This is by right THE best RPG/turn-based strategy game I have ever played or seen.
The graphics are also truly exceptional. This game was released in 2008, probably about 6 years before its release on Steam and almost 7 until the writing of this review, and the graphics are still stunning. The unique engine the game uses literally makes the scenes in the virtual book to come alive, while they still look like drawings with pencil and watercolours. Even if you normally don't like anime, you should still play this game. It is exceptional.
The plot is also amazing. I don't normally watch anime or play anime-based games, but this one is exception. This is the example of what an amazing story can be told through a video game and of how well it can be told.
The characters are really life-sized. Like what you could normally find in a book - and  I mean, a really, really good book - here, the characters are also so alive, so real, that you forget that they are imaginary.
The characters you meet in the game are very diverse and in many cases simple black-or-white morality would not apply to them. You are a squad leader in militia and all of your squad members are individuals with certain likes, dislikes, medical conditions, phobias and talents. Some of your key squad members are racist or sexist while others can get distracted by their squadmates to chitchat. At the same time, in certain conditions, they are able to perform significantly better due to them being in a very familiar environment or surrounded by close friends.
Many of the enemies are not really just ruthless psychopathic murderers either - many of them were really just made to fight you by their superiors while actually they easily relate to you and on certain occasions when it matters, they will arrange your survival even though it thwarts the goals of their commander.
The gameplay is fun and frequently is also very tactical. You will have to use the advantages the given terrain offers you and exploit weaknesses in the enemy's defence to your advantage.  There are several unit classes and as I previously said, each of the units is unique in his/her way.
Really buy this game. You will never regret playing it. I assure you. 10/10

LuckCatchers immediately gave me the impression that it was for boring PC gamers.  You know, the ones that sit in front of their computers hours a day and don't move.  The game opens up to a hangar with very little information as to what to do.  After several clicks and button presses to figure out how to even get your starter ship out, you are told to just accept the same 1 mission type over and over until your cargo hold is full.  So for the first few hours, you are literally doing the SAME mission back to back: take load from this place, and move it over here.  Repeat about 50 times until you get 100g so you can buy your own property or whatever.  THe game needs alot of work.
Character creation is just two portraits, humans and orcs.  You name your guy and voila, you look like everybody else.  There's no music from what I experienced, and the sound effects are very lackluster.  Learning how to control your air ship is easy enough, but takes a long time to get it anywhere.  The game sort of reminds me of Eve online.  You click a place to move.  But here with the lack of sound decent sound effects, it's just boring to fly anywhere
You can tell the game was made specifically for nerds that are willing to sit on their asses for hours a day and just do the same repetitive nonsense.  It needs alot more funding and care to make the game more fun to be in.  Right now, its not very immersive....but, I will give it this, if you are a fan of Eve's user interface, you'll feel nostalgic while playing this crap.

Ok, time for one of my rare reviews.
LuckCatchers, an online F2P open world game in the likes of eve but in a steampunk setting. For the combat oriented, there are thousands of dragons to hunt, pirates to fight or join, and clan wars to battle in with the ominous threat of the "Russian" invasion ever permanent. There are various different types of ships with different attributes to min max, plus enhancements and magic, different types of weapons and ammo with its own enhancements. And you also get to create and customize your own fighter ships (strekolets) to allow to use them for different roles.
There is a cash for gold store in the game. Gold is the currency in game and can be earned in game fairly easy in many many ways. You can use that gold not only to buy things in the markets, but to also speed up construction, resource extraction/refining, and even speed up skill research. People may complain that because you can buy gold its P2W game, but i would disagree for two reasons. 1. Gold is very easy to make in game and the costs for speeding skills and boosting constructions/etc is, with only a few exceptions, very very low, 2. The stuff that is really really expensive, like top tier skills and speeding certain items construction, is so expensive that it doesn't make sense to spend gold you bought with cash on it. Plus a lot of the gold that gets sold gets put back in the game through the market and contract system for transportation of goods.
Overall i don't think that the sale of gold is a bad thing in this game, in fact i think its needed for the stimulation of the economy.
For the more adept at economic and crafting combat, there are trade routes to discover, plentitude of goods and consumables to manufacture as almost everything that you will need and use is craftable or extractable, plenty of local economies to conquer and monopolize,There are resources to mine, potential settlement sites to explore, and political conquest through governmental territory control.
The game is vast, entertaining, more complex than meets the eye, and quite pretty to behold too. Having said that it still has some bugs and server issues that can be quite frustrating. The learning curve is steep, and the game may be too frustrating to some players at the beginning which combined with an at times akward interface may lead them to give up. Its a shame as the game has a lot to offer and potential to grow to the same heights as the other big names in this category.
Pros:
Contract system. You can make sales, purchase, transportation contracts that anyone can claim and fullfill for you. You can add security deposits, and break orders into any size packages.
Player driven economy, all the way from extration, production, logistics to sales. Everything is done by players and can be delegated out with gold. The economy is completely demand driven.
Combat system is fun and more complex than appears. From fall off on amunition and ranges, enhancements, magic, turrent angles and rates of fire, ship speed and fuel consumption, demon level and max altitudes, different types of ammo and guns, strekolets. There is a lot to think about, customize and tinker with.
Game world is vast and beautiful. The cities feel like they have a story, products they sell/buy tie in with the resources, lore and geolandscape that surrounds them. The different races, gnome island, the island of reconcilliation, it all fits with the larger lore and makes the game feel cohesive. Plus flying a zeppelin through the clouds over a beautifully rendered landscape is fantastic.
Dragons, farming dragons is fun. Having this horde of flying flame breathing nimble creatures coming at you while you hover over your town with a bunch of guns blazing in the night is awesome. Running across them through the world adds to game athmospheric feel, the dragon migration monthly event brings that annoyance level into full threat adding even more character to the game and a boost to all ammunition sales!
Strekolets, they add a whole new dimension to the game. Completely customizable you can fit these for anti fighter duty, bombers or torpedo runners that will take out a fully decked out ship in no time. They are extremely powerful in the right hands! If you are of the pirate persuasion, then outfit yours with a grappling hook and that shiny cargo ship you just downed will be all yours.
Cons:
Learning curve is a bit intense for most. There are tutorials on youtube that will help you and are listed here on steam under guides easily accessible from the shift tab menu in game. This includes learning to use the interface which can be dauting at first glance.
Bugs and Server issues, most of the bugs i've encountered have been interface bugs. Sometimes buttons just seem to stop working for no reason. It ends up resolving with a redocking or restarting the game. But there are small bugs here and there throughout the game that gives it an unpolished feel. For example i've travelled uncountable miles but my screen on login still shows 15miles. Server also seems to crash once or twice a day over the last week and there seems to be a lack of communication on game roadmap of features/fixes to come or server issues.

Note: this is a short review of both Metro 2033 and Last Light, since I played the games back-to-back and can't be bothered to write 2 separate reviews. I've played Redux versions of both.
***
2033: a well crafted mixture of an old-school and modern shooter (leaning more to the modern side) with an incredibly well crafted atmosphere and visuals. The combat is decidedly average, but is saved by great-feeling and great-looking weapons and by the fact that it's well paced and I very rarely felt overwhelmed by it. The story keeps a lot to itself (which I liked) and offers some choice with regards to the ending (which I don't like, since Last Light picks a canon ending and throws everything else away), the supporting cast is reasonably memorable and decently voice acted (with Russian VA at least).
The only two things I can really criticize are the facts that the game at times feels very inconsistent with its combat mechanics (trolley ambush and Librarians were a pain and felt more luck-based than anything else) and that the cutscenes were extremely repetitive and at odds with the gameplay itself.
If you're looking for silly comparisons, it's kind of like the narrative gameplay of Half-Life 2 and the atmosphere of STALKER (and I'd say that the Andrei Tarkovsky film had an even greater influence than the STALKER games) had a mutated baby.
***
Last Light: to me personally, this is a strictly worse version of the original game. While the story is, broadly speaking, more fleshed-out and filled with characters that develop a closer relationship (for better of for worse) with the protagonist, it feels a bit too exposition dump-ey at times. While that in itself isn't a huge problem, more and LONGER and still repetitive cutscenes were added (sure, a few select are really visually impressive and break the mold a bit, but most were still just you getting captured and then rescued, both COMPLETELY out of your control), there are more large combat encounters (which just drives the point that the combat in these games is average at best home ever so painfully) and for some weird reason, now we get a bunch of weird boss-fights that completely break the combat mechanics established by the game up to that point, and are then never reused. Now, this would be fine if this was a throwback-oldschool shooter, but it still tries to be grounded and 'realistic', and those boss battles feel completely out of place (I'm not even going to mention the fact that in some boss fights you have to shoot specific places at ONLY specific times, and are guided by glowing red signs...) and... boring.
Even with all that, I'd still recommend the game to anyone who enjoyed the original, just bear in mind that you might find yourself disappointed with the sequel.

Well this a hidden gem if I ever saw one. It was sitting in my Steam library for years before I finally got around to playing it too. I don't know what took me so long.
Everyone praises the XCOM games. I don't get the appeal. I think the tactical combat in it is fantastic, but everything else seems more than a little lacking. Take that type of gameplay and apply it to a proper RPG, though? Now you're speaking my language. Harebraned Scheme's Shadowrun series is that, and I loved those games. Expeditions: Conquistador is that in a historical setting.
It does a few things different from the games I'm comparing it to though. For one thing, the percentage to hit mechanic only applies to ranged weapons. This doesn't make the game easier or less frustrating. Instead it forces you to change your tactics with almost every battle. The battlefields are extremely varied too, and overall this game is much harder than any of the Shadowrun games.
There's a bit of The Oregon Trail in here too. It's up to you to properly manage resources such as rations, medicine, and your party's morale. You can only travel so far per day and the game is filled with random events that will screw you over or help you out.
As for the roleplaying options and historical accuracy, well, it's gonna depend on how you form your party. You choose who joins before the game begins. So you can go in with an all white male party of racists, or you can go with a more modern gender balance and an emphasis on open minded people. It's up to you. There's also a random button and I highly recommend going that route if you want to hear everyone's collective groans with every other decision you make, as you're unable to make everyone happy no matter what you do.
It's pretty awesome. I highly recommend it.

Spoiler alert. The tips I share below may contain spoilers of a sort. Or not.
Tips. Set the game to easy mode on your first play through. Do the tutorial. When the tutorial is through, grab all the quests in the starter town. Run the bibles to the village. Use your money ( Treasures) to buy as many supplies/food as you can. Wander around in the jungles, away from the roads, and hit the camp button often. Look for "harvest medical herbs" in the contextual window on the right. Harvest and process these herbs into medicine until you are low on food (around 20-30 rations) then go to towns/villages and trade the medicine for equipment and more food. Rinse and repeat as many times as you want. But at least fill the equipment slots on your main six fighters/healers/support team.
Lastly avoid looking for the rebel camp and Esteban at the mines until you do all the other quests in this area. This will prevent the random battles where the rebels attack you, often with a surprise attack. And you are almost always outnumbered. Or,  fight these battles to hone your tactics.
Mexico, wich is your next area, is huge and the enemys are better equipped and smarter (if you have the settings on normal or higher) and getting your main battle group fully equipped and leveled up a few times before getting there will allow you to have fun instead of getting your butt kicked by the AI.

I have played this game for over a 100 hours now, and I can confidently say it's one of my favourite games ever. Which is strange, because it isn't the best game I've ever played - there are games with far fiewer faults than this one. But it just stole my heart...
You start by choosing your expedition members. Each has a combination of 3 traits, which determine what affects their morale. For instance, Agressive followers love to fight at every opportunity, while Peaceful ones prefer to avoid combat; the Openminded gain morale when you recruit natives into your adventuring party, while the Racist ones lose it; a Proud follower's mood depends on the success of a battle, while Narcissists like being promoted; and so on. Of course, nobody like going without food or having their injuries untreated. High morale gives a critical hit chance in battles, but let it drop below 2 and you've got a mutiny on your hands. Every follower has a back story. If you aren't the type who reads them, fear not - there are random "conversation quests" during which a follower will tell you about themselves.
The quality of writing is consistently superb. It reads like the best interactive novels, and is broken up into paragraphs, so it never feels like a wall of text. Most conversations have 3 choices of reply, which can be described as "dignified, ferocious or charming" in tone. The majority of battles can also be resolved in a number of ways - you can avoid it altogether, use diplomacy, use the Tactics skill to put yourself in an advantageous position before the fight, or simply ride forth with guns blazing. Overall, it's an RPG in which the role-playing actually matters!
The battles are the most challenging part of the game by far. They are usually 6 versus 6, but there are variations. The objectives also vary - from the standard "Eliminate all enemies" to "Reach the escape zone" or "Stay alive for X turns". There are 10 classes - 5 Spaniard and 5 native, each with it's own strengths and weaknesses. There are also traps, barricades, attacks of opportunity...
The main reason why I've put in so many hours into this game is what I like to call "a Non-Binary victory system". What I mean is, you don't just win or lose. Any follower that gets incapacitated in battle has a chance to end up injured. An injured follower cannot fight and is useless in camp until fully healed. Healing takes time, medicine and doctors. So it is very important to not just win a fight, but win it without too many serious injuries, otherwise you'll run out of resources, and your party members will deteriorate and die.
And that's where most of the problems with this game lie. The interface, especially the combat interface, is of patchy quality. Your troops stand in blue circles, while the enemy is in red ones, but they are not very well highlighted, so during nighttime battles you can barely see who's where. The game isn't open-world, more like a series of passages you can travel along, but the map doesn't make it clear where they are - it only shows roads and mountains. So much time, especially on Hispaniola, is spent bumping into rocks and trees. Your quest objectives can be tracked in the quest journal, but it only tracks the main storyline quests. Even then, if your objective is on the part of the map you haven't discovered yet, you wouldn't see it!
Despite all this, the faults are minor compared to the good stuff. And I'm eagerly awaiting Expeditions:Viking, in which the faults I've highlighted have been mostly resolved.

I love this game. The animation style, the gameplay, and the storyline all come together to make a game that evokes the feeling of a blockbuster movie with the strategy and Role Playing you know and love. Thats not to say the game doesn't have its downsides, but the heart of the game is amazing.
Pros:
-Amazing story- I have only jsut begun, but already I can't wait to continue the story and see how my team interacts, not to mention how the plot thickens!
- Rich gameplay- Not only do you have to select a team to fight for you, but each have their own quirks which really help to make the characters feel alive. You don't have troops that you throw away, there isn't any cannon fodder-like troop, and each man or woman you command brings a personality with them.
-Tactics- The game has a great tactical base, though it can be somewhat nonsensical at times. Sneaking up on an enemy trooper by being slightly to their right can be ridiculous, and crouching negating headshots is just silly. However the game does reward creativity and persistence with victory. Rushing your enemy is rarely a good idea, but splitting your team and hitting either side of their main force? Hell yeah!
CONS:
-Tactics- I know, I know, I put this in pros as well. Sue me. The tactics at times can just be stupid, and the map sizes limit your tactical ability significantly. Hills end where invisible walls begin, etc. Crouching enemies taking a tank and two snipers to kill, and other things like this make the tactical portion of the game annoying at times, but rarely really affect your immersement in the game.
-Accuracy- The enemy has snipers? Say goodbye to any trooper left in the open. The enemy makes ridiculous shots look easy (though they can fail to hit at point blank range) and all the while you are trying to hit them with a fully upgraded sniper rifle only to miss by a millimetre. Infuriating! But, this just makes victory al the sweeter, no?
-Villains- Very Arch, very cleche at times, and altogether an unimaginative lot. They can make you weep with laughter as they say/do the stupidest things. Altogether, not a brilliant bunch.
Overall- I would give the game a 9/10. Not perfect, but an amazing game that keeps you coming back.

Probably the best in the series in terms of gameplay, or at least offers the biggest improvement over its predecessors.  ME2 fixes most of the annoying gameplay issues from the first game, upgrades the graphics, grants Shepard greater range of motion, doubles or triples the size of the Normandy, and dispenses with the tedious and unnecessary Mako levels.  Also introduces a handful of new characters--most of whom are even likable!--and gives the crew of the Normandy a disreputable new playground in Omega.
The combat is about a thousand times more fun than the first game, and I slightly prefer it to Mass Effect 3 simply because there's a bit more variety in the fights--you're not just facing wave upon wave of husks/Cerberus mooks.  The Thresher Maw on Tuchanka and Archangel's recruitment mission are particularly noteworthy.  Oh, and the final boss fight might just give you nightmares.
In terms of story, I feel that the third game has a slight edge, but the process of upgrading the Normandy and prepping for the final mission is a lot of fun.  Encounters with returning characters genuinely feel like meetings with old friends (or enemies) and the new romances are certainly worth checking out.  The voice acting and some dialogue can feel hammy at times, but it fits in well with the faux-gritty space-opera feel.
Even if you weren't thrilled with the first game, it's worth giving this one a look.  (I recommend importing a character from Mass Effect, if possible, because the default past decisions that the game sticks you with when you create a new character are somewhat unsatisfying, particularly for players who went the extra mile to save the council and complete the various side missions.)

I'm enjoying this game a lot so far (70 hours in) and some of these negative reviews from people with 0.5 hours were kinda bugging me, so I'll keep this succinct:
* This is a slow-paced sandboxy trading and base-building game. If you're looking for instant gratification, look elsewhere.
* The graphics aren't stellar, but they don't need to be. It's got a nice style. The ships look good, and the sunsets/sunrises are genuinely beautiful over the landscape.
* The economy is player-centric, supply & demand. Think EVE. Ship cargo, mine & craft with your settlements, or kill & loot dragons (or players) to earn gold.
* Skills cost gold & time to learn, but if you stay logged in you'll regain the same amount of gold you spent learning the skill. The game rewards you 5 gold per 30 mins.
* For a F2P game, there are no feature lockouts or specific advantages of paid players vs. free ones. You can buy gold if you like, but it's not required. Very generous!
* The tutorial is weak, and many of the guides here are outdated, but it doesn't take long to get the hang of the basics. There's not much info out there, no handy spreadsheets or the like (at least for English players). The game is still pretty new to Steam and it'll take some time for people to write resources for it.
* The ingame chat almost always has people willing to answer questions, and the general mood of the English community is friendly and welcoming. I've seen virtually no chat drama, and most people seem mature.
* New players have 30-day PVP protection, which can be skipped with a special (cheap) item if you like. PVP works on a reputation system, and if you go into negative rep with either of the factions (Human/Orc) you'll be marked a Pirate. (Tip: don't swear in chat when you're new. Certain words will give you a 100 rep penalty, and considering you start with 0 rep, this could be dangerous!)
* Yeah, there are some annoying glitches. You will occasionally crash (I've had 2 crashes in 70 hours of play). I haven't encountered any game-breaking glitches though, and whoever said you can lose the gold you buy for no reason is talking out of his rear.
All in all, this game is nice relaxing fun, something to tab back and forth into while you do other things and your ships are travelling. I'm looking forward to what future updates may bring!

In my thirty plus years of gaming I can honestly say I have never once played a worse game than this. There is little to no guidance for first time players. The navigation "system" if you can call it that is a complete disaster, Just finding your location in the game world is a awful chore and travel even between nearby settlements is painful.
The moment you engage any of the mobs you get immediately swarmed by dozens more. Your ammo supply is ridiculously small and while killing the mobs is fairly simple, the sheer number they throw at you makes it impossible.
The UI (and I hesitate to even call it that) is so terribly cumbersome, You constantly have to open your cargo hold, then open the market to find the general values for an item then reopen your cargo to select the item and try to place it on the market for sale. Only to repeat those steps to a nauseating level.
Manual ship controls are about as sluggish and poorly designed as the rest of the game. If you set your elevation then set your direction of travel, your desired elevation setting is erased and set to your current elevation so you have to reset that every time you change your point of travel.
The only positive thing I can say about this game is I didn't get suckered into paying for it.
For those who say they like this “game” all I can say is you are a Masochist. It's an exercise in patience that rapidly loses any possible draw to try it.

I have played this game for over a 100 hours now, and I can confidently say it's one of my favourite games ever. Which is strange, because it isn't the best game I've ever played - there are games with far fiewer faults than this one. But it just stole my heart...
You start by choosing your expedition members. Each has a combination of 3 traits, which determine what affects their morale. For instance, Agressive followers love to fight at every opportunity, while Peaceful ones prefer to avoid combat; the Openminded gain morale when you recruit natives into your adventuring party, while the Racist ones lose it; a Proud follower's mood depends on the success of a battle, while Narcissists like being promoted; and so on. Of course, nobody like going without food or having their injuries untreated. High morale gives a critical hit chance in battles, but let it drop below 2 and you've got a mutiny on your hands. Every follower has a back story. If you aren't the type who reads them, fear not - there are random "conversation quests" during which a follower will tell you about themselves.
The quality of writing is consistently superb. It reads like the best interactive novels, and is broken up into paragraphs, so it never feels like a wall of text. Most conversations have 3 choices of reply, which can be described as "dignified, ferocious or charming" in tone. The majority of battles can also be resolved in a number of ways - you can avoid it altogether, use diplomacy, use the Tactics skill to put yourself in an advantageous position before the fight, or simply ride forth with guns blazing. Overall, it's an RPG in which the role-playing actually matters!
The battles are the most challenging part of the game by far. They are usually 6 versus 6, but there are variations. The objectives also vary - from the standard "Eliminate all enemies" to "Reach the escape zone" or "Stay alive for X turns". There are 10 classes - 5 Spaniard and 5 native, each with it's own strengths and weaknesses. There are also traps, barricades, attacks of opportunity...
The main reason why I've put in so many hours into this game is what I like to call "a Non-Binary victory system". What I mean is, you don't just win or lose. Any follower that gets incapacitated in battle has a chance to end up injured. An injured follower cannot fight and is useless in camp until fully healed. Healing takes time, medicine and doctors. So it is very important to not just win a fight, but win it without too many serious injuries, otherwise you'll run out of resources, and your party members will deteriorate and die.
And that's where most of the problems with this game lie. The interface, especially the combat interface, is of patchy quality. Your troops stand in blue circles, while the enemy is in red ones, but they are not very well highlighted, so during nighttime battles you can barely see who's where. The game isn't open-world, more like a series of passages you can travel along, but the map doesn't make it clear where they are - it only shows roads and mountains. So much time, especially on Hispaniola, is spent bumping into rocks and trees. Your quest objectives can be tracked in the quest journal, but it only tracks the main storyline quests. Even then, if your objective is on the part of the map you haven't discovered yet, you wouldn't see it!
Despite all this, the faults are minor compared to the good stuff. And I'm eagerly awaiting Expeditions:Viking, in which the faults I've highlighted have been mostly resolved.

You are El Conquistador. You are bound for the New World to gain fame and riches. How will you do it? Your call. Nobody holding your hand, telling you what to do (except tutorial sequence on Hispaniola). You have absolute free reign on how to achieve that goal:
Raze native villages, kill helpless women and children, and claim the land for King Carlos?
- no problem!
Befriend natives, free slaves, and fight against the Spanish Crown?
- no problem!
Can i do both of the above?
- yes you can!
What i like in this game - it is not you classic "good vs evil" b u l l s h i t, it is more realistic, dark and "shades of grey" game. Just like real life.
Example: Trade with the village, marry the chieftain;s daughter, accept gift and be worshipped as the sun god. Then - raze village to the ground killing all inhabitants. Il con Dieu! Stupid Heathens! :) - and the game is full of such options.
P.s. I STRONGLY recommend playing in Ironman mode. Its how this game meant to be played. You will only feel the weight of your decisions if you play it like that. And don't worry about losing battles and thus game over - in most battles, while you have at least 1 of your units alive, you can always surrender/flee. Yes, you will be humiliated, lose many valuables, fail quests, some of you companions may permanently die, but you will be able to continue, and in some cases, have your revenge (or second humiliation).
Overall: 9/10 go play it now, Conquistador :)

I don't write reviews everytime I play a new game I enjoy. I need to really love it or hate it. Why? Well, I am a lazy geek that enjoys procrastinating and well, do nothing. In this case, I really need to say a couple of things:
I bought this game on a whim. I liked the concept and the music in the trailers sounded cool. The price was just right for my "I buy a new game on steam every month" thing, and so I did.
This game brings back memories of old. The soundtrack is awesome, our opponent is awesome as well and the replayability is absolutely tremendous. Everytime you play, it is a different game. You don't quite understand if the card dealer is a friend or a foe, maybe both, but you'll love him for it.
It is as much as an RPG as it is an Adventure game and well, a card game as well. You keep playing, betting on your luck and mixing it with micro-management and you'll eventually finish it all. It's not as easy as you might think though, you need some combat skills as well. The game is not all about playing cards, you do need to fight your way through various combat situations, which is cool. The combat system reminds me of games like Batman, where you need to counter enemies attacks. Of course you'll need some nice equipment and nice equipment you get throughout your gameplay session. Never the same mind you. The bosses - yes, there is a boss for every "playthrough" - are hard enough, but you'll probably won't find any real difficulty, unless you've been real unlucky in the past like getting robbed by goblins of your food and pieces of equipment, or even a tough unfortunate card you've chosen that made you lose life etc....
All in all, it's not exactly up to you how you end the playthrough. It depends both on luck and skill, which is like in everyday life, where most of the things are outside your margin of control. The game is an awesome improvement on card and rpg games alike, and should be played by as many people as possible. The price is awesome, for an awesome game. Hand of Fate is my new favourite game, buy it.
Not worth the money.

A very interesting and deadly game of cards.
The story telling in this game is amazing. I love how the dungeon master (or whatever he is called) always works against you. Outing his anger when you gain something and laughing at you when you are closer to death. The cards are just as intruiging as well. A big variety of encounters, roleplay (aka find the right card out of 4) and shops. Endless mode is just a bunch of fun so you can play to your hearts content.
However the game is not without it's flaws ofcourse. During every card encounter the game gives you the option to "take the challenge" or "leave". If you are low and you skip it you will most likely be dead on the next card as you can't skip everything.
combat is it's biggest flaw I'm afraid. It's very nice to get down and personal in a fight but the mechanics are a bit lacking. You can easily win every combat you encounter. There should either be a more complex version of it or a difficulty setting (as there is none in the game, just default difficulty). If you want a better version of it, go play one of the pc batman games. Same combat style but better designed. On a side note I also love how the arena constantly changes by what card you drew. From deserts to castles to forest etc.... depending on the card you drew and the boss you will be facing (so far I encountered: dust, undead, rats and lizzards as monster mobs, I guess that's also the only ones in the monster decks)
Overall I'm enjoying it very much! I would recommend it if you are into card games, but not if you're a combat veteran.

Well♥♥♥♥♥♥ Color me addicted.
First let's talk about what I like about this little experiment. It's free, for one, and although it has premium content the only reason you would want to pay for it to be able to play with more people in a lobby (which would amount to ending up having the same people as the free lobbies because no one in their right mind is paying 7$ a month for this game. Now back to the positives!) So the premium content is very minor.
Once you get into a game, you are randomly assigned a character from a grab bag of famous, and infamous people. These people go from a wall street employee looking to blow his weed with his new "friends", a tennis player looking to find an orphan a home, to a man on the run after screwing over the russian mafia, and thats not the half of it. The character's are so iconic, and diverse I couldn't help but get attached to the one I played as after reading his backstory (this is given to you in full at the start of each match.). Also, each character is fully voiced with a text to talk voice that's different for every character. That's just neat.
You may be wondering, "Whats the goal?". To explain this, im going give an example using a character i didn't mention before. Alex is a troublesome man from a wealthy family who thought it best to put him on a luxury cruise to give him the chance to calm himself down. He woke up this morning with a fierce headache, no memory of last night, and a red thong left on his bed. Alex's personal objective (being the gentleman he is... >_>) is to return the thong to its owner. But now you find out something that not even someone who has played Alex would know; something that's different every time. Alex is an undercover agent of an oil company called 'Explon' who is looking for evidence of an attack on an Explon oil rig by their competitor "Balboil". He knows there are Balboil agents onboard the yacht, but he's also aware that Explon has more then one person at work here. Theres also a thief with a taser... yeah, he can be a♥♥♥♥♥♥
The character interaction is the main selling point of the game. Each time your given a new situation with new variables that amount to the game never playing out the same way twice. How do you want to find that data? Who are you working with to begin with? Who are the people on this yacht with you? These questions will burn holes in the back of your mind as you scramble for an answer that isn't there at the start.
Now on to the negatives.
Before i begin, it's important to note that, in my opinion, the good outweighs the bad very heavily, but the bad is there.
The bad. Is. There.
Player interaction can go either way. On the one hand you have people playing as themselves no matter what character, that's fine by me. You get the people who are hardcore roleplayers that try to delve into the very psyche of the person they play. Then you get the people who are specifically trying to get enjoyment at your expense. Yep, you guessed it. Trolls. These guys can ruin the immersion of the game in about three seconds flat. "I WANT TO ♥♥♥♥ YOU. LETS ♥♥♥♥" being popular vernacular. Honestly, the trolling isn't as bad is it could be. I had a really interesting conversation about how Jack (the wall street drug dealer) sounds like Shrek, and Morgan Freeman. That guy was cool. Then theres this other guy. There always is. Who literally started every conversation with "Wanna ♥♥♥♥?". That guy was an♥♥♥♥♥ and it was just my divine luck that he was my oil company spy buddy. Can you smell that? Disappointment; Disappointment in the human race. Mmmmm, ripe.
The game is very lacking in it's animations, and for the most part isn't very cutting edge. You'll do a lot better if you think of this game as a chat room roleplay that does a lot of the imagination for you. All in all the game works, but the scenery outdoes the motions at every turn. Enemies almost always match or better you in quality AND quantity save for the odd encounter.
What you SHOULD do first of all though?
Buy the game.

I've started playing this game quite a long time ago, and this game came a long way, at the time, it was an above average game, now, it is oustanding. Let's see why.
The gameplay in this game is extremely well executed. Moving is intuitive, fast pace, and satisfying, it is extremely easy to make your 'frame do what you want it to.
Shooting is extremely solid too, from your sidearm to your rocket launcher, every weapons seems to work as it should, and it never feels out of place.
The abilities of your 'frame can change the tide of the battlefield, you can support your team, dish out a lot of damage, become invisible, etc etc, each frame have a specific ''feel'' to it, and their abilities can be quite enjoyable to use.
One of the best selling point of warframe is the content, there's quest, events, challenges, secondary bosses, end-game content, a ♥♥♥♥ ton of weapons / 'frame to plat with, thousands of mods for them. Actually there is so much to do in this game it can be overwhelming at time, but if you just take your time with learning how things works, then you should be just fine.
Customisation-wise, the game can be pretty fun there too, you can switch the color of specific areas on your frame/weapons, giving them specific looks/feels, you also have access to thousands of mods to further customize their fighting abilities, maybe you want your weapons to dish out critical damage ? or maybe you'd rather deal with elemental damage ? Maybe you want your 'frame to be more resistant, or maybe you want her to deal more damages with her abilities, etc etc.
This game is free, so you might expect it, microtransactions are present.
they are far from necessary, thanks to the trading system. Quite early in the game you unlock the ability to trade with other players, and this allows you to trade goods for platinum (the paid currency), depending on what you are trading you can get quite an amount of platinum. This sytem is pretty much enough to pay for everything that you will need in game (weapons / warframe slots, wich are not unlimited).

Let's get one thing out of the way: "Murdered: Soul Suspect" is not your normal action game. Actually, it is actually not an action game at all; it is more a story-driven adventure focused on exploration and (very logic) puzzle-solving that centers around clue finding and logic implications among them; the plot is thick, with lots of twists and turns all along the way which will nail you to your chair until you're done. There's only one caveat: it's rather short -- I managed to complete it in under 10 hours.
There are also "combat" sequences against demons (ghosts that turned evil after forsaking what they were meant to "fix" in the living world before leaving it) that are more annoying than anything else as they involve hide-and-seek mechanics; I think that there is a lot of room for improvement in that area but I am not complaining too much.
There is one more thing that I dislike though: the whole collectable item craze that the game is so soaked with. Some are in obvious places, others in less-obvious ones, while others are really unfindable unless you comb the town of Salem systematically -- and it's rather hard to do it without a map of the place. Through the collection of clues and items, you either go forward with the main story or unlock sidequests or insights about the protagonists and the town itself.
When it comes to presentation, graphics are really good (locked at 30 FPS but there's no sensation of lag at all), the audio acting is well done and the music hits the spot without being particularly memorable.
I recommend this game if you're into ghost stories (or well-written stories in general) and like to enjoy a slower-paced game that requires a minimum of thinking.
My vote for the game: 7/10 (with a gameplay vote of 5.5/10 and one for the story of 8.5/10)

Valkyria Chronicles blends real time strategy with turn based tactics so well that it's basically a genre game of its own. It also has a highly unique story and setting that deserves much praise. The one area that I wasn't particularly fond of, however, was the extremely corny dialog in a number of scenes. Maybe that was to be expected, though, as this is a somewhat light-hearted anime that contrasts heavily with the dark overtones of war and deceit. The cheesy dialog comes in the form of in your face morals when confronted with growing friendships and relationships. Really though, it wasn't that bad, it just came off as super corny sometimes.
Let's start with the story, the game is set in the 1930's in a fictional content called Europa (Europe) where an imperialist force (the East Europan Imperial Alliance) is attacking the Atlantic Federation. It's basically a fictional WWII, but here, it's called the Second Europan War. Well, the central character is Welkin Gunther, a citizen of the neutral country Gallia. Because of Gallia's abundance of Ragnite ore, which is the alternative fuel to petroleum, the Imperial Alliance attacks Gallia. Welkin, while visiting his home town of Bruhl, comes across Alicia Melchiott and find that their town is under attack. The two escape with several other civilians, including Welkin's sister, to the capital city of Randgriz. There, the pair join the Gallian militia and that's where the journey really takes off. Welkin becomes Lt. of Squad 7. The rest of the story involves militia based missions, including espionage, tactical operations, and full out war. It's really great. The story is amazing. And I really loved it.
On the technical side of things, the game really is a tactical RPG, as you can level up the characters for more HP and what not, but it also employs what is called the Battle of Live Tactical Zones (BLiTZ) which is the real time strategy element I had mentioned. During battles, you have an overview map where you can view your characters' placements. When you select a character for movement, you transition to a third person view where you can traverse the map for a duration of how much AP you have. In the map, you can take cover, climb ladders for better views, prone around in grass to hide, and, of course, battle enemies. When you battle enemies, you freeze time, allowing you to aim, much like VATs in Fallout 3. All of these aspects are what make this game so unique. It's a tactical game truly like no other and another reason why I love it so much.
Which leads me to the graphical side of things. Being an anime game, don't expect super realistic graphics, but allow yourself to be pleasantly surprised, anyway, when you see the detail put into the buldings, tanks, outfits, geography, etc. It's a very good looking game, and ported to PC with full HD resolution, the game looks absolutely fantastic. This is a great port. And a truly amazing game. What keeps it from being perfect is just my disdain for some of the cheesy/corny moments; like the pig you rescue that joins your squad. Like... okay.
One last thing before I finish my review; this game can be really difficult. I mean, you really have to strategize and allocate your team to positions that favor winning. The slightest mistake or allowing an ally in your squad to stand out in the open could lead to their death. And if you make that mistake often enough, it'll mean losing the battle. There are probably 5 or 6 battles that I found really difficult and was frustrated throughout, but I eventually prevailed.

The game is a TBS, where you move your planes on a board.
You have 4 pilots, which you can:
- Choose plane type for (you get 1 new plane type each location)
- Upgrade, when they get enough kills for the next "level" (types of manouvers they can do) and plane upgrades (if your planes take less than 50% damage)
- Give 1 special skill each, after a set number of skills.
These pilots can also suffer from injury (shot down), repair time on their plane (heavily damaged plane) and captured by the enemy (shot down over enemy territory.)
It is a simple, easy to learn and fun little game, with 4 nations to choose from (US, UK, France and Germany).
If you like TBS games, I highly doubt you will dislike this little gem.
8/10

I was a founder of this game, played the beta and hundreds of hours post-release off steam, had a guild of great people of which I eventually became an officer, and through all that I must still give it a thumbs down because of Trion Worlds who run the NA/EU servers. Getting to the endgame (lvl50-55) is a journey that is amazing your first time through, the sheer variety of quests and monsters is great, but upon reaching endgame and looking into the crafting system, you will realize this game's biggest flaw IMO.
There are 5 levels of gear for high level players, and when made they roll one of 5 or 6 types, only 1 of which can be upgraded to the next tier. Then, there are also 12 different item colors that determine quality, and you have a chance to downgrade, or even destroy the item when attempting to upgrade it. Considering you must begin with the lowest level items and craft them up one tier at a time, crafting armor and weapons is the most tedious and annoying process in the game.
While the crafting system is terrrible, most of the game is still great, from taking world bosses as combat pets to raiding ships at sea with your guild, its easy to go have fun by grabbing a friend or two and just go look for a fight or do a dungeon. Sadly as of recently I have stopped playing due to how terrible Trion Worlds is and how badly they have screwed this game up with their incessant pay2win offers, destroying and laughing at the masterful in-game economy as they flood the market with previously-rare materials and basically give no promises as to the value of anything.
Overall I still love this game, but I cannot recommend it due to Trion Worlds' idiocy, if they handed the game off to a company that understands how a game should be run i'd expect many players like me would return, but for now my sub in cancelled.

Well, folks.  Here we are.  The Hype is real and still is!
I bought ATS as it is called by players because I loved ETS2 and wanted to play an American Truck game, like the old 18 WoS days.  So far, I'm not disappointed by the game one bit.
Yeah, you only get two trucks at the start, and I'm fine with that.  The reasoning for the lack of immediate content is actually a good one for once.  It is because rather than put fake brands in the game, SCS wants to get licenses first.  But, as said by Pavel Sebor himself, getting licenses from truck manufacurers that aren't used to being approached for licenses of their product is like the chicken vs egg debate.  So, they are going about it the right way at least.
On to the gameplay.  Those of you that are familiar with ETS2 will have no problem getting used to the ATS Gameplay.  There are a lot of new things to compliment to already very good base gameplay that I hope will be making it's way to ETS2 soon as well.
Delivery Points are the biggest advancement in the gameplay system.  You can choose how difficult you want the delivery to be.  From a zero point quick drop to a 90 point drop that is so complex, even the most Veteran Driver will have a challenge are available for choosing.
Weigh Stations are new to the game.  You can be randomly chosen to go to the Scale House for Inspection.  It's an interesting feature, but a bit of a waste of time and ruins fuel economy.  Hopefully, SCS will be able to do something to give this feature more meaning.
After talking about weigh stations, we have no choice but to talk about the new police engine.  Now, the dreaded Rozzers are mobile and sneaky.  I got a Speeding Ticket for not being at 30 MPH right after the sign changed.  There needs to be a Reduced Speed Ahead sign, like in real life here in the States.
So, lets break it down to the Pros and Cons.
Pros
Familiar yet tweaked Gameplay
American Trucks
Nevada included
Scenery that will blow your mind
Easter Eggs, yes, there a few, and no, I will not tell you what they are
No curves every 20 feet like ETS2
Cons
Only two states at the beginning
Only two trucks at the beginning,  Not really a con, but may put some people off
The UI is completely Copy/Paste.  Would have loved to see the Route Adviser remodeled.  Maybe next time.
Only 64-Bit

Explore life as a 16th century Spanish Conquistador in this indie, turn-based RPG. The game consists of 2 campaigns that follow on from one another, with the second campaign being noticeably longer than the first.
Gameplay consists of recruiting your party members, exploring the world map turn by turn, whilst managing resources like food and morale. Every turn, your party must make camp and then you assign a different camp duty to each party member (hunting, preserving meat, scouting, guarding etc.). Where you choose to make camp will affect the probability of success of different activities. Resting will then trigger different scripted and random events.
Encounters can be resolved peacefully or aggressively - if you end up fighting, then (turn-based) combat is resolved on a separate hex grid. Party members have different classes and gain new skills as they level up, in traditional RPG fashion.
Warning: the turn based combat can be brutally difficult even on the default difficulty level if you aren't prepared!
+ Incredible atmosphere full of lore and flavour text
+ Excellent soundtrack and voiceovers really add to the immersion
+ Challenging turn-based combat
+ The game tries to follow history by allowing you to be a completely evil, racist conquistador if you wish. You can massacre and enslave native villages in the name of God and the Spanish king. Innocent villagers will tremble helplessly in combat which is a nice touch.
- In the second campaign, the scripting can be a bit buggy. You are tasked with rebuilding a fort and sometimes it can fail to be completed. I recommend focusing exclusively on this quest to make sure it gets completed.
- The camping mechanic gets a little repetitive after a while.
- The world map view feels too zoomed in and it is easy to miss objects and locations on the edge of the screen.
- Graphics are adequate but feel slightly dated.
The followup game Expeditions: Viking is due out in 2017 - can't wait!

This game is hard to describe, but that's because the structure is so fresh and original. The experience is like playing one of those great fantasy board story board games like Hero's Quest. I think when most people hear it's a card or deckbuilding game they think Magic or Hearthstone, but it's much more akin to a tile based RPG where you move around a board having little narrated story encounters, which sometimes drop down into 3D action combat. It just happens to be that the "board" you're playing on, the monsters you encounter and the gear you gain, are drawn from decks of cards that you can configure (or let the game choose) beforehand. Really what makes this game sing though is the presentation. The wonderful moody thematic voice-over of the wizard you are playing against, where he comments on every card and action thematically, the awesome art of the cards, the general graphical polish makes it feel like playing a real fantasy RPG card game come to life. The combat is... workman-like and servicable, but it's honestly only a portion of the overall experience. Highly recommended and I hope that DLC comes to expand it as this is an amazing structure for a game.

The game has a very simple concept; you create two decks of cards, one of equipment and one of encounters. As you play you unlock new cards that you can add to your decks, but there's a catch. You wont know what a specific card does until you encounter it in the game for the first time. The dealer also has his own deck that will also be enhanced as you collect more cards for yours.
Something that some will consider a downside is that the combat is fairly simplistic. You can have some abilities in the form of artifact cards or special equipment, but for the most part combat consists of basic attacking and countering with a shield. The combat still manages to be intense and extremely satisfying when you win despite, and perhaps due to, it's simplicity.
Overall I would recommend the game wholeheartedly to anyone looking for a fun and satisfying adventure.

I've been a big fan of Disgaea ever since the initial release on the PS2. When I saw that it was being ported to PC I was all for it. However, what I ended up getting was a bit of a mess.
I personally hadn't experienced any issues with the game within the first couple hours of the game. I had seen many people having issues with the frame rate, and stating that textures weren't loading. I had a smooth 60fps experience and all my textures loaded fine. I had to change all the new graphical settings off and use the old textures and UI, but that didnt' bother me much. I didn't even change the settings because of performance issues. I did it because the enhanced graphical options look terrible. Funny that the enhancements didn't enhance anything.
My real issue is when after having played the game for three hours it just stopped working. Not like it would crash in the middle of playing it, but the game just wouldn't start up. Every time I tried to play it it would crash before the game window would show up.
I can say that Disgaea is a great game, and I encourage anyone who is a fan of strategy games to check it out, but honestly you'd have better luck buying it for any of the other platforms that the game was released on then buying it on PC in its current state.

Ever thought about being a ghost?  Pass through walls, posses people, teleporting,  making the T.V. go wild, things like this make it fun to be one. Of course, being a ghost has to be somewhat dark and taken seriously. After all, being a ghost means you’re dead.
Murdered Soul Suspect is a game where Ronan, a detective that follows a lead, dies but stays in this world as a ghost and the only thing that keeps him from finding peace is solving the case. The story is very noir like, despite the presence of modern objects, since the dark atmosphere and the mystery  are the things that are unavoidable in this game.  The plot is as it should be,  clear, logic and ended with enough closure to make you realize what a good story it is. In a world where ghosts have many questions, where are mediums that can see that and a killer that hunts those people down, you are the one that provides the answers.  There are ghosts that you can help find peace. There are collectibles that give you a lot of backstory on various topics and characters. There is one murderer that can’t be stopped still loose in this town. All of this is obvious throughout the game and that’s what will keep you hooked.
Gameplay wise, the game is easy. To put it simply, you’ll  take walks,  find clues, conclude investigations with the correct solution, execute demons by taking them from behind and collecting stuff if you feel like it. To put it as it is, things are more complex than that, but not much more.  In order to gain clues, you’ll need to look for them at the crime scene , you’ll need to interact with someone or something to find more, which sometimes mean possessing a person, influencing them to think about the topic you need or looking through their eyes.  The things that present a challenge in this game are the demons, that are very much alike with the dementors. They’ll consume your soul if you are exposed to them for long enough.  You can pass by them, or you can execute them by going behind them and using one of your ghostly abilities. Ronan can hide from them by possessing people or hiding in different entities. At the player disposal is also the ability to see the demon from afar, even through walls.Facing the demons are the stealthy section of the game, but they’re not frustrating enough to make the game challenging at all. For completitionists, there are a lot of collectibles to be found, which contain backstories of characters and places, or a separate story.  They aren’t hard to be found and there are more than one good guides, so you could say it’s easy to get all the achievements. The town of Salem is beautiful, varied but after you explore it all, it feels like a small place.  There is free roam until the last mission, but that is useful for those who want to get back to specific locations to get the rest of the collectibles.  Also, if you see an NPC that looks interesting to you, you can posses him and hear what he thinks.
Is the game a great one? No, it’s simply good. It lasts for about 10 hours, it has great concepts and executes them simply, which may be a fault for it, since many said about the game that it had great potential. Still, there’s no other game that can make you have fun for being a ghost like this one.  Passing through walls, possessing people, talking with other ghosts, potterghasting different object to perturb the living ones, it’s all very enjoyable. The theme is dark, some details are gritty, it’s a game where you solve a mystery which has a solution that isn’t obvious at all(the plot-twists turned out to be mind-blowing).
All in all, Murdered Soul Suspect is a good game that delivers on what it describes itself to be and doesn’t take risks in being something more.

Comrades, this is not a game, certainly not a detective one. The puzzles are not really puzzles and there are no options of getting it wrong. The game is quite short, only has few side quests, and three types of enemies (demons, train and controls).
The thing is that as a detective game Murdered: Soul Suspect fails, it fades away into the shadows if compared to Sherlock Holmes and L.A. Noire.
The game play is very basic, pretty much point and click on clues and then select the most relevant one. As such on a gameplay and mental levels the game is not challenging or stimulating at all.
The story is simple and the plot can be guessed, but it is not a cliché one.
I can't recommend this as a game, however I will recommend this as an interactive story if available to purchase below $7

I have very fond memories about two specific titles from the past - Over The Reich and it's sequel Achtung! Spitfire. Ace Patrol does look a bit like those games, but with more colorful/kid-friendly approach.  After a few hours of gameplay I can honestly say, It's not even close to level of grand those aformentioned games represented.
Ace Patrol feels like a mobile game (and it is a mobile game too). Gameplay is a mostly fun, turn-based dogfighting with light rpg elements. Scale is a first dissapointment -  you won't command more than 4 planes at once. Most of the time, missions involve two or three of your pilots. That's just sad - no chance for grand strategy battles. Rpg elements are barebones. There's no real way to customize your pilots - you just make them better and add new skills. The same with new planes - every time you get a new one, it's better then the previous.  If you hope for a long campaign - you can finish all missions (diveded into 6 offensives) in around 2h. Single mission takes around 5-10 minutes to be completed.  Offcourse the main goal of the game is to win the war on the highest difficulty setting, but most of us, will be perfectly happy with medium. Ace Patrol can be punishing at times. You are not obliged to win every mission, but failures will cost you.... points. Yes, it seems that Ace Patrol is more of a score attack game. Sure, shot down pilots will end up in hospital for a while or be captured and put into POW camp for the rest of the offensive. Also, failing missions will change the final outcome of the offensive. Nevertheless, it's all about your final score, not about ranking up your pilots or enjoyable mission objectives.
After finishing the game with one of the factions, I'm not really interested in playing it again. Factions don't really differ from one another,  so replaying the game as Americans or French changes nothing. Also, i don't think there's enough variety in mission objectives or rpg elements. It's just so basic and bare-bones.
TL,DR :
Ace Patrol is perfect game for "so-so" score. Middle grade. There is no "mild recomendation" in Steam Reviews. Yes, i would recommend it. I was pretty negative, but it's fun little game, for a 3 or 4h. It was a nice distraction, opened in a small window, on my work computer - just to finish a mission between sending emails and making phone calls. I'm dissapointed it's not fleshed out as i hoped it will be... but i guess i need to dig up old copy of Achtung! Spitfire to scratch my itch.

Ace Patrol is a fun little hex-based air combat game set during World War I. It is important to keep in mind that this is a casual game. The gameplay is not especially deep or complicated, but that is not necessarily a bad thing. It is easy to pick up and play through a few quick missions if you don’t want to get sucked into a full-blown, drawn-out strategy game like Civilization V or XCOM. (Not to say that the gameplay of Ace Patrol isn't incredibly addictive, because it is.)
Missions take just a few minutes to complete, and there are roughly twenty-four missions per campaign (There is one campaign for each of the four playable nations). During a mission, you maneuver your little squadron around the playing field to complete the objective, be it shooting down enemy aircraft, destroying supply convoys or escorting reconnaissance planes. But it isn’t enough to simply shoot down other planes as quickly as possible by selecting the move that gives the most damage… doing so might put your plane directly into the enemies' line of fire. Instead, you will need to decide the best course of action of how to destroy the enemy planes and still bring your guys back (relatively) undamaged.
Ace Patrol is quite fun, however, there are a couple of downsides. The graphics are so-so (I find they have their charm). And even though there are “campaigns”, there is no storyline or narrative, which is a bit disappointing. You level up your pilots, add upgrades to your planes, fly out on a mission, come back to base and repeat, so you never really feel a sense of purpose or connection to your pilots. At the very least, it would have been nice to see a few historical fun facts or something. And because there are a limited number of mission types, eventually you may find yourself flying the same missions with only different configurations of clouds and friendly/enemy territory.
If you are looking for a pick-up-and-go casual game to play every now-and-then or a “light” strategy game that does not take hours to beat, I highly recommend giving Ace Patrol a try. Although it lacks the scope of other turn-based strategy games, there is still great potential for “just one more mission!”

I've played through Expeditions: Conquistador multiple times, and likely will again someday. There's just so much here. To wit:
- The tactical combat is excellent. You will be punished for mistakes - especially on higher difficulties - but you can also win against the odds with careful planning and team composition.
- The storytelling is fantastic, and every possible combination of characters you take with you subtly changes how your expedition unfolds.
- The "tutorial" island before arriving on the mainland is so good that I can't imagine playing a full game without it. It does more than introduce you to mechanics. It tells its own compelling and entertaining story.
- The soundtrack is awesome.
- The UI is functional, though hardly groundbreaking.
- Ditto the graphics.
- The game throws some excellent surprises at you if you explore enough. Indeed, this is the rare game that - while ostensibly a tactical RPG - is truly about exploration. Take your time. See the map. Once you learn how to survive in the wild, you'll be rewarded for poking into every corner.
- Ironman is truly rewarding. It's an accomplishment to make it back to Europe in one piece, much less to achieve higher glories and honors.
On the whole, I unquestionably recommend this game to cRPG fans and tactical strategy fans of all stripes. The biggest caveat I would make to my recommendation is that there IS some randomness (more than some) build into Expeditions: Conquistador's core mechanics, and at times it feels unfair to miss that 95% chance. You can and should strategize around those possibilities, of course (in a long game, 1 in 20 will happen!), but players who get frustrated when RNG doesn't go their way will likely want to play on the non-ironman setting.

One of the most heavily-underrated games of its time, Expeditions: Conquistador is a well-written and deeply-engrossing masterpiece that has hours upon hours of content on top of having great replay value.
The player is given the role of a hidalgo of the Spanish aristocracy, sent to the new world after a first attempt at colonization disappears. Sent first to the island of Hispaniola to quell a rebellion, the player is then given the freedom to do as he wishes, whether that means mapping out the island, helping or hurting the natives, or even in how he deals with his fellows in the employ of the Spanish crown.
The level of freedom players are given is enormous; you are free to pick out your own companions, each with their own personalities, and then develop them as you wish; you are also able to play without worry of game-overs as there are very few choices that will end the game prematurely, allowing the player to continue even past tragic and traumatic experiences. It goes without saying that there are multiple endings and each of these is a direct consequence of a choice the player will have made much earlier in the campaign; will the Spanish king be pleased with your conquest of the new world or will the Aztec empire be forever grateful for your efforts in their name?
The combat system is also nothing worth shaking a finger at; as an isometric strategy RPG, how one develops and balances out their characters is important and because of this, it's very easy to find a party that suits ones's playstyle: whether that means a party focused on long-range bombardment or close-rance aggression is entirely up to you.
Truly, it is the freedom in combination with a fantastic storyline that makes this game worth playing. With engrossing gameplay to keep a player in thrall of this game, this is truly one of the great hidden gems within the strategy RPG genre.

It almost physically hurts me not to recommend Metro Last Light Redux. I loved Metro 2033 Redux, and all the things that made that game great have translated to the sequel. Very little has changed in terms of gameplay or setting, which I suppose could be a good thing or a bad thing depending on how you look at it.
Unfortunately, none of that really matters. About halfway through the game (in the "Bandits" chapter), you run across a lengthy sequence in which you have to move a railcar down the tunnels, pausing every now and then to sneak around and pop bandits in the head with a silenced pistol. This is fun at first, but it grows tiresome as the sequence drags on and on and on for about an hour. Then things get even worse.
Right as I was getting ready to leave the area and breathing a sigh of relief at the thought of moving on to the next chapter, I encountered a game-breaking bug. I can't move or shoot if I crouch, reload, or activate the objective. This obviously makes it completely impossible to survive the scripted onslaught of monsters that occurs immediately after ringing a bell for a ferry ride. Not fun.
I tried everything I could think of to fix the problem, including restarting the game, reloading the checkpoint, remapping the action keys, unplugging other peripherals, and other things. Then, while scouring the internet for a solution, I discovered that this bug has been in the game for YEARS and has never been fixed. The only possible solution I've found is to restart the entire tedious chapter and play it again--at which point the bug may or may not occur again. I'm sorry, Metro, but I will not be wasting my time like that.
Maybe you'll get lucky when you play Last Light Redux. Maybe this won't happen to you. But I can't endorse a game with such a game-breaking glitch embedded in it, especially given the fact that the devs must know about it and simply haven't bothered fixing it. I may come back and retry the game when my patience rebuilds itself, but for now I'm done. And that's a real shame.
EDIT: Even after replaying the entire chapter in a rare fit of patience, the same glitch recurred. There's no way I'm trying again. Uninstall.

After playing 4 hours straight with a friend on PVE I can say this is, for better and worse, Ark without dinosaurs, and rust without as much grind.  It's a lot of fun.
My setup is an i5 4670, R9 290, 16gb Ram, and the game played at a comfortable 30-50 fps with most things high or ultra.  Mostly it was right under 44fps, which is really annoying for me because my freesync monitor kicks in at 44fps-144fps.
It looks better than Ark in a lot of ways, and some of the traditional fundamental ways of collecting crafting components is just so much smarter in this game.   Common resources are easy to find, but look natural.  Enemies can be pretty easy but don't get comfortable.  We wandered away from the starting area after crafting some base armor, shields and stone swords, and bows and arrows (which are buggy but do work).  We found ourselves surrounded by spiders, which we easily dispatched.  They spat poison at us which seemed to slow us down.  So we thought we were OP - and took on 5 at once.  These spiders must have been a slightly higher level because they weren't as easy to kill, and what we soon realized is that the poison which slows you down also STACKS.  Pretty soon we had 18, 19.. stacked poisonings, slowing us to a crawl and making us unable to block these new meaner spider attacks.  And then we died.  But it was a fun adventure!
Overall, for 30 dollars I recommend it.  4 hours was not enough time to give it a full nod, but if you like Rust, Ark, the Forest, and other crafting and survival games, this is a fun one that takes some rather OBVIOUS cues from those games and polishes the things I like about the genre up to a nice shine.  I suggest playing on a PVE server to get used to the interface and understand the systems first.  I love that this game can just be PVE.  It's a lot more laid back for that reason.  It's got a few bugs but only crashed once when I was playing.  I think the water effects were the thing that most dented my performance, but at 1440p and knowing how UNOPTIMIZED Ark is (seriously, we don't need more dinosaurs or maps, we need optimizations) it ran quite well.   I liked the setting and the vibe the game has of being a barbarian in a dark fantasy world.  The creatures were cool, and tribes were scary.  It was fun cutting them in half with my sword or bashing them into the ground with the large stone mallet.  Funcom has never let me down, and this game is no exception so far.
Anyway, give it a try if you have the extra cash and don't mind a few bugs.  If your system can deal with Unreal Engine/Ark it should take nicely to this.

After nearly 3 hours it MIGHT seem a bit early to actually write a review. But I might edit stuff later on soooo...
As with many games these days you either have trouble due to bugs/EA or you don't. In my case I don't have any technical issues on two different machines AND a dedicated server, except for the usual EA bugs (day/night cylcle not working on the dedicated and so on). Most negative reviews seem to come from people who try to play on either offical servers or servers not belonging to themselves, so I can't tell if that might be the reason why I haven't encountered any issues as of now.
However heres pros and cons.
PROS :
- The graphics are fine. Beautiful at times, depending on where in the exiled lands you are.
- Character creation is hilarious XD I mean come on...there's a DONG-SLIDER! Think about that for a minute!
- The survival part is unforgiving. You don't hunt, you starve. You can't fight your way to a water source (and I mean fighting like in "bashing somebodys head in to get there....") you die of thirst. Balancing is a little off but that's surely going to change.
- Crafting and building look alright.
- You can have thralls, slaves and stuff!
- A lot of stuff to craft and build that IS already in the game. So content wise theres much to do
CONS :
- Balancing.
- Combat is basic at best. Right now it's unresponsive and pretty much spam LMB and hope the enemy dies before you die because blocking or dodging are not an option.
- AI...it has basic pathfinding, which is nice...well and....uhh...yeah that's all actually.
- The usual EA glitches and bugs, one would expect (stuff disappearing, glithing through things and so on)
- NO BEARDS! I haven't found a single f***** beard during character creation or ingame! As it seems there will be beards implemented later on but come on...not even a stubble?! Nothing?!
- Dedicated server options aren't well documented and some things don't seem to work (yet)...once it's up and running it's good, but most will have their share of issues before getting one up and running.
So would I reccomend it? Sure! If you know what you're getting into. It's early access. It's not finished and it MIGHT be buggy at times. Give it a try or leave it and wait. I for one enjoy it already quite much and will do so in the future :)

This is a F2P game which means MANY MANY microtransactions.  If you want to complain that this game has too many or that its game breaking, please cry elsewhere.  Costumes are the only essential thing in this game that you can buy from the item mall.  However, you can get yourself 4 costume pieces for 250mil ED if you dont mind your costume not matching.  250mil sounds like a ton at first, but given you earn over 1mil ED per level 70 run, and there are now lvl 80 dungeons, you can earn that ED fairly easily.  Whats that? 250 runs just for costume pieces sounds like a grind?  Fear not.  As you level up, just make sure to hold onto your ED and you will have plenty.  I am not even including items such as secret dungeon materials.  You can obtain somewhere between 3-25 of these per run depending if you do lutos mode or not.  Currently these prices went up to roughly 300k-400k per piece, so you can sell those easily.  Not to mention, almost every event has free accessories or costumes that you can earn by simply playing enough (usually involves logging in for 10 minutes each day).  PvP is limited by your gear, but PvE is not at all.  I know someone who is ranked top 50 with a +9 weapon, which is now extremely easy to get if you understand the concepts of making money in this game.
The game is starting to see some growth in NA, despite the server population dying.  Merchandise has been officially released, and content continues to be released.  3rd jobs will be released shortly, bringing back old players.  On top of that, it is possible that a raid may be in the near future (1-2 years)?  It's never too late to play catch-up, so start playing now!

Wow. I always heard good things about this game but never got my hopes up. Its amazing that a game originally released in 2008 could hold up by today's standards in every way. But if they had a team this talented, they could have given them any number of projects. Skies of Arcadia, Phantasy Star (single player not the mmo series), Shining Force (this would be the most intriguing imo considering the team already showed mastery of the tactical genre) and maybe even Panzer Dragoon Saga. Sega has a rich history of RPGs that fans have been begging to see return. Instead, they continually run themselves into the ground. Interesting little game, it's a turn-based tactical game, very basic in its design - set in Europe during WW1, you can choose to play as the British, French, Americans or Germans.
In terms of challenge - On easy there is very little skill involve - simply get behind your opposition, not in front of them, and continue to shoot them until you've defeated them. As you increase the difficulty the challenge really does ramp up and you will need to plan what manueveres to upgrade your pilots with and understand how and when to use them, it becomes like a chess game.
The set up of the game is that your participate in 5 battles, and there are 5 engagements within each battle. They are literally just randomly generated engagements based off the same 4 engagement types - Combat Air Patrol, Search & Destroy, Recon or Escort. However you can choose from one of 3 engagements offered, this means you can choose to challenge yourself or avoid doing that one engagement type that you've become bored of. There are also some random bonus or "Challenge" missions which get thrown in too.
Overall if you like turn-based tactical or even if you're just a fan of WW1 it could be and interesting way to waste a few hours.
