Well, folks.  Here we are.  The Hype is real and still is!
I bought ATS as it is called by players because I loved ETS2 and wanted to play an American Truck game, like the old 18 WoS days.  So far, I'm not disappointed by the game one bit.
Yeah, you only get two trucks at the start, and I'm fine with that.  The reasoning for the lack of immediate content is actually a good one for once.  It is because rather than put fake brands in the game, SCS wants to get licenses first.  But, as said by Pavel Sebor himself, getting licenses from truck manufacurers that aren't used to being approached for licenses of their product is like the chicken vs egg debate.  So, they are going about it the right way at least.
On to the gameplay.  Those of you that are familiar with ETS2 will have no problem getting used to the ATS Gameplay.  There are a lot of new things to compliment to already very good base gameplay that I hope will be making it's way to ETS2 soon as well.
Delivery Points are the biggest advancement in the gameplay system.  You can choose how difficult you want the delivery to be.  From a zero point quick drop to a 90 point drop that is so complex, even the most Veteran Driver will have a challenge are available for choosing.
Weigh Stations are new to the game.  You can be randomly chosen to go to the Scale House for Inspection.  It's an interesting feature, but a bit of a waste of time and ruins fuel economy.  Hopefully, SCS will be able to do something to give this feature more meaning.
After talking about weigh stations, we have no choice but to talk about the new police engine.  Now, the dreaded Rozzers are mobile and sneaky.  I got a Speeding Ticket for not being at 30 MPH right after the sign changed.  There needs to be a Reduced Speed Ahead sign, like in real life here in the States.
So, lets break it down to the Pros and Cons.
Pros
Familiar yet tweaked Gameplay
American Trucks
Nevada included
Scenery that will blow your mind
Easter Eggs, yes, there a few, and no, I will not tell you what they are
No curves every 20 feet like ETS2
Cons
Only two states at the beginning
Only two trucks at the beginning,  Not really a con, but may put some people off
The UI is completely Copy/Paste.  Would have loved to see the Route Adviser remodeled.  Maybe next time.
Only 64-Bit

TLDR: Devs are cool, game is hard-but-awesome; read the beginners guide while you download/install or risk fiery death.
If you're unsure about trying this game and are looking at the 'mixed' rating it currently has, then you should know that the majority of complaints (such as NPC markets, new-player protection, bug-fixes etc..)  have now been addressed, but naturally people are too lazy to go back and change their review.
Since this game was released on steam, the devs have been actively responding to community requests, questions, whining, and even the occasional nasty comment; whilst being consistently professional, courteous and friendly.  I can think of very few games which can make the same claim.
It's also worth noting that this game is pretty hardcore.  When you lose a ship; you LOSE the ship, it's gone, with nothing left but a burning wreckage and regret; Not everyone is accustomed to this type of gameplay.
That being said, there are a plethora of guides out there; you don't have to read every single one of them, but many players  (myself included) have gone down in flames in circumstances that could have been easily avoided by a little reading.  Further to which, there are now a number of clans/groups who are willing to equip new players and help them get started. (Seems 30 days of PVP invincibility makes you pretty popular, who knew?)
After playing this game for a couple of months (at the exclusion of all others, which I've never done before), I'm convinced this game is, at least in part, a labor of love, and is worth absolutely your time on that fact alone.

It almost physically hurts me not to recommend Metro Last Light Redux. I loved Metro 2033 Redux, and all the things that made that game great have translated to the sequel. Very little has changed in terms of gameplay or setting, which I suppose could be a good thing or a bad thing depending on how you look at it.
Unfortunately, none of that really matters. About halfway through the game (in the "Bandits" chapter), you run across a lengthy sequence in which you have to move a railcar down the tunnels, pausing every now and then to sneak around and pop bandits in the head with a silenced pistol. This is fun at first, but it grows tiresome as the sequence drags on and on and on for about an hour. Then things get even worse.
Right as I was getting ready to leave the area and breathing a sigh of relief at the thought of moving on to the next chapter, I encountered a game-breaking bug. I can't move or shoot if I crouch, reload, or activate the objective. This obviously makes it completely impossible to survive the scripted onslaught of monsters that occurs immediately after ringing a bell for a ferry ride. Not fun.
I tried everything I could think of to fix the problem, including restarting the game, reloading the checkpoint, remapping the action keys, unplugging other peripherals, and other things. Then, while scouring the internet for a solution, I discovered that this bug has been in the game for YEARS and has never been fixed. The only possible solution I've found is to restart the entire tedious chapter and play it again--at which point the bug may or may not occur again. I'm sorry, Metro, but I will not be wasting my time like that.
Maybe you'll get lucky when you play Last Light Redux. Maybe this won't happen to you. But I can't endorse a game with such a game-breaking glitch embedded in it, especially given the fact that the devs must know about it and simply haven't bothered fixing it. I may come back and retry the game when my patience rebuilds itself, but for now I'm done. And that's a real shame.
EDIT: Even after replaying the entire chapter in a rare fit of patience, the same glitch recurred. There's no way I'm trying again. Uninstall.

Hand of Fate is a unique combination of adventure/card/rogue-like with
well done audio, and decent enough graphics.  The character you play as is a
male warrior, so if you're hoping for a female character or a different style
of character, this may not be the best game for you.  I give the game devs
props for creating a card based game that is expanded, and pushes the envelope for a new style of game, and they did it well, but did they do it well enough?
Each level is an individual dungeons where you follow a path of
cards, at the end of which you fight that levels boss.  This game would
more appropriately be titled 'Hand of Chance', as the random elements that
make up a rogue-like combine with the card game elements to make an experience that relies more on the luck of the draw rather than skill or strategy.
You start over on every level, and by that I mean you lose any items
or money that you have, making every dungeon its own mission.  This negates the impact of dying, as you start the level fresh. The only loss you have would be of time spent playing.
As to the equipment cards you have for your deck;  it is unlikely you
will be able to play that perfect card you need or want during a typical dungeon; of the 28 cards I had in my collection, it would be generous to say that I  saw 10 during any one dungeon. Obviously you want to have more cards that are chosen based on what you enjoy, but overall the gear or weapons in your deck become less important, due to the small chance you will actually see them.
Every level is randomly selected, which may give it a new look and feel
as you progress forward, but it takes away control or any sense of power as there is no choice in where you go.  The randomization of what gear you may get combined with the random level you may end up on, and the random number of traps on that level can determine how well you do on a level.  The combat was not challenging; a matter of mashing the  mouse button and dodging when the green light flashes.  Skill and tactics play no part in the battles, only having the correct timing.  This gets quite boring very fast after a few battles.
This game boils down to chance;  equipment, levels, perks, relics,
weapons, traps, all is dependent upon the chance that you get the right one.
There is no tactical challenge in this game; what combat there is is simplistic
and offers no challenge.  If you're looking for a casual game, and like card
games and rogue-likes, this may be for you, but if you're looking for a game
based on skill rather than chance, I cannot recommend it.

I'm giving this a thumbs up based on the hopes of funcom reading and listening to the people giving actual reviews.  I gave it a solid 2-3 hours of playtime and noticed a LOT of things that need to be worked on.  So I'll just cut the butter and spread it.
-The wall needs a countdown warning instead of insta-gibbing your character. This is going to frustrate a lot of new players exploring the "world" created for them.
-Materials on some simple crafts make no sense. 50 branches and 50 stone to make a fire?  I'm just trying to cook my meat so I don't instantly die from being hungry; not build a complete backyard smoker with variable heat adjustments.  The materials for the fire and water bladder are just stupid, especially after dying.
-The ease of breaking structures.  3 arrows should't blow up a door, and punching a wall shouldn't destroy it. Simple.
-The lag on official servers is almost unplayable unless you're on a very low pop, gazelle teleporting around me and players skiing all over the place completely breaks the immersion, ESPECIALLY in a PVP based Conan game.  You can't even fight other players without it feeling like your character is stuck to a pole with a bungee cord on his waist.
-The world is frankly just too small as it is, with 70 players building civilizations the current map is going to get plugged up so fast, especially since half the map is useless.
Now I only stated the negatives above, I do believe the game has a lot of potential if funcom pulls through.  Even MORE props if they actually release the game, but I'm predicting a cash grab.  I hope to be proven wrong because this is one survival game I could get into.

About the game in general:
Disgaea is a comedic srpg, it features a funny story in a high fantasy setting featuring several greatly written and designed characters.
The gameplay features more options than most other srpgs do and there are numerous ways to customize every single character, the game has great long time motivation, featuring a lot of content even after the main story is beaten.
However by now the gameplay is outshined by that of it's 5 successors, and the ai of the enemies is too low to put up a challenge even to a little child.
About the PC adaption:
Disgaea PC is the third version I've played, after the PS2 and the PSP version.
For these not suffering technical problems some users complained about, the PC version runs smoothly and features the added content of the PSP adaption.
However the controls, especially regarding the mouse, are a little awkward and sometimes lead to minor problems like throwing, attacking or walking in a different direction than planned.
Resume:
The game is a must have for friends of comedic manga style games and worth a look for any friends of the srpg genre who don't already own one of it's successors.
However for these who own a PSP, I would recommend the PSP version over the PC version, as it has more intuitive controls and a screen resolution just better befitting to the optics of the game.

Shortened version:
Pros
-Side character designs, vices, and backstories are diverse and interesting
-This is a good concept, even if it's horribly implemented.
Cons
-This game is SLOW. There are a LOT of loading screens, cutscenes you need to go through, in game cutscenes you can't skip, dialog bits, and even waiting for the enemy to move takes a long time
-On that note, you can't fast forward enemy turns. Minimizing pauses the game as well.
-This is a strategy game with a HEAVY reliance on random number generation and probability. Many chances are a complete hit or miss--you either succeed or fail catastrophically. Some people also refer to it as a JRPG, but the RPG elements are very limited.
-That said, the game is also horribly imbalanced. Many of the super difficult missions can be beat in a single turn by exploiting certain properties of your classes, while others can be beat quickly with a scout rush. The random aspect actually contributes to this.
-Characters fail to come across as realistic. They feel almost there, but still a step away from human. Repetitive dialog doesn't help.
-Plot has some decisions that are questionable or just stupid. The ending in particular is senseless (more on that below).
Full review:
Valkyria Chronicles seriously felt like a giant 30 hour sludgefest. As in I was slowly wading knee-deep in swamp.
Good god why would a strategy game rely on random chances and probabilities for 80% of its actions?
Why are there so many loading screens? Why are there so many goddam cutscenes that, even if you can skip them, you still need to load and watch a second of them first?  Why are the credits unskippable?
Why is the dialog so long? Half the time it doesn't feel at all realistic. When characters interact, they usually reaffirm what each other said about 3 times, and they do it via repetition. (E.g., paraphrased: “Wow this bread is good! You should open a bakery!” After saying this like 2-3 times, instead of responding with “I’ve thought about doing so” or whatnot, the other character responds with something much more repetitious like “I’ve always wanted to open a bakery.” This is just paraphrased and isn’t word for word how it went.) Character interactions constantly feel a step away from human, which while it gets the point across, rarely feels genuine.
There was only one character death in the game that made me upset. The only other death I sympathized with wasn’t even a character with a name, nor were they an ally. The rest were anticlimactic, predictable, or just outright stupid. (”I love you so I’ll kill myself in a blaze of glory for your honor!” f**k my A-HOLE.)
The worst offender was at the very end, when you defeat the final boss. You literally have him about to surrender. He's disarmed, his super weapon’s been powered down, he’s weak and surrounded. Yet even one of your friends shows up and grabs him only to kill the bad guy in a suicide maneuver to atone for how he hurt you and and another team member earlier int he game AND IT'S SO GODDAM UNNECESSARY I'M ACTUALLY MAD. There was literally NO realistic reason for him to kill himself nor the final boss when they could’ve easily apprehended him. The icing on the crap cake? He kills them both by pulling the baddy-mc-badguy into a pit on board the carrier you’re on, which causes his deactivated weapon to explode, which causes the carrier to start exploding and basically screws the two main characters over. (GOOD JOB ATONING FOR YOUR DICKISH BEHAVIOR.)
Being an anime game of course there’s supernatural aspects, but it’s only ever used against you. One good character has special abilities, but they only show up in game context once for the first half of a single mission and you don't even get to control them at that time. That's literally it. It's a huge  letdown--I would've LOVED to turn the tables and command a super soldier against an impossible objective. If they wanted it to be a plot device, they should've kept that in cutscenes only, not actually put it in a mission and not let you use it.
Gameplay wise I love the concept and attempt at the approach, but the reliance on random factors is maddening and outright stupid. The way the game is set up, either things will go perfectly, or they'll go horribly wrong. There is no in between.
So you wind up saving at a spot just to avoid watching the debriefing cutscenes, and the unit positioning, and the map-start cutscenes, etc. Probably the start of your turn, or right before a big play. Now you have to hope a perk you have will activate or your character won't suddenly develop Parkinson's and miss a nearly point blank shot, and when things do go wrong and you do absolutely no damage because of it, you'll reload. If you forgot to save recently, then prepare to watch all the cutscenes that played all over again since your last save, watch all the dialog bits, over and over and over again, until finally the RNG system stops jerking with you and you can move on.
Whether or not it works in your favor, because of the random aspect most missions you can just rush a full scout team and have them slip in and capture the objective. Balancing is non existent. There is no difficulty curve, just a probability curve. Skirmishes can be beaten in 1-3 turns via a scout rush. Campaign missions can be anywhere from as much of a cakewalk, or can be absolute bull difficulty unless you know how to exploit the class imbalance. (One 'difficult’ boss that can kill your units in milliseconds if you don’t have cover can be beat in a single turn with just a smoke bomb and 3 snipers. Another can be beat in a single turn just by rushing shocktroopers.)
Oh and of course, as you’re moving a unit around, if a perk activates randomly you’ll suddenly freeze and have a little mini-cutscene appear on screen as they say something gloaty, and then they get a perk to activate. Sometimes they can activate repeatedly during the same turn, btw. (Yay perk, boo WASTING MY TIME AND DISRUPTING MY MOVEMENT. One of Ted’s perks activated literally 3 times in a single move.)
The game has a horrible habit of also changing mission objectives on you at random, without warning. One mission has two tanks spawn on opposite ends of the map. The only way to beat this mission is if you knew in advance that these tanks were going to spawn, and you equipped both of your own with anti armor rounds so you could actually kill both of them.
My profile shows 30+ hours of play. About 40% of that was actually my gameplay. The rest was watching (and rewatching) cutscenes (some of which were unskippable), waiting for loading screens (there's plenty to go around!), and waiting for the enemy to make a move (even after they pulled some RNG bull and killed a key position of mine. Wanna restart? Too bad: you can't pause in the middle of enemy movement. You have to wait for their AI to tediously and meticulously finish. Even if they can easily kill you in their first move of their turn, they may decide to wait and finish you off during their last move.)
I like a lot of the side characters you can put on your squads for their designs and backstories, and I feel like this system has a lot of potential, but beyond that this game was incredibly frustrating and slow as crap.

- Gameplay is quite straightforward.
CONS:
- The graphics are a bit childish for the most part.
- Too arcadish. Don't expect me to care about the life of my pilots when some of them have these silly faces. Don't include female pilots. I don't care about political correctness.
- Lack of strategical decision-making. You can choose between 3 missions, select some pilots and upgrade them. You don't really have influence on a strategical level.
- Don't play for too long, it could get a bit repetitive. That said, it's not really a con.
So, the game is okay, but as soon as there is a game like this that is historically more accurate, graphically more attractive and strategically more challenging I will probably never play Sid Meier's Ace Patrol again.

Coming from Euro Truck, I pretty much knew what I was going to get. Gameplay was going to be pretty much the same with some new and improved visuals to go with it. Which is ok, because the basics didn't really need fixing.
There are things that make it stand out though. SCS improved city modelling the ETS2 Scandinavia DLC by quite a bit, but what's in here is another step up. Even though everything is scaled down by quite a lot, you still have the feeling you can drive through a big sizable urban area instead of a few roads on the outskirts that ETS2 gave you. And the detail is pretty damn impressive as well. Waiting for the lights, I could now actually look into some of the shops through the reflective windows. A far cry from the old flat facades. And the cost of all this additional graphics? Nothing! In fact, I think I'm getting higher FPS in ATS than I do in ETS2.
Another very welcome addition in ATS is having a choice of parking. You can now opt for putting the trailer in more difficult spots, which occasionally requires quite a bit of effort.
So is it all perfect?
Nah, it has its issues. The AI vehicles can behave a bit weird at times. I've had quite a few incidents with AI cars turning right on red when it wasn't safe to do so. There are also quite a few smaller issues with map and definitions. But if SCS continue to improve the game over the coming years, like they do with ETS2, then that stuff will be sorted out soon enough. I'm also not too fond of the overuse of some standard road structures. The stacked interchange looking junctions with standard clover leaf ones underneath really annoyed me. I hope this is just there to have something to change over time.
Which leaves the big topic of the amount of content. Due to the scale factor, the map doesn't really feel that big. If the three states that will eventually be included with the base game would be the only thing ever released, then you would probably have seen everything in about 30 hours. Which is not bad for a 20 Euro/dollar game. But it's quite obvious that the scale is meant to have a full map of North America in it. Driving from LA to Boston would keep you busy for quite some time and really give you that feeling of having done an epic journey.
The two trucks are also a bit limited. Especially since they are very much alike. Hopefully the licensing deals will come through quickly so there will be a bit more variety.
Since I play ATS on Linux/OpenGL, a few words on that. Performance is very good. In fact, I haven't seen any frame drops that I've heard mentioned by Windows/DirectX. My GTX650 Ti BOOST gives me pretty much 60 fps all the way providing I keep scaling at 100%. There are still plenty of Linux specific issues that are identical to those in ETS2. I can't run 1920x1200 fullscreen and 1920x1080 won't properly switch to fullscreen unless I alt-tab out and back in. This seems to be specific to Ubuntu. Also getting Force Feedback to work on wheels requires drivers that aren't in standard systems yet (not the fault of SCS of course). But even if you get those new drivers, it feels a bit flaky and requires setting the level way down. Not too surprising since the support was probably based on a best guess. I still had a lot of fun with a G920 wheel though.
So is this recommended? Absolutely! As long as you realize that this just the start of something bigger. I look forward to getting the new map extension DLCs and expanding the trucking world. And if ETS2 is any indication, the modding scene should explode quickly. I expect it to be an awesome ride.

If you're into any kind of relaxing type simulation, be it flying, buses, trains, tractors or just cruzing around in cars, you must have a look at American Truck Sim.   The developers (SCS) are not new at this, and with the success of Euro Truck Simulator 2 (and many previous trucking titles) they've raised the bar once more here with a great level of eye catching details in the world around you as you drive through the countryside.
The simulation is not without it's challenges.  Driving some of these longhaul trucks with long traillers is not as simple as you might think.   If you're used to Euro Truck Sim 2, be prepared for a new level of difficulty with these longer wheel base trucks and longer traillers.   The truck models look and sound great, there are two truck types so far, the Peterbuilt and Kenworth and two states to drive in, California and Nevada, with another on the way that is included in the purchase price.   This may seem a bit limiting, but for $20 it's probably a fair deal.
It's playable with a keyboard or game pad, but to really bring this simulation to life a wheel is the way to go.  Working those turns and shifting throught the gears, when you collect your virtual paycheck you really do feel like you've earned it.

Dislikes:

First things first: The gameplay of this game is VERY niche, its not something that I am personally likely to put more hours into, however I will say that the skill cap and complexity of the game could easily attract some cult following of a hardcore playerbase.
A lot of reviews read along the lines of "Cargo simulator." The only downside to this, is (also as listed in MANY other reviews) the tutorial is massively lacking. It seems like the dev's are actively working on this, though, and it took me maybe 30 minutes to figure out all of the basic functions. After that, I just used the world chat if I had any questions. The game gives the option of manual or RTS-style movement with the larger airships, the smaller fighter types (strekoleks I believe) are a dog-fighting flight style, kind of neat to mess with though I didn't put enough time into the game to really give them a full go.
Overall, it shows about 20 hours of gameplay whereas in actuality it is probably about 4-5hrs. Every hour you play the game gives you gold, which is INCREDIBLY helpful early, so I had left the game running so that I could check out a couple of the features out of a newbie's pay grade, because as I mentioned before it is a VERY slow start either way.
Overall, honestly for most users this is not recommended except for as a casual game because of the extremely slow pace. But, for those of you looking for a very intricate, almost completely player based-economy with a very unique play style all around, you might give it a shot.

I never imagined that I would enjoy being a shopkeeper this much. The game is broken up into two components: Buying and Selling goods, and Dungeon Crawling. The merchant aspect relies on keeping track of market trends to know when to sell high and buy low. There is something about mastering this portion that I found irresistible. The dungeon crawling serves to obtain new items either to sell or equip on your adventurers to increase their stats. There are different modes unlocked after playing through which helps with the replayability factor. I also enjoyed the chibi and anime graphics style, though this may put others off.
Unfortunately this game does have some weak points. The story is lacking to the point where it loses the spotlight to the shop keeping and dungeon diving. Because of this there is very little dialogue or character interaction. The fighting becomes repetitive quickly and the extra adventurers do not offer enough variety to keep it interesting.
Overall the game has solid gameplay with a refreshing pace. You could spend a few minutes or a few hours playing and feel satisfied either way. If you are a fan of hunting/gathering games, or are looking for something just a little different, this game is for you. I highly recommend it.

I have over 700 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #59 - Expeditions: Conquistador
I was intrigued by Expeditions: Conquistador, as there aren't many games with a 16th Centry New World setting.  But I was happy to find a few more reasons beyond just the setting to enjoy myself.
First, I'll say I was surprised by the emphasis on the story.  I guess I am used to playing turn-based games which are pretty light on the story and more about getting you to wander the map and fight things.  Instead I discovered there is as much emphasis on the RPG as there is strategy.  One warning, other than a little voice acting at the beginning, it's going to be a lot of reading, so depending on how you like your RPGs presented, this may be a turn off.
I imagined as I set out that I'd be doing my share of exploring and fighting, and I wasn't entirely wrong, but it didn't play out the way I expected.  Instead of being in charge, I found myself having to work for the local governor, and starting out as an errand boy of sorts.  I enjoyed the fact that the story was twisting my expectations here.
The game does provide a tutorial of sorts.  Before you can go exploring you have to go through a friendly battle in the town, and this gives you a chance to pick up some of the basics of combat.  What I liked here is that the basics were pretty easy to pickup, but there is definitely a deeper strategy at play.  The characters you command will have different classes, and each class will have a specialty.  So for instance, you'll have characters that focus on melee attacks, or ranged attacks.  Each class also has a special ability, such as the doctor who can heal an ally.
So the combat starts out pretty straightfoward in regards to moving around and attacking things from either up close or at range.  But then the tutorial starts to layer on some of the other aspects of strategy like taking cover, flanking your opponent, and attacks of opportunity.
Once you finish the first fight, you are able to leave the starter town and explore the area.  Although before you actually leave town you'll visit a few places of interest around town, and pick up a few quests along the way.  You can also stock up on additional supplies (like food) before leaving town to go explore.
Exploring felt a little different from other games I have played.  You still have the concept of turns and only being able to travel so far in a single turn.  But once your day is up, instead of just advancing to the next day, you make camp for night.   Camping actually involves a few different activities that you assign to your crew.  You'll have someone guarding the camp.  You can also go out and hunt for food to add to the food stocks you already have.  Also, if you have people who have been injured, you can treat them with your doctors.   You can specify all of this manually, but the game also has an auto-assign to help speed this process up.
My first fight outside of the town did not go well.   The quest I got from the governor directed me to this temple where I proceeded to get into a fight with it's inhabitants.  I ended up retreating from the fight after most of my crew got injured, and limped my way back to town.  What I found interesting was, I ended up failing the quest.  I'm used to either having to reload or do the quest over, but in this case, the story simply went on in spite of my failure.  This also made me realize that this is not an easy game, even on the easy difficulty.
And that's where I ended my first hour of play.  It was enough to get a good sense of what the game was about, but otherwise barely scratching the surface of it, and definitely leaving a lot left to learn.   I can see where the early game may be frustrating while trying to learn everything and figure out the right strategy.  But even so I certainly enjoyed my first hour of playing, and have no problems recommending this to others.

I love entertainment with a supernatural spin and I love trying to solve mysteries, so this was right up my alley. Though the game is very simple and certainly not the best game I'd ever encountered, I've enjoyed it immensely.
The game is overall extremely simple. This may be a drawback to some, a bonus to others, or something that is totally indifferent. I fall in the indifferent category as I don't play games based on their difficulty at all. There is very little combat and I didn't mind that one bit as it was extremely easy to advance the story. The collectibles can be somewhat challenging and you want to be sure you've collected all of them in an area before advancing too far, especially before advancing to the next area. Check every room, nook, and cranny. If you are in an area where you have to do something special in order to get past something, make sure you gather everything on the other side before heading back. I missed one item in the church and I am kicking myself for it. I will probably not be creating a collectibles guide for this game, but there are many out there. If you are uncertain and really care about thorough completion, try to find one without spoilers that you can use. Any challenge or gameplay the game lacks is definitely compensated for with its story.
The story is very solid. The side ghost stories are somewhat unnecessary, but the effort to expand the storyline seems to be in earnest. I found myself gathering collectibles simply for completion as opposed to the enjoyment of the stories, though I didn't hate them.
My only real gripe with this game is that they chose to set it in Salem, Massachusetts. I am currently sitting about a 30 minute drive away from Salem, spent an immense amount of time there throughout my life, and had lived there for a time after graduating high school back in 1998. I feel very strongly that things based on some aspect of real life should remain true to the history and reality of the place or story. This could have been very easily set in a fictional Massachusetts town near Salem, with the emphasis on *FICTIONAL* or really anywhere else. Of course, it looks nothing like Salem in any capacity and the history...is beyond inaccurate. It is obvious to me that there was no attempt at historical or geographical accuracy and that should simply not happen. Part of the reason I wanted to play this game was the Salem setting. I get more enjoyment out of seeing things set in my stomping grounds than I do anything else and I am not the only person who feels this way. I was immediately let down. It irked me a little further with the introduction of historical names into this fiction. Those accused of witchcraft were not burned at the stake, for starters. The "Judgment House" seems to be based on the "Witch House" which was the home of Judge Corwin, not John Hathorne, during the 1692 Witch Hysteria. Things like that really got my goat. The nearest mental hospital to Salem was the once great Danvers State Hospital (in Danvers which was the historical Salem Village), and in my opinion one of the most beautiful buildings that ever stood. It was abandoned for years and then eventually mostly demolished and converted to apartment buildings. Judge Hathorne actually lived where they ended up building the asylum. There is great potential for ghost stories within the actual history, lore, and locales of the real Salem. Of course, if they went too literal, the map would be way too big. They could have used real places, landmarks, and history as all of these places exist within historical Salem and are not incredibly difficult to research. I am going to stop with all of this negativity as I could go on forever on just this topic. I was ultimately able to separate the story from Salem and enjoy the game. However, had the game been disappointing in any other way, that enjoyment would have been traded for outrage. If anyone ever decides to set a video game in the actual Salem, please come to me first. ;-p~
I know I have fixated on mostly negative aspects of the game, but my experience was positive overall. My complaints about history and geography are merely my personal pet peeves, though others may feel the same. If you like mysteries, ghosts, rich stories, and simple gameplay; I strongly recommend this game.

Yeah, very promising. And this all also wrapped with pretty good graphics with good visual art and detail, good score and voice acting. The catch? - Dull story and mainly boring and repetitive gameplay.
The story had a good potential but authors were unable to pull it off. Eventually it slipped to so trivial and dull finale, that I began to regret for my wasted time. Authors tried to fill it with the notes of Salem's history, Ronan's personal story and love tragedy, but it didn't worked, something was missing and the main story felt... shallow. Throughout the game there is almost no progression in gameplay: after you learned how to discover things, collect evidence, solve the case, possess people, counteract the opponents - you'll do it till the end with almost no diversity or new meaningful mechanics. The investigation part is very dull and making conclusions is not particularly interesting - especially when doing it dozen of times.
I know this might look silly to blame a story-driven game for lack of gameplay (it's not
though), but we're talking about the game with also sort of 'open' locations for your discovery, where you can freely go and explore it, solve some side-quests (they are also trivial and repetitive). On the contrary, I never got bored in story-driven
, even though it's mere third-person shooter, because of its constant progression in fascinating story, locations design, changing circumstances, obstacles and gameplay.
In
, besides that you can wonder around the locations doing side-quests, looking for collectibles (fun at first, become boring and useless later) or navigating your way from point A to B there are a lot of times during the second half of the game when you forced to revisit old locations and more often than not run through it from one end to another.
The locations themselves are not very distinctive and did I mention you can't run through every wall? To clear up any potiential confusion, this is a port not a remake. Even though the developers made some improvements to the quality of terrain, menu items and text, much of the game's graphics are still fairly low resolution and pixelated.
The game play is the same from its original release years ago, and might be a bit off-putting to players that are only familiar with more modern takes on strategy games. Level ginding is a requirement and you will be repeating maps over and over before you have any chance of progressing the story. The game can be quite difficult as well -- which may be a positive or negative depending on your preference. There is something of a tutorial to start but much of the gameplay is only briefly explained in optional tutorial text leading to a fairly steep learning curve. There are no in-mission saves and some parts of the game require marathon like runs to complete.
Despite all of this, Disgaea is still a fun, deep game with massive amounts of replayability. Maps provide a variety of strategic challenges and there are numerous paths to improving characters. This is one of the few games I have played  that manages to be consistently funny even though the English tracks are not as good as the Japanese version (The English voice acting is decent, but the English translation is fairly weak. If you happen to understand Japanese you will notice that the English translation is often much shorter and leaves out a lot of information and in many cases is very different from the original text). Replayability is off the charts and I suspect very few players will ever get close to 'completing' this game.
Overall Disgaea is good enough to recommend if you are willing to overlook its age related short comings -- particularly given the shortage of good turn based strategy games on the PC.

MURDED: SOUL SUSPECT (apparently the CAPSLOCK key of the developers is broken!) is a really good game. Really good. Repeating for emphasis!
Of course, I'm going to complain about something, so lets get the irrelavent bit out the way first.
I'm playing this on a PC. So tell me Airtight, where is the Start button? I really hate the consolification of PC games. I don't need a silly screen where I have to "Press Start" to continue. When I want to quit the game, I don't want to be returned to "Press Start" so I can then choose "Exit Game" from the menu. I thought I made my intensions clear when I initially said "Exit Game" from the in-game menu. Meh, who am I kidding. Might as well wish that developers didn't include stupid not skippable logo's and videos each time the game starts.
And... CHECKPOINTS? This was almost a deal breaker. MSS is an adventure game. Since when did adventure games need checkpoints? This leads to my major crisitism of the game, but as I'll defer that until the end where it belongs.
So, what's good about the game? Well, pretty much everything. Atmosphere is brilliant, I really enjoyed the juxtaposition of the ghost world ontop of the real world, past mixed with the present. It worked amazingly well. Graphics and environment design top notch.
Audio is generally good, but there's a few places where you had "what is making this sound" puzzles and two of these the proported sounds didn't really match the clues, but no biggy. I also confess to jumping out of my skin on more than one occasion when the demons annouced their arrival.
The investigations were nicely done and nothing too complex (which is both a plus a minus, sometimes it felt a little easy, at other times I was greatful I wasn't trying to work out some insane and illogical inventory puzzle), and the story was engrossing. Each major area in the game also has a themed set of collectibles, which once all obtained give a nice little backstory to the area.
The checkpoint system generally works, but take heed - when you get to the final act, the game mentions if you continue you can't go back. By this point I was treating MSS as a open world type game, running around picking up things I'd missed and so on. I assumed, like all open world games, that once I'd finished the main mission, I'd be free to find the last missing side quest in the town center. Nope, I was wrong. When it said you can't go back, you really can't. And there's only a single damn save for the entirely playthrough.
Fortunately I have a backup from a couple of days ago so I can at least replay the latter half of the game to find my missing items rather than the whole game, but I did think this a pretty dumb design decision.
One other astoundingly bad design decision is the very final act of the game. Remember that MSS is an adventure game - you play it at your own pace, looking around for clues, collectibles, backstory etc. There's a few semi-quick time events involving demons that spawn. These aren't too bad, just annoying as each event uses a randomized key combination. There are similar QTE for demons that come through the floor but for most of the game you'll avoid these.
The final scene however involves two very brief timed events where you have something like 20s to do one thing then 10s to do another. This made me pretty angry actually, I've spent hours playing this lovely creation, then you force the last 30 seconds with no time to do anything but try and do the right actions.
Combine that with the fact that I couldn't return to the open world, meant my last memories of the game are negative, which is a shame because the climax of the story was excellant, and the little twists amazing. This is a game with an excellant story! What a shame a couple of silly design decisions have offset that.
I've just read on a wiki that Airtight closed a month after releasing MSS, which seems a travesty along the lines of TTLG closing after Thief 2. Disappointing news, as I was greatly looking forward to the possibility of further games in the series.
In short, excellant game, buy it, play it, enjoy it! And commiserate over the fact that they might not be any follow ups. (And probably spare a curse for the publishers that probably cause the shuttering)

Sid Meier's Ace Patrol is a Turn-based strategy game that uses small squad tactics with different types of planes as you fight through World War I. Sid Meier's Ace Patrol was developed by Firaxis Games and released in 2013.
You know how World War I goes in your history classes? Yeah, pretty much the same story here. So instead of giving you your history class again, here's the basic gist that the story relevance to the video game follows: There are breakthrough in technology on both sides that give the Axis or the Allies a technological advantage over the other, you should take advantage of when these occur before the other side catches up and you're forced to rely on tactical maneuvers, again.
Sid Meier's Ace Patrol fills a unique strategy game "niche", this is the first game that I personally have played where it's all about flight combat tactics. Depending on different positions your planes will do more or less damage; if you're attacking from a flank or behind the enemy you'll do more damage. If you're firing while banking away you do less damage, or depending on the range you are from your enemy you might do greater or lesser damage.
The achievements generally require a great deal of commitment to first, learning the game mechanics, and then accomplishing successful campaigns with the different nations, earning ____ amount of victories as each respective nation, Victories with pilots, and defeating the harder difficulties. (this game is already plenty hard on easy difficulties by the way)
Sid Meier's Ace Patrol is priced at $4.99, that's a fair price for the game, and for people who may find this game very enjoyable it's a great deal! Unfortunately this game will only appeal to certain gamers, most people won't grasp the subtle nuances or simply be pushed away because of the complexities of the game itself.
I recommend this game to people who already know they Enjoy strategy games. I suggest watching a few videos on how to play before making a final decision to purchase. Don't get me wrong, it's a good game... but there's just nothing that will grab and keep the normal player playing.

This game is hard to describe, but basically you drill rocks in space, which gives you gold and allows you to collect resources (tiles and collectables), which in turn you can use to hire crew members (who can be upgraded with the gold as well after they gain experience), build your base (which improves your drill's stats and allows you to place more crew members), buy upgrades (including expanding the size of your base, so you can have more rooms, crew members, and ultimately stats), etc. -- there are also some enemies to avoid.
The main strength of the game is that it's pretty unique, there aren't that many games like it that I'm aware of, and it's quite addictive after you get into it and learn the game (which can take a while). There's also quite a lot of content, I'm 17 hours in and feel like I'm barely half-way through the game. The music is minimalist but pretty nice.
On the other hand, the game does suffer from a clunky and often non-intuitive GUI, a lack of notifications where needed, an unnecessarily wordy tutorial, and often poor English with an amazing number of typos. It also has fairly primitive graphics (not just in terms of being 2D and simple, but also in terms of poor color harmonies). There are no hotkeys -- none. Not even escape. Everything is done with the mouse, which can get very tedious, particularly when you are exploring a large map and clicking a square, clicking 'explore' (half the screen away), then going back and clicking the next square, then going back and clicking 'explore' again, repeating 400 times, when it could easily have just had a hotkey for explore ('E' or something) and been ten times as fast. Speaking of speed, the speed at which the text scrolls in is glacial; maybe I'm just a fast reader, but the tutorial text always felt like it was appearing at least half as slow as I wanted to read it. There are also almost no mouseovers, which is annoying when you want to know what type of collectable or what type of tile you are hovering over. Instead you need to memorize what it looks like, go to HQ, and then look it up in a big list. Similarly it'd be nice if there were an easy way to get a list of the levels that you've been in that have a particular tile or collectable, it'd be useful for finishing collections for medals or research. The whole GUI just screams 'argh!@#$%' to me whenever I have to interact with it.
To me those downsides did actually distract from the experience quite a bit, it's hard to get into a game where every other sentence contains a typo (I've been messaging the developer about these typos and eventually many of them may be fixed, but it really needs a professional editor; thankfully most of the text is flavor text and not essential to understand, and the game has no real story and typos aren't quite as bad if it's just flavor text rather than dialogue or story text). But it's still addictive enough that despite those problems I'm probably going to get to the end game.
Though speaking of getting futher into the game, it does feel like the game eventually gets more and more repetitive. For instance, I was able to notice patterns of block and crate placement, it seems to use not a truely randomized level design but something more akin to Spelunky HD's level system where large blocks of content are randomly mixed together. And while that made sense in that game, it makes less sense here because you can dig, so there's no reason that I can see to have the same exact configurations of enemies and crates over and over again (e.g. the big blowfish with the left/right create right above it, or the enemy that turns tiles purple and dangerous is almost always next to a grenade create 1 tile to the right and above it; maybe most people won't notice these patterns, but to me they were distracting and took away from the immersion, because I could sort of see the algorithms by which the levels were put together).
What I'd really like to see is a sequel to this game which fixes all the GUI and other problems I mentioned, upgrades the graphics, and adds a greater variety of enemies, crates, maybe gives the drill some more options to fight off enemies, etc. -- overall this sort of felt like an amazing but flawed beta for a game rather than a finished game, I think a few more months testing and ironing out the rough spots would have done wonders (and I know it's difficult to find playtesters prior to release, but if all else fails they can be hired on Fiverr, I have a Fiverr there for playtesting games that very few people take advantage of).
Note: I got this game for free from the developer, who is a fellow indie game developer friend (but that didn't stop my criticism of the game haha, as you can see).

A lovely addition to the truck sim family to follow up Euro Truck Sim 2, which I also thoroughly enjoyed. It's great seeing the new game assets that are entirely different to those in ETS2 - new trucks obviously, but also a large range of new vehicles, new scenery props, new architecture, new road designs - and some fun things that enhance the ambience like helicopters, jets, shooting stars and flocking birds. There are some new mechanics too, including police cars that tag you with flashing lights and sirens when you get a fine for speeding/crossing red lights.
The company extensively researches truck sounds and handling to give you a more genuine experience when driving the trucks, and they spend an inordinate amount of time getting the locations looking like their real-world counterparts (within the limits of the game), which is all very nice (and you can see side-by-side comparisons with Google Street View shots) - but the main reason I enjoy it is that it's just so damned relaxing. If you're looking for a serious, hard core driving sim with realistc crash physics, go play something else - this isn't that game. This is a casual game about driving a big truck around, taking in the scenery, listening to some music, and gradually building your trucking empire.

Coming from Euro Truck, I pretty much knew what I was going to get. Gameplay was going to be pretty much the same with some new and improved visuals to go with it. Which is ok, because the basics didn't really need fixing.
There are things that make it stand out though. SCS improved city modelling the ETS2 Scandinavia DLC by quite a bit, but what's in here is another step up. Even though everything is scaled down by quite a lot, you still have the feeling you can drive through a big sizable urban area instead of a few roads on the outskirts that ETS2 gave you. And the detail is pretty damn impressive as well. Waiting for the lights, I could now actually look into some of the shops through the reflective windows. A far cry from the old flat facades. And the cost of all this additional graphics? Nothing! In fact, I think I'm getting higher FPS in ATS than I do in ETS2.
Another very welcome addition in ATS is having a choice of parking. You can now opt for putting the trailer in more difficult spots, which occasionally requires quite a bit of effort.
So is it all perfect?
Nah, it has its issues. The AI vehicles can behave a bit weird at times. I've had quite a few incidents with AI cars turning right on red when it wasn't safe to do so. There are also quite a few smaller issues with map and definitions. But if SCS continue to improve the game over the coming years, like they do with ETS2, then that stuff will be sorted out soon enough. I'm also not too fond of the overuse of some standard road structures. The stacked interchange looking junctions with standard clover leaf ones underneath really annoyed me. I hope this is just there to have something to change over time.
Which leaves the big topic of the amount of content. Due to the scale factor, the map doesn't really feel that big. If the three states that will eventually be included with the base game would be the only thing ever released, then you would probably have seen everything in about 30 hours. Which is not bad for a 20 Euro/dollar game. But it's quite obvious that the scale is meant to have a full map of North America in it. Driving from LA to Boston would keep you busy for quite some time and really give you that feeling of having done an epic journey.
The two trucks are also a bit limited. Especially since they are very much alike. Hopefully the licensing deals will come through quickly so there will be a bit more variety.
Since I play ATS on Linux/OpenGL, a few words on that. Performance is very good. In fact, I haven't seen any frame drops that I've heard mentioned by Windows/DirectX. My GTX650 Ti BOOST gives me pretty much 60 fps all the way providing I keep scaling at 100%. There are still plenty of Linux specific issues that are identical to those in ETS2. I can't run 1920x1200 fullscreen and 1920x1080 won't properly switch to fullscreen unless I alt-tab out and back in. This seems to be specific to Ubuntu. Also getting Force Feedback to work on wheels requires drivers that aren't in standard systems yet (not the fault of SCS of course). But even if you get those new drivers, it feels a bit flaky and requires setting the level way down. Not too surprising since the support was probably based on a best guess. I still had a lot of fun with a G920 wheel though.
So is this recommended? Absolutely! As long as you realize that this just the start of something bigger. I look forward to getting the new map extension DLCs and expanding the trucking world. And if ETS2 is any indication, the modding scene should explode quickly. I expect it to be an awesome ride.

If you're into any kind of relaxing type simulation, be it flying, buses, trains, tractors or just cruzing around in cars, you must have a look at American Truck Sim.   The developers (SCS) are not new at this, and with the success of Euro Truck Simulator 2 (and many previous trucking titles) they've raised the bar once more here with a great level of eye catching details in the world around you as you drive through the countryside.

Expeditions: Conquistador is a turn-based tactical crpg set in the early years of spanish colonization of the Americas.
Visuals are decent, nothing too fancy. It looks okay from afar while still acceptable from close-range. Battle units look good with easily distinguishable appearance. An extensive amount of bloom applied at some places, especially in towns which looks awful. It can be turned off, but other areas will look rather bland if done so. Also, most of the map consists of forests and places with vast foliage and the view is getting obstructed too often by objects. Some sort of transparency or alternate view would have been good.
The game itself features various South American locales. You are some rich kid who set sails to conquer the new world but soon realizes that there are already people who control places where you do not have as much influence as you hoped for. There are tribes to handle and deserters to slain. The options available during quests and various encounters are similar to those seen in old crpgs like Wasteland or Fallout, however much simpler. It is still nice to read background stories about your people who you picked by hand at the start or settle disagreements via diplomacy instead of violence. It feels disjointed and without proper consequences at times, but gives the game the illusion of choice a bit.
Gameplay is pretty much Heroes of M&M with a few extras like survival aspects and without the extensive kingdom-building. There are towns where quests can be taken. You have unique people with classes whom can be leveled up with the gained experience. Classes are soldier, scout, hunter, doctor, scholar. Each of them has their own use both on and off the field. The survival part means that turns become days and camping is important for survival. You have to assign people to hunt, patrol, guard, tinker or preserve materials. The system is simple with exact numbers, however the randomization can be quite frustrating. You can lose stuff during the night because of one bad 'dice-roll'. You can save anytime while being on the world-map, but there are a few encounters which happen no matter what you do, even moving to a safer place and having 90% of guard at night result in theft. And these are not even the story related 'hard-coded' events. The game screws you over from time to time no matter what you do. World-movement is also pretty clunky. The game automatically sticks to the road - because it is faster I presume - but if I run out of steps on a path I will have a big chance that I get robbed during the night. I constantly have to move away from the road which sometimes really hard to do due to movement and camera restrictions. And the camera is really restricted. No proper zooming, so you can only see things around you. Also, camera is stuck into tree and other objects. After some time I started to constantly use the "vontrier" 'cheat', which detaches the camera and allows free spectating.
I am not a big fan of the overall system and I would not say that I am satisfied with combat either. It is turn-based with hex-movement. There are combat skills. Flanking is present. Everything seems to be in order at first glance, however right in the first battle I noticed that those percents which would show how likely is for a ranged attack to hit the target are pretty much useless. My archer with 72-76% hit chance missed 4 out of 7 shots, while my soldier missed only once out of 3 with his supbar 30-35% chance. I do not know if there is some kind of background balance, but the interface should show values that I can base my choices upon. This one thing makes the combat a frustrating mess. Melee attacks succeed all the time - though they can be blocked -, so it is easier to gank the hell out of the enemy with a few soldiers. Battles could be tedious after some time because there are not many type of units. Most of the time I fight against soldiers just like mine which is either boring or frustrating because even freaking fishermen look and fight like well-equipped soldiers. Even with higher level well-equipped units I did not feel more powerful. In one pre-determined situation my camp was attacked by rebels. I faced 10 of theirs but I could only use 6 of my 11 people as always. Unfairness once again comes to mind here and the game full of these unlogical punishments. Also, their hunters are much better than mine for some reason constantly hitting my troops while I never had the chance to use them properly due to the high miss rate. This just does not make any sense whatsoever. One more thing that I have to mention is how chaotic the battlefield is due to the absence of any kind of tactical view where I can see all the troops and movement tiles clearly. Foliage is ever-present on these maps thus it is really hard too see anything sometimes. Actions are also hard to make due to everything including troops, rocks, tents, etc. get in the way both visually and mechanically. It would be much if I would only have to select the tile where I want to perform an action instead searching a dozen of units for a clickable point.
The audio presented in the game is quite bland. Sound effects are repetitive and low quality. Ambient soundscapes are really plain. There are no voice-overs for dialogs. Music is good but repetitive. I feel that despite being a lower-budget title EC should have better assets as the ones featured in the game are pretty inconsistent and overall insufficient.
Content wise the game brings a fair-sized world to explore. There are two campaigns available. Decent amount of land can be covered. Repetition should be the main concern here as the filling is pretty much the same during the whole game.
The ideas implemented into Expeditions: Conquistador are rather mixed. There are really good parts of the game which should be developed further and worse which should be reworked from the ground up. The handling of units, questing, dialogs and basic combat is good. The randomization and unfairness the game hands out to the player is far from it. Being difficult is one thing but the constant punishment just makes the game frustrating which does not go well with the flawed controls and sometimes repetitive nature of the game.

The story line itself, story wise, is good. The developers clearly put alot of effort into it, unlike me typing this review, and even though its relatively short for someone like me who plays video games for the majority of there life, its long enough for the majority of the populous and the other things to do in albion (the name of the world) more than make up for the short story. To be honest i spent days on my first playthrough however i was very young at the time and after i completed it the first time i started to clear games quite quickly.
I love the games mechanics, the combat system is fun and not to hard to use but reasonably difficult to master. The magic isn't over powered whatsoever and the way you level yourself up gives you an amazing sense of achievement even if (like me) your completing the game for the quadrillionth time. They really balanced it perfectly but the glitches really give you an easy time if you chose to exploit them.
Now the bugs. The game is solid most of the time and it has a few loading problems every now and then but overall i don't take much notice to that. But the thing they really ♥♥♥♥ up on is the hero save system.
Now if you have ever played fable before for longer than one playthrough you would have realized how bugged the herosave system is. Basically if your in the middle of a quest you cant save the game normally, you can only transfer your current hero to a previous save file as to not waste all the time you spent grinding experience in the current quest. however herosaving also transfers items...
If you don't see the problem here I'm kinda surprised. By going into a quest and picking up an item of value and then herosaving to before you started the quest you can get infinite of that item. But don't get me wrong, i love this glitch, you can complete the game then herosave to before your first ever quest and complete it again with an over powered character and one shot all the bosses ;D
Basically the only "gamebreaking" glitch in the game makes it better and most fans were horrified when they realized the remake had removed it.
Its a solid game good gameplay good leveling system and good story. I have no problem with anything in the game except the aging system and as long as you don't abuse the herosave system that doesn't effect you to much anyway.
Good luck fighting the final boss on your first run though. xD

This game is pretty fun and I do enjoy it, although like a lot of indie titles it does have some annoying quirks.
The setting is very unique and the game does not push you towards certain moral choices. You can be as altruistic or selfish as you wish. The game is also unique in that when you lose a battle the game doesn't end; it incorporates the defeat into the plot/questline, although the repercussions of that defeat may make the game next to unwinnable in a chain reaction of bad consequences. Each rock you trip over makes the next rock harder to get over. Expeditions: Conquistador is very difficult (I feel that some missions are virtually unwinnable) and very rewarding when you accomplish a difficult mission. It feels very similar to the XCOM reboot with a historical twist.
This game is utterly punishing in some of its RNG events.  Alligator bites your soldier in a random event. Soldier can't guard camp at night. Camp gets raided. RNG your troops have to fight off attackers with only knives while outnumbered. You lose battle, doctor killed, other party members injured. Doctor can't heal party members post-battle, so most injured party members die from infection. Load last save.
The leveling system is a bit flat. The classes gain fixed activated abilities and combat stat boosts as they level up with a list of passives to choose from, some of which seem next to useless while others are clearly superior.
The combat can get somewhat tedious. When your 6 soldiers are facing 8-18 enemies with no form of fast-forwarding the opponent's turn, the battles really start to drag.
Some parts of the game are opaque. Native units have some abilities that I'm completely unfamiliar with (that guy cursed my guy...what does cursed do?). One unit can reduce the defense of one opponent by 10, but on your units defence is rated in % damage reduction. Should that be 10%? Another ability allows the unit to ignore 7 points of armor on opponents, but you don't know how much armor opponents have (or if some opponents lack armor), so it's very difficult to see the effect.
Don't let the less polished parts scare you off, I'm glad that I purchased the game and look forward to wrapping up the campaign.

First off for the people like myself that like to play PC games with a Xbox Controller this game isn't compatible, but it isn't needed the controls are as simple as can be. Point the mouse in the direction you want the ball to travel hold down the right mouse button and move the mouse forward or backwards for power to hit the ball. This a mini golf type game the difference is all players take their turns at the same time. This causes mayhem and hillarious situations at time especially if ball collision is enabled.

Custom ball mechanics (low gravity, bouncy surfaces, Misc ball shapes and sizes, ect.)
Custom ball Colors
up to 12 players at the same time online

Murdered: Soul Suspect is actually a really good game. Okay, maybe that's an overstatement, but I really enjoyed it's approach to detective work and solving the mystery of your own murder as well as the recent string of murders in Salem in a single night.
You play Ronan O'Connor, a former petty criminal/turned detective who is hot on the trail of the Bell Killer, only the opening cutscene is your own death. The game picks up right from there as you search for clues and get used to being a ghost. The devs handled the ghost mechanics rather well as far as being unable to walk into buildings from the outside unless there's an open doorway or window. But you can move through walls, bushes, benches, etc.
The story is really intriguing and it seemed like it was going to be predictable, but I was wrong. I didn't know who the killer was from the get go. So, I tip my hat to the devs for pulling a decent M Night Shamalamadingdong. Sound design is eerie, as it should be. Unnamed NPC's that walk around Salem that you can possess, well, a lot of them looked the same and had the same responses when reading their minds, that bugged me. And for being an open world town, it seemed more restricted than anything because of the ghost walls that you can't pass through. It just made the town section of the game seem a lot more linear, but like a maze.
The graphics were decent enough, but it's clear that the game was held back due to last gen consoles. I mean, some of the modeling and textures look like games from 2010.
The mystery work was a lot of fun though, searching for clues and whatnot. Good game.

Do not install this game and, if you have already, follow the instructions below - this game installs a rootkit named "Hackshield" which most people would not want hanging around on their machine.
Removal Instructions:
WARNING: You should uninstall ArcheAge and Glyph before removing HackShield. While it is possible for the game to function without HackShield being enabled, you are guaranteed to become reinfected by it, since it will eventually reinstall itself in an ArcheAge or Glyph update.
Note: People using a 32-bit operating system will see a slightly different file, but the instructions remain the same.
Windows 8.1:
1. Right-click on your start button and select the "Run" (without quotes) option.
2. When you see the run dialog, type "regedit" (without quotes) and hit enter.
3. Using the tree-view in the left pane, navigate through the following folders: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE -> System -> CurrentControlSet -> Services
4. In the left pane you want to locate a folder called "XEagle64" (without quotes). Right-click on this folder and select the delete option. (May show up as "EagleX64" instead)
5. Reboot your computer.
The Hackshield service is now uninstalled and the included system driver should not run unless you try playing ArcheAge again.
Windows7:
1. Open your start menu and type "devmgmt.msc" (without quotes) into the search and hit enter.
2. On the top of this window you will see a menu entry called "View". Open this entry and select "Show hidden devices".
3. Navigate to the Non-Plug and Play section of devices.
4. Locate "XEagle64" then right-click and uninstall it. (May show up as "EagleX64" instead)
5. Reboot your computer.
The Hackshield service is now uninstalled and the included system driver should not run unless you try playing ArcheAge again.

Since it's a modern JRPG, expect at least some grind, terribly cheesy characters, a weak depiction of war, and some uncomfortable cultural gaps. I expected that, so I'm not going to criticize it, but my negative review is based on the following:
1. Combat rankings. Post-battle, you receive a rating and it's respective reward, which comprises the majority of what you need to progress in the game, especially without extra grinding. Story missions are non-repeatable, so while it isn't vital you get a high rating, it will save you a lot of time and sanity if you do well here. Unfortunately, these ratings are entirely based on how few turns you can complete the mission. This wouldn't be so much of a problem if game balance wasn't completely lopsided and scouts werent the final word in achieving high ranks in basically every mission. You buff up your scout, speedrun to the end, on to the next chapter. Terrible design decision.
2. Cutscenes. This game is 90% cutscenes, especially when actual gameplay is around <10 minutes of speedrunning as a scout. It's one thing that they're painful to watch, even for JRPG standards, but a chapter consists of 7-8 cutscenes, all with loads between every one of them, and then another several cutscenes for the actual mission. For how many cutscenes there are, you'd hope gameplay would be more fulfilling, but it really isn't that special.
3. Requires omniscience. I've pretty much restarted every mission, even the ones where I've won with no casualties, mostly because of the ranking system, but also because of how vital it is to know where things are in advance. While intel is important in any strategy game, here, you are briefed in the most unrealistically uninformative way possible, giving you no idea of what is to come or what to expect. Even for missions where you SHOULD know according to the plot, you have no idea, because the game is showering you in cutscenes and platitudes. Worse, the overhead map in deployment modes doesn't show obvious terrain features to give you a good idea of where to place units. You might end up placing a sniper in a gulch rather than a hill simply because the map isnt topographical. After deployment, the map is just as awful, poorly conveying LOS, and forcing you to spend CP simply to see if the giant pile of debris infront of your troops is high enough to be a barricade or just some flattened bricks. Simply start the mission, suicide-run your scouts through the map, then restart. Or maybe check out the notorious chapter 7 mission, and see how it's all about abusing script triggers, pre-defined enemy movements (wow, am I playing a tower defense?) and predictable spawn positions.
4. Frustrating RNG early on. Want those high rankings? Good luck when not even your snipers can hit the ground underneath them. Every weapon has a firing cone where the shot may spray, so your best bet is still to rush and shoot in CQC. Of course, you can save scum your way through, but it drains the fun out of the game to either play dirty or be robbed. Later on, you unlock more upgrades and weapons which alleviates this problem, but it doesn't feel like skill or tactics has much to do with anything.

Definitely a game worth checking out. Why? Read on.
The aesthetics of the game are borderline peerless, with every tank, character & class looking visually distinct from one another in what must be one of the most consistent pieces of art in the gaming space. It perfectly fits the motif of the games pretty unique setting, which is loosely based on the events of World War II, with its own fictional supernatural sprinkle on top. It's an interesting mix that thankfully treats the events of the War with the utmost respect, while also inviting us into it's wonderful & scary world in a relaxed manner.
The characters are mostly great, with Welkin & Alicia's relationship surely going down as one of the greatest & most believable in the history of video games. A few of the villains are a tad predictable, and a lot of the minor characters are done to extremes (Jann & Leon being good examples of this), but they're for the most part ignorable, and do not detract too much from the overall enjoyment of the game. Sadly, the voice acting is nothing special, but the audio design as a whole really is top notch, and ties in perfectly with the games beautiful, unique style.
Regarding the gameplay, combat is a bit hit and miss. It's overly simple & easily exploited, with a ranking system that makes little sense but still remains important, and minor issues like the odd invisible wall that bullets cannot penetrate, and tiny lips and dips that can foil the movement of a ten tonne battle tank. There are a couple of high quality combat mods that are supposed to be worth checking out, and while I can't comment on those personally, I'd definitely recommend checking them out if you have the time.
Overall, as a lovingly crafted tactical JRPG, Valkyria Chronicles has a lot going for it, but there's also quite a lot to overcome if you're wanting to see it through to the very end. Very much worth your time, though!

I cannot believe the rating this game has on Steam. This is a fantastic experience revolving around being an Airship captain and the martial and economic responsibilities that go along with such a position. If you want a game about airships where you just shoot everyone go play Guns Of Icarus. If you want a game that actually tries to simulate a world where such technology exists but must be maintained by an infrastructure of production much the same way Eve Online is laid out then this is the game for you.
Unlike Eve, there is no subscription fee, and everyone gets ‘paid’ in premium currency just for being logged in. There is no pressure to ‘pay to play’ nor is there an extended and indefinite assault on ‘noobs’ for not having the same in-game qualification as someone who has been playing longer than they have. You are actually free to take up a career as a pure trader who plays the market to their advantage – and there are plenty of opportunities to do so. You can actually make a pretty penny by speculating on the value of currency!
This is a game where traveling across the world takes a realistic amount of time. This game has more in common with a naval warship simulator than it does with some arcadey crap like Elite: Dangerous. It takes several REAL minutes to adjust your altitude to meet threats, and not a world where a simple dive or climb or some usage of a power-up that lets you magically achieve the perfect tactical position just because you decided to equip it. You need to think and plan what you are going to do, otherwise you do not succeed.
In light of this, it is still a game that one can pick up in less than an hour, and it is quite rewarding knowing that everything in the game except for certain goods which are exclusively traded by npcs – consumer goods and the starter ship, if you’re wondering – is produced by other people. When you buy and exchange ‘gold’ you are injecting a premium currency that isn’t just extra money and experience points for YOU, but rather a valuable resource which is necessary for the advancement of all pilots. Put another way, when you get premium time in, say, Mech Warrior Online the only person who will ever be effected by this is YOU. In LuckCatchers, that gold is an integral part of everyone’s growth and not just your own. It is a real thing that exists, and depending on your acumen, you can accrue quite a bit without spending your own money – the caveat is you actually have to do something useful for someone in order to get paid.
And now we come to why this game has such a poor user satisfaction rate. Look at all the people rating it down – 0.1 hours play time, too ignorant to read the tutorial which pops up as soon as you open the game. Too ignorant to tolerate a game whose developers don't speak the same language as they do but nevertheless try their damndest to help. In all honesty, these people are a bunch of illiterate ♥♥♥♥s who close every window that pops up and then pretend the game has no tutorial. These are the same idiots who give crap like Rome II a 10/10 because it has Romans in it and they’re cool, yo.
This is a thinking man’s MMO and a poor man’s MMO in the best possible way – those who cannot afford premium currency can get it off of those who can simply by helping them produce things that every player needs. Also, again, the developers give you premium currency just by being logged in. what, in the name of all that exists, is not to like about this game?
