With the huge success of Euro Truck Simulator 2, I made the critical decision of buying this game. In this review I will tell you why I hesitated, as well as good and bad things about the game.
I initially hesitated to buy the game because it literally looked like a clone of Euro Truck Simulator 2, as if America was supposed to be a DLC, not it's own game. Despite this, I still bought it to give it the benefit of the doubt.
The game graphics are fantastic and the roads feel slightly wider, making it rather easier to turn. If you played Euro Truck Simulator 2, you know how narrow European roads are!
I love this feature, for some reason. You can turn right on a red signal! I know it's small but it's a traffic law that was ignored in Euro Truck Simuator 2. How many times have you been stuck at a red light, wanting to turn right and there are NO cars coming and you just want to go?
You can also discover cities without actually entering them! A few basic routes fall right on a road leading to cities and you can discover them without actually entering the city.
The speedtraps in this game are very difficult to manage. Speeds on roads will drop very suddenly without warning, causing speeding tickets. The AI usually slam on the brakes so fast that it's easy to rear-end people.
The UI in this game is exactly the same. From the main screen to your navigator, they didn't change anything except a few minor tweaks. They also changed a few icons on your map. I personally think this should've been looked into a little more, considering you're paying for a new game, it should have something different about it!
Only two trucks exist in the game right now, Peterbilt 579 and Kenworth T680. SCS has a reasonable excuse for this, because they need to have legal rights to these brands in order to release them in the game. They are definitely going to release more brands, it's only a matter of time! I'm excited to see how the Kenworth T900 will turn out, that truck is a beauty!
There are only 2 states to start, California and Nevada. Arizona is expected to be released as free DLC, but how many states will be released as free DLC before SCS decides to release a DLC that you need to pay for?
You can now park your vehicles in multiple different spaces to increase your XP gains for parking. I think this is a good adaptation for those who are NOT good at parking trailers and those who are good.
-----------------------------------
A few things I wish the game had:
1. Driving School - I think adding a driving school would be a better way instead of a "Tutorial".
2. Real Cops - The game would feel much more immersive if you actually needed to pull-over in order to receive a ticket, and you would be penalized more if you didn't pull over.
-----------------------------------------------------------
Would I recommend this game?
Personally I would recommend this game, but if you are not one to wait for new content to be released, I would recommend waiting to buy the game until more DLC is released.

This is truly a hidden gem.
Initially, the $10.99 ($9.89 on sale) price tag seemed a bit steep for what the screenshots and description showed.
But I gave it a chance, and I'm glad I did.
If you're familiar with any sort of 'digging' game, where you start at the top and dig your way to the bottom, this will feel familiar. There's lots of features that you can unlock, in order to directly boost your drill.
Initially, the game seemed pretty simple and straightforward (for the first area.) But once you unlock more comets/planets/etc, you'll find that each of them is a bit different. They can have monsters, or other factors that make that planet harder to drill on. (The first planet doesn't give you any sort of time constraints, but once you progress to others, time becomes a factor, so you have to make quick decisions to min-max your drill run.)
There's a lot of repetition, but only in the sense of "you're bettering yourself with each attempt." There's always something to unlock and strive for. (That actually feels worth getting!)
I hit the 110 minute mark, and didn't think twice about continuing past 2 hours. It's a lot of fun, and you'll definitely get plenty of value for it.

Velvet Sundown is a game of great potential, but only being in Alpha stage makes the potential very hard to believe.
A game where straight-forward communication to achieve your goals is a challenge in itself, considering communication in online game is as it is right now. But it's remarkably fun in it's challenge; encouraging roleplaying, opening doors for trickery and deceit, and building alliances and rivalries. You get to play a variety of characters, each with the main objective everyone has, as well as a side objective that doesn't really have much of a point, in that it helps with roleplay and gives the player something to do.
It's gameplay falls short. The premise is wonderful, but the movement is stiff and robotic, using the arrow keys with delayed turns, or using the mouse to look with extremely high mouse sensitivity (at least in my opinion). Talking to people, giving/using items, and interaction is pretty straightforward though, but that's about all the game has to offer. Talking to people is another section of this review in itself, being the core of the game
The look of the game isn't anything remarkable. Your characters look like dolls though, staring into an endless void infront of them, and jerking around, and looking sexy while doing it. The animations are pretty hilarious, considering the lack of props, expression, and exaggeration that's really needed. The only level you can really play is the ship the game is named after, which isn't surprising, and it's not all that bad. The ship though doesn't have much in terms of level design, with most people meeting in one general area. The game encourages you secretly talk to others in other parts of the ship, which works fairly interesting, considering you can eavesdrop and even just simply walk into a conversation without actually being a part of it.
The game has a strange soundtrack of way it's presented. With every action you do, the game shows off a cheap cutscene along with a small track. The soundtrack is not memorable in the slightest, with the outer ship having a rather unfitting score, but the inner ship having 2 fitting, but rather stock-sounding loops. Hilariously, whether you lose or win the game, the soundtrack for the end cutscene (which just shows your characters gorgeously textured face) is always triumphant.
Let's get into the core of the gameplay though, the communication. But I'll have to point out something that just makes the game fall apart: The community. Playing an actual game, including the roleplay and cooperation that's needed, is near impossible without trolls, or AFKers. the game largely depends on players PLAYING the game, and if 2 or more people are afk, the game will continue until the time limit, and you'll have absolutely nothing to do but leave yourself. The trolls though, are something else. In a game where communication is key, the trolls have the high ground and will control the situation. You just can't help but humor them until they give you what they want. This can range from just being out of character, to simply asking to cyber for teh lulz. But aside from the community though, the communication can be hilarious, since it's all text to speech. I found it rather remarkable though, that each character has a different voice, but it hardly matters due to the utter insanity of accuracy the text to speech implementation is. It is extremely hard to be immersed in such a game, when you or the players mispell, or speak as simply as possible. The Text to Speech can be turned off, but makes the game rather boring to be honest.
Lastly, let me discuss about the online experience itself. It's trashy. My experience was a lot of lag dealing with speaking with people, usually regarding the timing to saying something before someone leaves or enters a convo, but also with trying to give items to players. Also the lag may have to do with why players enter a game afk. Another thing that rather sucks about the online experience, is the lack of lobbies. The players will simply choose a 'story/mission', and wait until a game starts, but by no means do you enter a lobby with who you're playing with, nor will you ever find out until the end of the mission. I can understand why this would be done, since playing with strangers is the aim here. But lobbies can help configure players who are actually active, and those who are only idle. The players will instead instantly join a game with whoever signed on, and have to work with them. I actually ended up in a game where only 2 other players were active, and we left within minutes. During this period though, you have to wait until the game ends, or it'll reconnect you back into the already broken game.
All in all, TL;DR, my 2 cents, the game is still in Alpha, still has issues, but the designers have something going on, and I like it. The stiff gameplay and the community sucks, but the thrill of being immersed and roleplaying make it bearable. The game isn't very replayable though, so don't expect to play for several hours... at least until the map changes after a week.
I would recommend this game, but tread lightly, and play patiently. You'll end up playing an actual game, and it's rather satisfying.

E:C has elements from some of my favourite games; Party skills like Mount & Blade, role-playing like Baldur's Gate and turn-based combat like X-Com. There's a variety of traps to use in combat, but you can't place them very far and they take up slots that can be used for cannonballs and the like. Every character including the player has 6 skills, but especially on party members these don't seem to help much.
The absolute worst part of the game is camping. First you have to make sure to not camp on the road so you won't get robbed. Then you have to distribute food in a poorly designed menu with buttons that don't always respond when clicked. There's a handful of tasks but most of them have little effect on the game. I harbored no illusions about what it meant for us to explore the New World. Exploration is first and foremost a conquerer's act - over nature herself, if not the natives who inevitably resist the tides of change. I was a soldier, with senses long inured to the stench of blood, and I chose my companions accordingly. I needed grim warriors. None pious. We were not missionaries. I wanted the aggressive sorts, those fueled by bloodlust and goldlust. Nevermind I found their racism and greed distasteful. They were exactly what would be necessary in the heart of the jungle.
My choices proved apt, as Mexico was as treacherous as I feared. In those wild lands, we were alone. My predecessor, a man commanding a force of hundreds, had come here and vanished. He had made mistakes. I knew I could afford none.
When my servants rebelled, I slew them to a man. I would not have them slitting our throats as we slept. After defeating a native patrol, I might have spared them. These young men and women were only defending their lands from strangers in shining armor. I left none alive, none to report back to their village about our arms, numbers, and tactics.
Again and again, I had to face the hard choice between surrendering my tactical advantage and attempting a diplomatic solution. Always I chose to strike swiftly and decisively. Yes I killed where peace might have availed me. But what if it had not? What if those peaceful overtures had led to ambush? I had a duty to my soldiers. They looked to me to keep them alive. That is what I did.
Yet the land soon began to work its magic on me. There was a vivacity here that could not be found in Spain's stone streets. The people possessed an earthly wisdom and a refreshingly naive curiosity. Many welcomed us openly, asking about our ways and our lands. They were, it turns out, not so different from us, finding joy in a good meal and a bountiful harvest.
We found common ground with the Totonac peoples, and sided with them in their rebellion against the Aztecs, true barbarians whose temples ran slick with the blood of pagan sacrifice. I allowed the Totonac Chieftain's teenage daughter, Anacaona, into my group to serve as translator. She stayed by my side throughout. I taught her to wield sword, spear, and musket. I shared our language and our ways. She was ever eager to listen to my stories, and each night as we camped in the swamps and jungles, I told her of past battles. Her eyes shone with the fires of these remembered glories, and a hope for her own.
Of all of us, she was the truest and best adventurer. It was she who translated the glyphs on a golden gateway and led us into the legendary El Dorado, that shining City of Gold. It was she who manuevered through the temple of death's diabolical traps, braving a pit of snakes to uncover mounds of treasure. Without her, we would never have found the Fountain of Eternal Youth, which spring must have originated in Heaven itself.
Ah, Anacaona. She became the daughter I had always wanted.
It must have broke her heart when, following our triumphant battle over the Aztec Empire, I turned on her father and slew him in the same garden I had killed the Emperor. I know it broke mine when she chose him over me.
I buried her with mine own hands, outside Tenochtitlan, its plundered temples and palaces alit with devilish infernos.
I had been given a duty and an obligation, and I had fulfilled it to my utmost. I returned home with every companion but she still alive. Our ship held such treasure that it bobbed low in the water, our hold bursting with plundered gems. The king welcomed me home a hero, bestowing upon me lands and titles. My ambitions fulfilled.
Yet as I sit on my estate, watching the sun plunge beneath my tamed fields, I discover that somewhere along the way, my ambitions had changed. The jungle had transmuted them. The glory, the riches, the titles: all hollow now. I would give them all in order to go back and make a different decision. To choose the path of peace, so that Anacaona might have lived.
As a child, I thought the title Conquistador a grand one and never imagined I would hold it. As an old man, I carry it with a heavy heart. I will take it with me to the grave. Murderer. Betrayer. Conquistador.

One part Oregon Trail, one part XCOM: Enemy Unknown, and one part decision-based narrative RPG, Expeditions Conquistador is an intriguing mix of genres in a unique setting understandably avoided by both game and film media. You play as a conquistador in 16th century Hispaniola then Mexico with the power to be either an oppressive, slaving, genocidal warmongerer or an easy-going humanitarian.
You begin by selecting a backstory and a retinue of party members with different attributes and attitudes chosen from multiple classes. Each of these potential compatriots has a well-developed backstory which emerges throughout the game and informs or explains their attitudes to the world around them. Depending on these attitudes and the dialogue-based decisions you make throughout the game, party members may follow you to the ends of the Earth or grow to hate you. Gentle and humanitarian characters will not like your genocidal warmongerering ways, after all.
Most of the game is spent on a strategic map. As an explorer, you choose where to go on these fairly large maps which take dozens of turns to traverse, Along the way, you pitch camp every night, deciding on the allocation of limited resources such as food, medicine, and manpower for scouting, defending, and forging.
The turn-based squad combat resembles XCOM: Enemy Unknown's cover and dice-roll based system but with pikes and arquebuses on maps depicting open-pit mines, Mayan ruins, or other areas expected of the time and place. As would be expected in a party-based RPG, you can change weapons and allocate experience points to your party members and each class has unique abilities. Combat is challenging and the strategic use of abilities and flanking is necessary for victory.
Despite the unique setting and mix of successfully implemented borrowings from other games, Expeditions Conquistador does wear its welcome and feels repetitive after a few hours. The historical setting likely inhibited the developers from introducing exciting mid and end game enemies and mechanics that would be possible in a Wasteland or Baldur's Gate.  Enemies are obviously always humans and while you do fight against both American Indians and Spanish, the expected different feel of fighting two vastly different cultures with different armaments never materializes. The decision-making is shallow because it is not nuanced; it is always very obvious when you are going down the path of oppressor or humanitarian.
Overall, Expeditions Conquistador is an intriguing game worth checking out if you are a fan of squad-based tactical RPGs and interested in the Spanish Conquest of the Americas. Let your inner Cortez or Pizarro reign free for at least a few hours, as long as you can find this game on sale.

The endgame content is rather braindead & trivial, making there to be no difficulty whatsoever. You'll be grinding the "Warframes", basically your characters. While a majority of these are simple to get, the game punishes you for not picking Excalibur at the beginning. If you want to ever obtain Excalibur, you need to do very annoying & extensive farming that is there to make it difficult (which was there intention, but it just turns out to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.) This also applies Warframes like "Mesa", "Octavia". For example, in order to get a chance at Mesa, you need to sit in the same couple missions over and over mindlessly killing the same enemies type till you finally got the parts for one key (lol, just one), and that's just a chance to get one part. The real struggle comes in when you finally get 2 parts of the Warframe (remember, it's just a chance to get a part of the Warframe (let me explain - you need a Helmet, Chestpiece, and Systems to make it easy), and the parts have ABOUT equal drop rates. When you are farming Octavia, it's pretty simple... except for one part. Keep in mind you can purchase these Warframes in full form with the premium currency, platinum.

I would like to preface this by saying there are a number of optimisation issues that are causing some users to experience low framerates (below 30 FPS) and some graphical glitching. NISA are aware of the problem and are trying to fix the issues, but please be aware that until it is fixed, you may experience some issues. EDIT 06/03/2016 - NISA have released a number of patches that seemed to have fixed most of the issues. There may be a few remaining minor issues, but the major ones have been fixed.
The Good:
Its Disgaea on PC! While the story is pretty basic, the writing is very self-aware. The main story will take about 20 - 30 hours to complete the first time around, but the meat of the game lies within the Item World and the bonus bosses. The Item World is a series of random maps that are used to strengthen items. As you progress through the Item World of your chosen item, it will gain levels equal to the number of floors you have cleared, which will improve its stats. Something to keep in mind: the more powerful the item, the stronger the enemies are.
The Bad:
Its Disgaea 1 on PC! This is a port of the original Disgaea game, with the addons from the PSP port "Afternoon of Darkness", so the complaints are the same: Many bills in the Dark Assembly are locked until you reach a specific rank in the Dark Assembly. Some Item World maps can be unwinnable because the game creates sections of land too far apart. If you execute a series of actions, any unused actions cannot be undone (ie, if you attack an enemy with 5 characters and the third one kills that enemy, the last two characters will still be counted as having taken their action for that turn). Also keep in mind that when using a controller, the game will only offer prompts for generic buttons (ie Button 1 is accept, Button 2 is cancel)

Definitely a game worth checking out. Why? Read on.
The aesthetics of the game are borderline peerless, with every tank, character & class looking visually distinct from one another in what must be one of the most consistent pieces of art in the gaming space. It perfectly fits the motif of the games pretty unique setting, which is loosely based on the events of World War II, with its own fictional supernatural sprinkle on top. It's an interesting mix that thankfully treats the events of the War with the utmost respect, while also inviting us into it's wonderful & scary world in a relaxed manner.
The characters are mostly great, with Welkin & Alicia's relationship surely going down as one of the greatest & most believable in the history of video games. A few of the villains are a tad predictable, and a lot of the minor characters are done to extremes (Jann & Leon being good examples of this), but they're for the most part ignorable, and do not detract too much from the overall enjoyment of the game. Sadly, the voice acting is nothing special, but the audio design as a whole really is top notch, and ties in perfectly with the games beautiful, unique style.
Regarding the gameplay, combat is a bit hit and miss. It's overly simple & easily exploited, with a ranking system that makes little sense but still remains important, and minor issues like the odd invisible wall that bullets cannot penetrate, and tiny lips and dips that can foil the movement of a ten tonne battle tank. There are a couple of high quality combat mods that are supposed to be worth checking out, and while I can't comment on those personally, I'd definitely recommend checking them out if you have the time.
Overall, as a lovingly crafted tactical JRPG, Valkyria Chronicles has a lot going for it, but there's also quite a lot to overcome if you're wanting to see it through to the very end. Very much worth your time, though!

Firstly, I'd like to prefix this with stating that I'm a Founder (lowest tier), and racked up many hundreds of hours of play prior to  it being re-released on Steam.
This review is of the game as it is today, April 2015. I specify this because the launch of the game was pretty terrible, beating out D3 and UO's Malas opening as "worst launch I've ever experienced." The game is developed in Korea, and published here in the west by Trion, and up until 3 months ago it was absolutely an afterthought. Little consideration was given for the player base in any decision, and it seemed they were determined to milk it for every cent and then kill it.
There is now a new AA lead at Trion, and he seems to be doing a much better job - although there are still huge foul-ups, like the recent Dolphingate fiasco.
Trion are also obsessed with releasing Gambling Boxes.
That's the negative. The positive is that this is, quite simply, a great game. It's not as sandboxy as it might lead you to believe, but the term used to describe it is "Sandpark" - a themepark (i.e. EQ style) MMO with some sandbox options. The housing system, while not as good as that in UO or RIft, is decent and solid. I enjoy farming, fishing and trading, but my wife and I often go out fighting. The game has a HUGE open-world PVP component for those who like that, but it can usually be avoided completely by those who do not.
You must subscribe to place land or pay Land Taxes, but subscription can be bought in game for Apex (about 500g for the 2 required at present).
Try it free, you've nothing to lose but time. (And avoid the official forums. As with every game, you have nothing to lose there but faith in humanity!)

Heavily simplified civ game
Ace patrol is about unit tactics.
In the campaign you start with four pilots as they face off their foes in World War one. You can customise your first pilot's voice and portrait who will go on the first mission. Each pilot command their own plane. As you progress through the game you can unlock new planes, which each have varying stats. Your pilots will also level up during the game. As they do you can select an ability for them to learn which varies between their movement during play. If you meet certain requirements, you can unlock perks for pilots after each mission which includes improving accuracy and defence. Each plane has a set amount of health. When your pilots get shot down, they remain unavailable in later missions until they are released. Injured pilots may also be unavailable in later missions as well. You get to choose different mission types in campaign:  defence and attack. In defence missions, you basically have to defend a certain building or units from being destroyed by the enemy. In attack missions, you need to bomb/destroy a particular building or unit. As you win one country's campaign you unlock another one (you start off with playing as the British)
Combat is turn based. You generally select your units and move them on the highlited pads. Certain pads may glow red, indicating that you will shoot at the enemy plane when you move there. You will be provided with the amount of damage you will do to the enemy plane. Furthermore, you can only shoot at plane from the front and to the side only, so you need to turn around if enmy planes are behind you.
There isn't much music to this game. The title screen music is like classical 'Civ' games, but there is no tracks during gameplay. Your pilots may say a few words, but they are forgettable anyway.
If you enjoy basic civ game which only focuses on unit combat then you may like this game. If your expecting a 'civilisation' game, you will DEFINATELY be dissapointed.

Summary.
A really fun game, that is also in places horribly designed and often a terrible experience to play.
Pros.
*Beautiful art style and a great soundtrack
*Really interesting concept and execution, seamlessly integrates RTS and FPS elements into a really enjoyable and replayable package, especially in the skirmishes.
Cons.
*A lame and predictable story
*No restart button and autosave means if you ever screw up, you're better off intentionally losing instead of returning to menu to try again
*Lack of explanation of a number of the exact numbers with given features (Such as auto dodge and the like) can leave you befuddled when a unit can dodge, from behind, multiple times in a row, perfect sniper rounds to their head.
*Easily exploitable mechanics that seem to be present solely for the purposes of exploits (Orders) which actually discourages actual squads of mixed units when one or two boosted units can do the missions much much easier and faster.
*Almost every story match has a mechanic that is not explained, and will be, often seemingly intentionally, completely contrary to the way the game has played up to that point, and will play from that point on, almost every time causing serious problems if not total wipeouts to your squad (IE, level 14's infinite spawning waves and the giant tank boilers in level 7 to name the two worst offenders of this).
Conclusion.
*Even though the game itself has a number of VERY large flaws, I'd still reccomend it, however for casual players I would HIGHLY reccomened at least skimming a summary of the unique battle mechanics for each fight before going into them. Even for less casual players, unless you wish to suffer at the hands of unexplained mechanics on an almost mission to mission basis in often unrealistic (In the scope of the fictional world created for the game) ways.

Other positives include:
A much improved skill system and more gear that grants abilities (no cast limits yet either).
Naturally, the music and VO are both great. The atmosphere of just Fort Joy so far is wonderful, really drives home the feeling that it's a ghetto/mass prison and torture facilty. The random humorous moments juxtapose the dread nicely as well.
A good balance of new and old skills. Can't wait to see some of the higher end stuff.
Looks great visually, and the character models and clothing are really well done. I really like that each model has unique clothing even when it's the same item. Makes me glad I started off with Sebille ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)
The only gripes I have so far are these:
The armor system is a bit meh tbh, I don't really care for it just yet, but we'll see how it goes further down the line. I like to think of it as simply an extension of the enemies health bars so it's not too bad. I went with a 50/50 magic/phys group so I'm pretty prepared for whatever comes along. I think.
Not being able to customize two characters stung a bit at first, but I quickly realized it ultimately doesn't matter since you can recruit any of the origin chracters to your party, with any specialization you want them to take up.
A few dirty release bugs that will likely be fixed in the coming days. The most notable I saw was global chat, while a wonderful idea, didn't work for me all night. Not surprising really, and doesn't detract from the experience.
Adding certain consumables to your bag automatically drops them onto your hot bar whether you want them there or not. I drop the bag directly onto the hot bar and access consumables from there, so it's pretty annoying to have to keep unlocking the bar to dump all the crap it put on there for me even though I didn't ask it to.
Overall though, so far so good, can't wait to not leave my seat for about 12 hours tomorrow while I see what kind of charms Rivellon has for me this time!
60 hour edit - Well so far I'm still only on act 3 of at least 4. Level 18, rolling through the game pretty easily at this point. My healer is largely useless since my tank can now amass over 4000 physical armor and has 8000 health, along with a 4000+ armor summon, so I'm basically a 5-man wrecking crew. Definitely a few bugs along the way, one crash to desktop around 40 hour or so, and some things I'd like to see changed, but all in all, still a very solid experience. Finished game edit: Borrowed this from a post I made on the discussion board, mostly griping.
I disagree with some aspects of the gameplay, especially some brokenly overpowered abilities (charm/madness causing your characters to waste valuable consumables etc), omniscient enemies in more ways than one, and very weird limitations on what is considered "out of line of sight" or "blocked." I also think stats could have been done better. I would have preferred things like leadership, perseverence, and retribution to be on a different point system ala OS1. Right now there is 0 reason to put actual points in, when attributes and skill points are vastly more useful, and gear only provides so much.
I don't really care for attributes or skill points giving flat bonuses either, as it simply encourages mass stacking of the most useful attribute. I also don't like the fact that some things, such as healing abilities, don't stack with intelligence, but with skill points. I feel like this is a limiting factor in some cases, especially late game, when I'm only healing 1900 health on a 14k health tank for example.
And then there's just good old fasioned technical problems like severe lag, in my case especially when trying to fly with the dragonling. 30 second freezes + game crashing from one ability is painful, and on an only moderately useful summons since only Red Prince can get it, and in my game was a tank with only 2 summoning from gear. Decent only as a 2-round meat shield if that.
That being said, I still enjoyed the hell out of it, and I still enjoyed it more than OS1. I wouldn't have played 90 hours of one campaign if I didn't, and I'm really looking forward to playing with Ifan and Beast this time around, and finishing all the quests. There were moments of shear frustration which I haven't experienced in a long time, but also quite a few triumphant moments too.

Geo
Released
Windybeard
Windybeard
Economic Simulation
31st of January, 2017
Single-player
What we have here is another clear example of an indie dev who’s sticking to the formula he already tried and tested. It’s the second 2D game in their case and I’d say that those 4 years of development hiatus between Sweezy Gunner and Geo have been time well spent. Luckly instead of another arcade shooter (of which Steam most certainly has its fair share already), in Geo we have a very interesting hybrid of multiple genres. It features elements from economic sims along with a sprinkle of casual arcades thrown in for good measure.
A rare case in which the actual screenshots don’t do a game justice. We’re more used to “doctored” footage and images on the Steam Store pages, which trick potential buyers nearly as efficient as those juicy burger ads which thoroughly disappoint, after you’ve unwrapped your next meal. Geo may not look any better or worse than the screenshots but its hidden complexity, surely cannot be described in words or pictures. Don’t let the drilling part with all those different tile shades convince you that the game is reduced to that singular and repetitive activity. Managing your interstellar drilling company is the better half of the game and that is most fortunate.
At a brief and superficial first look, I honestly thought that I’m being handed over for review another lazy clone of Candy Crush or Zuma (I’m far from being a fan of casual games in general) but I couldn’t have been more wrong. You don’t even start the actual drilling bit until you’ve set up shop, with a shiny and initially small HQ plus a couple of crazily cheap for hire (but mostly, just crazy) employees. The headquarters serve as both a base of operations and a research facility which will allow future upgrades to be implemented and thus, making your business ever more profitable. You will continuously expand both the building and the skilled team of workers under your command.  A balance between income and expenses serves as a natural restraint from becoming “overpowered” too fast. At least in the early stages of the game, grinding (or drilling, if you may) isn’t much of an issue.
You do have to keep an eye out for mining opportunities since that “O” from G.E.O. does stand for “Observe”. “Gather” and “Explore” do require a keen eye as well, not just quick reflexes and intuition. I’m also glad that there aren’t many obstacles to steer you from your path. The randomly generated exploration part most certainly guarantees a new perspective every time you play. No time limit either but your drill does have hitpoints which simulate the wear and tear level and the inevitable damage the machines sustain when piercing the many types of soil and materials found underground. Other than that, gameplay is pretty straightforward: aim for the trasure chests filled with goodies (coins and upgrade points). Luck will only get you so far. Familiarity with the aforementioned soil types will make the job easier and the shortest path towards the buried treasure may not also be ideal, if your drill explodes from too many pierced tiles made of metal. The main objective of any mining location, is to reach the core and collect its essential resources which ultimately fuel your business and subsequent HQ improvements via Geo’s upgrade tree, which is referred to as the “Coretrium”.
The graphics while not impressive by a long shot, are still pleasant enough but the sounds are a tad too repetitive for my tastes. The presence of a proper settings tab (along with options for resolution or effects) would be a welcome feature in a future update. Also a price drop won’t seem out of place. If you can overlook these shortcomings, you will be pleased by the gameplay itself and the inclusion of both Cards and Achievements.
+ Interesting concept and hybrid gameplay.
+ Adds humour into the mix.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards.
- Repetitive sounds.
- Slightly overpriced.
- Game progression is dependent on grinding after a certain point.

Windybeard, Windybeard ....hmmmm ah yes! The Developer of the cool SWEEZY GUNNER. I remember.
SWEEZY GUNNER was a cool Retro Shooter with many nice features and a special Graphic Style, a little bit like a comic.

Starting the Game it was like coming home to SWEEZY GUNNER, because it has the same graphic Style and if i`m not wrong has Characters from Sweezy Gunner. The shopowner in the game, can it be?
Anyway. The music sounds also similar and so i began to play. A little Robot was trying to tell me the facts and how to play and i was into action. Well, that is no shooter like SWEEZY GUNNER, that is ... something else.
How can i describe it, hmmm. In this Game you are the owner of a Space Mining Corporation. At the start you have nothing, absolutly nothing and it is your target to get everything, absolutly everything.
Okay, nothing is wrong, you have drills. This drills are your key to Fame and Glory and of course to Money. oh yes you also
have building where you can build special rooms into it, where you can hire peolple who raise the abilitys of your drill. All right. So i went to a star sector and clicked on an asteroid and the Graphics changed to a playfield. You are controlling a Drill, that looks a little bit like Dr. Snuggles Machine or the Drill from Jules Verne that moved to the Center of the Earth. Was it Jules Verne? Don`t remember, was an old movie. The playfield is full of squares and your Job is to move the Drill to the ground, deeper and deeper. Thats sounds easy of course, but isn`t.
Your drill has a lifebar that continuesly goes down. How fast depends on the obstacles that you have to master. The squares are different. Some go down fast, some go down slowly. But there are also many usefull sqares like treasure chests or Liferefueller and many more. One Kind of squares also bombs a big hole into the playfield, what very usefull is to get faster to the core. Later there will be monsters that will disturb you and when they hit you, your lifebar goes down faster, and here comes the bad news, your drill has no weapon systems. You have to avoid them but thats not easy, but possible. Also, the deeper you go, the more you are confronted with the inner core of the planet. Ice Planets get colder and colder and that effects your Drillhull. So, move fast and have an eye on the kind of squares and avoid hard ones.
If your Lifebar reaches zero your drill explode and you get points and gold for your going. You have infinity Drills, so don`t worry. Try again. The Goal is to reach the Core in each asteroid, planet and more to get special points that helps you raising your Mining Corporation. With the Gold you can buy usefull things and the more you upgrade your Drill the easier are you Mining Visits.
This game has tons of content. There is much to explore, much to find, much to upgrade, much to achieve. Like SWEEZY GUNNER there is really much to do and it is fun to explore the Star Systems and drilling on the Planets and Asteroids.
It is fun to explore secrets and upgrading your Homebase.

With the huge success of Euro Truck Simulator 2, I made the critical decision of buying this game. In this review I will tell you why I hesitated, as well as good and bad things about the game.
I initially hesitated to buy the game because it literally looked like a clone of Euro Truck Simulator 2, as if America was supposed to be a DLC, not it's own game. Despite this, I still bought it to give it the benefit of the doubt.
The game graphics are fantastic and the roads feel slightly wider, making it rather easier to turn. If you played Euro Truck Simulator 2, you know how narrow European roads are!
I love this feature, for some reason. You can turn right on a red signal! I know it's small but it's a traffic law that was ignored in Euro Truck Simuator 2. How many times have you been stuck at a red light, wanting to turn right and there are NO cars coming and you just want to go?
You can also discover cities without actually entering them! A few basic routes fall right on a road leading to cities and you can discover them without actually entering the city.
The speedtraps in this game are very difficult to manage. Speeds on roads will drop very suddenly without warning, causing speeding tickets. The AI usually slam on the brakes so fast that it's easy to rear-end people.
The UI in this game is exactly the same. From the main screen to your navigator, they didn't change anything except a few minor tweaks. They also changed a few icons on your map. I personally think this should've been looked into a little more, considering you're paying for a new game, it should have something different about it!
Only two trucks exist in the game right now, Peterbilt 579 and Kenworth T680. SCS has a reasonable excuse for this, because they need to have legal rights to these brands in order to release them in the game. They are definitely going to release more brands, it's only a matter of time! I'm excited to see how the Kenworth T900 will turn out, that truck is a beauty!
There are only 2 states to start, California and Nevada. Arizona is expected to be released as free DLC, but how many states will be released as free DLC before SCS decides to release a DLC that you need to pay for?
You can now park your vehicles in multiple different spaces to increase your XP gains for parking. I think this is a good adaptation for those who are NOT good at parking trailers and those who are good.
-----------------------------------
A few things I wish the game had:
1. Driving School - I think adding a driving school would be a better way instead of a "Tutorial".
2. Real Cops - The game would feel much more immersive if you actually needed to pull-over in order to receive a ticket, and you would be penalized more if you didn't pull over.
-----------------------------------------------------------
Would I recommend this game?
Personally I would recommend this game, but if you are not one to wait for new content to be released, I would recommend waiting to buy the game until more DLC is released.

Oh, Miranda. Oh, dear Miranda...
Mass Effect 2. You've had to have heard those words at least once in your gaming life. Whether if it was a Youtube video, or maybe just chatting with a friend. You had to have heard of this legendary title. Well, I'm here to say that Mass Effect 2 is EASILY one of the finest games of last generation.
I'll start with the visuals. I have to admit, the visuals in this game are still very impressive, even after nearly four years. If you are a friend of mine, you would probably notice that I frequently take screenshots of in-game stuff, usually something about it's beauty. Now, I've played numerous games that are really stunning, but I haven't taken this many screenshots for a game since Skyrim. I'm HIGHLY impressed with this game's graphics.
The gameplay is a very strong point in the game. Mass Effect 1 was more tactical and people didn't like that, along with squadmate abilities, some in-game choices, and more. However, Mass Effect 2's gameplay was much smoother, even if lots of ME1 RPG elements were taken out. The gunfights were heated and awesome. Choosing squadmates and using the abilities they have make the game have a slightly more strategic approach. However, when you could actually have an option to do something else. In one mission, one of my squadmates said that we could sneak past the enemies, but when I attempted to do so, there was no way of actually sneaking past them without triggering the alarm, thus making some missions pretty linear.
The story is a step down from the first Mass Effect and even the third Mass Effect. It goes completely off topic. But, there's a reason why I'm praising the game in the "story" section. It's simple. The lore in this game is INCREDIBLE. When you search planets for resources to survive missions, you need to scan the planet and send probes to retrieve your materials. Before you do scan though, there is a decent sized blurb that describes life on the planet and lots of facts about the planet. There's lots more, too. However, you'd just have to buy the game so you can be amazed by that. Also, the CHARACTERS. The best part about this game is the CHARACTERS. Tali is a little clumsy, especially around me. Grunt has an aggresive attitude and lusts for bloodshed. Mordin is crazy, and seems like he cares little for death, and talks in an extremely fast pace. Should I describe anyone else? I didn't think so. Although the plot was rather off-topic and poorly done, I praise this part of the game highly for lore and characters.
The audio is just alright. It seems like A. The same music is played over and over again or B. All the songs sound the same. This is probably the weak point to this unforgettable RPG. Even friends of mine agree, the music in this game is just meh. However, I do think the voice actors did a strong, strong performance for their roles.
The replayability is actually pretty good. Beat the game? Play as a Renegade, or maybe play as a heroic Paragon. Play as the opposite gender. Side with someone else. "Do it" with another romance option. There's lots to do, and there's even some DLC you can download. You have quite a bit to do.
The key problems to this game include the following: Lots of glitches, the space bar seems to be overused, making cover/run/interact/etc a bit clunky. The game is somewhat linear. That's about it!
In the end, Mass Effect 2 is one of the best RPGs of last gen, but also one of the best GAMES of last gen. It's amazing, and I highly, highly, highly recommend it. Go "do it" with Miranda, would you?

Racketeer - The game where you rip off small children and the elderly for fame and fortune! Capitalism ho!
Seriously, you play a shopkeeper of a stereotypical RPG, catering to both the regular townsfolk, as well as the occasional adventurer.
Oddly enough, the game actually has surprisingly good writing, with a unique and interesting assortment of eccentric characters set to a rather ridiculous plotline which works not just in spite of, but specifically because of how silly it is.
A lot of various addictive qualities show up in Recettear, such as RPG-style leveling of your character/shop, an economy where you purchase materials and have to buy low/sell high, as well as witty and charming dialogue.
You'll find a modest variety of characters enter your store; a small girl, an elderly man, a housewife and a generic common man for the regular townsfolk, each with their own personal buying habits. Toss in the more unique characters such as your brattish rival with a cynical faery of her own, a runaway princess-turned drunken assassin, a cyborg who is kind of new to the concept of "money", and a down-on-his-luck wannabe adventurer, to name a few, and you'll find yourself entertained for quite long periods at a time interacting with them.
Haggling is an artform, and you get significantly rewarded for giving an offer that will be accepted on the first try rather than just going back and forth until someone either gives in or they meet in the middle. As such, there's actually some pretty shrewd tactics to manage when trying to haggle with customers, and learning their personal traits and spending habits can be quite beneficial.
As a whole, it's a fairly unique game. There have been others vaguely similar to it before, where you buy low and sell high... but none which have have nearly as much polish and just sheer charm to the personalities you interact with in Recettear.
Final Verdict:
It's really quite enjoyable for what it is. If you like shopping, or even just anything similar to facebook or flash games, you'll probably adore Recettear. It's value for retaining a player's interest can be a bit less than ideal, however, as there is an "end" to the game. There are some nice options for increasing replay value, but you'll probably only find yourself doing one or two playthroughs every few years. It's a nice game to come back to once in awhile, but not on a consistent basis.
Overall Score: About 80%. It's really probably the best game of it's kind out there, and the writing is great! The content duration's a bit short, though, and considering the game type... you might want to wait for it to go on sale; $20 is a little bit much. $15 is reasonable, and $10's a good, ideal price for it.

I was really looking forward to this game as I enjoy tactical RPGs and am always intersted in games with rich settings, espeically historical ones.  Unfortunately this game doesn't do justice to the historical setting it's placed in.  It takes the complexity of the Spanish exploration, colonization, and conquest of the New World and reduces it to a politically correct misrepresentation of the era.  Feminism is endemic in the game and, if my first interaction with natives is any indication of how the game treats religion, you're either stuck making live and let live decisions or you're oppressing and murdering people in the name of God, Church, and country.  There was no middle-ground.  I guess I should have expected this given this line from the game's description: "Re-write the history of the Conquistadors: Forge diplomatic alliances with the natives... or crush the savages and bring civilization to the pagan tribes!"  It's still disapointing to see such a fascinating and rich piece of history represented so poorly.
I found the gameplay to be less egregious but not terribly entertaining.  The camera in the game's traveling mode was maddening in how limited it's field of view was and the tactical battles were boring.
I think the game had a very promising concept.  Certainly one that really hooked me into buying it.  It also has some interesting features and mechanics, but nothing so great that I was motivated to keep playing after experiencing the above.

Absolutely solid indie rpg for the price. Tabletop RPG fans will feel at home. The mystical theme works well, and the "Dealer" is executed elegantly with his dark wit, personality, voice acting, and nuanced gestures.
The gameplay consists of a set of cards dealt faced down on the table in a random path. These represent the "level". A figurine represents you on these cards, and you move across them in a direction of your choice, one card at a time, revealing them and resolving them as you land on them. They might be fights, traps, or story events, or some combination of the three. While doing this, you are balancing how much food you have left (it is lost every move), whether your gold is better spent on food, blessings, or equipment, whether it's worth it to explore further or look for a shop on the next level, etc. You are also engaged thematically with the style of the scene, and the banter of the Dealer, while making story decisions for the cards, or engaging in combat.
Fights bring you into real-time combat using the gear your have found, in a freeform twitch / reaction combat style similar to the batman arkham series or Middle Earth: Shadows of Mordor. It is not perfect; the camera is a little rough and the animation and targeting can be slightly shaky, but it is still very good, especially for an indie game. I grew comfortable with it pretty quickly, and I haven't had any significant issues. I enjoy it, and I think it's the best form of combat for this game.
One of the cards on the level is an exit to the next level, which will clear the table and draw a new map of cards. Depending on the mode of play, you are either descending to ultimately fight one of an impressive number of bosses (story mode), or descending indefinitely into ever-increasing difficulty (endless mode). Endless mode uses all cards that you have found. Story mode uses custom decks that you build ahead of time.
The customization and collection aspect of this game really make it shine:
As you play, you unlock cards that are added to your collection. You use this collection before each game to build 2 customized decks: Equipment, and encounters. Your equipment deck isn't what you start with, but instead represents all the items that you may find in shops, chests, and as combat rewards throughout the game. Your encounter deck represents the cards that make up a level. So you are putting together the pieces of your story. You are deciding what you'll run into, and what you'll find, with some other things added by the dealer. You unlock new cards to add to your collection as you go.
From a developer perspective, these guys put a lot of care into this game. There are elements of conditional dialog, animations, and menus; things like the dealer saying something different or being aware of your stats, things like a menu screen that changes based on whether or not you've completed the tutorial level, and other things that may seem trivial, but took consideration, time, and effort to include, when really they didn't have to. Bigger games have been released with far less intelligent scripting.

This game makes you feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. There are dilemmas that stretch from the plot to the game's mechanics themselves. This game doesn't have "Moral Choices" this is the new world, there is no morality, only survival. You constantly have to be making decisions in this game that kill people, and most of the time it's up to you if those people are part of your party, or the locals. You're gonna feel like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by this game's conclusion, because being nice is just not pragmatic. Many of the hardest hitting moments in this game are non-scripted events, you may lose your best soldier to disease or desertion. You may have several random conversations with another soldier under your command, learn about their life, their family back in Spain, and then lose them to a native ambush. Maybe you really wanted to tend to everyone's wounds but you have three wounded men and only enough medicine for two.
In most other games, the moral choices are usually nothing more than fodder for repeat playthroughs, they might effect the plot or maybe your character's appearance, but the moral choices in this game always tie directly into the game's mechanics, maybe you really do want to be the generous savior of all the people, but if you gave that starving village some food you would be left with none of your own. I always felt like each choice actually mattered, but not in some telltale games way where characters react to me differently, each choice mattered because it was the difference between being alive and guilty, or dead and innocent.

Crusader Kings II balances realism and accessibility to create a dynamic, interesting look into this oft-portrayed era. Historical enthusiasts and the "as-it-was" crowd can get a lot of enjoyment out of this title. While certainly not a page out of history verbatim, Crusader Kings II does an excellent job at keeping itself honest. For those who dig this age of history, look no further.
But this game offers a truly fun experience for everybody else, too. Playing it for the drama-mongering, whether political, carnal, religious, or otherwise, rates quite highly. If one of your vassals is bothering you a whole lot, have them killed. If that is too risky, arrange them to be married to someone with the plague. The level of detail and creative freedom is deceptively high. You're left to create much of the nuance yourself, however. This isn't a title that holds your hand much.
Unfortunately, sometimes the level of detail and micromanagement can be irritating. It would be nice if you could delegate more to your inferior, but it's by no means a game-breaking annoyance. Of course, with any complex game, there are issues within the game here and there, though never enough to break immersion.
So, fellow kings and lords, fulfill your birthright and rule like you've always wanted. Just hope you aren't born disabled.

turn-based aerial combat in WW1 setting.
From the description it's hard to see how a game like this could be so compelling but it actually is.  You control a group of pilots fighting in the front of WW1.  Each turn, you get a set of possible moves for every pilot.  Some are basic, like flying straight ahead fast or slow, banking left or banking right, climbing or diving.  As your pilots build up skills, they get more advanced manuevers like half loops, Immelmans, slides, and spins.  Each move limits you to the next possible set of moves, factoring in altitude and plane condition.  Moves that bring you close to the enemy give you the opportunity to fire--or be fired at.
The appeal of this game is its puzzle-like quality.  The emphasis is less on action than it is on tactics.  It's a pretty cerebral game.  The missions are varied, too, and range from straightforward air combat to strafing runs to escort missions to aerial cover.
Rounding out its play value is the skill tree, new airplanes, pilot personalities (both for your own squadron and the enemy's), upgrades.
Highly recommended!

This is Disgaea.  You know what that is, right?  It's why you're here.  So what you want to know is:
How is the port?
The answer: It depends.
There have been many reports of people attempting to run it and have it lock up, play sluggishly, or have graphical tearing.  I am not one of these reports.  My computer is old, my graphics card is out of date (AMD says it's a "legacy" product now, yay!  no more support!), and by all rights, if there are going to be optimization issues, I should be feeling them.
But here's the thing: I'm not.
I get smooth FPS, the updated UI looks good, configuring my old GamePad Pro was a breeze (plug it in, switch two buttons on the Config screen, and I'm done), and I have had absolutely no issues at all.  The closest thing to a CON I can think of is that the mouse cursor stays visible even with MOUSE: OFF.
So TL; DR - if you like Disgaea, get this.  Why are you even thinking about it?  If you have a computer that has issues with the port, you have 2 gameplay hours to request a refund.  If you don't, enjoy yourself some Disgaea!

Collaborating once again with Injekted to bring another unforgettable soundtrack, this really is a brilliant project that has clearly come to a successful conclusion.
Highly recommended if you want a game that gives you way too much bang for your buck and for anyone who wants a new, immersive experience to get addicted too!!

The critically acclaimed PS3 title 'Valkyria Chronicles', inclusive of all DLCs, was ported over to the PC by Sega and released on the platform late last year. It is a turn-based squad strategy game incorporating strong flavours of a third-person shooter.
The game is set in a neutral and non-partisan fictitious small country, Gallia, situated in the continent of Europa. The land is rich in the mineral ore Ragnite, a much sought after ingredient due to its vital properties that see it being used both as fuel and medicine. The Empire, an alliance of autocratic Eastern Europan nations, declares war on The Federation, an alliance of democratic West Europan nations, to kick-start the Second Europan War (EWII). The Empire has its sights set on Gallia's ragnite rich deposits.
You play as Welkin Gunther, a Gallian and son of celebrated war-hero, General Gunther, as you command a troop of organized Gallian militia soldiers known as Squad 7 whose job is to thwart The Empire's advances in Gallia. During the course of the playthrough you command foot soldiers and tanks as you set forward to complete objectives and, thus, win battles in the process. The game is divided into chapters which is further sub-divided into small episodes.
First things first, the game is gorgeously good-looking. The art-style is inspired by Japanese animes while the visuals are unique, feeling as though the entire game is a sharp watercolour painting brought to life.
The game has five combat Classes; namely Scouts (Rifle), Shock Troopers (Infantry), Lancers (Anti-Tank), Engineers and Snipers. In addition, you also get to control Commanding Officer Welkin's tank. All equipment is upgradeable, relying on XP points which are gained as missions are completed. The Combat system is an amalgam of turn-based and third-person elements. You deploy a squad of your choice and each time you click on a squad member, the camera pans to third-person and he can be moved to an appropriate place. The camera then swings back to the bird's eye view of the map allowing you to plan your next move. Combat is challenging and is easily the best part of the game. Level environments are well-designed and test your strategic skills to the hilt.
The game's setting is inspired by real-life incidents, with a mix of fantasy and fiction elements thrown into the mix. The plot is, frankly speaking, nothing to write home about. It's B-grade anime with trope characters and a cliched predictable story. There are a few instances in the game where the plot impresses but, highly unfortunately, those are few and far between.
I really liked the game. The war-setting negated some of the cheesy anime moments and the combat was fun and challenging. I'm glad Sega ported this over to the PC. Valkyria Chronicles is a definite recommendation from my side, if just for a refreshing change of art-style and grueling turn-based gameplay.

GEO is by all means a thinking man's game. You have to have patience and no super A.D.D. to appreciate the complexities of it. At first it can be a bit overwhelming with the amount of things to do here, though there's a helpful flying droid named NAVI who is always there to help you with information when clicked upon (no doubt named for Zelda OOT's notorious helper fairy).
I'll try to break down the basics: You are in charge of a mining company in outer space, which is a hard premise to go wrong with  (will the Nostromo make a cameo?? Only time will tell!) Anyhow you can hire guys to work for you whose specialties range from punk rock engineers to dumb as a stump grunt laborers with questionable hygene. After hiring guys you can build rooms for your HQ and pop them in. Lucky one of the rooms includes a shower- and good news, ladies- it's coed!
Placing guys in the rooms gives your drill spaceship bonus stats like more HP. Once ready you can explore outer space one quadrant at a time. Each section is initially hidden and revealed only after spending some money. Luckily, money is not super hard to come by at the start so this isn't an issue. Uncovering these hidden sections of space is actually really fun, as they appear to be randomized and can hold different events like improved shop stock or even new places for your drill to visit.
It's here that you'll spend the lion's share of time while playing. Take your drill ship to drill down and destroy different 'tiles' or materials like dirt or metal. Each tile requires a different amount of time to destroy, and every second spent drilling anything will eat away at the drill's HP. Drill enough tiles and your drill will explode (thankfully for your crew these seem to be remote controlled).
At first I wasn't sure if having a constantly exploding drill ship would work, but it does so surprisingly well in practice. Since your company provides an unlimited amount of drills, you can in turn make as many trips down into a moon's crust as you'd like. And what you find is always randomized and different, from resources to more money to exploding do dads and more. This is my favorite part of the game. Since missions like this tend to be over quickly, it wasn't unusual for me to retry one over and over again for like 15-20 minutes.
Getting enough resources through digging will eventually unlock medals back at the HQ. Unlock enough medals and other collectible materials to open up new blueprints for other rooms. You also have a room called a Coreatorium which acts sort of like a passive skill tree, fueled by cores you can drill out at the very bottom of each planetoid.

complicated. And isn't that what we're all on Steam for anyhow? To find new and cool ways to spend our off-time? Wouldn't you rather be mining for carbonite than sitting in a stuffy cubicle right about now?

Valkyria Chronicles is one of those rare anime-based games that truly does not suck.  It's both a interactive novel and a turn-based strategy game.  The story takes you along to points of conflict, then you must engage in the conflict yourself.  If either of these elements had not been up to par, then the game would have suffered.  However, to my surprise, both the story and the action parts of this game are very well done.  Any anime worth watching will at some point make you cry, and this game accomplished that.  As for the gameplay, it's also quite good, if you are a fan of turn-based strategy games like me (X-Com, Civ).  Though the gameplay is a bit different than most turn-based strategies I have played, the basic concept is the same.  You get X units of time to perform actions during your turn, then the enemy does the same.  The way Valkria Chronicles implements this moves the action along at a faster, smoother pace than with games like X-Com and Civ.
Overall, this game surprised me at how good it was.  I bought it on sale not expecting a whole lot, and it has ended up being the game I have played the most recently.  Both the story and the gameplay keep me coming back for more.  Terrific job by the developers.

Play Mass Effect 1 to port your gameplay results to change plot, port saves into that legal copy of Mass Effect 3 on Steam, and play with 3D Vision assisted by Helix Mod.
Well balanced Sci-Fi RPG designed and built by Bioware with  just enough EA meddling.
$35 (for Mass Effect 1 and Mass Effect 2 Deluxe)
Bioware is an interesting studio. They have pushed out some very note worthy titles such as SWKOTOR (Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic) and Dragon Age: Origins. They are both worth a go, but are not for "modern" gamers who like action packed games.
If you have played Mass Effect 1, you will find that Bioware had moved on from the classical "RPG" elements such as attributes (Dexterity, Strength, etc.) and inventory (limited slots, customization items take space). You will also discover that you can port your save game data and input the results to affect gameplay in Mass Effect 2.
The stripping of core RPG mechanics was done to allow for as many people to enjoy the game as possible. The plot was re-designed to make it more action packed. The 3 plot necessities were focused, being: gore, sex, and humour. This unfortunately causes a problem for some; there's more on this later.
The result was a much more interesting, action packed title which should allow anyone to play it.
You should however, take into account that Unreal 3 is more of a console porting engine. You can see this with the lower quality textures, limits on the detail of scenes, field of view (FOV), hidden frame rate smoothing, and loading in between decks of the Normandy.
When I think of consoles, one of the first things I think of is DLCs. While I describe them to be the evil of all evils to some, there are some ok "patches" such as the Shadow Broker, which adds to the story, save porting abilities, and even highlights the back story that I wasn't aware of from the comics.
Another issue with porting is that meaningful keyboard shortcuts and keys are not used. This is where the concept of "spacebar does everything" comes in. While most games use the "e" key for interactions (failing that, the "f" key), Mass Effect 2 uses the spacebar. This is quite the switch from the original Mass Effect.
Comparing to another successful title such as Dragon Age: Origins, you can see how the game has improved and worsened.
Improvements range from not being so dry thanks to humour, to less about fine tuning character attributes and more enjoying the story.
The list of things that you can say have become worse include: "The getting laid simulator" romance mechanic, the plot is too simple, and that the game is generally "dumbed down".
It should be up to you to evaluate what is important to you, but I will make as side note here to say that the game has replay ability. You can even replay Mass Effect to change how the story unfolds in ME2 and ME3.
Another point that should be made apparent is that the 80% process is used.
Due to the 80% process, cut scenes don't use weapons assigned by you. While not a “game breaking” issue, just could have been worth the weight (thanks gabe for the comment). In this process, studios finish things to 80% and move on, hoping to come back and finish them later. Sadly, most of the time this means picking the more meaningful features before shipment.
Stereoscopic 3D done via Nvidia's 3D vision and improved via Helix Mod, really make this title a treat and greatly improve immersion.
To end this off I will say this. The beauty of Mass Effect 2 (as with the others) is that you can play a different style or character the next playthough. Go with male Shepard once, then with the Female another. Things change, and thus I have played 4 times all the way though. Yes, you will feel like doing that one day. Maybe Romance Tali in one, Garrus the 2nd, or Miranda in the 3rd.

I absolutely love this game. The gameplay is absolutely minimalistic. The people make the stories. You need to have a strong sense of humor to roll with the inevitable trolls, but when you've got one or two other people in the game who are putting their all into it (as, hopefully, you are), the wondrous magic of human interaction happens.
Instead of telling you anything about the actual gameplay (which is 99% human), let me tell you about my best round so far, which had caused me to fall in love with this game: I found myself in the role of Alex Obolensky, young Russian aristocrat and also a thief looking to rob someone of their data with his trusty taser and resell said data to accumulate riches. Also, he had a spare thong, and no idea who it belonged to.
So, after waking up, the first person Alex talked to was Mary, apparently an official on the ship. She wanted Alex' passport. Still drunk from the night before, Alex tried giving her the thong instead.
The person playing Mary played the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the role - Mary stuttered, not knowing what to say.
Eventually, Alex realized that what he had found in his wallet was a thong. Mary took the thong, anyway. Then she quickly aborted conversation and left.
Quickly, Alex managed to gain the trust of the people on the boat. Someone gave him their CID, which Alex used to his advantage; only someone affiliated with the oil companies should have one of them, and those are known to pay a lot of money for data. Alex found someone who had data to sell and lured him away from the others. When they were alone, Alex apologized and tased the man, taking his data.
However, a religious man and Shaina, who had become his disciple, witnessed Alex' deed and were appalled. Alex tried selling them the data, but they didn't want it, apparently not interested in worldly affairs anymore. Eventually, Shaina agreed to give Alex one hundred thousand dollars, but, bizarrely, she wanted Alex only to tase her in return, and she paid the money upfront. Alex could've just taken the money, which he may have done if she would've wanted the data, but he didn't see why he shouldn't give her what she wanted. Alex was unsure if that was meant to teach him some kind of lesson or if it was something entirely else.
A much richer man now, but still with data to sell, Alex kept looking for people who were buying. He found Mary talking to Boyle, the bartender. As it turned out, Boyle would've been eager to buy what he had, if it wasn't for the fact that he had lost all his money. He had paid a hundred thousand dollars to see Shaina naked, and he didn't even get to see what he had paid for. Alex was outraged. He loudly proclaimed that he had seen Shaina and that she wasn't worth that much. It wasn't right. He promised to get the poor man his money back. He wasn't sure of himself, whether he had told Boyle the truth or not.
He sought out Shaina, not noticing that Mary was following him. Alex yelled at Shaina, asking her how she could do such a thing, and also asked if that meant she still had another hundred thousand dollars in hand. Before Shaina could reply, Mary interrupted. Nervously, she said it was her who had tricked Boyle.
I'm unsure what had happened there. Either me or the one playing Boyle had gotten the names mixed up. I like to think it was Alex.
Chaos ensued, as another plotline which had been happening along the way collided with the first - the search for the lost thong. Shaina had claimed it was their own, but so did Boyle. Quickly, several people were yelling at Mary, demanding justice, a hundred thousand dollars, and a thong.
Mary was absolutely unable to handle the situation and eventually stopped responding.
Alex should've been happy. He had a hundred thousand dollars, and still had the data on him. But he just didn't feel accomplished.
It only seemed sensible that he would return the data to the one he had robbed it from. But he wasn't done there - he felt ashamed that he was unable to reclaim Boyle's money and so he gave Boyle all of his own money, instead.
Later, Alex said on the matter of the lost thong:
"Too much alcohol, too many women."

Ok so a few hours invested in this game, it's about time I gave it a review.
Firstly, keep in mind when reading any review, positive or negative, that this is an early access game in it's alpha state. It is NOT a finished product and all info given in reviews is liable to be rendered inaccurate at some point.
The good:
Ok let's start with the description. Note this from the game devs -> "This is a social-economic sandbox RPG". So if you are looking for a fast paced PvP game or action packed adventure game, stop reading now and go away. This game requires patience, time, a little intelligence and certainly commitment.
This is a game where you work, trade, hunt or just blag your way to fortune. You start will a little airship hanging from a balloon and you set off into a world that is 500x500 miles in size to make that fortune. There are 2 playable races. The fantastic awesome Orcs, and the pink skinned lilly livered humans.
Game progression is simple. You take some jobs, deliveries mostly. You float across the sky in your balloon and complete your job. You get paid some copper and get a little reputation. Rinse and repeat until you can afford a bigger better airship or two (yes you can command a whole fleet of them with skills). Then you can take on bigger jobs or try your hand at buying and trading in consumables between cities.
A little further on, a little more money, and you can establish a settlement of your own. Produce your own resources, airships, weapons, ammo etc etc. All can be traded on the market or directly from your own store.
Another viable option is hunting dragons. The other denizens of the world. Trophies from dragons are used in crafting some of the more advanced items in the game and are in high demand.
Level advancement is done in the Eve Online fashion (one of many similarities). You train a skill over time, even when offline. XP earned from skill training increases your level. Simples. There are crafting skills, pilot skills, magic skills, resource gathering etc etc. There are not too many at the moment but there are enough for you to specialize.
The community is great. At least the English speaking one. There is a large Russian player base too, doing what Russians do, but I have had no real interaction with them. The Dev team is really good. They are constantly updating the game and helping players out. They have a passion for the game, and that is usually one of the most important traits a dev can have. They want you to tell them what's wrong, and then they fix it. Communication can be difficult, but not impossible.
Combat-wise there is not much. Apart from fighting/hunting dragons, there are also the pirates and rogue players. So far not a problem to me but they will be. Combat can be done with the auto attack feature or by manually aiming your weapons groups. There are also planes that you can launch from your ship like a carrier that will defend you, or you can station them in your settlement and have them fly combat air patrols over it. You can also launch as a pilot of one of these planes.
The economy is a work in progress. There is one, but it's a bit iffy with the small player base and the early players dominating the best settlement spots. Prices can be ridiculous too. That will change as more players join and there is more competition. There are 3 currencies in game. I shall simplifie them as copper, silver and gold. Gold is a premium currency you can buy. And it's actually dirt cheap really. You can trade all currency for one of the others but the prices are stupid in some areas. You need to look about for the best deals.
The Bad:
Well, there are certainly going to be no prizes for graphics. They are minimal at best. But, as you spend most of your time high in the air there is really no call for high level ground  detail. So it actually works just fine. And will run quite happily on most machines.
The economy is a bit broken, as I said above. However there are many players trying to improve this by selling their wares at sensible prices instead of the greedy ones. It will take time but it will happen. The majority of the community is interested in promoting the game and making it accessible to new players. Including the prices they have to pay when starting out.
Server restarts are a pain as they reset the consumables on the market and you have to wait for them to restock. This is an unfortunate consequence of the Devs being very active in fixing and updating things. We just have to suck it up.
Scammers are present. Some of the jobs you will see are just unrealistic. Very high deposits that require you to take ridiculous loads over long distances. I would not expect to reach your destination, you will probably be jumped on the way so you fail the job and the job poster gets your gold. There are also players with names I can not pronounce who like to add newbies as enemies in the hope they will attack them in a safe zone etc. They get nothing financially if you do, just a good laugh.
The game has no useful tutorial really and can be very confusing when starting out. It shows some tips but they can be a little bewildering and misleading. The whole translation of the game to English is seriously bad. The names of some items are just strange or wrong. There are a lot of things that just won't make sense at all or give the wrong information. Devs do seem to be fixing this when its pointed out though.
Conclusion:
I recommend this game if you are the sort of player who likes a relaxing game and doesn't mind the slow pace and time required. Economists and traders will love it. If you are a more combative type, then you probably won't like it much unless you go down the pirate route. That's your call. Even then though, combat you have isn't going to be fast paced and intensive. You are going to have to chase down targets over distance in a slow moving airship and work for your kills. And probably be hunted by a lot of others in return.
The game is rough around the edges and needs a lot of improvement. However it has 3 things that make it stand out. An active and passionate dev team, a great community and a whole boat load of potential. With some major improvements in certain areas, this is going to be a classic for players who like this premise. It's free to play so just try it. Introduce yourself in game and you will get a warm welcome and a lot of help.  (Please though, read the guides and watch the star vid, we do get sick of answering the "how do I play?" question every 20 minutes) My in game name is Crom Cruach, feel free to add me on steam or in game if you require any help. Not sure it will be of much use, but still :)
