Although I'm not entirely a fan of how Nippon Ichi didn't choose this game to make their PC debut four years ago, I will do my best to put aside my personal dislike towards the developer. However, because the game does not appear to look updated at all moving on from Disgaea: Afternoon of Darkness, I feel that it would be important to review its performance on the now archaic
to gauge its playability on low-end machines. (scroll to the bottom of the review for tl;dr)
Yes, I know that this is was originally on the PlayStation 2 and the PC version is based on the enhanced PSP re-release, and the reason i wanted to start my review with the graphics first is because at a first glance, one would think that you shouldn't need too much to run Disgaea. Having sat through the game's intro on my secondary machine, I have noticed that the game runs at a consistent 30FPS when rendering the 3D map despite the game's logic being tied to 60FPS.
While one might argue that this is a turn-based strategy where FPS doesn't matter, Disgaea is known for having flashy and convoluted special attack animations, which you will need to turn off on low-end machines due to a lack of automatic frame skipping. I'm probably a
harsh about how low-spec Disgaea is when testing the game on a 5 year old laptop but please, feel free to argue that
is the more demanding game than
with a straight face, and I'm pretty sure i'm seeing some upscaling on the first screenshot.
Moving onto my primary system, it would seem as if the game runs slightly better than on my laptop (36-41 FPS). Upon closer inspection, I have found out that somehow, the game only runs like crap when you don't have a controller plugged in. From what i've read on another review, the game seems to do a constant check on your CPU if you don't have one plugged in.
On the bright side, it's definitely an improvement from NIS' first PC game, the options menu has a decent amount of settings to tweak and the window can be freely resized (doesn't stop the game from upscaling), though one might nitpick about the lack of borderless mode.
In terms of keyboard and mouse support, the game is pretty barebones in this regard, since there aren't any dedicated camera controls outside of Q and E to rotate the camera and zooming in and out with the mouse wheel (only two zoom levels). In full-screen mode, you can't even move the cursor to the edges of the screen to move the camera. To move the camera with the mouse, you have to hover your mouse over the tile you want the camera to center itself on and hit any of the WASD keys. What I just said sounds pretty dumb and I know people are gonna say that i'm shooting myself in the foot for not using a controller, but my main gripe with Disgaea's controls is that it has no Xinput support. While this may sound like good news for those without an Xbox 360 controller, the game will treat your left analog stick as a D-pad, so no analog cursor movement like in the PS2/PSP and you can't use your actual D-pad as a D-pad.
Moving back to how the game plays with the keyboard and mouse, the battle camera seems to be the only issue I have so far, as everything else seems to work just fine. Outside of combat, you can click on the map to move Laharl around or if he's standing next to an NPC, you can talk to them by left clicking them. In combat, the right mouse button serves as the △ (menu) button when hovering over an empty tile and ○ (cancel) in menus or when hovering the cursor over a tile occupied by one of your characters. the left mouse button is used as the ✕ button and for some reason, is also used to move the camera around. Alternatively, you can also use the I key (not Esc, since that is multi-bound like the right mouse button) to access the menu. While UI is geared towards console play, you can at least access all of the menu options with just the mouse.
In my honest opinion, I feel as if both the controller and kb/m could've been handled a lot better, the latter moreso.
Full disclosure, I have not played the PSP version in a very long time, so this will probably be the worst part for me to explain.
To the unfamiliar, one would first think that it's just a clone of Final Fantasy Tactics. Perhaps one would not be incorrect to say it has drawn inspiration from it, though it does have its fair share of unique mechanics and arguably a larger class diversity. In addition, there are a few mechanics that are common throughout the entirety of Disgaea; the first one being team attacks, where if you have allies adjacent to a character initializing a basic melee attack, they will join in on a gangbeating. The best part is, said gangbeating only uses up the action of whoever was given the attack order.
Another mechanic is the Lift and Throw system. You can literally tell one of your guys to lift someone else over their head(friend or foe) and depending on their class (monsters can't throw), toss them a certain number of tiles. In most cases, it will look as if you can only throw at 4 directions, though if your timing is really good, you can also throw diagonally.
Another mechanic unique to the franchise is are the Geo Blocks, which give passive effects on colored tiles. In addition to this, you can also destroy these blocks to change colors of a certain tile (assuming the geo block isn't the same color as the tile it's on), which can be used to deal damage to multiple enemies at once, though in the early game, you’ll probably want to preserve geo blocks that are beneficial to you.
Overall, I feel that the combination of all these give for an enjoyable deviation from Final Fantasy Tactics' format, even if hindered by the game's less than optimal controls on both the mouse and the controller. As for the $20 price tag, I think I would've waited for the Steam Summer Sale before buying this game, since the controls and performance issues I had with this game prevent this from being worth $20, and I'd also like to think that the issues I have now would be fixed between now and said sale. However, since I already burned a fair amount of money on 3 copies of Cladun X2*, it would’ve been wrong to not pre-order at this point. Ultimately, I’m gonna give the game a thumbs up since I think it’d be better to buy the game on a sale than to not buy it at all because it’s still a pretty good game.
And yes, I know I forgot to cover things like the dark assembly and item world, though most of my play time has been spent analyzing the porting quality. I will (hopefully) cover the more advanced aspects of the game the further I play through it.
+Geo Blocks, team attacks, class diversity and the lift/throw system add to a fun take on the turn-based strategy RPG format
-Pretty unoptimized, especially when you consider that there are other options available for low-spec games.
-Keyboard and mouse controls are barebones and no Xinput support
±Game's only worth $10-15 IMHO, but it's better to wait for a sale than to not buy at all.
*Before you ask, all three copies have been redeemed.

Bejeweled 2 is the second installment in the main trilogy of the games. The later spinoff titles do not count, such as Bejeweled Twist here on Steam. In this installment, the sequel takes the foundation of the first game, and adds a bunch of new features and game modes to the mix. For example, the original Bejeweled literally only made the jewels disappear when matched. However, this time around, when you match 4 of the same jewel, it will morph into 1 shining jewel. And, when matched, will explode within its area for bonus points. When you match 5 of the same jewel, the jewels will transform into a Hypercube, which will strike out any jewel it comes in contact with on the board itself. In addition to the new gameplay features and changing atmospheres when completing levels (another nice touch), PopCap also introduces 3 total new modes; Endless, Puzzle, and Zen. From the sheer relaxation of endlessly playing through, the strategic thinking of the puzzles, and topping the whole game off with Zen, Bejeweled 2 makes such a simple concept as a matching game work so well and deserving of sequels. I recommend you give all 3 games a try. You'll enjoy them!

This game has an incredibly cool concept, and was fun for about a week. But now, I can see that this game has as many holes in it as swiss cheese, which the developers clearly don't care to repair.
Positive:
- Sweet customization: plenty of cool options to choose from.
- Immersive gameplay; awesome war-like atmosphere.
- Intelligent integration of technical striking, such as slashing, overhanding, uppercutting, jabbing, parrying, kicking, etc.
- Interactive speech in-game.
- Feel like a boss when you win a fight.
Negative:
- "Dragging", a flat out abuse of the game's striking system which makes you nearly impossible to beat when holding a two-handed weapon. Throw's game balance off completely. (Specifically Claymores and Zweilhanders)
- Cancerous community. People generally use all the abuses, and find all the loopholes to make the game hell for people who just want to have a fun, balanced game. People who abuse the system also mock you for pointing it out, and try to get you kicked.
- Team killing. Not like this is that big of an issue, because you can't just walk into your allies' swings, and this makes it to where it's much harder to gang up on an opponent, which is perfectly okay, BUT half the time, teammates don't give a single crap about killing teammates in order to get kills, even though the game tutorial teaches you how to avoid friendly fire. You will find yourself the having more deaths by friendly fire than fire in some matches, which I find infuriating.
- Team stacking: another example of total garbage in this game, is that strong players (usually draggers) like to all join one team, so they can have a field day with less experienced/less skilled players, giving some teams virtually no chance of winning at all.
The bad far outweighs the good, and is only fun when playing low ranked matches against people who haven't learned how to abuse the game's loopholes, or with friends. Even in low rank games, I've caught obvious people smurfing just to feel good about themselves for annihilating a bunch of noobs.
My recommendation is don't bother downloading, because this game will get your hopes up with its awesome, and immersive gameplay, but then destroy your hopes with the distinct, and obvious imbalances, that people don't mind abusing to ruin the entire game for everyone. You will be excited, because Chivalry: Medieval Warfare seems like a really awesome game on the surface, but then crushing disappointment will follow, because the community will suck the fun right out of it for you. So, again, I recommend that you don't put yourself through it, and don't waste a red cent on this crappy, beta, unrefined game.

There are some good things here, but overall the game doesn't hold up well after the initial 30 minutes of play.
* The visual style is cool, and I appreciate the board-game-feel that they've achieved. However, it's mostly obscured by the scrolls of text that pop up during gameplay. You never really get to enjoy the novelty of visuals.
* There are a LOT of situations where the choices you're asked to make come down purely to guessing. There is very often not enough information given to make an informed decision, and once you've chosen your course of action, additional information is given. Often, that additional information occurs chronologically before the act you chose, and had you known it you wouldn't have taken the action. This feels like a cheap kick to the groin when it happens.
* Combat is very simplistic. After a handful of encounters there's not really anything else to learn about it. This goes back to my earlier comment concerning the game not holding up after the first half hour or so of play.
There's just not enough here to be worth my time. It's a game targeted at people that enjoyed things like Legend of Grimrock, but it's not at that same level of quality.

Turn-based strategy with an original twist and a reach story.
*Story* The plot is derived from WW2 and contains several twists that left me surprised. It is told through a great number of cut-scenes and dubbed dialogue. The characters are often likeable, but also often annoyingly naive for a setting that references a war and a genocide.
*Gameplay* Unlike Fire Emblem and X-Com, instead of moving on fields, you have a meter of agility points that tells you how much longer you can keep running with a soldier from your troop. The game manages to be a turn-based strategy and almost a third person shooter at the same time.
*Graphics* Originally this was a PS3 exclusive, so the graphics are decent unless you hate the Anime look.
A must-play for fans of the genre. And overall a solid game.

It's always a bad sign when a PC port's title screen invites you to "Press Start button."
Unfortunately, this common oversight really does signal deeper problems. Valkyria Chronicles has terrible PC UI. Sega doesn't seem to have bothered to do more than map controller buttons to semi-arbitrary keys. In menus, there is absolutely NO option to use a mouse - you must navigate with WASD or arrow keys. Confusingly, however, some menus (not all!) require you to click with the mouse to confirm your selection once you have navigated to it via the keyboard.
The half-baked interface is a shame, because other aspects of this port actually do seem to have been done with some care. The game looks great and ran smoothly and problem-free for as long as I tried to make myself get past the interface problems. Ultimately, though, I just can't. Your mileage may vary, especially if you are willing to break out a controller.

THIS IS NOT MY DESCRIPTION OF THE GAME. READ CAREFULLY.
Since Archeage is my favorite game at the moment and I come from a long history of loving wow, I thought I would do a quick comparrison between the two and what makes them worth playing and/or different.
First, let me say, Archeage is not a Wow Killer. Not because its not a better game but because it is an MMO that does not try compete with Blizzard in its space. Where Wow excels is creating content around the PVE experience. While there is some PvP, it is more an afterthought than the main focus of the game. Archeage is more PvP (on a grand scale) foccused with raiding content and world bosses more as an after thought.
Where Wow players require that Blizzard keep releasing updated content to keep interested, Archeage moves around high value trade packs and PvP. Archeage relies on politics, skullduggers and spies to keep it interesting. Since this content is player generated, you never run out of excitement.
In Wow, they try make an equal playing field. Every season the gear gets better and every expansion you get new PVe gear. Due to this you have insane gear inflation, and something you worked really hard for last year, is worthless this year. In Archeage its unfair. It mirrors life in this way. The gear almost never inflates. Gear you worked (for a long time) on 2 years ago, can still be imba today. Archeage does not try level the playing fields. Its absolutely brutal. Sink or swim. Until you have your gear, you better be quick.
Archeage is a different beast to Wow. Where I find myself playing with young kids mostly in Wow, I find myself playing with mostly adults in Archeage. Its one of the hardest MMO`s I have ever experienced. The depth of the crafting system is phenomenal and nothing in Blizzard can compare. If I want to make something simple like a plank to build a chest with, I have to plant the seeds, grow the plants, chop down the lumber, and then use a sawmill to turn the wood into lumber. Only then do I have the base mat!
However, this level of crafting means I can build almost anything. I currently have several homes in Archeage, ranging from mansions, to tree houses to farming cottages. I even have several storage silos in smuggler areas. Whats great, is I can take a picture of my family, and have it framed on my wall in my in game tree house. Other people can view this as well. One of the first things I did was buy a bunch of flags, and then make them into South African flag. In this game I can build wagons, ships, cars, carts, airships and just about anything. The crafting menu is so vast, almost no one knows all thats available (even the online documentation is useless and the Korean developers often introduce new stuff without telling players)
Archeage has a more real feel to it, in so far as world physics go, in wow you can walk through someone, in Archeage you can block people. This leads to some insanely fun trolling.
The class system in Archeage is far more advanced than Wow. In wow you get a handful of classes, in Archeage you get over 100. Your class is defined by what 3 skill trees you choose. Do you tank and heal? Cool, your class is paladin. Wanna be a tanking mage or a DPS healer, yup, you can do that in Archeage. My favorite classes are abolisher (melee, defense, buffs) and my nimble daggerspell (sorcery, rouge witchcraft (super cc)). The PVP spells are also more complex that wow, with combos and everything coming into play.
When I say archeage is brutal, its unfair. You are going to whine about how unfair it is, expecially if you are an unproductive or poor player. However, when you work hard at your goals, join a productive guild, and get involved in some of the most epic pvp you will ever experience (and on a scale you have never experienced). It emulates real life this way. Real life is unfair.
Archeage politics is insane, there are two major factions. Nuia (dopey looking elves and blonde pedobears) and Harnya (cat people and Japanese looking people). Each has their own continent. I was playing Haranya, but the Nuia on our server were stacked. A powerful guild grew up on the Nuia side and basically dominated the server. The pirates (more on them later) and Nuia used to eat us, even on our own continent, and we never stood a chance in all the major naval battles.
However, that all changed two weeks ago. Core (the powerful nuia guild) got so strong, that they claimed so much territory (in this game, a guild can conquer and own certain territories) that they were big enough to become their own faction! They promptly allied with us the Harnaya, to get access to much of our unused farmlands. Its pretty awesome going from zero to hero over night.
Now those pesky pirates, the bain of my life. Screw em, seriously, screw em. Any player can join the pirate faction. Pirates can not live on any of the main continents, but are able to inhabit small islands in the ocean. To become a pirate you need to PK players on your own side (or steal from them). When you get enough infamy points you end up on trial. The jury is made up of real players. If you are found guilty you are sent to prison. If you get sent to prison too many times you are exiled and become a pirate.
Most of the day you will find me in the ocean. My ships are my crafting pride and I spend hundreds of hours pulling up shipwrecks from the ocean floor. To pull up a shipwreck you need to find one, blow away the sand with a submarine, and then attach recovery pouches to the wreck, this will slowly raise it to the surface where you can pillage it. Getting the loot means nothing, everyone on the server is notified that you pulled a wreck up and have high value cargo. You now have to do a chicken run to a safe harbour to try deliver the loot.
Even a safe harbour means very little as I found out the other day. There I was, minding my own business, offloading my cargo, when I noticed a clipper come up behind my merchant ship. It fires a harpoon at my ship and they start dragging me out of the safe zone and into the PVP zone. I had to do everything to try avoid being pulled out, and they complicated my efforts, by putting someone on my ship to keep dropping my sails. Thankfully I was able to deliver the cargo, but the simple act of dropping off the cargo in a SAFE zone became a hardcore event where my adrenalin was pumping.
I cant compare this game to anything else. Perhaps a cross between minecraft and wow. It is a very very hard MMO to get into, the learning curve is huge, but if you get into the game, if you work out your trade routes, the thought of playing wow will make you yawn in boredom.

I bought this at the latest sales, and I didn't expect such a pleasant surprise.
This is a really great turn-by-turn RPG/action game. The battles are nice and challenging, the graphisms are refreshing and really give a sense of immersion, and the story / scenario goes deep.
As some other commentors said, it's quite a lot story based, so there are a lot of cutscenes, but the fights will still give you a lot of work. The classes system is nicely done and you'll clearly need to manage your 5 classes of soldiers in order to win your fights. The fact that all chars of a given class level up at the same time is a nice touch, since you don't have to grind your chars.
Basically, I only had to do one or two "skirmish battles" (ie, replayable battles that are not part of the main plot and that allow you to up your XP) so the main plot by itself is almost sufficient. There is also a challenge/completionist aspect: you earn ranks for each battle depending on how many turns you needed, and there are quite a few "unrelevealed" achievements that you need to find.
You can save as much as you want, which, IMO, is nice.
A few negative points, though:
* Quite a few times, the battles can turn around on just one "hit or miss", so the chance aspect is quite present. Be ready to load/save around this kind of shots.
* It's a bit slow: when it's the ennemy turn, you have to watch all moves in x1 speed, and you can't skip this. I found that a bit frustrating.

I don't know if the five Hidden Object Games (HOGs) in this "Hidden Object Bundle 5 in 1" could be considered to be bottom of the barrel.  But, they certainly aren't top tier.  Of the five games, two of them I found to be unplayable:
- Vampire Saga:  Pandora's Box.  I stopped playing after 20 minutes.  The graphics are too bad (low resolution) so it's very hard to see the objects in HOGs.  Also, there are some very blatant translation issues ("founded objects" instead of "found objects," "can't go ashore" instead of "can't go upstairs").
-  Behind the Reflection 2:  Witch's Revenge.  The story is so unbelievably bad that brain cells were dying as I played.  I had to stop after about a half an hour.
The remaining three games are playable, though not all that good.  In increasing order of "goodness" they are:
- Twisted Lands:  Shadow Town:  I got about 5.6 hours of almost tolerable gameplay out of this.  The biggest problem is that the story is pretty bad and the ending makes no sense.  I thought that was because the game is part of a series.  But, this is the first in the series (Shadow Town, Insomniac, and Origin).  Even ignoring the nonsensical ending on the assumption that it's explained in later games, the story is full of holes (gaps and logic errors).  Plus, the protagonist is a cad.  Other things:  the graphics aren't that great, there's no voice acting, the HOGs are foggy, fairly colorless, and too small (far away?  resolution issue?).  In-HOG issues: 1) won't accept an actual ships wheel, but will take the shadow of one just below it, 2) an electric fan not acceptable, but a paper fan just in front of it is, 3) a spade is not a shovel, 4) hedge clippers are not pruning shears.  Closely related in-story issues are 1) pliers don't cut fences, and 2) a microchip is not RAM.  More seriously, at one point there's an open electrical switch (the old Frankenstein type of switch) that works underwater.  For game mechanics, the diary sometimes gets populated when entering an area and not necessarily when things are encountered.  Also, HOGs get re-activated without story-driven reasons to return to an area.  You spend a LOT of time going back and forth across the island retrieving things and just looking to see if a HOG has re-activated.
- Weird Park:  Broken Tune:  I got about 4.6 hours of tolerable gameplay out of this.  There's no voice acting except the introduction narration, but two characters go through speaches with us but they're just text dialog.  The graphics are pretty good, the HOGs are good but simple, and most of the mini-games are good.  But three were hard for me (square flipping, rotation, and tune memory).  One bug I saw was that I needed a hair dryer at one point but it wouldn't let me use it.  Exited and restarted and it worked.  The biggest problem with the game is the story:  it's very weak.  The first half is reasonable though thin.  But the second half seemed to come out of the blue and just ramble.
- Mountain Crime: Requital:  I got about 5.3 hours of tolerable gameplay out of this.  First, the good:  the HOGs and mini-games are well done (the HOGs are interesting in that they're sort of Fractured Object Games (FROGs) but with whole objects instead of shards).  The plot is complex and interesting.  Now the bad:  even though the plot is interesting, the character behavior getting through the plot is stupid.  Plus, the voice acting just horrible.  It made me want to tear my ears off.  Then there are too many deaths and too many murders (9 in-game murders and several more backstory deaths).  The bodies pile up so deep you can't keep the dead straight.  But, the penultimate badness is the ending:  it's utterly HORRIBLE.  I can't explain it here as it would be a massive spoiler.  But, ugh.  It's terrible.
So, even though there are five games in this bundle and you can get probably more than 16 hours worth of gameplay out of it, at best, that 16 hours won't be well spent.  I certainly would never recommend spending the list price on it.  Heck.  I'm pretty sure I got this 5-in-1 bundle as part of an 8 game bundle and IT was on sale.  And, I still don't recommend it.

So having sunk several days into this game let's give this a shot
Common lies perpetuated by first impression reviews (ones from players that have less than 10 hours of game time)
1. "Cargo simulation" Yes, flying from city to city is a major part of the game. Just like every other game with ships and an open world. The game feels a lot like a steampunk Eve online in this way, but far more accessible. The issue is that combat is only accessible if you understand the game, and the game makes it really hard to get any idea of what to do.... JUST LIKE EVE ONLINE. I had to spend a month shooting rocks in Eve to get a better rock shooting ship.
2. "It's pay to win" many people seem to think paying money in any way is paying to win. In many Moba games you can pay real money to get rune pages, bonuses, experience boosters, etc to directly make you better than other players. Paying money in Luckcatchers gives you a large sum of golden coins, which you can then exchange with other players to buy goods and resources. Pay to win implies you are paying to do better than other players, while in this game you are paying to stimulate the economy. My business owning friend who I told about this said it made sense, because he likes the ability to pay to avoid grind he could avoid. Buying gold negates a LOT of grind in this game.
So it's not a cargo simulation and it's not pay to win, what is it? I don't even think this kind of game has a genre beyond MMO Airship Sim.
The game has no tutorial and if you aren't familiar with RTS games you will have an extremely hard time figuring things out on your own. The rough Russian translations don't help, but the devs are actively listening to the community and fixing any translation errors that we spot. On top of that the game tries a lot of concepts that american gamers just are not familiar with.
There is very little direction towards what you should be doing, being a wide open sandbox game. There is nothing that lets the player know that they have the weaponry starting out to sail away from town and shoot dragons, so they get stuck doing cargo jobs because they are so afraid to explore the game world; that's where all of those thirty minute "P2W cargo sim don't bother" reviews come from. A person has no business reviewing video games if they scream P2W without buying something to see how it works.
I think what confuses people about the ability to buy gold with real money is they think that LC is like any other game where having a lot of gold just makes you better than anybody else. Having gold gives you spending weight, since players will do anything for gold. You will be able to buy a bunch of ships, goods, and services from other players. In essence, if you buy a lot of gold you are essentially a Lannister, capable of throwing around economic weight.
Currency is based on a realistic barter system. Copper for petty purchases, silver for middle class, and gold is rich people money. You want to buy or produce things for copper and sell it for silver or gold. There is no magical conversion rate for money (since its a barter currency) and since the average american lives in the age of fiat currency and global banking they FREAK THE HELL OUT when they find out that there is no cold and fast exchange rate, or they see the inflated basic conversion rate and assume that is the global rate when it is not. You also get 5 free gold every hour logged in, which those first impressions guys would of known if they played games they reviewed.
Combat in this game is serious business. There are several kinds of machineguns and heavy cannons you can strap to varying sizes of airships, load them out with fighter planes, etc. You take all that firepower and you either go hunt pirate players or if you feel really brave attack the other factions player cities. Players don't immediately understand they can buy several shibay ships and tackle poorly developed bases. They assume you need all late game stuff, when the 1/10th pound guns you start with require days of base and skill development to produce and is a pretty efficient weapon itself.
Orange loot is free, it's dragon parts you can sell at towns or use in crafting. Blue crates belong to other players and appear as shipping containers. if the player has a negative rep with your faction you can open it with a master key without losing reputation yourself. The one problem is the reputation system is not well explained so players don't feel too brave indulging in combat yet like any mmo sim. Players often don't realize taht they can attack other players cities and steal their resources, because destroying ships and buildings ONLY destroys that, and it ejects everything else as a shipping container. Alternatively, planes with grappling hooks can steal crashing ships.
Bases are investments, money sinks, and vital to the economy. But if you get them built up enough you can produce your own ships and weaponry. Once you get to the point where you have several bases churning out goods and ships you will start to amass other players gold, that's where you want to be. Just don't grow too attached to them, people can strip it of buildings and steal yer stuff. Thankfully the reputation system keeps most players honest.
Pros
* Deep early access MMO
* Airships are usually equipped with several high caliber machine guns
* Huge pretty to look at world, devs say they want to make it bigger
* There is a time in the game year when thousands of dragons take to the skies and harass everybody.
* Reputation system enforces a truce among players of the same faction, allowing players to feel safe... too safe.
Cons
* Frequent server disconnections
* Rampant abuse of one use items and upgrade slots
* No tutorial or attempt to give players direction, which leads to many confused new players
* The realistic economy seems staggering to new players because of how hard it can get to make money starting out. Eventually the server will become more populated and this will be rectified
* It takes extreme bravery to be a pirate right now, there are few hostile players and that has lured the server into a false sense of safety.

(I'll put my overall opinion at the top for those who don't want to read anything about the individual titles.)
The bundle is a decent little treat for fans of Hidden Object Games. If you're not already a fan of those, however, you should probably look elsewhere for a smooth entry, as these games are not really the cream of the crop of the genre. Still, though, you get two good games, two decent ones and only one bad one for a rather low price, which is why I'm giving this a thumbs up despite its shortcomings.
- A strangely bland game, I thought. I really like evil clowns, and an abandoned amusement park sounds like a great setting for a creepy game, but still, I was a bit bored with this one. It felt very much like a by-the-numbers kind of thing, where not a single idea felt fresh or intriguing. Things get slightly more interesting (and surreal) towards the end, but overall, it's an underwhelming game.
- This one's more interesting. Both the setting and the story had me quite intrigued and motivated to keep going (the whole premise is a bit like Lovecraft's Shadow Over Innsmouth). The puzzles, HOGs and minigames are good, too, however, one problem with this game is that some paths between locations are maze-like, and you can *never* skip them. If you find yourself having to walk from Point A to Point B a couple of times and there's a maze section between them, then you will have to click through the maze *every single time*. It's not a major issue, since the mazes are short and easy, but it's still a minor annoyance. Overall, however, a good game with an interesting story.
- My favorite of the bundle. It excels in pretty much all areas: The Hidden Object sections have an interesting little twist to them, the minigame puzzles are well designed, the setting (a recently re-opened grand hotel) and the story (a string of grotesque murders) are intriguing and the presentation compliments the atmosphere. I have no complaints about this one at all.
- By far the worst game this bundle has to offer, in my opinion. It's a very bare-bones, visually off-putting experience for one thing, with bland environments, bizarrely ugly character models and the barest minimum of item combination puzzles,  but the real problem with this one is its actual Hidden Object gameplay. All the HO screens you encounter throughout the game suffer from one issue or another; they're either too dark to adequately see the things you're looking for, or they have a strong color filter that make the items blend in with the backgrounds, or (and this is my personal cardinal sin) they show you *more than one item that matches the description, but only one of them is actually correct. For example, there are screens where you're told to look for "a brush", but there are at least three different brushes lying around. Another screen has you looking for "a lamp", but there are four lamps to pick from, and of course you get penalized for too many consecutive wrong clicks. Unless you're a total HOG nut, you might actually want to skip this one altogether. The story has a few interesting and morbid moments, but it's not worth putting up with the bad gameplay, in my opinion.
- Very much like Weird Park. There's nothing damningly wrong with it, but the whole experience is rather drab. However, the HO gameplay is well implemented and the presentation is nice enough, so I still had some fun with it. One thing to note: This game's story is very closely tied to its predecessor. You might want to play that one first.

As a fan of the books my opinion can be a bit biased because I am not only playing the game but also reliving some of my childhood.
For the regular person experiencing just the game, its presentation and mechanics can feel a bit weird. The game plays like a tabletop game where a rigid, un-animated figurine travels throughout the dungeon doing "hops" as if moved by a human hand.  Imagine a beautifully 3D rendered world of a D&D board game. Something like that.
While crawling through the dungeon/mountain, items will be scattered throughout that might help you (or not) during your journey. As going through the book, every intersection, door, NPC or special event originates a pop-up with a textual representation/description of the situation and possible a decision to be made, sometimes depending of the items that you could have found. Such as, when finding a door, if can you bash it, knock, open, ignore it, etc.
Enemies will of course be found. When this happens, the map transfers you into a chessboard-like matrix board where you will face one or more enemies in a turn-based fight. For every turn, each creature (and you) will choose to either move 1 position in x/y axis or attack. When attacking, each creature has its own style. It can attack just one position ahead, two ahead, diagonally, an entire line ahead, etc. This is also valid for you and is dependant on the figurine you choose at the start of the game. Different attack types allow for different approaches and each has its own damage value.
Combat feels a bit weird in its design and I'm not sure i'm a big fan of it, but it's strategic in a way that it's mostly positioning and trying to predict where your opponents will move into so you can reach to attack them while they cannot. Regaining health is not that abundant and with a lot of combat in the game a careful approach is a good investment.
There are three base stats: Skill, Stamina and Luck, just like in the books. These 3 stats will vary greatly with each figurine of choice. They will be used either directly or for dice-roll-checks where virtual dice will roll to simulate the randomness and dice-rolling necessary that is then added to your base values.
Staming will be your life, Skill and Luck for some checks. Skill is also used in combat do determine the winners of "clashes" when you and your opponent directly attach each other's positions.
The dungeon is very well rendered, the text explanations and images taken from the books to complement the game feels very appropriate and a good hommage and respect for the original. Exploration is nice, there is a vast amount of forks along the dungeon that take you through numerous different paths that require some replays to explore fully as the progress rarely allows you to backtrack your advancements.
There are lots of figurines with different skills and attack combinations to increase replayability, each with their own "quest" that you are given to fulfill inside the Moutain.
All and all, it's a very peculiar game with many attractives but might also feel very off to someone that can not relate to what the game is trying to accomplish.

This game is a fantastic rpg. The storyline is extremely quirky and rediculous, definitely not something to be taken serious if you're coming from something like Final Fantasy. The gameplay is where the magic begins. It's a tactics based rpg in which you essentially keep leveling up. As far as I'm concerned, once you finish the main story line, the only real goal is to simply see how absurdly powerful you can get, which wouldn't seem like a very deep concept, but is somehow extremely addictive.
The level cap is 9,999. Yes, almost 10,000 levels. Not to mention, you can reincarnate whenever you want, further increasing your stats with every level up. For example, a level 200 character is typically pretty weak. If you say, level up to 5000 and then reincarnate and THEN level up to 200, you now have a hell of a character. You're also able to level your equipment, skills, and expertise with weapons. Virtually everything is able to be trained. You also have the ability to create characters, modify how strong/weak enemies are, how expensive/rare items are in the shops etc.
Ultimately, it's a fantastic game if you have the time to put in to it. Once you start hitting post game levels and manage to overcome the initial difficulty, you'll start powerleveling pretty fast and that's where things really get entertaining.
Did I mention how disappointed I am that Pleinair isn't available? :'(

I've just finished the first part, and am about 1 hour into the second game arch.
This game is fantastic. The gameplay, the story, the art, the sound - it's all done so well.
The game sets you up with a backstory which isn't unique to each time you start up the game from what I've been able to tell, but it's written well enough to support the rest of the story. Soon after the game starts, you must choose your crew members for your expedition that each bring different skills to your campaign as well as three character traits that vary from peaceful, aggressive, cautious, pious, racist, etc.
As a general tip, choosing expedition members that are similar will make your game easier, considering that a lot of the choices you make along the way will favor certain character traits above others, which will either boost or lower your individual members' morale depending on which choice you made. I ended up choosing a varied group that made the game a bit harder. On one of my saves, I had a mutiny due to the choices I made and just some general bad luck.
The game does a great job with presenting you different choices along the way that feel authentic, with very little circumstances where the choices didn't matter or felt like there was only one "real" choice the whole time, as is often the case with games of this type. There are no true "right" choices, especially when dealing with groups that are either pious or racist, and later on in the game you will actually have to think about some choices because either way you're going to have a bad time dealing with the political consequences.
I found the combat to be simple, and completely engaging. The majority of your battles will deal with 6 of your expedition members. Each battle proceeds the same way, usually: you are notified that you may "begin battle"; you must choose 6 individuals for this battle, with the ability to move equipment around and read their stats before you make your selection; you *may* have a preparation phase depending on the circumstance where you can set up traps on the board, or position your units in more advantageous ways; your turn is usually first, and is played by A) moving your units if you choose and B) Attacking with your units if you choose; then the opposing force has their similar turn; you do this until you either win, lose, or surrender; after which, you will have to treat your wounded individuals with your doctors and whatever medicine you have available. It’s worth noting that you don’t actually lose units in battle. Instead, you lose them from your inability to treat them afterward.
I haven’t finished the game, but so far it is completely engaging and fun. My expedition has a total of 14 members so far, and I believe I may keep it at this level because it *right* at the line of being too much of a drag on resources while still being able to achieve a lot via their character abilities.
Pros:
+ Amazing Art
+ Great Story
+ Fun/Addicting Gameplay
+ Difficult, especially in the beginning
+ AWESOME level design - very creative ways they implemented different battle scenarios.
+ Great UI design, with tooltips available to almost everything in the game, which was a great way to keep the player informed with all sorts of data without creating a cluttered UI.
Cons:
- The only thing I can really say if I HAD to be critical, is that it feels "indie" only during the few cutscenes they had. Instead of moving animation, they were still graphics with subtitles. They could have made these parts more engaging just by adding sound, music, and acted dialogue. However, there have only been 3 (more or less) of these cutscenes so far, and the rest of the game is so well done that it doesn't feel like an indie game at all when it matters.
- I would've liked to see more sidequests. This may be a plus or a negative depending on how you see it. The game creates an engaging story for the main campaign, but neglects any sidequests. I only bring this to attention because it says "RPG" as one of the tags, so it is worth noting.

Like many others, ignore my play time.  I downloaded this via steam, just so I could write another negative review among the masses, so that it the reviews would reflect the state of the actual game, instead of the Early Access reviews.  I played a Harani on Kyrios, as part of <The Soggy Potato Trading Co>.
Play as a pirate?  Kill your own faction?!  CARS?!  BOATS?!~?!  I'm on a boat~ I'm on a boa- wait a minute...*
ArcheAge had a lot of potential, and I was part of a group of 8 friends who decided to play the game together.  We all got to 50 and had a lot of fun, but it progressively worsened.  There were many problems that Trion simply did not fix, and I'm just going to write them as a list, instead of a wall of text for people to decipher.
1. Bots: After the implementation of needing to be lv15 to use the Faction and Nation chats, a surge in bots appeared, impeding the ability to complete some quests in a timely manner.  I took a screenshot of nearly 100 bots in a small area, killing all the mobs as soon as they spawned.
2. Hackers: The most obtrusive problem with hacking exists in the form of claiming land.  Farming crops and trees is a main part of the game, so to protect your plants while you are away, you need to own land in the game.  To own land, you must have the Patron status(which is basically a subscription service), but sometimes people quit the game, or decide to stop caring about the land, and it becomes open to be reclaimed by anyone willing to try.  The problem is that there could easily be 20+ people waiting next to the plot, hoping to be the one to claim the spot, but it will be claimed by someone hacking, sometimes by a toon that is halfway across the continent.  It's a guarantee at this point that you can only get land by hacking or buying the plot from a hacker.  This was a problem before Auroria was launched, to which most land on that continent was claimed by hacking, and it remains a problem many months later.
3. Pay2Win: With the launch of Auroria, came an increased need of a material known as Thunderstruck Trees(can be broken down into Thunderstruck Logs).  These materials were set at a reasonably high price in the economy beforehand.  It was something that only occurred as chance to any tree in the game, but with the introduction of the Rumbling Archeum Tree Sapling, there was a large influx of Thunderstruck Trees in the market, and for a few days, the prices of nearly everything in the economy was unstable, at least on my server.  These tree saplings still exist in the game as something you can buy with real money, and while I do not know how much of a value they hold now, it was just one of many things introduced to create a significant advantage to those willing to spend more money on the game.  Patron Status already had large advantage over free players, because of the Labor Point system.  Coercing players to create AFK macros to stay logged in the game, so they can actually do something in the game that earns in game money.
4. Unbalanced Class System: Something alluring about ArcheAge was the relatively large amount of classes the game has, but in the end, there were only a few viable classes with specific skills needed to survive.  There were classes that could either 1 shot, 2 shot, or 3 shot, anyone that wasn't one of those classes.  While gear matters quite a bit in the game, the class has a much larger influence.  If you're wondering why that matters, then you're simply limiting yourself to less than half the available gameplay, by playing how you want.  Going out to sea, which is roughly half of all existing playable area, would just be you going out to get yourself killed, and probably your ship getting wrecked by pirates or anyone doing pirating activities.  Yes, that's right...  Your ship can #GetRekt
5. If you need a number five, it's there and more, but I'm done wasting my time on anything related to ArcheAge.  Unless someone else were to manage the game, and spend the time to really fix it, it will be a broken, unplayable mass of data.  Occupied by bots and hackers.  Floating in the void of the internet.  If people are still playing this game, they need to #FindJesus.
*That was the only humorous line, in the entire review.

I am incredibly excited to say that this game is all that I could have asked of Larian Studios. As someone who loves Dungeons and Dragons, Pathfinder, etc, Divinity: Original Sin 2 simply blows my mind. The dialogue can be witty, comedic, even tongue-in-cheek, but at times it is also grim, dark, and serious. Each character has their own way of coping with situations, and you as the player must work to keep the group together. You can choose the class of all of your adventurers, and tweak your main character at the start screen - in effect, you can multiclass from the get-go. Abilities synergize and can create opportunities that can be exploited by other party members - or, if you're not careful, by the enemy!
In terms of customization, the game is lovely. In summation, you can advance your character in a non-linear fashion if you so choose, but you might find it easier to create classes that are symbiotes (they benefit from each other's abilities).
In terms of audio, the game is FANTASTIC. The voice acting is wonderfully immersive, and the sound effects are well-timed and well-orchestrated. Speaking of orchestas, the soundtrack is incredible. If you don't believe me, give it a listen on YouTube. The ability to choose which instrument will play at turning points of the campaign really gives you that feeling of audio customization, and lets you feel like you are in control of every aspect of the game.
In short, I may sound like a "yes-man" when I wholeheartedly recommend this game. I may sound like there's nothing wrong with the game, but there are several bugs which are still unfixed and exploits that can be exposed to the savvy gamer. But, if you are like me, and you simply enjoy a game for what it has to offer (a complex storyline, diverse characters, entertaining combat, excellent audio, above-average graphics), then this game is for you!

At first glance, my 23 minutes of playtime might put you off of reading this review but bear with me for a second. LuckCatchers, I'm fairly certain is a game made in Russia that was poorly translated to open it up to an english speaking audience. The loading screen starts out with some Russian text that I could not interpret. Next you are brought to a main menu with no sort of pretext or introduction. Upon searching the UI for 2-3 minutes, we found a plus button at the top of the screen where we could make our "Avatar". I had two race options, an Orc or a Human. The lore for each of the races was pitiful (only about 1 or 2 sentences long). There was no sort of character customization aside from a portrait change that required you to spend "real life" money to acquire.
Upon hitting the play button I was thrust into a multiplayer world. There were several common elements present, such as a health bar and my character portrait. However, those were the only familiar looking things to me. I only received a few tooltips about how I should take a job to earn money and no other sort of gameplay elements were introduced. I had to ask the world chat (which was split up by russian speaking and english speaking peoples) how to even launch my airship. From what I could gather (as there was no sort of lore) this was a sort of trading game where you ventured city to city doing jobs and selling goods. To do my first job I had to travel to a city 8 miles away and I received a bit of money. So I loaded up my cargo hold with the goods (which was arduous enough in itself to find) and began to travel to my destination.
There were a few options present that allowed me to control my ship. I could change my altitude, change course and check my cargo. There was however, no  option to attack another player, despite the game claiming you were able to, and again, no tutorial to tell me otherwise. Upon reaching my destination after about 8 minutes, I unloaded my cargo and received my pay.
At this point I thought I was getting a feel for the game and I decided to try and tackle some higher paying jobs. The only high paying jobs available required you to have submit a security deposit greater than the payout of the job. This was the point that I stopped playing because I saw no feasable way to progress without my spending a good portion of time trying to figure out the game's unintuitive UI or paying real money.
Tl;dr: An untuitive trading game attempts to simulate creating your own trading empire, but falls flat in so many categories (even in the first 20 minutes of gameplay), I would avoid this one.

tl;dr: This game is really good. For a dynamic and enggaging combt system, a less-than-toxic community, and an overall good time, I recommend this game.
If you're like me, and you enjoy an mmo experience but hate repetitive combat with no real fun or purpose, then you should give this game a try. There is a huge amount of fun to be had in this game! Many MMO traditions are thrown out in favor of creating engaging, dynamic combat.
For starters, Elsword takes an entirely different approach to how it is played by using a Side-scrolling Beat-'Em-Up format. By removing the average open world gameplay, and instead using this format, the game has an easy time creating a fun combat system. If one wanted to, they could forget all about the MMO aspect of the game, as it is never overbearing about player interaction, and is more about combat and leveling up.
Speaking of leveling, the playable characters in this game are done pretty well. Like some other MMOs, this game lacks a true character creation menu, and instead provides several premade characters with their own moves, special attacks, and fleshed-out stories. While this may sound restricting, this was never a problem for me. All of the chracters look really    cool, and each character brings an entirely new playstyle to the table.
Plus, there is a chracter progression system, in which you are able to access new special attacks and combos at certain levels. At level 15, you are able to choose a new class for your character. The class you choose can drastically change how you play, and leads into another class progression later on. A lot of the draw for playing new characters comes from this system. I spent hours just figuring out which character to play, and how they'd help my friends in combat.
This is, however, an MMO, so how are the other players? Well... I never really noticed them. No one ever bothered me, which is nice. You will likely only encounter other active players in the bigger towns, and occasionally in the battlefield. You can choose whether to involve yourself in that sort of thing; I personally chose to stick with my current friends. I'll say this: The community for this game is unobtrusive, and will not bother you unless you choose to be a part of it.
Overall, I enjoy this game thoroughly. At the time of writing, the Season 2 update just came out, adding upgrades and such to Elsword (the character) and Rena. I just hope that they game's creators will do something similar for all characters, as that would be a fun sight to see.
11/10 would spend too much time on this review again.

Hidden Object Bundle 5 in 1 is yet another series of Hidden Object games. As such, gameplay is conducted in fairly the same way as all the others: You get a first person view of scenes and you navigate with your mouse by pointing and clicking. Through the story you will find hidden object games, puzzles where you need to move pieces, or find pieces, or find pieces and then move pieces, and so on and so forth.
The bundle contains 5 games, I'll be quoting the store page here:
"Behind the Reflection 2: Witch's Revenge
A witch's quest for revenge spells trouble for a young mother and her son in this haunting hidden object adventure! Guide the mother as she pursues the witch through time and space to save her son from a fate worse than death. Interact with a variety of characters, find useful objects, and then use the items to solve cunning puzzles. [...]
Mountain Crime: Requital
Someone is killing the guests at a mountain resort, and you could be next if you don't solve the mystery at the heart of this chilling thriller! Take the role of a doctor who's summoned to a remote hotel to tend to a patient, and hold on to your sanity as you discover the first victim moments upon arriving at the retreat. [...]
Vampire Saga: Pandora's Box
With a chilling crime at the center of its spellbinding story, Vampire Saga is not intended for the faint of heart. Join Matthew Ward as he steals aboard a cargo ship to escape the violence of the Spanish-American War, passes out and then wakes up to find himself alone with several sinister-looking coffins. [...]
Weird Park: Broken Tune
Take the role of a private detective hired to investigate a rash of "accidental" deaths that befell those who worked at the park before city officials shut it down. Search for clues as you explore creepy carnival environments, solve puzzles as you pursue a mysterious joker down shadowy paths, and find hidden objects that can help you solve the mystery of a portal that leads to a realm beyond insanity.[...]
Twisted Lands: Shadow Town
[...] Welcome to Twisted Lands: Shadow Town, the first game in a new saga that will explore the emotion of fear. Guide the actions of a man as he searches a deserted island for his wife, who disappeared when their boat crashed on the shore. Along the way, gather hidden items, solve hair-raising puzzles and make one spine-chilling discovery after another as you draw ever closer to a shocking conclusion!"
Because they're all mostly the same in general terms, I'll be reviewing them as one item.
The puzzles are extremely easy to solve. In fact, in one of them I was solving them so fast I kept glitching the game every time I would get the reward or need to move a piece - they would end up disappearing and I had to go back to the menu and back into the game to get the item.
You can tell some of the games are older. The game play where you don't have a decent map in half of them, the graphic design as well are easy indicators, some don't even have voice acting (and trust me when I say: that's almost a blessing lol). This doesn't mean they're bad, but it makes them challenging and more annoying as you need to backtrack several times to find your way to things. this isn't necessarily bad if you don't mind all the back tracking, and in a way sort of makes up for the easy puzzles, but for me it just didn't cut it. I missed having a map (I think only a few had them), and more than that, I missed using the map to fast-travel to locations. Those items were a looot of clicking away.
Story-wise they've done nothing new. Someone close to you gets lost, you're trapped somewhere, gotta find them or/and a way out... and all of a sudden you're a pretty dumb human who can't do anything. "Gee, I'm trapped in this room in a creepy old house, and I think there's a key under the ashes; but wait! I can't just sweep the ashes by hand!! I need something to sweep them out of the way!"
Screw that, I'm sticking my hands in if that key can get me out. And if for some reason I didn't really want my hands all ashy, I'd grab the nearst thing to get the key out, not go through 50 different things to get to a sweeper. :P
That, however, is a fault all HOG games suffer from (and I do mean all of them), so if you're into them you should be used to it by now.
Visually speaking the areas and the hidden object scenes are quite lovely. I liked all the details, the items were neither too hard nor too easy to spot, and they didn't go out of their way to hide them in ridiculous places, most the time. Characters, however, were rather hit and miss, leaning heavily on the creepy side of 'miss'.
The music and sounds were fairly good too, but the voice acting was truly, truly terrible.
If you're a fan of Hidden Object games, I would still definitely recommend this bundle despite its shortcomings. If you aren't, they might still be a good enough place to start, as they are better than the average - and hey! you get 5 in 1! ;)

The bundle is worth buying and offers good value for fans of hidden-object games. The individual games are not stellar, but most are pretty good. They are all straightforward games: none of them have achievements or bonus chapters.
Note that you can play the first episode for free (with ads) on Android, and I indeed recommend that you start there. Both offer a forgettable, very dumb story with many hidden-object scenes and puzzle/mini-games, but no real point-and-click adventuring. The hidden-object system is innovative, but ultimately annoying. Behind the Reflection 2 is longer, but is also woefully unbalanced, with some of the puzzles being ridiculously easy, and others frustratingly hard. I used the "skip" button a few times. This is the worst game in the bundle. (The first free episode is actually better.)
The hidden-object scenes use an innovative system, but it ends up being far too simple. Otherwise, the puzzles are OK and the gameplay interesting enough. The story is quite intriguing: various clues left around can help you figure out the mystery, though you can just wait patiently and have all revealed in the end. The dialog and voice acting are
, but that's the norm for this genre.
Though the resolution is low, and there are no animations nor voice acting, this is a solid, satisfying HOG. The hidden-object scenes are challenging, even hard, but usually fair. There is good point-and-click adventuring to be had, and a handful of puzzles. The story, though predictable, is revealed in a restrained pace, carefully building up on the atmosphere, well-crafted with graphics and music. The timing of the cut scenes is very slow, possibly due to using a "modern" OS, but just be patient and you will get through them. It's worth it for this lovely, understated little story.
A classic HOG, with good scenes and gameplay. If you play it in expert mode, you will get quite a decent point-and-click adventure that requires logical thought. The background story is spooky, but doesn't take itself too seriously, and there a few jokes. Fun!
Though there are a few excellent hidden-object scenes, and a handful of mini-game puzzles, this game is primarily a good point-and-click adventure set against a nicely designed and scripted spooky atmosphere. No voice acting, but that also means no *terrible* voice acting, which is too common in this genre. The one flaw is that there is quite a lot of backtracking to be done for the point-and-click work. Still, this might be the best game in the bundle.

This game has improved immensely from when I first played it.  There is a fair amount of lore scattered throughout the maps and they do a lot to tell the story of what happened in the Exiled Lands. While this is a multiplayer, online survival game--with everything that entails--it is not a completely empty single player experience.  The more I played this game, however, the more I began to think that the world Funcom has crafted would make for a fantastic, open-world single player experience.  Add in some friendly NPC tribes, the ability to level-up thralls with you (or have more than one follow you at a time) and the game would be fantastic in that arena as well.
As a multiplayer coop game, It is definitely worth it.  If you like to play alone, it is less so--it can become punishingly difficult and the world is simply devoid of any life that isn't trying to kill you.  This curtails one's ability to focus on exploring the vast world around without use of mods or the admin menu--which is realy unfortunate, because this world has the potential for SO much awesome adventure and exploration.  Here's hoping Funcom continues to pack quests, dungeons and more monsters and heroes into this game!

I enjoyed it tremendously.  Absolutely a unique experience.
Playing as a ghost was well implemented in my opinion.  They used what I found were convincing concepts in order to limit your navigation where needed, establishing clear rules from the outset.
The mystery-solving was great.  It reminded me of L.A. Noire some (but I much preferred L.A. Noire I must say, as a game and specifically in its mystery-solving methods).  My one problem with it is that there really isn't a penalty for being a poor detective.  It's up to you to challenge yourself by not selecting all the answers until you get it right.  Of course, your 'ranking' is lowered for each incorrect guess but that's not a gameplay penalty as much as a pride penalty.
The story was compelling and the voice-acting was brilliant for anyone with a name you learn in the game.  Unfortunately, most of the NPCs with names you don't know, are comically wooden and not remotely human.  I loved Joy, notable given I thought I'd hate an angsty teen written by someone that's not an angsty teen, moreover one that's meant to be comedic and have an attitude; the media don't seem to be good at that in general, so this was a nice change.
Then there's the voice acting in the ghost stories.  That was phenomenal.  The stories were well written and well performed.  Absolutely a brilliant touch.
I really felt connected to Julia, your wife in the game.  She's hardly in the game, but you can collect her memories, and they're written.  If you read them, you begin to develop a real sense of who she is.  I have to commend that sort of characterisation.
The main character is believable.  Probably someone I'd laugh at in real life (even though I'd still like him; he's a good person and he certainly takes things in stride), but I can't say I haven't known people like him.  And the writing and acting make that believeable.
Speaking of taking things in stride, that's one flaw in the writing; too many people take too many things in stride.  But that's negligible in the face of everything else.
The combat system isn't much of a combat system, but I felt it worked well.  In fact, had they called your one move 'exorcise' or something instead of 'execute', you could have had a true example of a great game utterly devoid of combat, where overcoming your enemy isthe best thing you can do for them.  There's a nice stealth element alongside the one move you have.
The dæmons are extremely creepy in design.  I love it.
The music is great, but I wish that in a place where it becomes tense for enemies, that it would become less tense once the enemies are neutralised.  It doesn't.  A minor flaw I suppose.
The game feels like an indie game and was developed by Airtight Games, who were apparently independent according to Wikipedia.  I say this because the graphics are rather poor compared to contemporary games, and like many indie developers, the engine used was the old UE3 engine, rather than what was most current.
There's a lot of history in the game.  Old Salem bleeds into the modern Salem as the main character (and all ghosts I imagine) sees things.  You can collect snippets of history, which were probably all accurate, as the ones I was familiar with were all correct.
Bonus:
I'm a linguist, and I liked that a lot of the accents were notably correct.  The game takes placein Salem, which isn't too far from Boston.  I'm very familiar with the Boston accent as it's rather high-profile in dialects of English, and moreover as it has a significant Irish influence.  I'm not terribly familiar with Salem's accent but a lot of characters possess Boston traits so I assume they were trying to localise the accent at least as Massachusetts, which is really interesting to someone like me.  Also, a lot of Irish turns of phrase are used, which on looking them up are apparently common in that area of America, from Irish emigrants.  Nice.  Not only that, a lot of people have Irish names, which is rather realistic and once again interesting.
Oh, but the old-time Puritan accents were cat.  Absolute rubbish they were.
Speaking of cats, you can possess cats and meow and climb things and jump on things.  Another nice touch.

THE SHORT REVIEW:
Great RPG with good 3D graphics and a very interesting cast of characters.
THE LONG REVIEW:
I've been playing computer games based on Fighting Fantasy gamebooks since the ZX Spectrum days and I can say this is the best one so far by a wide margin.
Unlike previous Tin Man Games gamebook adaptations, The Warlock of the Firetop Mountain is not just a pen and paper gamebook with an electronic interface.
The Warlock has something for everyone. It has the original illustrations from the original book by Russ Nicholson, but it also has gorgeous 3D graphics. All the classic scenes from the book are there, from the drunken orcs to the final duel against Zagor, but there are also new locations (such as the Magic School or the Domain of the Dead) for those like me who read the book in the 80s. And of course, plenty of Easter Eggs for FF fans!
To me, the most interesting change from its literary source is the cast. In the book, you are an unnamed adventurer in a dungeon crawl whose morality (kill a wizard and steal his loot) is... questionable, at best.
However, in this version, you can choose from twenty different characters, each with a very interesting background (often tied to other FF books, such as City of Thieves or Creature of Havoc) and unique combat moves. My favorite is Lynette, a badass redhead paladin.
Only four characters are available at the beginning, but you can unlock others paying "Souls", the in-game currency, increased every time you kill enemies or complete a quest.
The best thing is, since each character has their own storyline and special abilities, replay value is huge, because the gameplay completely changes depending on your chosen character.

So, basically, this is a followup to Euro Truck Simulator 2, but taking place in America.
If you don't know what ETS2 is, then it's basically a truck simulator that takes place in a compressed version of Europe which is roughly 12 times smaller, and the cities are really only represented by a small industrial park on the outskirts (although you can often see geographical features in the distance that you can't actually drive to).  It's meant to capture the experience of hauling cargo between shipping depots and warehouses, and so only really includes buildings relevant to that job (so shipping depots, ferries, tunnels, truck dealers, service stations, repair shops, garages, etc).  If ETS 2 has a "point", it would be to open a garage in every city.
American Truck simulator is that experience, but taking place in (for now) California and Nevada.
This is better understood as an expansion/sequel to ETS2.  It uses exactly the same engine as ETS2, the UI is identical, the features are identical, etc.  The main differences are that ATS only has two kinds of trucks right now, and the map is different.
Now, for a $20 game, this isn't really a problem.  Another state is coming (which will be released as free DLC), which will add three states worth of area to the game, which is probably roughly about as much area as ETS2 had when it first came out.
The other thing that needs to be highlighted is that ETS2 has a
mod community.  There are maps that expand the Europe map well into Russia and North Africa.  I can assume that the mod community is going to expand with this title, and start creating some more states to attach to the existing map.  There are also countless truck addons that exist in the mod community, which isn't currently hooked up into Steam Workshop (which is probably for the best).  If you're interested in that, you should exercise some google-fu and track some down.

First things first: Expeditions: Conquistador its NOT a game for everybody. It is a HARD game with LOADS of text and a dense historical and political context. If you dont enjoy reading walls of text and cant handle defeat stay away from this game.
That said, I'll list the pros and cons and at the end give my overall opinion:
Pros:
- Rich, interesting and unexplored historical setting. For lovers of history (like me) this game came as a refreshing breeze.
- Combat is well developed, complex but fun though it gets repetive over time. But its HARD, especially because the tutorial doesn't cover it very well. It took me about 3 or 4 hours of gameplay to effectively understand how to use the medic in battles and I can't say I mastered all the other 10 classes.
- Beautifully written story and quests that makes you feel involved with the game, with your own character and your companions, thus making the huge walls of text actually a pleasure to enjoy. The writters picked up the historical atmosphere and the political complexities of Precolumbian Mexico really well (apart the female conquistadores, seriously?!). Previous historical knowledge about the Spanish Conquest of Mexico is recommended for the utmost fun though the game presents you very well with the minimum necessary for enjoyment.
- Pretty interesting camping and resource micro-management. Not only the mechanics are very good but it also fits pretty well with the whole setting of the game.
- Your choices DO matter! Not much for the story development in itself but for your party morale (covered in the next item)
- Companions are very well written, each with an unique personality and historical background. This influences the way they will react to your decisions. Managing their different personalities and maintaining an overall high morale is essential for sucess in combat, making party management a vital part of the game. I just missed an option to directly talk to a companion, instead of waiting for random events with or about them to pop up.
- Nice Soundtrack. Not really a masterpiece but fits well with the overall climate.
Cons:
- Graphics are simple for a 2013 game. I recon this is an indie game with limited budget but in my opinion they really could've been better, especially in the world map.
- As I've said, this game is HARD. One random event or one small mistake in battle or in camp management can ♥♥♥♥ up an entire gameplay. This can be very demotivating for most players and it is especially painful when added to the bad auto-save mechanics.
- Camera movement and trees. You will spend most of your time in the world map and the  top-down camera has its center always locked in your character. This hugely discourage exploring by making it very painful to see things far from your position. Wouldn't be a big deal IF collecting food, herbs etc from the map WASN"T essential to survive (There's a console code that unlocks the camera). Also trees not becoming transparent when you get near them can hide important collectables from your view.
- Bumping into enemies. When walking through the world map, you will sometime bump into an enemy patrol or hunting party. Sometimes you will have the option to not engage them. If you do so, after finishing the event, they still stay in your path and touching them makes the same event pop up again forcing you to fight them or to make a detour for progressing. This is a serious issue as even the easiest looking combat can turn into a complete disaster with one or two small tactical mistakes.
- Autosave: As said, this game is very hard and to add it up the autosave mechanic is very strange. I myself havent yet figured out how it works, so its safer to manually save often. Back in the days of Ultima and Breath of Fire this wouldn't be a flaw, but nowdays, in my opinion, it is.
Overall: Expeditions: Conquistador is a GREAT game for an indie company. It offers a lot of entertainment for it's pricing tag and it was a great efort by the guys at Logic Artists to delivery a solid and enjoyable game. Its cons are hugely surpassed by the pros and makes it a must buy for RPG, turn based combat and/or historical settings fans. Just keep in mind that this game is HARD and has LOTS of text in it before buying.

First off, if you are having ANY issues with the game performance wise, visually, etc. Turn OFF the enhancement/visual upgrades for this port. Character filter should be fine, but the other settings either look terrible (IMO) cause graphical glitches, or are reported to cause severe performance issues.
If you are having trouble with the game detected your gamepad, make sure your mouse is plugged in. There are also some people reporting the game running much better with a controller detected, I've only seen a few people say this and I'm not sure if that's truly the cause, the game runs fine on MKB with me, I just prefer gamepad.
As for the actual gameplay. There's MASSIVE MASSIVE amounts of content for you to go through. Essentially unlimited. The main story is quite good with probably the strongest story of the series and some serious character development for the entire cast. Plenty of hilarious moments. Gameplay wise this is the weakest of the series, only for the reason that the other games simply added on more and more mechanics and things to do. It's still a very solid game. The artwork for the characters is nice. It's a strategy RPG with some solid mechanics even in the first entry. And it just feels fantastic to wipe out a massive enemy and see your characters level up a dozen times.
If you like micromanaging characters, you can do plenty of that. You can level up every character hundreds of times. Re-level them from scratch with improvements to their next reincarnation over and over. Make your own custom units and do the same with them. Deck them out in expensive gear and then go into your gear (yes, you can go inside of a sword/gun/boots) and fight through dozens of floors to improve the gear's stats.
None of this is neseccary for the campaign for the game, only for the post game content. So if you simply want a good strategy RPG, this will scratch that itch. We get so few of these types of games on PC, so give it a look if you want a game like this. And remember refunds are a thing, so even if the game runs poorly you can always refund it if you are disatisifed. Two hours should be plenty to see if this is your type of game.
