ArcheAge is both the best and worst MMO I've played. I found the gameplay and combat to be fun and intuitive. The crafting system is very intricate, the housing and farming system was well done (I like non-instanced housing, it puts more value on property. It would be better if bots didn't claim all the land right away), and the Naval combat...oh man..this is what got me hooked on the game! Sailing around the ocean looking for enemy trade ships or fishing boats, stealthing into the water and swimming up to an enemy fishing boat and stealing and and turning in THEIR fish for your profit! I was so addicted to sailing the open waters searching for prey. It was one of the best experiences I had in a game.
But now, the game is sadly dying and at a rapid pace. The game is a blatant pay to win model. It is almost impossible to obtain end game equipment without paying a lot of money. It is incredibly tedious to even play the game without paying for Patron status for your labor regen and making a lot of gold in the game is practically impossible without patron status. Sure, you can get patron with in game gold. But to get in game gold, you need Patron, See the cycle? To break the cycle, you pay real life money for patron. But you want that shiny end game Delphinad weapon? It's obtainable. But it'll cost you at least 40k+ gold for a single weapon (at the time of this review). To get 40k gold, you can grind trade runs, but you need a lot of labor and it will take about 100 days (lots of math to pull this figure). And that's IF you have patron status AND you pay real money for the farm hauler upgrade AND you grind nothing but trade runs AND you are online the entire 100 days. Labor recharge is halved if you're offline. So what people do instead is spend a lot of money on RNG boxes that contain rare items or buy APEX (what people need to get Patron) and sell for in game gold.
The entire crafting/regrading (enchanting) system is RNG based. Which wouldn't be so bad if there weren't cash shop items that increase your chances of procing regrades. This appeals to the gambling habits of people and sucks in more money. As long as you keep paying money to Trion, you can keep crafting and regrading and eventually you will proc an end game tier piece of gear. And because people spent so much IRL money to craft the gear, it sells for unreasonable and unobtainable amounts of gold on the auction house. And the cycle goes on...
So props to Trion and XL Games for destroying one of the best MMOs out there. I hope all other developers can learn from them. Your game can be amazing, but blatant cash grabs and a pay to win model WILL destroy your game.

I don't know why I haven't reviewed this until just now, but its my 3rd favorite game of all time. There are so many good things to say about that I'm going to have to try really hard not to ramble.
1. The amount of lore is absolutely insane. It could fill entire books. This makes the Mass Effect universe seem so much more real and enchanting. You can tell that hundreds of hours of work went into developing the details of the setting. There is a detailed backstory for the game's variety of alien races and for the galactic history, for example.
2. You can't talk about Mass Effect without mentioning the characters. As usual, Bioware (the developers), have done an excellent job creating well thought out and developed characters. The numerous crew members who will assist Commander Shepard on his quest all have detailed backstories and fully fleshed-out personalities. They are each totally unique and extremely memorable.
3. Mass Effect 2 is revoloutionary in its roleplaying aspect. Out of every RPG, its probably allows the most freedom in how you choose to roleplay. Conversations have a cinematic quality and give you a variety of options. You typically get at least 4 options to choose from: a goody two-shoes type of response, a more rebellious response, a "neutral" answer, and sometimes the option to question NPCs for information. But it doesn't end there. You can also occasionally attempt to persuade NPCs my drawing on your charming nature if you have enough paragon points, which are earned by choosing more friendly responses. You can aslo intimidate them into doing what you want if you have enough renegade points, earned by choosing cocky or rebellious dialouge. There are also "interupts" or both paragon and renegade nature, where you can impulsively do something in the middle of dialouge. Are you sick of listening to this cocky mercenary ramble on about how tough he is? Choose an interupt and open fire on him with your gun before he finishes.
4. Mass Effect 2 goes the way of KOTOR or Dragon Age the way combat is concerned. It is a third person shooter but it is really tactical. You can pause the game and issue orders to your 2 current squadmates, or use Shepard's powers as well. You earn experience and level up as normal for RPGs. You will also pick a unique class when you create your character. Basicallly, the game feels like a smooth combination of old school D&D mechanics mixed with third person shooter mechanics. The combat is satisfying and unique in that it is action-packed AND tactical at the same time, while still giving you freedom to build your talents any way you choose.
Some people were dissapointed when it first came out because they simplified the combat a bit and made the talent system less complex. I played ME 2 first, so I may be biased, but I hated the talent system in Mass Effect 1. It was too complicated and very linear, not giving the player enough freedom. Mass Effect 2's talent system has a good balance: enough complexity and just the right amount of freedom.
If you love RPGs, buy this game. You won't regret it, I assure you.

This game is The Hero's Journey: The Game.
The quests can get repetitive but the main story is good pulpy stuff. If you grew up watching Hercules, Xena, and/or Highlander, Excalibur, Dragonheart, you'll love it. The gameplay isn't anything extraordinary but it can be fun thwacking hordes of bandits with your BFS spamming Enflame and Multi-Strike. The stealth is unnecessary. Fishing can be tedious, and escort quests suck but all you need is to make them wait, clear out enemies, follow. Magic is fun.
What can you do? You can slaughter a village and buy up all the vacated buildings, or you can lead the inhabitants out to a different zone and buy their property if mass murder isn't your thing. You can collect silver keys, treasure clues, and goofy outfits. You can change your PC's hair, tattoos, and clothes. You can grow horns if you go full evil-and you get a halo for being fully good. You can sacrifice innocents for a sick bow, you can trade goods between shops for a limited profit, join Fight Club, show off trophies, shoplift, go fishing, figure out what the hell the demon doors want, and walk around in your Union Jack undies.
It's ludicrously easy to gain EXP once you fully understand how the combat multiplier works in conjunction to Physical Shield and how much EXP carrots, red meat, fish, and combat-oriented actions pay out. Hint: eat 150 red meats (3xp) with a x20 multiplier to equal 9000 Physique XP.

But don't let it being short, deter you. I found this game to be quite amazing. The graphics are good, not the best cutting edge graphics, but still decent. The ghost abilities are great and it's quite refreshing to not have to walk around everything, just walk through. The voice acting was alright and the sound track suited the game even if it was lacking a little in variety. The lip syncing of the models when speaking was a bit off but other than that it was a pretty solid game.
This is NOT your standard action adventure game, you can't use weapons so there is virtually no confrontation and what is there is pretty basic and very easy.
I encountered no bugs throughout the game, it was solid and polished and I admire that. The story I found extremely captivating and the side quests with the ghost stories were quite chilling at times.
This game is played for the story and it just happens to be delivered to us with a nicely polished game. I could definitely have seen this game being pushed to 3-4x the scale with extra mechanics, locations, characters, side quests, etc introduced throughout and I'm a little sad to have hit the end since it left me hanging on to the story up until the end when everything came out in a giant twist.
For what it was, it was great and I'd recommend it to people but I wouldn't expect anyone to pay any more than $30 for it due to the length and lack of content within the game.

The premise is cool, the environments are pretty... but the game itself is a chilling purgatory of unfinished-feeling, clunky, boring slogs from cutscene to cutscene.
The whole game feels like they ran out of money, or time, or will to live - and just slapped together what they had at the time into the misshapen turd that was squeezed out of the interwebs and into my computer.
-the console-portyness makes my peepee wilt
-the controls are, at times, derptastic (especially helpful when flailing your view around a room to detect super esoteric clues)
-the demon 'stealth combat' made me want to gouge out my eyes with a spork just due to the PURE UNADULTERED TEDIUM
-after a few (uninteresting) base abilities at the beginning, gimmicky abilities are abruptly and unceremoniously shoved at you via random pop-up boxes of text, and then only useful a handful of times (mostly for unimaginative 'collect 67 spatulas in order to READ a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ghost story' sidequests)

For the record, I didn't hate the game (I really wanted to like it), but it wasn't fun - and I guess it's the waste of potential that really bugs me. I had high hopes for this game, but yet again the game falls short... Definitely not worth full price. luckily I only wasted a few bucks on it.
here are my unorganized thoughts on it:
you have a limited number of lives and very weak attacks, while the enemies have absurd amounts of health and attacks that cover nearly the entire itty bitty grid that youre forced to play on. there's not really any way to get all of your health back once you lose a large percentage of it in a battle. You only have 20 health to start out with, but the max you can gain back is about 10, so once you lose more than ten you will never be able to get it all back. The other thing is that you are forced to face 4 or 5 enemies at a time, so if RNGesus hates you and they all move closer to you at once, then all attack the next move, creatures that normally do 2 damage a hit, now wipe half of your health in one move. additionally, most of the hazards you encounter as you are traveling are purely scripted and your choices have no real say in what happens. The only time it does is when you come to a path/room with multiple exits and if you pick the correct one you go on your merry way. But if you pick the incorrect one, which there is no hint from the ungodly amount of reading you do that would indicate it as such, you lose half your health because you chose the stairway instead of the archway (it gives no other explaination why you got hurt for taking the stairs other than 'Oops, I guess you should've taken the archway').
What it comes down to is that the game has a weak story line, poor fighting mechanics, a nearly complete lack of items to use, and a nonstop stream of "gotcha's" that wipe your health, and the lack of ability to meaningfully regain health. Your ability to play this game does not affect the outcome, as it is entirely dependent on having the moves pre memorized and not on how well you paid attention to the story. The game has the potential, but in reality is garbage due to the shear lack of ability to affect the path the game takes... don't waste your life and money on this.

I drew some enjoyment out of this game but that doesn't mean I recommend it. In fact, I do not recommend this game.
The best summary I can think of is this: "Things go poorly and people die."
This is a game about being uncomfortable and frustrated, facing the harsh reality that enthusiasm and hope do not produce sucess. You will run out of food, and will have to decide who goes hungry. You will run out of medicine, and must triage your party to determine who should survive a failed hunt or even a spider bite. You will lose combat encounters because you are consistently outnumbered and have only the same options and attributes your enemy does.
The caveat is that despite all of your failings, the game will rarely, if ever, hand you a simple game over. Enthusiasm and hope may not produce success, but tenacity comes close. In the end, though, success in Expeditions: Conquistador won't  look like traditional video game success. It will look like you failed forward with some unknown force preventing your necrotic body and hollow spirit from simply dying and escaping this hell.
To reiterate and elaborate: I do not recommend this game. But, if you read all the above and still want to experience limbo and/or eternal damnation in the form of Spanish Conquistadors exploring Hispaniola and Mexico, by all means go ahead and purchase the game.

A turn-based strategy game about exploring Mexico as a Spanish explorer. Graphics and sound are fine, story is pretty detailled and there's a good amount of events to read as you progress through the main storyline. The setting is pretty unique to me (not used as much as a world war setting) but don't expect complete historic accuracy.
You travel across the overworld and do quests, events, collect resources, and progress the storyline with the end goal of returning to Spain. It's turn-based so there is a limit to how far you can move each turn. As you do quests and events, you get XP to rank up your followers (which improves combat stats, unlocks a skill and increases equipment slots). At the end of the turn, you're forced to camp, set rationing of food, and set tasks for your followers (gather food, convert herbs to medicine, convert supplies to battle items, heal a wounded unit, patrol for a chance to find supplies, and guard to prevent theft). The resources you have to gather are food (each follower requires 1/day), valuables (used as currency and how well you did at the end of the game), medicine (used to heal followers), equipment (used to improve follower combat stats), and craft supplies (used to craft battle items).
You can lose a lot of resources from theft so may want to end your turn off the road (which has a very high guard difficulty) if the terrain nearby is any better. In the second part of the story, you'll find somewhere to store your valuables (instead of carrying them around to be stolen). However, since you deposit in intervals of 100, you can end up with a negative balance (which is kind of weird).
The camera is an overhead camera that gives you some degree of control but there are a few quirks. Going uphill seems to mess with the zoom so after you go downhill you need to manually zoom out again. It feels like the overworld camera is restricted for artistic vision (you can only see so far ahead of you) but I would've liked to zoom out a lot more (with fog for unexplored areas and unlit areas to show vision range) so I could see further and reorient myself easily.
The battle camera is alright but I'd still like the option to zoom out more for a big overview so I could quickly check where each enemy starts at the beginning of battles (instead of holding alt and panning around).
In battle it would be nice to check enemy stats in more detail than rank and class.
You can only set waypoints on the map on points of interest, it would have been nice to create your own waypoints anywhere. It's a little annoying that your movement waypoint disappears if an event box pops up so that you need to set your destination again.
All in all, I enjoyed playing through the game. The story and events were the best part of the game for me. They were fun to read and it was nice you could roleplay a personality through different choices. The combat TBS part was good enough- there was unit variety, skills, combat cover, traps, and tactics. It's worth a try if you like reading story and turn-based strategy games like heroes of might & magic (without the fantasy setting- no magic/spell system).

I am torn. Do I give this a positive or negative review? I think I'll put it down as a positive one but do not misinterpret that as me saying you should play this game.
On the one hand, I really like the game, it's fantastic, probably the best MMO I've ever played rivaling even World of Warcraft in content, replayability, level design and genuity. The game also has a lot of amazing features that most MMO's just don't have. (Court cases, sailing, own-faction-PvP, a pirate faction to name a few.) For these reasons I have trouble saying that you shouldn't play this game. The reasons why I'd give this a negative review are personal and I will explain why below.
The developers for this game do not deserve the money. I've played this game since beta, got a maxed character with level 50 in every skill and 90k proficiency in 2 skills. I had 3 large pieces of land, a galleon and a nice set of gear, and I was in many of the best guilds on the Ollo server. I was also a part of the game's first full release Kraken kill. I also want to clarify that I had well over 800 hours played in this game before the game was released on Steam.
On the release of this game, the developers promised us that the game would never come pay-to-win, and for the first few weeks it didn't. (Although that may have been because they were too busy fixing the 8 hour queue times, not an exaggeration..) But, as time went on, the developers became more and more hungry for money. Now, whether this is Trion's fault or the fault of the company that originally created ArcheAge, (XL games,) and had more creative control is up for you to decide, but either way, I am not comfortable playing a game where I am able to be so easily screwed over.
I'd love to go into extreme detail on how they screwed us over but I'm not going to, but I will mention as many as I can without being too descriptive.
First of all they brought out boxes that gave out some of the rarest materials in the game very cheaply. You could buy them for real money. (Thunderstruck logs.)
They promised us 10% off the real-money currency in-game, but didn't give us that until 4-5 months after the game was released when many players had already quit.
They sold some of the rarest armour making materials in the game for real money, (which in turn translates into in-game money.)
They made it so you get more labor whilst being online compared to being offline. (This encourages you to sit afk on the server rather than log out, hogging server space. It also means there is no incentive to take a break.)
Sold the best gliders in the game to players for 20 dollars each, and took all of the best gliders in-game with distinct advantages over these gliders and nerfed them so that people could buy the gliders without feeling like it was going to be wasted once they got an end-game glider.
They released some end-game gear to the public right as a patch was released, making the weapons people had spent thousands on almost irrelevant. (This gear was designed to be released years after the game had been released to allow new players to catch up more quickly, but Trion decided to release it 3 months after release, messing up the economy hardcore.)
Refusing to deal with "land grabbers" who would hide in areas where you could build a house, and as soon as a piece of land was available they would instantly steal it before anyone else even knew what happened. These people were around for the first 5 months of the games release. (I assume they are gone now, but they might not be.)
Bots. They must love bots because the GM's hop in-game and tell everyone to "let them know where the bots are" and none of them were banned. Ever. I'd stand with a bot for an hour or so, PMing the GM every few minutes and it never happened. The GM's instead preferred to stand at the docks of Austera and spawn un-released ships for players to exploit.
Oh, and they have the worst customer support you've ever seen in your life. It took up to a month to get a response. Their live chat was also only available to paying members, so if your issue was about anything to do with not receiving your membership after paying then you were screwed.
This last one isn't really the same as a fault, but the game does not have spell queuing, meaning that people with lower pings have a distinct advantage over those with high pings. It essentially means that if you have a low ping, you can use spells more often, which literally means you have a higher dps. Here's a good video that explains it:
Anyway, for this reason I can not honestly recommend this game, but as the gameplay is good I'm going to give it a positive. If you don't care about the devs behaviour, then go ahead and play this game, you will like it, but be prepared for disappointment and poor decision making from Trion.
TL;DR: You should not 'play' this game, but you should 'experience' it.

This video-game-book costs 20 bucks... What is a mistake. It's interesting, some of the encounters are great, but only a very specific audience would be interesting in beating the game more than twice. I got it in a bundle
The major strength is the huge cast of characters you can choose from. Not only they have various combat abilities and base stats, but also different goals, skills and playstyles. A dumb minotaur-like monster won't climb on small ladders and persuade anyone to help him; an illiterate peasant won't be able to read signs, maps and books; various warriors will approach various encounters differently. However, the playthroughs don't differ so much that you would be excited about facing the first corridors and late-game mazes with an excitement. Because of that, the grindy "play and grind to unlock new characters" approach doesn't really support the experience.
If you can get it cheap as well, you may have quite a nice time playing it for maybe 2-4 hours. But don't expect it to be an amazing, 20+ hours game where "every time you play you experience something new".
Not every part of the game is equally interesting. Some parts are actually very boring and annoying, and parts of the game have a questionable design. Killing your character for making one choice instead of another (not a "wrong" choice, just not the choice that the developers decided you need to choose to overcome a specific obstacle) is not very rewarding. One of the especially easy randomly generated mazes is not as much a maze as it is "find door A, find door B, find door ... F, walk, walk and walk some more without doing anything interesting". It tilted me pretty hard during the second time I got there.
For example, during the main-boss fight you have a couple of choices how to approach te encounter. You can even try to find a helpful item in the chamber he sits in to use it against him. However, the game doesn't do much to help you judge which route would be the best one, so you just pick blindly. If it's not going to help you, you just need to remember to choose otherwise during the next playthrough. It's not very fun if the game doesn't allow you to judge the situation and requires you to just take a chance.
I was also annoyed by not being able to explore the area more freely. You can very rarely backtrack, or rather - sometimes you can, sometimes you can't and you never know what the game is going to do.
What amazes me is that I feel like the developers try to make this game something really ambitious. They add DLCs, new characters, new events for the community and it feels like someone would like to turn  it into a masterpiece. I doubt it's going to work, though.

The reason I don't recommend this is that when you get to a high enough skill level, the gameplay drops to a level of absurdity that involves confusing the game engine by contorting your character's body in all sorts of ways that are impossible in real life, to cause the side of your weapon's hitbox to collide with back of the enemy's exposed hitbox. I.e. turning your character 180 degrees while cutting straight down (or stabbing forward) with a very long two handed weapon, trying to make the flat of the blade (not the edge or tip) touch your opponent's back at the last second of the swing. Your character being off-balance and stumbling forward gives you a great range advantage when you can spin on your heels with the mouse to guide the already finished strike (but still active hitbox) into your enemy. This is just one of the styles to guide a vertical strike of any kind for a hit, and there are many other awkward and unnatural ways to make contact and kite with different weapons at top level play.
I'd recommend this game for casuals since its fun when its casual vs casual, but then those casuals end up having to face the pros on the same server and don't have a prayer because of the abnormal weapon styles.
The devs missed the mark with this one by a small margin, and hopefully a sequel to this game might be able to improve on some of the failures from the ground up with new code.

A fantastic title that reminds me highly of Fantasy Flight Games' X-Wing Miniatures series, Ace Patrol is a turn based strategy game focused on WW1 air combat. Each side takes turns performing various maneuvers with a handful of aircraft from America, France, Germany and Britain. Most missions are simple, ranging from one on one ace combat, reconnaisance, bombing and zepplin attacks.
Pilots add another layer of strategy as they level up with successful kills. Each level allows the player to choose from three different sets of maneuvers for that specific pilot. Should the player keep damage levels above 50% in a scenario they will gain a part unlock to attach to a plane. This comes in the form of accuracy, damage, speed and maneuverability upgrades.
All in all, a wonderful game with high replayability. Recommended at any price!

That alone, especially if you always wanted to experience the genre but were turned off by the above, is enough reason to try this game.
But I understand that's a very personal stance, so let's speak objectively. The art direction is fantastic, the setting is satisfying and rich, the gameplay is a bit trial-and-error at times but it's only a problem if you absolutely must get that S-rank (remember, speed > efficiency when it comes to that). You're actually encouraged to treat your soldiers as people and not cannon fodder, because their individual potentials synergize with each other and friends will team up against enemies. So in short: if you didn't play this game on PS3, play it now. You won't regret it.

It has a lot of attention to detail and in general a lot of  has been done to realize a game that does what it intends to do well. In the details I mention you will find crew members being jettisoned out of a ship that is about to be destroyed, radio chatter with all sorts of sane or insane messages, a good variety of weapons, subsystems, ship hulls. Also, ship designing has been implemented well and smartly. You can store up to 3 ship designs per Hangar (you have 3 hangars! and of course 3 ships at the same time) with 4 different ship sizes.
Combat can be as involved or automated as you prefer, depending on the ship hulls and systems you equip on them, and it's nice to unlock new types of hulls by destroying ship hulls you don't already have unlocked. Also, you can have a tractor beam that automatically picks up stuff left on the map. In terms of weapons you can use cannons, lasers, drones (even stealth ones!), missiles (and torpedoes, with various effects), mines and deployable turrets.
Exploration is simple and fast, each systems needs to be unlocked by clearing the blockade that gives access to it (or by bribing the guards), provides new missions as well as farming for either Rez (ore, needed to modify or rebuild your ships), goons (crew, needed to repair your ships faster) or data (experience, needed to upgrade your ship systems) and all three resources are quite useful and integrated into the game perfectly.
On top of all that, you generally follow a main story line towards the center of the galaxy, you can set the number of systems you want (default is 225 but you can go quite higher).
Overall, this game is great value for money and can provide many hours of fun, so I definitely reccommend it and will definitely look into SPAZ 2 (which is in Early Access but almost at release at the time of writing).
Have fun!

The game itself is fun in my opinion. However, it is also good and bad.
Here are some good points on why itself is good:
I rate it 8.5/10
-Controls are easy
-Fun/addictive
-Many different characters to choose from as well as many variations via Job classes etc.
-Lots and Lots of combos
-They consistently bring up new content and updates
-Fun with friends
-Major co-operative game and is dependant upon teamwork
-If you don't plan on wasting cash on this game then there's always new unlocks, items that you can have with a time period (Kind of a downside)
-Dungeons are great to mess with.
-There's a PvP
Here are the major downsides of the game itself and in my opinion should be fixed:
-Pay-2-win. You see, for example, they release out a new cool and awesome character. And you really wanna be good at it or play it alot or in fact enjoy it. Ahem, well, you're going to have to check your wallet if you wanna enjoy it to the core. Hint hint whispers* There's a time period.... All the good items will disappear... Pay me if you want it all back..... That's right,that is the message they're giving you. I mean you don't have to spend a single buck on it, it's really up to you.
-Some characters combos are bad and lack of it. In the game's description, it says "Amazing COMBOS!!!" no, not really PVP players spam out "ZZZZZ" ">>ZZ>X" or "ZZZZX" and "ZZZXZ" They also spam skills.
-PvP is unfair and not balanced, based on my experience, I myself was a previous Grand Chase player, the base of Elsword. And so when the game had to shut down I gave this game's PvP a shot to see how fun it would be. But nope instead it gave me a LVL 70 beater who kept calling you noob if you managed to get an edge. So if I were you, I'd level first before PVP and/or if you want to be lvl 70 or 80 wait for an update because they usually level boost any characters.
-The costumes have stats??? To me this is so unneccesary I mean really??? Stats? Desperate to be stronger are we?
-The pay-to-win players, Are 100x better than you if you don't spend a buck on this game. And I'm not saying that you should but it's your choice. But anyways they're better than you in every way via Items, weapons, and armor.
-The basic mechanics on this game are complicated via in order to check mail you must go to a certain place instead of  being automatic.
Conclusion:
Overall, this game is both bad and good, it could get revised more often to make it alot better. So if you're looking for a fun side scroller/ beat em' up game then this is for you. However, if you think my review made it sound bad and you don't want to get it's up to you really. But I'm not trying to make this game sound both good and bad but this whole review is just basic knowledge that going to help you if you're going to get the game. I just gave this game a chance when Grand Chase close, so you should too. It's not the best out there but definitely not the worst. Bejeweled 2 Deluxe is a classic match-3 game, which has held up well over time. In it, you are presented with a series of maps which have a variety of jewels of different shapes/colors, and can swap any two adjacent tiles in order to get three in a row, which will cause them to disappear and those above them to fall, potentially causing a cascade. Additionally, getting either 4 or 5 in a row will provide special power ups which can also help.
In addition to the classic "high score" mode, there's a variety of other levels with puzzles where you try to clear the board, etc.
It holds up well after all this time, and is certainly worth the asking price (or especially a sale price) if you're looking for some classic match-3 fun.

I was excited about this game before it released. I think I got an e-mail from Amazon advertising it. After it released, however, it sort of just faded away; I never really forgot about it, but I would always look at its cover and sigh (I listened to the haters). I picked it up in a Humble Bundle sale, and when I started playing it I didn't stop until I finished it. It has now entered my (mental) top 10 list of my favourite games. I recommend this game highly if you're interested in a big production game that works a bit different to the current ones on the market. There's very little combat (or none at all; depends on how you define combat) but that's perfect for me. I actually would have liked to have seen even less combat, just to show you can still make an engrossing, captivating game.
So let's get down to the real question: is it worth your money? As much as I loved the game, I don't think I could recommend it at $29.99. There's just too little to do. I finished the game with just under 13 hours, and I went slow and did a lot of the collection achievements. You could easily finish this game in under 10 hours - maybe even 6 or 7. However, if this game comes up for less than $10, I would say get it because it really is a very nice game and a delight to play.

I wish there was an option to give games a mediocre vote rather than just 'yes' or 'no.' Since there isn't, I'm giving this game bundle a 'yes,' but only barely. Unlike the poster before me, I was able to download and run the games with no trouble (I'm using a laptop with Windows 7). I have different opinions on each game in the bundle, so I'm going to break my review into a section for each game.
_________________________________
Mountain Crime Requital. Overall Rating: 3/5
Plot: 2/5. You play a doctor who has been summoned to a secluded mountain resort, under the pretense that the owner has suffered a heart attack. Once there, you realize that the owner is nowhere to be found, and the other guests start turning up dead.
Voice Acting: 0/5. The voice acting in this game is horrid to the point of being remarkable.
Artwork: 3/5. The characters look awful, but if you can ignore them, the overall scenery is decent.
Puzzles and HOS: 4/5. The puzzles aren't bad (some may find them too easy). The hidden object scenes are set up so that you have to locate objects in order to assemble an item you need.The scenes are drawn nicely and are not too dark or full of unnecessary clutter. Occasionally there is an item that has been named strangely due to mistranslation.
Getting Around: 3/5. You are provided with a map of the resort, and when you open it, it will indicate areas in which there are actions to be performed. Unfortunately you cannot click on the areas and be instantly transported, so there is a great deal of backtracking.
_______________________
Weird Park: Broken Tune. Overall Rating: 4/5
Plot: 2/5. You play a journalist who is sent to investigate the disappearance of a fellow journalist at an abandoned circus. Once there, you begin having random sightings of a ghost clown and a midget dressed as a harlequin. As for the midget, he is supposed to be more than he seems, and is linked to a broken music record, which you find shards of throughout the game. Although he is supposed to be a major factor in the disappearances, the only interaction you ever have with him is seeing him darting around walls.
Voice Acting: N/A. Your character doesn't have any conversations with anyone.
Artwork: 3/5. The characters leave much to be desired. The overall scenery looks nice though.
Puzzles and HOS: 4/5. The puzzles are pretty good (some may find them too easy). As for the HOS, some are typical HOS, in which you locate various items, while others require you to find broken parts in order to assemble a useful item. The HOS are nicely done.
Getting Around: 1/5. There is no map provided, and there is a great deal of backtracking in order to figure out what you are supposed to do next.
________________________________________
Behind the Reflection 2: Witch's Revenge. Overall Rating: 0/5. I was unable to complete this game due being unable to find items that are needed in order to progress.
Plot: ?/5. This game is a sequel, so why wasn't the first game in the series included in the bundle? You play a mother who defeated a wicked witch in the first game, and now the witch has used her magic to escape jail, and has absconded with your son’s soul by using mirrors as portals.
Voice Acting: N/A. From what little I did play, there seems to be no voice acting.
Artwork: 3/5. The characters and their animations are poorly done. The scenery itself is nice though.
Puzzles and HOS: 0/5. Unfortunately the niceness of the art is trumped by the issues I (and other players whose comments I found on various forums) have with being able to find items we need to continue playing. The items are often hidden to the point of being too difficult to locate amidst clutter and things of the same color. To make the matters worse, is the hint feature in the game proved useless for me. I got stuck and clicked for a hint. It directed me to go in the church. I went in the church and clicked the hint again. Instead of showing me what to do in the church, it directed me to go back outside, over and over. On top of it all, I could not find a strategy guide anywhere online either.
Getting Around: 1/5. There is no map provided. Plus there is a great deal of backtracking to find items (or parts of items) you need.
_______________________________________
Vampire Saga: Pandora's Box. Overall Rating: 4/5
Plot: 3/5. In this game you bounce between playing a young man and his grandfather. You start in the 1950s as the young man getting a bizarre phone call from grandpa, in which he sounds distressed, and is claiming to have just killed a woman. You rush over to his house, and once you make it upstairs, you find grandpa has barricaded the bedroom door with furniture. He is outside the door, still insisting that he has shot a woman. He goes on to indicate that he knows this woman from years ago, and that she has tracked him down. It is then that the gameplay switches, and you are playing grandpa as a young man during the Spanish-American War. He is a deserter, who has stowed away on a ship. Unfortunately this ship is carrying dangerous cargo.
Voice Acting: N/A. The dialogue between characters is all text.
Artwork. 2/5. The characters are expressionless, rigid mannequins. Scenery is okay.
Puzzles and HOS: 2/5. Puzzles are okay (some may find them too easy). The HOS vary in enjoyability. I found myself having to use the hint feature an awful lot because some of the HOS were dark, so items were hard to see. In others the items were hidden behind things to the point only a tiny sliver of the items were visible. In others the items were placed on the very edges of the frame, so they were barely visible. Additionally, there are some items that are incorrectly translated to English.
Getting Around: 2/5. There is no map, and there is a huge amount of back and forth between areas. You will find yourself too often wandering between areas trying to figure out what to do next. In these instances, the hint feature will simply tell you "There is nothing to do here right now," instead of directing you to the area you need to be. Sometimes reading your journal will tell you what you need to do, but not often enough.
______________________________________
Twisted Lands: Shadow Town. Overall Rating: 2/5
Plot: 1/5. You play a man who is washed ashore after a boating accident involving him and his girlfriend. The town he discovers is within a dense fog, and is strangely deserted. The man believes his girlfriend must be somewhere on this island, so he embarks on a mission to find her. During his explorations, he finds evidence of a serpent cult, yet journals of missing residents and other shipwrecked people describe victims being transformed into fish folk with gills. I’m trying to see the connection.
Voice Acting: N/A. In this game, the only dialogue is between the protagonist and his girlfriend at the beginning, and it is all done via text.
Artwork: 4/5. Of all the games, I think this one had the best artwork. Though the characters still looked like mannequins. The scenery was very nice.
Puzzles and HOS: 4/5. Puzzles were okay. The HOS were well done- items were detailed, and some cunningly hidden, but still able to be found.
Getting Around: 1/5. There is no map, and there are a lot of different areas to visit, multiple times. So you will spend an enormous amount of time backtracking. The hint feature is helpful in that it will light up an arrow and direct you where to go.

I might be a fake casual gamer girl, but I'm a connoisseur of match 3 games since way back in the day.  No shame, no regrets.  Bejeweled 2 was the last of the really great old-school match 3s.  I'll tell you why!
Match 3 games, at their core, are just about matching and watching the matches, watching stuff fall and maybe cascade into more matches or blowing up and stuff.  It's a simple pleasure, and it's a kind of game that's always fun.  It doesn't require you to be in any kind of special mood, you don't have to not be tired so your reflexes work, you don't have to grind or farm.  It's just matching, and trying to get as far as you can until you can't match anymore, then starting over.  I love hardcore platformers and rpgs and all kinds of other more particular games, but Bejeweled 2 fills the gaps when I don't want to play anything else.
What do I mean by "old-school" match 3?  After Bejeweled 2, match 3 games started doing other crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥  They started letting you slide gems all the way across a line or column instead of forcing a match right next to it, which made these kinds of games way easier.  Just a little bit of challenge is important; this isn't They Bleed Pixels but it needs to not be completely mindless.
Games like Puzzle Quest and its sequels added rpg mechanics, but then you're spending time in menus (i.e., not matching things), and plus the computer cheats in that series and it's very frustrating.  Match 3 games aren't about frustration and menus, they're about matching.
Candy Crush is designed by the devil, and plus it sucks anyway.  Weird, offputting graphics, flat boring sounds, candy gems that fall too slowly and match in strange ways, arenas that aren't a simple square anymore and instead have holes and other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t going on.  Easily the worst match 3 I've ever seen.
Come back to Bejeweled 2.  If you add it to your collection, you will have something that will never not be fun, forever.  The gems look good, matches sound nice, after a match the gems fall really quickly, nothing about this game is designed to get in the way of just pure matching and watching.  It's very satisfying.
Protips:  Pick a gem type that you're going to ignore as much as possible.  Just don't match them until you have no other options (I like red for this).  Then you always have extra cascades happening from the surplus, and you've got a store of gems to draw on when you feel it getting close to No More Moves.
When you make a bomb gem or a clearing dealie (match 4 or 5), resist the urge to use them right away.  They can really help in later stages, when the game isn't being so generous with dropping things in nice orders, to shake loose some more matches.  Just be careful not to accidentally blow up your clearing dealie!  That always sucks.
Try to keep your matches low on the board.  If you match up high, you're eliminating the possibility of cascades from stuff above you getting shuffled around.
There's some RNG involved.  Part of the reason games went to letting you slide all over the row/column (or like Puzzle and Dragons where you can just put it wherever the ♥♥♥♥ you want) is that after a while, it will become impossible to make matches.  Sometimes you can get really far, sometimes not.  But Bejeweled 2 isn't designed to be played forever.  Just start again if you like, or go do something else.

There are many flaws with this game, still I quite enjoyed it (at a discount purchase).
- There are way too many collectibles (nearing 200). You need to collect a random number of things to unlock a story (e.g. 14 chainsaws). That's way too many and after collecting the necessary collectibles in the first section of the game I never did it again.
- Sometimes you need to collect clues and the prompt for them are very precise. You need to angle the camera in just the right way which is very annoying for a game that's focused on that.
- You need to battle demons in this game. It's by far the worst part which consists of teleporting between safe spots and trying to sneak up behind them. When I had the opportunity, I just ran by them to enter the next section.
- It can be hard to find your way. This is partially because you can just walk through walls which is disorientating. At a later point in the game you learn to teleport which makes it even worse.
- There are stealth section in this way where you need to guide your human partner while distracting guards by ringing the phone and other poltergeisty stuff. I didn't mind this is as much since it's easy and you don't seem to be able to fail (which I consider a good thing).
- You sometimes posses a cat and run through vents because... you're in Salem?
- There are (near) instant death traps and you die so incredibly fast, it's kindof funny? They just consist of black spots on the ground and are easily avoidable.
I enjoyed this game the best when I ignored the side stuff and just focused on the main case where you're trying to solve your own murder. I bypassed the demon battle sections as best I could. The cat scenes were ok but unnecessary. The stealth sections where you guide your partner was kindof fun. The main meat was the investigation stuff where you collect clues and try to figure out what precisely happened at the crime scene. I completed this game in 5 hours which is probably not worth it at full price but it was for me and I found that the story didn't drag.
Go buy it in a sale!

Crusader Kings 2 is a dynastic family simulator set in the middle ages and is a game that gets incedibly complex very quickly. The game has a steep learning curve, so only buy if you are prepared to spend a few hours learning the game.
The game has a lot of DLC, but Pardox's DLC policy is pretty good. Each major DLC release accompanies a major patch which includes some features present in the DLC. In addition, in multiplayer, everyone connected to the host will have access to the same features present on the DLC active on the host, ex: My friend connects to me, I have Old Gods active and he doesn't, He has access to the Old Gods features.
By default you can play as a Christian (both Catholic and Orthodox) landowner, or even a vassal of a land owner. Muslim and Pagan rulers are locked behind DLC becasue they are mechanicly different in many ways.
DLC I would recomend:
Sword of Islam (If you want to play as a Muslim, if not don't bother)
Legacy of Rome (Retinue!)
The Republic (Republics!)
The Old Gods (Earlier Start Date, Pagans)
If you like complex, historicly theamed games set in the middle ages, I would recomend. If not then this isn't for you.

This game... Oh my, is it good. I finally finished story mode, so I feel like I can give an educated opinion now, so lets get down to the details.
Hand of fate is a mixed card game and action RPG. On their own they are both average at best, but they complement and enhance each other very well.
You have two decks (Sets of cards, for those not familiar with the lingo): The equipment deck and the encounter deck. The encounter deck will be used by The Dealer to construct the levels you play on, along with the cards he add himself to help and/or screw you over. These cards can be everything from a shop to buy and sell items in, to assisting (alleged) druids with their rituals. You start the game standing on a card, and you can move to any adjecent card to get closer to the boss so you can beat it and win the game. Every card is initially hidden, so you have no idea what awaits you before you move to and flip a card (certain items can reveal cards under certain conditions, though).
A session consists of several levels, which are each constructed by a bunch of the encounter cards. For example 10 cards can build up a level, and one of these cards will be a travel card which lets you travel to the next level, where more cards will be used to construct it. Every encounter card can also have a golden symbol on it, which means that if you handle the encounter card in a certain way (usually defeating the monsters or getting another positive outcome), you will unlock more encounter and/or equipment cards.
The equipment cards in your deck are the cards you will be able to obtain during a session. You can gain these by completing encounters in certain ways, or buying them at shops. As you complete more encounters you will, as mentioned earlier, obtain more equipment cards. This increases your potential power for each subsequent session (you start every session with basic equipment, although you can obtain better starting gear as you progress in story mode). Like the Encounter deck, the dealer can also add cards to the equipment deck.
Equipment comes in seven different types: Weapons, shields, armor, helms, gloves, artifacts and trinkets (I suspect they are all rings as I haven't seen other types yet, but the category is called trinkets. Possibly for DLC down the line?). You can use one of each at a time, except for trinkets who are all active as long as you own them. Equipment can have both passive and active effects. The exception are artifacts, who only have activated abilities (they are your spells, basically).
There are two different modes: Story and Endless mode. Story mode will put you up against one of the bosses of the game
(SPOILER::::::
The last boss forces you to fight every single boss in the game, three at once four times
:::::ENDSPOILER).
In story mode you'll start with certain curses and The Dealer will add certain cards himself to your different decks as mentioned earlier. Usually these will be encounter cards. It is possible to just play a story session with almost any kind of deck (as long as it's not outright terrible), but specializing your deck for the stuff The Dealer will throw at you is probably a good idea unless you're like me and put as many "unfinished" encounters you can into your deck to unlock more cards more quickly (warning: this will likely result in a lot of rage as you try to unlock more stuff, fail, and get screwed over for the session).
I have yet to play a lot of Endless mode, as Story mode kept me occupied for a while (I've slept with my computer running the game and such, though, so take hours/played with a *grain* of salt). From what I can see, you don't get to construct your deck here (you use all your cards), and the session continues until you die. In addition every time you travel to a new level of the session the dealer will throw in more bad things you have to deal with (feel free to correct me in the comments if I'm wrong, and I'll update it. I'll play Endless mode more now that I finished Story mode myself, though). As you start without any curses, it's probably an excellent way to go for unlocking encounter cards.
Speaking of curse cards. There are two kinds of cards I haven't mentioned yet: Curses and Blessings. These are persistant effects that will buff or debuff you for the duration of the session (or, rarely, until a condition is fulfilled and it fires). Examples here can be spending food to counterattack, but doubling counter attack damage (a curse), or a lightning bolt striking down one enemy at the start of each combat (a blessing). Curses are usually really expensive to get rid of (at least the ones you start with), and blessings are expensive for their cost to obtain, and have varying levels of use. You could get a blessing which won't be of any use for an entire run, or a curse you will barely notice. On the other hand, you could also get really powerful ones which will be a great boon, or completely screw you over.
Whew, ok, only a few mechanics left to mention now. In addition to what's already been mentioned, you also have health, food and gold. You start with 100/100 health, and both your current and maximum health can change during the course of the run. Current health can be knocked down both by encounters, and by taking damage during combat. You spend 1 food every time you move, and if you run out of food every movement will cost you 10 health points. Gold is simply used to buy things at shops (equipment, blessings, removing curses, food, etc.). All these resources can be refilled through encounters, or purchased at different types of shops (selling in the case of gold).
The combat itself is a very simple Batman ish combat system. You attack and counter attack, and can dodge roll. You can also use the activated abilities of your different items. The combat itself can feel a bit sluggish (animations are a bit slow), but the controls are VERY responsive, and I hardly ever felt like I didn't avoid something which shouldn't have hit me. Combat itself can be triggered during an encounter card, and you will draw from the dealers monster deck whenever combat has been initiated by an encounter (although what strength/kind of monsters you can draw is usually decided by the encounter card).
Do I recommend this game? Hell yeah I recommend this game. It might peter out a bit after you finished the story mode and start just screwing around in endless mode (I don't know yet, although I've yet to unlock all the encounter cards), but so far it's been a LOT of fun. That said, it can be ridiculously hard towards the later story sessions (it starts out easy, though). If you don't mind the difficulty you should definitely take it for a ride. I'd be very surprised if you end up regretting it!

If you felt this isn't helpful at all, you can of course vote it down, but I'd appreciate being told what you feel is wrong so I get an opportunity to change my review if your points are valid. Have fun gaming!

This game is fantastic, a nice mix of deckbuilding, choose your own adventure and fable/arkham style combat, the narration of the game is comes from the card dealer, a kind of forture teller character who you could refer to as your dungeon master for the game.
Other reviewers have complained about the combat style, btu having played the game since it first came out on early access I can confidently say it feels Kinetic and viceral, while allowing the player to dodge and counter easily.  While the game might start out a bit easy the difficulty curve does start to ramp up as the game progresses.
The Sound design is very nice, the music in particular lends a nice fantasy feel, and does a good job of lifting the player up and making them feel good about their victories, and as previously mentioned the narrator keeps the player engaged at all times, even coming out with different remarks based on your actions that keep you wanting to push on.
The graphics are simple but look very pretty when turned up all the way, some of the small arenas may get repetitive at the start but once again the game does a good job of pacing itself, while adding new traps and environmental risks into the mix as play progresses.  The actual graphics style gives me flashbacks to the slightly cartoony aesthetic of the fable series.
I have yet to finish the game, but I am over halfway through it and so far it has kept me well satisfied and the developer has already said they plan to add more content based on community suggestions and feedback.
My only bit of dissapointment would be that there is no option for changing the look of the character, even a couple of presets would be nice, hopefully now that the game is out this may be added at a future date.
In conclusion, Hand of Fate is fantastic, and if you have any quarms about paying the full near £20 for this game (which I think is a very reasonable price for a game of this quality and length) then stick it on your watch list and grab it as soon as it does, I love it!

TL,DR; Awesome.
Let's start by summarizing by expectations: Seeing some EA advertisment, some mentionings on streams and a 25 letsplay (from July 2014), my expectations were: An Indie title with a love for detail, a rouge-like which revolves around cards and deckbuilding, stale combat with glitchy controls, bugged encounters and a short playtime.
Now, let's review those expectations after I played 11 hours (in one day), beating all 12 bosses (hint hint) and unlocking about 75% of all cards:
Is this really an Indie title? I can't tell, it's quality is pretty much flawless and probably higher then quite a few AAA titles we saw last year *coughUnitycough*. Does it have love in detail? Yes, pretty much. Except for a ridicolous animation bug in the intro, the whole game scene has an unique, authentic atmosphere. I love the card-laying animations.
A rouge-like revolving about deck-building? I think so, albeit I got to admit I rarely play rouge-likes. But the deck-building aspect is just genius. You enjoy every round, even the losses, simply because you progress in the Questlines of the various cards, adding new to your deck, recycling old... I love it.
Now, for the negative expectations: Stale, uninspired combat a la AC/Arkham and glitchy controls? No sir, the combat system is no doubt the same genre as AC/Fable/Akham (enemies surround you, you punch towards a target whilst blocking attacks from other sides, add in some special moves, etc), but it's very well done and so far I can't call it stale in the least. Maybe because I keep getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked against certain enemy combinations.
The controls are quite fine, too. Once you notice that TAB serves as back button, the menu controls start becoming much more reasonable, too, albeit you DO notice that the game was originally designed with gamepads in mind. In combat itself, I DO have the occasionaly moments where my character does not move towards the enemy/direction I intended him to, and whilst this is frustrating at times, it doesn't happen too frequently to be a major issue.
As for bugged encounter, I've seen zero so far. Must have been an EA thing.
What I need to add though: The complete lack of camera controls. At some points you won't notice it, at some maps it'S annoying and on some maze (aka trap parcour) maps the camera controls are outright hostile because you will NEVER see what is behind that certain wall. Might be a lethal trap there, or a path.
Summarizing, this is an OUTSTANDING game. Great art style, intricate strategic gameplay, mercyless (un)luck, challenging combat and one of the best atmosphere of any game I've purchased in the past months.
Really, the only complaint would be the control scheme for a non-gamepad user, but that's about it.

TL;DR A fresh take on turn based stratedgy gaming, with an interesting setting and plot, hampered by some very cheesy exploits/balancing and the PC port is good overall, but could be better. Controller recommended. Worth it in my opinion, it was one of the better games on the PS3.
I played a  bit of Valkyria Chronicles on the PS3, but rebought it on PC as I never finished it. The port is pretty good, though you should know that the framerate affects an important game mechanic called "intercept damage". Which means that as you move a unit, being within range and line of a sight of an enemy unit will damage the unit you are moving. So if you play at 60 FPS, intercept damage is twice as effective. Though I personally think it makes shocktroopers a little more balanced, they now do their damage/defensive role better. It also makes the game more difficult, and I like that extra tension myself. Besides, 60 FPS makes it look so much better in motion that I couldn't pass it up. There are also some mods that enhanced character textures and remove the white canvas border during gameplay segments that I appreciated asthetically.
Onto the game; it is an interesting take on turn based stratedgy, and it comes SRPG, Third Person Shooter, turn based and real time elements. The classes all serve a purpose, and while Scouts are a little too good because they can move so far each command, they all work fine and have interesting pros and cons. I found the shooter and real time elements were more appealing to me than usual SRPG mechanics. Also, each unit in any of the 5 classes of units will level up together, so you don't need to worry about micro-managing experience points I've been told happens alot in games like Fire Emblem. If one scout is level 10, all scouts are level 10. Though not all classes have to be the same level, so you could have level 10 scouts and level 8 lancers and level 5 snipers if you felt like pumping most of your experiences points into scouts. Though the equipment on each unit can be customized individually.
The story is actually really good, with the game set in episodic chapters where Cutscenes and Visual Novel elements tell the story in between the battles. The setting is a dieselpunk, alt history ww2 world, but with anime and water colour asthetics and I absolutely love it. The story can get pretty dark, with themes racism/antisemitism and loss, though it has brighter moments too. The characters that make up Squad 7 tend to be pretty interesting, and everyone has perks that represent their personality, some good and some bad. While these perks are not necessary, they add flavour and depth for those who seek it.
The game should take a while to beat, probably 20ish hours for the standard playthrough. With side mission skirmishes, include DLC missions from consolesand a new game plus to keep you playing if you really want to keep going. Though there is no multiplayer, which wasn't added until the PSP sequel Valkyria Chronicles 2 was released.

I was not all that impressed with this game. The first impression was good. The artstyle is lovely, the story was entertaining enough and at first glance the combat seems fun. But i found myself losing interest in the game quite fast.
Lets start with the story. The story so far has been interesting and the characters have been nice enough. Each character has a distinct look which is lovely and it great that this is also true for all of the characters in the squad. The story and the characters are certainly animehhhhh which might turn some people off but i have no problem with. They way they jump from being serious to lighthearted can sometimes be a bit odd but there is a certain charm to that in some way.
But my problem with the story is just how cutsceny the whole game feels. Every chapter is filled with cutscenes and there is also a ton of downtime in the actually missions. So far all of these cutscenes have contained no interactivity at all and there is just so much of it that the game feels more like a movie with some interactive parts than a game with some movie parts.
I did not personally enjoy this and i would have prefered if they either made the story more interactable or allowed me to move around in the base as a character and actually feel like a character instead of simply dropping a bunch of movies on me through the interface. But this is very much a personal preference.
The interface is by the way obviously designed for a controller even though it works alright with mouse and keyboard.
But the combat sections of the game is where i think that the game dropped the ball. There is some strange stuff in the combat that becomes very obvious very quickly. The hitboxes for stuff in the environment are often larger than the visual representation which is extremely annoying in a game where every attack matters.
The game is also full of invisible walls for your characters movement. At best this is simply annoying when it leads to you wasting movement points but it also forces you to go exatly where the developers wanted you to go. In practice this means that you can't go a couple of meters in the forest next to you to get a clear shot or to flank your enemies and i think that this is a very odd design choice for a game that is supposed to be tactical.
But there are just a bunch of stuff in the combat that does not makes sense. Crouching behind cover means that you get a defense bonus and immunity to vital shots. Ok fine, but these bonuses are still in effect when the attacker is at the same side of the cover which leads to certain units being able to take a silly amount of shots from an attacker which stands just beside them.
Some people might just accept this and see it as another rule in the rulebook that they need to take into consideration in combat. But the way is see it is that the rules should fit to the gameplay and the visual representation and this rule does not fit into what i think should happen if the player flanks and shoots an enemy behind cover in the third person perspective.
The AI is also quite weird and it often throws away a large part of its turn doing nothing. Which is fortunate in a way since it otherwise could quite easily screw you over. The way units return fire when its not their turn is very odd and the computer could really screw the player over if it actually just stayed behind and focused on a single unit.
In the end i just found myself forcing myself to play another chapter every evening and that is not a good sign. I can see how some people might really be into this game but it was not for me.

-1VS1 PVP in the arenas are heavily P2W and yield very little profit.
-Open World PVP depends more on group coordination and party makeup (Healers, melee, range, seiege weapons)
-PVE is based around the holy trinity. There are currently 2 endgame dungeons that drop gear and other dungeons that drop more specific/vanity items.
The game is hard to enjoy without patron, but once a player obtains patron they can easily make gold from offline labor regeneration to pay for the apex needed for next months patron.

The game is definetly not a bad one, but there are several caveats one should be aware about before deciding to buy it:
1) It has almost nothing to do with WWI/WWII settings or tactics (I saw many times it being advertised like it has), it just hasn't. It falls short in its attempt to recreate a WWI/WWII battlefiled (I doubt there even was such attempt at all), and actually it's a very casual and intentionally non-realistic game. So any hard-core fans of real life tactics and lovers of mentioned historical periods shouldn't expect it deliver any of those when buying. It's just an anime tactical fantasy game (yes, there will even be magic, revivial of old legends and stuff), slightly stylized to look like something distantly similar to WWI/II battles.
2) I don't remember when I last saw a game or a movie for what I could recommend this, but.. That's probably the rare example when english dub is actually better then original (japanese). Many will probably be objecting to this, but just a word of advice: if at some moment you'll feel infuriated and frustrated about how unbearably voices of many characters contradict the overall setting and the scene you currently experiencing - just try to switch to english dub (can be done any time, from the main screen); the odds are you'll find it much more.. not better, but more appropriate, lets say.
3) As I already have said, the game is very, very casual. It may not seem like this from the first glance, but many of these features you are looking at (like all these special trates etc) make almost no difference in most cases. Yea, some negative trate could screw you a turn or two, and latter in the game you are even allowed to trade some firepower for range or chance to inflict status effect when arming your soldiers... but doing bad choices here rarely will screw your mission, not even close to what could happened in really complex tactical games, like jagged alliance 2 or 7.62. In the end I stopped care at all about all this, and just chose people based on their speciality, and their looks (:)). And when it comes to actual battle, it's not getting better. Yes, the gameplay is fun, and somewhat addictive, but, you know, so is the gameplay of Zooma, or Plant VS Zombies. You got the point. If you like deep and complex tactical games, this game will fail you.
4) A plot.. is okay, I guess. In my 14-18 I would had said it's great, but all these "burst in tear" moments and "horrified by knowing how the world is actually works" moments just won't solicit any emotional response from older audience. That's like a very polite and censored introduction to the world of armed conflicts for kids.

The current early access status of the game shows quite a bit of promise, but at its current form does not have much to offer. The game is somewhat slow and built more of an RTS civ builder rather than an RPG as it is described above. It still seems interesting, but there's not enough to the game to really intice people to continue playing after they start the game itself. The opening area is confusing, as you may not know where to go at first. Controls are wonky but it's early access so theres no deducing points for that. I personally would say that the game would have more positive reviews were it built as an open-world RPG rather than an RTS civ builder. An RPG aspect would give the player a sense of adventure, gaining a ship would give a player a view of the world from above, and the combat aspects of an RPG would give the player an invigorating feeling as a fighter.
Although, as I say this, the game is still interesting. It has some gameplay concepts which make it complicated and require the player to think a bit before acting. It also allows you to manage your fleets and ship and know when you're strong enough to take on an adversary or not. It can look less than appealing, and be rather complicated and sketchy in the beginning, but as you progress it becomes more of an adventure, living as a pirate or a soldier. It depends on your style of play, and you have to have an open mind in order to stick with it. Should you prefer a game with higher graphical intensity, then this game isnt for you. I would definitely suggest trying this game out, but at the same time I would heavily suggest some major tweaks. It'll take some work, but I'm confident in the creator's abilit[y](ies) to change this game for the better, and I wish them the best of luck in their continuation of this game.

Yes.. it is a huge copy paste from ARK. And not only the engine (UE4) but many aspects of game like farming, crafting, leveling, building, etc... There's no doubt that Funcom developers played ARK alot :)
And yes.. this is Early Access so there are performance issues, animation glitches, bugs, unbalanced items and that combat system is just ridiculous.
However my first impression was very positive. Here are some positive things compared to ARK:
- Game initialization is nicely done. There is some narration, there is some backstory, there are steps for character creation and personalization. Compared to ARK's sliders (which most players use to create some ridiculous character) this is very nicely done.
- Optimization is much better. While it's true that Conan Exiles don't have much content at the moment I was able to get 70-80 stable FPS (versus ARK's 30-40) on my GTX 980. Can't remember when I had such FPS on ARK.
- Building is more user friendly compared to ARK's building. Everybody had this problem on ARK where you can't put a structure properly, or it is showing one thing but building something else, or even worse it is destroying an existing part to put the new one. Here I built a 5x8x2 structure and didn't have any of these issues, it indicates inner/outer sides with a label, it immediately allows to put next piece, and so on.
- Structures and items look natural here. Structures on ARK look artifical, here you put various structures and items and they just fit to the map nicely.
There are however some negative aspects compared to ARK also:
- The content. Obviously this game needs tons of new content to catch ARK. There is however this strange feeling on ARK that we have too many useless items and dinos, I hope Conan Exiles will find a better approach here.
- Network and performance issues. ARK is not perfect itself, but it has more or less stable servers which is unfortunately not true for Conan Exiles. I hope developers will solve this in near future.
- Game's price is higher than it should be.

I have put in 12 hours into Conan Exiles to this point.  Overall, I am pleased with the game so far.  It is rough around the edges but that is to be expected in an early access game.  But I will break down into the PRos and Cons:
Pros:
-Crafting system is easy to use and intuitive
-Overall look of game is spot on for me.  It is desolate and forbidding.
-Overall character design looks good at this point.   The breast and endowment sliders provide some amusement during character creation.
-Building is time consuming but easy to manipulate.   It is basic (a good trait, yet bad).
-Seperate PVP and PVE servers allowing folks to play according to their preference.
Cons ( this is more a list of things that I think would make the game better, in my opinion)
- Limited to global, local and guild chats.  Would be nice to have private emssaging between players available as game moves on.
- A little finer controls when building.  I like that it is basic, but being able to raise up foundation when placing, for example, would be cool
-  Battle system is basic, but is pretty standard MMO fair, figure that will be improved as game developes.
-  Server system is a bit frustrating.  I put in 10 hours ona  server, too a couple hour break and then came back to ahving server not even listed.  Is it down?  Is it full?  I have no clue and I am faced with playing single player or starting over on a new server and possibly faced with it being unavaible the next time iw ant to get on it.  That leads to frustration.  Starting over again and again doesn't let a person experience all the game can offer.  This is probably my biggest and true complaint.
-  there are some graphical rough spots, but again, i figure that will be improved as game moves forward, so not really a complaint.
Overall I give it 3 our of 4 stars and well worth playing even in early access.  I am looking forward to improvements in the game and playing it with my friends.

Got this game via. a Humble Bundle and despite the recommendation, I'm glad I didn't pay full price.
This is not a bad game. However, it isn't a spectacular one either. I enjoyed playing it, and think it's worth the purchase, but only within the $5 - $10 range.
The game isn't particularly long--7 - 10 hours not including collectables--and due to the murder mystery-esque storyline, has little replay value.
Combat is non-existant, and instead the few enemies met in the game are dispatched using "sneak up behind them and perform a button combination" tactics. The encounters are never difficult, and with the exception of perhaps one or two near the end, pretty straight forward.
The meat of the game involves crime-scene investigation, or at least a simplified version of it. Once you get the hang of what the game expects from you, they become fairly simple, but several times throughout I found the prompts given to help you select relevant clues had little to do with the actual clues the game expected you to select... not that the game really penalizes you for choosing the wrong ones.
In short; decent game, buy it cheap, play it once, enjoy it, and move on.

For those who enjoy the particualar kind of game that Crusader Kings II is, it is worth every single penny. However, if you are one who is less excited about roleplaying, in-depth history, and boardgame style strategy, this game will simply be a waste of money.
Crusader Kings II is possibly the most accurate and immersive historical game, and is one of the most detailed and complex on the Steam market. To lovers of Europa Universalis and strategy games in general, you will play this game for unhealthy periods of time. You will feel like you are a Medieval noble, conspiring against his king, conquering large swaths of land, or defending against barbarians. This game is truly one of the most immersive I have ever played.
Unfortunately, one has to wonder if the publishers used this game as a money-grab. Without payed DLC content, you will be LOCKED from playing beofre the year 1066 and from playing as a non-Christian even after 1066. This restricts the player from the entirely different playstyles of the Pagans, Muslims, and Indian nations. Without DLC's you cannot become a mighty desert warlord, or raid the weak Christian kingdoms as a VIking warrior. Even the so called "Crusader Kings II Collection", which sells for an astronomical price of 80 dollars does not contain the three largest expansions.
If you are able to get past the obvious money-grab, and if you are a lover of the genre, this game is a must-own, and is a masterpiece of the strategy genre.

By all accounts, this game should have never been made in 2014.  The market for AAA games demand experiences much different than this one.  This is a niche game, and throwing so many resources at it is a terrible, terrible business decision.
The game has almost no combat, and is driven by dialogue, information gathering, and narrative.
That said, I am writing this after just completing it, with a huge grin on my face.  The story in this game is STELLAR.  It evokes the slower pacing and murder mystery elements of games like the Blackwell franchise and LA Noire.  It's also compounded with supernatural elements and a heavy influence from the Salem Witch Trials.
At it's heart, it's a murder mystery (your own, in fact.)  But once it starts unfolding, there is an incredible narrative to be experienced, one I highly recommend, if you don't mind slow pacing in video games.
I can't recommend this to everyone, but if you love a good mystery, and prefer dialogue to gunplay, then I cannot recommend this game enough.  Like I said, it's a niche game, and if you fall into that niche, then please, please, play this game.

Unfortunately the game has a sort of battle system in the game with demons that look for you and try to eat your soul or something like that. Personally I hated these areas of the game the most, it didn't feel scary or add anything to the game, it actually just seemed really annoying, so I always rushed through the demon areas executing them as fast as possible (which just means walk behind them and press the execute command that was on screen). For me they could have just left the demons out and I would've enjoyed the game more. Or they could've made it hella scary and borrowed the run and hide system from "Amnesia: The Dark Descent". Oh well there aren't that many demon areas so it was ok.
Conclusion: It's a fun, easy, detective game that lasts about 6 hours  (10+ hours if you want to 100% the game) filled with fun cut scenes and an interesting storyline.
