First off, I feel I have to write this review just to defend the game from the ignorance that is being spewed all over these reviews.
Anyone who thought this game would be completely different from ETS2, or anyone who expected more than 2 states and 2 trucks and is going to bash the game and developers over it aren't fans of the series and haven't been following the development.
Yes, you infact are getting 2 trucks and 2 states right out of the gate for your $20. A third state Arizona is close to the end of development and will be released as free DLC once completed. Then as time passes, more DLC involving more trucks and more map sections will be released. Some will be paid and I'm sure some will be free. My understanding is that ETS2 had quite a small map at release as well and they have added much to it over time. Why would ATS be expected to be done differently?
Now as for gameplay. Is it perfect? No! But I'm sure it will be improved as time goes on. Yes there are too many tickets issued in this game. Typically in the US, you're not going to get a ticket for 56 in a 55. I hope they adjust red light tickets to only occur if you actually cross the intersection as opposed to slightly going over the stop line. There are tweaks needed. One thing I haven't seen anyone discuss is the three levels of parking. This was a great addition because the parking in ETS2 was just too easy. The skilled level parking really does take a lot of patience and is a great addition to this game. I have not seen any issues with the AI yet. I've seen people complaining that the AI runs red lights. I'm assuming that these people are not familiar with the laws in the US that allow vehicles to make right turns at red lights, unless otherwise posted.
All in all, this is a good game. It will likely become a great game with further development. SCS may have rushed the release of this game because the public has been calling for it for a while now. ETS2 had to grow through additional development, so there's no reason to expect anything less from ATS. If you're not interested in playing a semi-watered down version of what we all expect this game to become, then wait. Play ETS2, and wait for this game to grow. I'm perfectly happy with this game, even though I can see all the imperfections that need to be fixed.

This is the first Disgaea game and probably my second favorite after Disgaea 4. The story is excellent, the main story (with some grinding of course, this is a japanese srpg after all) is crazy long (I think last time it was 80 ish hours for me on the PSP version), the characters are generally likable, there's a bunch of zaniness with random bouts of seriousness, and it's just generally very enjoyable if you like SRPGs (Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem) without requiring it to take itself too seriously.
Granted, this is a PS2 game ported to the PSP and then finally ported to the PC. The main place this starts showing this age are the graphics, which look only slightly better upscaled and are otherwise unchanged (unless you choose to use new map textures). The other is the lack of class/combat/quality of life features in later disgaea entries. For instance there is no option to change text display to instant, many later classes are missing, you can't toss towers directly on to people you need to throw them next to people, etc. But those features (aside from the text display one) are mainly only going to be noticed as missing by someone who has been playing later entries into the series while the older graphics are probably going to be up to taste.
This game series has a history of INSANELY long post-game content. In addition to the usual alternate ending fair/NG+ (and Etna mode) there are also massive challenges that require a huge amount of grinding, reincarnating, grinding more, etc, etc to even accomplish. But if you're the kind of person that can handle it the content is there and it will eat a lot of time.
I really like the entirety of the series and I hope that they also begin making their way over here (hopefully in their PSP/PS Vita versions with all DLC/extra content included in the base game) but for now this is a great first step into a giant, complicated, grindy, funny, and lovingly crafted series. I hope you decide to try it, dood.

What a unique experience; and I mean this in the most positive way possible. I usually get negatively surprised when I decide to try out a title that is not part of a series, style, or game type I know I'll enjoy. It's rare that it happens, but this time it is the exact opposite.
I have often wondered what it would be like if you combined "Magic the Gathering", "Dungeons & Dragons", and some kind of "Diablo" based game. Looks like this it. The way medieval styled fantasy deck cards are combined with a very pleasant story narration, and action based dungeon crawl elements, is truly well done. Very well done. I cannot stress this enough.
The game/cards/session is randomly generated, which technically makes the replay value pretty much infinite. This title is very atmospheric. The music is utterly great; it reminds me of folk tunes similar to what you would expect from artists such as Loreena McKennitt; it's soothing, but also thrilling at the same time. The narration is top notch. Truly a story teller, something that certainly is the ultimate game master. Wouldn't we all like to be able to shuffle cards like that?
I wish the graphics were a little less cartoon-ish looking, but I also think that the 'polish' of the game is just right. It looks like an old board game has come alive, and shows you all the magic in beautiful effects. Playability wise, I think it works perfectly fine with mouse and keyboard. I don't have a controller, I don't like them, and I find it no better or worse to control than other games of the same kind.
To me, this is a game with barely any shortcomings, except for the fact that I agree on the repetitiveness of some of the fighting sequences. That's a minor issue though, and is hugely outweighed by the rest of his marvelous experience.
For an Indie game this is a true gem, and I wish some of the developers of AAA titles would take some notes in regards to originality. I'm from a generation that played games before the first 3Dfx cards came on the market; nice graphics are certainly awesome, but the narrative, presentation, immersion, atmosphere and originality outweigh any kind of shaders, ambient occlusion and anti-aliasing for sure.

Chivalry Medieval Warfare.
Chivalry is a medieval based MMO game that allows you and your friends to to play as medieval knights vanguards archers and more.
There are several game modes for chivalry such as Team Objective, Team Death Match, Last Team Standing and more.
There are four basic classes in Chivalry.
The Archer.
Though the archer has no armour it has the second fastest speed of any class. Equipped with either a Bow which has good speed and descent damage however it lacks in range and is a bit weaker than the crossbow. The crossbow with devestating damage and descent range it lacks in speed. Javelin with medium damage range and speed the javelin also comes with a small sheild which helps allot when blocking against other archers and soldiers. Or the sling with medium damage but low speed and low range, the sling however increases your movement speed and allows you to run faster than archers that have a bow javelin or crossbow equipped.
There three variations of each of the weapons that you can unlock by playing and increasing your characters level.
This is a class best suited to someone who likes to look at the battle from afar and pick off enemies one by one rather than charging in head first.
Man-At-Arms.
With the second lowest rating of armour and the highest sprint speed in the game the Man-At-Arms weilds a range of short to long range primary weapons as well as a short dagger and throwing knives. With this class you can chose to either have a ranged weapon or a shield equipped with you, if you use the default Broadsword you will have medium-high damage with medium speed and low range. If you use the hatchet you will have slightly higher speed but lower range with the same amount of damage. If you use the morning star mace you will have slightly more speed than the default broadsword but lower damage and the same range. If you use the quarter staff you have greatly increased range but with lower damage and raoughly the same speed as the other weapons.
This is as close as you'll get to a beserker in this game. Fast, and deadly the Man-At-Arms truly brings devestation to the game.
Vanguard.
the vanguard specialises in heavy but fast close quarter combat with medium armour and speed. Equipped with either a Great sword or a pole arm you make your enemies truly know what pain is. Also equipped with throwing knives or tomahawks you can rush in and take your chances or damage your enemy from a distance first then take the final blow up close. The Greatsword with high damage low speed and medium range. The Spear with slightly reduced damage but increased speed and range. The Bardiche with very high damage reduced speed and medium range. The Pole Hammer, with extremely high damage low speed and medium range.
This is a class for people who like to get up close and personal but also keep a good distance between you and your enemy using you long close quarter weapon.
Knight.
With the highest armour ingame he also has the lowest sprint speed in the game. Depending on your primary weapon will determain if you have a single heavy weapon or a shield and primary. Eqipped with the default double axe you have devestating damage but with very low speed and range. With the war hammer you have high damage, medium speed and low range. With the longsword you have very high damage with medium-low speed and medium range. With the flail you have medium-high damage, medium speed and low range.
The knight is a class best suited for a player who likes to charge straight into the battle as they can take a hit and definately deal one back.
With allot of messy blood, gore and violence this game isn't really suitable for people under 15 years of age.
All in all a great game difinately worth the money and time.

MLL is Fear meets Crysis meets Stalker with a hint of Half Life thrown in. It's an excellent 'on rails' FPS, mature without falling into the torture porn trap that so many games have adopted these days. It can be too easy on normal difficulty then punctuated by impossibly hard sections (I died zero times from enemy bullets, dozens of times from 'falling in water'). It's too much on rails to warrant a second playthrough I'm afraid.
I do hope the next game will have a better objective management (the current one requires to switch weapons and hold the right mouse button, what gives?) and that we'll see maybe a shorter game that's a little more consistent (some levels were absolutely superbly designed, while others felt bog standard). The loadout mechanism is also hit and miss, as you have no idea if you will face humans (in which case the game is entirely stealth-based) or mutants (read: bullet sponges). It doesn't sound so bad until you get stuck in a death loop as the game reloads with you have 0 oxygen or armed with the 'wrong' weapon, which forces you to reload the level (gah).
There are absolutely hours upon hours of spoken dialog that breath life in the game. It's full of details that will remind you a bit of Duke Nukem , just messing about with the environment. The scripted sequences are good for the most part, and the sound design is excellent, the graphics brilliant and the framerate buttery smooth at 1440p on an i7 GTX980. Tons of extra content in this edition, too!!! Get a recommend from me, especially at the very low sales price.

This is the best MMO I have ever played, and that only makes me hate it even more.
The "free" model of Archeage is a lie of omission. A person can, in theory, earn premium by grinding enough gold to buy a special item off the marketplace from someone else who payed real money for it. The problem with this is that you need a premium account to ever have any hope of making that kind of gold. The tradeskill system is the most interesting and varied part of this game, which is why Trion Worlds decided people should have to pay in order to use it. Sure, you can collect wood from that tree, but you need twenty five minutes worth of labor points in order to do so. Oh but don't worry, labor points regenerate offline... if you're a premium member. Other wise it's five points every five minutes for free players as long as they stay logged in, which is half the amount premium players get.
This is pay2win at its absolute most insidious. The subtlety of the paywalls that exist throughout the game are so well thought out that whoever thought of them should be given an award alongside a much more deserved punch in the mouth. I cannot tell you how many times I attempted to do something before being told it was only available to premium members, even though the game never tells you this at any point other than right before you try to do it. Oh by the way, remember that subscription item I mentioned? You actually need TWO of them to have enough credits to buy subscription days, a little fact this game specifically does not mention.
It's a shame because I've really been looking forward to playing this ever since it was announced, but Trion Worlds proves once again just how much they are willing to siphon the fun out of everything in the hopes of suckering players out of their cash. Their business model is to conceive a product that people want, and then transform it into something that nobody asked for.
I'm not paying for premium, even if the game itself really is fun once you are allowed to play it. After what happened to End of Nations, the idea of giving any of my money to Trion Worlds makes me want to tear my own skin off. I hope now that they've ruined Archeage as well, more people will understand why I feel that way.

First thing, the keys are a bit odd to get used to and even though rebindable, they still feel a bit weird to get used to because some actions are bound to the same key.
The game sells itself as a tactical turn-based strategy RPG where after fights you earn money to upgrade your equipment (or purchase side-chapters) and EXP to improve your squad (or acquire new Orders).
You can't replay the main story Operations to try and acquire a higher rank for them until you move on to its New Game +.
Not too long into this it starts to feel more like a game of memory & luck instead of strategy because throughout most of the game a good chunk of the enemy operatives stationed are only revealed & visible if you let them have a turn and it just so happens one of your guys sees them or if you have a unit run somewhere and they happen to stumble upon them showing where they are.
There's a system in this game called Command Points that determine how many times you can control a unit(s). You'll see these during your turn on the overhead map view. They regenerate by a set amount every turn and can be saved up by skipping the current turn. CP can also used for giving Orders (buffs) and you can use one CP to move a soldier (two for tanks) and decide where to move them and possibly do an action at the same time such as healing, shooting, and a few other various things depending on the class of the unit you chose. Controlling a tank in this game is bugged when using the mouse. When looking around with the tank, for some reason, you waste AP. Normally you spend a very minimal amount of AP by turning but for some reason the game thinkgs you're trying to turn when you're just looking around.
A single unit moves in real-time using Action Points which determine how much distance they can cover before the AP are depleted. I don't believe the real-time part works here because way too often there will be invisible walls and little gaps that look deceptive enough for me to think I can walk through, for example a tree close to a wall with what looks like there's space to fit someone through. However before it's too late I stumble upon an invisible wall because apparently either the tree or that wall has a bigger blockage range than it made it out to be and so the AP I wasted trying to go between that small gap is wasted and you can't exactly have do-overs because the whole thing is in real-time. You can save the game and load while you're in the overhead view in case you don't feel comfortable with the turn you've made but doing so becomes real bothersome.
To get a higher ranking in an Operation, the highest being
, you have to finish each while making the lowest amount of "turns" possible. With the way it works though it feels more like I'm trying to exploit the system by rushing as opposed to playing a turn-based strategy game using actual strategy to complete the Operation. An example of this is one of the very last missions where a boss is an overly defended tank where I have to keep shooting it until its armor HP is down to 0. I skipped my very first turn to save up CP and let the enemy with its incredibly unstellar AI do its thing without bringing any of my people down to 0 HP. So my turn comes and all I did was move one of my tanks as close to the boss tank as my AP can handle while after exhausting my AP I take aim & shoot the tank, slowly decreasing its armor HP each shot. Because I saved up all that CP in the skipped turn I can keep moving and shooting until its armor HP is down and reveal the boss tank's weak spot. With enough CP I managed to get behind the tank and shoot its weak spot with two attacks thus ending that boss fight within two turns giving me an A rank. It didn't feel like a strategy more than it did a rushed play.
You can also almost complete an Operation with one person because most of the main objectives are basically just capturing a specific flag. If you have enough CP and the right Orders and you place those Orders on that single unit you can pretty much make them a possibly bullet spongy killing machine that can just run towards the main objective.
The enemy AI are almost abysmal. During a boss fight, way too often they'll waste their own CP making unnecessary and sometimes completely pointless orders such as the boss making the order for a Heal Request when everyone of their units are at full health. The enemy AI will also often waste CP to control a unit of theirs to barely do anything or something worse that doesn't put the enemy AI in good light.
They'll also often waste their own AP literally running in circles and running to extremely dangerous spots & getting instantly killed. It's almost as if you'd have to actually put yourself in front of them for the enemy to act proper.
The English voice-acting is tolerable at best though you can set it to Japanese.
The game's story heavy but it's not too bad. Because it's story heavy however it often felt more like I was going through a visual novel and 3D anime episodes more than I was playing a game.
I suppose if you play "normally" it's not bad but so many of these what seem to be exploits feel like they ruin some of the fun.

A good game for what it is - casual, tactical adaptation of board game about two small flights of WWI planes trying to outmaneuver and shoot down one another.  It is *not* "Civilisation with planes" or anything close; people who saw Sid Meiers name and came here looking for another long strategy full of management and compelling player to play "one more turn" before quiting are in wrong place.  Ace Patrol campaign is more a series of scenarions each about 15 minutes long, connected by campaign mechanism just complex enough to give sense of continuity. It is not a faithful representation of WW I, either, but I'd say more faithful than not :).
The Good: The game mechanics make sound representation of planes behaviour in the air; most of tactics and moves you need to win would make sense in historical fights (if not always between planes presented). You don't have feeling that you are playing abstract board game that uses plane icons to represent pieces. Despite it being a turn game, the feeling of movement is always present. I'd even say I've learned a thing or two about Boom and Zoom tactics when playing  a squadron of SPADs against Dreideckers - knowing it needs patience and discipline from pilot is one thing, seeing how many turns it takes in turn game is quite another. The short but satisfying scenarios mean you won't spend long hours over this game, at least not continously, but makes it good game for short breaks while doing other things, especially office procrastination :) . It does not mean it can't be played for hours - happened to me - but you don't need hours of free time to play it.
The Bad: While the way game represents the planes characteristics and behaviour in the air is mostly sound, putting the roll rate and sustained turn rate in single "maneuvrability" stat (which seem to govern how easily plane changes direction, IE roll rate) leads to some breaks from realism. For instance, the way to defeat Albatros with "maneuvrable" Sopwith Camel is not to outturn it, but to outscissor it - historically, it might be the best way to snach a defeat from maw of victory :). It's still a possible situation between two different planes and Ace Patrol is a board game that is not supposed to be realistic, but it still ruins the immersion.
The Ugly: Each of four featured nations (Frenchm Britons, Americans and Germans) has choice od six plane types to fly, and the way planes have been chosen is idiosyncratic to say the least. The decision to shoehorn Americans (who skipped most of tech race of 1916-1918 and did not have own early plane types) as full-blown faction is probably to blame here; we have French flying planes they designed but never used (Hanriot HD.1, Nieuport.28) , Americans flying iconic French and British planes they barely used (SPAD 7, Sopwith Triplane, Sopwith Strutter - to add insult to injury, N.28 was widley used by Americans while french made more use of Triplane than Americans). Thanks to campaign mechanics, sometimes we see unhistorical fights like F.kker Eindeckers vs Bristol Fighter. It still makes a fun game, but much less immersive than it could be.

I'm going to start this off with a "not recommended" with a follow up tag of "As of the moment I write this."
Basic plot: You somehow done screwed the pooch hard and got your self a REALLY old fashioned Roman funeral. Conan finds you hanging out somewhere unspecified in Tur*mumblemumble*gastan and the Hyborian king gets you down and gives you a Dark Souls style welcome before wandering off to fight Cthulhu or something. On the plus side....you got that shiny new bracelet. Just take it from me....NEVER try to take it off EVER. The downside? There's nothing else to do but lose your souls again and again and again.....err never mind I mean just die a lot. Not even the single player has anything for you to really do. If Crom will not help you....then to hell with him!
Now before I get into the meat of this, all my time as of writing this is done in single player and with a garbage computer. I'm not going to bother about frame rate or graphics, my comp couldn't max it out anyway.
What I will get into is the rest of it.
1) Single player- Its simply an offline mode like Ark did, no story and you still have to "Host" the game though you get full control of many variables that are available to full server admins. You can tweak the offline to your liking.
2) Character- First thing you see when making the character is that the options for race/nationalities is fairly large. Unless I missed something they mostly all share the same hairs and such, picking the origin is purely cosmetic and won't do anything in the overall.  Religion currently seems to do little, but I chose Crom (He doesn't care about worship) and I could at some point make altars to the other gods anyway. The face sliders and body sliders are serviceable, but unlike Ark the sliders stay fairly reasonable so you won't stray too far from whatever face structure you pick and undoubtedly run into clones left, right, and center. The Bust and Package sliders are fun to play with but other than seeing a woman run around with her♥♥♥♥♥♥smacking her face or the guy with his junk trunk dragging on the ground (and maybe getting some true teabagging action going in PvP) they really don't add that much, just makes more sense to me that if you aren't wearing anything...well you aren't wearing ANYHTHING. Plus serves have nudity off by default, admins can change this.
3) Survival- Lets face it, you aren't going to survive, unlike Ark though you won't start the game dead five times before you spawn away from a predator. However there are only two or three non-hostile creatures and an herbivore that will only get hostile if you are close. Everything else will kill you and hunt you down to do it. As of now, the default settings have predators every few feet with some fairly high respawn rates. Fighting them is a bad idea, running is even worse. Basic resources are fairly common, but you need so many to get things done that for the first few levels you likely won't keep enough to make things you need. I made the mistake of building clothes for my character first when I should have been keeping the fibers for making twine, I spent a while building enough to stuff to make a campfire to eat only to die in the hunt for more branches (A basic campfire needs 50 branches and those are different from wood. While they can be gotten from trees with an axe, the quickest way is to pick up the ones on the ground) plus running from one predator only to aggro another leads to a chain that would see me out of stamina with no way to fight back and die. I built the stone pick and axe at least seven times before I had enough space to even start the foundation of a house. Food can be difficult to get, if you fight a lot you will have meat but unless you dedicate time to collecting branches you generally won't be able to cook it, eating it raw is a fairly bad idea. Collecting plants will yield small bugs, and occasionally you will find big grubs on the ground. Eggs will likely be the best source of food until you get a fire going. Water snakes throughout the map but the food and water bars do go down fairly quick so not wondering far from it is best at teh start.
4) Combat- Basic Skyrim hack 'n slash. You stand in front of something and hit the mouse button until one of you dies. You will however need to be observant of the weapon. Swords are good against things of your height, they swing wide and will hit other stuff, but against smaller things you will either need to aim down or try to aim a little right of the target so your blade actually makes contact with their body, Otherwise you will swing over them with no effect. Picks will hit high directly in front of you, smaller creature you will need to duck. Axes hit mid-level on the right side try to aim a little left so it makes contact, smaller things you will need to duck. Crouching generally won't help you, you make less noise but enemies seem to go based on proximity and line of sight. If you cross their sight at all they will aggro, crouching and walking behind them will still activate aggro as well. There are two creatures I currently have great difficulty fighting: Antelopes which while not hostile in anyway take at least 12 hits from a sword to kill and you will be chasing it all over the map, the rewards aren't worth it either, they give the same amount of useable items as any of the easier to kill large creatures. NPC Human exiles are also a pain. I have yet to take one down in a one on one fight, even naked with only a stone axe and me with a shield and sword and some clothes I haven’t been able to kill one before they do me in. The side hops you get as a dodge mechanic are ok, but either my timing is bad or the enemy hit box is wide because I have yet to mount a successful evasion even when I hop as the enemy winds up I still get hit.
5) Crafting- Less to it than Ark, but that goes with the setting. Similar to Ark you have skill points you distribute when you level up and those can be put into crafting plans. Unlike Ark though many of the basic things will be difficult to get needing the apprentice/journeyman/master crafting first (and unlocking a small set to build in the process) and then needing to be purchased themselves afterwards. In four hours I got to a grand total of level six which had me very limited on what I could build. Buying the sandstone buildings got me the foundation/wall/roofs but to build more of the house I would need to purchase the pillar/stair/ect. separate. Basically Ark made you buy everything independently and gave you points to buy one or two things a level, Conan lets you unlock random stuff with some skill points and then have you buy supporting items later on, on top of that there is no promise of one crafting plan per level. Again, I had settings to default, your server or admin may vary
Overall- Wait to buy. The $30 price tag is steep for what little it offers. Yes it’s a Beta, however if Ark's performance is any indication of a trend, we are seeing 90% of the final product here. They've covered quite a bit of what the era and terrain had to offer in tech already. Outside of magic (which may or may not be in the game I didn't build an altar or anything) I don't seen too much they could add outside of new maps.

Got this as part of a recent Humble Bundle.  Had never heard of it so there's no nostalgia clouding my review.  If you like exercises in trail and error, this game is for you. You get 3 lives for any run, where in case you die you return to the latest checkpoint you found.  Sometimes this sends you back quite a distance to replay a bunch of fights and redo choices you just made.   There is little room for error during fights. I'm sure I could finish the adventure given enough attempts but I despise retreading the same ground over and over memorizing the right choices at each turn.  Even then, there'd be little reason to replay it.

First off, I feel I have to write this review just to defend the game from the ignorance that is being spewed all over these reviews.
Anyone who thought this game would be completely different from ETS2, or anyone who expected more than 2 states and 2 trucks and is going to bash the game and developers over it aren't fans of the series and haven't been following the development.
Yes, you infact are getting 2 trucks and 2 states right out of the gate for your $20. A third state Arizona is close to the end of development and will be released as free DLC once completed. Then as time passes, more DLC involving more trucks and more map sections will be released. Some will be paid and I'm sure some will be free. My understanding is that ETS2 had quite a small map at release as well and they have added much to it over time. Why would ATS be expected to be done differently?
Now as for gameplay. Is it perfect? No! But I'm sure it will be improved as time goes on. Yes there are too many tickets issued in this game. Typically in the US, you're not going to get a ticket for 56 in a 55. I hope they adjust red light tickets to only occur if you actually cross the intersection as opposed to slightly going over the stop line. There are tweaks needed. One thing I haven't seen anyone discuss is the three levels of parking. This was a great addition because the parking in ETS2 was just too easy. The skilled level parking really does take a lot of patience and is a great addition to this game. I have not seen any issues with the AI yet. I've seen people complaining that the AI runs red lights. I'm assuming that these people are not familiar with the laws in the US that allow vehicles to make right turns at red lights, unless otherwise posted.
All in all, this is a good game. It will likely become a great game with further development. SCS may have rushed the release of this game because the public has been calling for it for a while now. ETS2 had to grow through additional development, so there's no reason to expect anything less from ATS. If you're not interested in playing a semi-watered down version of what we all expect this game to become, then wait. Play ETS2, and wait for this game to grow. I'm perfectly happy with this game, even though I can see all the imperfections that need to be fixed.

I've had more fun with this game than any of the myriad grand stategy games I've played over the course of my entire life. If you're new to games like Europa Universalis, it might take a good 10-15 minutes to get used to the pace of this game as opposed to other strategy games (don't be afraid to use the fast forward button often!), but once you do... There's such an amazing amount of depth to this game it's astounding.
The bittersweet fun of building a dynasty off of a single noble couple and watching how the tendrils of your bloodline spread throughout the medieval world is something that has never, ever gotten old for me. This is a game less about military strategy and more about political scheming. Sure, there's plenty of military action, but it involves placing armies who are automatically raised and limited in number by the land you own. It's not so much a matter of "produce a mass of units and SWARM THEM" as some strategy games are. (If you HAVE played Europa Universalis, the mechanics are pretty much exactly the same.)
Because militarily challenging for the throne of Norway with a few hundred troops from the Isle of Man is an utterly impossible task... you'll want to pursue more subtle options. This game is largely about the people you surround yourself with. While you can play a king, stepping into the shoes of the likes of any historical ruler of any of the nations featured in the game from Scotland to the Mongol horde (or placing your own created character in such a role, with a bit of very inexpensive DLC!), it's just as fun to take the role of a small count at the start. With deft political maneuvering and plenty of well-placed marriages, that day you finally claim a royal throne of your own will make you feel like legimiately feasting on the finest fatted calf in the land.
I've gotten a bit long-winded here, but even the above paragraphs don't adequately describe how much I love this game. It's not for everyone; fans of games paced along the lines of Warcraft or Age of Empires might want to do some research and spend time with the demo before committing to a purchase. But I promise you that if you're a thinker at heart who enjoys long term strategy and scheming (or if you simply like to build dynasties, trying to breed the most capable warriors and spies the world has every known), you'll lose yourself in this game for hours if not days at a time.

It is interesting to see how 4A Games made exploration so rewarding in such linear level design to the point where even the last shell or cartridge is a joy to find as you turn the corner. This must've been the reason why I stuck with the bundle for so long.
The campaign is barely any different from what you last remembered if you played the original version back in the day. Now that I have also played Metro 2033 Redux's campaign I can say that Metro Last Light Redux's campaign holds up pretty well to its predecessor. Aside from being a little bit more action-oriented it is nonetheless a worthy sequel if you are ready to get into the mood.
Now for those of you who were probably interested in the DLC's, here they are:
THE FACTION PACK DLC (consisting of the HEAVY SQUAD, KSHATRIYA and SNIPER TEAM) holds missions which are mostly modified versions of Metro 2033's levels (or Metro 2033 Redux's, for that matter) but even so they are unpredictable and reused in such a great way that you will find yourself satisfied. The  KSHATRIYA level is one good example and if you have ever found yourself shaking your head in denial at an open-world Metro game just give this a try before speaking again. This is probably the best level out of the DLC which overall focuses on the different types of combat.
THE TOWER PACK DLC is an Arena mode which pits you against all the enemies you're familiar with and puts you on your toes like never before. If you're interested in the lore the presence of what is essentially a VR kit in the depths of Metro might seen wrong at first but it gets manageable the more you get used to it. Let me throw in a little the fact that the preparation room reminds me a lot of System Shock 2.
THE DEVELOPER PACK DLC (consisting of the DEVELOPER level itself and an additional level called SPIDER LAIR) is for those who were interested in modding or just learning the mechanics in order to become experts. Although there are no modding tools available this is pretty enjoyable as unless you're rushing you'll probably spend more than an hour trying and firing everything out. I got the "Developer" achievement without realizing. Also the SPIDER LAIR level is one of those that brings the worst out of the series in a good way, making you run for ammo and filters more than Metro 2033 Redux ever did. I might be overlooking something but since when you can't carry more than 3-5 minutes worth of filters? Was the protagonist wearing his suit or not?
And lastly THE CHRONICLES PACK DLC (consisting of ANNA, KHAN and PAVEL) is yet another set of 3 levels but instead this time they're very story-focused, making this a spoiler-heavy area. Instead of just seeing things from a different perspective you're also learning new stuff. Like one friend suggested I reccomend to others leaving the KHAN level for last.
Overall Metro Last Light Redux is a worth sequel and even if you're in it for the DLC you might find yourself sticking longer than you should. If you are able to get it during a sale then that's even better.

So far this game has been more or less what I expected of the port. Being that this game is almost 15 years old, I won't be reviewing the game as much as I will the adaptation to the PC.
The good:
-Option to switch between English and Japanese voice overs
-Mouse support, even in menus (though more on this later)
-Options between classic and updated graphical styles
-Keyboard/mouse and gamepad button mapping
-Framerate not locked at 30fps
The bad:
-No resolution choices
-Mouse controls can be clunky/unresponsive
-
I will start this off by saying that I have had none of the crashing/low framerate problems that have been reported so far. I kept the graphical settings at stock with the sole exception of turning shadows on.
--PC Controls--
When it came to the controls, I found the default mouse commands to be very intuitive. L-click to select, R-click to cancel/go back. The entire game could be played entirely with the mouse, although keyboard shortcuts do prove to be useful for faster interactions. Plus, they added a nice detail of having a custom mouse cursor for the game, which I personally liked.
However, I did notice that the mouse commands could be a little clunky. If you click somewhere outside of a menu, for example, you have to click twice for it to first, put itself back in the menu, then again to actually select what you wanted to click on. In combat, clicking on tiles proved to be a little hit or miss for me on what I expected it to do. It seems the mouse detection boxes are very small in the grid, and you have to be pretty close to the center to actually click them. Sometimes, it would even seem to just stop working altogether, and I would have to click several times to get the clicks to register. Maybe this is just because I'm not used to the controls yet, but so far they don't feel 100% accurate.
Talking to people is a bit of a pain as well. You can click and drag to move your character towards your pointer, or you can use WASD in the overworld. Talking to people is done by running into them, face to face. This proves to be difficult no matter what movement option you use. I do remember this being a problem using the PS2 controller as well, but it's even more difficult to do with 8 directional movement (like WASD). The mouse movement isn't much better, but I had better success with it.
--Updated Textures--
This port release did upscale some of the textures from the original 2003 release, and it really shows on the menus and backgrounds. However, the character sprites didn't look as crisp as the rest of the game. While the new textures are a higher resolution, it ends up making the characters look blurry as opposed to crisper. The original sprites were much more pixilated, but they were carefully stylized to make up for their low resolution. Fortunately, the game allows you to switch between old and new character sprites, as well as backgrounds and maps. Personally, I like the updated maps and backgrounds with the old sprites.
--Conclusion--
Overall, I do recommend this game. If you are a fan of the original game, this port is worthwhile. If you are new to the Disgaea series, I definitely recommend starting here, with just a few warnings: 1) I would recommend the use of a controller, being that this game is a console port, but using a mouse and keyboard is doable if that's all you have access to. And, 2) While the port is better than I expected, it is still lacking in some areas. If you expect a full PC experience, you are going to find this game lack luster.
If you are looking for a top down strategy game that can go as deep as you want it to, this is the place to look. The humor is wacky and very anime, with a very self aware "over the top" spin.
Love the art, love the music, love the characters.

The popular opinion on the internet in regards with suggesting which game to start with in <insert any JRPG series here> is usually something old but gold. Part of this motivation is that making you play 40+ hours of an older game first makes you appreciate the latest additions and the improvements they brought.
I 100% disagree with that notion.
While Disgaea 5 is the current game and console owners are able to be introduced to the Disgaea universe in a smooth and up-to-date world, we're stuck getting the old games in order of appearance, partly due to companies wanting to milk their old products down to the last drop and partly because the fanbases are "Jehovah witness" the hell out of the old games through their nostalgia goggles.
I'm of the camp of people who actually believe that a newcomer to a series has to be sold to the series right off the bat, and there's no better way to do it than suggesting them to play one of the top 2 entries, not top 3. Top 2.
While Disgaea PC is "okay" its age is showing compared to the new additions. If you want to satisfy your nostalgia that's fine. Me? I'd rather get off the nostalgia milk train. Somebody wake me up when we get the console buyer treatment.

Wow, what a truly wonderful surprise this game turned out to be. I picked it up on a whim without having any real knowledge of the game till it hit the market. It's a procedurally generated set of dungeons (akin to the old 'choose your own adventure' novels from  20+ years ago) based on cards in a deck that you have a hand in designing. You traverse this dungeon using gear from a separate deck that you also have a hand in designing, which is comprised of gear you found throughout your journey exploring previous dungeons. It's really quite genius.
The game is surprisingly deep too. During play you'll see the following:
-various weapon damage types
-various enemy types
-mazes
-curses
-blessings
-merchants
-buffs
-traps
-chests
-path choices
-bosses
-magical items
-random loot
-artifacts
-item activation during combat
I'm sure theres more I could add, but I'm still not even 2hrs played.
You walk across a board comprised of over turned cards from the deck, randomly laid out in a grid. Each step consumes a food resource, so must monitor your food as you travel. You'll run into decisions in  your journey...do you give some of your food away to a weary traveller? or just pass by them. How you respond will affect the outcome of your journey.
While I was originally concerned combat during story mode was too simple. The further I got, Not only was I becoming stronger, but so was my enemy.
I definitely recommend this game. It's new and refreshing. Well done!

I do not drive trucks for a living, nor have I ever.
In fact, I don't even drive a car - I live in a major US city, and some medical issues prevent me from driving safely. When I could drive a car, I didn't enjoy it.
So why am I in love with this game?
I bought this on a whim. Hey, it's $20. If I hated it, I could always get a refund. I played for about half an hour the first time, barely making it out of the tutorial. I had chosen the third "level" of controls (shifting and mouse steering) out of four, which made the game unintelligible to me. I considered, and discarded, the idea of getting a refund. It was a neat game, but definitely not for me since I never knew how to drive a standard anyway.
Then I started it up again later that evening... and I've been playing for hours ever since.
Something about this game is so soothing, so freeing - it's unbelievable. The graphical fidelity reminds me of GTAV, although (obviously) less detailed and not bothering with animating humans. Neon blinks uselessly in open starry nights, proclaiming doughnuts here / left turn only / ACME goods. A year ago, I took a ride with a friend out into the wild empty desert around Barstow (and yes we did have Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas audiobook playing while we did so). This game does a wonderful job at capturing the grit and loneliness of that open, alien world.
I finally figured out how to not roll backwards when I get to the top of an onramp. That was a good thing. I feel clever when I do things like this - I understand now why people drive, I think. Downshifting to slow down when I see brakelights flash briefly in the distance... and then, sure enough, there's a traffic light I didn't anticipate but I'm already slowed down!... these things make me feel that private sort of joy you get in any video game when you make a particularly difficult play.
I don't know why I like this game. I'll never be great at it, and that's okay. I have no interest in trucking, or driving, in the real world. But I wanted to write this review to let people know that this game might grab them in the way it did me.
Give this game a try.
One quick edit while I'm thinking about it: Most of the negative reviews here are due to two main factors:
1. Actual, real, live, human truckers disappointed that the game does not perfectly capture the depth or distance of driving for 40+ hours at a stretch (I am okay with this; I have no desire to sit for that long). I understand, but I disagree with, that as a criticism. Games must remove some of the tedium from real life.
2. People giving temporary thumbs-down because the existing world is rather small. True. There are only two states out of the forty-eight that comprise the continental US. The company has stated they will add more.

I find this to work more like a board game.  If Talisman tried some rogueish influence you'd have Hand of Fate: an interesting game where you play levels: first the jack of a suit, then you restart and fight another suit's boss after a level, rinse, lather repeat.  Simple enough.  The game is played by using facedown cards as tiles, moving one space at a time (using food as a resource), discovering each card and playing out each scenario -- Might be an enemy ambush!  Might be a shop to get new armor, weapons, spells, etc.  Completing some cards in certain circumstances (like score a critical success) will reward you with new cards for later levels. You get to pick some of the cards that are used on this playing field, though there are other cards involved in it to.  Combat isn't terribly exciting, just whackwhackwhack counter chance! whackwhackwhack counter! Roll!!  The adventures themselves are still quite enjoyable, though not too difficult.
An overlooked part of this game is the Dealer character. The only speaking character is the monologuing Dealer, who has a very good attitude for a 1-on-1 DM. He has some interesting things to say, no matter how small: Sometimes when I get a blessing, he'll say he made the card a little overpowered, and should rebalance it sometime.  Things like that just come across as genuine, though you'll hear him say much more interesting things.
As far as pricing goes, even $20 seems a little high, I'd recommend picking it up around the $10-15 range.

Okay, so this game is REALLY unique and cool. You play as a recently-deceased man who has passed onto the afterlife, and is reliving broken memories of his life in the form of a card game, played against a mysterious hooded figure known only as "The Dealer." The game's cards correspond to various memories of the man's life; trials he may have endured, enemies he may have faced, and the items and powers he may have wielded to vanquish his foes. Don't be fooled, though; this is definitely NOT a card game. It is more like a text-based choose-your-own-story adventure game, interspersed with hack-'n-slash combat encounters. The cards you possess on the table manifest themselves as equipment and abilities in the combat portions of the game, which are crucial to being able to take on the enemies you will face.
The combat encounters will seem very familiar to anyone who has played the Assassin's Creed or Witcher games. The flow of combat follows the same attack/dodge/counter system that players will recongize from those titles. The real brilliance of the game comes from the sheer replayability. You're dead, after all, so the Dealer is perfectly content to sit at the table and play cards with you for the rest of eternity, and once you get the hang of the game, you might be, too. Matches take the form of multi-level dungeons, the floorplans of which are laid out face-down on the table, using a mixture of cards chosen by you, and by the Dealer. As you win matches, the dungeons become longer, harder, and more complex, but always different. Winning matches will earn you new cards, which equate to new weapons and armor, stronger powers, and even persistent quest-lines that you can explore or replay over the course of multiple matches. As you become more skilled, though, the Dealer will become increasingly frustrated with your success, and throw even harder obstacles in your way. Despite there being only one fully voiced character in the game, the Dealer's voice acting, model, and animations are rich and full of character, and you may even find yourself reveling in your rivalry as much as he does. Overall, this game is a solidly designed, well-polished, and unique experience that any mortal would be pleased to devote the rest of eternity to.

Bland, limited & repetitive gameplay is what you can expect from Sid's Ace Patrol. I really tried to enjoy this (I put in the time!), but it has none of the 'one-more-turn' addictiveness of his other games.
So why is it so bad you ask?
Each map looks almost identical, graphics look like direct port from mobile platform, the mission types you can count on one hand & the game itself is very short covering 24 missions across 4 campaigns. They can go quick too! You do not feel there is any progression as you go through as the game centres around your score; having little in the way of feeling like you are winning a war. There is no territory to defend or conquer instead you choose from 3 random missions then up to 4 pilots to progress through each level. Pilot & plane upgrades are rewarded as you proceed through your game, but only really make it easier to win & that isn't really a strong point when the 'Legend' difficulty is not really very challenging. Legend (besides boosting your score) just makes it more frustrating than anything else since the opposing pilots get big stats boosts making it take a painfully long time to shoot them down yet much easier for you to be shot down.
Tactically you will find many dogfights are reduced to both of you flying around in circles for multiple moves until the AI decides to fly out giving you an opening to attack. You can try different tactics but it always comes back to 'circling' from my experience. Once you get behind someone it is very hard for them to get away (unless they're an Ace pilot), and likewise when the roles are reversed. It makes the first few turns of your engagment most important, but then very predictable after that. To add to this, I also couldn't play this on my old PC with ATI graphics as it wouldn't render the display, showing all white, so I have only been able to play recently since I got my new PC with NVidia graphics.
All said & done, I can't help but to ask myself why Sid would put his name on such a sub-par game, let alone make a sequel! Also milking it further by charging almost twice as much locally in AU @ $8.99 instead of US @ $4.99 (still well overpriced for what you get if you ask me).

Hand of Fate is a clinic in good game design.  Yes, it borrows from many sources:  choose-your-path books, collectible card games, arcade fighters and more.  But it blends those diverse elements into something you've not seen before.  When you've been gaming for four decades as I have, playing something unique is a rare treat indeed.
+ Eye-catching art
+ Interesting writing and voice acting
+ Understated sense of humor
+ Gameplay that appears simple but becomes more complex and challenging the longer you play
+ S T Y L E.  Oodles of it.  In an endless sea of MMO, RTS and FPS clones, this stands out like a bright beacon
Nothing is perfect, of course...
- The basis for the interface design is obviously consoles, which makes keyboard and mouse slightly awkward.  Not game-breaking by any means, but it is noticeable for PC Master Race types such as myself.  Still, it shouldn't stop you from buying.  You'll quickly get used to it -- or just plug in a gamepad.
- A few minor spelling errors.  I'm a self-admitted grammar nazi, however, so most people probably won't notice or won't care even if they do notice.  A niggle, nothing more.  Pardon me while I stroke my neurosis.
Summary:  Just buy it.  I promise you haven't played anything exactly like it before, and at the price point you'll easily get your "movie standard" value out it.  If nothing else, it shows support for game designers who aren't swimming in the blood gutter of money clones, and we could do with a lot more of that.

A sequel to one of the best games ever?? SHUT UP AND TAKE MY MONEY....or...perhaps it falls short of the glory of its predecessor? As the global recession slowly chewed away at business stability, Bioware was bought out by E.A., who were ready to chop down the quality and crank out sequels. Mass Effect's tragic decline was in motion....
Plot 7/10
The plot was a little weak this time around. I felt like I was just being retold the same story. "But I already know this story." I thought to myself. The opening of the game is jaw-dropping visually and emotionally, but you'll get very tired of it from watching it about 16 times trying to make your Shepard ideal (player character's name). After it though, you are immediately met with several crazy plot elements and twists. A short time passes, however, then the main plot takes a back seat and transfers over to minor conflicts with dialogue that doesn't pack the same punch as the first one. By no means is it boring or sub-par, but a noteable downgrade. Just when I thought this game was going to be another stroll to the ending credits, the excitement of the plot EXPLODED! One major twist had my adrenaline pumping so hard, I had goosebumps and stayed awake 'til about 2:00am on a work night to keep playing. I haven't had a story reach out and pull me into full immersion like this since Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater. I couldn't stop; I had to know what happened next! Plot-wise, the game makes up for it all at that moment near the end. The new characters and their backgrounds are of the same, satisfying quality of Mass Effect 1....except: Jack - the grumpy, tatoo freak and Jacob - the personality starved black man. Jack's background was rushed with no answers besides "I don't know. Bad things.", and Bioware played too cautious with Jacob. They were too scared to write him a personality without getting 'OMG RATHITH' so they made him a very generic, overly pure-hearted, black-skinned paladin who's dialogue doesn't stray far from "Ok, whatever you want, Commander." In summary, the plot is good, but it could've been better.
Sound 10/10
Not much to say in the sound department. It's the same quality as the first game, so WHOOHOO! (but robot voices sound a little TOO much like the robobrain from Fallout 3). Same praises goes for the superb voice acting. It's back in all it's immersive perfection! Weapon sounds are little more dull and not quite as satisfying, but this is minor. The music is good too, but during that great climax of the plot, there's a song titled "Suicide Mission" that deserves to be called legendary.
The sound is perfect...oh, and the sound glitch is fixed on this one.
Graphics 10/10
Beautiful and running smooth as butter, the graphics deliver on every front in sync with it's predecessor. I want to save my character limit for other things. Graphics are perfect (aside from the sometimes stiff animations of characters i.e. when Shepard first "wakes up".)
Gameplay 5/10
It breaks my heart to give Mass Effect 2 a five in gameplay. The weapon loot and equip screen was completely removed in favor of an overly dumbed down version of it. You can change your weapons a bit, but armor is purely cosmetic. Combine this lack of progress with the game being far, far too combat-heavy, and combat gets old very quickly. It was obviously done to coddle to the mass of CoD.
There's also little-to-no variety in enemies. You get your grunt, the tough guy, and the dog-like creature. Throughout the game, this is the "evil trinity line-up" of every foe you face.
My biggest complaint is how almost every ability has the same paritcle affects, so they all look the same aside from being colored purple or orange which makes most of the classes feel the same. The only one I really liked was Infiltrator because you slow down time when you scope in for a snipe and can go invisible. I loved that! Another huge gripe I have is how crazily glitchy this game is. I can think of at least 8-9 times that I either ran through a wall, got stuck in a box, or suddenly started flying through the air. All the above are game-breaking glitches that force restarts.
ME2 funnels into a vanilla, average, glitchy, console-shooter that - at the same time - is the scenes where the story takes a back seat. This leaves a long, long drought of entertainment for a large portion of the game. This "drought" is bad enough to even turn you off from replaying the game after you complete it. The ending is also disappointing. While it freaked me out, making me shout "HOLY FREAKIN' S*@!" from the EPIC last 4 seconds, it didn't do anything to satisfy the story. Following the trend, I had a feeling ME3's ending was gonna be bad too, because Bioware never gave ME a good ending in the first place. Summary...sigh...just average.
Side note: Even being a male, I was slightly offended by the portrayal of Kelly Chambers. While I loved her personality at first, I found it sexist that Bioware tried to subtly blur "affection" with "nymphomania". She is a spectacular example of character design/voice/script except for her depiction as a ditzy sex slave. Ironic that they were cautious with Jacob, but portray a woman's only affection is in her crotch. I don't appreciate this at all.
The Verdict
ME2 has great graphics, sound, voices, good script, and a great climax, but half-hearted plot, dumbed down combat, and 3 characters we could have done without hit the game in the leg for a bad limp during a fun trip. In the end, the game shouldn't be passed up. Get it because the game earned one good run from every gamer. ME2 scores a 7/10. It's cheap, it deserves one play through.

This is a very mediocre “game.” Let me explain that. If that were all there was to this, then I would obviously have given it a thumbs down. As a game, it’s just so-so, but as a piece of entertainment, it is fantastic. The actual gameplay has its ups and downs. There are really only a very few elements to the whole experience. You have exploration (walking around large/medium sized areas.) Collection (there are little glowing things liberally sprinkled around everywhere to pick up, and they all have some interesting tidbit to share.) There are a few stealth sequences, and then there are mysteries to solve. As for exploring, and collecting; I love and hate this sort of thing in games. A lot of games have them these days, and I have an unhealthy compulsion to collect all/most that I can. It’s not even for the achievements. I just have to. It’s like wringing out every bit of value that I can from a game. There are objects to be found, and I must find them. The stealth, is pretty horrible. This actually drags the gameplay as a whole from being good-ish down to mediocre. Plainly put, the stealth sections hurt this game greatly. For people who don’t play games, and would like to experience the story, these sections are going to be too difficult and very frustrating. For people who DO play games, these sections are just going to be annoying. They aren’t very difficult for a gamer, they just become tedious. Luckily they aren’t in there too often. Just, once in a while, when you are on your way to something interesting – boom. Ohh noos. Demons. I suppose I will have to watch them float around their 3 different way-points until it’s facing the way it’s obviously designed for me to kill it. Then, there are the mysteries. These are pretty fun. They are not unlike Phoenix Wright. There is a smallish area. and within that area are clues strewn about. Once you find all (or most) you can solve the mystery by selecting the correct “clue(s)” to answer whatever question the game is asking. Unfortunately this sometimes causes problems because the clues that they are asking for sometimes don’t make sense. The mystery asks for what seems like a specific answer, but instead accepts answers that are just vague repetitions of themselves. You’ll find yourself annoyed at the end of some of these sections when you find out which answers the game actually wanted you to pick. You’ll be able to think, “I guess that kind of makes sense?” but also roll your eyes because it doesn’t directly, and you are penalized for selecting incorrectly. Luckily the penalty isn’t too harsh, and you have unlimited retries. The only punishment is that you might get less “badge points” for how well you do. As far as I could tell, these points literally never had any bearing on anything. That is all of the gameplay that there is to this game.
So as a game, it doesn’t do very well. However, most everything else about it is great. Great story, interesting characters, interesting setting. Great music, great voice acting (mostly), pretty decent graphics. The ending was a little bit abrupt, but there’s a little twist you might not quite see coming.
Luckily for this game, to me, the gameplay didn’t matter too much. I kept coming back to find out what was going to happen next, and to see what little mysteries I could uncover in and around the spooky city of Salem. I ended up having a really good time with Murdered: Soul Suspect, and if they were to make a sequel, I would most definitely give it a purchase.

BLUF: I recommend this game for the player who likes tactical turn-based combat, mixed in with some exploration and resource management.
-Interesting story where your choices have actual implications in the game world
-Combat can be brutal, but there are ways to win most battles. You may have seriously wounded party members at the end, though. In some cases, bringing fewer than six members into combat encounter is key to victory. Scouts can move really fast....
-Pretty solid underlying game mechanics. While some players may not like the design decisions they are mostly consistent in their approach. Bad player decisions lead to bad outcomes and loss of troop morale, for instance.
-Resource management can be a challenge at first. Random travel events can quickly cause loss of rations, valuables, and medicine if you don't assign party members to correct tasks.
My only minor issue is the interface. Camping screen is click-intensive and can become tedious, considering you will be there several hundred times during a game. Likewise, a few more hotkeys for combat would most welcome.
Overall, a game worth a look for the right kind of player.

Murdered: Soul Suspect tells the intriguing story behind Detective Ronan O'Connor's death, all wrapped around a ghostly and spooky universe, filled with stories and events that will complete Ronan's adventure in the town of Salem, Massachusetts. While the ghosts stories add to the frightening aspect of Salem and its legends, and Ronan and Julia's stories scattered around the town add to the complexity of the story's main characters, there is little to do around the town apart from collecting things, which is such a disappointment since Salem is a great place to explore and finding a few more things to distract you from your main objective along the way would increase the length of the overall campaign and make the experience feel more diversified, because as it is, you can easily complete Murdered: Soul Suspect's campaign in less than six hours, adding a few more if you're willing to collect everything and complete the few available side quests for the restless souls. Speaking of those restless souls, you are not the only soul in Salem trying to find eternal peace, as you will find people with different problems around Salem, but sadly you can only interact with a few of those, as most of them will feel like pointless NPCs as they only have one line of dialogue, even if their stories had some great potential for a follow-up side quest. While Ronan's story is definitely an unique experience, as the whole adventure takes place after his death, trying to find eternal peace by solving his own murder, the way in which it is told makes it obvious to draw a conclusion before your character does, making what lies ahead story-wise foreseeable from a mile away. There are still some great twists in the story, but the moment those will happen in your head do not coincide with the moment they will happen on screen, making them less enjoyable as you will already know what is about to happen from the very first moment you step into a new location, and the only surprise will come from clues that you will often find at the crime scene giving you the impression that there is more to it, but in the same sense of disappointment in most cases those are there only to fill the space.
Murdered: Soul Suspect goes for a simplistic gameplay, trying to be easy to pick up and play, and on that side it succeeds as almost anyone can get into the action after just a few quick tips. For most of the campaign, you'll be wandering around looking for something or making your way towards the next objective while following the basic rules of being a ghost: you can pass through anything, as long as it's not part of the spiritual world in which case that particular object will be highlighted using a pleasant light blue colour, just as anything else around the spiritual world including the ghosts themselves. The game does a great job combining those elements, leaving you to experience the thrill of being a ghost by passing through walls and objects while still limiting your access by using spiritual objects in order to create puzzles and hidden areas. The interesting concept comes in the form of investigation scenes, where you will look around for clues and connect those to answer different questions that will lead you towards your next objective, even though for most cases the item that will answer that question will be the most obvious one. While combat is certainly not the main focus of Murdered: Soul Suspect's gameplay, you will have to fight demons from time to time, as the mechanic used in those encounters is annoying and boring at the same time, forcing you to sneak behind those demons and use a quick time event to defeat them and jump from one hiding place to the next one if a demon spots you until it will eventually stop looking for you, the game would've probably been better without those sections. The main problem with Murdered: Soul Suspect's simplicity is that it takes away any sort of challenge, as solutions for puzzles will be more than obvious and the combat will feel boring once you get the hang of it, since it only requires you to sneak up behind your enemies without being seen, which isn't hard to do at all; once you realize that is all there is to the gameplay, it does become boring and repetitive, and there is no higher level of difficulty to turn it up a bit, even with the broken mechanics.
Murdered: Soul Suspect is a pretty game and Salem is a perfect fit for its ghostly story, as it's full of historical landmarks filled with opportunities to make things scary at times, but even with all the ghosts and history, Salem ultimately fails to impress due to the lack of life, and that's not even a reference to the spirits, as the living people of Salem are just as dead as the spirits when you approach them. There are countless clones of people around Salem that will all give you the same lifeless dialogue line, and even when you do encounter a restless spirit such as yourself, the level of interaction is kept to a minimal. The character design and effects are okay, but facial animations can be messy at times, even when you're looking at some of the main characters; as for the secondary ones, let's just say they are way worse.
The spooky tone of the game is kept in place with a great soundtrack and combined with the audio effects of abilities and other ghostly objects it manages to come pretty close to a scary experience, especially in natural spooky places such as a mental asylum or a cemetery. The voice acting is okay for most parts, some of the main characters such as Joy profiting the most from it, but it's hard not to notice the limited dialogue in conversations or the completely wasted Mind Read ability that will only provide you with a pointless sentence. The narration of those ghost stories is the greatest part as it will feel naturally scary, but since those are only a reward for collecting a number of items, not all players will get to experience that scary aspect of the game, as the main campaign feels left out from that perspective.
It takes no more than six hours to complete Murdered: Soul Suspect if you're only focusing on the main objectives; combined with the search for all the collectibles and the four side quests helping restless souls find peace, maybe it can add up to ten hours total, but once that is done, there is absolutely nothing else to do, as there is no other mode to keep you busy or reasons to revisit the campaign any time soon.
It's such a shame that the world around Ronan's story isn't developed to it's full potential as it dragging you away from the main experience that is, with its flaws, a great story, rather than letting you enjoy what is actually fully developed, but in an open world such as this, it's impossible not to stop by and see what else there is, and five minutes later be disappointed because there was nothing else.

I wasn't sure about this game when I bought it. I figured there was a good chance it would end up on my "wasted money Steam purchases" basket. Only a few days later, when I bothered to check it out, this game became one hell of a pleasant surprise.
Recettear is a weird mix of simulation, hack & slash and role-playing, with the cute japanese kind of graphics and animations that I really love. You play Recette, the cute and naive item-shop seller girl, who's teamed up with Tear, the fairy, who at first seems like the tough business...fairy(?) personality, but already a few hours into the game, I'm getting the feeling she has a totally different agenda than the one she's letting out.
As Recette, you need to manage your items shop and make money, so you can pay a debt to Tear's agency (whatever it is), so they wouldn't take your house. In addition to buying and selling routine, you can also hire adventurers and go to dungeons. In return for your payment to the adventurer, you get to keep the items you find in the dungeon, and sell them with nearly 100% profit.
All in all, this game is a lot of fun, definitely worth its price, in my humble opinion.

Hand of Fate is a clinic in good game design.  Yes, it borrows from many sources:  choose-your-path books, collectible card games, arcade fighters and more.  But it blends those diverse elements into something you've not seen before.  When you've been gaming for four decades as I have, playing something unique is a rare treat indeed.
+ Eye-catching art
+ Interesting writing and voice acting
+ Understated sense of humor
+ Gameplay that appears simple but becomes more complex and challenging the longer you play
+ S T Y L E.  Oodles of it.  In an endless sea of MMO, RTS and FPS clones, this stands out like a bright beacon
Nothing is perfect, of course...
- The basis for the interface design is obviously consoles, which makes keyboard and mouse slightly awkward.  Not game-breaking by any means, but it is noticeable for PC Master Race types such as myself.  Still, it shouldn't stop you from buying.  You'll quickly get used to it -- or just plug in a gamepad.
- A few minor spelling errors.  I'm a self-admitted grammar nazi, however, so most people probably won't notice or won't care even if they do notice.  A niggle, nothing more.  Pardon me while I stroke my neurosis.
Summary:  Just buy it.  I promise you haven't played anything exactly like it before, and at the price point you'll easily get your "movie standard" value out it.  If nothing else, it shows support for game designers who aren't swimming in the blood gutter of money clones, and we could do with a lot more of that.

I did not enjoy this game at all. The gameplay is mostly the sort of thing you'd get in an old-school Choose Your Own Adventure novella (if you GRAB THE SKELETON, turn to page 18...) with some basic dice rolling mechanics tacked on. Neither your choices or your dice rolls are interesting in any way. It feels like you're just sitting there while somebody describes a bunch of bad things happening to you, giving you almost nothing in the way of interactivity.
Combat is servicable, and is the most enjoyable part of the game. It's shallow but you do have some interesting abilities and different monsters use different tactics, so you generally - with some notable exceptions - feel like you have control over the outcome of the fights.
After beating the game once I had no desire to play it again, but I thought I'd try a few of the other characters to see if there was any replayability. While there are numerous 'flavor differences' between characters, the story remained the same. Your path is linear, with little branches of no consequence peppered throughout. It's very strange to me that a game with over a dozen characters to try has so little in the way of offering an actually new experience.
If this were all, I'd merely rate this game mediocre, for fans only. But there's one last aspect of this game that absolutely dooms it to the shitheap: the mazes.
There are at least two (possibly more) large mazes that are pseudo-randomly generated out of corridors, turns, scripted events, and dead ends. Each bend in the maze asks for your input, even when there's only one way to go, or you're just backtracking through after hitting yet another dead end. It's horribly tedious - over fifteen minutes of mindlessly exploring empty corridors with the occasional identical "trap" room taking away your health then sending you back to wander aimlessly some more.
Don't buy this game. If you got it for free in a humble bundle like I did, don't bother. Read an actual book or play an actual game, don't waste your time.
