A sequel to one of the best games ever?? SHUT UP AND TAKE MY MONEY....or...perhaps it falls short of the glory of its predecessor? As the global recession slowly chewed away at business stability, Bioware was bought out by E.A., who were ready to chop down the quality and crank out sequels. Mass Effect's tragic decline was in motion....
Plot 7/10
The plot was a little weak this time around. I felt like I was just being retold the same story. "But I already know this story." I thought to myself. The opening of the game is jaw-dropping visually and emotionally, but you'll get very tired of it from watching it about 16 times trying to make your Shepard ideal (player character's name). After it though, you are immediately met with several crazy plot elements and twists. A short time passes, however, then the main plot takes a back seat and transfers over to minor conflicts with dialogue that doesn't pack the same punch as the first one. By no means is it boring or sub-par, but a noteable downgrade. Just when I thought this game was going to be another stroll to the ending credits, the excitement of the plot EXPLODED! One major twist had my adrenaline pumping so hard, I had goosebumps and stayed awake 'til about 2:00am on a work night to keep playing. I haven't had a story reach out and pull me into full immersion like this since Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater. I couldn't stop; I had to know what happened next! Plot-wise, the game makes up for it all at that moment near the end. The new characters and their backgrounds are of the same, satisfying quality of Mass Effect 1....except: Jack - the grumpy, tatoo freak and Jacob - the personality starved black man. Jack's background was rushed with no answers besides "I don't know. Bad things.", and Bioware played too cautious with Jacob. They were too scared to write him a personality without getting 'OMG RATHITH' so they made him a very generic, overly pure-hearted, black-skinned paladin who's dialogue doesn't stray far from "Ok, whatever you want, Commander." In summary, the plot is good, but it could've been better.
Sound 10/10
Not much to say in the sound department. It's the same quality as the first game, so WHOOHOO! (but robot voices sound a little TOO much like the robobrain from Fallout 3). Same praises goes for the superb voice acting. It's back in all it's immersive perfection! Weapon sounds are little more dull and not quite as satisfying, but this is minor. The music is good too, but during that great climax of the plot, there's a song titled "Suicide Mission" that deserves to be called legendary.
The sound is perfect...oh, and the sound glitch is fixed on this one.
Graphics 10/10
Beautiful and running smooth as butter, the graphics deliver on every front in sync with it's predecessor. I want to save my character limit for other things. Graphics are perfect (aside from the sometimes stiff animations of characters i.e. when Shepard first "wakes up".)
Gameplay 5/10
It breaks my heart to give Mass Effect 2 a five in gameplay. The weapon loot and equip screen was completely removed in favor of an overly dumbed down version of it. You can change your weapons a bit, but armor is purely cosmetic. Combine this lack of progress with the game being far, far too combat-heavy, and combat gets old very quickly. It was obviously done to coddle to the mass of CoD.
There's also little-to-no variety in enemies. You get your grunt, the tough guy, and the dog-like creature. Throughout the game, this is the "evil trinity line-up" of every foe you face.
My biggest complaint is how almost every ability has the same paritcle affects, so they all look the same aside from being colored purple or orange which makes most of the classes feel the same. The only one I really liked was Infiltrator because you slow down time when you scope in for a snipe and can go invisible. I loved that! Another huge gripe I have is how crazily glitchy this game is. I can think of at least 8-9 times that I either ran through a wall, got stuck in a box, or suddenly started flying through the air. All the above are game-breaking glitches that force restarts.
ME2 funnels into a vanilla, average, glitchy, console-shooter that - at the same time - is the scenes where the story takes a back seat. This leaves a long, long drought of entertainment for a large portion of the game. This "drought" is bad enough to even turn you off from replaying the game after you complete it. The ending is also disappointing. While it freaked me out, making me shout "HOLY FREAKIN' S*@!" from the EPIC last 4 seconds, it didn't do anything to satisfy the story. Following the trend, I had a feeling ME3's ending was gonna be bad too, because Bioware never gave ME a good ending in the first place. Summary...sigh...just average.
Side note: Even being a male, I was slightly offended by the portrayal of Kelly Chambers. While I loved her personality at first, I found it sexist that Bioware tried to subtly blur "affection" with "nymphomania". She is a spectacular example of character design/voice/script except for her depiction as a ditzy sex slave. Ironic that they were cautious with Jacob, but portray a woman's only affection is in her crotch. I don't appreciate this at all.
The Verdict
ME2 has great graphics, sound, voices, good script, and a great climax, but half-hearted plot, dumbed down combat, and 3 characters we could have done without hit the game in the leg for a bad limp during a fun trip. In the end, the game shouldn't be passed up. Get it because the game earned one good run from every gamer. ME2 scores a 7/10. It's cheap, it deserves one play through.

Mass Effect 2 plays very much like Dragon Age 2... tactical corridor combat with a bioware famous conversation tree wrapper and companion interaction... but in outer space.  More like a space opera at times with action interludes.  The pros and cons here are almost identical to DA2.

> Tactical combat is consistent in its difficulty with reasonable, occasional spikes
> Unit abilities are varied and interesting enough to warrant another playthrough
> ALL conversations are fully voiced... including a male or female main character
> Generally immersive atmosphere with good sound and visuals
Cons:
> Occasional terrible textures.  I mean epicly terrible.
> Although you can control your companions during tactical battles, it is rarely necessary to do so.  On my playthrough they never stayed put when I did decide to give commands.
> The "paragon/renegade" system, which assigns points to either based on conversation choices, seems to have little effect on actual gameplay, other than making it potentially impossible to bang Miranda.
> Action sequences revisit the same boring levels over and over.
> Many environs lack clutter and details.
I did like the game in general, especially for the fiction.  After some time it starts to feel very grindy though.  The story is what kept me playing, more so than the other game elements.  I hope ME3 does a better job raising the bar everywhere else.

TLDR: The game still needs polishing, but is definitely on the right track for becoming a beautiful gem. <3
There are tutorial guides on steam, READ them! - it's a temporary tutorial, that will tell you what you need to know to start.
As for the game, it's a different take on the true sandbox MMO's as boats, air balloons, and fighters with quite a bit of depth if you can push past the few quirks. (Open world, hardcore - I.E. you die, you lose everything on you, base building map.. PVPVE - although seems to be quite strict on the pvp and also has safe zones)
Yes, the game was developed by Russians with Russian dev's, and a mostly Russian playerbase. But you'll find a few people who speak's english to play with, and the text is translated quite well. - on top of, the devs are very active and speak better english than the majority of my country.
The main thing, in which you start out doing is by trading. - you pickup a trade job here, deliver it there... simple. But from there, that's where you start carving your own path in what I consider a 'true' sandbox.
--IN depth!--
Some things to note about true sandbox:
Things don't transport everywhere automatically.. there is no global market, there are no seeded objects (apart from the few starter items) - if you want to bring something from another town, you have to go get it.. or create a job for another person to go get it for you. :P - or simply sell it there to another player, and buy a new one where you are.
Every item in the game was manufactured or found by another player (apart from the simple base items) - Meaning somebody else gathered all the materials, crafted or processed it, and then had it hauled to your location and placed on market. (and pretty much every item is pretty good about staying on the market - ty russians <3)
You can build your own bases, from hidden outposts, to mining facilities, to castles. (run your own communities and clan's - and war with others) (about 90% of the bases in the game currently are player made, and player ran... only the base NPC towns aren't.)

A charming romp through semi-mystical pseudo-Europe, Valkyria Chronicles is a lovable underdog story, told with all the cliches and stereotypes that are commonplace to the narrative. Though it offers nothing remarkable in terms of story, the characters shine through and the tale of this quirky group of  outnumbered, outmatched militia-men facing off against a monolithic war-machine will keep you spellbound. With its lovable cast of protagonists and secondary characters, who succeed in evolving as the story progresses, beautiful cell-shaded artwork and intuitive mechanics, Valkyria Chronicles promises to entertain you, as you fall in love with its cast of misfits.
There's no denying Valkyria Chronicles follows a cookie-cutter plot. It tells the tale a vicious and nearly omnipotent empire seeking the valuable unobtainium hidden within the borders of a small, neutral nation. Galia fins itself caught in the middle as two superpowers clash in this backdrop of magical pseudo-Europe at war. The story is simple but its overtone of acceptance, resistance and camaraderie still carry weight.
Th true strength of Valkyria Chronicles lies in its cast of quirky and unforgettable characters. While some of the primary cast fall into typical JRPG roles, most of the characters, including a slew of unique and remarkable secondary characters, are fantastic. You'll find yourself weighing every decision and regretting the loss of every felled squadmate. The unlockable backstories and models are a nice touch that help you feel more intimate with the soldiers under your command.
Additionally, Valkyria Chronicles sports some of the most beautiful artwork to date. A throwback to the dawn of cell-shaded games, the graphics can feel a little dated to some, but the charm still holds. Characters, background and every detail from clothing to weaponry has something to love, even if it lacks the polish of more recent releases.
Unfortunately, this charm and love does not follow through to the control scheme. The fact that the game is a port is obvious from the awkward and clunky key mapping. Despite these faults, the game's mechanics are intuitive and undeniably revolutionary.  Playing through your turn in a third-person perspective, with immediate repercussions for miss-steps and mistakes, adds an additional layer of depth and enjoyment to an already phenomenal game.
Though the game lacks much of a story, or challenge, its lovable cast, charming artwork and enjoyable gameplay make it a worthwhile purchase, despite the cliche narrative and JRPG tropes.

ArcheAge is a fun sandbox with plenty to do, or be prevented from doing depending on who's trolling who. Unlike some games you are not entirely class locked, there are classes, but you can change what you are at any time (for a small in game fee of course). You can fight, you can craft, you can quest, you can also do any of the above or all of the above to level.
While one of the big draws for this game is that you can own land and build different homes or farms on that land I feel you should be warned of two things. First, you need to be a patron to won land, stop paying and you lose your land. Second, there is almost no land depending on what server, what location, and of course who you talk to. Botting and scripting land grabs ruined the beginning of this game for many people. While I went into the game wanting land and a house I now see it as being too much of a constraint so I'm fine with having no place to call my own... no lonely little shack in the middle of nowhere even... no place to hide the bodi.... err nevermind.
Players should also be aware that no matter what you do if you have any hope of hanging onto every little piece of crafting items, armors, weapons, etc etc (ok ok so I horde) then forget it, even with paying to expand your bank and inventories to max and mailing items to your alts, sorry but you're going to run out of room. Land owners have more options with chests but those chests and all items will be mailed back and possibly lost if you stop paying (Who knew the Sword of Damocles was held aloft by money).
One big plus is that patronage can be purchased with in game money (sort of) it's not direct but one player can buy a cash shop item called Apex and then sell it to other players for in game currency. When used Apex gives the player credit in the cash shop they can use to purchase patronage.
The game has also progressed pretty well at lowering the number of gold spammers, I now rarely see any and the few I do I can block.
Overall I recommend that anyone looking for an MMO to either settle down in or play casual give this one a try.

Are they all well-executed? Well...
The story is probably this game's strong suit. You play as Ronan, a cop with a dark past who is investigating his wife's murder when he himself is killed by the infamous Bell Killer. The buildup is fantastic and the atmosphere is great, but the ending? It was certainly a twist but just not a satisfying one.
Anyone who has played Ghost Trick (a far better game) would feel right at home in Murdered: Soul Suspect. You possess people and items to obtain clues, sometimes manipulating them to your will. In some parts you control cats, which control frusturatingly bad. Thrown into the game at random intervals are Demon sections that, honestly, I hate. I try not to hate things in video games, because, you know, people put a lot of work into them, but the Demon sections are just awful. You can try to sneak by them, but it's impossible - they will see you, sometimes through walls. You can execute them through quicktime events, but if you fail, you have to hide, and they will look for you for what seems like an hour. It's just tedious and every time I heard their shrieks announcing their arrival, I audibly groaned.
This is not the best-looking game this year, but there are a lot of nice touches I enjoyed, such as ghosts appearing off in the distance, staring at you, only to disappear when you approach them. I love stuff like that, it's immersive and creates a genuinely creepy atmoshpere. What I don't like are the bugs. And there are a LOT of them. About a third into the game, my mission indicator froze on something and remained that way for the rest of the game, which was really confusing later on. Small bugs like this really hurt immersion and I wish there were less of them because, really, it's what holds this game back from a high score from me.
Murdered: Soul Suspect was fun while it lasted (about 7 hours), but once it's over there's not much else to do. There are 242 collectible artifacts to find, but I find little motivation to go back in and get them all; once the story is over, there's not a lot of reason to play the game again. What saddens me is that it could have been so much better. The large amount of bugs and disappointingly short story could have been solved with a few more months of development. Looking back on the game, I just see it as an underwhelming waste of time not worth 30 dollars. Buy this game on sale if you want to buy it at all.

I was really pulled into this game; its immersion factor was quite high. There is much to say, for I have played it at great length and to completion. Warning: spoilers ahead.
Things I liked:
The tactical combat was rewarding. I found that most battles tended to end as either Flawless Victories or defeats; there didn't appear to be much middle ground in terms of outcome. I relied on a team of 2 soliders, 2 scouts and either 2 medics or 1 medic and 1 scholar. At first I eschewed the medics, as I felt that the in-combat healing was a little too fantastical for what I took to be a historical RPG. (More fool I, for the apparent rise of 3rd wave feminism 5 centuries early should have clued me on to the fact this game is quite fantastical.)
Things I didn't like:
"Your guards failed to prevent the theft of 2444 valuables during the night." What in the holy hell. I understand the concept of RNG, but it felt like A) this happened way too often, as though some factor was not accurately reflected in the Guarding percentages (I never camped at below 85% and always tried my best to max it out at 95) and B) the amount stolen was way out of proportion to the value of other things that could be stolen, such as medicine, rations or various construction materials.  As a result, despite discovering El Dorado, I finished the campaign with Carlos♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at me for bringing back a paltry ~15000 valuables.
And that's another thing. El Dorado. While I enjoyed the quests and puzzles, I found the reward in valuables to be quite underwelming. Anti-climatic, even. In fact, I will say the same about raiding Quetzequoatle's temple. I wish I kept track of the figures, but I'm fairly certain my scouts rounded up more valuables on their nightly patrols getting there and back to Tenochitlan.
I felt robbed of my glorious victory upon slaying Monteczuma. If I had known I didn't have enough troops in my barracks back at the Stone House, I wouldn't have embarked upon those final quests. I had resolved early on to do as the historical Cortes had done, but could not. I had to let those dirty savages keep their filthy empire of heresy. This was outrageous. The fort/barracks mechanic was introduced too late and not very well explained. I guess I was supposed to have my hermandad sit around and do nothing until some arbitrary number of soldiers was recruited.
Part of why I went into the ending when I did (and thus losing Mexico for Spain) was that I was sitting on more XPs than I could spend and so felt that it was time to wrap this game up. The leveling needs some work. More promotions. More things to spend XPs on. I did use my hermandad from the Hispaniola campaign, so perhaps that explains the overage, but honestly, why wouldn't you use the same character?
The equipment system was flat and unimaginative. It inspired me neither in terms of cool factor nor in utility nor in versimilitude. Am I to believe that my 15th century Spanish soldiers would find value in weapons made of glass? Or in armor made of feathers? Give me the classic model of equipping units anyday; weapon, armor and accessory.
Arquebusses are♥♥♥♥♥♥ Not the♥♥♥♥♥♥ but♥♥♥♥♥♥ These weapons were a big part of how the conquistadors did their thing. That they were inaccurate is well represented, but remember, these ignorant natives had no conception of black powder weapons. Where's the shock and awe? I tried using them but was profoundly dissapointed. Not even a leveled up hunter made them worthwhile.
The battle maps were sometimes confusing. It wasn't always clear to me if I could move into a hex or not; sometimes foilage would cover the grid.
Conclusion
Despite my criticisms, I did find myself playing the game to completion. I think at some point it became an obession. Which is highly to be desired in one's video games. I do not see much replay value in it, but I do look foward to the Expeditions: Viking game, which I will most certainly be purchasing.

In this game you are a Spanish Conquistador. You can choose if you want to trade and intermix with the natives, or if you want to brutally kill them, rob them and burn their villages!
For that you get to choose you followers, which can be racist or open-minded, greedy or altruistic, pious or narcisistic, peacefull or agressive, etc.
There are several classes of followers, like soldiers, hunters and doctors, and when you gain experience you get to promote them, giving them more abilities to help you in the game.
The game is based in the exploration of the main map, with battles every time you encounter someone and don't get the chance (or don't want to) deal with them peacefully or run away.
The battles are turn based, and the goals can be to kill every enemy or just to survive a certain number of turns. Most of the times you can set up barricades and traps, or use items like torches and lanterns to set the scenery on fire! The AI is not to clever, but as you are regularly outnumbered these battles turn up to be quite chalenging.
You get to manage your resources, like food and medicine, and if you run out of them, you're in big trouble as you can't feed or heal your people!
In the course of the game you'll have many dialogues, with your followers or with other characters, and the decisions you take in those dialogues (wheter to fight or trade, wheter to punish anyone or leave him alone) have influence on the morale of your followers. If this gets too low they will rebel!
All in all a very engaging game that puts you in place of a Conquistador, trying to win glory and fame!

ALPHA PLAYER REVIEW:
Please note, I had this far before I got it on steam, hence my low hours
DO NOT support this game, it hurts me to say this but DO NOT
Because:
1.) The game is on life support, not due to player density, but due to people actually working on the game, trion layed off a ton of people who were working on archeage before it was even released, even multiple programers who worked on this have stated that it is beyond fixing at this point
2.) While it is not pay 2 win, it is pay 2 progress. What does that mean?
All actions you due in terms of crafting or farming or anything else requires "labor" every action has its own point value, no big deal, but free to play players only have a cap of 2,000 labor, you can go through that in a second if you craft to level up your character or try to increase your trade, this is where a portion of the micro trans come in, you can buy potions to recover your labor (labor usually takes a long time to recover if your a freebie) OR you can upgrade to prem or buy potions and pay for prem for a month or so, or buy these time prems from other players via the marketplace, which boosts your labor to 5,000 with an increase recovery rate. (I was a prem due to buying alpha) Now why is this a bad thing you might ask? On paper it is great, players who work hard can get the benifits of prem without ever cracking open their wallet, but I have friends and guild members who on multiple times the game would not register their activation of these items but still concidered it used, this is not fun when you paid a lot of gold or items to get these time cards.
3.)  Yes, there are a TON of classes, a huge buy for the game was the insane amount of classes you could make, only one issue, not all classes are created equal, when it boils down to it, there are really only maybe 4-5 classes that are the best or "top tier" you can be kicked from parties or dungons for not being one of these, and these 5 classes are OVERPOWERED compared to all the other classes, at one point all I ever saw was daggerspells, what fun is diversity when it is obvious the game is catering to certain playstyles/classes?
4.) This goes back to 1, you can literally never touch a quest, or mob, or anything if you are premium, why you might ask? Because of crafting and mining, if you have the labor and an XP boost, you can max in a week, this is why I said pay to progress, while it is not needed, it is such a HUGE difference in the time it takes, which kills any point of even doing PvE
5.) The game tries SO HARD to show you how pretty it looks, yes it looks amazing for an MMO, massive props to the devs on this, but the world itself seems so bleak/uninspired, it feels like any other MMO you've played, the quests are generic, the fightinig is generic, the art style is generic, even the music for the most part seems like it was just smacked in the middle.
6.) Servers and updates; There have been MULTIPLE times that servers have been offline for DAYS with no real answer from the devs as to what is going on, nobody is expecting an instant answer, but when it gets to the point where people start making "HL3 confirmed, archage servers are up" jokes without a single responce from devs, that's a little bad.
7.) Housing; Yeah, good luck with that, unless you are on a fresh made server, you'll have to hawk every spot that hasn't had it's bills paid on time, and usually either someone will just PK you so they get the spot or a bot will insta build when the property comes up for sale, this can be massivly frustrating for anyone.

Overall the game was great for a while but it is like a giant inflatible castle with a hole in it, it only goes so far.

While a majority of these are simple to get, the game punishes you for not picking Excalibur at the beginning. If you want to ever obtain Excalibur, you need to do very annoying & extensive farming that is there to make it difficult (which was there intention, but it just turns out to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.) This also applies Warframes like "Mesa", "Octavia". For example, in order to get a chance at Mesa, you need to sit in the same couple missions over and over mindlessly killing the same enemies type till you finally got the parts for one key (lol, just one), and that's just a chance to get one part. The real struggle comes in when you finally get 2 parts of the Warframe (remember, it's just a chance to get a part of the Warframe (let me explain - you need a Helmet, Chestpiece, and Systems to make it easy), and the parts have ABOUT equal drop rates. So they make you farm these "keys" forever to fight the boss ONCE and the parts have equal drop rates, it's going to take you days if you aren't lucky to obtain all three pieces of this Warframe in a row (lol, very unlikely). When you are farming Octavia, it's pretty simple... except for one part. The part that's so troubling is a part you have to obtain by AFKing in a mission for twenty minutes to have a 20-ish% chance to obtain the part, and then you leave and try again if you didn't get it. Keep in mind you can purchase these Warframes in full form with the premium currency, platinum.
The crafting system is pretty solid, while only having a couple items that are insanely ridiculous to craft. They did a nice job on this making the GUI clear and less confusing for new players, and you can mess around with it a bit.

Every time I play this game, I think I'll only invest a small amount of time but always end up losing so much more time than I'd intended because it is so addicting and sucks you in. You get attached to your dynasty (family) and want to keep conquering and expanding your nation's borders whether it be through marriages and inheritence or more direct military or plotting.
This game is really about the relationships between characters and making the best of your situation as a given ruler and dealing with his or her strengths and weaknesses. It is very rare to have a "perfect" character- you will have good traits and bad traits, and sometimes there will be good and bad things about those traits that aren't immediately apparent. Unless your character is very skilled in diplomacy, you will rarely please everyone and that is the point- you have to learn how to make sure you please the right people and in doing so, they will (hopefully) please you.
I think that the wars in this game are underappreciated. You don't get to command many units and watch them battle it out in the traditional sense, but you have army generals you can appoint to lead your men (who are only numbers to you) to victory. We all like to crush the enemy fast and hard, but when you fight against someone of equal or greater strength, you'll likely lose battles. This is where the ability for real strategy shines- just because your army loses one huge, colossal battle doesn't mean you've lost the war. It will severely dishearten you, making you mad, want to give up, but I've found that if you stick with it and use your head, you can still overcome the defeat and win the war in the end.
There was one time that I was under attack and my army was overmatched and the war was essentially us sitting in my castles and hoping the enemy loses men while besieging me while plotting with his lords to try to arrange an assassination, and succeeded! He was murdered in his own camp outside my walls and with his dead, the war was ended! It is that kind of satisfaction you get from pulling off an unlikely win that makes me love this game so.
I could go on and on about what I love about this game, but this is getting pretty lengthy, so I'll just say:
PROS:
-Focus on relationships between characters
-Growing your nation on a global scale depends on your different abilities as a ruler. You can go from the lord of a single county to managing a massive empire.
-Wars can be intense and can be won and lost through different strategies.
-Expansion packs add cool flavors and gameplay mechanics to different groups
-You have to keep your dynasty/family going through marriages and education of your children and protecting your interests
-Council members can be put to use on a variety of helpful tasks
CONS:
-Battles are represented by numbers (I don't think this is too bad, because in a war there might be a lot of battles being fought and you will spend a lot of time managing everything as it is, but some people will always want to see the action. That's total war to me though)
-Some minor bugs like council members randomly quitting. (Maybe it's not a bug and they just don't like me, but there's no popup message about it) Nothing game-breaking
I reccomend this game to anyone who likes the idea of growing and expanding your own kingdom.

Oh dear, I'm dead - pretty much the main mechanic of the game.
starts out with the death of the main character who goes by the name of Ronan, a local Detective investigating a murder. It's not the most unique premise out there, but it handles it in such a way that makes it intriguing, but can ultimately fall a little short thanks to the way the game itself is structured.
While Ronan and the other main characters look pretty good and the environments themselves look pretty top notch, I can't really say the same for the NPCs. I noticed they re used qutite a LOT of NPCs without as much as trying to hide it somehow, which can definately break the immersion this game tries to set in with it's dark and drab setting. The lighting is top notch also, and really helps give the game the sense that you're in some ghostly world in an already dark setting.
The environments, as stated above, look very nice and I really like how they themselves tell their own stories because of the way the game places just random objects in an area. You can have, for example, a train inside a museum to let the player know that in the past, where the museum stands now used to be a regularly used train track and the game's chock full of little things like that, as well as it uses flat and ghostly images that sorta just fade out as you get closer to them to help accentuate that you are indeed in a ghost world. It's really good.
Even greatly influencing the atmosphere the game has, is it's sound design. You can occasionally hear ghostly wails in the backgrounds, and the game is very light on music, only really playing it during tense moments like when there are Demons around, it knows when and when not to play music and it handles it pretty well. Voice acting is pretty par for the course, Ronan and the main characters sound decent, but some of the VA's for the NPCs can be pretty hit or miss.

is pretty much a glorified adventure game. The very linear structure the game has is done to help accentuate the story, making it feel actually more like a 3D Visual Novel than an Adventure game. The game is pretty much divided up by "stage" sections and an overworld (The Town). Each "Stage" has it's own set of collectibles that, once fully completed, gives you insight into a usually very dark and grim backstory into those items you collect as well as having it's own story section and more in general collectibles.
What can feel detrimental to the game's pacing, is the way each stage is handled. It always ends up being a straight up Move from Point A to Point B sort of ordeal while exploring through every nook and cranny to find collectibles.
As far as mechanics go, the game can sometimes feel a little messy since there's no map to indicate an overall layout of the area you're in, thankfully, no one area looks exactly like another so it's usually easy to tell when you're going the wrong way - you can also walk through certain walls, and railings on stairs but not all of them. You can also posses people and read their thoughts (random NPCs) but sometimes they just end up repeating lines, other times, for story purposes, you can posses people to get over obstacles, you can posses objects to cause noises and distract NPCs and you can influence people to think about certain events by using clues. Clues are items you inspect during an "Investigation" phase which can be used occasionally only during said investigation, or sometimes long term throughout the whole game.
That being said, the only challenge this game does bring, is some half baked stealth sections involving "demons", creatures that live to suck out a spirit's soul and re-kill them I guess? These sections can be very tense thanks to the musical cues and the great wails they tend to do, but they merely serve to give the game padding and often can break up the pace of the story. The demons are also never used in any meaningful way to complement the story.

is a pretty fun and short adventure game that can clock you in anywhere from 4-12 hours depending on how much you decide to focus on collectibles. There's no real punishing methods the game uses outside of demons catching you, it has a fairly uneven pace that can otherwise dull a pretty nice Murder thriller story.
Pros
+ Amazing atmosphere   + Great sound design accentuates further the atmosphere  + Decent Voice Work
+ Interesting and fun story  + Fun mechanics that makes you feel like a ghost.
Cons
- Uneven Pacing  -  Game is on the short side, story alone clocks in at about 4 hours or so  - Repeated use of NPC models can break immersion.  -Demons serve no purpose to the story and are used as padding.
Overall, if you can pick this game up at a decent price range, it's definately worth a playthrough if you enjoy Murder/Crime Thrillers, outside of that, this has very limited appeal.

Truly surprised at how much I enjoyed this game. If you liked XCOM: Enemy Unknown but want a more story driven experience, I highly recommend trying this out. In all my years of gaming (about 20 or so), I don't think I've ever really played a game with a story that felt so mature. It's extremely refreshing and I think that everyone should try it.
This game has a lot going for it
+ Really good writing. The writing in this game is a serious step above your average video game writing. I'd love it if more games put this much effort into their writing. The characters you choose to join your party all have really interesting backstories and personalities. This is definitely the strength of this game.
+ Tactical combat that is challenging but still forgiving. One of the great things about this is that even though your people can go down in battle, you can still bring them back once the fight is over, granted you have enough medicine saved up. The game ties its combat and survival mechanics together nicely. There's even a little economy system. It's very basic supply and demand, but it's nice to see thought put into all the little aspects of this game.
+ Meaningful choices and consequences that aren't always obvious.
+ Catchy music.
Things not so great:
- Graphics are simple I suppose. I honestly thought this was a game that came out in the 2000's. It's not going to put your PC to the test.
- Minimal graphics. The game really only has two views: overworld and battle mode. The story is mainly told through dialogue with portraits next to them to show who you're talking to. They do not change expression based on their dialogue. Instead, emotions are conveyed (very well) through character dialogue.
- More reading than most games that will probably intimidate people who don't liked to read. Now I know that sounds pretty bad, but I feel like I should point out that I don't read anything other than the internet. So don't think you have to be a book worm to enjoy this game. The game's solid writing and the fact that it asks you to make choices that actually have some weight will keep you engaged in whats going on. There are rarely ever walls of text. I'd compare reading the dialogue to participating in an online conversation with fancier vocabulary.
I really cannot recommend this game enough. It's really nice to see a game not pull any punches and just be so driven by its narrative. I honestly think this game makes a great case for video games being art. Play this game.

This Murder Mystery if filled with its uniqueness and presented with a story where the mystery actually gets a hold of you. Frankly speaking it is a big underrated game and i blame official mainstream reviewers, this may not be the best game around but its certainely worth playing.

The gameplay is little bit different than the first Mass Effect but the storyline just as good. Many new interesting NPCs in addition to recurring characters from the first game. The missions are more interesting than the previous series because the levels are better defined compared to ME 1 where the interior of any building looks very similar.There is wider selection of squad members so you can employ many different tactics according to a mission's need. The squad members also have unique personalities and history that they can share with you, given you spend some time to talk to them. The loyalty missions, squad members confrontation with each other and romance really adds flavour to the game. Squad members can die in the final mission (dubbed as the Suicide Mission) resulting from failing to secure their loyalty, not making ship upgardes or choosing non-ideal person for a task in the mission. This forces the player to carefully plan and prepares for the mission. The were so many different way the game progress and ends, even the main character may be killed in the suicide mission. This gives the game a very high replay value and the player did get a bonus to the character and resources should we choose start a new game after finishing one.
Overall, Mass Effect 2 is a story rich game that continues the greatness of the first game. If you want to play the game, I suggest you finish ME1 first and carry forward your character into this game. Forget about wikis and walkthrough (except when you completely stuck of course) and just follow your heart and be yourself when making decision throughout the game and you will find out the Commander Shepard you're playing really reflects the person you are (Paragon and Renegade choices). You always can play it again later if you want to experience another options that you missed before, or choosing different character to romance or whatever different options the game can offer. But remember, the outcome of the decisions can be carried to Mass Effect 3. For score, I'm giving ME2 a solid 9/10

2.5 hours in and I am impressed with this game. After a few small headaches with getting connected, mostly due to day 1 bugs and connection issues one would expect with a game in beta, I experienced some of the most enjoyable gameplay I have had the pleasure of experiencing since Rust first came out. Early creatures feel dangerous but once you get a handle on combat and move up past the basic cloth armor and driftwood tier shield, you start being able to fight back quite effectively. Archery seems like it will be incredibly strong if you are skilled enough to land shots, but while i wait on some of the kinks with rubber banding and desync to get figured put, I am enjoying sword and board combat.
Unlike with some survival games, the first tier of buildings do not require a massive time investment to make. You can get a basic building set up in about 5-10 minutes, complete with a sleeping back to respawn at. The buildings provide very little in the way of defense, but protect you from sandstorms and require a commitment of time and effort to break into.
i have thus far sacrificed 8 players to Set. Having a reason to kill human NPC's and players adds a level of immersion to pvp which I like.
What I am most impressed with is how quickly Funcom has been addressing what would be considered game breaking issues in a finished title. Multiple patches for stability and crash fixes have come out already and it's the first full day of release.
Thus far, my only complaint is a bug that allows players to punch through tier 1 walls with their fists. However Funcom has confirmed, they are already have a fix on the way.
After I hit the 50 hour mark I will update this review, but thus far I am extremely happy with this game.
67 hour edit:
Still hooked, can't put it down. It's been just over a week since the game deployed and it's in a MUCH more playable state. Performance has increased by leaps and bounds across the board, the only lag I get now is related to my 6-year old computer.
Now that server lag has been drastically reduced, I must correct myself about creatures being dangerous early off. Even basic creatures continue to be a threat well into the game, requiring you to always bring some healing items with (or antidotes, for the spider's crippling poison) or risk death all the way up until you have steel. This has made the environment seem much more scary, which makes the game continue to feel exciting. Now that the lag's gone, I can no longer safely take on 5 pirates by rushing them, I have to fight strategically while also conserving my stamina.
If you're on the fence about buying this game... just know that your experience will be easily 10x better if you take the time to find a stable, lag-free server. Some hosts are much better than others as far as stability, and it's more than just ping, it's hardware. Since picking up the game, me and my group have also picked up a 50-slot server and it's been running stable even with 30+ people online.
Your cross awaits, Exiles.

ALPHA PLAYER REVIEW:
Please note, I had this far before I got it on steam, hence my low hours
DO NOT support this game, it hurts me to say this but DO NOT
Because:
1.) The game is on life support, not due to player density, but due to people actually working on the game, trion layed off a ton of people who were working on archeage before it was even released, even multiple programers who worked on this have stated that it is beyond fixing at this point
2.) While it is not pay 2 win, it is pay 2 progress. What does that mean?
All actions you due in terms of crafting or farming or anything else requires "labor" every action has its own point value, no big deal, but free to play players only have a cap of 2,000 labor, you can go through that in a second if you craft to level up your character or try to increase your trade, this is where a portion of the micro trans come in, you can buy potions to recover your labor (labor usually takes a long time to recover if your a freebie) OR you can upgrade to prem or buy potions and pay for prem for a month or so, or buy these time prems from other players via the marketplace, which boosts your labor to 5,000 with an increase recovery rate. (I was a prem due to buying alpha) Now why is this a bad thing you might ask? On paper it is great, players who work hard can get the benifits of prem without ever cracking open their wallet, but I have friends and guild members who on multiple times the game would not register their activation of these items but still concidered it used, this is not fun when you paid a lot of gold or items to get these time cards.
3.)  Yes, there are a TON of classes, a huge buy for the game was the insane amount of classes you could make, only one issue, not all classes are created equal, when it boils down to it, there are really only maybe 4-5 classes that are the best or "top tier" you can be kicked from parties or dungons for not being one of these, and these 5 classes are OVERPOWERED compared to all the other classes, at one point all I ever saw was daggerspells, what fun is diversity when it is obvious the game is catering to certain playstyles/classes?
4.) This goes back to 1, you can literally never touch a quest, or mob, or anything if you are premium, why you might ask? Because of crafting and mining, if you have the labor and an XP boost, you can max in a week, this is why I said pay to progress, while it is not needed, it is such a HUGE difference in the time it takes, which kills any point of even doing PvE
5.) The game tries SO HARD to show you how pretty it looks, yes it looks amazing for an MMO, massive props to the devs on this, but the world itself seems so bleak/uninspired, it feels like any other MMO you've played, the quests are generic, the fightinig is generic, the art style is generic, even the music for the most part seems like it was just smacked in the middle.
6.) Servers and updates; There have been MULTIPLE times that servers have been offline for DAYS with no real answer from the devs as to what is going on, nobody is expecting an instant answer, but when it gets to the point where people start making "HL3 confirmed, archage servers are up" jokes without a single responce from devs, that's a little bad.
7.) Housing; Yeah, good luck with that, unless you are on a fresh made server, you'll have to hawk every spot that hasn't had it's bills paid on time, and usually either someone will just PK you so they get the spot or a bot will insta build when the property comes up for sale, this can be massivly frustrating for anyone.
8.) In the end, the game later on feels more like a job rather than a game, you usually end up becoming a slave to the economy in terms of just spam trade packs across the sea or to your local dealers or making items for others and selling them on the auction house.
9-ish.) This is more of a subjective issue, but on my server there was a well known youtuber who would stream and record his gameplay, getting a ton of his drones to hop on and try the game, long story short, a lot of stuff pointing towards some GM's giving him little extra's for advertising their game, such as buying stuff that was not out yet for the game. I do not have proof to link, but if you search around you will find a lot of talk about this issue.
What did I like?
1.) This game shows you how to do PvP right, even if the classes can ruin it, it always feels responsive and fluid
2.) The crime system is pretty fun, getting a bounty on your head and having to defend yourself in court ran by player jury leads to great and funny confrontations
3.) Sailing, beyond fun with a band of friends or guild, feels like windwaker in that aspect that you can sail forever and not get bored, just look out for pirates or the other continent or worse...THE KRAKEN!
Overall the game was great for a while but it is like a giant inflatible castle with a hole in it, it only goes so far.
Are you looking for a long term MMO to get into? I would skip this one
Got some friends who play this and want to hop on every now and then? Go for it
Is this a "WoW" killer? No

If there is one word to describe SPAZ, it would be "ambitious". If there are two words, they would be "over ambitious". It has all the parts needed to make a grand space adventure but ultimatly the various systems are not deep enough to support this. The game is divided into two parts.
The strategy part has you designing ships, plotting a course around the galaxy and managing relationships between three factions. But those relationships carry only over between systems for one of the factions so there's no long term planning in relationship building. And those relationships can be turned very easily so ticking someone off only takes 1 or 2 missions to fix. The one faction that does perist relationships is only ever hostile towards you so your interactions are limited. The ship design system is deep enough but it requires way too much farming. Advanced ship designs require several blueprints which can only be obtained by destoring enemy (or friendly) versions the ship. Advanced weapons also require several blueprints which can be bought or stolen from the faction bases. On top of all that, the weapons can only be used if you reach a certain tech level which again means more farming.
The second part of the game is the tactical action combat. This part has you commanding your ships and piloting one of those ships in space battles. This is where you use the ships you grinded for. Ships handle differently and learing to lead your shots and manage your momentum is key to success in this section of the game. However, because of the slow build of new ships and weapons many battles are the same.
But despite all the negatives, it is possible to loss yourself in the universe and just enjoy the ride. It's a fairly cheap game and is often on sale.

I've actually logged in more hours than Steam says. From my experience of ArcheAge is well... it's your standard Korean sandbox-MMO. Pretty new to us and it does look amazing (providing you have the system requirements.)
Summary: While to progress smoothly and with good pace, take that hard earned income, pocket money or get a friend to pay for Premium. Or at least, pay to progress. Many people will say that it's pay to win. I'd say "Not quite. Star Wars: The Old Republic is pay to win". For a F2P can you really complain at the restraints? It's free. Mean, come on. It's 2015. It's time.
Simply put: Pay to progress with ease. Go free for a long arduous experince but still entertaining none the less.
For those who are intrigued by ArcheAge or want to blow off sometime till the "next big thing", then continue to read below.
ArcheAge is one of those gems that you rarely find, it's unique and pretty amazing but a gem is still a rock and you've seen a lot of rocks. One of the key features of ArcheAge, seen very little in newish to older MMOs, is its sandbox feature. Love tree just a little more than you should? Welcome to ArcheAge! Were you can plant trees amongst other things. However, it's not all that great see if you are a F2P user, more than likely, you can place items down, grow trees and po-ta-toes, and chickens for crafting. However... other players can steal your items. For F2P users, your items aren't protected and anyone can take them whereas if you pay, you get a nice little house or farm to grow your po-ta-toes and they'll be protected. Now I'm not saying that if your F2P your items are going to be stolen at every turn just like 60% - 85% of the time they will. So better find a really good hiding place.
Labour Points (LP): ArcheAge uses the system of Labour Points which generates 5 points every 5 minutes, I believe. Not sure if they've changed it. Unless you're paid user in which you get 10 points every 5 minutes while online and 5 points when you're offline. Also the standard labour point cap is 2000 for F2P users, for the account. Not for each single character. I believe for paid users it's 5000 cap.
In addition to that: Crafting, Harvesting, Mining, placing items, Identifying items etc. (The list is like huge, just my♥♥♥♥♥♥) Requires labour points. If you want to chop down a tree, it does various, it will cost you 25 labour points. If you're free, you'll have to be online for 25 minutes just to chop down one tree and you may get one Log to 10x Log. Want to make something out of that Log(s)? First turn it into Lumber, gonna cost LP (can't remember how much >.< just playing aswell). Now you've got lumber, get the other necessary items. Guess what? You need more LPs... It's a long arduous process to make one. ONE. Item. Imagine going through that process for making armour, it's 7 pieces for a set and the lowest of crafting armour requires 100+ LP per armour. So umm... F2P guys, you're gonna be there for awhile, max level, crafting basic armour. You can make it, it's not impossible just gonna take a long time.
Environment/atmosphere: Graphics. Well it's not Black Desert but it's better than what most Western companies are producing. Mean, have you seen the trailers? Screenshots? It's pretty stunning, if you've got the system to run it uber high.
Factions: You've got 4 playable races and you've got two of those races on two continents. Those two continents happen to be at war with each other. So if you want to play as a cat person and your friend wants to play as an elf, you're better off finding new friends. For you'll see each other as enemy players unless you're pirates but becoming a pirate takes ages. There's nothing really good about this. Also each continent is better growing jazz than the other or you can only get specific item/materials. Furthermore, you row your little boat to the other continent for one stupid quest to get a farm and everyone will try and kill you, unless you're a high level then you should be fine.
Ships/Mounts/vehicles: Like boats? Like sailing the seven seas? Well how about you harpoon your ship across land. It's just brilliant. Okay, there you are, deep in the jungle killing 10 of something and in the distance you see a large ship. Reeling its way across land. It's just magnificent. It's soo stupid it works. Think that's what sold me on ArcheAge.
Okay so mounts. Ever played that MMO where they give you a mount, free of course, and it's movement speed like 5% - 15% faster than your character and some other guy, whose paid, has got this majestic mount that moves like 60% faster? Yeah we've got that too. BUT! You don't just get that one terrible mount that's actually kinda good, oh no, you get three! The first one being race specific, you can get the other mounts through other means but it's gonna cost like 50gold or real money, the other two is a fluff tauntaun and♥♥♥♥♥ Oh one last thing, you get gliders and steam engine cars. Well everyone gets a glider but the cars... don't go there is you're a free guy.
Armour: Oh hey, you're a Tank class? Well then you can't wear cloth armour, that's only for mages. Yeah no. ArcheAge has one of these features that is quite brilliant. You can be any class/build and wear any armour you want. Squishy mage? How about force-lightening fortress? Though each class of armour has it's pros and con but you don't need to wear the same type. Armour comes in three classes: Cloth, Leather and Plate. And like 12? different qualities. You can mix and match the armour to your preference or just go style over stats.
Classes: If you don't know by know, ArcheAge has 10 classes and you choose three of them. Not at once mind you. You build the class to how you want to play and you can change those classes at anytime. Gone full on tank and you have no healer friends because I mean, who plays healer? Then change of your classes to a healer one. Play style changes but you can heal... kind of. Best leave it to a dedicated healer. Basically, you build a class on how you want to play and not is required or what some wants you to play as.
Playstyle: Just like every, empathise on the every, MMO it has the quest system on: go collect this, kill 10 of these, to this dungeon. It's the same like every MMO so don't expect anything new there. However! You don't have to play ArcheAge just for the quests. You can just be a farmer, crafter, pirate or part of commerce. Personally, I'm tired of doing the generic quests but I like to play MMOs, ArcheAge provides another mean to play. Mean I had more entertaining crafting item, travelling to another city, making travelling companions and selling golds to an NPC instead of grinding. You still get EXP from this and other jazz. It's refreshing having this option in the game, providing you can do that jazz.
Rather short review so I've probably miss a few things but you should get the gist. Would I recommend this game? I'd say give it a try. If anything it can pass the time until you find another gem. To be honest, this review doens't makes sense. Enjoy.

First of all - Ignore the negative reviews. 90% of them are "omg just released, there are sever problems and some game problems. The game is only avaible for 20 minutes but HURRDURR♥♥♥♥♥♥GAME HATE IT."
Now to the actual Review - It is an interesting game for now (I've played 6 hours so far). You can do a lot of stuff, you can die due to a lot of reasons.
The "bugs" I've experienced so far:
- The NPCs still move a little bit buggy (they seem to slide over the ground until they get closer to you).
- Animals and weapons bug through walls when they attack (so you can hit them through the walls as they can hit you through the walls).
- the physics feel a bit clumsy sometimes, I don't know if you'll actually take damage if you jump down a mountain.
- If you reach the border of the map (at least I think it's the border) in it's current state, you'll see a green shimmering wall. A warning that you'll die if you walk through it would be very nice.
The positive things I've experienced so far:
- The graphics are nice. If you play and survive long enough to witness the sunrise, it's beautiful.
- Gathering ressources and crafting makes fun and is very interesting. Hopefully they'll adjust the amount of stuff you need for crafting in the future tho.
- It makes a lot of fun to create something with friends and/or randoms. But it's also enjoyable if you want to play Solo.
Hope this Review is helpful for some of you.

For those who enjoy the particualar kind of game that Crusader Kings II is, it is worth every single penny. However, if you are one who is less excited about roleplaying, in-depth history, and boardgame style strategy, this game will simply be a waste of money.
Crusader Kings II is possibly the most accurate and immersive historical game, and is one of the most detailed and complex on the Steam market. To lovers of Europa Universalis and strategy games in general, you will play this game for unhealthy periods of time. You will feel like you are a Medieval noble, conspiring against his king, conquering large swaths of land, or defending against barbarians. This game is truly one of the most immersive I have ever played.
Unfortunately, one has to wonder if the publishers used this game as a money-grab. Without payed DLC content, you will be LOCKED from playing beofre the year 1066 and from playing as a non-Christian even after 1066. This restricts the player from the entirely different playstyles of the Pagans, Muslims, and Indian nations. Without DLC's you cannot become a mighty desert warlord, or raid the weak Christian kingdoms as a VIking warrior. Even the so called "Crusader Kings II Collection", which sells for an astronomical price of 80 dollars does not contain the three largest expansions.
If you are able to get past the obvious money-grab, and if you are a lover of the genre, this game is a must-own, and is a masterpiece of the strategy genre.

I was looking for a RPG with an original setting, and was not disappointed.
OK, not really a RPG to be honest. If you think computer-RPG à la Baldur's Gate, it isn't. Expeditions: Conquistador is more an illegitimate child from Heroes of Might and Magic series:
- explore the map day by day with limited movements
- tile movement combat
- micro management of your party
So to be short, what's OK and what's not.
YES:
- setting, perfectly captured and rendered
- graphics, I've a small computer and the game runs at maximum details 1920x1080
- sounds (you can almost feel the steel and gunpowder in combat)
- music (world, combat and story, special mention to the eerie title music, which is just perfect)
- immersive story
- most of the game mechanics
NO:
- healing kinda sucks: no way to heal in a town (seriously?). To heal your party you must camp outside in the woods, with the right amount of medicine. If you fail to do that, you lose followers.
- morale management is... strange. You'll have hard time to raise your party morale (thanks to quests and tough social decisions), but hunger alone will ruin it.
- camera is fixed on your character, so you'll lose precious movement points losing yourself and taking the wrong path.
Fortunately (unfortunately?) to these NO, there are cheat codes, respectively heal your characters (I authorize this to myself only in towns because DAMN), modify your party morale or add rations, and release the camera from the character.
Despite these small gameplay flaws, I recommend this game, notably to HOM&M fans, and historic games fans.

I played this game from start to finish in two separate nights. The game immediately pulled me into it's atmosphere of supernatural mystery and maintained it's low hanging horror throughout. I'm glad it did not try to be a horror game; it was smartly realized to keep that element very passive which just supported the backbone of the game's overall flavor. This particluar "flavor" is set in Salem, Massachusetts and plays heavily off of the historical witch trials. You get to experience this through the character known as Ronan who dies in the first sequence of the game.
. In order to avoid spoilers I won't say anymore about the story than that.
Gameplay-wise this game relies on an investigation mode where you have to search specific areas for clues to piece together a shard of the story. Sometimes finding all the clues in a given area is really easy, othertimes they aren't all so obvious, but that's okay, beacuase you don't need to necessarily find all the clues to complete the investigation.
.
There is a strange component to this core mechanic in the form of what seems to resemble a score system. It was never made really clear, but basically, whenever you have to put the final pieces of an investigation together a menu is brought up in which you usually have to choose three clues that explain that particular scene. At the bottom of this menu are three police badge shaped icons and whenever you make a mistake in choosing clues one of them goes away. However in my experience the badges will never drop below one and create no pressing incentive to just randomly click on all the clues until you get the right answer.
.
The final main mechanic you will run into are these "stealth-action" sequences. You will occasionally run into areas that have demons blocking your progression. You must sneak behind them and perform a short series of QTEs to destroy them. I played this game with mouse and keyboard, and my expereince with these QTEs was frustrating to say the least. You start by holding R, then have to follow up with a combination press of W, A, S, or D + left or right mouse button. It is a little akward and to be frank they are QTEs which I already despise. I did run into some areas where these demons could be ignored and you can progress by just being sneaky, but not many. And when the demons see you, you have to go run into hiding spaces and then teleport between them when they search the hiding spaces. This entire mechanic is a bit akward and I don't feel it added to the game in a positive way.
.
The game doesn't have a whole lot more to offer mechanically, but it should be expected seeing as this is a very narritive focused game. So as I said above, I reccomend this game only at a discount.
EDIT: Oh I forgot to mention. The final sequence to the game is irritating. You have a limited amount of time to figure out what to do and if you fail it takes you back two whole cinematics. Luckily cinematics can be skipped, but it was frustrating.

This is the first review I have ever written and I'm writing it due to my conflicting interest in this game. It's a very good game. It's optimized to the point that it runs on a generic 2016 HP laptop at 60fps (except earth, ♥♥♥♥ that tile set). There are just over 100 weapons in each catagory (melee, primary and secondary). I believe 30 different warframes to build and a lot of them have prime variants (various increased stats). The combat and movement is enjoyable. You will be flipping and sliding and spinning like a wheel of death after you learn the controls. The other mechanics in the game aren't hard to learn. A lot of people say they are but they aren't. They aren't deep mechanics. There are just a lot of different systems in place. If you decide to play this game then spend time on your ship clicking on stuff (after you finish the few tutorial missions). The game is also packed full of content. You will be learning something new and grinding for different reasons constantly. Alerts, syndacites, fissure missions, star chart, clan contributions and a ton more, but you are doing the same thing constantly and that's what I don't like.
It's a grind. It's Grindframe. To the point that you won't even be looking at stuff in the levels and just hauling it to the extraction point. The objectives do vary but getting there is the same thing every time. The devs try things (like spy) but the ai is dumb. I don't really blame the devs for that. In a game about grinding we don't need a ton of difficult enemies. Bosses show the same kind of dumb and will just glitch out a lot. They tried to vary bosses too but a lot of them are lackluster. Who cares though. You're going to be fighting said boss 3+ times for the warframe parts. I don't want to go on about the grind forever though. I didn't enjoy it but maybe you will.
I would definitly give the game a chance. It has a lot going for it and if you enjoy the grind then this game should keep you coming back for a long time. Especially if you decide to grind trade chat. One of the best parts to me.

But oh well, there aren't so many after all and the game is more oriented towards exploration than "fighting". The side stories are also interesting and it isn't too hard to unlock them. I didn't like that there were no consequences whenever you guess something wrong, or if you make a mistake when solving a mystery or investigating something. If that happens, you can just try again until you get it right, which makes the detective work kind of pointless sometimes.
There's no doubt that the best thing about Murdered: Soul Suspect is its plot, so if you like ghost stories, or ghost movies/TV shows (I'm looking at you, Ghost Whisperer!) you're probably going to enjoy this game. It may not be perfect, but it definitely does its job. I only encountered one bug (couldn't exit the menu) at the beginning, but restarting the game fixed it and it never happened again in 10 hours of gameplay. I'd also like to congratulate the Spanish dubbers and localization team for the great job they've done adapting the game. Oh, and one last thing! I MUST mention that this game includes 'Cat Simulator 2014'. Well, kind of... See it for yourself!

TL; DR Despite gorgeous 3d modeled terrain and great faithfulness to the source material its very limited replayablity, some poor UI choices, very basic combat mechanics, and old school "killer DM" sensibilities make this a tough sell at full retail.
Warlock of Firetop Mountain is a video game adaptation of an adventure book.  After
18 hours and
11 successful runs (
6 of which were full warlock kills) and
only 1 complete failure, I have to say it's a mixed bag, not requiring enough skill to create fair difficulty or possessing enough variety of content to be a proper rogue-like which it almost feels like it wants to be.  It’s mostly just a short, mean text adventure/turn-based strategy/dungeon crawl, but not one completely devoid of charm. As I said, it's completely gorgeous! However...
While I never read the book the game is based on, I can only surmise it is rather faithful to the source material, as it’s overflowing with  early 80s pulp sword and sorcery charm.  However that faithfulness is probably also its biggest drawback.  There is a reason why "Choose Your Own Adventure" books went out of style, and that is the limitations of how many branches you can have in a book format.  Procedural content
have remedied that, but that’s not how they choose to handle this game, prefering a straight 1:1 adaptation.  Puzzles being almost completely set in stone with almost no variation between heroes don't really justify repeated runs.  Yes, each hero has his own side quest to achieve and minor differences in move set, but of the
12 runs I've finished so far, none have been different enough to feel like a unique experience.  After your second or third run you will know exactly what early encounters to hit, which to skip, and how to handle them with a minimum of harm and hassle through sheer repetition.  After a half dozen or so runs, you might have memorized multiple paths to the warlock complete with every puzzle solution and enemy attack patterns.  Even the best books get boring once you’ve read them enough, and this
game is painfully short and shallow.
Further, literally every step drops massive text dumps on you, requiring a click every few paragraphs to scroll them and then another click
on the screen to move to the next encounter.  That UI inconsistency is probably the worst aspect of this text adventure and you will quickly want to stop reading the same purple prose paragraphs that you've already memorized, but you can't because otherwise you may accidently take a wrong turn by clicking the wrong box.
The only thing differentiating your runs, your hero selection, doesn't change the encounters very often or very dramatically.  I think on average there are less than 4 encounters in the whole dungeon per hero that play out even the slightest bit differently than the last hero (excepting the italic text for the hero telling you how much he hates orcs or doesn't want to actually fight). After a few times of seeing the exact same encounters in the exact same places, solved the exact same way, the game feels less like a cRPG and more like a Choose Your Own Adventure copied word for word from a book with a very, VERY basic turn-based strategy game stapled to the side of it... which is exactly what it is.
And it’s not even a very good TBS.  As a TBS connoisseur, I can assure you that the TBS elements do not have a lot of meat on their bones.  Most of the heroes have very little to distinguish themselves from each other combat-wise.  They can attack one square ahead, perhaps stronger diagonally, sometimes rarely two ahead, but they mostly play the same.  The tactics that work well for one hero (basically force them to come to you and attack at which ever enemy moved last round while ignoring those that attacked), usually work just as well for the next hero due to the very simple, predictable AI and abusable combat system.  Turns are one action, either move 1 square in a cardinal direction or attack and enemies almost never make you come to them, being mostly willing to dance around you, alternating between move and ineffective attack patterns.
Finally, puzzles with absolutely no foreshadowing or clues to their solutions have not grown more enjoyable with age.  It has the mentality of old “killer DM” modules, where every door knob could be a disguised monster or instantly lethal, no-save, trap.  The kind that both reward and vicously punish in turn the "10-foot pole" ultra-conservative and reckless "let's see what this does" play styles with no rhyme or reason for when it favors either.  That wasn’t satisfying game design then, and it hasn’t aged well for anyone other than the frustration masochistics, people who are amused by cheap deaths, ultra-traditionalists, and Awg.
Overall it’s not unfun, at least in the first few plays, (it has beautiful 3d modeled terrain and a lot of early 80s dungeon crawler nostalgia) but it wears out its welcome surprisingly fast, not something I’d recommend for a $20 game.  If it were under $10, perhaps $5, sure!  It’s a good afternoon of dungeon crawling nostalgia, but unless 3-5 hours justifies $20 for you, I’d pass unless it’s on a steep discount or this sounds like EXACTLY the game you've always wanted.

To start this off... Is this game perfect? No.
Do I enjoy it? Yes.
Since you are reading these reviews you must be torn to get this game or not. If you have only played the newer Disgaea games - Ie, 4.D2. and 5, I would stay away from the computer port, and just  emulate the psp/DS version of it, as it had a few nice Quality of life features, such as faster dialog. If you have played all of them before, give this game a chance.
Gameplay- Disgaea follows a typical TRPG system- Make unit, Select unit, Move unit, Kill unit. Gain exp... Oh, and throw Prinnys Dood. The place where Disgaea is different, is the exp system. Most games let you go to level 99, or if your lucky 999. Disgaea says no to that, with a soft level cap of 9999 and a 'optimal' level cap of  186,000.
Given that TRPG's are the best kind of RPG's I have to give this part a 9/10
Story- Demons, Demonesses, Angels, Flonnes, Prinnys. You play as Laharl; a 1313 year old demon child, who has just awoken from a 2 year slumber to find out that his father, King Krichevskoy, ruler of the Netherwold is dead. This has caused most of the Kings vassals to take off, or to try to take Laharls place as the overlord. Thus, Laharl needs to take the throme back by force.
8/10. Probably the best story in the Disgaea series,  A good mix of comedy, story telling, and drama.
(My personal story ranking- 1,2,5,4,3, D2)
Port- I have not put enough time into the game to give this too much thought, however, it seems to be an almost identical port to the Psp version, with a few extra options added. The options are- New maps, new sprites (Which look terrible) New menus, V-sync, screen size, SSAO, DOF, Screen Blur, and Shadows. (30-60 FPS)
7/10. Not much to say, seems like a straight port.
Performance- This is where the problem lies for some people. Do you have an AMD GPU? Your in for a bad time. Do you like the new features they added? (V-sync, SSAO, ect) Your in for a bad time. Luckily for me, I have neither of the main problem causers, so the game runs at a smooth 60 fps.
9/10. This score is only based on the performance I get.
Overall score- 8/10.  It's a decent port of a great series with a few quality of life features missing. If you like the series and want NIS to port more of the series, go ahead an give em $20.
(For context- Running Windows 7, GTX 970, 16GB, i7-4770)

Probably one of the best and most surprising (because of it originality and innovations) games to ever come out of Kickstarter. It it so much fun you wouldn’t believe it.
The gameplay is like this: a card game mechanic where you make your own deck of skills/items/encounters is the main focus, you move just like in a board game and each card is either one from your deck or one of the cards the “boss” puts in at the start to spice things up. The encounters are either text based stories with tons of decisions (and some of the quests you do can take multiple cards that are unlocked by succeeding) or combat. The combat is very similar to games like Batman or Shadow of mordor, very simple yet very exciting and it fits the game well.
Pros:
-the narrator is probably the best out of any game(both acting and writing), that includes darkest dungeon and Bastion
-the way the gameplay flows is incredible. Even if you might think this is a roguelite game, based on luck, because of the cards, it is very surprising to see how well balanced the luck and skill elements are; in all my time playing I don’t remember ever dying because of  complete randomness; you chose the cards and most of the encounters have 2 or more ways out and combat is completely skill based
-the game doesn’t waste your time, all the story based bosses don’t take long to beat, but as usual exploring might help you
-all of the boss stories are highly replayable, especially if you change the difficulty and deck you use
-multiple difficulties that don’t just give the enemies more health or other such garbage, but instead make the game faster or give the game different modifiers to make the way you play the game different and challenging
-combat is fast and very fluid and different equipment and useable items can change the flow of it quite a bit
Cons:
-the graphics, especially the combat animations of pretty basic(all weapons have the same animations with slower/faster attacks and all of them are 1 handed)
-camera isn’t controllable and sometimes can be annoying
-different effects added by spells/items in battle can really clutter the screen making it hard to see what’s going on especially if you have a lot of enemies
Overall this game, in my opinion, defines “having an adventure”. It can be replayed any time you crave some action with a bit of card game antics thrown in. The only area that could use improvement is the combat, by no means bad, just a bit too basic. It’s A fantastic game that anyone can play and have fun with.

The system here for Warlock of Firetop Mountain makes for a more interesting gaming experience than a digitized rehash of the 30 year old books.  I'm old enough to have purchased and read those books many times during the 1980's, but had more fun playing this than I did going through Tin Man's earlier games from this system.  This system is a lot tougher (you can't spend 15 minutes rerolling dice until you get nice stats), but adds to the replay value of the game, particularly with the different characters available.  The combat can be very tough (especially against multiple opponents.  Even a group of 4 bats, which would be a joke in the books, is challenging here).  I failed my first several attempts through the game before finally finishing it.  I look forward to playing the available DLC and hope that they will add more books to this series soon.

The first thing you should know about this game is that it is just a grind. You grind resources and blueprints to either sell for premium currency or use in order to farm more efficiently.
If you do not like endless farm with constant upgrades and new weapons and skillsets then this game is not for you.
Pros:
- Best part of the game; the movement system.
- Tons of very different weapons (most of which have a normal and upgraded prime version)
- Many different characters to play as (again, most have normal and prime versions)
- Very well optimized yet visually pleasing in every way, even on lower settings
- Constant progression
- Highly customizable playstyles with the mod system
- Great variation in environments
- Linear-ish procedurally generated missions as well as open world with bounties and random encounters
- Great for groups of friends up to 4
- Microtransactions are very optional as the currency can be traded
Cons:
- Focus on farming (wouldn't necessarily call it a con but its definately not a pro)
- Slow in the beginning without help from experienced players
- Confusing without help from experienced players (or google)
- Microtransactions with many reasons to get them
