Hand of Fate melds roguelike(lite) with action adventure, and even some CCG elements. You, a figure on the board, will be traversing through a dungeon made of cards. As you land on each card it'll reveal a new event. These events are varied, and can range from loot drops, to enemy encounters, or even a quest, just to name a few. It's a very interesting take on the genre.
Hand of Fate features incredible visual aesthetics. The dealer, the table, the cards, almost all aspects of the game is masterly designed, and executed with incredible technical finesse. The game is gorgeous visually, and the audio, though subtle, is very memorable and suiting to the game. The dealer is voice acted well, and there's a snarky charisma about him. He's a likable character, and that's good, because you'll be with him for the majority of the game.
Mechanically it seems so simple. A card based roguelike where the deal of the cards IS the RNG system. Once you play the game you'll be wondering why it took so long for some one to come up with this concept. It seems so obvious and fitting once it's played. The game also offers a great deal of meta gaming and offer a fair amount of complexity for players who like to dive into the nuance of a game.
Though there is plenty to love about Hand of Fate, there is one area that seems lacking, or even uninspired in comparison to the rest of it. The combat. The combat will play out very similar to say the Batman Arkham games, where there's an attack, a dodge, stun, and counter button. You'll be mashing that attack and stun over and over again until either the counter or dodge prompts come up. Like I said, very similar to the Batman games. Though it shows some similarities to other games, it's not as smooth, and feels rather stiff and clunky by comparison. It's certainly not my favorite part of the game. Luckily for us, the combat is not the center ring of this, and it's very much a side mechanic, used to enhance the true character of the game, the procedurally generated dungeon running.
Overall, Hand of Fate is a fantastic entry to the roguelike(lite) genre, that introduces some very interesting concepts that seem to fit right in. If you're interested in the game, I think I can safely recommend the buy!

This game is -inarguably- niche. It comes out like a classic CRPG right to the core, an extremely well made translation of pen and paper gaming to a cigital medium. If you like pen and paper games, both RPG and skirmish style games included, you'll love this game. If you like squad-based strategy like Xcom, you'll love this game.
Along with its very robust take on traditional RPGs the game offers quite a diverse list of skills and assets right off the bat before we even have been given access to its modding API.
That being said, the game's primary strength is its greatest weakness, at least in respect to the main campaign mode of the game. It's an RPG unfettered by the tropes and clear story path of modernity. Even frequent PnP gamers are going to be left scratching their head for a while out of the gates. You can and will fail quests inexplicably, get left behind by NPCs if you go to loot more when they are proceeding to something else, and the slightest mis-step can irreversably change your playthrough. For example in one of the earliest dungeons, you can step through an unlabelled door hoping its an exit or a way to proceed only to find out it leads right into the courtyard of the fort you were infiltrating. A moment later you realize this turns many NPCs hostile, some of which are very powerful at that level and patrol the starting town.
If the game is such a throwback to classic RPGs, why isn't there some kind of dungeon master feedback to when you're about to accidentally do something very dumb?
-----
Act 1 Update:
Now on the final fight of Act 1, I'm still not thrilled with game's main campaign. Its main problems are the pacing, lack of dungeon master feedback, and chaotic difficulty curve. It's very stop and start with the pacing, letting you calmly explore at leisure before randomly throwing in URGENCY with no prior DM feedback. You cross a line and scripts trigger with very little nuance. There is little to guide you through the zone to meet each encounter at an appropriate level on top of that, so expect to spend your first few hours save scumming around to find just the right order in which to defeat every encounter to come out powerful enough to defeat the act boss.
-----
Acts 2-4 Update:
Once you've finally managed to use a cheesy enough set of tactics to get through the final 2 fights of Act 1 it's all smooth sailing from there. HAHA. Nah that's a lie. You can still accidentally skip crucial plot points, fail to recieve plot crucial powers, and have literally nothing to guide you accept the need for more EXP. Unless you by chance end up on the developers' intended story path you not only can become completely lost and unable to progress... You can completely break the progression! You can end up in Act 4 without powers you were supposed to obtain in Act 2 that are critical to gameplay and progression. You can end up doing everything needed for the story along one path, but the game won't recognize it because you didn't do things in the exact order the game wanted.
The main campaign of this game is a flowchart of chaos and bad scripting. It's got Tommy Wiseau's "The Room" levels of WHAT IS EVEN GOING ON without the unearthly charisma of Tommy's complete mania.
Do not buy this game for its main story alone. It's 30+ hours of potentially wasted time. If your game offers that many hours of content, there shouldn't be conditions in which you have to completely restart it because you missed something at hour 4 you need for hour 26.
----
Game Master Module
Always save the best for last. That is something that I should not have done with this game. I almost would not reccomend this game if not for the raw potential it had with the Game Master module. Not only does it allow you to make your own custom campaigns to upload for everybody, you are able to play as the invisible hand of god with your friends and build a campaign as you go. It's a PnP gamer's dream game.
It does have its flaws though. The GM mode's sucess is going to hinge very heavily on support from a modding community to add more assets and maps to the system and potential future updates from Larian. It is almost barebones right now, and you sadly cannot build dungeons tile-by-tile. If you want completely custom maps you will need to learn how to make them with the modding API itself.

The first thing I have to say is do not be put off by this game because it's a port from the IPHONE. AGAIN I REPEAT DON'T BE PUT OFF BECAUSE GAME IS A PORT FROM THE IPHONE!
Now that I have told you that, let me tell you why you need to get this game if you like taticle turb based strategy games such as Frozen Synapse where you attempt to get into the best situation possible so that you may obliterate your enemy, than this game is for you. Here are the basics. You control a squad of 4 WW1 airplanes. You do missions ranging from shoot down all enemy pilots to protect your recon plane. You must than issue orders to your pilots based on their abilites and manuvers to complete the mission. Use each of them to cover the other. Deal with altitude, cloud cover and evasion. In other words, the combat is deep and satisfying. Missions can take anywere from 5 minutes to 15 minutes depending on how you play and how risky or safe you play.
How much gameplay is there? I've played 3 hours so far, still British (which is the first nation you get to play as) and just started the 3rd level out of 5 (I believe) After that you get to pick the next nation you play as which has different mission types, locals and planes.
The graphics suit the game just fine, a bit cartoony but not over the top cartoony. The planes have nice modles as does the ground. But your not playing this game for the graphics, your playing this game for the combat. Again, think games like Frozen Synapse or Advanced Wars mixed with the Hex Based grid system of Civilization V mixed in with Altitude, upgradable manuvers, cloud cover and hours of fun and strategy.
The game never feels cheep when your plane is getting shot up. More than likely there was a way to forgo the situtation you are in, but you can undo turns, keep going and get your self out. Some missions only allow 1 pillot while others require all 4. But you have to manage your pilots. Each pilot has a different skill set of manuvers ranging from rolls, loops, ace moves and many more and even a special perk such as being able to shoot from farther away, copy all plane upgrades or escape from POW camps. So you have to look at the mission your going to do and pick the best pilot(s) for the job.
There's still so much that I didn't cover in this review because I havn't even touched the surface of this game. Am I filling this review full of BS and lies? No. This is all true and better than I can explain. Should you get this game? If you like deep tacticle strategy games, than yes.

Spent 40 minutes (or so) in the game before requesting a refund. It's not that the game is horrible. I'm not a "graphics snob" either, and think the game actually looks rather nice and I can see that the gameplay would be decent, from the videos online. The problem is, I've had a more of a fulfilling experience watching videos of others play this game, than I have of actually playing it myself.
This game is an axample of a game that demonstrates the major flaws of an "Online Gmae" vs. a "Massive Multiplayer Online Game" (MMO). The latter has official servers, capable of housing thousands of players at a time. While it is a resource hog, it allows players to have some sense of security in their game play; their characters, options, progress, etc. and a guaranted place to play.
My first 30 minutes in this game, was spent creating characters for each server that I lagged out of and was then unable to connect back to and forced to connect to a different server instead. No, as far as I could see, there was no way to enter a queue for a server, like other online Steam-based games allow. This meant having to manually load and refresh the list every few seconds before giving up and trying a different server.
The next server issue came in location. With a 70 player cap on official servers, there was all of 1 available with a remotely payable ping and that was fully populated. So... options? I can connect to the next server in the list with a 68 server pop and 120ms ping? Tried that, and immediately received message that it was full. Ok... try the third sever with a ping of 180.... nevermind!
It's not like I'm using a sattelite connection from Guam for my Internet. I have a pertty substantial provider with a high speed connection. Other games I have no issues finding dozens of "official servers" in the Western USA wtih <50ms pings. Funcom seems to be incapable of providing this. Then again, I experienced the same thing with them when I signed up for Anarchy Online over a decade ago... fool me once.
Conan Exiles allow you to host a game, but who wants to connect to another player and play only on their terms in their time frames? This is an option for Local Networks, or a group of close friends, but not a viable one for large groups of people.
The final option was Solo mode. That's all I can critique this game on for the 15 minutes I was able to sink my teeth into it for.
I've played survival games now for, what must be 7 years. The only thing that allows solo games to be fun is a sense of immediate danger and a threat around every corner, with every tick of the clock. Exiles does not have that feel to it. Unless you go super-hardcore, even dying is just a slight nuisance. Staying alive though, is just plain easy. There's plenty to eat and plenty to drink. The rest is just grinding resources to craft things.
Yes, this game needs to be played online, with massive groups of people. And that brings me back to square one of this review.
At best, I can say this game appears to be on par with Ark, Rust and all the others. I'd give it a hesitant "recommend" if you liked those games. The network/server issues though, tip the scales ever so slightly off that balance and into the "not recommended" zone - the $30 price tag is just icing on the cake at that point.

What a game, what a work of art for a two-person team.
It's so beautiful, from the debris-strewn starscapes to the twinkling spaceships and spinning starbases. The sound effects are good, too. The background chatter could have used more variety, but it was so well done and unobstrusive that it never annoyed me. The misanthropic humor is pervasive throughout the game, from the main characters' dialogue to the way slavery is tacitly endorsed by everyone.
There are lots intriguing ships, weapons, and upgrades to try, though brute-force lasering was how I usually settled things. The beams-cannons-missiles damage system makes you carefully weigh your strengths and weaknesses, while the rez-goons-data economy keeps you hunting for ways to exploit and score. I would have liked more missions and factions, though.
The difficulty of the game is quite well balanced until the very end. I got stuck many times, but getting unstuck often required just a different fleet or loadout. And when I needed a break, I could look for other things to do like collect components or free up warp gates.
Still, the game is undeniably a grind. With there being only two factions and not much in the way of plot and missions, there is a lot of looking for other things to do. When the game got too repetitive, I'd play it intensely for a few weeks and then stop for a few months before playing again.
What bothers me most is how the game ended. In the last chapter, I did the minimum I had to do to proceed to the finale. I then saved the game and went ahead to the finale just to take a brief peek at it, expecting to be defeated right away. Fifteen minutes later, I'd won the game without breaking a sweat. That was really disappointing. I was playing on Normal difficulty with a tech level of 113, so I don't think I was overleveled. In fact, the unique side missions were still very tough for me. Even the story, which I found fairly interesting, ended flatly.

ArcheAge a game that had so much potential to become a great only to get ruined. Does the game still contain some great elements yes but there is just so much locked behind paywalls that a person with out subscription is restricted from so much of the game.
Almost every action and task is locked behind labor and to gain that if you don't pay for the monthly fee is restricted to 2k cap and 5 labor every 5 minutes while your logged in and 0 gain while offline. Now if you paid them you get a 5k cap and 10 every 5 and 5 while off line. Now whats locked behind labor you ask. All forms of crafting, trade runs which is a good source of income, opening money pouches which drops when your killing stuff which is your source of money/gear/crafting resources. Harvesting resources as well as refineing those said resources also takes up labor. You can easily burn through 5k labor just performing simple tasks in less then 30 minutes and then could take you almost a entire day just sitting around afk waiting to get some labor to once again burn it in 30 minutes.
Also if you want to own a house which alot of the higher end crafting and resources is restricted to well you got to pay for that with the monthly subscription to and of course thats if you can even find a place to put that house. Oh and of course that also takes labor to craft that said house plus resources to gather to craft it and everything else.
Now there is alot of elements this game that is great like the class system is unique as you can mix and match 3 differnt class types to form a unique blend and your not forced to that blend for the life of your one characture. Though there is a credit cost to swap out which if you do alot can get costly but there is some methods to offset that cost but then again alot of those methods are locked behind labor.
There is alot that makes up the world and its fairly easy to get around as you can basicly teleport where ever you want between towns as long as you visit them once and have the resources to do so which to craft is easy though once again a element placed behind your labor.
Alot of the elements that make up the community are about your standard for any mmo with a few being helpful and alot of them being toxic and troll chat all day and rather grief then help you. And while there is times of peace in that zone where you can quest safely that rarely happens except in a small handful of the more popular areas.
But while there is alot of elements that can make this game great if you like being stuck behind alot of time sinks ranging from labor to resources to crafting to leveling then sure play the game it can be great but be warned there is alot of pay to win elements as well as a ton of money sinks.

Murdered Soul Suspect is a 3rd Person Ghost Walking Simulator. You are a cop, who has been murdered in the intro and must now try to solve your own murder (and several others). As you can barely interact with real worlds objects, you mainly walk around and look at things. From time to time you have to answer questions about the things you looked at, these questions are normally either embarrassing easy or the answers do not make much sense.
There are some nice "ghost mechanics" included, mainly walking through walls, but they do not carry the game for its full (or half or quarter) length.
So, what else can carry a game with stale gameplay?
Visuals? They are nice, but no unique sales point.
Music? There are mostly mysterious sound effect.
That leaves us with: Story. And the build-up is great. Your dead cop character has a checkered past and is full of hurt, you have your run of the mill serial killer to follow, your teenage side kick complains a lot etc. The first third of the story is good, then not a lot happens, then a few foreseeable plot twists and it ends with ... a deus ex machina.
In a nutshell:
+ really good concept, no open end
- gameplay is mainly walking around looking for stuff
- story starts out good, then becomes less so and leaves you unsatisfied

Original review: Simply epic. A very awesome game which seems impossible to learn at first, and it does take a while to get the economy running due to low income rates. But after that you can basically conquer, assassinate or diplo your way around the old world. Very steep learning curve though but I'd still recommend it to anyone who has an interest in grand strategy games.
New review: This story actually doesn't start with CK II, but with several of the other games made by the CK II developers. To make a long tale short, which can be hard with Paradox titles, I bought the first Crusader Kings, several Europa Universalis, Victoria and Hearts of Iron in the hardcase cd/dvd version and played them all for several hundred hours. Most of these titles were however notoriously buggy and unstable, yet still fun, enjoyable and playable.
However with the release of Crusader Kings II a new era of stable grand strategy games began. I have sunk so many hours into this game, following dynasties from their beginning followed by games of scheming, plotting, court intrigue and rather interesting family relationships to small skirmishes over border regions and large scale invasions of realms across the sea. There is quite frankly so much you can do in Crusader Kings II and with the developers still adding stuff to the game it is still evolving.
One of the only downsides is that the base game with all dlc's is very costly- still considering I've spent 892,6 hours in the game as of now- the money spent vs actual game time is quite decent. That said CKII is not a game for everyone, yet it plays on factors like history (both real and alternate), kinship, economics, religion, culture, statemanship, politics, peace and war which makes it interesting to invest time in.
I've nominated this game for the 2016 Steam Awards: "Test of time"- category, but it could also fit in the "one more turn"- category save the fact the game actually has cycles instead of turns.

This is something of a Choose Your Own Adventure novel, but with a LOT more depth and replayability, and a great ambience. I got it on sale, so the $15 for the game + DLC was a pretty fair deal. If the devs were to add a World Editor and Steam Workshop, this game would probably gain a lot of followers.
TL;DR Version
The game starts with you choosing from one of 4 pre-unlocked characters (you can unlock more later). Each character has hir or her own backstory, unique abilities, and combat options, and as a result, each playthrough with a new character can result in a dramatically different run through the dungeoins. Each room you explore, and many of the objects in the rooms, can interact wtih the player quite differently, based upon which charactter is being played, inventory items, and other factors.
Little details in your character's bio actually surface during exploration. Alexandra of Blacksand, for example, is quite famous according to her bio. Her fame precedes her in quite a few places in the dungeon, sometimes in comical ways. Some of the creatures in the dungeon know her face and/or name, and have a number of different reactions, from attacking on sight to hugging your leg while begging for an autograph.
Combat is somewhat chess-like, with your character and enemies all having their own unique movement and attack patterns. These can range from simple front-facing melee attacks to long-range arrow volleys with knockback. All units, both player and AI, select their movement or attack options, then everyone moves / attacks simultaneously. This requires you to observe AI movement and attack patterns (each creature type is different), and learn to anticipate their movements in advance. You aim where you think your opponent is moving to, not necessarily where they are standing at the start of the turn. Some creatures have some powerful capabilities, including long-range attacks, debuffs, etc., and managing / fighting larger groups of monsters can get pretty complicated.
There is a fair amount of reading in this game, But the game's approach to presenting it doesn't get boring with repeated playthroughs. There are a surprising number of little things that change each playthrough to make the written material stay fairly intriguing, even when you've visiting an area you've seen 10 times already with different playthroughs. There is a luck element thrown into combat and other gameplay scenarios through die-roll "saving throws." Meaning, if you roll a certain number or below, you succeed at whatever it is you're rolling for. You get one re-roll if you think the dice might be about to give you a bad number, and there's an element of skill to this die-roll mini-game.
Finally, there are a few things in the dungeon that will just kill you instantly. You might fail to see the giant spider lurking behind you, only to wake up in a cocoon with baby spiders eating you alive. These sudden and ignomeous deaths are usually the result of exploring something nasty. There are lots of hidden nooks and crannies in the dungeon, and some of them only show up for certain characters. You will probably have a few "What the actual **** just happened?" scenarios that leave you somewhat mind blown.
I've won the game only once so far, with Dekion Strom. Unfortunately, I didn't find any keys or finish the individual character quest, but managed to kill the final boss. The actual ending of the game was pretty interesting, as the story continues on a bit after escaping the dungeon.
Graphics are great. Story is great. Replayability is great. An instant classic, IMHO.

I grew up on these books and was hoping for a nice refreshing trip back through memory lane. Unfortunately not. Just like the book which is basically a maze, there is only 1 way through with little variation coming from which hero you pick. Sometimes you get a different option at a particular section with an opportunity to either avoid combat or spot something different. But the game eventually gets very repetitive. The combat is not like the other books. You have to maneuvre around a small grid and success comes at guessing whether the targets are going to move or attack into which square. There is no reliable way to predicting - even if a piece is facing one way it can still move into the opposite direction. Granted, some creatures have different behaviors and can perform different actions, just like the heroes. If you both swing at each other you have a "clash" roll which are 2d6 with skill value modifiers. So its all hex-based guessing and luck, as opposed to just straight up dice luck as in the other FF games. Some creatures are larger than one square and have a slightly more predictable behavior but usually its just tic-tac-toe hit/miss. At least the combat here is better than Sorcery! The game is long and unforgiving which means you eventually develope the habit of quickly skipping over most passages when you have to restart trying to get back to where you were before. Sometimes you have a resurrection option that lets you continue at the last rest point but sometimes you reach a literal dead end and its immediate game over. But usually its the combat that makes the worst bottlenecks. I only noticed one area where the map is randomly generated each time i did it but i only wish the rest of the game had the same replayability. Let me put it this way: it's not so good that I don't feel that twinge of pain when I see how many hours I've played...but it's good enough that that doesn't stop me from playing more.
The story is fairly interesting, the visuals are decent (better than Fable Anniversary in my opinion), the voice acting is decent, and despite the simplistic good/evil moral choices (save your sister or kill your sister?) I've found that there are more than two ways to play this game.
You can grow old or you can forgo leveling to remain that scrawny 20-year-old who wouldn't look like an adventurer in armor made from balverine bones. You can be a scar-covered warrior or a spellcasting mage. You can glow with goodness or you can sport demon horns. Eventually you will be all of them. You can (and are in fact encouraged to) run around in your underpants...and still marry any girl/guy you want. Speaking of which, this is one of very few RPG's in which you can marry people of the same gender.
If you like action-RPG's, you'll have a fun time.

Love this game. If you enjoy ETS2, this is the game for you. It is a little underwhelming, with only California, Nevada, and the Peterbilt 579 and Kenworth T680. This should change soon, with the state of Arizona being added soon as a free DLC, and the Peterbilt 389 and Kenworth W900 are on their way. The devs have shown us sneak peeks at a International Lonestar, Volvo VNL780, and a Freightliner in the works, and have stated that they will be supporting the game long-term. ATS is not as forgiving for new truck drivers as ETS2, so I would suggest you be extremely careful if this is your first trucking game, as the fines are horrendous. $1000 for speeding, $900 for hitting a car, and $700 for running a red-light. The cops are merciless, and when you only have $1500 to start with, it adds up quickly. I would highly recommend the game if you are like me and love details and eye-candy. The map is beautiful, very detailed with small additions such as skateboarders in parks and workmen at delivery points. The delivery points are much more varied and detailed compared to ETS2. This game does feel like a standalone DLC to ETS2 at this point, but I think that once more content is released it will begin to come into its own. While people are complaining that the whole map is only about the size of two ETS2 UKs, they have failed to note that the map is much more detailed than ETS2. In ETS2, every town looks pretty much the same, while in ATS, there is actually some fun in discovering new towns and cities, they actually look different from one another. I love this game and at $20, it's very reasonably priced, especially with more content to come.

I seldom write reviews, yet I feel a need to share my story. My first experience with Larian Studios was with Divinity Ego Draconis. I was an adolescent and didn't like it at first, ready to dismiss it on graphics alone. Yet the mind reading intrigued me. I never finished that game and down the line returned and found myself enjoying it much more.
I then discovered a kickstarter campaign for either Dragon Commander or the First Original Sins. Impulsive as I was, I decided to pledge money because I thought that I would then get the game at a cheaper price.
I never actually finished any of the previous divinity games. Dragon Commander frustrated me while I felt that the Original Sins lacked something. Then I learned there was a kickstarter campaign for Divinity Original Sins 2. You might be asking, "If you never finished any of their games before, why do you keep help them with kickstarter"
I could give a number of reasons from the top of my head. To support an indie developer to create games which others clearly enjoy. To give the finger to the greedy AAA developers by spending my money elsewhere.
In all honesty, I supported their kickstarter because I knew that they were reliable. That even if I haven't completed their games in the past, that I acquire the taste to truly enjoy them.
The day which this game launched, I went home from work with such a vigor and childish glee that I've not felt since I was a child at Christmas. It was a moment of rare bliss which I doubt that I will experience again anytime soon. I can honestly look back with no regrets and I already look forward to continue my adventures in Rivellon.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

A true example of a carefully written Sci-Fi epic, Mass Effect 2, similarly to its predecessor, grabbed my attention during the first five minutes (and hasn’t lost It ever since). While the RPG element has been downplayed somewhat, the story, setting, characters, even the music make this game a superior sequel. Class dynamics have been changed – most interesting cases being the Vanguard and Sentinel classes and the action is considerably faster, even chaotic in some instances. Some minor technical mishaps aside, this game is a must play for any fan of either science fiction or RPG games. Once again, when compared to the detailed RPG system of, for example, KOTOR, another BIOWARE game, ME2 is quite simple, but still fun. On the other hand, the game world is so immersive you’ll tend to forget that flaw. DLC’s are worth playing, especially since most of them are F2P (the best ones are not, of course…). The game looks pretty good on the graphic part, just another reason to try out one thoroughly  enjoyable product.

This review comes from a person who once called himself a Grand Chaser, and as one, I cannot help but compare their gameplay every time I play this.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is shallow and limiting, compared to GC. There's a noticeable lack of dodging mechanics when it comes to combos, and the main mechanic for gameplay is called "looping" where you spam combos that you're aware have the lowest chances of knocking people down. It's also very rusty, compared to GC, since you have abilities that allow for dodging behind an ooponent during a combo, but they cannot be performed spontaneously. They have a preset combo you must go through that won't save your bum, unless the move the monster makes lasts as long as the necessary combo. The only options you have for dodging are either jumping or using skills that provide momentary invulnerability. These, however, can only be activated in between "loops," making it difficult to dodge various powered attacks bosses or monsters use. I frequently find myself initiating a skill, but as I've released it, the boss/monster prepares for an attack. My window for dodging after this is only .3 miliseconds. Spamming jump never works even with "normalized values," and neither did the skill activation, because of the delays between skill activation. (Ara can cancel her skills into the next, but she's the only one I've seen do this.) Most of the time, I don't have enough mana from using the initial skill, and at other times the skill I use to save my HP only gives super armor. It also turns out, that skill that gives "super armor" also gets easily interrupted, so I still knocked down. I think this game needs a dodging mechanic for such a circumstance, since there's no way to tell when they'd turn red, for their special attacks. Coupled with this game's marketing, it is only fair that we get such a mechanic, since you need real money, or event boxes for resurrection stones. Granted, you have a chance at one with the pin code cube, but that only goes for one character at a time. Since their dodging mechanics are basically non-existent, they're practically forcing you to spend money on it, whereas GC gave you resurrections for logging in. You could save points you get for stamping attendance to easily purchase resurrections. This leads me to talk about the game's marketing.
Marketing:
As many have talked or complained about, the marketing is way too expensive. It requires around $30+ to complete an entire set. You can buy an entire AAA game with that much, and the set only goes towards one character. It also has no help gameplay-wise. It just makes you look slightly better than the common free player. The marketing also panders to those who are easily susceptible to gambling, with its Ice Breakers, and Fossil Readers that give sets with stats just a bit more powerful than the ones you can spend $30+ for. With $30, you can become far more successful in other games, most notably DCUO, which really gives you a lot of replay value, since many of the things you get in their marketplace can be shared between characters, even the ones you haven't made yet. On the plus side, though, you can can buy cash items from other players using ED, so it's not at all a pay-to-win game. I think they need to take DCUO's example, where with $10, you can unlock a full set of armor, and weapon styles, which can be used at any time, upon equipping. At least making the armors unlockable instead of "purchasable" would be nice. Like, buying one set would unlock them on different characters. Similarly, it would be nice to be able to have inventory spaces shared between characters, like how DCUO does it. Over all, it's way too expensive, but it definitely is NOT Pay-to-Win.
Honestly, the more I play this game, the more it convinces me it's a piece of garbage. It's like sprinkling really stylish designs onto a piece of crap, then selling it for an overpriced amount. Underneath all that style, it still stinks. As an anime, I could see myself getting into this, but as an overpriced game with shoddy mechanics, I just can't seem to enjoy it, whereas Grand Chase was able to satisfy that through smooth gameplay, plus some really good dodging mechanics. Granted, GC was also overpriced. ($10 for a lousy weapon? Really? xD)
Opinions on the revamps:
The revamps offer a new skill tree system, where you can finally preview your abilities before using them, as opposed to before where you had to waste points to preview. It also comes with English voices, which make the game feel more familiar, in a sense. Plus, they were giving out free styles, and skill unlocks for leveling up during the revamp event period.
In the end, I'd rather recommend DCUO (or even Grand Chase, if it was still around) over this. If you don't mind DCUO's heavy files, then I'd suggest going there instead of staying here. I cannot bring myself to recommend this stylish, but overpriced crap to anyone. Elsword doesn't work as a game, and I will only be playing it when I'm over at my brother's place, where not many games in my Steam Library work. Every time I play this game, I am reminded of how shoddy it is, so I can only play it with friends, and although I can play it with them, I still end up ranting during gameplay, which is an unhealthy amount of stress from something that supposed to entertain me, by a game's definition.
I think the experience people have for this game is different for different people, which is why some people prefer this over Grand Chase, while others were in the middle, and people like myself prefer Grand Chase. So, my final verdict is a "Give it a shot," since who knows? You might end up liking it. It is less than 10GB, and might even be less than 6GB, which is a lot lighter than DCUO, which is 24GB. So, because of its light data, I suggest picking it up and trying it for yourself, anyway. Time and money are all you have to lose. I just can't recommend it from my personal experience with it.
Additional Notes:
Despite my complaints over its shallow gameplay, I still get SS grades in solos. It just bugs me that I have to get hit, and I hate getting hit. How 'bout including an actual dodging mechanic in the revamps, huh, KOG'?
Now, just because I compared it to DCUO in marketing doesn't mean DCUO is a perfect game. It is just the new one I am moving on to. It, just like Elsword, is not a perfect game, and I also have a review of that, detailing what I hate about the game, which includes stationary powers.
And lastly, Grand Chase > LoK > Elsword ;P

I really enjoyed Valkyria Chronicles in many ways. The characters are well-developed, the romance is excellent, and the story itself is amazing. The gameplay is quite unique as well, obviously combining elements from strategy RPGs such as the Fire Emblem series with more action-based combat. Each turn has a sense of urgency, as even when simply moving, you need to be sure to keep an eye on your surroundings. An enemy hiding in tall grass or behind a building could eliminate your character with ease.
The only flaw I can find with Valkyria Chronicles on the PC are a few issues with controls. It seems the port from the PlayStation 3 didn't go as smoothly as one might hope, as controlling certain characters with keyboard-and-mouse controls can be difficult. The Edelweiss (tank) sees these issues more often than anything else, but the game is far from unplayable even with this issue. I would recommend playing with a gamepad to circumvent this issue, but don't be afraid to play with a keyboard-and-mouse. Controlling the Edelweiss just takes a little bit to get used to.
The graphics are absolutely incredible. Just like the anime, everything looks hand-painted and watercolored. The music is just as amazing as well! These are the types of graphics that hold up regardless of time, as they have their own unique flair to them that just doesn't seem to age.
As a side note, the game does not have the same Japanese voice actors as the anime. This was a little disappointing, as the voice actor that portrays Alicia in the anime is one of my all-time voice actors. It's not really a flaw, but certainly something to note. (The English voice actors are surprisingly good.)
All in all, Valkyria Chronicles is an amazing game that I would recommend even at full price. It is definitely worth the money for the experience it provides. (Also, may I recommend that you watch the anime after playing the game?)

A dungeon crawler through and through with the added element of cold, hard, capitalism.  You take up the role of a young girl named Recet.  Her father has gone off to become a hero and leaves her to live on her own.  One day a fairy named Tear shows up and announces that unless the loand on the house gets paid the bank is going to repossess it and Recet will be kicked out onto the street.
Tear comes up with the idea of having Recet open an item show and thus Recettear is born.  The game is centered around paying down the debt in installments that get bigger each month.  It is quite easy to miss a payment and have to "loop" into another attempt.  When you loop you keep everything you currently have (pix, items, state of the shop) but you start over from day 1 and your adventures are set to level 1 and you have to reattain them.
After completing the game there is also an endless mode where you can continue playing the game and unlock new dungeons.
If you are a fan of JRPGs this game should be an instant buy for you.  Even if you are not I highly reccomend it.  9/10 stars.

One of the best MMOs to come out for a long time.  Unforunately, it's been completey ruined by the short-sighted, money-grabbing TRION who are clearly only in it to see how much they can get out of the game before it crumbles.
F2P is an illusion - you can play for free, but you're constrained at almost every turn to the point where you have to spend $$ or quit.
P2P is also an illusion - even if you pay via APEX or subscription, you're still hampered by the labour system which charges you for doing almost anyting in the game:
Want to open a purse you just looted from a mob?  That costs labour
Want to dig up that corn you just planted?  That costs labour
Want to craft something? That costs labour
Want to mine / chop something?  That costs labour
Run out of labour - well you can wait 5 minutes for a bit more, but dig up another plant and that labours gone again.
I can't think of any other game that practically forces you to stops you doing whatever you want.
The game itself was full of hackers / bots and gold-sellers.  Whilst some of these have been addressed, many have not.  Furthermore, griefing is practically supported in this game with TRION calling it 'emergent gameplay'.
Marketplace / Cash shop items cost a fortune as they mainly in RNG boxes - I read horror stories of people begging to pay $100 for an item as a one-off cost as they've already spent $500 or more trying to 'win' it from the RNG Boxes.  The latest mess?  TRION GAVE AWAY ONE OF THOSE RARE ITEMS AS A FREE GIFT TO NON-PLAYING PLAYERS as a mean to win them back - they hacked off their own player-base and ended up having to give the item out to everyone (but no refunds for the 100's of dollars spent trying to 'win' it.
All-in-all I'm more disappointed with this game than angry.  Here was a WORLD that I was willing to spend a lot of my time in and yet TRION saw it as nothing more than a GAME CASH AND GRAB.  They would have made thousands out of me over the next few years on a regular subscription, instead they opted for a quick gain from the 'whales' and regular players like me didn't count.  So, I've quit and couldn't recommend this game for any amount of money....

Valkyria Chronicles has 3 main areas of interest: Story, Art, Gameplay.
The art is peculiar - as you probably already know, it's a drawn/manga style and it's really pleasant to watch. Animation during cutscenes is minimal, it feels more like reading than watching, but it's quite good.
The gameplay is GREAT. You have all your different units, you can level them up, buy equipment, and everyone has potentials and attributes that alter their stats in combat, effectively making each unit unique.
This variety means that you've got several ways to play. You potentially COULD have a full sniper team and make it work, if you wanted.
The story is infuriating and left me really bitter. I'm not gonna go into the spoiler zone, but there is that one character that YOU KNOW has to die from the first moment you see it. And what do you know? It does. In the most stupid and illogical way, because apparently that's plot advancing.
And everyone will rub this character's death in your face until the end. It's like the storywriters saying "CRY YOU LITTLE♥♥♥♥♥♥CRY", and I don't really appreciate this stuff.
If this is good enough for you, you'll find the rest of the story satisfying and lovable main characters.
Overall, Valkyria Chronicles is a very good game and will keep you playing for hours and hours.

I'm not a big fan of these turn based games really, and typically prefer a different type of open world game.
Yet, when I picked up Expeditions Conquistador, I got inexplicably hooked.
You're going to absolutely fall for this game, especially if you're into the time period.
Kinda like Mount and Blade, in the sense that the game is mutli-genre'd. You're combining turn-based combat/map play with a survival game, with a classic-style RPG, with intricate companion management, with many rougelike elements thrown in. Your time as a Conquistador/a is dependent on how you use/build your team's strengths and weaknesses, and how you choose to interact with the world.
Many Conquistadors and their bands in reality died by the dozens in this New World, and I think the game's execution of that reality and fear makes the game very exciting. You really get the sense of the danger in this New World. But you're constantly presented with options of choice, allowing you to play the good guy or bad guy or ugly guy to your heart's liking.
And of course, decent historical games are a rarity... much less one that takes place in early, colonial Central America. But there's something very historical fiction about this done right that makes it charming. You start off around the same time Cortez had his journey to Tenochitlan, as if you are racing him to the shores of the New World. After a long while docked at the isle of Hispaniola, you eventually head to the land of the Mexica, where the Aztec rule. Many factions upon factions are against each other, much more than the famous Spanish vs Aztec quarrel. In this way, you are able to influence the Mexica/Aztec people, or topple the Empire if you want before Cortez even arrives.
Overall every part of me was immersed as ♥♥♥♥. The way you progress as a Conquistador leading a band, and interacting with the vibrant world, the telling of rich stories... I'm a sucker for text based RPG♥♥♥♥♥♥too. The survival-ish/game-y elements all throughout play kept me excited and hooked. Wasn't a fan of the combat coming in, but its implementation was easy for me to grasp and became an unexpected addiction.

One of the most interesting RPGs I've played in recent years. Using cards to represent everything from encounters, monsters to equipment and stats, you start off with a limited deck but earn more cards as you beat major encounters, and can essentially customise the deck to stack encounters/drops in your favour or limit yourself for a more challenging game.
As someone who is tired of the whole roguelike trend that's swept indie games recently, Hand of Fate is surprisingly fresh and isn't difficult for difficulty's sake. There's just the right balance of randomness with a consistent, well-written RPG experience, and superb narration (probably my favourite narrator since Bastion) and attention to detail to back it up.
Very happy to see it out of Early Access. I had to stop myself from playing too much prior to launch!

It's a little bit like the Heroes of Might and Magic series, minus the fantasy. The setting is interesting and not often explored in games, so it's nice to see it done justice here. The combat is challenging and fun, and the management aspects will require you to pay attention. Each team member has a story and a personality, some will vehemently disagree with your decisions and others will come to you for advice about their personal problems. Graphically, it looks ok and runs well on older hardware. The soundtrack, although short, is excellent and I often find myself whistling the tunes when I'm not playing the game. You can choose to be a care bear, a ruthless genocidal maniac or something in between. You will often face tough moral questions and your decisions will impact the moral of your followers.
If you are interested in this period of history, or if you like turn-based strategy, or even if you are suffering a bit of genre fatigue and want to try something different then Expeditions: Conquistador is definitely worth a shot.

You proceed through a dungeon, where each room is a card that has some kind of encounter on it.  Some encounters are about making choices, some will lead to a fight scene, in which you need to win a combat against mobs.
It works well as a dungeon crawl, due to the random element, but it seems to have decent balance.  The encounters comprising the dungeon are made from a combination of cards put in by the dungeon master (an NPC) and your own deck, which you build over time.
There is a reasonably strong RPG feel.  Partly this is because some cards progress based on your choices (if you "win" during one encounter, the reward is often a new card with a follow-up encounter).

This game gives you the option to play in two ways and I would definitely recommend choosing the classic Metro: 2033 "Survival" style, but if you're looking for fast-paced fps choose the "Spartan" mode. For me, this game is great at atmosphere: it creates this eerie, desperate world that works well with the "Survival" gameplay.
Play 2033 first and try not to get too spooked.

Originally I bought this game on the Xbox over a decade ago. I liked my time in the world of Albion so much that I jumped at the chance to buy TLC just so I'd have an excuse to revisit the world, albeit with some welcome changes and additional content that broadened the world and further refined the game play.
The Steam release of Fable is thankfully the latter, and it's never been better.
The game supports psuedo HD, which is to say that although it runs native at, I believe, 800x600 it can be scaled up to whatever display you require. Much to my delight, widescreen support is also present.
Sadly controller support is not available in the vanilla release, but if you felt so inclined there are some readily available mods that place that functionality in there.
Many are of the opinion that the first Fable game was the pinnacle of the series, I share in that opinion. Though even if you are new to the series or a returning fan, this game warrants a playthrough. It clocks in at a modest 30 hours, but the real charm of the game is the morality system which tailors events and content of the game to how good or bad you are in interactions or story choices. People may delight in the sight of you just to run to you and cheer, the inverse would have the population of the world running in fear and screaming.
The sole complaint I have with this game is that the player character feels a little lifeless. Some of that can be forgiven if you take into account that he's intended to be a cypher for you to project your own emotions upon. Still, it is disheartening to see in the games cutscenes a mute character that for the majority of the game reacts like a wooden playdoll.

Sid Meier's Ace Patrol is a fun, although highly unrealistic at times, turn-based strategy game set during The Great War (aka World War I). How much you enjoy it, however, depends on several factors, all of which shall be discussed in this review.
The first thing many gamers on Steam will notice is that the graphics aren't particularly high-res and the options menu within the game is severely limited. You can't even set the game's resolution and as far as I can tell, there's no anti-aliasing at all.
The reason for this is because SMAP was originally an iOS title.
What's the difference between the iOS app and the PC game? The mobile game is free, but requires that you pay for additional content. The PC version demands payment up front, but there no additional fees, optional or otherwise. The iOS version also uses a touch-screen interface as well, while the PC uses the mouse.
The game's audio is quite nice, especially the sound effects. Whenever you move one of your planes you hear the associated propeller-driven engine noise. It even changes depending on damage or what maneuver you're attempting to pull off.
The music fits the game, although I turned it off. This wasn't because it was bad, but because I generally dislike background music in games.
Unfortunately, your pilots' voices (the few times they speak) are sometimes weird or just plain buggy. One of my German pilots had a voice that sounded like someone had slowed down an old tape recording. It was amusing, but somewhat creepy at the same time.
The gameplay is standard turn-based fare, with some RPG elements tossed in. While in combat, your planes move over a hex-based battlefield, and have to keep an eye on their location. If they pass over an enemy base, for instance, anti-aircraft guns will fire at them. Fly into the clouds and you'll have temporary cover.
Your position also determines when you can fire at the enemy and how much damage you can potentially do. Attacking an enemy from a higher altitude generally inflicts more damage on them, just as lining up shots while on their tail. Likewise, trying to attack an enemy while head-on or from a lower altitude does less damage and exposes you to return fire.
The RPG elements come into play by leveling up your pilots. They can gain rank and medals, including ace status. If you win missions and have less than 50% damage on any pilot, you gain a bonus that can be applied to any pilot. These bonuses improve weapons, flying, and armor.
After a certain number of kills, each pilot gains a callsign, which denotes a  special ability, some of which are offensive and other defensive. Examples of offensive callsigns include "Deadeye" (long-range attack and better accuracy) or "Executioner" (potential to kill enemy during first attack) while some defensive callsigns are "Lucky" (anti-aircraft guns do no damage to you) or "Grease Monkey" (repairs plane faster).
Each airplane also has its own stats, which gauge its speed, maneuverability, climbing rate, diving rate and hit points. Some planes have extra features, like a rear gunner or a machine gun mounted on the top of aircraft itself. These features let you shoot behind or up above you, when normally you could only shoot straight ahead.
If one of your pilots is shot down behind enemy lines, he'll be captured and become a prisoner of war. All prisoners are automatically exchanged every Christmas, although its possible for a pilot to escape. If your pilot was shot down within friendly territory, he'll be sent to the hospital and have to heal up before flying again. Finishing the mission with a severely damaged plane also necessitates repairs, which temporarily removes your pilot from active duty.
At the beginning of this review, I also noted that SMAP is unrealistic at times. How so? Well, for starters, you can play as one of four nations when playing a new game: American, British, French, and German. The problem with this is the campaign always begins in 1916, one year before the United States entered the war.
In addition, there are active-duty female combat pilots, when there were none at this time (or at least, none officially part of those four nations' armed forces). No pilots ever die, either. They can be captured or wounded, but that's it.
Of a somewhat more minor nitpick in regards to realism, the ranking structure makes no sense at all, and fails to take into account each nation's differing ranks and language. I know this doesn't really make a difference in the game as rank is meaningless and imparts no benefits of any sort, but it's still annoying if you know better.
So... would I recommend this game? Yes, but only if you really like turn-based strategy, and the military and history inaccuracies won't drive you up the wall.

Cute and fun game. The game is about a girl whose father is gone and left his huge debt onto her. She must now open a item shop to pay for his debt. Basically you buy items from the guild which is worth around 80% of the true price. You then sell it at your shop at around 130% the true price. You do this every week until you pay your debt off. There is also a fluctuation of prices like the stock market so it is best to buy stuff that are low and then wait for the prices to normalize and sell them. You can also craft items by getting materials. You get materials by hiring a hero to enter a dungeon with you and at this point in the game, it is a like a dungeon crawler where you control the hero instead to defeat enemies and bosses to get ingredients as well as loot for your shop. You will do this for about a month in-game time. It is very challenging to beat the game in one run because the debt you are required to pay each week increases very quickly from 8,000 to 500,000 which is the 5th or 6th week. It is very possible to do this but you must manage your time and play the "stock market" carefully. If you fail, don't worry about it. You will continue from the first day with all your stuff you obtained (minus your money) and attempt to play through the game again like a New Game+. It's a very fun game even though i beat it in 5 hours in my first go. (Estimated 20 hrs of gameplay) The shop mechanic is unique and the dungeon crawling is fun. There isn't much to do after you beat the game except start over or go for the timeless mode where you play just to amass a lot of gold. Overall its a good game 7.5/10

This used to be my absolute favorite game growing up.
I'm a huge fan of Hitoshi Sakimoto's musical work, I found the messages in the game endearing, I loved the heavy story elements that made me have a relationship with every character.  I even enjoyed the sharp difficulty curves and the punishing DLCs that came out.  This was one of the few games I played to 100% on the PS3.
Coming back to it again, It doesn't hold up.  I think the biggest issue is that VC is a game that DOES NOT want to be PLAYED but rather WATCHED.  It takes so long to perform a series of actions.
For example, say I just want to move a character (not attack, just move) three times.  I have to go through a selection menu, a dialog prompt, a zoom in transition, then I move once, then a menu confirms if I want to end my turn, then I watch an ending animation, zoom out, I'm back at the selection screen--I click the same character again, dialoge prompt, I zoom in again, I  move the character (a shorter distance this time), confirm I'm done moving the character, closing animation, zoom out, selection screen, pick the character for the third and last time, dialouge prompt, zoom in, move character (just a few steps forward by this point), confirm I want to end my turn, closing animation, zoom out, and finally I'm back at the selection screen.
All of that just to move in a straight line?  Three times?
It's only now do I realize how terribly designed that was--especially for a game that's come out after other tactical games and franchises such as FF:Tactics, XCOM, Advanced Wars, etc.
I guess, at the time, I was more won over with the anime-astetic than I was with the actual gameplay.  In retrospect, I only remembered enjoying the story and relating to the messages of fighting for peace as an underdog.
But even the story in upon critical review makes me frustrated.
For example, Galia is played to be an underdog protecting it's own land from two much more powerful forces (The Empire and the Federation) that are in conflict with each other.  However, the status quo in Galia before the Empire even invaded was essentially a country that was openly racist against it's indigenous  people, the Darcsens, who were wrongly blamed for the actions of the invading Valkyria, who brought the ragnite technology to Europe and ultimately cultivated  actions the great wars told in this stories anthology.  The Valkyria are baiscally the root cause of this entire mess, they're the emotional antagonists, yet they're worshiped as gods/royalty by Gallians and no one ever exposes the truth to the world by the end of the game.  The entire crux of Galia's culture is a fraud and it's only made more severe when it's revealed (spoilers.....) that the leader of Galia is actually a Darcsen who was part of a tribe the double crossed it's own people for power.  That's just sours my impression of the team I'm fighting for.  The Empire is "evil" but at least they're straight forward about it.  "We want what you have because we're more powerful than you."  The Federation is shown to be underhanded with their politics, trying to kidnap Galia's sitting regeant.  But Galia's even worse for worshiping a race that destroyed the lands, subjugated it's indignous people, forced a traiter tribe to rule over everyone, does NOTHING to improve race relations since, perfectly happy to lie to it's people as they draft younger and younger citezens to march to their death (Squads 6 and 8 of the Galia militia are utterly obliterated--and the Valk with comedically large boobs literally obliterates the entire standing Galia military), hides weapons of mass destruction in their towers (Valkof), all while propagating themselves as this innocent bunch of people that like bugs and bake bread.  It's like.  Dude.  We may not be the bad guys, but we suck worse that everyone else.
Also... ugh, now I'm just venting.  But the story really goes off the deep end once the supernatural elements are thrown in.  I loved the minor tank on tank battles, but once Selvaria (the big boob Valk) comes into the picture it just becomes... dumb.  It's like all the more subtle elements of the warfare completly fall the wayside.  It's like, before we were charmed with the concept of Isara building a plane and Alicia planting flowers in a time of war with nothing but rifles, a single tank, and a band of spunky misfits--then out of nowhere there's this giant slug like tank/train that can mow down an entire forrest and carries a giant lance that blows mountains apart and on top of it is a SUPER Valkyria and you have to use your Valkyria to punch a hole in the tank so you can take down the Super Valkyria on the top.  It's so stupid.  What happened to the charming Europe-envisioned alteranate universe I was playing in?  When did this become this terrible Japanese sci fi land where all physics are out of the window?
This is coming off as a rant, but if I were to conclude, I would say that the gameplay itself tragically breaks at around the same time the story jumps the shark.  The first time I got angry was when I was doing a mission, using my tactics, having a good time, and then the Valk shows up, mid-mission, and the only recourse I had was to reload saved games and save after every move (save scrum) just to get through the mission.  It just added to the number of menus I had to go through and I felt a bit cheated because the dynamics of an overpowered enemy Valk that I am NOT ALLOWED to defeat because of STORY ruined the careful tactics I had prepared at the start of the mission.
But whatever, I moved on to the next mission... and soon I'm having fun again until the Valk shows up again and now I'm ready to beat her but the STORY will NOT ALLOW me to beat her for BECAUSE, so I have to suffice with hitting her with tank shells over and over again until a CUTSCENE defeats her for me.  Now I'm getting angry.  It's like my fun game is getting lame on purpose.
Then my next Valk mission is that Alicia becomes an over powered Valk, and I'm like, okay, cool.  But the game won't let me use her to shoot down enemies... Okay.  And I just have to sit and watch while the game has fun playing with my scouts... Okay.  Oh, and by the way, this whole mission was a trap and your surrounded now.  Well at least I have my Valk right?  WRONG.  OH SCREW YOU GAME--look what you did?!  You put me into this position where I have to watch you put me into a trap and then watch me get out while you remove the only key to get me out?  Who could figure out this mission on their first time--after watching all of those intermissions of Alicia slowly walking and killing enemies on her own.  How the hell was I supposed to know that you'd sick a never ending stream of enemy fodder at me and take away my Valk mid mission?  NOW I HAVE TO SAVE SCRUM AND REWATCH THIS WHOLE SEQUENCE just to make up for your inability to properly inform me of how you changed the games rules.  The objective of that mission was to claim the base--now it's destroy two tanks?  I don't even have lancers out--ugh, what a terribly designed mission.
Every mission with a Valk friggin suuuuuuucks.  Even Ghirlandio sucks, when you kill the Selvaria--no, I'm sorry, THE GAME WON'T LET YOU "KILL" SELVARIA.  Even if she kills hords of your own squad, even if you surround her with stormtroopers and take pot shots at her head over and over again, even if that was the MAIN OBJECTIVE OF THE MISSION, no the game won't let you kill her because then you'd get in the way of the STORY.  Ugh, such a terrible mission.  It puts the priorities of PLOT higher than the gameplay incentives of the player.  It's like if Mario beats bowser and Toad is like, "Sorry, Mario.  The Princess is in this castle, but you can't save her right now because she's going to save herself in cutscene.  So... good job making it this far."
I can't recommend this game anymore.

First of all, as you can tell by hours played, this game consumed my life...  Secondly, over half of my hours played are spent AFK due to the stupid Labor regeneration.
I stumbled across this game last summer, and thought my wife would love it.  I wasn't wrong.  But what surprised me is how much I found that *I* loved this game.  From the time I started playing during the closed beta/Alpha stages, I was spending a large portion of my weekends living in ArcheAge.  It quickly became all-time favorite game.
The game itself is amazing.  Never before have I played a game where you can do just about anything.  Make a farm, grow what you need.  Use those materials to create ships, potions, food, houses, trade goods, etc.  Spend time tending to you home/garden/farm, take trade packs across the maps for gold, go deep sea fishing, steal other people's trade packs and or fish, PvE world bosses, Dungeons, PvP arenas, pirating... There is literally so much to do, that it is overwhelming.
Where all of these negative reviews are coming from, is from an administrative perspective, and that IS this game's single biggest failing, and it is  major one.  Trion has made mistake after mistake, seemingly on a monthly basis like clockwork.  These mistakes usually revolve around the "Marketplace" (Cash Shop) and involve them placing very rare (and coveted) items in Mystery (RNG) boxes, where people pay real money for random items.  The game is based on an in game economy, which Trion seems to influence for the worse.  But, they do seem to be doing better.  Most major things are being addressed.  Will they ever be a good publisher? Definitely not, but if they can stay out of their own way, this game might just live on it's own.
People complain about this game being Pay 2 Win (P2W), which is an over exaggeration. You CAN play the game as a Free 2 Play, but yes, you really do need to be a Patron to enjoy this game.  But I don't consider a monthly fee as P2W.  But due to Trion's marketplace, and APEX, you can dump as much cash as you want into this game and get gold, to which you can buy whatever you need.  So that part is very much P2W, but definitely NOT a requirement to play, enjoy, and succeed in this game.
This game is an online game with other people, and as such, other people influence this game.  Mostly, everyone in game is having fun and enjoying playing the game.  A small and vocal minority spend a lot of the time creating drama anyway they can, and whine, complain, and cry.
As for my initial comment about Labor regeneration.  Labor is used in the game to do tasks which generate income or materials.  Such as, 100 labor to catch a fish to sell for gold, or 10 to chop down a tree, etc.  As it is, you generate 5 labor every 5 minutes that you are offline (as a Patron) and 10 labor every 5 minutes that you are online.  Therefore, everyone tries to stay online all the time... which is ridiculous.  They ARE changing this soon though however (finally) so it will be the same whether you are online or not.
TL;DR
The game itself is amazing, I could go on for hours about the hundreds of different things you can do.  I have spent months playing this game, and probably several more to come.  Trion's management as a publisher has been a nightmare, but hopefully the worst is behind us and they improve.  Don't get sucked into the drama, game bashing, and general ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥gery that the community has created.  Just play the game and experience for yourself if you can find your place in this amazing game world.

A refreshing mystery game, light on action with some straight-forward navigational puzzles, and a solid narrative as far  as video games are concerned. There's some above average voice acting present here, with atmospheric and sometimes spooky visuals.
The content and subject matter of Murdered: Soul Suspect is what makes it a breath of fresh air in a sea of violent action games.  How do people cope with their own deaths? You'll learn a lot about that subject if you take the time to talk to other ghosts in the game's world. Some are flat-out in denial, others have embraced it. Some are recently deceased, others are ancient ghosts, still troubled by their tragic (or not) fates. You'll encounter spirits that offer  side quests requiring you to help them figure out the circumstances  of how or why they died.  It's rather interesting if you're into that kind of thing.
To nit pick, the game goes on for about an hour longer than it should, revisiting areas previously visited and therefore becoming a bit tedious, but the obligatory mystery genre twist at the end makes it worth it. There's no combat to speak of -- sometimes you have to dispatch "demons" which requires a bit of  stealth combined with quick time events -- that's the extent of Murdered: Soul Suspect's "action". These  scenarios are few and far between, but only serve to slow down your investigative process, and caused me to roll my eyes, particularly at the end of the game, when I just wanted to move forward with solving what I wanted to solve to complete the game.
Murdured: Soul Suspect is not a perfect game but if you crave a break from shooting things in the face, instead gathering clues, solving mysteries and exercising the more analytical side of your brain, Murdered: Soul Suspect is for you.

I got this game from buying a new video card, and had heard good things about it before that. When I finally got to play it, the first thing that struck me was how much it felt like a console game. The world is very limited, and it feels like one is railroaded from crime scene to crime scene.
Gameplay is limited to finding clues at each crime scene and then selecting the most relevant to "solve" the scene, with some side cases sprinkled in for flavour in between. Occasionally demons arrive and must be dealt with (or evaded), but this is very tedious and not fun (or challenging) at all.
Adding insult to injury is the fact, that Interaction with the environment is extremely limited, and dialogue choices are non-existant.
The game also isn't entirely free of bugs, which sometimes make it necessary to load an older saved game.
What saves Soul Suspect from being a complete disappointment is the setting, in which the protagonist perceives both the mortal and the spirit realm. This does grow old after a while though, and there is absolutely nothing that could possibly add a level of suspension (while there is the occasional strained-strings-with-something-unspeakable-about-to-pop-out-of-nowhere-background music rest assured, nothing will actually happen).
If I hadn't gotten this game for free I would most certainly feel that any amount of money spent would have been a complete waste. As far as crime games go they mostly revolve about finding and combining clues, and it is also the core mechanic of Soul Suspect. The execution, however, is so uninspiring (and sometimes insultingly simple), that I simply could not recommend this to anyone.

Each game session is designed to last about 45 minutes, and millions of game possibilities exist, making each game truly unique.
I personally found this game to be pretty fun and well thought out, you don’t find many games quite like this. Because it is free you might as well take a look into it and if you really enjoy it, you can pay for a premium version which allows you to play a new scenario called “Story of Fathers and Sons”.
Overall I recommend it and that everyone should give it a try.

To describe Warlock of Firetop Mountain needs a history lesson. Fighting Fantasy gamebooks were a series of Choose Your Own Adventure gamebooks decades ago. "If you take the ladder up, go to page 58." That sort of thing. These were bare bones, with thin theme, just enough to invoke the imagination of a P&P RPG player but not enough for a fantasy novel. They were also arbitrary, full of silly choices that lock off needed items just for picking the wrong fork in the road. But for all that nonsense they were the best of the time and their earnest charm won them a deserved following.
Warlock on Firetop Mountain is one of the first and most well loved of those gamebooks. Tin Man Games has been keeping the CYOA Gamebook format alive digitally with their excellent Gamebook Adventures series (See An Assassin in Orlandes and Curse of the Assassin on Steam.) with modern design and strong writing.
But these Gamebook nerds at Tin Man Games love the classics and were absolutely thrilled to get a shot at the original Fighting Fantasy stuff. Warlock on Firetop Mountain is their most ambitious project. It is still the same gamebook, but with overhauls to the combat, additional encounters, different preset characters with unique side quests, and a really cool presentation of your pawn moving through a dungeon that builds itself as you proceed.
The text and choices of the original Gamebook are still all intact, with the infamous and terrible maze now randomly generated (and skippable if you play smart) and the combat tweaked into a simple simultaneous move chess game where you try to predict the AI and attack where it will be next turn and avoid getting attacked yourself. Healing and checkpoint opportunities are added to counterbalance the original game's brutality as well and a lot of the arbitrary bad paths are given a bit of foreshadowing to hint there is trouble ahead (while at the same time there remain dangerous rooms worth the risks so of course it's worth exploring every route over multiple plays).
In the end, it is still the same Gamebook. It is just one dungeon that always ends the same and has a few branching routes. It might be much to expect you to replay it with nearly a dozen different characters and see all their unique content and what their skills unlock, but the effort added to give you incentive to replay is appreciated. The smart combat system and many other ways the game had it's rough edges smoothed over are welcome too.
I still wish for more of Tin Man Games own original series, but if they treat other classic gamebooks as well as they have done this one, I look forward to whatever they do next, old or new.
