If I were to pretend that I spent $0 on this CYOA game, I still wouldn't have much to reccomend it for. Most of the good stuff comes from the usual Fighting Fantasy fare--the imagery, lingustic style, and sense of danger is well-crafted. The issue is that there is barely any of it. The dungeon is five floors long, two of which are pseudo-random mazes which are rather obviously intended to grind the player to meat with no other purpose. I personally do not mind scripted instant-kills in CYOAs, part of the charm of the genre is how difficult it is to get to the end. Procedural generation slamming 5 halls of enemies in a row, however, I do have a problem with.
Getting to the Warlock is quite simple even if you have no idea what to do and ridiculously easy if you do know how to do it. Other Fighting Fantasy titles have immense replay value due to their large amount of secrets, this one has almost none, and most of them are instant-kills. The dungeon is structured in such a way that it actively kills whimsy or interest. Basically anything that doesn't involve killing people for loot is guaranteed to be trap. Extra content is split across the different characters you play, but only a few of them can do anything interesting with their extra content. These characters have laughable "bonuses" such as the ability to 'perceptively' notice a key lying right out in the open, or being 'educated' enough to know the very obscure fact that dwarves are good at building things.
The combat system is basically the Fighting Fantasy system put on a grid and it isn't interesting. It is also incredibly random, because attacking an enemy as they attack you results in a dice roll. 2d6 + modifiers is simply not enough differentiation for characters to meaningfully impact fights with their stats. Especially when the master gladiator character has 8 in his skill attribute and a freaking rat has 6. That's like a 9% higher probability to win the struggle. You might as well be flipping coins at that point. Thankfully the AI is stupidly predictable so you're in no danger of dying at most points.

This little gem is actually quite intereresting. Made for smart phones and Tablets originally but ported to the PC and beamed into our collective HD using the magic that is STEAM Ace Patrol is about two things. Biplane Hex Combat and more importantly fun.
Gameplay is basically this. You pick a nation (UK, France, Imperial Germany or America!)  and each nation has a selecton of randomly generated pilots with aeroplanes of the era and you dogfight the enemy using a turn based hex combat system. Your squadron can have up to four Pilots who fly a series of randomly generated missions over four different offensives against NPC pilots who like your own can be captured or forced temporary out of the war to repair their damaged crates. Both friendly and enemy squadron Pilots unlock RPG-esqe skills, upgrades for their planes and learn special manauvers that give them the upper hand in combat. Oh and as the offensive progresses so does air technology for both sides. You might be flying easy one moment and then the enemy has a fancier crate with another set of wings and a bigger gun to keep you on your toes!
Combat itself is pretty simple, get a good shot under or behind the enemy plane whilst not exposing yourself to the dangers of their wingmans guns or AA gun fire. You are graded with a score system that is tied to the general STEAM achivements and online leaderboard for said game. To increase the score obviously you'll have to ratchet up the difficulty level (or be lucky enough to get a Pilot with the DOUBLE SCORE ability).
The other feature to keep you playing again is once you complete a Offensive with a certain nation the first time you unlock famous WW1 Ace Pilots with their own biplane livery schemes.
Bugs wise I've only encountered one and that sometimes you have some trouble clicking on a hex, this gets really fiddly when your Pilot has a million manuvers and you really don't want to select the FORCE LANDING one. I expect this is to do with it being more of a Tablet game really. Also, some of the art assets are slightly bland (Don't get excited about seeing the Offensive Victory screen more than once)  despite the fact they did their best locked more or less in a single location.
Is it worth buying though? sure, why not if you want a addictive but slighty short turn based aeroplane game . But for the best value get it in a Sale and make sure you pick up the rather decent WW2 Pacific Campaign sequal at the same time.

So at roughly 400 hundred hours played I am neither a left button mashing noob or a rainbow swinging killing machine. Which means I have good days and days my head spends more time on the floor then it does on my shoulder. But at 400 hours I have no plan to stop playing. There is something about the game which brings me back over and over. That is why I can recommend this game, but It is a game which is not for everyone.
First lets start with what is good about this game. Firstly the game becames hard after level 15,bloody hard. I have been a gamer since before the 8 bit era where games like Ghost and Goblin taught you how to cure up a storm based on how hard it bloody was. Chivarlry can be difficult in that way but rewarding once you start to improve your ability as a warrior. In many ways Chivalry is really like the sword of warfare it tries to recreate. The swordsman who spends hours and hours in the courtyard,dueling and fighting will be the guy who steps on to the battle field and destorys his enemies. While a peasent who is jst handed a pitchfork while me face in the grounds in no time flat. So being a good swordsman requires practice and learning the techniques. Its time intensive sure,but that first time you fight an opponant and keep up with him parry,for parry and finally best him with a move he did no expect is really rewarding. There are frankly game mechanics i really dislike and feel should be taken out,like rainbow hits for instance, but once your learn the timing behind such hits,it becomes easier to parry and counter. Like i said before,the game is hard but if you have the paitience it can be very rewarding. Classwise I honestly feel there are no real imbalances,every class,if played by a skilled player can wreck me on any particular occasion.Good players exploting the right situation can own with any class in this game. Graphically the game looks good after 3 years and the overall look is changing due to promotions and workshop items. The sounds and voice acting are both brilliant and hilarious. I love the feel and difficulty of this game and its why I still play.
And now for the bad. The game,has a Chivalric code you need to follow. If your ping is over 100 expect to be kicked,ping has an an impact on battle,so stick to low ping servers. Try not to hit your teammates and if you,or even manage to accidently kill them apologize. Its what I do and 99% of the time players will handle it graciously. If someone is a♥♥♥♥♥♥to you,just ignore it and move on. Its just a game and you are play with people of all ranges of maturity and certain players will be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  Stick to this code and you will be ok. People say this game has a toxic community, so do others, but this game makes it easy to troll people and that can make it worse for some players.
Then there is the learning curve, if you want to be good and fast,this isnt the game for you. It takes time to become a good fighter and maybe some players dont want to invest it. In chivalry there are many many good players,who will go medieval on your♥♥♥♥♥and it can be frustrating to lose over and over,but learning the mechanics is what level 0-15 are importantly about,come to think it it,0-61 is about learning how to fight. Some mechanics as well such are dragging,feinting and rainbow attacks new players find annoying and cheap, but its the fact of life in Chiv, you can learn to counter them and learn to do them as well.
Thats the game in a nutshell. Medieval warfare was a cruel and bloody affair and only the fittest and fastest make it out alive. If you want a challanging,fun game this is one for you. If you want quick and easy there are many other games you would enjoy instead.

Mass Effect 2 was the very first game I ever brought on its release day, It took me completely by surprise when the original teaser trailer was released, as I was a big fan of the first game - regardless of its issues -, I was hyped and could not wait for the sequel, when it finally arrived, It blew me away and remains strongly one of my most treasured and favourite video game experiances of all time.
The Story takes place 2 years after the first game, without attempting to spoil anything, I'll keep it as brief as I can:
On the far edges of space known as the Terminus, a mysterious enemy has begun abducting human colonies, there are no signs of any sort of attack, only that every man, woman and child is gone. as Commander Shepard, you must assemble the most deadliest and fearless team in the galaxy to travel through the Omega 4 Relay - a "jump-gate" in which no one has returned after using- and take the fight to this new enemy, the chances of survival are slim. A Suicide Mission.
Whilst Mass Effect 1 had you travel through civilized communities throughout the galaxy, Mass Effect 2 takes you into its dark underbelly, where crime, slave trade, corruption, mercenaries and drug trafficking run rampant and freely with no ill will on the criminals part. This gives the galaxy a more intimidating feel as you travel to recruit many of the Soldiers, Scientists and Mercenaries that will assist you throughout the game.
Of course, recruiting people for a Suicide Mission isn't as easy as it may sound, Missions in this game are nicely structured and area enviroments give each mission a differant feel, what makes the missions so fun is the revamped combat system and classes, combat feels satisfying, reliable and fun and the differant player classes are reason enough to replay the game, Soldiers and Vanguards are seriously a blast to play with.
Everything you do in the game is building up to the Final Mission, throughout the game a sense of foreboding looms around you as you get one step closer to passing through the Omega 4 Relay, in which everyone on your ship may not return from, as your decisions throughout the game will have impact upon Suicide Mission.
A highlight of this game is that each crew member has their own loyality mission, your crewmate will ask for your assistance to help resolve a past, or present issue, allowing you to bond with said crewmate and learn what makes them who they are and how they tick, the assasin character is more than just an ruthless killer, the scientist is more than just a book worm.
DLC is also some of the best I have ever seen in a game, the Cerberus Network houses free Downloadable mission packs and even some bonus weapons, there are some priced DLC but all is worth picking up, if you can only choose one, Lair of the Shadow Broker.
All the praising I give this game, there are only 4 issues I have with it.
Weapon selection feels very limiting, alot of the customisation was removed, streamlining the experiance for better or worse, without DLC packs, you have pretty much 2 choices for each gun type (Save for 5 heavy weapon choices) with a powerful version you can obtain later on in the game.
Although extremely rare, it is possible to get stuck in the enviroment, but this does not happen often enough to ruin or tarnish the experiance.
Where Mass Effect 1 was fair in its Renegade and Paragon options, this game might as well force you to be one or the other, as I don't see this much as a spoiler, but I would say it is mandatory to be pure hero, or pure badass.
The last point I can make a paragraph about:
Do I recommend this to those that haven't played the first game?
No. Alot of the revelations that will occur in the game will not go over strongly with you if you havent played the first in the series, I would strongly recommend that even with Mass Effect 1s problems, you push through it, as your decisions in the first game will be carried over into Mass Effect 2, making the story feel so much more personal to you and you alone.
With all that said, Mass Effect 2 is an astonishing achievement, Winning over 90 awards and Game of the year 2010, It's graphics still impress me making the aliens and the galaxy around you feel so alive and real, The soundtrack is superb with special mention going to Suicide Missions theme itself, it's fast, fun combat with class based powers is vastly entertaining and story grips me each and every playthrough, if Mass Effect 2 isn't my favourite game of all time, it's Top 3 for sure.
They say it's a suicide mission, you should prove them wrong.

There is a ton of content it seems for this game, but most of it you will likely not use during the main course of the game. The reason being that taking advantage of such usually requires risk, and since you have to meet monetary goals within a certain amount of time in the main story, you may choose to go a safer route. Valkyria Chronicles is an interesting game for sure. Not only it's a weird genre mix making it very hard to describe, but also there are many strong and weak points worth discussing in both gameplay and story.
Story excels at world building. Not-Europe at not-World War II is a very interesting and compelling setting on it's own. There is also ton of flavor text, both written and voice acted, going miles to give, for example, characterization of every soldier you can command in the game, with quirky personalities included. World overall is really inviting. That said, core plot has some very noticeable problems. One: it tries to tell a war-themed story in probably most non-violent way possible, implementing massive amount of well-known anime clichés, where Spec Ops: The Line simply eviscerated and deconstructed this genre to the bare-bones. It leaves the game without cohesive message and consequence, making it hard to take serious. Add pretty long cutscenes to the mix and you will receive something that not everyone can stomach. I ultimately liked it, but everybody wanting a serious story or having an anime allergy, take caution.
Gameplay is a weird mix of strategy game, RPG and third-person shooter. I would compare it to Worms, Fallout 3's V.A.T.S. system and Supergiant Games’ Transistor. Many others also use X-Com as a reference. The gameplay may have some "first-installment-oddities" like: unbalanced classes, clueless buff/debuff system, slow leveling requiring additional skirmish battles (just to keep on par with the enemies), annoying randomness and unexplained mechanics... BUT at the end it's real, genuine fun and battles feel like chess matches. Tanks are awesome, sniping enemies from distance is awesome and owning the AI in pretty hard battles is awesome too. It's a solid gameplay worth your interest if the description feels compelling for you.
Music? Top notch! Japanese people certainly know how to make symphonic music. I also cannot say a bad thing about graphics that have their own charming style. This cell-shading will not age quickly. I also commend a good PC port, free DLC, New Game+ mode and good content/price ratio (even with long cutscenes, 32 hours for one playthough is pretty neat result).
Valkyria Chronicles is a weird mix, but for those who want to take risk, it may be a bullseye. Not for everyone, especially those with low anime tolerance, but definitely worth a look for the uniqueness sake alone.

The game has an EXCELLENT story, but only if you take the time to read the "cutscenes". I love the variety of characters and their job paths which all are fun to play and have great backstories.
I would love to give it a Positive Review, but sadly the Cons outweigh the Pros.
Pros:
> Beautiful storyline
> Characters have interesting backstory and personalities
> Tons of character classes to play, different from one another in play style and looks
> Dungeon maps are versatile, pretty, and not flat
> Community is mostly friendly (outside of PVP)
> Not much thinking is involved for PVE until later dungeons
> It gets more strategic in the endgame dungeons (but not by that much)
Cons:
> No tutorial for your specific character/class. You have to eventually (if ever) figure out your character system on your own.
> Pay to look good (customization) which also leads to:
> Pay-to-Win skins and accessories, and utilities. You need money to get more skill slots. The skins cost either real money, or lots of in-game money because of:
> THE SUPER BROKEN ECONOMY. Where you really can't make much until endgame levels.
> SUPER GRINDY. You have to do the same dungeons over and over again because of level restrictions starting around late level 40s.
> Unfair prize gambling system for $1 per try. If you don't buy skins off other players with in-game money, you have to buy items that have a CHANCE to give you a skin. They don't say what those chances are though. Most of the time, it gives you stuff you can cheaply buy with in-game money.
> Want good PVP gear? Grind for it.
> Events are terrible. You either need to grind for something, run a dungeon a certain number of times, or just WAIT 10-60 MINUTES FOR AN EVENT REWARD and you can't switch or log out otherwise the timer resets. All just for a crappy reward that usually has a 15-day expiration.

Short version: potential wasted and not enough skill from Trion to stop the hackers. Plus, Trion is a TERRIBLE company.
Long version:
I played from Day-1 (Gamanek here) until November 2014. I bought the Silver Pack and played 2 months, everyday, constantly, with also a guild under my command (a medium-large guild with 20+ members).
Things began to fall apart as soon as more people kicked in: after the problem of the constantly full servers dissipated, the real problem began: hackers, bots and whatnot. All the land for housing was taken before you could even click it, thanks to an exploit regarding your character not actually being near the house, but letting the game think you're there, clicking to place the house.
Housing is actually REQUIRED in the game, in order to create most of the things, without housing you're in for AN HELL HOT farm, and a lot of social demanding (knowing crafters, farm money for them, pay them, rinse&repeat) plus, obviously, the actual fun of the game being locked away from you. There are ways of circumventing this: have a friend pay the monthly subscription (you need it to being able to pay the taxes for the houses) and you then use his/her house. Still, you need that actual friend to do it for you. And find a spot for the house.
After the house problem, there is the gilda problem: everything for housing costs Gilda Stars: every single advanced bench for your house vary in cost, and you need to pay also designs for house, scarecrows and a lot of things. These stars can be acquired through the chapters of the storyline (which at one point obviously ends) and doing daily things. The daily things, though, are somewhat boring things and sometime even HARD (like killing a certain number of monters which spawn in a precise hour of the day, without getting partied because there are already 1 or 2 full parties) plus, the range for things to be bought is around 250 gilda, while you make AT BEST 5-8 gilda PER DAY.
The fighting mechanics are okay, not Guild Wars quality, but still bearable, PVP is obviously "I've got the best equipment" and overall the game COULD BE really good. However, terrible company behaviour and a lot of unhappy mechanics really make this game fall apart.
If you've got money to waste on this, play FFXIV instead. IF you've got no money, then try this out, and go away when you're bored.
DON'T PAY FOR THIS.

Just played the game for couple of hours, and I must say I'm not disappointed. I bought it only for single player, since this is, I think, the first 3D non-zombie SP survival game with friendly NPCs available. I always wanted a single player typical survival where I can build a settlement and see some NPCs roam around. This game delivered exactly what I needed.
Survival elements sometimes resemble ARK; overall optimization, at least on my pc, is almost good (there were some minor stutters sometimes, but not something gamebreaking — and I play on high settings, not ultra, but with 2K resolution on nvidia GTX 780).
I don't know about multiplayer, saw complaints here and there about servers unavailable, etc, but MP is not my thing at all, so I don't know anything about multiplayer issues.
During my gameplay I've seen some minor issues, typical for early access game — some NPC tribe warriors were floating over the land, combat feels a bit clunky at the moment in first perspective mode, etc. On Steam Discussions I saw some complaints about hunger/thirst mechanic, but it all is customizable when you start new game ("new server"), so I found a balanced option and had no trouble with this aspect of game (in case you want to completely turn off this game feature, you can do it in admin menu, at least in single player game).
I hope developers will make more options for RP in single player, not only multiplayer, and will make an option for thralls to be available to join you as followers in future release.
And please, add a functionality for your thralls to do simple jobs/missions for you, for instance, gather some resources or hunt (I don't know, maybe it is already implemented in game, but I had no chance to find it yet). It would be perfect if you could send them on some time-based "fake missions" with probability of failure/success (in single player only, of course), to have a clan simulation.
Overall, Conan Exiles seems a decent game to me, and enjoyable already. Just needs some polish and some additional gameplay elements. And yes, there will be mod support!

I can't recommend this. I don't mean to diminish the efforts of those who worked on this game. I want to acknowledge it, clearly a good bit of work was put into this game, but in the end if someone was to ask me "Should I spend my money and time on this game?" I would have to say no.
Really great. The models and textures are finely detailed. The environments are beautiful and cluttered, as they should be. You can really have a lot of freedom when your character doesn't care about most collision. Only one texture stood out to me as bad: the police badges. It was sort of distracting when it was right in the camera sometimes. The engine runs beautifully as well, I was able to turn everything to its absolute maximum and run with only a few hitches, even with the anti-aliasing at x16 and HBAO at high definition. I don't think I've had any other game run so well with similar graphical settings.
What really confused me was the pre-rendered cutscenes, they were
! This game probably would have been a couple gigabytes smaller without all the unnecessary pre-renders. I don't know if it was for consoles or something, but they never did anything in the cutscenes that they didn't also do in live render. The most baffling cutscenes were the dialogue trees where characters would just sit in their idle animations waiting for me to select something, then pop into a pre-render. They were actually rendered at worse settings then encoded with Bink Video, resulting in a pixelly mess that just made me confused and annoyed.
Very good with some few nitpicks. Stumbling into the little spirit traps on the ground makes an annoyingly loud orchestral sting, which isn't really necessary when Ronan's gasping in terror and the screen is doing everything it can to make me feel attacked. There was a weird bug where sometimes cutscenes wouldn't have audio until I restarted. Overall however, the ambient music was subtle yet evocative.
Well-paced and keeps you interested. Unfortunately it's kind of short. It's not that it needed to be any longer, I felt it wasn't rushed at all. The main characters are well written and voice-acted and the random citizens are well voice-acted, but the stories you unlock for collecting all the things are not so good. It was sort of a letdown after running all over the place, only to be rewarded with the actors sighing and pausing and "ohh what a terrible experience" when somehow they all sound like the same person being told how to be scared rather than feeling it.
This is a large part of why I can't recommend this. It's a murder mystery where you run around collecting clues at various scenes and putting them together to come to conclusions, but it wasn't done all that well, really. I felt quite often that a clue I had to pick didn't really make any sense, because I HAD to pick three or I apparently couldn't come to a conclusion. Sometimes I knew what the game wanted, but was able to pick out several other clues that could lead me to the same conclusion, that I could see people picking and being annoyed that they got it wrong. Sometimes the conclusion didn't make any sense. Are you sure she's being taken to that gallows in particular? Salem, Masseschussetts has no other gallows sitting around? All the other murder scenes were improvised and scattered everywhere, it didn't have to be right there and it didn't have to be a hanging anyway.
There's no real consequence to being wrong except that you don't get "three out of three badges". Frankly, I wish there was just no consequence at all. The game doesn't need to tell me that I have to solve the murder, I
I have to solve the murder because I'm invested in the character and I care about the story. The annoyance of the game telling me I'm not perfect at its flawed system really dragged me out of the investigations. The only real consequence happens at the very end of the game in a terrible timed sequence that isn't really timed anyway because it pauses while you make your selection.
Okay, but ultimately pointless. Demons float around on limited paths and you have to execute them from behind. They can't see you through walls, but you can see them through anything. If they see you, they'll start sucking out your essence which works through walls, even walls that you can't normally walk through. It doesn't even matter if you get really far away from them, you'll die. However, sometimes I could break the drain for seemingly no reason by running through a bunch of walls or going down stairs. What you're supposed to do is hide, but that system sucks because the demons just go straight to the spot you're in, despite "not being able to see you". If you don't move to another one, they'll push you out and then your camera will probably get stuck in them, so you can't hide again. If you are able to, they'll immediately go back to searching for you even though they just saw what you did.
That ended up being kind of a mess, but that's the whole logic of the combat in this game. It makes zero sense. They can't see you when you're behind a wall, hiding, or just more than ten feet from them, but they can ALWAYS see you if they're draining you, but not if you hide, even if you were just about to die and they're two feet from you. Other demons won't notice you killing their "friends". Ronan instantly knows how to kill them even though he can't do things as basic as teleportation (which he also instantly learns when he decides to 'figure it out') and it doesn't seem remarkable that he's able to kill them with ease, even though everyone else is scared of them. So basically, it was slapped into the game to pad the length and fill out the environments.
Get a facial animator! Please for the love of God get a facial animator, Squenix! Every game that you make is played by terrible over-body-animated mannequins! I wish I was exaggerating! The models are great, but the fact that they rarely move their eyes, eyebrows, nose, cheeks or even lips to do anything that isn't lipsyncing is so frustrating. A few scenes had me watching the characters' backs while they talked, which was really immersive. The good acting, writing, sound design and rendering, all of it worked together, just to be ripped apart when I saw their faces.
Literally every resolution in the ending happens offscreen. Deadlines, budget cuts. I don't know.
The ending is all of thirty seconds long, but they're more than happy to force you to sit through the credits for five minutes.
In the end it's just a letdown of an experience, even if it is pretty.

4/5 Stars
CONS:
To someone who has never played this style of game it can be daunting to see the different options at the start. The UI isn't as good as it could be and occassionally I get confused when I'm cycling between characters (since they all look the same in their pictures and names.)
A huge con for me in this game is actually one of the tactical commands. They don't describle combat at the start. You literally are just thrown in without explanation and you have to divulge on your own that movement and your ability to attack after moving are color coded. You also don't learn the abilities without trying them out, which is really annoying when you want to level characters up.

Honestly they could have done a better job with the abilities and just scrapped them all together for pre-made builds. I think it would speed up my leveling and make me focus more on the story and less on the numbers game that E:C creates that ultimately isn't that important.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 is one of the best RPGs I have ever played. It's challenging, engaging, and encourages the player or players to get more involved with the world of Rivellon.
There is a lot of freedom with how you develop your character, the relationships they have with the NPC's, the way they solve problems and how the party interacts with each other.
The game is certainly enjoyable alone, but it truely shines when you have others to play it with. It really gives a lot of D&D vibes when you play it with a full coop of players. That said, it is best played with people you know already and not just randoms, the game is much to long to played in one session and organizing times to play can be difficult for some people even when they already know each other quite well.
The mechanics of the combat are challenging and every fight is a unique experience. If you struggle with combat, its important to look over your party and make sure there is some balance. If everyone is warrior type you may struggle in the fights.
The game doesn't really hold your hand with telling you what your next task is, its not hard to figure out if you read the journal though. Many of tasks/quests (whichever you want to call it) have a relatively straightforward way of being solved and several alternate, sometimes more rewarding ways of being solved or completed. It's important to look around and not just simply rush through everything, you will miss a lot if you do.
Overall, the game is very fun for me and my friends. Larian Studios did a great job with this one. This is without a doubt the game of the year for me.

After having beaten the entire game (and having gotten to about level 40 in endless mode), I figure I should give my opinion about the game.
In my opinion, this game is fantastic. Not flawless, sure, but definitely worth the price of admission.
The Good:
No two playthroughs are the same -  You are able to select what cards are in your deck (with the exception of endless mode, where every card is included), but not every card is drawn, and the path of the cards changes in each section. This changes the game's story in a dynamic fashion.
Success/Failure Screen - One of the game's most charming mechanics. Your every decision is faced with these cards, and those wary enough can track the wearabouts of each success and failure. Granted, that never seems to help me (usually I get the huge failure cards when I try), but you can succeed on (almost) every decision if your vision is clear.
The writing -
"gets the Mister Lionel card"
Lionel gives me a shield.
The dealer:
"I'm beginning to think you put that card in here just for a free shield."
0_0
Anyway, the writing is fantastic. I love the dealer's sarcastic and mocking inflection, and I love the fact that the game doesn't mind mocking you when you start to cheese the mechanics. For example if you find the maiden too often, and you can be sure that you'll be mocked for your inability to go without her.
The atmosphere - If nothing else, the game is just charming in its presentation. Everything from the dealer's shuffling of the cards to the memorable encounters screams theme and suspense. Definitely one to pick up if you're looking for a unique atmosphere.
The bad -
No camera controls. The game does a pretty decent job of tracking your movement, but being able to move the camera would definitely improve your awareness during combat. USE THE TABS, DYNASTY WARRIORS STYLE!
No customizeable main character. This one doesn't really bother me, since it's an indie title and all, but the only way you can customize your character is through equipment you get in game. Personally, I think this would be much more tolerable if you could switch between male and female avatars. Perhaps somewhere down the road as additional content?

No "main story." - The game has a sort of Dark Souls feel going on, in that you can learn about the world through the cards and equipment you gain. However, it's more about building your own story using the cards as a framework. I know, however, that this will put some people off.
The bugs - Yes, there are bugs on launch. I haven't encountered anything game breaking - instead, it's just been a few irritating ones (like the sfx being switched off after death). I expect these will get patched soon, but I had to include them.
The okay:
The combat - The combat is done Arkham style, with dodges, counters, and stuns. One of my favorite parts is that you become unable to do certain things if you lose equipment. Lose your shield? You lose the ability to reflect projectiles and enemies stop displaying their "attack icon" indicating that you should dodge. However, the combat itself is both slower and less flexible than Arkham. It's one of the game's weaker points, but it is serviceable.
The slowdown effect - This one can be both good and bad, depending on your opinion. Personally, it gives me more time to take in my situation, but it does noticeably slow down the game's pace.
The RNG - You will be screwed over, both randomly and consistantly. Sometimes you simply won't find what you need, and you'll die. A lot. However, this is kind of a basic element of the rogue-like genre, so this depends on your tolerance, I suppose.
Overall, I believe that the game is worth every penny. The developers (Defiant Devs) listen to the community and are willing to change elements that simply don't work. Even more amazingly, the developer ACTUALLY USED EARLY ACCESS LIKE IT SHOULD BE USED. No cash shops, no broken promises, no controversy. They even rewarded their early access users by giving them the first DLC free. Take a note, game developers. This is how you do Early Access right.
Anyway, that wraps me up. Guess I'll include my coolest attempt (sorry, couldn't resist).
VS: The King of Scales
Started off immediately by finding the royal treasury
Got cut to bits and lost 2/3 of my HP
Got the "skin rash" curse, which makes you draw pain cards
Got hit with 2 max health reductions, bringing me down to 20
Got hit with midas appetite, making my gold food
Ran out of gold next to a shop, had to sell my shield and weapon
(finally) got lucky and got a huge success at an encounter, giving me a weapon and food
Ran into the sweetnymphs at 5hp and reset my character
Knocked that scaly mongrel into the ground, bringing me to the final challenge....

The bit above was my original review, i wrote it about 3 or so hours into the game.
Now, having finished it after about 45hrs of playtime (that's a single playthrough, so if the game can keep you engaged, there is very good playtime value in it... Most of it was repetive/grind-ish missions however), i am somewhat torn.
In the long run it was better,  than my first impression. Certainly not terrible. However, was it good enough, to change my vote?
I don't think so. On a more refined scale, i would have voted differently - a 6 out of 10 perhaps.
But with only "Yay" or "Nay" as possible votes, i'll stick to my initial negative vote.
After all, after wrtitng that original bit, i stopped playing for a few days. Might havenever returned, but was really-really bored, so took it up again.
A few nice extras came up, but my two main complaints - grind and awkward controls - remained in place.
The story was ok for a open world-ish combat game, where no one really cares about story anyway. Predictable and very cliche, but enough to keep you moving from chapter to chapter.
Actaully, when changing chapters there were a few interesting changes in the mechanics. Late game even had something a kin to a basic strategic layer, with defense chokepoints and ressource management - very-very-very basic, but nevertheless, an interesting change of pace.
However, it did not do away with the grindy-ness. Rather the need for ressources increased. To progress the story i had to do the same missions over and over again (same objectives, slightly different maps). In the end i was just cherry-picking the missions, that i could do the fastest (cloak, destroy the target, get out).
I had unlocked all the ships, all the modules about half way through the game. Picked my favorites rather quickly too. Most new unlocks i only tried for a short while (one or two fights), found them inferior, to what i already had and never used them again.
Now, i am willing to believe, that there is some bit of personal prefference involved - other player might select other ships at some point. However, there is also somewhat poor balance - some ships of the same class, are clearly and stricktly superior to others - more health, more equipment slots.
Bounty hunter designs in particular seem very strong - perhaps a sort of power creep in the development process.
My main complaint remains the control scheme, even after 45 hours of gameplay i still wasn't fully used to it. I can't even rightly describe it - it's just not intuitive.
Basically the strafe controls are pivoted on the ship, rather than on the screen. And since the ship can be spinning all willy-nilly, depending on where you aim your mouse (which is where your target is, so you can't just say "screw it" and steer with the mouse), the direction of strafing is kinda flipping around, so sometimes ushing left, will make you move left, while other times you push left, yet go right.
That made strafing completely unviable for me.

Delightful turn-based air combat. Every turn is an agonising choice as you choose between maneuvers. The game mechanic of trading altitude for speed and advanced maneuvers is breathtaking in its clarity, simplicity, and plausible authenticity.
The early days of air combat lead to a game of jousting and attack runs, both sides clawing for altitude and position, weaving in and out of clouds and flak zones, trying to line up a shot or trick the enemy into lining themselves up for another pilot's power dive kill shot. Taking to the air knowing you're facing a supremely skilled enemy Ace is a daunting prospect as he dances his bird across the sky, crossing your engagement lines in a lightning sprint and performing daring aerobatics to bring himself up into your squadron's six, but even the best pilot can find himself hard pressed if he lets himself get caught at low altitude, exhausted by constant high-gee flying.
It's a light, tight, satisfying game that shows its mobile roots on the surface but the underlying design shows an understanding of what makes a game work that dwarfs most AAA releases.

I wish there was a "I liked it but I don't think it's worth getting" option. I've played through this game three times, two to completion; and the third time is why I don't recommend getting this game. My first time I played a warrior, the game was a piece of cake. I had like two points in mage and so when I got to the point where you had to used ranged -- it was slow and I went through a ton of healing potions but doable.
The same thing with playing a mage. If anything after a few levels it was beyond easy to run around and basically wipe the floor with anything that came close. There's lots of threads that talk about how OP mage is for good reason, the game is a cake walk with it.
But the third playthough I wanted to do a pure archer. Only turns out you can't. There are certain quests where you will get mobbed even trying to be extremely sneaky and one shot people with max range -- certain quests essentially require close combat.
I don't mind when a certain combat style or class, is overpowered and much easier to play through. In fact that's sometimes a plus; but to have a whole class be nearly impossible to win with does bother me. I don't actually think you can complete the final boss battle as an archer -- it's again structured to give an advantage to mages and warriors who can take damage close combat style.
Maybe I'm missing something, because there's certainly gear and setups for all three combat styles, but it just feels like range is really underpowered throughout.
Overall, you really do become insanely powerful proportionally quickly. The later levels were honestly overly easy, even with the additional content added, I still breezed through it all. Wearing plate as a warrior you're essentially invulnerable; and you can get several swords that can single shot almost everything. There's no real challenge to the game.
That all being said -- I consider it "adventure game lite" in that it's short enough to beat in an afternoon and have seen all the content and feel satisfied that you played a whole game. Excluding silver key and demon door hunting there's about 7 hours of content per playthrough, which makes in a nice fix for wanting to play a RPG but not wanting to invest 100+ hours in an elder scrolls game.
I would say it was kiddie -- but there's enough sexual innuendoes, and a brothel outright at one point, that make it rated-M and so it just falls into a category where it feels like something I would let a kid play as introduction to the genre but it has moments of being a little to edgy for that.

===
+ Immense variety of weapons and modules (100+) to suit any play style
+ Astonishing variety of spacecrafts, from tiny fighters to massive capital ships
+ Customizable galaxy: decide number of systems, tech availability, difficulty and more
+ Many types of side-quests with always random enemies and objectives
+ Beautiful 2D art style and effects
+ Arena challenges: you get to pilot a random ship against random enemies for fame and fortune
+ Unrestricted gameplay: want that upgrade but don't have the money? Blow up the trader and take it. Or die trying.
+ Faction system with allies, enemies and an ever-growing bounty on your head
+ Tactical map to give orders to your fleet, with customizable AI behavior and commands
+ Modding supported and easy to use with a modular mod selection function
+ Good story, albeit a little stereotyped
+ A long journey: at least 30-35 hours on high tier difficulty levels. More if you aim for 100% everything. Lot more.
- In late game it takes a lot of rez (money) to do anything and often you will have to grind for it the long and boring way. Or let your AI ships do it while you tab the game and do something else.
- Booster Modules are REALLY overpowered used in certain ship designs / weapon combinations
- A particular quest in the Main Questline is borderline broken and WILL make you REALLY mad
- Respec debt is way too big: whenever you respec a skill tree you get your points back, but also a debt of XP equal to all the XP it took you to make the points you refund. Basically, you have to do that XP again after refunding and redistributing those points, and it takes AGES specially start and mid game. So think REALLY WELL what you want to put your points into.

…For a game titled “Valkyria Chronicles,” this game really isn’t about the Valkyria…
Anyway, I heard about this game while looking for more SRPGs to play – SRPGs being my favorite genre of video game. I enjoyed the game a lot. The story, while somewhat predictable at times, was well written and the character development was well done. Despite being a game set in a war, it has a relatively realistic take on war (i.e. it is hell). The game looks and plays well with one major exception that I’ll get into later on.
Tactically, the game suffers from its preoccupation with speed. See, like many other games in this genre and others, Valkyria Chronicles grades you after each mission. But instead of grading you in multiple areas, such as number of enemies killed or number of allies kept alive, the games only grades you on how fast you beat the mission. This means that to get the best rank, you need to make stupid choices like running through enemy fire just to get to your objective more quickly.
This wouldn’t be such a big problem if grades were cosmetic, like they are in most games that grade you. Here, the amount of experience you gain is mostly based on your rank. Later, you begin to receive the best weapons in the game only if you do well in missions. So…you either need to grind skirmishes to make up for lost experience or speed through the missions as much as possible...which I think is unfortunate design.
I have a few words on the battle system – you begin in Command Mode, where you get an overhead view of the map, and once you select a unit it zooms into Action Mode, where you control the unit in a real-time third-person shooter system. It’s unique and gives the game a bit of urgency – enemies will shoot at you as you approach in real time – but I feel they could’ve executed the system better. See, once you select a unit, each time the unit moves it uses up Action Points or AP. Once you run out of AP, the unit cannot move anymore. The problem is that if you misstep, that uses up AP.
Usually that isn’t a huge problem…except for the almost game-breaking issue I alluded to earlier, and that is driving a tank. The tank controls are atrocious. The game sometimes turns your tank in the opposite direction you’re trying to move in for some reason and that takes up AP. I’ve experienced blowing through a full bar of AP on my tank without it moving an inch. And some maps really necessitate you moving your tank quite a bit.
I still recommend the game heartily. You’ll have a good time outside of driving your tank.

Basically, it's Euro Truck Simulator 2 with some little tweaks, an American theme and currently with less content (emphasis on
). Which might not sound like a compliment, but as someone who adored ETS2 this is more of the same in a great way. ATS also features a few neat twists that are just icing on the already sweet cake that was ETS2. And all the wonderful little details and bits of authenticity really capture the feel of driving cross country through the highways, interstates, towns, and cities of the US. Even if said highways, interstates, towns and cities are a tad limited at the moment.
Now yes, there are only two states (California and Nevada) and only two models of truck to drive at the very moment. And I can completely understand why some might be apprehensive about buying this because of that. For me, however, it's been more than enough to satisfy my bizarre truck-driving fantasies. And the promise of more states and truck models added as free DLC in the coming months, combined with SCS Software's excellent track record when it comes to updating and supporting ETS2, made me perfectly okay with plopping down $20 for this game.
While it is limited compared to Euro Truck Simulator 2 in its current state, American Truck Simulator is still absolutely fantastic. And I genuinely cannot wait for what is to come once the extra content starts coming down the pipeline.

Oh Boy... where to start? As you can see, I've sunk lots of time into this game.
One of the most amazing MMO's I've ever played that has everything, yet made thoroughly unenjoyable by the mechanics, hackers, and cash cow decisions by the publisher.
Archeage has it all. PVP, PVE, Ships, Boats, Piracy, Farming, Harvesting, Crafting, player housing, good graphics and if the greedy developers weren't so well, greedy I'd still be playing.
So to the bad and why I quit.
1. Hacker & Exploits. At launch and for a few months after it, hackers were able to exploit some serious flaws in the game that allowed them to become super super wealthy whilst legitimate players struggled.  This shafted the economy which as of now (March 2015) is in one hell of a mess with everything on the AH incredibly expensive.  Hackers were able to land grab very early on and as land was in such high demand, people would pay silly money for a small farmhouse.  It's only now due to the fact most people have left the game that land is available all over.
3. Labor. In this game if you want to do anything related to farming, you spend labor points which once spent, regenerate over time. Now here's the giggle. If you log off, overnight you will generate enough labor points for around 10 mins of farming.  If you stay logged on, permanently, you'll gain double.  This system is designed to make money from the Korean player base who pay per hour for internet use. It has no place in the western market.  It's the main reason I quit the game.
4. Gear. The best gear is crafted. Unfortunately the crafting system is so RNG based the only way you'll get gear is to buy it but because the economy is so borked, the good gear is so rediculously priced it's unreachable for the majority of players. I worked out that one bow was around £600 real money if you bought enough apexes to buy it.  Generating that kind of income can only be achieved via hacking.  What this ultimately has lead to is a small majority of players with the gear being able to one shot people in PVP.
5. Cash Cow Attitude .Going back to point 3. Run out of labor? No problem, you can buy a Labor pot from the cash store or for around 100 gold on the AH.  Want to improve your gear, you'll need to play the RNG game with uber rare items. Don't worry though you can buy these uber rare items from the cash shop.. Want to sell your property? You'll need some appraisal tickets available from the cash shop.  Want that awesome weapon? Buy APEX from the cash shop and sell in game for gold.... The list goes on.
6. The don't like constructive feedback if it's not positive.  I made only 2 posts on their forums, one was about how the labor system was hurting the game and driving players away. A couple of weeks later I tried to log into the forums and found my forum account had been 'permanently' banned. lol...  I created a support ticket which 2 months later is still unanswered. lol  This for me was actually the straw that broke the camels back and 3 days ago, reluctantly I cancelled my 4 accounts.
7. Epic player abandonment. I've never experienced such an over subscribed game at launch which became void of players within 6 months. At the start the you had to queue for hours to get on. Land was so in demand, some folks after 3 months still could not find any free. Property was sold for silly amounts.  Every square inch of farming land was occupied. Fast forward 6 months later and land is available everywhere.  Go to arena and it's the same OP geared players over and over.
8... I could go on.
9... I could go on
10. I've lost motivation to continue listing the reason this game is one to avoid.
All in all Archeage is a truly ground breaking MMO that is a victim of poor management and greed. It's such a shame because in the right hands this would be an MMO to invest all your time in.
Seriously, just avoid it and spare yourself the inevitable pain and frustration that will come from playing this game.

Throughout my playthrough of Murdered: Soul Suspect, I could never truly figure out if this was just a game that took the modern game developer's philosophy of all-inclusiveness to an extreme or if they honestly just think gamers are all dumb as posts. That's the biggest problem with this game. I'm generally a fan of story-based games and can appreciate when they make games decently easy to complete so that you can follow the story at a good pace. Even for me, Murdered: Soul Suspect was so ridiculously easy that I just couldn't bring myself to care.
You follow the story of Ronan, a cop working on a serial killer case in the city of Salem. As the game starts, Ronan meets his grisly end but comes back as a ghost. He quickly finds out that in order to move on to the afterlife with his beloved, he must solve the case of the Bell Killer and thus, his own murder. It's not an uninteresting premise but curiousity quickly becomes tedium as you work to make Ronan catch up with what you probably figured out just from reading those three sentences. Supernatural occurances in Salem equals witchcraft. In fact, reaching this level of obviousness and not overthinking things is probably the most difficult part of the game.
While the game occasionally gives you action sequences involving sneaking around demons a la Metal Gear Solid, the primary bulk of the gameplay is exploring and using detective work to piece together the mystery of the Bell Killer. The kinds of puzzles you have to solve are similar to this: a body lies in front of you with a gunshot through the head. What weapon killed him: a gun, a knife or a rope? See what I mean about overthinking things? This isn't a trick question and the game is full of stupidity like this. One frequent puzzle that is honestly in the game is where you have to influence people to think about a certain topic so you can read their thoughts. You have to pick from a variety of subjects to get them to think about the Bell Killer. To do this, you pick the thought that is directly talking about the Bell Killer. There is no extra thought to this and the puzzle repeats FREQUENTLY throughout the game.
The other gameplay elements aren't much better. The stealth sequences are absurdly easy and simply require you to move behind the demons who follow the exact same path without variation in rooms where there are, at most, four of them. There is also a collect-a-thon throughout the game where you pick up elements of backstory about a variety of topics like Ronan's life, Salem's history and other topics. There are over 200 of these collectables scattered throughout the relatively small game world and while it's fun to find these at first, it quickly becomes boring like the rest of the game due to very little reward for collecting them all.
Due to the ease of completing the game and the stupidity of pretty much every character, the storyline is hardly fulfilling either. Some may enjoy making their way to the conclusion but you will likely guess what's going on after only a few hours of play time. Still, despite the bad gameplay, the controls felt great to me, using a 360 gamepad, and the camera worked surprisingly well, considering how much time is spent walking through walls. The sound is also decent with voiceovers ranging from passable to pretty decent. If you are looking for a mindless game to play through in a day or two, Murdered: Soul Suspect may be what you're looking for but if you're looking for something with even the slightest hint of meat to it, pass on this one. It will only disappoint.

I'm not really sure how to write a review for this, other than mostly just saying that if you know what you're getting into then you know what you're getting into.
I guess I'll talk about the differences.
Graphically, the new map textures are very nice, and if you'd rather go back to the olds one then that is an option. Character sprites don't really seem any different, not that there was really anything wrong with them, but there is a blur option to smooth them out a bit.
I can't say anything about the voices since the version I played originally was Disgaea DS, so I didn't get any voices.
Keyboard controls are pretty functional, and the mouse works fairly well in the Overlord's Castle. It's also fairly nice in the field (There's two controls that aren't immediately obvious with the mouse. You can hold left click and move the map around some. You can also hold right, move the mouse in a direction, and then release right click to spin the map. It's a bit awkward of an implementation, but otherwise the map would spin as though the Netherworld was on tornado watch.)
Using the mouse in the field feels a bit twitchy though, it'll easily decide to go out of bounds rather than stay on the map itself.
Also, oddly enough, they added a new feature that I don't think they mentioned.
In the Dark Assembly, you can now rename any and all of the NPCs in the Overlord's Castle. It's a bit odd of a feature for them to add, but it's there and it's neat.
I don't think that's in any other Disgaea game. It wasn't in the original, I don't think it was in 2 (Didn't play it.), wasn't in 3, wasn't in 4, wasn't even in D2, and I've never played 5.
It might've been in one of the ports, I don't know for sure. I didn't get the chance to play them.
Recommending mostly because it's 20$, and it's Disgaea. If you're a fan of SRPGs, then you really can't go wrong with Disgaea.
Hope someone figures out modding. That'll be fun to play around with.

I have only played Hand of Fate for through about half of the Story mode decks but, I must say it is one of the greatest games I have ever played.

Having the encounters with monster cards be played out in a slightly Arkham Style (Attack/Counter/Dodge/Stun) was an even further brilliant idea.  Although the combat is the weakest part with a fixed camera, it is still manageable and fun.  Trap Rooms are also played out in this 3rd person camera style as you dodge your way through a trap maze.
Even if you complete all 12 of the storymode levels there is an Endless mode to see how far you can go.  The game starts out relatively simple, but starts to become challenging about 1/4 of the way through the Story decks.
Add to this the amazing way it's presented, the dealer is well voice acted and doesn't get annoying.
I cannot recommend this game enough.

Mass Effect 2 is an adventure I will never forget.
In my personal opinion, Mass Effect 2 is one of the best sci-fi RPGs ever made, the world Bioware created is unique, diverse and wonderful, not to say everyone is hugging eachother while hopping over rainbows.
The game presents you with many moral and ethical choices, an exmaple is a mission which requires you to blow up a mass relay, but doing so will destroy a colony with over 300.000 residents, but if you don't do it the system will get invaded by the Reapers. (Giant robots with lasers, you have to play the game to understand.)
You truly get to form your own personality in the game, do you assert and be a badass, or do you show compassion and be a hero? as you advance in either direction you unlock new dialogue options and actions, ranging from giving someone a hug to kicking someone out of a window.
Every crew member has a very devloped personallity, and you will feel attached to most of them, you can even develop relationships and they aren't limited by species or gender (Sadly, you can't be gay, only lesbian, this confused me a little).
You can do them personal favors to make them loyal to you, increasing your chance of survining the suicide mission at the end of the game, I have seen some of my beloved crewmembers die in my first playthrough, I was actually crying over the death of a fictional character.
But Mass Effect is still a game, not a futurustic dating sim, you can choose to skip the romance entirely, and you don't have to recruit certain crew member sif you don't want.
The gameplay is solid, sometimes the 'one-button-does-everything' system gets confusing, running, taking cover and interacting with things is all bound to one button, which can lead to confusion sometimes.
When you start the game you get to choose a class, some specialize in weapons, others in tech (this means you get to use combat drones, tech to drain shiles and incinerate or freeze enemies from a distance, and others in biotics (space magic, you get to lift people of the ground, or throw them a few feet away or you can spawn tiny black holes), most of these powers are well balanced and satisfying to use, some of them feel a bit silly though. (I'm looking at you, shockwave..)
You can explore a lot of different star-systems, you can scan planets for resources and you may just find a secret side-mission, these do feel a bit cheesy sometimes though. (you enter a hidden facility and the merc leader just keeps saying 'you shouldn't have come here, prepare to die').
Whenever you investigate a planet you get a little information about it, like the surface temperature, atmospheric pressure, even travel advisory sometimes, and some even have traces of past civillizations who were space-faring long before that fish with legs on earth crawled out of the water to eventually become a monkey.
Mass Effect 2's soundtrack is great, the music in the main missions really made me feel like I was in a dire battle to save the galaxy from detruction, the music that plays during the suicide mission is just.. damn, I still get goosebumps from it, it's truly an epic piece.
Sadly, Mass Effect does have it's weak-points, as missions can feel a bit repetitive sometimes, hub-worls are smaller than they were in Mass Effect 1 and DLC is obtained in a very annoying way, you have to make a Bioware account and buy Bioware points with real money, these points you can then spend on the DLC, I would prefer to buy DLC directly through steam without using these Bioware points.
If you want to play DLC you need to be online when you launch the game, otherwise it simply won't load or show up.
There are also a few annoying bugs that never got adressed, sometimes I run into an object and get teleported on-top of it, then I either have to wait until I die or I have to quit to the main menu and then load the save again, sometimes during conversations characters are facing the wrong person or are doing some really weird stuff with their head.

Oh Boy... where to start? As you can see, I've sunk lots of time into this game.
One of the most amazing MMO's I've ever played that has everything, yet made thoroughly unenjoyable by the mechanics, hackers, and cash cow decisions by the publisher.
Archeage has it all. PVP, PVE, Ships, Boats, Piracy, Farming, Harvesting, Crafting, player housing, good graphics and if the greedy developers weren't so well, greedy I'd still be playing.
So to the bad and why I quit.
1. Hacker & Exploits. At launch and for a few months after it, hackers were able to exploit some serious flaws in the game that allowed them to become super super wealthy whilst legitimate players struggled.  This shafted the economy which as of now (March 2015) is in one hell of a mess with everything on the AH incredibly expensive.  Hackers were able to land grab very early on and as land was in such high demand, people would pay silly money for a small farmhouse.  It's only now due to the fact most people have left the game that land is available all over.
3. Labor. In this game if you want to do anything related to farming, you spend labor points which once spent, regenerate over time. Now here's the giggle. If you log off, overnight you will generate enough labor points for around 10 mins of farming.  If you stay logged on, permanently, you'll gain double.  This system is designed to make money from the Korean player base who pay per hour for internet use. It has no place in the western market.  It's the main reason I quit the game.
4. Gear. The best gear is crafted. Unfortunately the crafting system is so RNG based the only way you'll get gear is to buy it but because the economy is so borked, the good gear is so rediculously priced it's unreachable for the majority of players. I worked out that one bow was around £600 real money if you bought enough apexes to buy it.  Generating that kind of income can only be achieved via hacking.  What this ultimately has lead to is a small majority of players with the gear being able to one shot people in PVP.
5. Cash Cow Attitude .Going back to point 3. Run out of labor? No problem, you can buy a Labor pot from the cash store or for around 100 gold on the AH.  Want to improve your gear, you'll need to play the RNG game with uber rare items. Don't worry though you can buy these uber rare items from the cash shop.. Want to sell your property? You'll need some appraisal tickets available from the cash shop.  Want that awesome weapon? Buy APEX from the cash shop and sell in game for gold.... The list goes on.
6. The don't like constructive feedback if it's not positive.  I made only 2 posts on their forums, one was about how the labor system was hurting the game and driving players away. A couple of weeks later I tried to log into the forums and found my forum account had been 'permanently' banned. lol...  I created a support ticket which 2 months later is still unanswered. lol  This for me was actually the straw that broke the camels back and 3 days ago, reluctantly I cancelled my 4 accounts.
7. Epic player abandonment. I've never experienced such an over subscribed game at launch which became void of players within 6 months. At the start the you had to queue for hours to get on. Land was so in demand, some folks after 3 months still could not find any free. Property was sold for silly amounts.  Every square inch of farming land was occupied. Fast forward 6 months later and land is available everywhere.  Go to arena and it's the same OP geared players over and over.
8... I could go on.
9... I could go on
10. I've lost motivation to continue listing the reason this game is one to avoid.
All in all Archeage is a truly ground breaking MMO that is a victim of poor management and greed. It's such a shame because in the right hands this would be an MMO to invest all your time in.
Seriously, just avoid it and spare yourself the inevitable pain and frustration that will come from playing this game.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a Medieval based sword fighting game that is honestly pretty unique and can be a lot of fun.
The combat is fairly fluid, there's nothing more satisfying than a well timed strike slicing through your enemies neck, the pop as their head separates from their body. You will die a lot in this game, especially at the start - once you get passed that initial bump you'll slowly but surely start to pick up more advanced techniques and learn to string them together into devastating combos. Eventually you will start to predict where the enemy is going to hit and manipulate your character to duck under, run away from or even jump over their blade, while counter attacking and gaining the momentum for yourself.
It is easy to grasp the basics, but very hard to master. I feel fairly confident that I'm a decent player after 500 hours, but there are others who completely destroy me without me making a dent.
There are bugs, ghost hits, desyncing issues, but they don't crop up so often as to be a major concern, just a minor annoyance.
Do yourself a favor and do NOT join the level 15 servers. You'll be the best of the special class until join regular servers and go 1-15 every other game and quit.
The biggest downside? While the community isn't all bad, there can be the occasional jerks, but you're playing a video game so don't let it get to you.

by other players with hundreds of hours while being under 50-100 themselves. The reason they are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all over you is because they have far more practice. Go figure, when you spend 1000 hours doing something you get pretty good at it.

I wanted to finish the game completely before making a review, I have never touched a JRPG game in my life and I likely wasn't ever going to until I had saw Valkyria Chronicles during the Steam Summer Sale, after watching the trailer on the store page it had caught my intrest with it's intresting watercolour artstyle and world war setting, a glance at the reviews showed a large ammount of positve reviews praising it's story and gameplay, so I decided to jump out of my comfort zone and give it an honest try.
That said, Valkyria Chronicles takes place in a fictional World War 2, two great powers are fighting for control for the land of Europa, the western Federation and the eastern Empire and they are locked in what seems to be a never ending conflict. The neutral land of Gallia finds itself undersiege by the Empire for it's rich minerals known as Ragnite - a rare and ever fading resource known for it's all general purposes -, as protagonist Welkin Gunther and side protagonist Alicia Melchiott, it falls to you to defend Gallia from the Empire and drive them out of your homeland.
There is
of plot and narrative in this game, so if you're not a fan of story driven games, then this is not for you, as between each story mission there will be at least 4 to 7 cutscenes advancing character developement and game setting. The story is told through a book called "On the Gallian Front" which acts as a central menu to cutscenes, missions, headquaters which is where you do your upgrades and research as well as additional information on the world around you.
Of course the game is not all plot and cinematics, there is an actual game here to play, Valkyria Chronicles is rather a turn-based action hybrid game, Like in XCOM you have your units laid out on the map before you, but instead of clicking on them and telling them where to go and fire, you manually control each of their movements in a third person action camera, letting you move and aim freely as you want, so long as you don't exhausted your Action Points, those being represented in a small bar at the bottom of your screen, if you run out of AP, you can't move and will have to end your units turn, nothing is to stop you from moving that same unit again, but it will cost you another command point and will also have reduced AP. I didn't think the hybrid would work to well, but it kind of does, it lets you feel more involved if anything, rather than just watching AI fire back and fourth after giving orders, which is another thing I need to mention.
Orders are special commands that Welkin can issue his team that are unlocked very early in the game, some of these are increases in damage, resistance and other special effects that can help you in your current mission, never ever shun them as these can be huge difference makers in thier own right, however I will openly say that playtesting these Orders wasn't done very well, I won't explain in detail, but let me just say that a lot of missions can potentionally be finished in thier very first turns of the level using a scout (most likely Alicia because she is actually OP) and a combination of certain orders.
But like most JRPGs, the story is why most people would buy a game like this, so what did I think of it? I'm a fan of World War 2-esque settings and it was an intresting take on SEGAs part, I can tell that they tried to approach the game with alot of care and maturity, even going as far to include the equivilent of concentration camps, murder and slavery, not the kind of settings I expected from a company like Sega, but it's good to see that they did branch out of thier safety zones and into something more realistic. They also did a great job of giving the game a likable main cast of characters who all have some personality behind them, making each one stand out in thier own unqiue way.
As there is alot of dialogue, so to must there be good writing and voice direction, I don't have much to say about the writing as I tend not to really notice the writing if I'm enjoying the game enough, I like to learn about the world so I can get more involved in the game, which I was, I can say that the voice direction of the main cast is superb, they all gave a performance as if they was there and experiencing what their character counter-parts was, a big thumbs up for that, but a number of other characters sound like the absolute stock of stock, you know those really cringe worthy voices you hear in actual shows? There are a few present here, but it's easy to overlook them, especially since the main cast of characters are good enough in missions.
Art style gets a massive thumbs up from me, I'm not a huge fan of anime, but I'm a sucker for any kind of cartoonish art style in games, as mentioned it uses a watercolour esque look with an intentional anime art design, the both combine extremely well together, sound direction was also top notch, keeping in touch with it's world war style to making you feel like you're apart of a larger battle in some fights, the soundtrack as well, splendid and superb.
My only complaints come in the form of some tibids of gameplay and a rather weak late early to mid game story.
First off for gameplay, get used into the habit of finishing your units turn
because when you take control of a character, enemy units that are looking as that unit will fire on you due to what's refferred to as reactive fire, most of the time this will result in cheap hits and could potentially screw you over, so again, finish your action as soon as, there is also no way to speed up or skip the opponents turn, forcing you to observe every little thing that they do, not a huge complaint being a turn based strategy, but it can be noticible.
The late early to mid game story felt so weak to me though, the beginning of the game is so good, you are protecting the countryside land of Bruhl and introduced to your main characters effectively, learn a bit about them and such, then the empire begin attacking the evacuating civilians, like literally killing them, after buying time for the rest of the populace to escape, hope is slowly lost as you are forced to retreat, Alicia and Welkin then proceed to have a extremely well performed discussion of the horrors of war. Later on they would both go on to be conscripted by the military, sounds like it's going to get really rough for our protagonists doesn't it? Well after that, nobody seems to realise that they're fighting a war and it distracted the heck out of me, where was the panic of being young adults thrusted into the military backbone? A young mans uncertainty of being placed as squad leader with these lives in his hands? It's not until around chapter 9 where the story really starts to pick itself back up and by chapter 10 when you are introduced to Zaka (Voiced by the one and only Steve Blum) the cast really start to remember whats happening.
Honestly though, the more I played, the more intrested I got in seeing what happened next in the story after a mission, it definately gets more and more better toward the end as the tensions between the Empire and Gallia highten. The ending was actually really touching.
In the end, I really experimented with this game and I'm very glad I did, It was a surprisingly fun 30 hours of gameplay and I might play through it again at some point, If you like JRPGs, you'll likely love this, if you're a fan of turn based strategy looking for another fix, then I'd recommend giving Valkyria Chronicles a try, challenging, fun and intresting, maybe you should try to kick the Empire out of Gallia.

I shouldn't be fighting the urge to skip all the dialogue, and non gameplay sections after only 40 minutes into the game.
I also want to point out something that affects a lot of parts of the game, is that it takes it's time 'too' much. I'll start with the pros; Murdered has a great story, part of which you know a little from the beginning of the opening sequences.  The remainder, you piece together through out the game collecting "memories" of your life prior to the accident.  The game plays similar to LA Noire when it comes to looking for clues, albeit you're dead so you have a few obstacles to work around.  The pacing is good, but you can stroll through looking for memories, clues and help others who are lost between two worlds solve their own deaths.
What pulled me in the most was definitely the story, but the mechanics of how the developers pulled off being a detective caught between the living and the dead, is also well done.  Without giving any spoilers, lets just say there were different ways for the dead to interact with the living, all of which help you keep moving through the story.  The way the devs pulled in both past and present worlds, create some interesting puzzles when navigating rooms or even the city, but it really captured the feel for me, of Ronan being caught between two places.
There aren't many "bad" aspects to the game for me, but I will say the game could have used a little more polish.  First, I would have liked to interact with the living more, through some of the stories.  There are times when the interface is glitchy; selecting a clue sometimes will not work unless you select another adjacent clue, but it's nothing show stopping.  At times it feels like it was built mainly as a console port, althought both sets of controls work equally well.  I prefer playing mouse/keyboard, but the controller scheme works just as good.   The graphics are great but from time to time I would notice small sprites in spiderwebs or small tearing along seams between walls.  Again, hardly worth mentioning and nothing that detracts too much from the game play.
If you've come looking for action or gun blazing shootouts, this might not be your game.  However, if you enjoy a good mystery story, or if you're looking for something a bit different with some twists on some old mechanics, Murdered will show you a good time.
