As an archeum founder alpha/ beta tester and an in-game player for almost a year to year and a half, the game was fun. The scenery was nice, game play was enjoyable, and there was always lots to do. I personally enjoyed going with guild friends on trade runs and out to sea battles.
The game began to fall apart when there were lots of gold spammers and botting cases, though that wasn't the only problem. The game focused very heavily on the Item Market section with real money. Not entirely the worst system, but made it hard for many players to get anywhere in-game without it. If ever experiencing an issue in-game or out of game, there was terrible lack of support. In fact, it was lucky to get a response back. The official launch after alpha/ beta was released, there was very little sign of patching for the the bug and glitch issues. There was also a problem regarding a botting case in-game, which caused regular players to be banned in the process for no explainable reasons. Which Trion did very little to resolve, and for some didn't do anything at all.
In my case, I was one of those few if not many to fall into the regular player category that had their account banned for no explanainable reason. I tried submitting multiple support tickets and the company was terrible at responding. Normally took weeks to get a response, and when I did, the answers were not even remotely close to what I was asking. After about ten support tickets I wasn't even able to contact them... They had restricted contact, couldn't access forums, and couldn't log into the game after spending the $150 on the game, and another $150-200 in-game.
I decided to look up Trion on the web for any traceable evidence as to whether it was happening to others as well. Sure enough, the (BBB) or Better Business Bureau has a list of complaints regarding the same issue and more. I was shocked and surprised that a company could be this bad. Since then, I haven't touched foot in ArcheAge or in any Trion games.
As a previous alpha/ beta tester and player, I would highly recommend staying away from Trion games. They do not respect their players and they have a very bad reputation for purchase history.

This game is currently where most of my hours are invested in.
Unless you have friends that play this game, I wouldn't highly recommend it but it is still fun nonetheless.
I bought this game close to its release date, back then the community was casual, players were still adjusting to the combat system, class system and the plethora of weapons they had at their disposal. It was all fun and games, either dying to a dagger or having your face caved in by a maul. All players were deciding their play style. It was and still is fun, however one the main issues is the constant lack of good fixes from the developers, I'm not talking about the animation glitches such as reversal overheads but the hud, miscellaneous game changes as well as the map exploits. I've only came back a few months ago.
There are numerous times that the hud has become glitchy, when you're playing with friends and you see that green marker, you know exactly what I'm talking about. This has been a bug for quite sometime and these 'fixes' are not really doing anything. The gritty melee death camera is a notable example, having your character in first person and stay in first person when you die is gruesome especially when you see your head getting sliced apart from you body, it was all for immersion or when the in game voice chat has been removed because people were abusing it? Simply add the mute option to everyone and they themselves can pick who they want to personally mute,I remember when the King character would rally his men and lead the charge in the final minute of the match, it was exhilarating. Map exploits are still present, i.e spawn camping, spawn glitching as well as unorthodox map areas which were meant to be inaccessible such as the Arena.
Now how does the game currently fare? Excluding all the bugs or lack of proper fixes?
- The community
If you're playing for the first time, you need to know that the majority of the current chivalry community consists of very high level players most of which have over hundreds or thousands of hours of game time, you will get crushed by them, over and over, it is inevitable. Some even exploit the newcomers for the gain to finally reach level 50 for that golden helmet. Many will kick you for friendly fire, abuse your lack of knowledge about the game and overall they can be infuriating at times.Now you must understand that not all veteran players are like this. Many see that it's great that the game gets revitalised by newcomers, even with the occasional annoyance of friendly fire. This is where you see the duelyard servers, these servers contain a community that is more than willing to help you with the game, as well as giving you opportunities to have sessions with veteran players and useful tips they can provide, just ask. It will take time, that is for sure to be able to withstand pro players or even hold off 20 seconds of their slaughter but the more you do hold them off, that is an achievement you can be proud of as you invest more time into the game.
-The combat system
We now come to the combat system, we all had our taste of metal, enjoyable is it not? To visibly see the impact your weapon made to the enemy. This is what splits Chivalry from the rest of medieval games, the immersion. This has since been broken by the introduction of fighting techniques such as the reversals,drags and accelerations. But you must think, if the game resorted to just feints and left clicks it wouldn't be fun would it. To be able to pull those moves off is a testament to how skills players have become, whiffing such moves or having people block said moves is a death sentence. This is the skillcap of the game, despite the animation glitches when pulling such moves. As a new player, of course you aren't able to pull these off right away and you'll be dying to them a lot, but when you do pull at least one of them off, it is satisfying. Plain. Satisfaction.
-Tips when starting out
The optimisation is still poor, the developers need to get up and start dealing with these issues now rather than release more and more cosmetics.
In the end, you will find people who will destroy you, you will find people who will help you, you will need to take time in order to even 3v1 the absolute veterans. This is the process of any combat game. Is it a bit of a mess? Sure, but for only $5, it's a great mess.

Then there is what the others have said about limited replayability because it's exactly the same dungeon every time. Overall the game is frustrating. I'd say a solid hands down.  It is EXTREMELY eary access and servers are unstable as all hell.  I wasted about a half hour joining one and getting kicked constantly before spending the rest of this dinking around in singleplayer.  Graphical glitches and minor bugs abound.
But the 2 biggest worries and main reasons I voted no are:
Combat.  It feels like Skyrim, yet worse.  A very weak and dorky looking dodge to the side, a decent dodge back, and a shield that can take 2-3 hits.  Frankly, in a game that should be specializing in melee combat that's the least fun I've had in the game.  Feels like I'm just trading blows.  And there's no real weight to them either.
Right now it feels extemely basic.  Like they took the same survival starter kit that Ark used and didn't really change much.  Almost every system I've encountered is fairly similar to an embarrassing degree.  Granted it's a bit smoother, and I love the sliders when making your own server, but it all feels far too similar.  This should change after more systems get added, but for the next few months it's going to be really samey.
However there's a decent base here, hopefully they just need a few patches for stability and than can start adding/polishing content.  I'm not refunding it because I LOVE that there's no plans for modern equipment (screw guns) or for mounted combat (Ark left a sour taste in my mouth on that one) and the worshiping of gods and capturing thralls sound like fun.  Honestly, if they can make the combat fun this game will turn a 180.  More like Chivalry or Mount and Blade, just anything that feels more dynamic.

Being such a big fan of Fighting Fantasy, i had to get hold of this game as soon as possible.
As far as these adaptations go, i'm not too demanding. I'm fine with a plain book adaptation as Tin Man Games had been doing until now. This time though, they really upped their game, and it's a very interesting result. The main improvbements are a new fighting system, expanded writing, different characters to choose from and miniature inspired graphics.
Well, the first 2 aren't so much as a success as the latter 2, and this is why:
The new fighting system is fun for the first few times, and then it gets boring. It takes way too much time for something lacking in depth. I wished there was an option for the old simple dice system.
The expanded writing is a bit pedestrian, and it's very evident what's was in the main book and what wasn't.
Even still, i like the adaptation. The different characters are a nice addition since everyone whould reroll a 7 skill character anyway, and the graphics are just lovely.
I just hope this game is succeful enough for a few more adaptations like City of Thieves and Deathtrap Dungeon.

This game is really a hidden gem - unknown to the wide public, but a great pleasure to play.
Pros:
- Tactical combat
Although the combat system may seem too simple and limited at first glance, it nevertheless allows for a wide range of tactics to employ. The rules are sort of unique due to mainly melee-oriented combat, and you will find quite a few of challenges to overcome
- Setting and story
The not-so-popular Age of Discovery setting is great not simply because it is fresh, but the game does a lot to really engage you in atmosphere and spirit of those days. The story is also quite interesting, not the usual 'kill the arch-demon' type.
- Role-playing
You will really have choices to make, and you will face the consequences. You can be the conquer-the-savages type, or you can try and be more tolerant (maybe even too tolerant by the 16th century). The followers characters are sadly not unique, but defined by a number of traits. Nevertheless, you will have to deal with them having their own opinion.
Cons:
- 3D graphics
This is an indie game, but I still think that the 3D world and animations are mediocre. The combat is a bit better. 2D art is good though
- Interface
Mainly the adventure interface can be frustrating. Limited camera, bad pathfinding sometimes and the annoying bug when you're near POI but instead of interacting with it the game sends you to a journey around it.
Still, I had a great time in this game. With King's Bounty not available on Linux, Expeditions: Conquistador is a nice replacement.

As an 80's child I was a huge fan of the Fighting Fantasy gamebooks (along with others such as Lone Wolf and Way of the Tiger), having collected and played almost all of them, and it has been a shame that has been so few good computer game adaptations.   However, I feel that this game has bucked the trend and is definitely the best Fighting Fantasy computer game I have played so far.
The Warlock of Firetop Mountain is very clever in that it combines the original gamebook structure (where you make the relevant choices) with elements of another great childhood favourite, HeroQuest, as your character and the enemies you face are represented by models, and the graphics are of good standard with a good range of locations to traverse.    In terms of keeping to the original gamebook, the creators have added elements of the sequel, Return to Firetop Mountain, with their own additions - which do not feel out of place in the Fighting Fantasy world (although I do not know why Salamonis is missing from the game map).  The battle sections are also cleverly done with the option to use strategy to help narrow the odds against stronger enemies, as well as the obigilatory dice roles (skill is still the most important factor with these games).
The game also benefits from the amount of characters you can choose, and later purchase, each with a different backstory.  This gives them game more longevity, although the option to create your own characters would have been nice (maybe this is a hidden option I have not discovered yet).  This option also somewhat nullifies a problem that beset Fighting Fantasy in that there was not the levelling up option of gaining experience that Dungeons and Dragons and similiar RPGs offered (although the mighty Bloodsword gamebooks did implement this).
All in all I highly recommend this game, not just for fans of the original gamebooks, but for new players as well.  I would definitely be interested  in future titles  done in this style.  Citadel of Chaos next anyone?

I'd only wish this game showed the fall of Aztec civilization and evil doing of player's expedition more explicitly in art instead of written description (fall of Aztec Empire was a dark time).
On the tactical level, Expeditions: Conquistador provides player with interesting battles that can be often approached in different ways and player needs to keep his expedition in shape and manage the risks coming with leading his party into deeps of the jungle as many risks await for him there...
In overall, I give it a clear 9/10 score. Must buy for fans of history and tactical cRPG's.

Fable is a game about one thing - beating the snot out of everything in sight.  Many will say that it is supposed to be about choice, but in reality the choices don't matter aside from giving you specific weapons (or constantly having the village guards on you about simply existing).  Beat up enemies, search for relics to increase your power, do quests to increase your influence, follow the storyline.  Rinse, repeat.
In terms of environment I'd prefer a game similar to Dragon Quest 8 or The Elder Scrolls for this type of gameplay.  The world is segregated by zones and paths between them rather than an open world you are able to get lost in, quickly quashing any feeling of freedom in exploration you would otherwise have in the game.
Freedom in building your character, on the other hand, is much closer to the other end of the spectrum.  You can play as a melee weapon strength user, a ranged weapon skill user, or a physics-bending will user.  Or, if you want to put another 100 or so hours into the game, you can do all three and make yourself nearly untouchable.  Tons of melee weapons, ranged weapons, and spells make any of the three viable - but ultimately you'll be building these up by beating the snot out of everything in sight.

Now that I've come here to write a review I've discovered that SPAZ2 has just gone to early access and the video for it it making my heart thump already. Anyway, back to my review...
Cons (none of which matter to me)
The game universe is enormous but to be honest all a bit samey. You have to complete endless tasks to gain the technology and resources to upgrade your ships, but these tasks mostly involve battling enemies which is really the be-all and end-all of this game. In theory you're supposed to tailor your ships/weapons to the task at hand, but in practice it doesn't really seem to matter, you just equip the best weapons you can find and use them for everything. It's not the most intellectually challenging game.
Con (which does matter)
There is a storyline to this game, with an ending. After it had finished, to my dismay, I discovered that it was impossible to go back and play some more with the massive battleships I had worked for hours on end to build up. Bear this in mind before you tackle the final task, or make a data backup!
Pros
It's all about building bigger and better ships with more and more firepower and watching the battle mayhem. Especially towards the end of the game when huge battleships are blasting each other to smithereens it's a sight to behold, and the amazing thing is that all this glorious graphics action doesn't seem to lag or stutter at all, it's smooth as silk.
Now enough of this, I'm off to buy SPAZ2!

Elsword is an older MMORPG where you play as one of 10+ characters and go on a journey to defeat demons.
The gameplay is a bit sticky at first, but you can easily get used to it. The PVE is a bit boring at times, but the PVP is where it really shines. It acts as sort of a fencing type game where if you land a hit, you need to know how to chain into other attacks.

The music is pretty catchy at some parts, and isn't too bad, but like other games, you'll eventually want to turn it off. I keep mine on because I can ignore it.
The game has a way of keeping your level the same as the area you're in, but it forces you to do the same dungeons over and over at later levels. This is both useful, but annoying at the same time.
Overall, I say the game is about a 7.5-8/10. The game knows how to easily avoid P2W, and still allows you to acquire some things by using only microtransactions during events. So Elsword is COMPLETELY free.

Imagine a board game where the board "spaces" are cards laid out side-by-side.  You move your token from card to card, travelling across them until you reach the end of them.  As you "step" on each card, it is revealed.  Whatever the card reveals informs the adventure - an ambush by thieves, a mysterious cave, a helpful vendor, it's all randomized and set out under the cards for you to discover.
Now imagine the cards are composed of a deck of cards that YOU build, as well as some cards the "gamemaster" stuffs in there.  You don't know what you'll get in your travels, or in what order, and that is the core gameplay.
All combat is resolved in a simple, but elegant, action combat system similar to the Batman Arkham games (WASD, E to "counter", Space to roll, and sometimes # keys for specials) and it's fun.  Are you wearing a magic cap that makes your hits explode with gold?  Sounds good, until you remember that you revealed the "gold curse" card and the more gold you're carrying the slower you move.  Or not!  It's up to you.
So far only 4 hours in, absolutely loving it.  Why has it taken so long for this kind of action CCG to come out?

Don't let the hype-fueled positive reviews from pre-launch fool you. This game has fallen far from it's potential.
I joined up late in Alpha and experienced a sandbox with amazing potential, but dated mechanics. The gameplay was fun and I spent many hours through alpha learning the ins and outs of trade and farming. As the game launched, disappointment settled in because the land which was so crucial to success in the game was gobbled up. I continued to tough it out, slowly building up land for myself and alongside guildies.
Then Trion started making a mess of things.
In a game so focused around the player-driven economy, they continually made choices which turned the market on its head and took away the communities control over it's economy.
Lets start at launch. Trade certificates could be bought for cash shop currency. These items are needed to place and maintain your property. Whats the harm? Well being able to buy as much as you could afford in real money allowed the whales to dominate the landscape with massive amounts of buildings from the get go. This also devalued the tax certificates making it really inexpensive to maintain the land.
Another item...the wagon upgrade. The wagon is the critical tool to making money in the trading game. It allows you to carry up to 6 more trade packs and move at a greatly increased rate, massively increasing your gold payouts. The one item which could put your cart from 4 slots up to the max of 6? On the cash shop.
Finally, there was a rare material used for higher end items like these carts called a thunderstruck tree. It went for 2000 gold at one point. Then Trion put in a cash shop seedling which had an exponentially higher chance of spawning one. Within a day or two the price dropped to 200 gold.
The game is build on a flawed engine with many security holes, allowing for packet injection. This would not be a problem outside of PvP but it enabled an onslaught of bots and mods to dominate the real estate landscape, ruling out any chance of getting land beyond paying through the nose for it. Time and time again they claimed to have clamped down on this behaviour, yet the suspect land grabs continued.
This game has lots of potential but because of mismanagement by Trion and a terrible framework it has missed the mark by a long shot. The only reason this game has survived as long as it has is because there just isn't anything solid out yet for the sandbox fanatic to sink their teeth into. Once the rest of the industry rolls out it's sandbox options I would expect Archeage to fade to obscurity.
For now, I highly recommend not giving Trion your money for this or other titles. They have proven time and again that they are only keen on making a cash grab. No tricks, no traps, right?

I usually buy games during the summer or winter  sale, mostly because as I got old I became patient about my PC gaming. There are rare exceptions, when I buy a game full price...that is mostly because of some obscure principles, usually about supporting indie developers to survive in the dev-arena. You can guess, I bought TWoFM for full-price.
I was a huge fan of FF back in my heydey, forty-something people still remember fondly of the times, when those books were our _only_ entertainment. Now I have kids of my own, who are exposed to an array of different platforms, impulses bombard them from all directions. Yet, they rush to me everday and say "Daddy, let's play the labyrinthish game". And then we all do: I read the text (mild censorship is sometimes necessary), they happily make all the decisions about where to go or what to do, and we all enjoy the simple-but-entertaining fights. Older kid already demands to buy better heroes, and strictly supervises my pool of souls.
Frankly, I am tempted to play this alone, too. The changes are subtle, but helping the replayability immensely : the first time I noticed new dialogue options due Keen Eye ability, and realized that some things change during every playthrough, then suddenly the replay became more and more attractive option. Each hero also has an own quest to complete. The rougelike elements of buying new heroes based on stuff grinded in previous playthrough nicely provides the carrot at the end of the stick: we are 5+ hours into the game. We haven't beaten it yet, and we are not even close to getting bored.
All-in-all, this is a very-clever adaptation, that is elevated by the improvements of the original formula, while fully retaining the spirit of the original. I want Deathtrap Dungeons,  Scorpion Swamp and every other book to get the Tin Man Games treatment. And I want them now.

As a backer and long term Fighting Fantasy fan, this was very much a project I was looking forward to see come into fruition. Here are some general honest reflections taken from a post of mine on RPGWatch from my first 9 hours with the game:
Pros:
- Strongly faithful to the source material. Nostalgia will ring true for readers.
- Fun, bouncy and addictive game-play with many paths possible through the Mountain, expanding on the book's one true path.
- Reasonable variety of characters encourages replayability via the souls mechanic which unlocks different character tiers. (More higher skilled characters to choose from…)
- More DLC content still in development
- The engine shows great potential for future games.
- Unique turn based grid combat system rewards observation, positioning and experimentation.
- New artwork by Russ Nicholson gives that additional touch of authenticity.
Cons:
- Some bugs still remain; product still needs some polish. (Developers are liaising well with community)
- General linearity in scripted encounters leads to quick familiarity and a sense of repetition upon replay, which is critical to earn the souls required to unlock higher skilled character tiers.
- Combat can become tedious; possibly relying on too much player skill over character skill. (RPG factor)
- Group combat rules for traditional Fighting Fantasy not fully implemented. (No blocking skill checks, no luck use)
- The Maze of Zagor isn't really a maze. (Not disorienting enough!)
In short, this is a fun little game that blends traditional game-book ideas with table-top visuals. It is well worth your time, especially if you're a nostalgic Fighting Fantasy fan. It's also relatively short - you can fit in a single playthrough in around 2-3 hours and then return in a week or so to try out another character.  I could envisage playing this be great for an inter-generational activity, for interactive reading between parents/children and as a way for younger people to discover the adventurous wonders of Fighting Fantasy. This is pleasantly relaxing role-playing reduced to its core essence.
It's an exciting period for TinMan Games, hopefully success with this product will ensure more great titles be given a similar treatment. (Btring on Deathtrap Dungeon!)

Before you even read this review I will just say the following:
My reccomendation for this are soley for people who enjoy the genre, if you are unsure about it I suggest getting a physical copy of such a book and try for yourself first, as this is not your run of the mill RPG but a CYOA game, an old school type of game that have only recently joined the digital media in earnest and have gotten quite a few haters from those who do not know the merits of such a genre as a result, this is not for those who expect a simple journey, the game is more about trial and error, just like CYOA books of old, the game is NOT fair it will not hold your hand and if you mess up and make a wrong choice or your luck is not up to par then it will without a single hesitation END your characters life, it is actually rather realistic in that regard, the character doesn't know if opening the door with the odd noise inside will reveal a monster or not, so obviously neither do you the reader who take the role of this character, don't like that? Then deal with it or play somethign else.
This game is a good read and an interesting format for this type of game, one I honestly think does work if you like this sort of game, as it actually features more player interaction than just rolling dice, while still having the CYOA feel to it.
That being said the game is not all a dance on roses and it has it's upsides and downsides both from a gameplay as well as mechanically.
PRO's:
Every character have their own reason for being in Firetop, and have diffrent areas they can explore that others cannot or can do things diffrently, in one of my playthroughs i were ushered down the right turn of a T-junction corridor with no option to ever exploring the left one, while another character never had that encounter and could go left and explore that route, meaning there is actually a point to unlocking more characters than just to get diffrent atttacks for combat.
Likewise the side areas are varied and can take you on quite the detour before pushing you back into the main areas at times sometimes even skipping entire sections which means that there are room to explore without the area becoming too repetitive in just a few playthoughs.
Free Read Mode, this thing is a must if you plan to actually do harcore soul farming runs to unlock more characters, yes-yes I know what you are thinking "But you cant gain souls in Free Read" true, you can't, what you CAN do are practicing all the battles to know how to beat them with minimal damage as well as having access to infinite resurrection stones, allowing you to retry areas until you are comfortable with them, note that to unlock this mode you must finish your first legit attempt first (sucess or death does not matter here)
CON's: This game has the same "instant Death" posibilities as a CYOA, and while the "resurrection stones" and rest benches are made to make sure that isn't too much of a hassle it can become tiresome after a while, even moore so since such stones are limited to 3 outside of Free Read.
Soul Farming, this is a rather annoying yet understanding point of the game, you have to fam souls to unlock characters, sounds tedious and for the highest tier ones i have no doubt it would be as just tier 3 is 1k souls apiece with the cheapest being 250, that being said you start to gain quite a few souls per fight as you get further into the game so it shouldn't be too grind heavy, I suppose, but still a mark against it as it will take quite some time to unlock everything, even more so if you use Free mode to scout out the best oppertunities first.
The game, atleast for me, has a memory leak in full screen that will cause the game to just collapse in on itself after a while, and once it even locked up my entire computer this way, nothing would work, windowed did not have this issue, I do not blame the game itself for this, but Unity, the engine it's built in, which is known to have issues like this.

This is the first review I have ever written and I'm writing it due to my conflicting interest in this game. It's a very good game. It's optimized to the point that it runs on a generic 2016 HP laptop at 60fps (except earth, ♥♥♥♥ that tile set). There are just over 100 weapons in each catagory (melee, primary and secondary). I believe 30 different warframes to build and a lot of them have prime variants (various increased stats). The combat and movement is enjoyable. You will be flipping and sliding and spinning like a wheel of death after you learn the controls. The other mechanics in the game aren't hard to learn. A lot of people say they are but they aren't. They aren't deep mechanics. There are just a lot of different systems in place. If you decide to play this game then spend time on your ship clicking on stuff (after you finish the few tutorial missions). The game is also packed full of content. You will be learning something new and grinding for different reasons constantly. Alerts, syndacites, fissure missions, star chart, clan contributions and a ton more, but you are doing the same thing constantly and that's what I don't like.
It's a grind. It's Grindframe. To the point that you won't even be looking at stuff in the levels and just hauling it to the extraction point. The objectives do vary but getting there is the same thing every time. The devs try things (like spy) but the ai is dumb. I don't really blame the devs for that. In a game about grinding we don't need a ton of difficult enemies. Bosses show the same kind of dumb and will just glitch out a lot. They tried to vary bosses too but a lot of them are lackluster. Who cares though. You're going to be fighting said boss 3+ times for the warframe parts. I don't want to go on about the grind forever though. I didn't enjoy it but maybe you will.
I would definitly give the game a chance. It has a lot going for it and if you enjoy the grind then this game should keep you coming back for a long time. Especially if you decide to grind trade chat. One of the best parts to me.

I have very, very little time to play games these days and even less for writing reviews of them (three kids, teaching career, successful website to run...). But I just had to give "The Warlock of Firetop Mountain" a little write-up.
I signed up for the Kickstarter more out of nostalgia than anything else and I am really glad I did. The end result is simply beautiful. It maintains every bit of the charm of the original, not tempered by passing time in the least, and brings it bang up to date. The combat system is perfection, including the classic dice-rolling, but also a mental / luck element that the player controls.
The text is wonderful, the expansion on the core book doesn't seem at all cludged, the graphics are - frankly - beautiful and the replayability very good indeed. I love the way the scenery drops down an item at a time when you enter a new location. The fact that it's still text-based rather than having everything read out means I can hopefully introduce my modern-day son to Fighting Fantasy using this game and then ease him into the books, while still ensuring that he's reading a lot.
If there's one issue it's the save system and only as it doesn't suit my often very-limited windows for gaming. As far as I can tell, the game only saves when you sit at one of the rare benches which can be a little far apart for someone who may only have time for a 15-minute blast. However, I *may* be wrong on this and it could save at flagged waypoints. I need to check.
Highly recommended. Simple, deep, addictive.
One of the best games I have ever played.

I only played this game on Ironman, Hard difficulty. Thus far, only 0.9 % of players received the "Masochist" achievement ( for playing on Ironman mode ) 0.8 % received the "Pizarro" achievement ( for finishing the game on Hard ).
I first noticed that this game had an unusual design, in that the jungles were so lush, that you could not sometimes see your own character! Your screen is often filled with green, tree top canopies. You get a visceral, authentic sense of wading through a jungle.
There are two campaigns.
I think that the game trailer is misleading. Similar to 1990's RPGs, in terms of the time spent, this game is 90 % exploration, 6 % questing and 4% combat. The percentages are off, but that is only because the game is so exploration-heavy, that it's hard for me to get an accurate handle on the numbers. As an example, it took me a couple of days, just to uncover the fog of war, for each campaign.
You assemble your expedition of ten team members from the following classes: doctors; hunters; scholars; scouts; soldiers. Each class has three statistics of varying degree. As an example, a soldier would be better at "guarding" and "patrolling", whereas a doctor would be better at "herbalism" ( first aid ) and "tinkering" ( constructing mechanical traps ).
As you explore, you find washed up crates, containing random amounts of: wood, metal, rope and oil. You use these materials to construct different traps that can be used in combat, such as a spiked pit trap.
You have to manage food, morale and medicine.
During the turn-based, hex-style combat, the AI is fantastic and has fuzzy logic built in. On Hard difficulty, the AI will perform optimal moves most of the time and make mistakes maybe 2% of the time ( similar to playing against a strong, human opponent ). There is a separate slider, to increase the AI to maximum ( which would turn the combat into chess, I'm assuming ). There are 6 levels of escalating injury: "harmless"; "moderate"; "severe"; "critical"; "fatal"; "dead".
The quests are fairly straight forward and the writing was ( surprisingly ) very professional.
It took me a while, to warm up to the 18th century art style but the artist is talented.
I love the music, especially the combat music ( which is featured in the game trailer ). The ambient sounds of birds and crickets chirping is perfect.
The game is stable ( as a game with an "Ironman mode" would have to be ). In 119 hours, the game only crashed once and that was when I alt-tabbed into a different window, to chat with a Steam friend.
It was a joy to play a game, with such a well programmed, clean and intuitive interface. I'm looking forward to other products, from the developers. I think that I paid less than $4 for this game, which was a steal!

6180: The Moon is an easier, ambient,  minimalistic, shorter death platformer best compared to Super Meat Boy.    It isn't really derivative of SMB and feels like its own game, but the controls aren't as tight.  There's a little touch of looseness which has you missing platforms and touching spikes.  While I slogged through the addictive levels of SMB until I 100%ed the game, I found myself playing 6180 in short sessions, and I've completed it in 5 hours.  Like SMB, death is quick and restarts are quick.  There are little continue points sprinkled through levels to make it less frustrating.  The jumps have a wrap mechanic from the top to bottom, but you quickly get used to it.  Each set of levels adds a new mechanic, but boy oh boy was I sick of spikes at the end of it all.  The music is beautiful, but the levels get a little repetitive and it;s not nearly as addicting as SMB.  Actually, if SMB is an A+ game, this is sort of a C+.  I thought I'd recomend it when I started writing this, but really, go play Super Meat Boy instead.

The first thing you should know about this game is that it is just a grind. You grind resources and blueprints to either sell for premium currency or use in order to farm more efficiently.
If you do not like endless farm with constant upgrades and new weapons and skillsets then this game is not for you.
Pros:
- Best part of the game; the movement system.
- Tons of very different weapons (most of which have a normal and upgraded prime version)
- Many different characters to play as (again, most have normal and prime versions)
- Very well optimized yet visually pleasing in every way, even on lower settings
- Constant progression
- Highly customizable playstyles with the mod system
- Great variation in environments
- Linear-ish procedurally generated missions as well as open world with bounties and random encounters
- Great for groups of friends up to 4
- Microtransactions are very optional as the currency can be traded
Cons:
- Focus on farming (wouldn't necessarily call it a con but its definately not a pro)
- Slow in the beginning without help from experienced players
- Confusing without help from experienced players (or google)
- Microtransactions with many reasons to get them
- Very expensive cosmetics (specifically tennogen which are made by the community)

First played this game on console around the time it came out. I was young and stupid, and ended up selling all of my clothing to the Guild shop vendor then wondering why I was running around naked. I quickly became better at this game, and learnt everything there is to know about it, and it's been keeping me entertained for years. All together I've probbaly played this game for about 1000 hours.
The gameplay is fairly smooth, and the controlls aren't hard to get used to, although I personally enjoyed them a lot more on console. But if you're looking for a challenge, then this game might not be for you, although that can depend on how hard you make it for yourself. If you regularly level up and get the best weapons you can (which can be found pretty early) you'll blast through this game no problem, but if you stick with an iron sword and rarely level up, you'll have a bit of a tough time. You could always try and play through this game on the unnoficial "hardcore" mode and never level your character.
The graphics are part of this game's charm. The textures are well done, well detailed, and the lighting is pretty nice to look at as well. The music is decent, but I found it's stuck with me over the years, while the actual game sounds are nicely done as well. No low quality, and they sound like they actaully fit with each action.
This game is pretty short, if you do just one playthrough. You'd be lucky if you got more than 17 hours out of it, but there are tons of choices to make throughout the game, so there's a bit of replayability. There's a few easter eggs around as well, which are always nice to see.
That's my review for Fable: The Lost Chapters. Hope you like it and hope you enjoy Fable as much as I do! :)

6180 the moon isn't a bad game, but there just isn't anything special to highlight it in an overcrowded market. Whether you'll want it in your library or not depends on your tolerance for simple indie puzzlers that can be fully completed in under two hours.
My favourite aspect of the game was the serene atmosphere it presents. The soundtrack is good, calming and appropriate for the setting, and just sitting on a random platform while plotting your next move can be quite contemplative. I found the visuals to be hit and miss; very minimalistic, but the textures are somewhat jarring and jagged on some of the obstacles, and I found the collision hitboxes to be slightly wacky on the side of the spikes. YMMV.
The story is whimsical and vaguely irritating, but nothing offensive, just pretty standard indie stuff. The gameplay is quite fun at points, with the general idea being to get from A to B via a screen that wraps around from top to bottom, negotiating obstacles as you go. Overall, I found the game to be relatively lacking in challenge and a bit uninspired in terms of level design. As mentioned earlier, it's also quite short, even for something so cheap and cheerful.
This is more of a neutral review than anything else, but given the sheer volume of games available on Steam these days, it's hard to recommend 6180. There are other cheap games that do everything far better, particularly in the sales. For cool bouncing mechanics involving spherical objects, The Floor Is Jelly and The Sun & Moon are worth a look, whike NightSky is a very atmospheric momentum game. As for this particular moon, it's rather more crescent than full.

First of all, first impressions plays an important part for me personally to decide whether the game is worth investing the time in and even though I enjoyed my short experience with SPAZ, I have to say that it fail to get me hooked. Now, onward to the actual review.
, or
for short, is a real time roleplaying strategy game developed by the two-man team
and was released back in August 2011. SPAZ is generally well-received and the success of the game spawned a sequel with the same name released only recently as an Early Access title.
The game takes place in a distant future where the center piece of the conflict revolves around the discovery of Element 126, or Rez as it's more commonly known. With rumors of the abundance of Rez reserves at the galactic core, you and your crew of space veterans sets out on a voyage to seek the fabled promise of fortune. Of course, things weren't always that easy as the galaxy is in turmoil with the clashes of the oppressing UTA forces and the desperate civilians factions. Not to mention the rising report of zombies incident and the notoriety of the bounty hunters that stalks each system.
The gameplay is done in a top down fashion where you control a single ship while the AI controls, depending on how advanced your mothership The Clockwork is, several others and they will assist you to what nature that you've set them via the Tactic panel. This panel acts as your drawing board for devising strategy on how to approach the situation. The game is paused while the panel is open and you can select units and commands them either to attack, reposition or follow you similar to the conventional real time strategy games. Another unique feature is that while you're in this panel, you can access the hangar menu and customize your deployed ships, whether to change them to a different better-suited hull or switching out ship parts to better adapt to the situation. All of this are done in real time as you close the panel so make good use of the Tactic panel to turn the battlefield to your side.
This game relies heavily on exploration and the game is
! It amazes me of what two people can achieved with the right motivation. Moving back to the exploration part, you'll have to jump from system to system via the warp gate, searching for rare blueprints to outfit your ships better, recruiting vital crew members which provides significant bonuses to your whole fleet, reverse engineering various hulls so that you'll have more options in combat and various others. Based on what you've chose early on, the galaxy can contain to hundreds of system at once and this will lead to potential hundreds of hours of entertainment.
Generally, the game revolves around 4 factions, the United Terran Alliance (UTA), the Civilians, Bounty Hunters and... Space Zombies. Yeah, I'll get to that in a bit. In a system, every action that you take will result in these factions react differently. Anger the UTA too much and you'll have their ships raining beams and missiles on yours and vice versa. To make it worse, in some system where the Bounty Hunters resides, your actions might increase the bounty on your head and collect it too much and you'll have some skilled hunters on your tail. There's also an arena mode held in the Bounty Hunters space station where you can undertake specific challenges in terms of scenarios. Succeed and you'll be awarded with Rez and reputation. I haven't got too far into the game yet but the zombies seems to be the byproduct of a failed experiment and for some reason, it affects ships, or zombies piloting the zombie ships? I don't know but it's pretty whack to be honest but I guess zombies sells.
Now, let's move on to the pros and cons, shall we? I hope this will explain why I said the game didn't get me hooked.
Like I've said, the game fail to keep me interested from exploring any further, even the previously reviewed
appeals more to me. However, if games like this are your cup of tea then by all means, go for it. I'm sure in time you'll receive your money's worth because the contents are just enormous.

This is a game with a great core gameplay loop - load up a couple of ships with various items and fly them around frantically through a swarm of other ships blowing stuff up. The action-oriented 2D combat is great fun, with surprisingly great physics and object interaction for such a seemingly simple game. The fact that the plot and the elements in play radically changes halfway through the game is a bonus, and works great even though the zombies are spoiled by the game's actual title.
There are a few issues I had with the game though. Grinding for resources and data can be quite a hassle - the less you grind, the harder the combat is, because your equipment simply won't be as good. Updating your tech RPG-style is really compelling, but unfortunately not every tech is created equal. Techs all cost the same, but it seems clear to me that investing 50+ skillpoints in, say, Hull strength or Shields is vastly preferable to investing the same amount of points in something like Bombs (a really specific type of weapon) or Crew (only situationally useful). Maybe this depends on playstyle, but I tried investing in things like Subsystems or Launchers at first and found the benefits just weren't as tangible.
Also, for a game that probably takes even experts 30+ hours to complete, the fairly small number of mission types gets old fairly quickly.
That said, the core gameplay is really fun and made it worth it for me, and the sense of progress you get teching up and defeating fleets that would have smeared you to a paste several hours earlier is tangible and rewarding. If you've got a lot of time and like a simple 2D action game, give this a shot!

Running an item shop may not sound like the kind of thing you'd want to do in a video game.  As a sidequest maybe, but as the game's bread and butter?
Recettear, however pulls this off beautifully. For the micro manager, there's many things to keep track of in the shop: is the placement of your items bringing in the optimum amount of customers? Is your choice of decorations bringing in the kind of customers you want?  How much is too much to sell that piece of egg toast for?
For the dungeon crawler, there's plenty of opportunity for exploration.  How far down do you go in the dungeon?  Do you take the opportunity to go back to town and empty your inventory, or do you press on to avoid losing a day that could be better spent selling your newfound loot?  Can you topple the boss rush mode after completing the story?  Just how deep IS this dungeon?
The combination of humor and tight gameplay will keep you coming back over and over.  For 20 bucks (less if you get it on sale!), you can't ask for more.

The combat system is a combination of FPS and turn-based strategy like X-com. You have a certain number of "control points" to spend each turn on units. Each unit has a movement meter and can use a weapon for each control point used. So you can move a unit into position, and fire, and if there's any movement left, move them behind cover. This works better for some units, not at all for others (snipers).
The problem comes in the form of difficulty, unknowns, and RNGs.
-Some missions are easy enough to beat in one try. Others take 5+ tries because of hidden units, surprises in the form of hidden tanks, and general RNG aiming. Or the first half of a mission is easy, and the second half is super hard because of endless enemy reinforcements. Or an undefeatable enemy appears that you have to ignore. Or the fact that a certain weapon does significantly more damage than any other against a special boss, but that you could never know to use.
-You have to grind "skirmishes" in order to not be outclassed by enemies by two levels (which means a lot) at al times.
-When you aim rifle/machine gun/lance/sniper/tank gun, you have a small reticule that shots will land within. This is ok, but for medium range shots, you miss 75% of the time because even though you put your crosshair dead on the enemies' head, it will completely miss. This wastes your control point and, if the enemy is within a 'counter attack' range, will be able to shoot back at you.
-Most of the missions require you to simply capture a flag. That's all.
Despite it's shortcomings in design and thought, it's worth a play. But don't pay more than 10$ for it.

I finished the main story and played one of the DLC mission chains. I had never heard of this series before playing it and haven't really played many games similar to it before. The most similar ones I can think of are the 3D worms games and hogs of war (old playstation game).
Valkyria Chronicles is a turn-based strategy game. Every turn you get a set number of moves which you use to control your units. The different loadouts of the unit classes (snipers, engineers etc) and their varying movement points force you to think about how best to approach your mission objectives.
This basic premise works fine and I really enjoyed it all in all. However, there are a few things about it that aren't quite as good as I feel they should be.
A lot of the game is very counter-intuitive. This is moreso a problem early on, when you don't know the game's rules yet, but it sure is annoying. Quick example off the top of my head: If a unit is in cover behind a sandbag with only its lower body actually covered, a headshot from a sniper rifle will still deal reduced damage to it.
Worse, your damage is still reduced even if you circumvent the defenses and attack from behind them. Of course, the game gives you ways to deal with that, but it's not what you'd expect going into it.
The shining example of this point, however, is the game's rating system. Based on your performance in a mission, you get assigned a grade at its end.
This is important because a higher grade nets you more money and XP for upgrades. Unlike what you might though, the
thing that matters is how fast you finish your missions. Literally nothing else matters.
I generally favour a slower approach and this is a turn-based game after all, so this (seemingly?) weird focus on speed left me somewhat underleveled towards the end of the game.
To alleviate this, you can replay some of the story missions as so-called skirmishes, in order to gain more XP and money. One of these is insanely easy to finish in one turn and nets you a lot points, so you can grind yourself to max level in probably under an hour.
You're also forced to position your units in your starting area(s) before you actually know what kind of enemy units are on the map and where enemy control points are located. I also felt that the mission briefings were quite lacking at times, leaving me unsure about how to plan for certain mission and proceed in them.
In a game where it is vital to anticipate your enemy's moves, this can get really annoying. On occasion, events during a mission that you couldn't be expected to anticipate can screw up your planning as well. This game sure likes to throw your plans into disarray a lot. Add to that the fact that the same move can be wildly succesful or a complete disaster based on sheer luck, and odd hitboxes preventing you from hitting shots that should have connected and you have a recipe for easy frustration.
Another thing  that bothered me a lot was that there seems to be a delay on absolutely anything you do in game.
Want to switch menus? Fade to black into load screen. Want to order your unit? Cursors plays select animation, dramatic zoom in on unit. Want to move your unit around? Too bad, one of its special abilities activated,
forcing you to look at a useless animation that plays for a couple of seconds. Want to buff it? Here, look at another useless animation first. Killed an enemy unit and want to end your turn? Gotta watch your unit celebrating first.
I admit, I'm moving into nitpick territory here, but I'd much rather have a subtle animation blend in at the bottom of my screen and be able to move immediately, rather than watching one for a couple of seconds, unable to do anything. It would probably be less of a hassle if there was a large variety of high quality animations, but special abilities and buffs all use essentially the same animation and it's not a particularly interesting one, so the novelty wears off after having seen it exactly one time.
Less nitpicky is the fact that you can't speed up time/skip forward during enemy turns. That's simply annoying in missions with a lot of enemies on the map.
Keep in mind that you change keybindings by rightclicking the game and then going to "Configure Valkyria Chronicles".
During combat, controls are solid. The only gripe I had with them was that it was difficult to maneuver precisely. I only later found out that WASD moves you faster than the arrow keys, which make you walk slowly + the tank controls are a bit wonky.
When it comes to the ingame menus, it is very apparent that you're playing game made primarily for consoles. There is no mouse support and you'll be navigating through a ton of different menus, which is a minor nuisance, but it wouldn't be as bad if not for the
whenever you switch menus.
I swear, there is a delay on absolutely everything you do in this game.
You can switch between the English VO and the original Japanese one in the main menu, which is pretty cool.
I played with the English VO first and then switched to the Japanese one later. Why?
The English VO had that weird fake sounding style that seems to be used a lot for dubbed anime.
I don't speak Japanese, so I can't tell if it's the same with that VO, which made it more enjoyable to me.
Note that your mileage may vary here, the voice actors aren't bad by any means and I'm har
I'd say the soundtrack is good. None of it really stood out to me, though I'd recognise certain tracks of course. Since it never took me out of the scenes I'd say it does a good job of being a videogame soundtrack: it supports the game while not pushing itself in front of the gameplay.
I'll keep it brief, the sound effects are jarringly bad and it took me quite some time to get over it, but in the end I did. It's almost a shame the rest of the game is good enough to make up for how bad this part is.
If I had to describe the story in one sentence I'd say that it's the writers' attempt at using as many
war movie and anime clichés as humanly possible in their game. That said, as long as you're fine with
loads of cheesy scenes and predictable plot twists galore, you will probably enjoy the story, since it
isn't poorly told at all.
However, you'll have to get used to the way the game makes you select multiple cut scenes manually
after each mission. It makes for weird pacing and most of these aren't "true cut scenes", but rather
portraits of the characters imposed on a background. At times this makes it hard to get immersed
in the scenes at hand, since their composition is left unclear (you don't fully know who's standing where and miss
out on the characters' body language).
Oh yeah, the setting is a sort of anime version of WW2.
Valkyria Chronicles is clunkier than it should be, a lot of its gameplay is counter-intuitive, the sound is awful, it often felt like the game was competing with itself to see how many curveballs it could throw me in a single turn and the game was a lot harder than I thought it would be, but I'll be damned if I didn't enjoy playing it.
If you think you can look past its flaws, I definitely recommend giving the game a shot.

Thematically, it's like Advance Wars and Fire Emblem got together and had a love child.  A heavy dose of tsundere and cringingly corny dialogue, and you have yourself Valkyria Chronicles.
Every soldier on the battlefield is a separate character, with a separate class, personality, different stats and buffs, and different terrain preferences (Ex. sniper Catherine is extremely ammo-conscious, and firing her last bullet will give her multiple stat penalties).  Everyone has their own backstory and playstyle, making for an impressive number of combinations with a relatively small roster.  (They even have separate voice actors).
The actual gameplay is very solid, while also presenting a very unique mechanic.  Each mission is played out in turns, but as each unit is moved, there is real-time reaction fire, forcing you to act quickly *while moving*, but still allowing every action to be deliberate.
A great strategy game, but only for those who can muster an appreciation for the anime/JRPG influences; otherwise, the abundance of quality writing and storytelling will be lost on you.
Lack of a multiplayer option limits replayability, but still worth it.

Some roguelike games are great because they offer a unique set of mechanics (like Desktop Dungeons).  Others are great because they present themselves so well (like Rogue Legacy).  But Hand of Fate does everything well.
Hand of Fate is polished, deep, accessible, and rewarding both for the casual player interested in a unique game and the hardcore collector who wants to get every achievement.  Even when grinding for some of the more difficult cards available, I've never stopped enjoying the experience, the rich theming of the dealer's grim narration or the surprises of certain windfalls or turns of fate.
Hand of Fate is a rogue-like wrapped in a deckbuilding game.  As you progress, you unlock cards which represent weapons or equipment as well as enemies and encounters.  All together, these form your "decks" - the equipment you'll find available in shops and as random rewards, as well as what monsters or towns or characters you'll meet along the way.  As a result, there are multiple levels of strategy at play throughout the game as you decide which encounters are most rewarding, whether to include high-risk, high-reward cards or cards that consistently yield some small benefit.  Collecting these cards and building decks of rewarding encounters and a strong arsenal of weapons and armor will be the core of your experience.
But where Hand of Fate really shines is in its presentation.  The card-as-fate metaphor persists throughout, making for a surprisingly immersive game, even as it transitions between the navigation of your pawn from encounter to encounter and the Arkham-style combat instances in which you'll fight a variety of interesting enemies, each with its own set of different attacks and powers.  I'm reminded on the one hand of the old Lost Kingdoms games for Gamecube; on the other, of the grim atmosphere of Demon's Souls or Dark Souls; and also of FTL, with its emphasis on careful decision-making as you explore deeper and deeper into the unknown.
Bottom-line, it's the best-looking, deepest rogue-like I've played to date.  It looks good, plays well, and has tons of content, even at the $25 tag.  If you're even remotely interested, get it.  You may be surprised - you won't be disappointed.

My review for Rogue-like: The Card Game.
The Good:
-A unique blend of 3rd Person Action RPG with a deck building card game that works incredibly well.
-The voice actor for the game master is awesome.
-Writing is great.
-Top notch visuals and the art style is very Fable-esque.
-Runs at a buttery smooth 144fps on my rig max settings, no PC problems as far as I can tell.
-Branching paths on later levels which makes for a good amount of replayability.
-Random card generation that leads to very different outcomes every time you play, you could get great card draw and have an easy ride to the boss, which leads to...
The Meh:
-Random card generation that leads to very different outcomes every time you play, you could end up with a pain card that may cause you to lose alot of heath or cripple you early on and make it very difficult to finish a run.
-Combat is Arkham-like in which you fling back and forth between enemies and all too familiar counter system, its not as good as Arkham and a bit button mashy, but it works.
-Kinda lacking in options, but hey, its a Unity game.
-Encountered a small bug in one of the merchant shops where i'd pause the game and when i came back, my cursor was gone and i couldn't select anything...luckily i fixed it by alt-tabbing.
Overall:
An Early Access success, its nice to see a game come out of that hell hole and bring something very unique and special to the table. I hope to see this gain some huge publicity and enough sales to bring it to other platforms so that everybody has a chance to play this. Support the devs, buy this game!

Well, what can I say...  This game has improved a lot.  I was around with a few other friends during the closed betas, but the game fell apart at release.  As of right now, only one other person I started this game up with still plays (occasionally).  So why the thumbs up?
This game's been through a lot.  At launch it was swarmed by DDOS attacks (yes, they were real), bots, spammers, insane queue times, and bad management.  They even took the game off of Steam.
Now, they fixed it up and it's back.  The economy is normal, the community is surprisingly friendly.  There is almost no reputable source of a wiki on the internet, so people communicate!  The game almost has the old WoW feel to it.  There's no dungeon finder, no cheat sheets on the internet, and no cookie cut progression, going out of your way to capture cool pets with good stats.
it's true that it does have the same flaws old WoW did (some abilities/talents outweigh others by far), but it's a tradeoff.
All in all, I recommend this game.  It isn't nearly p2w as most people comment on, you literally can only but gliders (faster movement), mount armor (so people don't gank your mount as easily), and land (but pirating and illegal farming can get you the same revenue).  The rest are cosmetics.  Tweaked cosmetics with slight boosts, but nothing p2w.

This is the first review I have ever written and I'm writing it due to my conflicting interest in this game. It's a very good game. It's optimized to the point that it runs on a generic 2016 HP laptop at 60fps (except earth, ♥♥♥♥ that tile set). There are just over 100 weapons in each catagory (melee, primary and secondary). I believe 30 different warframes to build and a lot of them have prime variants (various increased stats). The combat and movement is enjoyable. You will be flipping and sliding and spinning like a wheel of death after you learn the controls. The other mechanics in the game aren't hard to learn. A lot of people say they are but they aren't. They aren't deep mechanics. There are just a lot of different systems in place. If you decide to play this game then spend time on your ship clicking on stuff (after you finish the few tutorial missions). The game is also packed full of content. You will be learning something new and grinding for different reasons constantly. Alerts, syndacites, fissure missions, star chart, clan contributions and a ton more, but you are doing the same thing constantly and that's what I don't like.
It's a grind. It's Grindframe. To the point that you won't even be looking at stuff in the levels and just hauling it to the extraction point. The objectives do vary but getting there is the same thing every time. The devs try things (like spy) but the ai is dumb. I don't really blame the devs for that. In a game about grinding we don't need a ton of difficult enemies. Bosses show the same kind of dumb and will just glitch out a lot. They tried to vary bosses too but a lot of them are lackluster. Who cares though. You're going to be fighting said boss 3+ times for the warframe parts. I don't want to go on about the grind forever though. I didn't enjoy it but maybe you will.
I would definitly give the game a chance. It has a lot going for it and if you enjoy the grind then this game should keep you coming back for a long time. Especially if you decide to grind trade chat. One of the best parts to me.

The type of game that makes me wish for a recommendation of "Only on sale"
One of the few games out there that lets you play as a ghost doing actual ghost like things, the game is marred by several issues that really prevent it from working enough for me to give it a pass at normal prices.
It's a puzzle game first and foremost that felt it had to add in some action in the form of stealth segments where you must avoid getting caught by demons, which usually boils down to accidentally getting spotted and having to waste time teleporting around safe spots waiting for them to resume patrolling so you can try again at doing a QTE to get them out of an area so you can go back to exploring.
And then there's the puzzles, that boil down to trying to find every object in a given area and putting 2 or 3 of them together to solve a small mystery, sometimes operating off of logic and other times suffering from the Phoenix Wright problem where you're ahead of the game's characters but are forced to answer extremely handholding questions in order to advance (such as "there was a murder" as one of an early mystery's "most relevant" clues when you are asked to investigate a murder).
However, that's not what really hurts this game. Instead, it's the simple lack of content. There isn't enough dialogue recorded for a game that features a mind-reading mechanic. There are very few side quests and after you complete them all the hub world you are forced to travel through seems very boring. Collectables are decent but don't seem to ever really be enough considering the amount of ground you cover between them. The main plot ends way too early for something that came out above $20. And those demons mentioned above? They are thrown in purely to prevent you from breezing through levels in 10 minutes.
As you'll probably get through most of the content you care about in the first run, the game really lacks a lot of replay value, so your first run through is going to be about as long as you spend with the game. I went through with the "I'm going to try to collect as much as I can, but more than an hour without any result and I'm moving on" mentality, and I clocked about 8 hours (which includes a bit of idling time spent away from the computer).
It's kind of sad, because the game isn't devoid of value, just not enough to justify purchasing it normally.
Its writing, especially concerning some of the ghost stories you come across, is engaging, even if it's not the best you'll ever experience. Meanwhile, it completely nails the "I'm playing as a ghost detective" thing it was going for, even going so far as to have the first thing you do be trying to get back into your still barely alive body by trying to slip into it. If you liked Ghost Trick or Geist and wanted more games like that, this scratches that itch nicely.
This game is worth playing for those who have a weakness for a somewhat noir detective game or one where you play as a ghost, but because you'll probably only need to play it once, get it on sale.

- Linear-ish procedurally generated missions as well as open world with bounties and random encounters
- Great for groups of friends up to 4
- Microtransactions are very optional as the currency can be traded
Cons:
- Focus on farming (wouldn't necessarily call it a con but its definately not a pro)
- Slow in the beginning without help from experienced players
- Confusing without help from experienced players (or google)
- Microtransactions with many reasons to get them
- Very expensive cosmetics (specifically tennogen which are made by the community)

This is a surprisingly good platformer with a simple premise: the bottom of the screen loops around to the top, and vice versa.  Despite the lack of pits as a result, 6180 still manages to present a challenge both by using spikes as obstacles, and by adding new concepts to the newer stages.  There is a very atmospheric soundtrack to the game, not only fitting for the space theme but also quite calming, rather welcome when some of the stages can present frustration and repeated deaths.
It is quite a short game, perhaps an hour or less to play through fully.  It certainly doesn't overstay a welcome, and if anything feels like it could've been longer.  However, it seems the developers wanted things to end once they had presented the ideas they had with the mechanics, and so the game ends with all the stages well designed but without it being drawn out and without stages repeating themselves.
6180 the moon is a game which I would recommend.  If you are interested in an unusual platformer, or want a quick game which does a great job of presenting its mechanics and challenges directly, then I would highly recommend checking it out.  If you are looking for a game with hundreds of different stages and variants, or where you can sink dozens of hours into, then 6180 the moon is not likely a game you would be interested in.

Do not let the price of this rare gem fool you, Because the content this game can offer is well worth more! SPAZ is a fantastic, well-made game developed by only two people who had a dream and made it reality, Creating a stepping stone for others to do the same. After 300+ hours into this game, Here's my experience so far.
PROS:
1. What initially brought me to this game was how alive it felt, With something always going on around every corner of the galaxy. There are many events and little side-missions that make it feel like it's a living, breathing environment
2. While on the surface the mechanics look simple, there is a surprising amount of depth put into how you can personally tailor and customize your ships to your own liking, Giving you the chance to get creative and make many different layouts and strategies on how you want to play.
3. The exploration, With the choice of either a minimum of 150 stars or a maximum of 300 stars, You can set the pace at which you play the game to your own standards. Regardless of what you choose, It takes a considerable time to explore each and every different system, Giving you a reasonable space to scavenge for tech that you may need.
4.The combat, the main focus of this game, Is very engrossing and addictive. The controls are tight, The gameplay is fluid and it's all easy to pickup, But hard to master. From blasting your enemies away with cannons to steadily melting them to scrap from far away, There's plenty of options for you to take down your enemies. (Or civilians, if you're not in the most merciful mood!)
CONS:
1. The game can become very repetitive, With most side-missions being recycled, And many tasks needing to be done in order to progress with reputation.
2. It can feel very grindy, especially early on in the game when you need to farm resources and levels if you ever get stuck on a quest.
3.

This game has brought me tons of priceless joy, I hope I had shared some of that experience with you all, Because even with all that I said, I still can't express or put into words how much I love this game, Thank you for reading this far, Have a pleasant day.

Back. Now what does this game does well and what poorly.
(EDIT: I think I could have been less excited and more informative about the game. I am sorry, I was way too hyped. So here goes...)
Foreword: this is a card collection game, unlike any other. Here you do not use cards to fight - the cards represent actions or encounters. In essense, the cards fight you - or help you. In the beginning of the level, a maze of cards is laid out in front of you, which you must traverse to the end, which results in entering another area (different card layout) or a boss battle. And of course, to make your life even more miserable, you have food, gold, equipment and life points. Food needs to be replenished at a regular basis, or you will start losing life points and die of starvation. Gold is used in shops and random events, equipment and life points are used in battles.
To make the long read short short you have:
- Random events - ranging from quests to finding a treasure chest or running a gauntlet to it
- Fights - there is a number of encounters you need to fight through, including a boss at the end of the level who play in a 3D Batman/Assassin's Creed style
- Shops and helpful NPCs who will give you buffs or food
Good:
1. No 2 games are the same, even if you play the campaign. Decks determine playthroughs, not scenarios.
2. Winning a whole encounter and beating up the boss of a level with a starter rusty axe has never been more satisfying.
3. Building a deck matters, molding it to your liking even moreso.
4. Some people complain about the slowmo attacks, but it is exactly these that give you a good view of the battlefield.
5. Mashing buttons can both win or lose you the game. Cool. Makes gamers learn something.
Bad:
1. Bind the camera to buttons, people. You have both tabs unused, make it like Dynasty Warriors 8 and you will be golden. While I agree that you can't see behind your back and it adds a realistic combat, rogue-like games are punishing as they are by default.
2. Boss battles become a bit repetitive once you learn how the bosses work and what is their attack sequence.
Semi-bad: this game is best played with a controller. I hope you have one. My RAZR is doing a magnificent job with it.

Imagine Hearthstone, Batman AA, D&D, Darkest Dungeon, and Gauntlet had a baby...that baby's name is Hand of Fate. Then add a card dealer that actually feels like a real person is playing cards with you....I just cant say enough good about this game but I'm going to try.
This game is unbelievably good. The voice acting is literally perfect. It is so immersive watching all of the little animations that the  dealer uses and his comments are so on point that it is akin to psycho mantis from mgs. I really get the sense that I am playing cards with a powerful, mysterious and devious being and he is talking to ME! His covered face was a brilliant idea to add to the sense of mistrust.
This is truly a seamles mashup of several components. TCG, action, RPG, strategy. While Hand of Fate isn't a complete experience in any of the forementioned genres there is enough of each one that somehow when combined...is so throughly entertaining and enthralling I simply cannot put it down. The concept is so simple yet so brilliant it's a wonder noone has made a game like this years ago. The gameplay is so fun that I played the game for 7.4 hours straight the same night I purchased it. It is realy a unique experience. What a gem! I really cant say enough about the dealer's character he makes every single moment of this game feel meaningful and the absolutely nailed the atmosphere. The presentation is top notch. there are so many wonderful details such as the way the candle burns down as the game goes on and as such the room becomes darker.
I was so filled with wonder, excitement, terror, joy and anger while playing this game. The games difficulty seems to ramp up nicely. I am not even half way done with this game yet but I am so looking forward to the bosses and cards that I will unlock next but most of all I am looking forward to unraveling the mystereis behind the dealer and what this game is all about.
Fascinatingly there is no tutorial you are simply thrust into the game and yet I can tell that this is not an oversight, it is deliberate and the dealer makes mention of it several times. If you've ever played a videogame before you will figure it out and the gameply is so intuitive that to my surprise, no tutorial is necessary! He will wager some precious artifacts if you win you earn them if you lose you will have to roll your deck again and he will deal the dungeons from the beginning.
I took a chance on this game because I really like TCG and the way that this suppossedly had an action elemant sounded interesting and unique and I am so glad I did. Now that I know how good this game is I would have gladly spent twice the price I paid. Unless you are some sort of gibbering idiot who only plays madden games you will definitely love this game. 6180 The Moon, as has been mentioned in reviews before my own, was so named as this is the number of seconds it took the developers to make its prototype - around an hour and 45 minutes (thanks for the correction
). But why is this so important? Well, it's my issue with this game; it feels like it never developed far beyond a fun little coding or development project.
Aside from the screen-wrapping mechanic you can see in the trailer, 6180 The Moon features all the typical "minimalistic puzzle-platformer" fare you might expect, albeit at a very rudimentary level. Move from left to right across the screen, get to the objective, and avoid the spikes. Levels are short and relatively uncomplicated, with difficulty in most puzzles coming through manipulation of the gravity mechanic. In essence, jumping pushes you out the top of the screen and in through the bottom; you hit an arc somewhere in the middle, and float right back down again. And that's the game.
I definitely enjoyed some of the puzzles, but felt from very early on that I was playing something made in a Game Jam. There's nothing wrong with that at all, mind you; but I feel the developer wanted this game to be treated as a complete experience. So that is what I am reviewing 6180 The Moon on, and why my review is negative. The strange, wishy-washy story, the sometimes "muddy" feel of control during a jump, and the little glitches scattered all the way through make this game feel more like a great amateur project than a good published game (if that makes any sense).
Now if this
been presented as a hobbyist's project or a Game Jam submission, I reckon I would have been a lot more forgiving with my review. It definitely has a number of real positives too, like the pretty soundtrack which I see is mentioned in almost all of the positive reviews here. However 6180 The Moon isn't a game I would recommend parting with any money for, whether at full price or on sale; there are plenty of other "puzzle-platformer with a unique mechanic" titles to pick up on Steam that feel a lot more polished overall.
