Recettear is a very interesting game that lets you play the role of an item shop owner which are the very common NPCs encountered in many typical JRPGs. You will now step into their shoes and get a feel of what goes on behind the shops while the typical JRPG heroes go about their business of monster slaying and saving the world.
The story is very light-hearted and simple, and basically presents a shop to you in which you are given 36 days to pay off increasing debts each week. The total amount of gold (or pix as the game's currency) required in total is 820,000.
The way you can go about accomplishing this is simple, which is to go scout for items in markets to buy in low prices and selling them high for maximum profits. The mechanic behind this part of the game is very simple and will be very instantly familiar to anyone who have played such business simulation games before. It is not a very hardcore system and will also be easy to learn for newcomers of this genre because of a very good tutorial that was presented.
If you aren't interested in doing trading however, there is another aspect of the game which allows you to recruit adventurers and go with them on dungeon trips to smack monsters around looking for phat lewt. This part of the game lets the player actually control the adventurer and feels very arcadey. Its a simple enough system and is a very welcome break instead of constantly just doing item trading.
If you just don't feel like doing anything, you can wander around town and sometimes there will be little special cutscenes that tell abit more about the story of the world. Every aspect of this game is very well designed, and the whole thing comes together in a very satisfying package.
Character and art designs are very cute anime looking and their dialogues make them very endearing. Although the original game was in japanese, the translation is done very well and doesn't look awkward. Music is very happy and light-sounding. Some of the tunes are also very hummable.
Downsides to the game tho, it can feel very repetitive on Endless Mode. (This mode is unlocked after you complete game, which is basically a Freeplay mode with no debts to repay.) The above mentioned dungeons are also very simple affairs and only consists of very simple interconnected square rooms. Don't expect any high quality dungeon designs here.
Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10

The zone of error is roughly 8/final fantasy tactics, if someone dies you have three rounds to get to them, where they will be evacuated by a medic. If you don't get to them in time, they are dead for good.

Most entertaining is the level of depth the game goes into each individual class, they work VERY hard to make sure everything not just levels up, but has a huge bonus when they become elite.
The only issues I have are the cumbersome menu system (not really an issue), and the lack of an autosave (My own personal bias because I am an entitled modern gamer). The old reminder from the 90's is SAVE OFTEN.
This game is a "MUST BUY" In my book. Grab it ASAP.

The Brave Mouse is a platform game, with nicely-drawn graphics and twelve levels.
You jump from platform to platform (some of which are in motion), grabbing pieces of cheese (three per level), whilst avoiding spears, wasps, and fires.
Whilst I quite liked the graphics, I found the gameplay rather frustrating.
Some of the jumps to moving platforms had to be very carefully timed, or guessed at, added to which you have to avoid various traps - and a slight mistake may mean you have to start the whole process all over again.
I had to do some levels again and again and again, until I just got really annoyed - that probably means that my skill level wasn't good enough, but it also means that my annoyance level was increased until I stopped enjoying the game.
When you die, it would have been good to be able to start from the last spot you were at - but that's not what happens, so I guess that's just the nature of the beast.
Since I bought The Brave Mouse at a special price, the cost wasn't a problem - its usual price on Steam is only $2 anyway.
However, the problem was the lack of enjoyment that I got from this game.
It's a shame that I didn't like the gameplay, because I quite liked the artwork in The Brave Mouse.
For those who like platform games, and are good at them, this may be worth buying, but I don't think I can recommend a game which I found to be so annoying.

This is my first review, and I'll try to keep it short.  tl;dr: Skip to bottom paragraph.
It seems to have its ups and downs, but more ups. People often refer it to Mario Kart on foot, however, this title can be a little misleading. First of all, it is NOT a racing game in the sense that there is a start and finish. It is actually an elimination-style game where your objective is to get your opponents off the screen by getting far enough ahead of them. I really like this system and it works well. Another thing misleading about the title because it makes it sound like how in Mario Kart you have somewhat of a set speed. In SpeedRunners, your speed is defined by how you move and how perfectly you perform certain things, but I'll get to that later.
I've seen this game said many times as "competitive", but I'm not sure how competitive it can really get. First reason being is the items. They are random, completely unbalanced, and some can be pretty annoying. They take the idea of slowing other people down rather than moving faster that everyone else, which I personally dislike. The game already has plenty of ways to get ahead of people without items, which leads to my second point about it being competitive. Like how I mentioned before, SpeedRunners has a few ways of moving fast according to how well you do it. This is very good in a competitive point of view (and in any point of view really). What's also interesting and important to note is this game has clever ways of letting players that are behind catch up. For example, if you are too far ahead, you can't see any obstacles that are coming your way, but if you're skilled enough and know where they are you can still manage to avoid them. It works quite well and can help to make some very close games. Whether you like that, of course, is up to you.
From a non-competitive stance, the game holds up pretty great. Items can be fun, but I still feel they end up being aggravating at times. I really love the characters, even though they don't have much personality considering they don't talk much. I'm not sure what else to say here, sooo... I'll just move to the verdict.
In the end, the game is a blast. It doesn't take much time at all to get the hang of it, its fast, it features some clever design, and very well done maps (I didn't get into the maps, but there's more behind them then what they first appear).
The only things the game needs to work on is the items, repetitivity of games, and bugs (which is expected and can easily be fixed because it is in early access). Plus, one of the DLC's come with PBG! Wearing a Link costume! How could it be bad!

Playing through this solid indie title made me wished I would have backed it when it was on Kickstarter. Expeditions: Conquistador is a pretty good strategy RPG that mixes exploration, resource management and hex-grid combat with a little bit of fiction and non-fiction. The end game was a blast to play through and I'm hoping the developer has had enough success to create new Expeditions in the future.
Pros:
+ Solid combat: good balance of classes, skills, traps and other items.
+ Great variety of random occurances: both good and bad situations can pop up while traveling or camping that keeps the           player on their toes.
+ Interesting locations: The first location is a bit more than a tutorial while the second one is pretty much the main game. Both are rewarding.
+ Choice and Consequences: The game expands on this towards the end. Not all dialogue branches off to a totally different path or outcome but there is enough variance.
+ Great balance of fiction/non-fiction: combat is intense because it only takes 3-4 hits to kill someone and you can't spam healing spells, however there are still curses, pagan Gods and legendary locations.
Cons:
- Stability issues: the first island was fine, once I got to the second location there were some crashes to desktop, some loading the map issues and some other small hiccups.
- Higher Level Skills: once the characters get into the higher ranks, their skills are no longer varied. They're still semi-useful but it felt cheap. Also no higher level perks.

To be honest, I picked up this game during one of its deep sales, and still wasn't sure what to expect. Though after seeing "Square-Enix", I had some clue. (Those guys are the kings of cutscenes, after all.)
That aside, it's hard to classify this game as much of an action game. It's defeinitely more of a casual one than anything else, and not that long of a game, either. I guess one could also think of it as a kind of roaming adventure game with a few side missions, plenty of collectibles, and plenty of 'Press X to Not Die' moments.
The investigations in the game involve searching for clues, some of them obtained from thinking a little bit out of the box. Though personally, I'm surprised that weren't any 'match-3' or 'hidden object' puzzles in here. Maybe I'm a bit jaded in that respect. Really not all that hard to deal with.
As far as action scenes, there aren't that many, and they're generally limited to Quick Time Events with maybe a little bit of strategy involved. Outside of that, there really isn't much that can kill you. Again.
All in all, it was worth the discount price, though. Square-Enix can weave a decent tale, and the storytelling here was pretty decent, and not quite that predictable. Biggest faults, though, were that the game was too short, and the action rather limited in scope.

It's easy to find no-effort platformers made from basic shapes, looking like a video game made by a five-year-old with refrigerator magnets. A simple aesthetic isn't the last word in quality, but the danger here is that the challenges presented might have about as much thought put into them as the presentation. 6180 the moon may give that impression at first glance, but it turned out far more clever and engrossing than I expected.
You play the moon, on a quest to find its eternal buddy the sun. This journey takes you across fifty levels divided into five regions of the solar system, broken up by adorable little cutscenes with other heavenly bodies. The game's gimmick is that the screen wraps around the top, so if you plunge off the bottom you'll drop back in above. That means no bottomless pits to worry about, but the numerous spikes are more than happy to take their place for ruining your day. Your jump sends you a full screen height and change so there's nowhere on the screen that's unreachable, giving you very pleasant freedom of movement.
Level gimmicks include spikes, moving platforms, breakaway blocks, spikes, switches and gates, spikes, and a few other not-spike features. Once you wrap your brain around wrapping around the screen the game goes quite smoothly, and you'll likely complete your sojourn to the sun in 30-40 minutes. This unlocks a new mode where you play through the levels in reverse, with gravity flipped, and this one little change blew my mind. The vast majority of the levels are completely unchanged, but become far move difficult because of their genius dual design. Playing through the first time was a subdued, relaxing experience, but playing through the second was a distinct pleasure.
The whole game will take you just over an hour to complete, and there are no additional modes or corner-case achievements to chase so it'll all be over before you know it. But the clever puzzles are truly a delight, accompanied with an excellent piano soundtrack and the aforementioned cutscenes that just ooze charm. It's a bite-sized puzzle platformer, but you're sure to relish it more than a lot of larger offerings.

This game both excells as an rpg and a strategy game. A very immersive experience, and an excellent game.
The game let's you make the decisions as you play a conquestador from Spain: are you an explorer, a seeker of new and lost civilizations? Do you seek peaceful trade? Or are you here for personal glory, or to conquer lands in the name of the King? How do you treat the people around you?
The tactical combat system is turned based and simple at first, but complex enough to keep one interested. There are five base classes, and you usually take 3-6 into battle. Often your troops are outnumbered and outmatched, and you will need to use strategy, cunning, and well made traps to beat your opponents. Many rpgs have a trap system, but most of them are clumsy and feel more of an after thought. This game does a great job at allowing you to set up the battlefield before battle with the resources you have (unless of course you are caught unaware!), and makes trap placing easy, useful, and sometimes necessary.
On the world map you must manage resources as you explore the unforgiving jungles of the new world: Food and rations, lest you grow hungry; medicine to keep the inevitable wounds you will receive from turning fatal (wounds received in combat will digress unless treated by a doctor with medicine!); and various resources to build traps, tools, and equipment. You will be ambushed in the night; your scout might wake up having been bitten by a poisonous insect, and must be treated immediately; and numerous other random encounters.
You will keep the company of doctors, scouts, hunters, soldiers, and scholars, and your party members will talk to you as you make camp making them feel as though they are a part of your adventure, and not just units to command. The morale system is more than just a combat mechanic, but your choices will affect the way party members perceive you based on their personalities, and may even provoke a mutany.
The skills system does a nice job of separating the combat and non-combat skills, so you don't feel as though you're limiting yourself by taking one over the other; and, every skill feels useful in some way (so there's no useless character builds).
Again, really well designed rpg.

All in all, February seems like it's been a bad month for highly anticipated ports of popular games. Street Fighter V was highly anticipated and released half-finished with a ridiculous price tag, Tales of Symphonia was a collosal wreck of a port, and now Disgaea is having problems, both with the pre-order soundtrack and the game itself. Hopefully, there'll be some speedy improvements from the devs based on customer feedback; like many people, I was super hyped for this launch and would love to have supported further Disgaea and NIS titles coming to Steam, but I can't really do that if the ports are going to be mediocre. Until fixes appear, pass.
Edit: The devs have released fixes, which at least in my own experience, have provided a lot of improvement. While there's still a little while to go (some graphics options aren't super stablised, cave of ordeals 3 crashes), the response from the dev team has been very good and I as a customer feel confident that these issues will be addressed in time. For now, this is far less of a gamble than it used to be, so if you enjoy yourself that crunchy core of Disgaea gameplay, I can recommend it.

As of writing this review, this port is completely broken.
I am a huge Disgaea fan, having played (and grinded excessively) the original on the PS2 and also spinoff titles like Makai Kingdom, La Pucelle Tactics, and Phantom Brave. This port is such a dissapointment I cannot even properly express it in words, but I will try.
First of all, there are no resolution settings and all the new "enhancements", when turned on, create weird visual bugs. Especially SSAO - turning that on resulted in a chess board design that covered my screen. I do not know, maybe this port was orignally based on a FTP chess game.
And WTF, the framerates. Considering the type of game this is, how is it possible for it to fluctuate between 20 and 60 frames constantly? I do not have a top of the line rig, but I believe my setup is decent enough (970gtx, 16GB RAM, i5 processor) to handle a game originally made in 03.
The only good thing about this port is that the new textures do look better. The background looks brighter and less muddy and the text is in higher resolution. However all of this does not matter when the game lags for no reason and the controls feel very sluggish. Speaking about controls, the game uses generic "1", "2", "3", etc buttons in the dialogue boxes regardless of what controller you're using. Yup, no way to set the control type to Xbox or PS.
Honestly, if you (the developers) do not know how to make a proper port, then do not do it, or find someone who can. Just leave these classic titles for the original consoles they were made for.
Maybe they will patch it, maybe not. We shall see.

Quite possibly the very best game experience I've ever had. This is, however, due in large part from playing ME1 first and establishing history in both the game and within myself. The first was great too, but there were certain aspects about it that made it boring and/or frustrating at times. For example, combat was too short. The skills in teh game are designed for more of a prolonged battle to use flanking techniques and weapon strength mixtures... that sort of thing. In other words, battles could be fun, but it was rarely long enough to fully enjoy and the time between battles was quite long in lots of cases. Inventory was a constant burden as well, which also took away lots of enjoyable play time. Others might say it was too boring, but role playing games are simply more designed around a story. And this story of Mass Effect is absolutely wonderful.
That said, they fixed the inventory and leveling problem completely in ME2, as well as the lack of combat. Add an extension the story that got even more eipc and you have what I believe has been my best gaming experience ever.

Although I just started it, I can tell a lot of things have been repackaged from ETS2, although there are also many differences.
When I started up, I immediately noticed the exact same intro screen as ETS2 except for the name.
The main menu looks identical to ETS2, even the character portraits are the same.
The tutorial is literally the exact same, word for word, as in ETS2, signifying that there havent been any major improvements in the gameplay itself.
However, there is a lot to look forward to:
The cities are a lot more realistic and bigger than in ETS2 and have many famous landmarks. I opted to start in San Francisco, and it the area looked a lot like SF. (More than it would in ETS2).
There is a lot more to explore, as there is 50 states with diversified terrain and a lot of free DLC coming out that grants access to these states.
There will probably be less of endless highway driving and more of exploring the cities. (As I mentioned, SF seemed a lot bigger than the cities in ETS2).
Overall, I have been looking forward to this game for years and it has finally come. Despite some of the similarities to Euro Truck Simulator 2, there will be many positive differences and changes that outweigh the cons.

A true piece of art, the best RPG I've played since Dragon Age: Origins.
I didn't play this game much yet, but I've been following its development, as I did for D:OS1. You've got everything you'd want from an RPG: good story, interesting universe and characters, tactical (and even one of the best I've seen!) combat system - varied skills to use and a lot of combos between different characters -
. And fun multiplayer (even if I'd advise to play only with friends you can trust).
So I'm only going to focus on what you may actually not like much:
If you're ok with all this, you're likely to enjoy this game. You'll also need a lot of time, obviously, but the "quest log" is sufficiently well done to not lose you if you can't play a lot, and you don't need a lot of time to learn the game (everything is pretty intuitive, you don't need to spend hours on a wiki to know what does what or why you can't do X).
Would kickstart again.

I remember paging through a Fighting Fantasy book when I was a kid.  Can't remember which one but the mechanics of the game really left a positive impression on me.  I was mostly into video games so never ended up getting into the FF books.
Upon discovering that this game was based on those books I had to buy it to see what it was like.  After playing 100's of RPG's on consoles and PC I must say this game is absolutely worth your time.  It's so different than anything else out there.  I am also really enjoying the combat system.
A couple quibbles that can hopefully be fixed soon:
1) Need XBox One controller support
2) Need the ability to manipulate the text window.  I would love to slide it to the side of the screen so I can enjoy the simple wonderful graphics.  They are almost completely obscured by the text.  It would add so much more to the game to read along while actually seeing the dungeon.  Especially with the fantastic music and sound effects.
If you consider yourself a fan of RPG's I hope you would consider this game.  It's a must-buy 8when it goes on sale.
*Edit - After playing as a few characters and dying quite a bit, I can say that there is significant repetition in the game as you play through the same areas over and over again.  I still give the game a positive review, but can't recommend for its full retail price.  Worth buying on sale.

I've been waiting for the release of this game a long time and it was definitely worth the wait!  An amazing upgrade of the adventure book with beautiful artwork and an interesting "tabletop RPG" style.  The environments have been painstakingly recreated from the book.
Though the dungeon is the same, each adventurer you play has a unique story and ways to move through it.  One adventurer can stealth past sleeping guards.  Another can barter with enemies for information instead of fighting. Your options can change based on who you play.  Each adventurer has a unique combat style which changes up how you fight.
The combat system is unusual.  Everything is on a grid and feels almost like a chess game.  Watching your enemy's move/combat positioning is as important as understanding your own.  And trying out another character means learning a different approach to fighting the same monsters.
You don't want to get too attached to any adventurer since death is common.  But every delve will teach you more about the mountain dungeon.  Where a cool item is, how tough a certain enemy is, ways around difficult areas, etc.  In one spot I found a disguise to fool the orcs so I could move around more freely.  But I was forced to kill a prisoner since he thought I was the enemy!  On a second run I didn't put on the disguise and got valuable intel.  Lots of choices, not all good or bad.
I've played some of the previous digital adventure books like Sorcery and the straight book adaptions.  And none of them had the immersion of this one.  I'm really hoping this is a success so they will convert more adventures using this engine.  The amount of art and design necessary to do this game must have been immense but if more come out I'll definitely pick them up.

Cons:

First Impressions:
Combining an ARPG with the deck-building genre is both gutsy and interesting.  I had a hard time wrapping my head around what such a game would be like until I actually sat down with it and gave it a spin. The encounter deck, combined with the narrator's own stock, will make up the obstacles you'll have to overcome.  You'll gain equipment, food, and other goodies by successfully completing these encounters, allowing you to improve your character.  In between games however, your character starts over with just your basic equipment (though the cards you unlock can be seeded into your decks so that you can discover them next game).  The combat portions put you into an arena where you'll be actively trying to be the last one standing.  The flow of combat and the combat mechanics reminded me a bit of "Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor", albeit an extremely simplistic version. As a fan of deck-builders, "Hand of Fate" is an easy recommend.

The game initially had some bugs with controller support, but once I got past those issues and started playing with a friend I really enjoyed it! I love the concept and if those minor control issues get sorted out, I'd highly reccommend this game!

This game is difficult to catagorize. When you start a game, it is like a DND setting. You are given a pathway of cards. Step on a card and observe it's effects. Some give you options to choose an action. Some don't. Some cards test your luck and give you rewards or punishments in turn. Sometimes, the cards force you to fight a band of monsters.
Combat is where things get interesting. It is a system similar to that of Batman: Archam Asylum, but takes more skil to master. I say this because there is a bit of a difficulty spike towards the end, fair warning. Different equipment give you different benefits and your remaining health carries over between the encounter, and the pathway board, though it is all reset at the start of every run.
In terms of playing, there is plenty of planing involved in going on the adventure. There is also a lot of skill involved in the combat system, but there is plenty of luck in the cards to keep things interesting with every time you play. The dungeons are procedurally generated, so every run is different, allowing for changes of strategy.
There is a lot to like in this game. I do recomend it.

I played this game from headstart until Auroria released, so about 3 months. During that time, I have witnessed the fall of what could have been the greated MMO that ever existed. It had exactly what MMO gamers have been asking for, it was a great sandbox. It felt a bit like a fantasy version of EVE. Needless to say, that came to an end.
It began when Trion pulled a bait and switch a few days before launch with their start pack items. It happened again a month later when Trion singlehandedly destroyed the market with the changing of the thunderstruck logs. It has happened time and time again with horrible servers during release periods like Auroria causing people to lose not only plots of land, which are essential to gameplay, but also entire castles which affect many houses in a wide plot of land.
As if the housing situation wasnt dire enough, balance is yet another aspect of the game that affirms the reasons you should avoid it. This game caters to 1 type of archetype: the archer. It has been overpowered for months and showing no signs of stopping. If you want to win at PVP, you need to be some form of an archer. Melee is underpowered and easily kited, Mages are a very strong second to archers, and by mage I mean 1 class: Daggerspell. Healers are absolutely horrible and its not possible to heal effectively and do any meaningful damage with how spell power work, not to mention nearly all the healing spells themselves are worthless. Complaints and balance issues aside, the class system is very well done and if balance wasnt such a glaring issue, the possibilites for class combination would be unrivaled....but we live in a world where balance IS an issue, so the effective class combinations go from 120 total combinations down to about 10. Yea, great job.
Trion has kept making mistakes over and over. It was a running gag between me and my friends where we just started to expect whatever could go wrong, it will, because of Trion. Granted, its hard to say what is exactly their fault and how much of the games failures is theirs or the actual Korean developer, XL Games, but from a customers standpoint, Trion is in a great place to take all the blame. However, that unrelated to the actual gameplay.
I cannot recommend this game to anyone. It has such glaring pitfalls that exemplify exactly the faults of F2P games today on the market. In fact, in my 20 years of gaming this is the first game I have ever had to do a chargeback with my bank for the misleading advertisements and bait and switch tactics employed by Trion. I downloaded this entire game from steam and booted it up for 5 minutes to write this review in hopes that it will save someone else from this MMO. Do yourself a favor, save yourself months of your time, and stay away from this game.
TL:DR: Game is pay2win nonsense, stay far away.

Quick Summary: Last Light Redux has fewer graphical improvements from the original Metro Last Light when compared to its counterpart Metro 2033 Redux. This is because 2033 Redux was upgraded to the Last Light game engine whereas Last Light Redux just gets a few smaller visual improvements. However, with the Redux version, you now get all the Metro Last Light DLCs and the Steam achievements were reworked, including removing some of the pain in the♥♥♥♥♥achievements, like “shadow ranger.”
Once again, you play Artyom, a survivor living in the underground Metro tunnels of Moscow 20 years after a nuclear apocalypse. The world above is blanketed with radiation and unbreathable air, so thousands of people scrape out a living in the vast underground tunnels and Metro stations, where the main threats are mutants and other humans. If you played Metro 2033, you’ll remember that Artyom “saved” the metro with a missile strike from the D6 military base he discovered (the game’s “bad ending”). Well it seems that D6 is so awesome that everyone wants the goodies inside, including your old friends the Red Line (communists) and Reich (Nazis). War is coming and the mutants are going to have plenty of meat to scavenge.
The game is played in First Person Shooter perspective, with regenerating health. So if you take enough damage that your screen is flashing red, hide for a minute and you’ll be good as new. Stealth plays a big role, and honestly the game is easier if you sneak around knifing people in the back rather than run and gun. This is because unaware enemies can be killed practically instantly while some armored enemies take a lot of firepower to bring down once they’re aware of your presence. Stick to the shadows, and you can sneak past about half the human enemies quite easily. This isn’t a RPG, so don’t worry about missing out on experience from killing enemies. You’ll also have more than enough money from scavenging off of corpses if you’re playing on normal difficulty.
Returning from Metro 2033 is the “morality” system, where you get points by doing good deeds (giving money to beggars or listening to conversations) and if you get enough points you’ll see the game’s “good ending.” If you’ve been playing a good guy, you can’t save right before the end and see both endings by loading, you actually have to play through again making “evil” choices to build up enough negative points for the bad ending.
You should get Metro Last Light Redux if:
+You liked Metro 2033 or the original Metro Last Light and want to try Last Light’s DLCs, and (mildly) upgraded graphics. The DLC consists of a new gun (now found during regular gameplay) and a bunch of standalone levels that take a few hours to beat, where you play various characters that Artyom met in the main story.
+You want a game with survival horror elements, including bloodthirsty mutants, giant spiders, choking gas, punching Nazis in the face.
+You want a straightforward linear story game, where you can either run through kicking♥♥♥♥♥like Jason Bourne or sneak through, throwing knives in people’s backs and sniping with silenced weapons.
You should NOT get Metro Last Light Redux if:
-You are expecting a significant difference from the original Metro Last Light.
-You are scared of mutated monsters, spider webs, demonic hallucinations, massive gunfights, etc.
-You are looking for an open world game where you wander the wasteland at your own pace, building up a stash of guns/equipment to stomp on everyone. You might want to try the Fallout or STALKER games instead.

A turn-based rps set during the age of discovery in the Caribbean and Mexico? Count me in. It's really a pity that instead of beating the nazis for the zillionth time, we aren't often given the opportunity to play games set in other very interesting eras, such as this one. I generally mistrust all these crowd-funded projects that have been trending lately. But the setting and style convinced me to give this game a shot when it was on sale. 30 or so hours of playing later, I'm happy I did.
Despite obvious similarities to HoMM on the campaign map, the setting and its heavier RP elements help it make its mark. The story is loosely based on the actual events of the Spanish conquest of Mexico and is quite compelling. The game allows you to choose the path you want to follow and how you will interact with your troops and NPCs. You can be a friend of the common soldier, or a distant general. You can be a ruthless conqueror, or a friend to the natives. You can be an ally to the Aztecs or their scourge. And so on.
Moving on to the tactical part now, the game offers a combat system which is both tactical and hard. The game has a finite and pre-determined number of battles. Which on one hand means that quite some attention was paid to them individually. On the other hand, there is only so many different ways you can play the same battle before you get bored of it. It would have been interesting to see what the combat system could do, if the game included completely random battles as well.
Focusing some more on the negatives, it generally feels that the game lacks polish. There are several bugs and it becomes quickly obvious that it sorely needed more funding and work. There is also the question of content touched upon when talking about battles earlier. To put it simply: I wanted more. I'm not implying that the game is short, at least by modern standards it isn't. But by the time I finished the game I haven't had my fill yet. I felt that the game could give much more than it did.
Still I will recommend this game. It hasn't really made me a believer as far as crowd-funded projects go. But at least it showed me that even in such projects, there are good ideas that can actually make decent games. I certainly hope the team will have better luck financing their next project.
Verdict: Buy on sale.

This is a cool game with one interesting mechanic and a few other "meh" mechanics that fails to stay interesting throughout the entire experience. The fact that the top of the screen wraps around with the bottom is quite cool. The goal is to get to the Sun and ask him some questions. Then after you do that, to go back to your place by Earth.
The Moon level set does a good job of making you understand the main mechanic of jumping through the screen.
The Earth level set gives you another interesting mechanic: a box which launches you in the opposite direction from where you hit it (up or down). It also plays a note that goes along with the background music which is a really nice touch.
The Venus level set has the best music in my opinion. It also introduces a sort of power-up which allows you to pause your upwards jump or downwards fall, stopping you in the air completely before gravity kicks in and pulls you downwards again. This allows you to avoid hitting spikes on the ceiling or to make longer jumps.
Unfortunately another mechanic is introduced which is boring and rather frusterating. It's a timed wall that appears for two seconds and vanishes for two seconds. There's nothing really cool or fun about it, but it does add to the difficulty and challenge of the game.
After the Venus levels, the game becomes a drag. It doesn't take too long to complete. While rushing, it took me about 1 hour 20 minutes. There are also achievements. These were fun to do. They add to the game if you want some extra, non-required challenge.
Overall, it was a fun game for a while. AND IT'S ONLY $4. It's definitely worth buying the soundtrack with it. I like my Venus music.

The game accurately advertises what you are getting and is a true
in the only way it can reasonably be done.
The Luck Based part comes from the fact that when you shoot each round/projectile/missile/etc. that fires will land somewhere within the firing circle, effectively large crosshairs. Where you hit the opponent matters, a headshot does more damage than a body shot... but the head is a smaller target, so have fun gambling.
In other words the game has action points, and a bar that depletes as you move, shoot, well do actions. You move as if you were playing a 3rd person shooter in which you can't freely jump (but can jump over barriers/cover/walls when prompted).
The major drawback to this point system is there is no reverse/rewind, so if you think you can go distance x and end up being a step short, your simply out of luck. A rewind feature would make this game near perfect if not perfect in regards to gameplay, thus at times you may get irked until you are able to gauge exactly how much you can do before doing it. I am playing this game on its’ highest difficulty and it is not punishing early on for instances like this.
if I had to liken it to anything, I would to Total Wars campaign map unit movement system but instead from a 3rd person "shooter" perspective, except it gives no indicators as to how far you can go... if you can be shot at as you move, you can stop moving and shoot, then continue to move (to cover). This game is not select action 1, then select action 2... this game lets you do any actions in any order, with the only limit being upon the number of times you can shoot a match and you being able to move until the action bar is depleted.
I have not fully played the game but it is on my list of games to (finish) playing), I own too many... but...

Valkyria Chronicles is a somewhat typical S/TRPG (strategy/tactical RPG) that's been wrapped in a beautiful artistic vision and unique gameplay persepctive.  Most of the common elements of tactical RPGs are here.  Take control of the units you've selected from your squad, place them within your starting area and using Command Points move them during your turn within their movement radius and take one action.  Once all the command points have been spent the turn is passed to the AI who does all their moves and then again back to you tiill either the objective is completed or failure on your part.
There are 5 of classes in the game, Scout, Shocktrooper, Lancer, Engineer and Sniper.  Also there is a tank(s) that you command as well as the different classes.  Before each map you can choose what number soldiers from each class you take into the battlefield, some maps may require to load up on certain classes while forgoing a class entirely.  Most of the classes are also able to choose between a couple of different weapons/load outs so you can either favour accuracy, damage or status effects.  In addition to different classes and load outs there are also various orders to be given in battle (each order costs command points).
The best parts of the game to me were the Characters, level design and perspective.  The third person perspective made for a unique experience in a tactical RPG rather than a typical grid.  The Characters were great.  The design to them as well as their lore all worked to drawyou in to the RPG experience.  And lastly the level design.  There was a good variety of levels, from cities, to forests and deserts.  The levels also had different design elements and objective focuses to make each level interesting as well as replayable.
Some of the things that I was Neutral on was the Story and Leveling/progression system.  After each victory you would be awarded a certain number of EXP points that could be spent on the training grounds to level up characters.  Leveling up the characters didn't really result in traidtional RPG gains but would be used to unlock various class traits that would affect how that a character of that class would react to certain battlefield conditions.  The leveling up seemed to have a minimal effect on things like HP (your starting HP won't be much different from end game HP).  I did like that there was a variety of skirmish missions that could be done to grind for more experience or gold.
Some of the things I didn't like about the game were the Story, the interface and randomness.  The story was okay, but was very typical of a JRPG.  There was only one moment for me in the entire story that wasn't just generic JRPG storyline.  Some of the big suprises were not very surprising and a lot of characters took very generic character paths, which is sad cause the I like the characters themselves, they had charm.  As for the interface, there are a few things missing from the game that feel like it should be there.  You can only save outside of missions, there is no ability to save mid mission and with some missions that are on the longer side, it can be a bit of a pain.  As well you are shown how many shots it will take to kill an enemy (body vs head) but you are not given any percentages on if those shots will actually hit the target, so you are told that it will take 4 shots to kill an enemy but you are not told that you might only have a 50% chance of hitting the target.  The AI could also be kind of infuriating because there is no option to skip the opponents turn animations (as far as I figured out anyways) and on some of the maps there is a lot of enemy actions to go through.  Some of the Keyboard and Mouse controls can also be kind of wonky.  Driving the tank(s) with Keyboard and mouse can be very very frustrating.  One last thing I didn't really enjoy was that for the majority of the game you could load up on one character class with 2-3 other classes as support to power through the game.
Overall I felt that the game is very solid and definately worth the time to go through.  The game can be found on sale pretty often these days for 5-10$ so it's pretty solid value as well.

If you can look past the atrocities (such as in-game pay-to-win shop items and forcefully showing the shop button in the UI, and letting hackers, cheaters and exploiters go wild just a month after it released) that publisher Trion has put this game, made by developer XLGames under, then you will see a truly vast, beautiful open world with no loading screens except for when you enter or exit dungeons or teleport.
If you see a mountain in the distance, you bet you can peak it! If you see an island, you bet you can land there!
The game has some of the best graphics, not just technologically but also artistically of any MMO game to date.
The combat is the classic tab targeting that we all know and love, and it works very well. The game also has a deep story if you want to get indulged in that, i've seen better ones but it's not a bad one.
The jewel of this game is it's class building system, you can combine 3 out of a total of 10 class trees, each combination with it's own name and it's own strengths and weaknesses making for an ever dynamic balance that the player themself decide.
Finally, the sandbox elements of this game, while perhaps not as fully fledged as one might imagine it could be, they are still very solid. You can own property and as much of it as you want, as long as you can afford all the rents. You can own ships and farm carts and even racing cars. And the beauty of it all is that it is all put in the same one live open world where everyone else on your server is playing, there are no instanced housing zones or what not as in some other games. The only downside, courtesy of Trion, is that you must be a subscriber to own land property.
I definitely recommend this to anyone with refined tastes and high standards in their MMORPGs.

Metro Last Light Redux is a re-release visibly identical with Metro Last Light except it includes all DLC.  If you own the original release, it's probably not worth buying this release.
Metro Last Light is an improvement on its predecessor Metro 2033 in almost every way.  It still isn't perfect,  but its definitely a must-have for any post-apocalyptic storyline lover.
What to expect if you've played Metro 2033 Redux:  Same graphics, same mediocre AI, similar linear experience that takes  slightly longer(10-12 hrs) to complete. It has better sound quality with excellent sound direction.  It has better level design(more open ended), better monster/mutant design, and a better, more engaging storyline.  It improves on its use of scripted events and lighting to create an  excellent atmosphere (yes, even better than the already excellent original).
SETTING (no spoilers): Moscow is completely destroyed in a nuclear armageddon. Out of its millions of residents, only several thousand remain. The old metro tunnels provide them shelter from the harsh nuclear winter, radiation, and mutants of the surface world. The telephatic danger posed by alien-like mutants called the Dark Ones in Metro 2033 is seemingly destroyed by a nuclear attack launched by the hero of the 1st game, Artyom.  A year passes, and Metro Last Light begins.
PROS:
-Graphics are excellent, great even by 2016 standards. Better than many released this year, actually.
-Great use of lighting, sound, and scripted events create one of the most atmospheric postapocalyptic FPS experiences, if not the most
-Manages to carve out a unique place for itself in an otherwise overused nuclear dystopia setting
-Weapon and human armor/costume design is top notch
CONS:
-While the textures are ok by 2016 standards, the animations are lagging behind. Weak visual feedback from weapons, and from enemies hit by your weapons
-AI is bad(though not broken). Enemies get stuck on corners, and are easily exploited with melee hits.  I get the feeling the game is meant to be played stealth-like.
CONCLUSION: As long as you curtail your expectations, this game is going to be great. I'd advise against coming to this game after playing something like Fallout 4 and expecting the same because they are both post apocalyptic FPS experiences. This game is much shorter, and much more focused in scope.
It's largely linear, its scavaging is much more limited and quick, its stealth elements are much more subtle, its combat is not as good/diverse, and its a much shorter game. It has very limited RPG mechanics (some weapon customization and buying and selling) That said, it does really well with what it has. Creepy tunnels, amazing swampy Moscow, awesome use of lighting and quality textures create a really atmospheric experience.  It uses many scripted events that serve to only improve on the experience.  It might be a shorter experience, but it does offer a unique experience which you can't get elsewhere. Provided you don't mind spiders, telepathic alien-like beings, or Nazis and Commies in your post-apocalyptic game, this  one is a must-have.

This game is a sleeper.. The first time you play it you will be convinced you don't like it. The interface is a little daunting. I was pretty sure I was not going to continue playing.. but for some reason I did. Then you take your party out of the city and your play sessions get a little longer each time. Next thing you know you are thinking about it when you are not even in front of the computer.
It is by no means easy. You really have to 'learn' the game. You can't waste a single resource or let your party sit idle at camp. Don't let fresh meat go to waste, preserve it! Turn those herbs into medicine, you will need it! Just figuring out how all that works was like a victory in itself (there are tutorials but they didn't work too well on me lol)
The encounters are fun, not always battles, but moral decisions too, and you realize you can't please everyone in your party with every decision you make.
The battles can be frustrating. I don't know if I have ventured too far too fast, but you come up against some tough guys. It seems like losing some fights is all part of the game. If you lose a battle, the game isn't over. You tend to your wounded, salvage what supplies you can and move on. It is demoralizing to lose but there is always next time, and when you pull off a flawless victory it makes it all the sweeter.
This game is like the great great grandchild of Seven Cities of Gold. The same sense of exploration and mystery is there. You never know how a village will react to you, or where your next meal is coming from. Sometimes diplomacy works, and sometimes it wastes time and loses you the initiative in an inevitable battle where every move counts. I can't tell you how many times a battle has turned because I made one bad move (damn that 'attack of opportunity')
I have a feeling I will be playing this one for a while yet, and I look forward to it more and more after each session. Recommended, but beware it might take a bit of time for it to really hook you.

It's a brilliant game, one of the most enjoyable I have played in a long time.
As a conquistador, the story involves exploration (of the new world). The mechanic for this is similar to early Final Fantasy games, in particular FFVII. In the exploration facet, you can collect herbs, treasure and hunt boar as well as other resources with which you can create tools to help in battle. These resources can also be used in a barter system at settlements. New locations can be found in which you can meet new settlements and peoples.
Meeting people is fun as the game provides a multiple choice story driven dynamic. Your choices, how you interact with the natives, determines your fate and how the story evolves. I was really happy with the choice as it involves you much more in the story and really allows you to play how you like. Diplomacy really is an element in the game in terms of which factions you want to eventually align yourself with (if you want to at all).
As well as multiple choice in dealing with other tribes etc. you must also manage your own crew! You choose your troops at the outset and this is also well done. Each person is given a backstory, general stats and three determining personality attributes i.e. Courageous, Open-Minded, Greedy. The characters all have morale which is affected by your choices in the game - greedy followers would gain morale from stealing from someone for instance while others may lose morale from that.   Therefore your relations with the natives will also have an effect, be it positive or negative, on your troops.
As mentioned, you harvest herbs, find treasure and hunt boar in the exploration mode but your troops will need to be carefully selected to manage your resources.  Doctors and certain other characters can create medicine from herbs while your hunters can preserve meat. You can also 'tinker' to improve elements such as rate of travel or items whcih will help in battle. Characters can be levelled as you like however. So, there is a lot of mini management involved in the game outside of exploration or battle - one must be strategic. If you make bad strategic decisions the game can be very unforgiving, even on a normal difficulty setting.
Finally, battle! Having explained other elements at some length, I will be brief here - it is essentially turn based strategy. If you have played and enjoyed The Banner Saga or X-Com: Enemy Unknown, you will enjoy this. Fundamentally the mechanic is the same though it is very well done.
I loved this game - 9/10.
Very much hope the developers have a follow up to this in the near future. The system would allow for any theme or universe to be applied - Medieval Europe, Zombie Apocalypse(!), Classical Era (Romans) etc. though I understand the most likely follow up will involve Vikings. It seems the developers want to keep with a 'Expedition' (i.e. coloniser) theme so Zombies are probably out!
Warning this game takes alot of time to get used to. After that, load of fun!

I'm really glad I picked up this game and gave it a try. This game is so refreshingly different from the other turned based strategy games around, and is great fun. I rarely write reviews, but feel like I must get the word out for this game.
In the game you lead a spanish expedition to the new world. You get to pick your initial party members from a pool of recruits, each of them has a unique bio, personality/traits, and skills. Your in-game decisions would affect party members differently depending on their personality. For example, trying to avoid a fight would please the peaceful members, but aggravate the aggressive one (morale dropping), killing natives would please the racist ones but anger the open-minded ones, etc. So far I found the "proud" ones are the best to keep because their morale always goes up after winning a battle, so it's easy to keep them happy as there are always battles.
The gameplay really consists of three parts, exploring, camping, and battles.
Exploring is similar to HOMM where you travel a set number of steps each day, picking up random resources, visiting towns and villages, and interacting with characters.
The camping system is quite original and the real meat of this game, where each night you assign different duties to party members. Hunters hunt, soldiers guard, scouts patrol (scanvenging resources), doctors make medicines or treat injuries if needed. There are also scholars who can research technologies or build traps that are used in battles.
There are not that many battles in the game (maybe 40 or so), but all battles are unique and very well designed. The battles could be harsh at the beginning when you havent leveled up or geared up. But once you get familiar with some of the battle mechanics like flanking and class abilities, it's not that hard. In the later Mexico campaign you would have access to most of the native classes as well as spanish ones. Mismatching the classes can bring more flavor to the battles. And just before you get tired of the battles, the game is over! Yes, the game is short by today's standard, but that's what I like about it. I can rarely finish a game nowadays.
Last but not least, this game's writing is top-notch and really helps immersion. Reading the event descriptions and dialogues is like reading a novel.
9/10, go get it!

I played this game a long time ago, and I remember having a lot of fun.
So nostalgically recalling all the good times I had, I recently purchased the original Fable to play, hoping to recreate the experience.
Sadly, I must report that I was severely disappointed. The game is just so outdated, I can't play for five minutes straight without rolling my eyes.
The biggest issue I had was with the combat system. I built a warrior/rogue character because I wanted to enjoy some skill-based combat. However, I found that I was locked onto an enemy, it was difficult to switch between multiple targets with accuracy. This made it hard to block incoming attacks from the flanks or focus on different enemies. So I stopped locking onto enemies, but this made it extremely difficult to use the Assassin Rush skill as it required me to lock on to a target (which is almost random), use the skill, and then stop locking on. Destroys my groove.
Also, the stealth mission at the beginning of the game is terrible.
Needless to say, this was an amazing game for its time. However, I think replaying this game has made me realize and appreciate how much game design has advanced in the years since its release.
So if you remember this being a great game, I suggest that you just hold on to those memories and spend your money on something else. I recommend something more recent.

Warframe is grindy. GRINDY! Grind-Tastic. And other things that go with grind.
The big question, however... "Is the grind FUN?", and the answer is an absolutely unqualified YES! Warframe is probably the fastest paced game I've ever played and, at least in my opinion, makes Tribes look slow! It's hectic, frantic and other similar adjectives.
On the topic of grind, though... there are massive chunks of grind that you can simply skip, if you feel like it. Warframe has dozens of armours and probably hundreds of weapons, and you can (if you choose) level all of them multiple times for additional benefits. That said, like any game with hundreds of weapons, there are definitely some that just don't measure up. You can freely skip those if you like. You can skip whole weapon classes if you like (I'm personally not a fan of the "Heavy" melee weapons... too slow for a game this fast, I feel!). It's perfectly possible to play Warframe with a single armour and a handful of weapons that you really like, so at least some of the grind is purely voluntary!
It's well built, well designed and (if you have the hardware) beautiful to look at. The parkour is fantasic, and warframes, their abilities and weapons have some major variety across the pool.
Warframe is free to play. If you're super short of money, you can play the game completely for free. You can even earn the paid-currency simply by playing the game and selling duplicate phat-lewts to more cash-flush players who can't be bothered to farm it themselves.
And as if that wasn't enough... the devs are great.The development of the game is very active and (as of writing) the devs have just released the biggest expansion in the game's history (all for free, of course). The pace at which they have been fixing the inevitable bugs in a project that large is HUGELY impressive, and they seem to be genuinely involved with the community. Personally, I believe it's worth dropping cash on, even though there isn't (yet) anything I particularly want to buy!

A rich, evocative and well-developed world, Warframe is sadly beset by clunky, unintuitive controls and a frustrating "die until you get it right" learning model for even the smallest of challenges. Out of 96 minutes played, nearly 30 were spent on simply trying to emulate the camera angles and control setup of other games, a process made more difficult by a relative lack of guidance (at the start of the game, you're thrown right into a desperate situation, and the tutorial mechanics convey that).
Players looking for immersion, or simply to relax with the feeling of playing an action hero at the end of a busy day, will be left feeling intensely frustrated long before the tutorial is over. Experienced action/MMO players with better reflexes might have a better t/ime of things; Warframe also presents another strong positive, in that it runs very well on older machines.

The story is pretty cheesy, filled with boring one dimensional characters, predictable plot twists, and needless sacrifices.
That being said, the art style of the game is very cool. It looks like everything is drawn on paper like a comic book. Your tank displays the word RUMBLE behind it as it moves. It's something I've not seen before playing this game.
The combat is what makes the game very good. There are lots of tactics to think about instead of just running in guns blazing. The mix of FPS and RTS is very refreshing. You have to keep things in mind like cover, assistance fire, and retaliation. The vehicular combat is also pretty fun with a wide variety of tactical benefits provided like smoke shells. Each mission has some kind of quirk to make it unique. This can be a bit of a "trial and error" challenge. Often the first time through a battle you'll learn that your initial placement of troops was terrible and lose and the second playthrough will be a breeze.
The RPG elements of the game are quite dull. You spend XP to level up each class of character instead of characters earning their own XP. Upgrades to weapons and tanks just come automatically as the game progresses (actually you buy them but you have plenty of money so you can get everything). There's no way to speed up the development of the weapons, you just have to progress through the story. Honestly, they could have just removed the XP/Money system altogether and the game wouldn't have felt like it was missing anything.
My only other gripe is the speed of the game. Unnecessary animations in battle can eat up a lot of time (incoming mortar... on the other side of the map where nobody is... can we just skip seeing that?) The cutscenes are well voice acted but also tend to keep the pace of the game slow.
All in all, the cool art and combat style make this game worth playing. If you're looking for a good story or an in depth RPG system, don't bother.

For the most part I would say that I have enjoyed my time with The Warlock of Firetop Mountain.
The majority of The Warlock of Firetop Mountain involves reading text and making a choice on how you would like to proceed. I really enjoyed this part of the game and it reminds me a lot of the Sorcery series of games. If you like tabletop RPG games that focus heavily on the story I think you will really enjoy this part of the game.

I also think the combat is well done. The combat is pretty simple which mostly involves moving around the grid based board avoiding and attacking enemies. The system works well and it is satisfying when you learn the enemy attack patterns so you can avoid taking damage. Some of the enemies are pretty stupid though and don't provide much of a challenge.
There is actually only one thing that I didn't really like about the game. Warlock of Firetop Mountain is a rogue-like game in that if you die you lose all of your progress and have to start from the beginning. I have never been a big fan of rogue-like games so this probably bothers me more than it will people that like rogue-like games. The problem is that the game appears to only have slight randomization and most of the elements you encounter are exactly the same each time you encounter them. This means that each time you die you will have to repeat a lot of content to make it back to the point where you died last. I just wish the game could have avoided some of the repetition. If that doesn't really bother you this won't be much of an issue for you.
If you like these type of story driven tabletop role playing style games, I think you will really enjoy The Warlock of Firetop Mountain.

PLEASE READ THIS BEFORE BUYING: The AI will hit a specific percentage of shots depending on difficulty, about 65% on Easy. This is determined BEFORE it fires. If it decides it will hit a shot, it will keep simulating shots until it finds a shot that will hit. This means most AI shots will look like crazy ludicrous trick shots, but do not be alarmed, as it should still be hitting a 'fair' amount of shots.
PROS:
Saving for singleplayer
Lots of replayability with friends!
Amazingly fun and satisfying to smack enemies with shots.
CONS:
No saving for multiplayer
Shots that hit a planet but did not hit any buildings are not visible
Will take several hours to learn
Enhanced edition was given to everyone who bought the first game for free, and it really shows the devs care about this game. Balance was greatly improved from the original, as well as a ton of helper features. Do be aware that the shot prediction feature does not take into account planetary movement, which is good as it makes hitting certain shots still fun and difficult. Also, the AI can feel a bit unfair with the crazy shots it hits, but the hit chances ARE fair and comparable to that of an experienced player.
Mid to late game gets crazy with the amount of shots arcing around on the screen. Defenses are powerful but can be overcome with AOE upgrades or with weapons that the defenses don't counter. There are also superweapons in the lategame which are massively powerful and cannot be blocked normally. There seems to be many different viable openers and strategies throughout the game, making two identical games next to impossible.
Overall, I will definitely recommend this game if you're a fan of artillery games like Scorched Earth and/or turn-based strategy games.

The remainder of the game is a blend of adventure, resource management and RPG which is also reminiscent of games like HOMM or Kings Bounty, but with the resource management component focused on you and your party of Conquistadors (keeping them busy, feeding them, and tending their wounds) instead of managing an empire of several cities.
The overarching plot provides an insight into Spain's pivotal and brutal role in the fall of the Aztec empire and the colonization of Central America, and was a learning experience for me, who wasn't familiar with the history of the region.

Amazing indie title, it's really mind-boddling how much these develepors have accomplished with just some Kickstarter money. The OST is both imaginative and entertaining to listen to, the art style is bright, colorful, and immersive, and the creative and experimental turn-based RPG elements are a blast to play once you get used to it. The writing is also very impressive, making you feel as if you are in the shoes of a real-life conquistador who has to face difficult challenges every day.
On a more negative note, the game, like most turn-based RPGs, can get extremely easy after a while, especially after you've been slaughtering hordes of Aztecs for hours on end. The interaction you have with your underlings, though well-written, is sparse, and doesn't give them enough personality so that you can care about them 100% of the time.
All in all, I think every stragety-loving person will find an amazing experience with this game. It's a damn shame that a well-made indie title like this will never get the exposure of the half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥AAA games that plague the market. I am anxious to see what these devs will do in the future.

6180 the moon is a charming little platformer with some interesting physics. As the moon, you must jump across platforms on your journey to find the Sun. There are no physical boundaries between the top and bottom of the screen, so if you fall down a pit, you'll just appear above it at the top of the screen, likewise if you jump past the top of the screen. This allows for unique level design, since platforms can become ceilings or hazards and the forced jump height can turn simple jumps into precise platorming tasks. 6180 the moon derives most of its level design from these unique physics, but also introduces a couple other elements later on, such as breakable blocks that will shoot you quickly up or down, depending on which side you hit it from, again making you consider your jump arcs. While the game is not overly difficult, it does provide a decent challenge and forces you to rethink basic platforming concepts. Along the way, you'll meet a few other planets who you greet with a short dialogue scene. These charming moments comprise most of the fairly sparse story. The art style is pretty minimal, but feels appropriate and the soundtrack is quite beautiful. The journey is short, but it's a pretty serene ride to the end.

Is the core game fun?
- Yes
Should you buy the game?
- No.
Problems?
1. Population imbalance.
2. New player difficulty on matured server is high.
3. Hackers killed the game. Game must be recoded to address the hacker infestation. Not a patch, a full rebuild of the game.
Concept and gameplay is really fun if you were in the early start. Even then the servers was really screwed up then with waiting time in the HOURS. That was the people that payed for the game. All the lands were already gone by the first 6 hours of the game. I had a group of friends that played this game and we were ready for the early start. We managed to throw down our farms and take up around 3072 unit of land during the first day. For the week of early access we just powered level ourselfs. Truthfully you can hit your first three level cap in one week.  Money grinding was excruciating but once we poured all our gold to obtain a single 2 slotted tractor, everyone in the group got one within 3 days.
PVP was increadibly fun and the dungeon raids were alright. We had our own ships and we went on a lot of pirating. Both allies and enemy ships were targets. We been to the enemy continent and enraged the enemy guilds to hunt us down. We had enough gold to buy each person subscription so we didn't need to pay for subscription when it expired. However we stopped playing after several weeks.
Why did we stop playing even though we can fair against pay to win players?
1. Population imbalance. PVP war? I was on the top guild on our continent and we had to fight against the biggest zerg guild in the whole game. For every 1 person on our continent, there was 5 on the other. So during the war, either we get the best guilds on our side to fight or we always lose the war.
2. Joined late, well you are screwed. Waiting for an expired land? Good luck competing against 20 people trying to grab the smallest piece of land.  Our friends that joined late have a hard time getting land. Buying land? Good luck getting one to sell at a reasonable price.
3. Hackers. The game was coded on the user end. My god, any company that is hosting the game can't do anything about it. They tanked the NPC trade market and caused inflations on the user market. They can teleport inside a terrain so you can't see their names. They just make their tradepack then teleport to the trade NPC. Then they use those gold to buy all the cheap materials and sell it for an increadibly high price. Can't buy it? Well read the spam message and buy gold with real money. PVP against hackers? You will never kill them unless they are stupid and forgot to use their hack.

Here's the best compliment I can give this game - I bought Hand of Fate and Shadows of Mordor at the same time, and Hand of Fate is the one that pulled me in the hardest and I'm playing more often, despite the polish of the other AAA title.
This game does something I've always wanted to see in a game - watching your encounters be created through chance or fate around you, while you actually play through it. Have been wanting this since way back in the days of Vampire the Masquerade - and it never really came.  Hand of Fate manages this really nicely, as the encounter you are about to face is created by the very cards you draw.  The smooth Arkham-style fighting rounds this out to be a solid, very layered game.
The graphics are unique and nice, a cool blend of fancy hand-drawn card/boardgame and more Diablo-esque arcade environments.  You feel like you're across from your nemesis/Game Master and that it's all playing out based on your interactions with him.  The voice acting of this GM-type character is critical to the game since you hear his voice so much, so thankfully they've got A-list voice work here.
Very replayable as you collect cards and expand the possibilities of each game.  Roguelike in that once you die, you die and your current adventure is over, but the cards you've earned along the way are still added to future adventures making for even more diversity.
This game is in early access right now and it still plays like a complete game.  It's awesome and in only 4ish hours of play I can already tell I'm addicted to it somewhat.  If the developer/s keep polishing and expanding this, I think it could potentially explode on the scene and start a beloved new franchise because so far it's as good as any I've played.
Think Talisman meets Magic the Gathering meets Diablo and you'll be roughly in the ballpark.  Thumbs up.

I recently finished Murdered: Soul Suspect..............
I read many negative reviews, but loved the concept of the game and wanted to give it a try. Imagine my surprise when the game turned out to be polished, nice looking, and so much fun I stopped playing other games I was involved in till it was done. (I was playing Dragon Age:Inquisition)
One thing i haven't seen in the other reviews is how this game is really similar to Deus Ex: Human revolution. In fact, the computers in the police station are runing the menu screen for DE:HR, which is a nice little nod. The game's layout is similar, in that the City of Salem is the Hub of the game, and there are areas that you branch off into once you get to that part of the story, but return to the hub afterwards. There are many sidequests and collectables though out the game, some in the hub, some in the plot areas. Collect the items in the plot areas and get a ghost story which I enjoyed.
The demons you have to avoid and sneak up on remind me of DE:HR as well, the game kept some of its mechanics for sure.
The plot was good and the voice acting was excellent, if you listen closely you will hear voices you might recognize from other games. The music and sound effects are well done, especially the demon shrieks, and the ghostly and gloomy enviroments set the mood well. I admit I wish they would have made the game a bit longer, I finished at 13 hours, and wanted more when it ended. If I had not looked for the collectables, I could have went through it much faster.
I highly recommend this game, especially if you can get it on sale at a good price. It's sad that airtight games closed its doors, as I would love to see a sequel, which will probably never happen. I don't understand the low scores the game has recieved, it deserved better.

Recettear is fun, charming, and an original take on the JRPG genre. It combines simulation elements with the RPG genre. In the game, you run an item shop in an attempt to pay off Recette's father's debt with the help of the fairy Tear, who also works for the company collecting the debt. That being said, there are a few gamebreakers. Basically the physical shield spell. With maxed mana pool that spell becomes basically god mode. I'd suggest not using it.
Besides that, you have pretty basic combat: Range, Melee and Magic weapons/spells are all availiable for use at any time, similar to Kingdoms of Amalur (except Amalur's skill and combat system is superior in every way and you should be playing Amalur as it is basically Fable 1 but will less herp derp and more polish.). It eventually comes down to standing in the middle of Oakvale with a badass sword killing an endless stream of guards before getting bored, sheathing your weapon and leaving to the adjacent town, who doesnt recognise nor care that you just killed like 100 dudes.
There are downsides though: Spellcasting is based heavily on the system introduced for the Xbox, that is, only having a limited number of buttons compared to the larger number of spells. Get used to scrolling through pairs of owned spells. At the very least the game has the courtesy to let you organise these pairs. I cant remember if you can use the number keys for spells, you might - but don't take my lack of a conclusive answer sway you towards the 'it does'.
Additionally the spells themselves are pretty hit and miss. Lightning is weak as ♥♥♥♥, until you max rank it and then you become the ♥♥♥♥ing god of lightning. Fireball is weak as ♥♥♥♥, until you max it, and you stand around charging it up to max damage while hoping you dont get interupted - that is to say, you will. Divine power/Infernal fury (or whatever thier names were) are OP as hell and basically become the only offensive spell worth noting at high level, even if it has a huge charge time. Slow time is godly. Heal is useless because healing potions do more, dont cost mana, and dont waste skill points.
I could continue, but you get the idea. You quickly realise that some of the spells are useful, others simply aren't. There is some degree of replayability in terms of going range/mage/melee or any mix of those (Multi-strike and Multi-arrow do exactly what they say and are really nice for Mage/melee and Mage/range hybrid playthroughs.) however the story itself isn't all that good for replayability, and the limited map space again limits it. Didn't stop me as a kid from playing this WAY too much though.
Basically, it's a fun 'old' (depends on your definition of old I guess, but by modern standards I'd call it fairly old - definately not oldschool though. DEFINATELY NOT) RPG that is worth a shot for its pretty low cost.
