equal parts ambition met with cordial shallowness, fable is a flat oddity. mind you, its not a generic game, nor is it missing anything crucial on a macro scale. fable's problem is that it's severely undercooked. yet simplicity itself can be a virtue within a sphere of confidence. sometimes a basic expression is all that's required to get a point across. it is fable's hinted aspirations among its genre identity that breeds contempt, yet it is no issue with the game itself. from the very start, fable makes apparent that the experience is going to be humble and straightforward. although it works on realization, it's too hard to deny a contradiction of the premise as expected when compared to the actual function. a broad comparison that falls apart as easily as its made would be likening fable as a western legend of zelda. both games are humble and straightforward action hybrids with identical targeting systems, but one game is serious, and one game is not.
in fable and in ocarina of time, the protagonist is a hero of a long bloodline, whose struggle is an inevitable result of that bloodline. in zelda, this is serious business, but in fable, it is not. though it took a total reevaluation of every event in the game to get to this conclusion, truthfully it is evident from the beginning of the game. the expression system of this game, likely developed to allow interaction than anything I’m saying, can only function in an atmosphere of normalcy, unseriousness, and even ridiculousness. yet, though I say heroics in fable are par the course, every person in the world takes it in with awe and reverence anyway. it’s an utter contrast, how unserious and whimsical the things you do are, and how great and magnificent they’re transposed on the world scale. eventually, the two ends meet, and the hero does things worth praising, and it further drives this rift. I think a work should properly separate what is serious and what is not and fable struggles mightily in that regard.
being good or evil is still treated with incredible importance. there are, of course, mundane acts that boost your karma either way. killing townsfolk makes you evil, while killing bandits and some monsters makes you good, among various other things, but consistency is not what I refer to. fable’s plot ramps up into clearly selfish and unselfish choices coinciding the the plot. though your choices have little mention, it is true that you’re allowed to do great good or great evil, and it shapes the tone of the story even if the choices aren’t totally integrated into the plot development. the great contrast of the choices makes them significantly less effective if the player harbors little malice; to me there was a single choice and its foil, never amounting to much weight. those who enjoy acting out villainy will find fable more accommodating, I believe, because the sharp contrast will create more viable choices. to be mentioned, no other pretense is at stake. fable wouldn’t work with morally gray choices, its charm is its exaggeration. if anything at all is successful in fable’s narrative, it would be the grand moral choices.
now, to put it bluntly, the gameplay sucks. fable borrows from the beat ‘em up genre ignorantly. its combat can be likened to prince of persia, which is the worst model on the planet for combat. block stops every attack with no repercussions for blocking, so if required, you can be invincible at any time. enemies annoyingly have the incredible block too, with no wind up or downtime on any of their attacks, making all fodder near identical. which is to say, unsatisfying and irritating. animations are awkward and contact comes with no good feeling or fanfare. a few lame hits in, the enemy will block. when you’re blocked, or you successfully block, the hero’s weapon will glow purple. the other attack button will let the hero do a slightly more damaging guard break attack that will knock the enemy down. unless you hit the enemy while it’s down, it’ll get up and begin blocking again. there are never any weak-tiered enemies; current level enemies will always take a few knockdowns before being defeated. battles only occur in mobs and waves, with the exception of two enemy types and boss fights. one of those enemy types is a flyer that has a limited window of vulnerability, the other and bosses have constant super armor. so, they’re annoying in different ways.
spells and ranged attacks can’t be blocked. it goes without saying they’re the mainstay of your repertoire. arrows are boring, but cost no mana, cost nothing at all, so they are vastly more efficient. offensive spells come out instantly, with a few exceptions, but have bland particles and effects. there are utility and summon spells which I did not use myself, so I can’t fully comment on, but considering the games difficulty and how quickly enemies were dispatched, they’re probably more effort than they’re worth. it doesn’t matter how you fight, despite my criticisms. the only requirement to win is to have potions. they’re very cheap for being basically full heals. I don’t know what revival potions do, because I didn’t die, but I guess they revive you on the spot. my arsenal of 50 potions defeated the game.
easily the best part of fable is its level design. areas are distinct and there are no repetition. they are busy with detail, a careful labor. that being said, every single quest area in the game is a corridor. there are few change ups and they’re in the form of loops or alternate corridors, but the levels remain corridors. towns are, at least, more open affairs. they’re painstakingly detailed too, but there isn’t much to do in them. not a lot to shop for with only 4 tiers of weapons and armors. you can play games at the inn or attempt to bed faceless people and that’s the extent of things to do in town. models are soft and rounded, built to look like toys instead of things. the style is a touch of unique, able to convey realism and fantasy. every character model in the game is ugly despite this. there aren’t that many models either. the guys look like apes and the girls look like dolls. seeing the same ugly models everywhere starts to become distracting and annoying. even the main character is unattractive by default. fable’s scenario design is ok. the main quest is a everlong chain of meniality and fetching until the plot drops, the sidequests are only terrible things like defend quests, escort quests, and timed quests.
overall fable is of poor quality. featuring embarrassing writing and voice acting, limited and blindly executed combat, and uninspired scenario. it has fantastic music and environment design, maybe top tier in both respects, so it isn’t an absolute pain. it might as well be, though, as those aspects are passive quality. the irreverent simplicity of fable’s world did not impress. I want bite with my satire or development with my seriousness, not a work that stops short of either. what fable does have going for it is a combination of things that cannot be had or found in any other game. it’s partly to how npcs react to your character and definitely how it frames moral choices, but fable is an adventure all to itself. it being curious and an obvious work of passion is not enough to overcome its massive flaws. being interested in odd combinations, fable was enjoyable to a point, but I can’t call it any more than a dead average title.

tl;dr An arcade racing game ala Mario Kart with less RNG (Good!) but tests memory more (Neutral), and has good matchmaking (Good!). Screen mechanics are slightly iffy at times (Leaning bad...) and sometimes matchmaking does fail, and then the screen just goes to hell because it can't handle bad connections (Bad!)
You've heard this being compared to Mario Kart millions of times, and this review is going to do the same thing.
However, Speedrunners is better in that the aspect of luck is extremely reduced. Unlike MK's notorious Blue Shell, no power-up is horrendously punishing without having a downside (e.g. Golden Hook gets stronger as distance between runners increases but is also easier to dodge). The reduction in RNG's power means this game rewards both skill and memory, though the "memory" aspect is more apparent, which in my opinion is unfortunate.
The reason for that and my biggest gripe with the game? The screen.
The screen is fine most of the time, but if you're in first place and the screen has started shrinking, eventually you're going to be running blind because the red wall is right in your face. This is where the memory aspect of the game overtakes everything else in importance. It can be argued that it's a mechanic to help the stragglers catch up so it's not
, but generally, I dislike the feeling of not knowing what I'm running towards.
The screen can be especially bad when you're playing against someone with a poor connection. Usually the screen won't shake too much while your opponent is flickering all over the place, but sometimes your opponent doesn't move, but doesn't die when he leaves the screen. His position is still taken into account when calculating where the screen is positioned, usually where
You're blinder than blind and when your opponent finally connects properly, he could be dead, or he could be in front of you because you had to tumble through every box you couldn't see. Now THIS, is
.
But even if that's said, I still recommend this game because while my dislikes are more vivid in my mind, overall I absolutely had a blast when everything was working fine, which it does most of the time. The matchmaking is fairly good and I tend to play against people with great connections.

One of the best games I've played in a while. With a fair amount of customization available (capability to swap weapons used by your soldiers for different battlefield purposes, same for your tank [though only one of them]), with a straightforward yet still welcome R&D tree (you buy upgrades for your tanks and develop more capable small arms for your foot troops), and the capability of choosing new recruits, with each of them having their own traits (they act as buffs or debuffs when triggered in game). All in all, you can tailor your squad for each mission's requirement, being able to obtain the most from the positive traits and avoiding the negative ones as much as possible. Basically, you have plenty of freedom when it comes to building your combat force.
The story is pretty damn good, and the characters are well written. The game mainly relies in cutscenes for the story-telling, which while plenty and long (much like MGS), are entertaining and very well made (graphically gorgeous. Reminds me about Okami). Further information can be read in the game's glossary (for varied information), weaponry (for information regarding the weapons used), personeel tab (information about each individual which makes an appearance in the game, except a few generic ones), amongst others.
Combat is done within the player's turn. This obviously means that you can only move your troops or make actions if it is your turn. However, said actions are done in real time. And it's the player who has to manually aim the weapon, or perform the required repairs/healing (though some classes will automatically engage the enemy if close enough). In order to do these, the player has to spend 1 (2, if a tank) Command Point, and these are scarce, so it's better not to waste them. Amongst the mechanics, the game features the so called "orders", which basically act as buffs or direct fire support against the enemy. They may be issued with Command Points, except if there's a special condition which doesn't allow you to. A problem I've noticed, however, is that tanks pathing is quite terrible.
In short, if you like strategy games rich in story and suited in a pseudo WWII scenario, then this game is for you. It plays quite a bit like MGS Peace Walker, actually; but trading the solo stealth approach of MGS with clashes of opposing armies in a turn based setting.
Overall, the only three cons I can find are:
1) Long and plenty of cutscenes (not a problem if you're an MGS fan. Even then, they're enjoyable, so that's not much of an issue).
2) Tank pathing (given that you can only move a limited distance every time you choose a character/tank, having your tank turn 90 degrees or get stuck into basically nothing can prove to be costly, especially with anti tank units around).
3) Some songs kinda get bland after a while.

The Warlock of Firetop Mountain is another Fighting Fantasy adaptation from Tin Man Games. It has more in common with Inkle's Sorcery! than with their previous work, however. Instead of reading a digital book, you're actually playing a kind of tabletop game. And in that regard, it leaves Sorcery! in the dust, as the presentation is far superior.
It does not offer the same amount of content, though. Sure, you have 16+ heroes (of which 8 were available prior to release) with different goals and abilities, but that doesn't mean the game changes massively. And once you know what to do, a single playthrough takes maybe an hour. Still took me six to actually finish the game, even when using all three resurrection stones the game offers per playthrough.
One reason is the most annoying aspect of these gamebooks: instant death traps. Be a bit too nosy and your character might easily end up dead. Throwing a dice to test one's luck would easily have alleviated that problem.
Another problem is the damn maze every player has to cross (unless, perhaps, they manage to amass enough gold to buy the Maze Jumper, which I never achieved). Since it's randomly generated, you never know which rooms are safe. And those that aren't contain annoying hand creatures that you can try to flee from, but it won't work every time. And if it doesn't, you take a few points of damage and still have to fight ... which my earlier heroes never survived. The only other option is to fight them outright, which might not end much better.
And then there's the second floor. Really easy if you know what you're doing ... but if your hero has for some reason exhausted all his luck, he can easily lose his life if a certain room gets in his way. I had to cross it four times the first time I got there, which brought me to the brink of death. So of course I didn't survive what little came after the maze.
One of the devs commented that the maze has been made a little fairer, though. So it might not be as annoying anymore.
But hey, contrary to Sorcery!, it actually offers an interesting battle system. It's based on a grid where both the heroes and the enemies move at the same time, which means that attacking an empty square can sometimes be more advantageous than going toe to toe (where the dice would decide the outcome).
Every hero has different skills to offer. Some can attack multiple squares around themselves, others can bind the enemies in place or stop them from attacking ... if you manage to hit them, of course. Sometimes their pattern is quite obvious. Or even stupid, like that of an ogre who simply turned and turned, never striking me once (which has sadly been changed, it seems :x). Other enemies are far more annoying, especially if they can guard against your attack, which you might never know unless you try.
That's why I'd personally recommend choosing a hero who can strike from afar. Makes it easier to survive more difficult battles. And if you don't, you'll respawn at the last bench you rested at. If you still have a resurrection stone, that is.

All things considered, I'd call The Warlock of Firetop Mountain a well done adaptation. But it shares some flaws with the original (or so I would assume, as I have never read it). And it simply doesn't offer the same amount of content you would find in Sorcery!

First game I spammed Railguns and buried the AI under a barrage of shells, second game I went the other route and sniped all their cities with high-power lasers. There is tons of playstyles and great concepts in this game which allows for a good deal of replayability.
About the AI accuracy, the issue is probably a perceptive one rather than a gameplay one. Evaluating the stats post-game, I can fairly consistently get higher hit-ratios than Easy and sometimes Medium AI. The AI misses a lot of their shots, but it doesn't aim the way a human would. Where a player would estimate and line up their shots fairly directly, the AI more or less seems to roll a dice on whether it hits or misses completely. If the (figurative) die roll says "hit", the AI will hit your planet, often even performing a ridiculous looking trick-shot. Overall the AI is fairly easy to beat (on Easy/Medium at least), you just need to not get salty about it landing some ridiculous hits and probably destroying a couple of your buildings too sometimes.
All in all, it's a very fun game that's very satisfying to play and see the fireworks. Highly Recommended.

This game is hard to explain. To call it a "card based RPG" is a misnomer, even though thats what it is. Its kind of like playing those old RPG board games like HeroQuest, mixed with the Lone Wolf books, mixed with an ARPG. Its really unique. I'm an old jaded gamer and Ive never seen anything like this. Its awesome.
Basically, you have a deck of cards, your opponent (a mage who you are playing against and who narrates the story - I think the voice is the narrator from Fable 2 but Im not sure) has a deck of cards (encounter cards). He lays out encounter cards face down, and you move a token across them, choosing where you go. When you land on a card, it is flipped over and an encounter ensues. Sometimes its good, sometimes its bad, and sometimes its combat. Sometimes it can be good or bad depending on what you choose to do and what card you draw (success, failure ect). There are item cards, weapon cards, armor cards.
As you move through the levels you gain more cards. At the end of each sequence, you start a new one and can build your deck based on the cards you won in the last deck. You also build your encounter deck, as you win new encounter cards as well.
Combat is resolved in a 3rd person ARPG style. Sometimes theres traps and environmental hazards as well. Its pretty simple, attack, counter, block, roll. You can also get power ups/downs and special one-use cards. Its really fun. It doesnt take a whole lot of strategy at first, but the enemies and maps do get more complex as you go. Certain attacks cant be blocked or countered and must be avoided, some enemies have ranged attacks, and so forth.
My biggest complaint is that the camera is fixed, which can be a big pain in certain areas. A "maze of traps" where you are dodging flames and spears comes to mind, as well as in encounters where you cant see the enemies attacking you from off screen because you cant rotate the camera to look at them.
That is pretty much the major flaw of the game. Fixed cameras in ARPGs are not a good idea. Fortunately, its reltively minor and since the game is still in E.A. at the time of this writing, maybe it'll be implemented later.
That shouldnt stop you from getting this unique and awesome game, though.

I love the idea of this game. Deck-building games are interesting and unique in their own way, but this one turns deck-building into a craft-your-own-roguelike game. Build a deck of encounters, enemies, and rewards to explore, fight, and loot, choosing encounters that suit your playstyle. As you defeat bosses and complete encounters you earn more varied and powerful cards to fill your deck with. A super cool mechanic, one that I think is pretty much unique. At least I haven't seen it before.
Visuals are pretty good considering the size of the studio. Voice work is fantastic, but sometimes wasted on somewhat dopey lines. Themes are nice, and the artwork on the cards is phenomenal; they've done a lot to give this game excellent visual character without straining development resources by being clever about it.
Combat gameplay is extremely similar to the Arkham Asylum series, if somewhat less smooth. This area of the game needs the most work, I think, as the controls are unresponsive enough to feel clunky, and the wind-ups that telegraph enemy attacks are choppy. But it's certainly not gamebreaking or even really immersion breaking.
All-in-all, this is a really interesting game that's easy to pick up and play. Totally recommend.

As a HUGE adventure fan that almost always prefers a classic 2D click'n'point adventure, Murdered: Soul suspect is a breath of fresh air to everything the adventure genre has to offer. The graphics are just amazing, and thanks to the Unreal engine, the game runs smooth as butther with everything maxed out.
V-sync limits the game to 30FPS, but you can switch that off and just enable V-sync in your GPU options (Catalyst Control or Nvidia center) which gives you all the smooth awesomeness of 60FPS.
The story of this game is brilliant, and the spooky atmosphere just adds to the overall setting of the game. The way you interact with your surrounding and figure out the clues is great, but I was hoping getting stuff wrong would give you a penalty of some kind... Then again, it is an adventure game and most of them are very linear.
There is no combat apart from banishing demons witch can be really difficult at some parts but nothing an average gamer can't figure out.
I was afraid that the ending will be a dissapointment compared to the massive build up of the story (and the bodies murdered) but the game really delivered. After YEARS of trying to find something different and new in the adventure game genre, Murdered: Soul suspect finally brings tons of new mechanics, great voice acting, an amazing story and a beautiful engine to finally burst life into a slumbered genre.
Hats off to the devs and the writters.

I'll do a proper review some time later when I get around to actually playing this. For now, I just wanted to point out a couple of things.
First, I was VERY disappointed that Etna's voice is not the same as before. The original voice actress was perfect for the part, and this one is just playing second fiddle. It will definitely take some getting used to, and I hope it doesn't curb my enjoyment of the game entirely. It's hard to believe such a small detail can change the immersion so much, but it does. Evidently the voice actress in this has been present since the remake and sequels, none of which I had the luxury to try. So for those of you who never played the very first game on Playstation 2, you won't even notice a difference.
Second, as of launch, it's probably best to disable some options such as Screen End Blur, Depth of Field, and SSAO, as they honestly make the game look worse. Most of the other options are probably more of a preference thing, and even though it's not as "smooth" or pretty, I kind of prefer the old user interface and map textures. I'm having a hard time telling if the music is actually different or the same, but it sounds slightly off to me. Maybe I'm just remembering wrong, as it has been something like 10 years since I actually played Disgaea.
Anyway, all in all, it is Disgaea, so I'm sure it's still a good game, and I'm not going to give it a negative review or anything unless I feel it deserves it after playing it. For the time being, this will remain as a placeholder of my initial thoughts until I dedicate some time to this old gem.

This is a real gem of a game. Not a "game of the year" gem, but a very solid title that's well worth the price of entry.
I don't want to tell you much about how it plays, because part of the fun of the game is the way elements emerge as you play through the various "levels", but basically you have a turn based "movement / exploration / RPG" mode which occasionally changes to a combat mode that's like a cross between Fable and the modern Batman games. The real time combat might be a dealbreaker for some, so it's important to mention.
$25 might be a *bit* pricey for this, but bear in mind it's an Australian developed title, so you've got very high costs of living and production costs to cover. If you can get it on sale for < $20, get on it.

Ok i've only played this game for sub 1 hour but i can already put together a review (i will update it when needed)
For those giving it a thumbs up yes with out even actually playing the PC port yet simply because this is Disgaea you are all to be ignored. Seriously why thumbs up a game simply based on the franchise alone? that's like thumbing up Dragon Age 2.....simply because it's the 2nd Dragon age agme and DAO was amazing.
Those looking for a genuine review with harsh truths please look here.
NOTICE! Yes this is Disgaea in all of it's glory yes i love the franchise i've owned every game to date excluding the DS port because...well...didn't have a DS at the time lol But i'm a die hard fan of the franchise and was soooo excited when i saw this listed that for the first time in at least 5 years since SKYRIM i pre-ordered a game.
NOW THAT THATS OUT OF THE WAY.
This game has a TON of issues
Graphical issues come down to 3 major and i do mean major problems
SSAO as people have pointed out breaks the visuals entirely with graphical glitches like messed up black lines all over the place. Turnning this off in turn removes the graphical glitches but SSAO should NEVER be the cause of such a thing and thus needs dire fixes.
Resolution: this is probably the biggest one because it's tied to a bunch of problems. For starters, trying to run this game in full screen (there is no borderless? why?) completely breaks the game entirely. Upon going into full screen (for me) the game minimized......and refused to come back up......when ever i tried to maximize the window again it would just go right back down after a few seconds and the ONLY way i got it to stay up long enough to go back into windowed mode was to rapidly spam click my mouse on the window as it came up. it was extremely frustrating and this was all with in the first few seconds of loading the game up for the first time NOT EVEN IN GAME YET TECHNICALLY.
now back to the resolution issue. This port is clearly a port from the PSP or DS version of the game because OH GOD the graphics are soooo blurry. Turning off every graphical enhancement makes it look worse like it's running sub 480p and resizing the window just makes it even more stretchy and blurry. Character filter is absolutely pointless beause regardless of it being on or off the characters are pixelated to no end. Seriously they NEED to update the sprites for this game to play it on PC.
the third graphical issue is more on a performance side of things. the menus take FOREVER to bring up and the scrolling text for things like tutorials and talking to NPCs in general do not have a speed adjuster. You can not alter this so if you accidentally talk to that one NPC that just won't stop talking....guess what? .....tough luck....you're stuck spamming your buttons away until the text goes away. PATCH IN SCROLLING TEXT SPEED OPTIONS PLEASE!
Now onto the rest of the....issues....
controls. if you have a regular controller you are set, it's fairly easy to figure out the game with that. If you're on a mouse and keyboard like myself, yes you have rebindable keys, BUT THE BUTTON PROMPTS ON SCREEN DO NOT MATCH YOUR KEYBOARD HOTKEYS. To skip tutorial story stuff when selecting a map it says 4? i pressed 4....nothing happened......what does this 4 mean? OH it means the 4th button for your CONTROLLER. Good job! SO IT DOESN'T REFLECT WHAT KIND OF CONTROLS IM USING. On the flip side this is just a minor inconvenience as the menus and game as a whole can be completely played and controlled via mouse. Your keyboard doesn't even need to be touched as a matter of fact. the menus are accessed via left click over a character and right click over an open space to bring up the regular main menus for ending your turn or swapping out equipment and checking on character stats. But as i pointed out, the menus and controls as a whole are just sooo off in terms of responsiveness. you can click twice on the screen and nothing happens when trying to pull up the main menu. it's very frustrating when the game itself runs at a perfect 60FPS for me. This is the first time a Jrpg of any kind has run so smoothly in terms of framerate on PC for me since most Japanese game developers don't put much effort into optimization in general for PC. Then again considering how old this game is IT SHOULDN'T BE SHOCKING THAT IT RUNS AT 60FPS.
Seeing as i have less than 1 hour of gameplay i have no clue what the rest of the game is yet but just think.....it took me nearly one hour just to get into the game, get past the first 2-3 battles.......and create my first character........HOW!? I CAN DO THIS SO MUCH FASTER ON MY PS3 OR PS2! It's soooo frustrating because this franchise is my favorite one....period....nothing on my games list compares to how much i like this franchise as a whole. So please NISA....FIX THIS GAME SO WE CAN PLAY IT PROPERLY ON PC!
yes i will say i recommend this game, BUT THIS IS A HEAVY HEAVY WARNING THAT THIS GAME IS NOT A GREAT OR EVEN GOOD PORT. THIS GAME IS SLOPPY ON PC. SO TAKE MY WARNING SERIOUSLY. The game at launch is not worth the 20$ they are asking for even tho the franchise as a whole is well worth the 60 they generally charge for each new game.

If you're looking for a fresh, interesting, and unique take on gameplay progression mixed with a heathly dose of fantastic voice acting and fun combat, this is the game for you.
You play against a mysterious being for... something? The actual goal is always hidden in mist, but the path to that goal is simple: travel through a series of events and misfortunes told by the cards, then fight the being's boss creature at the end. Along the way you'll be waylaid by angry peasents, marauding rat men, and a host of other fortunes and events that can either benefit or harm you.
One of the best parts is the ominous opponent you play against--whoever they got to do the voice acting has a fabulously gravelly voice, and the dialogue is top notch. I've played through 5-6 rounds of the game so far, and I don't think he has yet to repeat a single line. I'll be incredibly impressed if it keeps up, and even if he does begin to repeat a few lines or two the VA is still fun and the mechanics interesting enough to keep me going.
I first played this game at PAX East, and it was one of the few games that really stuck out in my mind as a game I wanted to check out afterwards. I'm so glad to see it continuing to improve, and I look forward to the final product when it releases.

Runs locked 60FPS. Resolution is set to whatever window size is.
1. TURN VSYNC AND SSAO OFF
2. Have a controller plugged in. It would seem this has the issue FF13 had where it constantly makes CPU calls to see if a controller is plugged in if one is not detected. I'd expect a fix soon-ish though.
3. Turn down all other settings if you are not already at 60FPS
4. TURN VSYNC AND SSAO OFF
Now, if you have tearing at this point put the game into Windowed mode. That will fix your tearing issues. Either drag the window size to whatever you want (The resolution will change to match.) or hit the Maximize button and bite the bullet on having bordered fullscreen. Alternatively use Borderless Windowed Gaming or some other borderless fullscreen app, but this has given me cursor-alignment issues so far and potential overscan.

As you can tell from my hours, I have played this game quite a bit. I'm gonna go for an unbiased review of this, but it may end up being a tad bit biased without me realizing it. Without further ado, I'm gonna just jump right in.
Pros: 1. Fun (but occasionally repetitive) gameplay

2. Decent graphics and visual effects
3. Really nice character design and backstories
4. Great diversity in combat styles for certain characters
Cons: 1. Slightly P2W
2. Certain overpowered classes (looking at you CrA and DiE)
3. Terrible economy
4. Moderately buggy at times
5. The majority of the pvp community is bad (this one is a bit of a gripe but it still remains true)
These sum up most of the major points, but there is a lot more to go in detail about. First things first, if you wanna play this game seriously, it's pretty much unavoidable to not spend money at some point. It won't be too much, but the major thing that's locked behind a paywall is the skill slot change medal. When you start out, you only have 4 skill slots, and getting that medal unlocks the other 4. It's $9 worth of k-ching to buy it, and even though you won't need it for some, the majority of classes benefit greatly from it, with some needing it as a necessity. There are some events that will give you a free permanent medal, but those don't happen too often, so you would probably end up waiting several months for one of those events. Besides that, there's nothing else you "need" to spend money on, although it's pretty obvious they made the skill quests extremely grindy to push you towards just buying the skill you need instead of doing the respective quest(s) for it. The quest for most second job changes takes quite a bit as well, taking as long as a couple of weeks for people who play casually (Note: this does not include ALL 2nd job changes quests). As for the rest of the game, even though there are some negatives, the gameplay makes it worth it. It's really fun to play, and even though there's a pretty sharp learning curve that happens around level 46, that's what makes it fun. Even replaying through the various areas as different characters, levelling them up can prove a completely different experience depending on which classes you've played already.
Graphics: 8

Overall: 8
Verdict: Even though there are some definitely noticeable flaws, the P2W factor isn't too high and it's worth at least a shot in my eyes.

Fable The Lost Chapters is an old Xbox port with some extra bits.The game has you playing through the story of a boy turned man who becomes either a hero or a villian.Like many of Peter Molyneux's games you have the constant choices during quest to do good deeds or evil ones.The world around you reflects which side you choose and your characters appearance changes .The story itself is interesting enough but its the storytelling presentation that won me over.
Weapons,skills & abilities in the game are your choice never being forced to pick any over another.They all have strengths and weaknesses but none outclass the others,other than in terms of damage.There are various outfits ,armors ,collectibles ,tropheys,and acclaim status to be gotten as you play.You can buy houses & rent them,barter for profit, get married,get divorced in the game as well.
The game world is linear but the world itself is decently sized and you will revisit area's often enough.The game sports teleporting from anywhere to specific nodes to help keep the ending running down well enough.The game is littered with humor and sidequests many of which the rewards are worth doing but completely skippable. For an old game its a good buy if you have never played it and want a decent linear action rpg.With a sweetfx mod the game looks even better. Get it 75% off on the cheap or get Fable Anniversary with all its new shiney looks.Either way worth that linear playthrough if you like rpgs.

I've spent 4 hours in Conan Exiles now, and there are good and bad things to say about the game.
Let's do the good things first. (In no particular order.)
It's Conan! Or at least, it's in Conan's world.
The characters looks decent. (Although when you sneak you look like a dork!)
Crafting works nicely, and it's not that hard to get the items needed.
The bad stuff. (Also in no particular order.)
I had to play solo, as I couldn't find ANY online servers to join!!
When you strafe, you lose a lot of speed making dodging hard.
Gathering materials takes up a lot of time. And I mean a lot!
It's laggy. In particular it's laggy around fires, like the bonefires some humans hang around.
There are no tutorials. (But most people will figure it out quite fast, so this isn't as bad as it sounds.)
Fighting is annoying, at least in the beginning. Some times you stand right in the face of your oponent, and still doesn't hit them.
The lists are sure to be longer after more time in the game. If you like games like Minecraft, and you like Conan, I'm sure you'll have fun in this game. If you're more into getting quests and killing mobs, you'll have a hard time.
I'll play it some more, hopefully on an online server, before I make up my mind if this is a game I'll keep or not.

I'm voting no because the AI has access to information the player doesn't have, allowing it to pull off godlike trick shots when shooting unassisted weapons like railguns that have no tracking.
The AI can loop a railgun round around the sun 4 times and around 3 planets to hit your planet. And amazingly it hits the planet exactly where your buildings are and rarely out in the wilderness.
Even more amazing, is if you have built defense shields protecting your city and buildings, the trick shot will hit *just* outside the radius of the shield, so that the splash damage still damages or destroys your stuff. And these are supposed to be the basic railgun rounds that everyone starts the game with.
The developer said the AI has less then 80% accuracy, but I call BS. I've played 5 games and every game is the same.
If the devs decide to fix the AI accuracy and bring it to normal human levels, I'll change this review.
As it is now, the game is unfun to play against the computer.

It’s a great game which shines in multiplayer, especially with friends in my opinion (although with friends is usually better in most cases). The mechanics are not too complicated to learn but there is a multitude of different tactics and choices to make, from what kind of weapons to focus on, and the required support structure for that, countering the strategy of opponents and predicting their next moves, and then the ever-fun firing of the weapons to curve around the solar system into another planet.
The ‘Enhanced Edition’ is awesome. The game generally plays a bit slicker and a lot of user-friendly additions have been made, especially to research and the UI. The visuals have been slightly improved, and it is especially fun to be able to be zoomed in on a planet while it is being bombarded and watching the kinetic strikes every so often. More weapons, buildings and game options add even more layers to the game, and the ability to have AI players mixed in with multiple humans in an online match is a great addition.
Be warned though, while a human will generally hit with maybe 60-80% of their shots, the AI will hit almost 100% of the time including some absolutely ridiculous trick shots slinging round multiple planets before hitting the target or arching far out of the system and back in, its a bit ridiculous, though impressive to see.

ArcheAge is the prime example of greedy incompetent devs.
Trion is milking as much out of this game as possible, you can clearly see this with the packs they sell, some going up to 140 euro. The cash shop is huge with a lot of options that make the game terribly pay to win. Sure, you can play the game without ever spending a dime, sure, you can buy cash shop credit with ingame gold, but the prices inflated so hard after they kicked out the gold bots that I wish you good luck selling anything.
Game design wise it had a lot of potential but Trion's terrible communication and demands to the actual devs ended up with some really bad decisions. For example: they released content that was released after the release, meant for newbies to catch up with veteran players in terms of gear, at the release of the game. This meant that everyone had very easy access (or so it looks like, you'll find out eventually that it's a tiny area in the world that's overcrowded and makes you employ asinine grind and tagging tactics to get anything out of that place) to big weapons, which in turn made one of the bigger crafting professions completely useless and worthless for the bigger part.
Another big example is the total overpopulation of housing property. In the korean version of the game fewer people had membership to allow them to place houses, and the server populations were also smaller and more divided. Housing space is limited in this game and you had to compete really hard in the past to get a housing spot, a select few people used to use cheats to steal property from other players camping a decaying house to sell them. They eventually got banned, but it took a bunch of months before they did anything about it.
- Boat physics.
- Classes (although some will always be top tier, while some wont ever be)
- Professions/tradeskill, although it's a typical tradeskill menu they're definitely more interesting than the cookie-cutter MMO tradeskills.
- Boat physics.
- Weather system (I heard from rumors some sort of focus group found weather too unfun and too impactful on gameplay, and they toned down the weather from more realistic to really subtle)
- P2W cash shop
- Housing system. Once you stop playing, you'll lose everything related to housing, and with overcrowded zones it will be hard to find a good spot again.
- Patch implementation choices and gameplay/game content changes compared to the korean version.

If you're looking for a fresh, interesting, and unique take on gameplay progression mixed with a heathly dose of fantastic voice acting and fun combat, this is the game for you.
You play against a mysterious being for... something? The actual goal is always hidden in mist, but the path to that goal is simple: travel through a series of events and misfortunes told by the cards, then fight the being's boss creature at the end. Along the way you'll be waylaid by angry peasents, marauding rat men, and a host of other fortunes and events that can either benefit or harm you.
One of the best parts is the ominous opponent you play against--whoever they got to do the voice acting has a fabulously gravelly voice, and the dialogue is top notch. I've played through 5-6 rounds of the game so far, and I don't think he has yet to repeat a single line. I'll be incredibly impressed if it keeps up, and even if he does begin to repeat a few lines or two the VA is still fun and the mechanics interesting enough to keep me going.

I wanted to love this game.  I really, really did.  So much so that I originally paid for the $150 Founders Pack.  Everything seemed amazing, and if the only factor was the gameplay and graphics, I would have loved it.  The problem soon became that this is one of the most pay-to-win games I've ever played.  I put in over 1,000 hours over the first month or so, but then things started appearing in the in-game store... RNG boxes with huge, in-game bonuses at a very low drop rate.  I'm not talking about cosmetic items, but items that were the foundation for the game's economy because they were as necessary as they were rare.  Then there was the hacking.  Land came at a huge premium and was highly coveted, however teleporting/land placement bots ran rampant.  So much so that many outwardly admitted to doing it.  From last I heard, most received 24-48 hour account suspensions.  The land they acquired they got to keep.
I requested and through many emails and complaints, received a refund about a month after the game's release and haven't played since.  It's possible that everything has been fixed since then, but I highly doubt it given that the Korean version was about a year ahead of ours at the time and players there confirmed that their version was even more P2W than ours.  It's really unfortunate, because had this been a subscription-based game with no in-game store and a much stronger stance against hackers, this could have been one of the best sandbox MMORPGs of all time.

A great mix of turn based strategy and action gameplay. Highly recommended
Pros.
A well fleshed out story and characters. And I don`t mean only the main cast as well.  As a great addition I see a great characterization of the secondary squad members. The way they do it is through the appearance, combat shouts and interactions with the game world and other squad members. It works to a great extent and it does not feel ham fisted, like jamming unnecessary actors in cut scenes. This is something I don`t see all that often done in such games and find it a shame :( This serves as a great example of how to do it right.
Combat is an interesting mix of turn based and action gameplay. While in the tactical view it acts as a standard turn based game, but when taking control of a character it starts to feel more like an action game. This is due to the interception mechanic, while you move your character around, enemy troops with a line of sight and range will be firing on you. It gives a great deal of tension to the action, since you must act fast and precise while still thinking of the overall strategy involved, of course your troops also have interception fire, which gives additional tactical importance to the position and the direction your troops are facing at the end of your turn.
Something to add is the tone of the narrative. While presented in a colorful and distinct anime style it does not shy away from darker parts of war, like forced labor camps and the stronger world powers using the smaller nations for their own gain.
Cons.
I found tank controls to be janky at best while using keyboard and mouse, especially after performing an action. To my understanding it was due to the fact that the way tank was facing and camera were pointing were different.  What makes it even more irritating is the fact that tanks use AP (Action points) to turn as well as to move(unlike infantry), meaning you might end up facing the wrong way and leaving your weak points exposed to the enemy, because it took too long to regain control over the unit.
Some of the maps and missions feel a bit too gimmicky. While I see the notion of providing different game experiences at times it felt like the AI is straight up cheating or putting arbitrary restrictions on your possibilities. These missions made sense in narrative, but were underwhelming or frustrating in terms of gameplay.
Menus don`t have mouse control, which I found annoying.

Ok, after a few hours spent on the train vs mostly AI aswell as a few attempts at multiplayer, heres a purchase review on Interplanetary re-release edition.
First let me just say that I (like everyone else who bought the original Interplanetary) found this in their Steam library a few days ago, so some bias might be heard here.
The game in its fundamental form consists of up to eight players and AI battling each other from their own planets orbiting the same star, pretty simple. The twist is that their are no military units, or moveable units at all, each turn goes as follows:
Everyone chooses what and where they build things from a resource/power pool (which has a nice bit of gameplay depth), they also choose what to research and deal with some other details such as city projects or building upgrades. Now heres the REALLY REALLY fun part, everyone uses the various offensive structures they have built to bombard the ever living s***t out of each other, and its glorious.
everyone attempts to line up the trajectories of their missiles, railguns and GODDAMN METEORS, once everyone has ended their turn the game plays the glorious chaos of stray weapons just missing their targets flying off towards another planet just to be blocked by a gas giant redirecting their trajectory into the oblivion of space. These few moments of but clench never get old.
As far as re-releases go, the Jolly Roger team handled it very well, and to be honest a re-release was likely their best option, heres why:
Interplanetary on a fundamental level is a very good game for fans of strategy games, people who played those gravity shooter games or those who just love chaos on their screen. Sadly the original game received little attention, due to a what I believe is a mix of bad luck, minor quality of life issues and some weird acting AI (in my experiece), with the last two problems butchering replayability for me, Enhanced Edition fixed MOST of these issues, the AI feels a lot more fun to vs, idk how they worked before or how they work know but it no longer feels like the ai is just shooting into the sides of other planets.
Pros:
- Decent Graphics, fairly glorious explosion sounds and an acceptable UI (will get into that) gives a game that crutches on its gameplay, and the fact im still playing says a fair bit about that.
- Gameplay has a LOT of replayability, different tech paths, different weapons and vastly different strategies leave a 'one more game mentality'
- Multiplayer has worked flawlessly in my experience, and a hotseat option is always appreciated
- AI are fun to verse
- AI take over AFK players in multiplayer, which is nice
Cons (Warning: very nitpicky):
- Turtling/defense strategies still feel pretty unimpactfull though
-
- You cant end turn from the tech screen  (as far as i cant tell)
- Games can be a little painfull to wrap up, a plague amongst strategy games
- THERE ARENT KEYBINGS TO DO MOST THINGS, sigh, not even a controls menu caus escape and WASD are about the only keys you can use, and escape can only take pause/menu screen.
Reccomendation to devs:
- Make defense buildings have a upgrade system, let there be a single defense building, that stops only railguns, the upgrades instead change the statistics on its defense, decrease some things and increase others, a huge buff to turtling and make it feel more interactive, maybe even add some things that feel impactfull/visible from space for defense builds, though thats up to you as to whether you even want to encourage that playstile
-
- add more keybinds, add to buttons to scroll between the 5 different tabs, and make Enter end turn, some basic examples, atleast put the options in a menus somewhere would be real kind.
- you managed to really avoid that tacky indie UI look, so gj with that
- REALLY like how you view intel now, much more intuative
- thankyou for not shoving down a political system or whatever down your games throat, feelsgoodman
- hope to see some minigames/challenges, eg practice shots or survive for 5 turns or win in 5 turns type jazz
TL:DR
Good game, the $15 could be spent elsewhere but if you think you might like it you will probably like it. each round is filled a brief calm before the storm followed with chaos and butt clench. A lot of depth with little complexity (a good thing) leads to a larger then expected amount of replayability and strategy, a competant AI to vs is supplied aswell. Great fun multiplayer, although public games can be few and far between at times.
Love the game, all of my problems are minor and hope to see it grow further.

Despite the odd title, this is a fun game if you like 2D space action, like collecting new ships and weapons, and don't mind having to grind a bit if you do poorly for awhile.
SPaZ is a top down space combat game where you mine resources and fight other ships. You gain power by gaining favor with two factions and buying weapon blueprints. You get ship blueprints from beating those ships. For me, getting those blueprints and seeing what each new ship or weapon could do was the most fun part of the game. There are many different types of equipment and you have limited upgrade points, so you'll have to pick a few trees to go down until late game when you can really pack on the level up. This gives the game some replayability if you like.
Combat is fun and you have a lot of options. You can put out a big, expensive ship and just mow down enemies, or you can put out a small fast ship that can't take much damage. While the small ships do die quickly, they are much less expensive, making it an important issue to consider. If you get low on resources, you can't build your big ships and have to either do easy missions or go mine. There are places to do so relatively safely, but that's the slight grind I mentioned.
I only had two issues with the game. The first relates to the factions. There are two and in each system they will have different feelings toward you. If you make them happy or mad in one system, it won't affect them in another. This is actually good. The problem is that one faction is always the one blocking the warp gates leading to other sectors. They must be cleared before you can move on. So you must either bribe the guards, which is extremely expensive, or attack them and♥♥♥♥♥♥them off.
The second problem is that the end game got very boring and "samey" as I cleared system after system. However, that was me being completionist. You can finish the game without doing so but more systems cleared will give more aid in the last battle.
Overall, I had a lot of fun. I'm not ready to jump into a second playthrough yet, but I'm happy with the time spent with this game and I will be keeping an eye on the second.

So i'm going to "thumbs up" this one, but I'd recomend you only get it if you catch it on sale. The game is just two short. I figured the story (minus the side quests) totaled somewhere around four and a half hours. The game is still worth playing though. I enjoyed the fresh concept of the game's detective gameplay. Most of the gameplay reads as a hybrid between the crime-scenes in Arkham City and those in the Last Testement of Sherlock Holmes, so expect to spend a good deal of your time looking through a kind of 3D hidden object game. What makes the game different is that instead of automatically adding up your findings for you like in the Arkham games, you have to figure out what evidence is important, and what's not, and remember important clues from earlier in your investigation.
The problem is that much of the answers just seem to obvious. Ever watch an episode of CSI or Criminal Minds, come up with the answer 15 minutes in, then sit there waiting for the characters to play catch-up? That's what alot of this game boils down to. You click on glowing objects while Ronan mutters "Why was the killer here?" to himself and you scream at the monitor "Because this is where the girl was hiding, stupid!" The setting is probably the biggest givaway. The game takes place in Salem MA and the escaped victim you need to save is a psychic, so three guesses what the killer's motive is.
The game also suffers from a semi-acute case of Console-idus. QTE's and odd button mapping choices abound, but it's not what i'd call "crippling", just annoying.
The story itself is farely decent. The voice acting is excelent for the most part. There's a lot of naration by the main character, probably trying to emulate old cop movies from the 1950's, and while it's not bad, I know a lot of people see naration as the anti-christ of exposition, so, fair warning. The dialogue itself seems well written, but it was written be Square Enix, and there are a few moments where the Japanese writing just jind of pokes it's head out of the bushes and glares at you, but only rarely.
My only REAL complaint, besides how short the game is, is the enemy encounters. They're tacked on, predictable, clunky, time consuming, and just all-around ANNOYING. In a game where your selling point is story and mystery solving, you do not need to cram in pointless, enemies that have absolutely no impact on the story, just so you can make me play hide-and-seek with your failed attempt at capitalizing on the recent survival-horror craze. This is precious time and recources that could have been spent giving us more murder mystery goodness to solve, instead now I have to wait in a hidespot for 10 minutes to get behind a baddy that can one-hit-kill me just by looking at me. Thanks Square.
Once again, I do recomend the game, and I am glad I bought it, but I'm also glad I didn't pay full price. 4 hour story and no replay value means buy it dirt cheap, or just leave it alone.

Collectioning was absolutely unrewarding experience, items were scattered all around the locations, sometimes requiring solving the puzzles (not really hard ones), and in return for collecting all items from a quest you only get a wall of text narrated to you in front of static picture (though flashback would be a perfect reward).
Sound: 9/10 - music and voice acting were good. Sometimes the thoughts of people you posess would match the thoughts of others, which is obviously not what you'd expect in a game that offers you to read people's thoughts.
Graphics: 7/10 - picture quality was pretty good at highest settings and the game was running smoothly at 60+fps, which is quite rare nowadays, when games with a lot worse graphics manage to lag on high-end PC.
Overall: 7/10 - I suggest you give this game a try, at the very least you get a nice movie.
P.S. I want to say "thank you" to the developers for making the game about afterlife and not including Zombies in it! We really don't need any more zombie games.

It's a pretty straight port of the PSP version, with keyboard+mouse support and the option to use upgraded map textures. Missing a couple of features, and appears to be running poorly on some peoples computers, which is unfortunate, as it runs perfectly fine on my rig. The best part, though, is running Disgaea at 1080p without any aliasing or jaggies, looks good and is now pretty much the definitive version of the game (in features and appearance!). Considering this is a port of a game which came to be in 2003, they certainly took their time getting it onto PC. Looks interesting to you and want to get into the series? This review will try to quickly give you an idea of the game without spoiling the things that matter.
As for the game itself, it's a heavily gameplay focused RPG with a story tailored to entertainment value. Things only get serious around the last few chapters. Disgaea heavily values the player, giving you a multitude of ways to strengthen your characters and eventually create a monstrosity that can one-shot everything. However, ther isn't much to guide you much making said monstrosity. These things are mostly for the hardcore audience, you can bring characters to level 9999, then bring them back to level 1 with bonuses to make them become even stronger. If you like streamlining in your games and having everything be simple to understand, this has very little. They explain the basic mechanics of the game, and let you figure out everything else and devise your own strategies, both in gameplay and system. You should not know everything about how to play Disgaea going into it for the first time. To close this off, I think it's a game that you should absolutely own if you enjoy customization, strategy RPG's and pushing the limits of a game.
By the way... This game is lacking in many convenience features that future games include to make things more fun or convenient. However I still reccomend playing this game first, as you could easily discredit the earlier games by playing more modern versions. There really are a lot of great features added in later releases, but you'll be missing out on a great game if you play them first.

Plays like Bit.Trip Runner, Rayman Legends, and Guitar Hero had a baby on top of a Jackson Pollock painting; and I promise that's a good thing.
Unlike most endless runners you actually have a lot of control as to where your character goes. Depending on the exact path you take you'll end up doubling back for more points or missing bonus orbs (points), it takes an almost 'strategy' to correctly play this game. In that regards, Color Guardians elevates itself from the rest of the endless runner pack.
Helping it ascend further is it's multi-lanes mechanic. Instead of playing exactly like a rythym game where you HAVE to hit Button 'X' at this specific time, the game lets you sidestep certain obstacles if you are out of sync or focused on a different path. It even rewards finding your own way through a level, by letting you double back.
Color Guardians has the precision of Guitar Hero, the goofy aesthetics of Rayman, and the gameplay of Bit.Trip Runner, but goes a step further than all of them by granting the player a level of control I've not seen in an Endless Runner. If you are looking for a break from narrative heavy and AAA titles and just want to hit a flurry of buttons for a hectic, fun time, get this game.

I've been playing this game for about half a year now, and to sum it up in a general statement: the game is enjoyable as a side-scrolling RPG.
Pros.

-Good amount of events

Cons.

And finally: -yes, sometimes a quest can be too repetitive- yes this could also be a positive thing when it comes to earning locked skills and extras for those dedicated to a character for a guild or just a general favorite, but it can also hinder progress in certain parts of the storyline.
However despite the minor negatives it is still a very enjoyable game, allowing you to create a character which really fits your play syle. Whether you're into pro/casual gaming means nothing towards recomendation for this game, either way it's still enjoyable, and hope you have a blast.

I've played Fable in so many ways over so, so many years. I was one of the poor fools waiting years for it to come out, and event hen I was kinda late to the party.
All you really need to know is that this game -should- be awful. It failed the hype more than any other game in the history of ever (except maaaybe Duke Nukem Forever, because that one is awful), the graphics were not what they could have been, the combat shouldn't be fun, the voice acting is painful, the story is simplistic, and a few of the design decisions for models still hurt my brain.
But the game is wonderful. For all that is 'missing', your mind is happy to fill it in, for all that combat should be a boring slog, every player will try a handful of weird rules and challenges, or, just goof off entirely, and get their fun. Collectibles are at once plentiful, and achievable without aid. Marriage is utterly pointless and unfulfilling. . .that's it, marriage is just pointless and unfulfilling. >.> Meta humor >.>
Point is, there is no reason this game should be so awesome, and that's why it stands out as the shining beacon of "See here! This is what matters!" - Aesthetics. Every individual piece seems mismatched, disjointed, and frankly lacklustre on its own. Put them together and. . .you know the rest. Personally, I find this games sits with precious few others on that point of pure aesthetic gold, and among western-produced RPGs? It almost stands alone.
Backing away from cartoonishness severely damaged the franchise, and I really do place 90% of the blame on that alone. I'm serious. If they remade Fable III, the exact game, but with Fable's graphics (and more important, use of graphics)? It'd be fine. $4.99 on steam sale?  Heck yeah!  I was expecting this to be graphically challenged, being released in 2014.  I was quite surprised this looks nearly as good as any 2016 title out there, and better than most.  The gameplay is excellent, although much easier than anticipated from reading reviews.  The story had the potential to be magnificent, but was only mediocre at best in practice.  Without giving spoilers out, the reason for the apocalypse was never really fleshed out or explored, and if it was it would have added quite a bit to the storyline.  Well maybe in the 2017 version they will flesh it out.  I also got the impressions from reviews that there were a lot of choices affecting the game, but in reality you have 2 or 3 major choices with the overused trope of "morality", and all they affect is which one of 2 endings you will get.  Certainly not enough for a replay, but at least they tried.  Outside of that the gameplay mainly consists of 75% shooting, 20% stealth, and 5% cut scenes.  I'm a huge stealth fan in games such as Thief, Deus Ex, Rainbow6, MGS5, Dishonored, etc.  But found it lacking in this game.  It is present, you can sneak around a bit, turn off light sources, backstab or choke enemies, but other than the "moral" ending there was really no reason to.
The strongest point of the game is environment.  Holy crap, it's rare to play a game with such an incredible and detailed environment.  From the refugee camps to the abandonded city and underground tunnels you just get sucked in hard.   But at the same time that environment can feel you slightly disappointed because the game definitely has only a single path and you cannot get off the rail.  You can slightly approach missions a slightly different way, which basically consists of a tunnel underneath the level allowing you to run and gun on the surface, or sneak and ambush through the tunnel.  But  most of the time you can only go forwards, with the usual assortment of plants, rocks, debris, heights, etc blocking you from going off the path.  I'm not saying this as a bad thing as it's the type of game it is.  NPC's also were both very detailed, but also hollow at the same time as they didn't interact or do anything other than their very small scripts.
If you are hesitating, press that buy button, especially when it's on sale.  This game has more satisfaction than 3/4 of the game released in 2016.   It's a bit short, but you can always ramp up the difficulty.

Valkyria Chronicles was one of the first games that I bought on PS3, and to this date I still don't think there has been a better game published on that console. The game features solid mechanics, story, and aesthetics, and with a decent length is one of the most complete experiences in gaming.
The PC version manages to make replaying the game a fresh experience by eliminating the restrictions of the PS3. The game is no longer hobbled by atrocious load times, and the update to 1080p resolution is a massive improvement on already fantastic visuals.
I do recommend playing with a gamepad, as Sega didn't do quite a great job with translating the game's original controls to a mouse and keyboard scheme. This is unfortunate, because the game really does fine in action mode with shooter controls, but the map navigation being tied to the movement keys in action mode make it a little too awkward of an experience for me. The sniper zoom is also too slow with mouse controls, making a key binding necessary if you choose to use the keyboard.
The core game design is solid, but does have some problems.
The first is the ranking system. Rank on a mission is tied only to the number of turns it took to clear the mission. This is fine if you are a low turn clear type of player, and it is also fine if you don't want to care about rank and clear at your own pace, but there is no real middle ground.
Because you cannot replay past story chapters, if you want to A rank all the missions you have to speed run every chapter. This isn't very difficult, but it does mean that A ranking missions requires you to play in a specific way that isn't necessarily more fun. In particular, the movement advantage of the scout class is so extreme that shocktroopers, engineers, and tanks are almost completely unused except in the few missions that force you to use them in some way or another.
My recommendation is to do your first playthrough not caring about rank and just enjoying all the things the game and it's unique classes have to offer - the game is easy enough such that the lost EXP for not A ranking is not really an issue. It does however suck that the game forces you to do multiple playthroughs if you want to A rank and "have fun."
The other issue I have with this game is power creep. Power creep is in general a problem with every SRPG I've played, but in Valkyria, it hits as soon as your scouts hit level 11. Once your units are upgraded to elites, the enemies never really catch up in strength. It can be fun to run around maps with relatively overpowered units, but in an SRPG, difficulty is something to be valued as well. You can keep the difficulty artificially higher by not leveling up your units, but it would have been nice if the difficulty scaled appropriately as your team gains more resources naturally.
Do these cons outweight the pros? Absolutely not. The game is beautiful, fun, and has great characters. If you only want to play hard games, then you're missing out on a lot.

TL;DR - Conan Exiles is currently fairly basic in comparison to the other survival experiences that you can have right now. The game will take a fair amount of time to hold water in comparison to Rust or ARK (though it's about on par with Hurtworld) - That being said, for a fresh launch optimization is much better than I thought it would be. The game is playable - With a group, it'd even be a lot of fun. I'm going to keep an eye on Exiles' development.
Specifications.
Windows 10 Home.
Intel i5-6600k @3.5
16GB RAM
EVGA GTX 1050 Ti
SSD.
I picked up Conan Exiles last night at release and put a couple hours into it to see how it is. My current impression is that it smells a lot like Hurtworld and ARK had a baby and forgot to give it clothes - Which is to say that it isn't awful. My framerate, at autoset high graphics, jumped between 28 and 96 FPS - The majority of the time I sat at a relatively comfortable 50-60.
I thought the combat was relatively satisfying, most of the time. Beating the tar out of the starter ferals with my fist was pleasant and brought me to the militia path right off the bat. The stone sword and shield combination had me clearing a dungeon without any kind of shack set down. Leveling in the early game VIA that route was fast paced even at vanilla XP rates, and the continual rush of monsters trying to eat me was surprisingly immersive.
The building uses the same socket system that Rust, ARK and Hurtworld do. The sandstone walls you start out with won't get upgraded until the mid to late game, at which point I assume raiding will be a little more than camping outside doors. At this stage, it's all very simple and grindy. While groups will have an advantage in the early life of servers currently, the lack of parties or XP sharing will make them vulnerable to people that grind their way to tools capable of breaking down doors.
I don't really like the inventory weighting system right now. I understand that it's a part of the whole ARK-esque RPG meets survival game deal that's been going on lately, but I've always been partial to killing gatherers who are just chock full of goodies.
Speaking of gatherers - The thralls are an interesting concept that I like a fair amount. I could see them actually having a heavy use later in the game, and genuinely speeding up the gathering process. I'm interested to see if upgraded wheels of pain will make thralls viable defenders for time spent offline - If Conan actually eliminated the necessity of base babysitting, I could genuinely see myself getting back into more frequent time spent with survival games.
I think at the end of the day, I'd recommend it. It seems like there's a fair amount to look at even with this first release, and depending on the rate at which the developers put out new content, it could genuinely end up being something interesting. Currently, the only thing I can see myself doing with it is co-operative servers between friends to do persistent world RPG shenanigans, but that doesn't mean that it won't change later in early access. Even if you don't buy it, I do recommend keeping an eye out for news about it - I do think that we'll be seeing and hearing more from this game, and I am genuinely excited to see where that goes.

Color guardians is a great addition to the classic runner genre with a new mechanic that makes the game have very fast paced and hectic gameplay. However it does have inherrant problems that need to be fixed.
The game is a classic runner game that is heavily inspired by experts in the genre such as temple run and subway surfer. Although that has a very interesting mechanic that makes it stand out. Your character you play as can change colours between yello, blue and red. These colours are used to progress through certain parts of the level and to collect different coloured orbs. The mechanic creates fast paced gameplay requiring you to very quickly change colours in order to successfully progress through the level.
You also have other obstacles to avoid. These can include walls, moving enemies or spikes. There is a very wide variety in these obstacles. The game never leaves you with repetitive gameplay. All the levels are very different and keep you amused throughout. They are very challenging and aren't easy to complete first time.
There is plenty in the game for collectors and achievement hunters. The levels contain optional orbs to pick up. These require you to be the colour of them. Depending on how many orbs you pick up, you get a different ranking for the completion of the level. This can keep people entertained trying to 100% every level for a long time.
The game has a very stand out graphics style. The cartoony look is represented throughout the game and is consistent. What I found really unique is the way in which the world reacts to how you are doing in the game. If you aren't doing very well then the levels turn very grey because you aren't colllecting many colours. As you collect more colours the world becomes more and more colourful. This is a beatiful addition that makes the gameplay more fun for people.
The game has multiple control methods. You can use classic mouse and keyboard. However I wouldn't recommend it. A controller is key to being able to play this game properly. The colours of your character is optimized to the colours of the buttons on your controller. Therefore it is very hard to remember the keys on the keyboard wheras it is very easy with a controller.
The game features 2 controller setups for this. They have one for a playstation controller, and another for an xbox controller. This convenience does make it much easier for people with different controllers. However this was very annoying. I was using an xbox controller to play the game. I found that every time I rebooted up the game it defaulted to playstation controls. So I had to go in the options menu each time to reset this back again. This was an uneccessary hassle and was an annoyance.
Color guardians options menu is also very lacking in the needed options. There are no graphics options besides the default fastest, good and fantastic. For a 3D game this is unnacceptable. Other seperate options should be present. You then only have 3 different resolution options to choose from. This is unnaceptable range of resolutions. Finally there is a full screen option. There are also seperate audio sliders for different settings. However this is all that is in the options menu. The menu is also extremely difficult to navigate with both mouse and controller and can be glitchy.
While I was writing this review I had a very big issue with the navigating of the menu. For some reason when I clicked the back button to go out of the options menu the game automatically by itself went onto the new game button. This means it completely deleted all of the progress I have made and I now have to start from the beginning again. They definitely need to fix this issue to make sure this doesn't happen to anyone else.
I would cautiously recommend this game to people. There are a lot of problems that could lead to bad gameplay for people. I would recommend waiting for a fix before buying it. I also think the asking price is a little high for the content at the moment. You should wait a bit and wait for a sale before buying in my opinion.

A coffeebreak puzzle platformer with a screen-looping mechanic.
An intriguing premise, but this game feels more like a buggy beta than a proper game ready for release. If the problems had been worked out, it could have been interesting. As it stands, it is a couple short hours of at best a mind-bending and fairly forgiving physics gimmick game, and at worst intense frustration, glitches and shamefully awful writing.
Music is excellent, but writing is abysmal, glitches abound, and when you reach the half-way point, the game reverses your physics and expects you to redo the levels backwards, while pressing the
arrow to jump
.

- This game comes with a buyable soundtrack and there's no mystery why. The music is atmospheric, floaty and zen, which blends in well with the simple aesthetic the designers were clearly going for.

- This might not normally be worth mentioning, but the menus introduce the game and its theme well. They fit the aesthetic and are intuitive and easy to navigate.

- This game makes use of a fixed jump height with a floaty arc as the base of its jumping physics, and admittedly it feels great and free just clearing a bank of spikes with a long, lazy, beautiful arc.

- So bad that it is noticeably the worst thing about this game. Each of the planets is depicted as a dry, one-dimensional stereotype that seems like it's trying to give a Sunday special moral lesson that in many cases isn't even true. The game would be improved greatly by removing the dialogue moments entirely.

- Above dialogue moments often show text popping in at one size and then immediately popping down to another font size. Sometimes two text entries appear on top of one another, rendering both unreadable. There's a negative space that you move through in between the moment you disappear off the bottom of the screen and the moment you emerge from the top of it, and while in that space you phase through moving platforms; it seems like they go through more negative space than you do. There are also a couple of glitches that can make you hit the wrong side of a bounce block, or freeze in place.

- One of the introduced mechanics are walls that appear, fade, and disappear. This is a platforming staple, but in this game, I found it hard to get a feel for how long they would spend in each phase. More distinct or more fluid visual cues might have helped here.

- Given how much time you spend bouncing from the top to the bottom of the screen and back again at times, it can feel awkward how different falling down feels compared to rising up.
However, the symmetry of controls becomes more important once you have reached the sun and are tasked with going back through all the levels in reverse - in this mode, you "jump" down (by pressing the up key, no less), "fall" up and stick to the bottoms of platforms, which is extremely unintuitive. Having come back to this game and completed the reverse levels, I can attest that many of the earliest levels are in fact designed to be much more challenging backwards, but nevertheless, the difficulty curve on the return is highly erratic rather than smooth.
