This game is really good.  I hope there is gonna more of it.
+ The story is interesting enough.  I like how you're not out to save the world.  In fact, what you're out to do is pretty much up to you.  I also like the historical setting.  This particular setting is not that often explored and they haven't been shy about it and didn't fel in the total PCness or gentle savage BS.
+ The narration is good.  Except for some voice acting (which is good btw) at the start and at the end, it's all text.  Fortunately, it is  not badly written.
+ The character you choose on your team matters.  Really.  Not only for their stats but also for their personality.  They all have qualities and flaws and you'll have to deal with it.  Really.  Some character won't get along or won't agree with your course of action.  This is a really intersting mechanics and it is well implemented.
+ They make you care about the character on your team.  Because they have a personality and will react to your decision you will grow to love them.  Or in some case, hate them.  I could have added this to the previous point but, it is so good, I had to make another point for this.
+ The choice you make have consequences and some of those choice are mutualy exclusive.  This is not a game where you'll be able to see everything in one playthrough. Also, the consequences of your choices are not always obvious and I personnaly enjoy the subtility.  Something something is gonna reward you, or come back to bite you, futher down the line and you might have not expect it. This also means the game has a good replay value.  You might want to try one game where you're a do-gooder diplomat and one where you're an evil tyrant.
+ Multiple endings that account for what you've done throuought the game.  Not only for one or two choice at the end but also things that might have seemed not so important at first.
+ Team management during exploration with random events.  You have to make sure everybody can eat, that food doesn't go bad, that injured people get healed and you can research some techonologies.  Your teammember can also get hurts during hunting, or  your cart can break and you loose your movement for the day or, you can get attacked during the night.  And those attacks can be really though.
- There is not enough variety of random events and you often see the same one coming over and over again.  At one point, they lose their magic.
- You can solve the team micro-management.  At some point, when you have enough competent member on your team, you'll have it figured it out.  The injured will be healed, everybody is gonna be well fed, medicine and traps will be produced, etc.  May be there could have been a little more strugle there.
+ Comabts where stategy matters.  Fights can get tough, you have to think and use your skills to overcome.  Not only you will to choose a good team for the fight but you'll also have to use the environement and, if you can, prepare the battlefeild (with baricade and traps).
+ The game doesn't necessarily scale to your progression.  You can venutre and encounter groups of enemy way stronger than you currently are.  And you probably will. And get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked.
+ Loosing a fight is not the end of the world.  Even some important fight in the storyline can be lost.  The game will account for it but there is no game over screen.  Adjust to the defeat and carry on.
+ Land exploration is not just to get to one point to the others.  You can find stuff.  Not only treasure but also quest, ally, ressource and even village.  It doesn't feel like you're just going through; ou have to explore and discover. And finding your way is not always easy.
- A lot of quest have you go around from point a to point b.  Those are fine when point b is new to you  but when it's a place you already visited, and you have go do a lot of back and forth, it can get boring.
+ Music is good and appropriate.
- Sounds effect are not that great.
- Graphics and animation are not the best. Also, the whole color palette is really bland.  I guess they were going for something more realistic but I wish they would have opted for more saturated colours.
- There is no enough of it.   Ok, this is not a real objection.  My first playthrought took me about 23h.  Pretty decent for a 20$ game.  But seriously...
- The map is a little small.  May be, once again it is just that I want more but, at first, the world seem really vast then, you realize it is no so.
That's about it.   I hope this will help you make an informed decision.
Final score: 8.5/10

Speedrunners, a game of reflexes and grapple hooking your friends.
You really should get this game, honestly. It's definitely worth the friend rage. Also, the only issue I have right now would be the blast zone lines aren't transparent, which they should REALLY do.
Analysis:
Speedrunners is a game of running around a big map, grapple hooking your way to first place. Of course, it's only possible to grapple white ceilings, so the majority (unless allowed) of the map is going to be running, picking up item boxes, and trying to get to first place. What you have to do is make sure you keep on running til you can't. By that time you've hopefully won your first round. The game is in Early Access right now, but it's getting a lot better! The controls are also configurable and it's really best with a controller.
The items while not that plentiful are actually really fun regardless. You have rockets to shoot at people, EMP blasts to destroy: grapples, golden grapples, boxes, and also rockets; invincibility shield drill which protects you from harm, golden grapples which hook onto the closest player in the direction you face, and 3 boxes.
Speedrunners also has a nice twist to it where you can choose different modes to play. The most frustratingly fun has to be the mirrored track mode. Rapture just shoots rockets everywhere, lethal spikes, all X (X being either rockets or golden grapples last time I checked), and there may or may not be another I'm forgetting at the moment, but that's the fun of this game.
tl;dr Speedrunners is a REALLY fun friend rage-inducing game that makes you want to keep trying to aim for the top, but also can be played casually enough for fun.

I'm not much of a reviewer but, I'll sumarise this game as best as i can. And I hope this review will help to support this game.
This game is what i would call a story telling rogue-like/lite adventure rpg card game with the Arkham Style fighting system. Seem like alot to put into game but it works well.
In this game you must traverse the card layed out by the card dealer. The cards are semi- randomised but, I'll go into more detail later. You click on the card adjacent to where you current position is and then experience the story behind that card which results in either a fight, a choice, a lucky dip or any combination of the three. Then eventually reach the end of the level.
The combat in the game seems to be solid for the most part. The way you fight is simillar if not the same to Batman games style of combat. You move with "wasd", "space bar" to roll/dodge,"q" to counter, "left click" to attack and "right click" to stun. There are also ranged units which can be blocked by your shield. Unless they have a rifle in which case you have to dodge. With as much as I have played so far, the combat seems to be solid, it's not as smooth as it could be and seems a bit jittery, but nothing too extreme. There are also ranged units which can be blocked by your shield. Unless they have a rifle in which case you have to dodge. I have had no problems with the combat so far.
The bosses seem to have a bit of variation. Their mechanics are different depending on their species and the amount and way they attack differ from one to another. There are 12 bosses and so far i have beaten 3, fought 4 as of initially typing this. I have yet to face the later on bosses so unfortunetly I have no experience against them to share as of yet. But, you can still tell when you are in a boss fight and you feel satisfyed to win against them.
There are 4 mains enemies you face against, Dust - Bandits, Skull - Skellingtons, Lizard and another which i have yet to encounter. They each are weak to a diffent thing which makes you fights easier or harder depending on the elements of your gear. There are other enemies such as golbins and rats which you face against from their specific event but they all got their own gimic to. Rats will leave a poisonous cloud, goblins will steal your items and won't fight back but will instead try to escaps, so on, so forth.
I huge mechanic in this game is the cards. The cards you get in the events you play depend upon the cards you use to build your deck. You get two decks, equipment and events. You unlock more cards through completing events. The cards you unlock are set so it's not all randomised. However, the cards dealer throughs in a couple of his own cards to teach you more mechanics about the game such as enemy types and to prevent you from picking cards which give you a load of free stuff.
When you start off the game, it start off at a beginers pace, to allow you to get use to the controls. It then steadily escilates in difficulty so you are more reliant on your skill and cards you pick. I personally think that the game scales well in difficulty, but you also affect it by the cards you choose. Exsample - If you choose all fights cards, then you could get good loots, but at the same time loose alot of health. If you choose alot of simple equip events, then you will be stuck with low level stuff against the boss. Finding balance is crucial.
I personally think this game is well made. It plays quite well and the combination and implementation of all the mechanics are great. I would recomend this to people who enjoy rogue-like and/or RPG games with similar combat systems. Regardless of the fact that this game is in early acess at the time of this review, I think if it was released how it is, it would be well worth the price.

Wow- pretty amazing game. It's a cross between Talisman (the board game), Pathfinder Adventure Card Game, and Diablo, and it integrates all of those into a consistently fun whole. I have found myself willing to fight a hard battle before the boss (even knowing I will die at the boss if I do) because I will get a card to add to my deck. The decisions create tension.
Even the luck elements - of which there are many - feel different than a die roll because you get to choose. Yes, it's still the exact same amount of randomness, but it somehow feels like "If I had only chose that one...I was going to choose that one..."
The negatives:
1) Luck can be a harsh mistress
2) On my very middle-of-the-road system, the frame rate drops on complex battles to where it's almost a guaranteed fail
3) I had to go get a controller - the mouse and keyboard were just too clunky
The positives:
1) The dungeon master's voice. I usually get annoyed by voice acting, but this is masterful.
2) In story mode, even though it's roguey, it still feels like a story
3) Fantastic mash-up of different types of gameplay - the ability to pick the encounters I'm going to face and the range of equipment I'll have access to is brilliant.
4) The arkham-style combat is fun, and as frustrating as it is to have goblins steal your shield (which makes counters and blocks unavailable), it emphasizes that these are not just multiple game modes strung together, but multiple facets of a single experience.
Even though I've died a lot, I have almost always earned something, and I've always wanted to continue. I tend to have a low frustration tolerance these days, but the thought of "having" to play a level again just doesn't bother me. Excellent game.

My favourite game (and it will stay like that for some time), Mass Effect 2 delivers a great story within this excellent RPG. I really reccomend playing Mass Effect first, because this game imports your save file and all your important decisions with it (although you may change your appearance and class at the start of the game). Choice is again an important element of the game and it makes it into a personal experience. The combat mechanics are again pretty good and the ai is a bit smarter than in the original game. The voice acting is once again great, as well as the supporting characters whose personal storylines make the game even better.
One minor flaw exept for the pc controls is that the graphics aren't always the best (low-res textures), even on the highest settings, but you need to keep in mind that the game is getting pretty old.
Windows 8 users might need to use Windows xp sp3 compability mode and (if you're using it) you need to turn of Lucid Virtu MVP to play without crashes.

A remarkably unique take on the space trading genre, Helium Rain is doing Early Access right.  You'll find bugs, typos, all the old favorites, but the developers are extremely receptive (they even have their own Redmine server you can log and track bugs in) and quick to turnaround fixes and enhancement.
Past the Early Access considerations, you're left with a very compact, but utterly hypnotic space trading/combat game.  "Compact" because HR eschews the current trend of "fifteen trillion stars!" for just a handful of planets and sectors, but those planets and sectors are never without plenty to do, from running simple courier missions to building space stations, developing a trade fleet, commanding an economic empire.  Fly one ship while the rest of your fleet is own doing your bidding (and hopefully making some money while they're at it.)  For me it's almost reminiscent of something like Euro Truck Simulator 2 in that regard.  Except in space.  And with guns.
On the surface, look at the screenshots.  The washed out, high-contrast colors and dreamlike music confer one of the most "chill" space games I can remember.  The clean UI is occasionally fiddly, occasionally brilliant, and while it might look a bit too much like your cable box UI, it does the job and continues to improve.
Even this early, I find it one of the more compelling space games in my library.  And unlike some games that provide an entire galaxy but leave you wondering what to do next, more than once I've forgotten what I'd planned to do because something else more interesting came up, and then forgot I was doing THAT because something even more interesting than that came up.  Even while you're blissing out to the celestial look and feel, you'll never be bored.
If any of this sounds good to you, and you don't mind the vagaries of Early Access, I'd say, hit that Buy button immediately.

And it has a ton of replayability. There are a wide array of skills that dramatically increase the effectiveness of certain mutually exclusive parts (like a shield or a cloaking device) and also allow access to interesting and unique versions of said item. So for instance you might play through one game using cloaks and missiles, whereas another game you might not use a cloak or a shield and instead rely on armor, hull and improving the capability of your crew to repair damage while you're taking it. Options, options, options. All quite well balanced and viable, even if some are 'more viable' than others.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a third-person adventure game, in which you play the role of a ghost, who needs to find out about his mysterious murder.
You're playing Ronan O'Connor, a detective, who gets murdered right at the beginning of the game. The Murderer itself gets away unidentified and you're staying in this world as a ghost, to find out what happend, why and who did it.
The game itself is very story-driven. You're walking (or running) around the different hubs, interacting with items or persons, trying to find clues (and combining them) about your murder or the victims of the serial killer, which you were after at the beginning.
There are also various collectibles to be found, which will keep you occupied (if you like things like this).
Graphics are pretty neat and i liked the atmosphere of the game, though, even as you visit different scenes and buildings, the overall look doesn't change drastically. A bit more variety could have been better.
The story kept me entertained quite well and had also some nice twists throughout the game.
There is one part, which could be frustrating: from time to time demons appear on your path, which you'll either need to evade or destroy. THis only happens at certain points in the game (not often) and if you kill them, they'll be gone forever and won'T reappear.
It's not *that* hard, but if you don't like things like this in an adventure game, then you might have a little hassle here.
Apart from that, i can recommend this to all players, which like fairly easy, story-driven adventure games.

This game is early access. That's something to keep in mind.
I've encountered a couple of very minor bugs, none of which interrupt the game. It runs stable, great frame rate, and haven't had a crash at all. Which can't be said for a lot of other games in early development on Steam (and in full release too).
The game itself feels like the X series with Elite and mildly inspired Kerbal Space Program. The physics make it interesting and while at first I was concerned it would be a chore to fly around with the momentum, the game is good about adjusting to your controls and where your mouse is pointing (or where you adjust your view if you use a gamepad).
The game does feel sparsely populated and stations are relatively close together. I haven't played very long (4 hours in), but there doesn't feel like much reason to explore just yet. On the other hand I'm still doing tutorial contracts and understanding the game, so there might be a lot that opens up. There appears to be a story/plot that you can follow, but seems to be ultimately an optional contract to start.
Trading works like you would expect. Stations require specific resources. Some produce specific resources. You purchase the products and sell them to places that have them in demand. One unique aspect in the game is a live economy. It's a welcome aspect that causes natural changes in prices and I look forward to using this to my advantage as I progress in the game.
While the interface seems relatively bland and light, it works very well. The docking information is very helpful in lining up your ship and feels satisfying to have the magnetic bonding occur when you get close. Finding the right information in the menus is a bit of an issue. It feels cumbersome to look up where locations are, how long it'll take to fly there, then enter another menu to look up economic information. On one hand I'd hate it if it made it extremely clear since half the fun of a game like this is finding a trade route, not just having it handed to you. On the other, I'd like to see this design improved in the future. As you start to get additional ships, this sort of management process is more crucial. However there is an option to make trade routes that I assume send your other ships out to do the route automated. If that's the case, then there isn't much issue once they go on their merry way.
Ultimatly I'm happy with this game at this price point. The game feels light on polish and interface, but feels relatively solid in features and content. I'm hoping to see a wider variety of locations, ships, equipment, and items to move in the future, but there's a lot of potential here and the developers are very active on Reddit and on their own forum. This is cleary a work of love, not for a quick buck.

Space Pirates and Zombies appears at first glance nothing more than a retro style, 2d space shooter. But after playing it a lot, multiple playthroughs and challenges, it has a ton of depth lying beneath it's 2d surface.
You start as the leader of a small band of merchant pirates yourself seeking your fortune by collecting mineral deposits call rez. There are rumors of enormous stockpiles or rez near the core worlds so you set off to seek them out. Along the way you encounter zombies and eventually take on the gargantuan task of ridding the galaxy of them.
The first thing you do is set your world settings. There's multiple difficulty levels, 5 or 6 in total so you can vary your experience immensely, as well as settings for galaxy size, pirate density and tech distribution. You can create a unique experience for every game.
Once you are playing the game has three main areas. First is the galaxy and system maps. You travel to different systems and you can select various missions in each one to level up your crew, buy or steal tech and collect rez and ship designs. The systems all have different levels so you have to decide what you can potentially accomplish.
The next big part is your ship loadout screens, tech and hangar. In the tech screen you spend data (experience) that you have gather to level up various ship systems like beam weapons or shields. Each level increases the effectiveness of your systems and some levels are a prerequisite to advanced tech. Like you need level three beams to deploy particle beams or something. Then in the hanger you choose which hulls to use and what systems to put on them. You start with three hangars at the beginning of the game and get four by the end with larger capacity for larger hulls.
The final major area is actually flying your ships on the planet or area of interest screens. They aren't always combat screens, some missions you might gather rez for example. But while on these screens you can switch control between all your ships as well as issuing orders to the other ships to do certain things like rendezvous over here or attack this target. Sometimes pirates show up, sometimes zombies, all depends on the mission. I found there to be a good variety of events and missions.
The actual combat is extremely interesting if you make it challenging enough. Because there are so many types of ships and systems the way you fight can be varied. You might make a fast missile boat ship and whittle targets down while keeping out of their gun range. Or you might make a stealth capable ship, get in close and crush em with high powered beam cutters. Or maybe you want to use rotating turrets to track fast moving targets. It's up to you, there's no wrong way to do it, and a lot of times you have to adjust on the fly based on the tech available.
Hull designs are obtained by killing enemy ships of that hull. Sometimes one ship is enough but most need 3 or 4 blueprint pieces. Tech for subsystems like weapons, engines and all that is obtained from planets either by trading with them or blowing up their bases and taking it. There's also specialist crew members who give you distinct bonuses like +10% cannon damage. So that has to be taken into account as well.
In all there's a ton of ways to customize your game and your ships and it's very fun. I enjoyed leveling in this game immensely. The only downside is the hardest difficulties are REALLY hard and you end up basically grinding resources in low level areas to advance. But hard should be hard so I commend the devs for doing that. I guess you could fly smarter, not harder, if you're really good and get by with less.
Finally there's challenges too via a little space arena the pirates run. It's a good way to make money and there's some achievements with it. Some are very hard.
This game simply rocks and you have to try it.

WARNING ! Do not consider the steam in game time, for I played it before and also offline. I was part of the alpha and beta testers for this game, but I promess you a truthful and most unbiased review ;)
Helium Rain is a game where you manage a company in an isolated space system, in a distant future. You start with only one small commercial ship, and you will have to progress step by step to become the best of all companies. You have a lot of ways to play. You can focus on a very commercial  approach, focusing on building up your fleets with gigantic cargos, establishing numerous trade routes and invading all the markets, you can build stations to produce or transform materials... Or try a mostly violent approach, using fleets of warships and destroying pirates, selling your services to companies in need ( and that can pay ).
Of course, it'll take time. You have to work really hard, and the game may seem to slow down after the first hours of gameplay. But it is here that you can really start exploring all of its possibilities, and as I said, there is an awful lot of them ( trust me, I saw when the devs implemented them in the game following testers reviews ).
Of course, the game is not perfect and will not suit everybody. It is a slow paced game, do not expect overflowing action, even though combats are there, and they are really fun and a bit hard to play. But if you like what I told you this game propose, then you shall like it, for what it does it does it really well. It is a truly beautiful game, the music suits the atmosphere very well, it is calm and a bit contemplative. The gameplay is really well polished and it is quite easy to do things once you have learned how to from the many tutorials explaining the various aspects of the game.
I do strongly recommend this game to anyone who likes this kind of games !

This is a very tentative positive recommendation, since Valve did not see fit to allow neutral reviews.
The first impressions of this game are outstanding. Starting by choosing a group with contrasting characteristics emphases the strategy which will have to be employed in making decisions throughout the game. Getting into the game itself, you are met with lush visuals, quality writing, some genuinely interesting strategic and moral decisions with branching results and nice music. There are lovely little touches, such as echos to sound effects when combat is in a confined area.
Over time, though, flaws emerge. Combat is the major one, being a significant part of the game. It is remarkably difficult and frustrating - not through particularly clever AI (indeed, it can be quite dumb, including soldiers standing still while you take potshots at them on one combat map) but through overwhelming numbers and often superior quality troops. Melee combat is overpowered and classes are unbalanced.
Combat can be quite sluggish, and the lack of a fast-forward key is an oversight (there is an option to increase the speed generally, but that's it).
The camera is frustrating, with your view on the world map constantly blocked by trees.
Some aspects of the game are quite unintuitive. For instance, some quests need to be turned in at a town in the first map. Once you have triggered an event in the main quest, though, going into the town will only allow you to access that. Win that battle, and you still can't turn in your quests. A very frustrating situation for players - at least those who don't somehow intuit that you will be able to turn quests in again a couple of days later.
The biggest problem, though, is constant crashes. These problems have affected a number of users and the only potential solution is to turn down graphics settings - even on some systems which meet the recommended requirements  (which really should be revised) - and even then it does not always assist.
That's a lot of negativity, but I still lean towards recommending it. It's rough around the edges, but well-written, attractive and challenging games deserve attention, especially when produced by a novice studio like this one. By all means give it a go, and I hope you don't suffer the same crashes that I did before buying a new system.

My personal experience with this was quite good. Despite being fairly generic on the surface, it bears mentioning that ArcheAge has a good deal of depth even in beta events. Improvised towns crop up in housing areas, and it seems that the Northern Continent will solidly deliver on the mass sandbox experience promised. Labor Points are a concept, limiting a number of actions. However they come at such a rate that unless you are substantially grinding as one might feel impetus to do in a limited closed beta, that they do not notably impact gameplay if at all.
Above all however, ArcheAge is simply fun, and that's what matters in the end. There's enough spread of features between sandbox elements and themepark elements that you have enough to do in one to support the other. The community can be annoying, but blocking problem players is always an option and in the end you're better off for it. Simply put, I recommend the silver pack if you want a somewhat to substantially different experience and a good time.

Lumini isn't really bad, but it is mediocre. It’s a game that dares to ask the question: What if Pikmin were really, really monotonous?
Lumini has some nice elements — the visuals are evocative, the story was told with mild competency — but it, once again, fails as a game. The entire game consists of moving to the right through tunnels and sometimes opening doors. The door puzzles start simple and stay simple, even as you power up your Pikmin-sperm. After you upgrade the red ones twice, you can 1HKO any enemy, and the puzzles are never more complex than pushing buttons and twisting valves. At the end, sometimes you have to push a few buttons in a row; this is the game’s idea of a challenge. The ‘secrets’ are all hidden in plain sight, and in some cases it’s not even clear what certain pickups do — what was the point of collecting those crystals? of the green orbs? I also found the lack of control explanation really annoying. Again, not explaining the game to me isn’t clever, it’s just bad game design. The most irritating was that I only realized halfway through that the upgrade orbs weren’t set — that is, if you switched your active color Pikmin-sperm, the cube color would change. I passed a bunch of them because they were all red and it was only when I started to wonder when I’d run into the other color upgrades and started fooling around with the controls that I realized it was based on your active color.
Relatedly, I thought the game used its own mechanics poorly. You could split your Pikmin-sperm into two teams, one controlled by WASD and one the arrow keys. But the only way the game could come up with to utilize this was to have you press two switches at once. And it wasn’t even like, you had to guide the two groups through two separate mazes or anything — the switches were always right next to each other. There is so much cool stuff that you could do with that mechanic, and they opted to do next to nothing. I actually get the sense that the dev couldn’t decide if it wanted an ABZU-style experiential thing — which, frankly, could have worked here — or a puzzle game, and so kind of ended up settling for neither, the worst of both worlds.
Also, while I found the story cute, it really doesn’t hold up to much scrutiny. Why did the Chozo-thing die so far away from their home base? Why not bring the lumini directly to the central one instead of forcing them to make this absurd journey there? Why not forgo the lumini and have the save-the-planet system self-activate? What kind of culture can create an elaborate system to revitalize their entire planet but can’t just fix a drought directly? Why did they wait until they were all almost dead to set the lumini into motion anyway?
Ultimately, this was just a game that promised a lot more than it delivered, and felt like it lacked the confidence to go all-in on any of its aspects.

Lumini is a pleasant, well-made game about destroying every living thing in the planet with your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ murderflies. It's described on its store page as "relaxing", more an "experience" than a game, and so on - which feels true but is not exactly so, since there are tons of secrets to find and enemies that to (theoretically) avoid or, more likely, shockwave into cute little corpses. Your horde of genocidal insect-things will quickly learn how to kill other living beings, and then it's kind of hard to stop before the whole world's ecosystem is brought low. I'm pretty sure that is how the game is intended to be played.
It's very pretty, with great music and a surprising variety of environments. Unfortunately I didn't really find it to be a lot of fun - I never clicked with the controls, with their weird dead zone while rotating the analog sticks, and the puzzles never really evolve into something that's actually interesting to solve. I never felt the splitting mechanic really came into its own, either. However, finding secrets and destroying every animal and plant in my path was compelling enough to see me through to the end. The difficulty is low enough that you can almost treat this as a flittering simulator, taking in the sights and enjoying all the murder. How dare these filthy vegetable-ish things try to spread their pollen in my vicinity? I'll show them. I'll show them all.

I am going to tell a story to all who are willing to hear of how our tribe of Lumini left our home to find a safe haven, but first I have to tell you the culture and the social structure of our society. First I think you should know who your Narrator is: I am a Purple Lumini who the other Lumini call 'Mythic'. The first group of Lumini lived peacefully for thousands of years. They lived a complex life and communicated like how dolphins do. Every morning we would send out Blue Lumini which were known for their speed. The Blue Lumini were known as the scouts who would search out and find energy orbs which is our way of life. Energy orbs is like how honey is to bees. The Blue Lumini would go out with Yellow Lumini which could gather the energy orbs and bring them back to our home so we could grow and expand. We built great structures and we improved our way of life day by day. Prosperity and abundance abounded. Then one day, our gathers came back and some were missing. The ones who survived told of terrifying tales of horrifying monsters and deadly wildlife. Soon we had to send Red Lumini out with the scouts and gathers so they could defend them. Even then we still lost some Lumini every time we left the safety of our home. Soon it was clear that our once peaceful home was riddled with a growing evil, and that we had to leave. This is the story of the jounrey of the Lumini to their new sanctuary.

I remember the day when our chieftain, a Blue Lumini named 'Big Blue', decided that it was time to leave our homes to find a new place where we could be safe and live like we used to. Big Blue was one of the wisest and the most trusted Lumini that I have ever met. He was the biggest Blue Lumini I have ever seen. His son, Lil' Blue, was being raised to take the place of Big Blue because Big Blue was very elderly. Ironically Lil' Blue was one of the smallest Blue Lumini. So when Big Blue said that we should leave our homes for a safe haven that might not even be out there no one doubted him. I feared that the journey would be too much for Big Blue physically. When I spoke to Big Blue about my concern he told me not to worry because he was youthful in spirit. I knew there was no way I could talk him out of it so I started to help with the countless preparation of getting ready for the journey.  The morning we were going to leave had an electricity in the air that I will never forget. Our group started out with one Purple Lumini (the narrator), three Red Lumini (the warriors), two Yellow Lumini (the gathers), and seven Blue Lumini (the scouts and Big Blue). The first few days the travel was light and we gathered energy orbs as we went. The more we traveled the more of the world I was able to see. Maybe the journey wouldn't be as bad as I may have feared.

The more distance we covered the more dangers slowly started popping up. At first there were just red spikes we had to avoid which was easy enough. Then there were deadly plants that would shoot out poisonous spikes which wasn't a problem with the great leadership of Big Blue. There were many obstacles we had to get through, but again Big Blue guided us with such wisdom that we got through them without a problem. As we traveled we found ourselves in a huge opening and up ahead at the only way to exit was a flying monster. . Its teeth was almost the size of Lil' Blue, and its size was bigger than our group put together. We waited hoping that the beast would leave, but it did not budge. The sun was starting to go down, and Big Blue knew if we did not find shelter soon that we all would be doomed. Big Blue knew there was only one option left. He signaled for Lil' Blue to lead the whole group through the opening once the monster moved. Big Blue went forward and zoomed past the monster and it started to chase after Big Blue. Once the opening was clear Lil' Blue lead the group through the opening. I took one look back and I saw Big Blue fighting back against the monster, but the odds were too much and Big Blue was stricken down with a fatal blow. As we found shelter for the night there seemed to be a fog in the minds of every Lumini in the group. Will Lil' Blue be able to lead us? Can Lil' Blue handle the new responsibility as chieftain? Only time can tell...

This game made me hate the now typical practice in not only "Free to Play" games, but in most MMO's in general.
I looked into this game a couple of years ago because I wanted something simple and easy to jump in/jump out whenever I wanted to "play" a game but not really play a game.  You know, do something to kill time until other obligations spring up or if I can't decide what other game I want to play instead.   I treated this game as a snack; something to enjoy in the meantime before the real meal comes up.
At first I was pretty happy.  It was nice, colorful, and simple.  And despite the atrociously generic characters (little girl with a big sword, little loli mage, blonde haired elf archer, etc), I still enjoyed playing with them for a while.
And then it hit me like an angry flaming brick wall;  You're not allowed to even have simple fun unless you're willing to shell out the cash.
"It's free to play!", you exclaim. "Of course they'll charge you for SOMETHING."
Fair enough.  But I shouldn't have to pay money out for an extra skill slot.  Little things the game throws at me shouldn't require extra cash when I never wanted the item in the first place.  And all the base, free costumes are incredibly ugly... which is to incentivize players into paying more money for their costumes.
And on that note; the Pay to Win.   If ANYONE tells you that isn't true just know that they're lying.   Those stat increases are insane!  It doesn't matter how well you are at the game because little Johnny Morebucks can buy an insta-kill weapon and BOOM! You're dead.  No glory, no skill.  Just a whiny kid with his daddy's money.
Typically I wouldn't mind handing over a few bucks for a neat costume.  But this is insane.   The stuff you can buy with real cash are incredibly overpriced and needlessly over-powered for no adequately explained reason.  And after a certain point it's almost as if the game expects you to start throwing money away just so you can progress.  That's insane.
Games like this are an embarrassment.  If you want to make a Free to Play game, then go for it.  You want to charge a little for a neat outfit or an accessory?  By all means.  But don't charge $40+ for a single complete outfit and then jack up the buffs to where you become unto a God.   I know what it means to have fun; it means to feel as though you've accomplished something.  That YOU became powerful on your OWN merits.  Not by buying it.
And this all doesn't even address the grind.  Dear god almighty the grind.  "Oh, an MMO that makes you grind? How absurd!"  I know, this isn't anything new to MMO's.   But this makes a grind and turns it into a tedious, required chore where the end never comes into view.  It's just over and over whacking the same bland enemies with the same bland backdrop with the same obnoxiously bland sound effects to the track of some bland, forgettable pseuo-electro pop nonesense.
I'm also ignoring the whole "weeaboo" thing but... hey, it's Elsword.  Young anime girl with unnatural hair weilding a big sword.  What did you expect?
No, I don't reccommend this game.  It should be pushed aside.  This sort of practice should not be encouraged.  And I don't care how much money you borrow from your family/friends, or how much you earn to justify spending it on this.  You're paying for numbers and pixel clothes.   That's depressing.
Fun and rage inducing at the same time!! Wouldn't quite reccomend if your friends don't have this game, it's 100% better with friends!

I will not comment on game play, since that has probably been explained a million times over in other reviews and videos. But this I will say:
The Dealer is your Narrator, as well as your Savior and your Opponent. He has offered you the chance to play his Game. As the Player, you are in charge of a pawn - a nondescript adventurer. You are given cards upon which the Game is played. You build the pawn's equipment deck, and the story's encounter deck. The Dealer will deal out the cards and lead you on an incredible tale of greed, hubris and honor. Your pawn will face endless, faceless foes as well as specific boss villains. There will be violence, traps, treasure and horror. The Dealer will attempt to entice you to send your pawn into situations most peril for the offer of a few tokens. These tokens unlock more cards, which unlock more adventure and equipment/treasure.
And as you defeat each boss villain, the Dealer will put the card into his cabinet, where you will be able to choose the next villain. Defeat a row of villains, gain a special item. But beware, every Game, every card, every victory will add to the complexity and danger that your pawn will face as you struggle to reach and win the final Game. Your pawns will die, but never fear - there are countless pawns waiting for you to guide them.
Who is this man in the robe, who created these cards that influence a world, individuals and items? Who are you, Player? Are we Gods who are meant to play with the lives of mortals? Maybe.
You'll have play to experience it.

Hello there! If you're reading this, you're looking for a review on Fable: TLC, and i aim to please you with such.
Fable - The Lost Chapters ( Fable:TLC for short) is the PC-Port of the game Fable 1 with added content & storyline, which also got released on the Xbox slightly after, the game focuses on being an action third player person view game which allows you to roleplay and costumize your character(hero) whether it be through skill, personality or appearance in various different ways.
Throughout the entire game, you'll be given choices of which are categorized by beither either "good" or "evil", and by doing said actions, you gain points for each one, being evil will modify your character's visual look and make him look visibly like a demon, otherwise, by doing good, you'll have a halo on your head, and your hair will turn white alongside having butterflies fly around you.
Do these actions actually matter towards the storyline? Yes, they do, you're given different cutscenes depending on what path you take and certain things change in the game as well as having different spells you can master.
I'll be appointing each section a numerical value between 1 and 10 to make it easier and to allow quick TL;DR for those who don't really care for the in-depth review.
-- Graphics --  (7/10)
The game was originally released in 2004, then had it's expansion released in the later year of 2005, i'd state the graphics are very good for it's age and that they do not look bad at all, even if you think that way, the game is quite customizable and you can use mods to enchance your gameplay performance. ( There's also Fable:TLC Anniversary on Xbox now.)
Are there any bugs regarding the graphics? Very little, you may experience some errors occasionally regarding character glows or weapon glows or entering a new area and the loading being awkward, but nothing out of the extraordinary.The game brings widescreen support so you also don't have to worry yourself about any of the screens bigger than 4:3 ratio.
Some may be annoyed by the character's textures, but i think they look fine for the age of which the game was produced.
-- Gameplay -- (7/10)
The initial parts of the game hold very little action as it is showing you the storyplot, but as soon as you're done with the "Wasp Queen" quest, you'll start to frequently experience more and more action.
The gameplay is very action-based and revolves around you as a hero focusing on the utilization of three main powerpoints, Strength, Skill(Speed, accuracy and stealth) and Will( Magical prowess), you spend points on these throughout the gmae in order to improve your character's statistics.
Similarily to an MMO, the way to gain those points is by killing enemies, or doing quests, which will gain you "experience points", points that can be used to tap in all three of the major areas, or you can utilize specific points to each one.
Ingame, you're given the option of going in full melee, sitting back with a bow or utilizing magic to enchance yourself, or a mixture of all of them, i believe that they did the variation very well and that there's no real downsides here, at times the characters may be able to hit you through awkward hitboxes, but that doesn't happen frequently.
You may experience annoyance at the GuildMaster's constant bickering if you do not heal your Will/HP energy points up by either eating/utilizing a potion.
NPC spawns are predictable and very rarely change with area when it comes to the enemy AI, they mostly repeat the same process over and over, HOWEVER, the AI is not to be underestimated as it is quite random and at times it will DECIDE to hit you when you least expect it, or block attacks and counter-attack you back, so it does increase the difficulty and i say kudos on this.
For some, the game will be considered quite easy, and you will most likely not die a single time, the replay value in the gameplay is very high, so you can consider re-doing the game and even imposing challenges on yourself, or doing the "boasting" challenges that they grant you for each quest after the starter ones, allowing you to effectively increase the skill-cap required. ( Begins at the Orchard Farm quest).
Weapon variety is high, from a numerous amount of 1handed weapons, 2 handed, and allowing you to even change between crossbows and bows for ranged endeavors, the modding is also well open and allows the modification of weapons to create new custom-content or even apply other character weapons into your own.
Same applies for customization, you can customize your character in any way you'd like, ranging from tatoos, different titles, armor, mixing armor parts( boots, shirt, etc) and all sorts of fun stuff.
IE: You CAN get drunk in this game or become fat, and there are various mini-games, easter eggs,jokes & Demon doors along the way so that the gameplay is not constantly filling your face with action, same for the side-quests which allow you to take a small break from the main one.
You can abuse certain points of the game to get your character stronger than it should be at the current time or grab items that you otherwise would have difficulty having through the "Hero Save" option, or by utilizing a trader glitch that allows you to gain more everytime you buy and resell specific items at the early stages of the game allowing you to rack up a large amount of gold. But these do not necessarily break the game for me, and you can choose not to utilize them in the first place as they were player-created.
More on the "Hero Saving", you have two types of save, a "World" save in which it saves your current position and everything you hold, and a "Hero Save" which saves your items currently held and puts you at the initial scene of the quest, you MAY not save your location ingame during an ongoing quest which may annoy some.
A trait that may be annoying for some is the aging system which is based on your skill progress.(age increases as you level skills)
Others may get bored out of the action-combat due to having too much experience with the game, however the replay value is great even then.
-- Performance -- (8/10)
The game's performance is great, it works even on older PCS with outdated graphic cards, and it has many numerous options in order to tone down the graphics, i did not feel at any time any moment of which i had a drop of FPS.
The game is compatible with different types of OS so you do not need to worry about having Vista, XP or Windows 7, as they all work.
There is a slight problem in that the game will SOMETIMES CRASH unexpectely and for unknown reasons, or simply NOT play Audio clips at times it should, however it does have a safe-mode itself and you can usually run that if you run into any performance issues.
-- Audio -- (6/10)
The OST is decent, i feel as though it could've been better and it is lacking in a lot of fighting scenes / cutcenes, the ones that do have it are fitting though, nothing majorly special.
-- General -- (7/10)
I believe the game is quite legendary for it's time, even if you dislike it or hate it, it has created a giant fanbase and was one of the best prequels imagineable for the Fable series, many people to this day still prefer Fable:TLC over Fable II &  Fable III.
I would recommend this game to anyone who wants a game with a lot of fighting & magic, but at the same time wants to roleplay, enjoy himself and fascinate himself with the good story plot that it provides, making full use of the unique story-dialogue cutscenes given to you.( they may be boring for some but i for one love them)
It is a must-buy for any RPG-lover and if it's on sale i would definitely say get it as it's worth every penny unless you are not into the genre.
Thanks for reading this review, and i hope that gave you a good idea of what the game is like, allowing you to reconsider and ponder your opinion on whether to get it.

A genuine gem of a game. After hearing several good things about it I thought I would check it out. I'm so glad I did.
I know the anime cuteness look may make some people want to vomit, indeed this was my initial thought (I know that's a terrible way to judge a game) and this will put them off even considering buying it, and that is a massive shame. Yes it's cutesy Japanese nonsense and you will get that from start to finish but if you can look past its aesthetic there is a truly great game to be played here.
The main premise is that you run an item shop in an fantasy RPG style town and sell various items to various different customers. You acquire these items by either buying them from a couple of areas of the town, buying them from customers who come to sell them to you or from hiring an adventurer and running dungeons. You have to make a certain amount of money by the end of the week in order to pay off your fathers debt. This amount increases week on week making it harder and harder to pay it off.
By all rights it should be dull, the main bulk of the game is simply selecting the price of an item that a customer wants to buy and then haggling the price until the item is either sold or the customer leaves, that's it, but this becomes strangely compelling and remains fun.
The other main section of the game is dungeon crawling, and although not truly great it is solid enough experience that doesn't become too repetitive and provides you with several different adventurers to play as with different play styles.
In addition the translation is simply excellent, and nothing in the good and witty writing appears to have been lost in translation.
All in all Recettear: An Items shop's Tale is well worth a look, it goes far beyond any expectations I had for it, and is still delivering to me after finishing the main story section of the game, which admittedly isn't terribly long but this does unlock several new game modes as well as being able to continue beyond the main storyline with new content, and for a game that is pretty cheap anyway you will easily get more than you're moneys worth. A truly excellent game wrapped in great humour and originality, that deserves to be played by all.

This is one of the rare instances where finishing the game leaves me with the same feeling as finishing a good book. There was so much to keep me interested in the story; the history of the town, the plaques, the various ghost stories, that every collectible seemed valuable. There was nothing I was gathering that was going to give me a preposterous Western-themed in-game costume or a new gun or some flashy-yet-useless ghost-power. They all just added layers to the story of the game. I completed all achievements not because I cared, just because I wanted to know more about everything.
The gameplay itself was not overly complicated, but it was rewarding. If you take the detective work from L.A. Noire and strip out the gimicky facial-tic rendering and the occasional schizophrenic-Cole freakouts, you have Ronan's basic mystery-solving kit. Look around, analyze details, put clues together. Throw in some of the more entertaining mechanics for stealth or getting around from The Novelist to help navigate a Salem layered with history, and I made it through the game in short order without ever getting bored.
More games should be like this. All the depth and thought that goes into a walking simulator to create a rich and fascinating game world. Enough gameplay to keep you engaged without shoehorning in reasons to use their Advanced Ducking-Behind-Dumpsters technology. A character covered with tattoos that don’t grant magical powers, only capture memories or tell stories (much like real ink), whose only weapons the entire game are lost during and just before the opening cut-scene. Enough story to make everything incredibly gratifying through to the end. I only wish I would have known earlier how good it was: I would have paid full price right when it came out instead of waiting for a sale, to help drive home the point of just how much I would love to play more games like this.

Players looking for immersion, or simply to relax with the feeling of playing an action hero at the end of a busy day, will be left feeling intensely frustrated long before the tutorial is over. Experienced action/MMO players with better reflexes might have a better t/ime of things; Warframe also presents another strong positive, in that it runs very well on older machines.

The writing is quite excellent and reminiscent of older RPGs where we were expected to have some form of reading comprehension. The moral choices you make are actually tough decisions. Do you put down a revolt by force or do you leave the rebels alone (knowing that the rebels seek to create a free nation in this new world)? Do you smite the pagan tribe in the name of economic expansion or do you leave them at peace? Do you fight to the death or cut your losses and retreat?
This game truly forces you to slow down and think about your actions and their consequences, since every decision has ramifications. It's a refreshing change of pace from the linear and bland first person shooters that we get today that have no challenging thoughts whatsoever.
The only real issue so far is that you can't really pan the camera all that far, so it can be difficult to navigate the map.
If you're looking for a mature gameplay experience with a gripping tale, strong strategic combat, and freeform gameplay, this game is for you.

If you are into strategy "thinking" games with a historical bent you will love Ex:C.  It has several qualities that have kept me interested for 40 hours (and still going on first playthrough):
> The writing is fantastic.  The story revolves around your character, a spanish captain charged with exploring the new world shortly after Christopher Columbus made his initial "discovery".  You hand pick your expedition members each with well conceived bios and character traits. The story unfolds as you encounter new people and places, and is told through text and stylistically drawn images and portraits... the writing is so good I find myself hoping that the next village or encounter will have some description associated with it.  Honestly this adventure could be converted into a book.
> There are hard choices to be made. Most encounters provide an opportunity to choose your response, often with very tangible benefits and consequences.  Like the Walking Dead telltale series, the best choice is not always obvious.  Many times I left the choices up on the screen and went to do something else for a while to think about how to respond.  Although I could have simply chosen one reponse then reloaded the game if I did not like the outcome... the "role playing" feel is so intense doing so would break the immersion.
> Its an excellent survival simulation.  This game captures the feeling of being at the mercy of the land, and effectively manging your available resources to survive... especially at the beginning of the game.
> Its historically accurate.  Many people and places you encounter are based on historcal fact.  There are historical codex entries that unlock as you encounter them... this adds to the immersion.
> The tactical battles are fun.  The battles are based on a hex grid and are turn based like most games in this genre.  The battles can be very difficult in the beginning until you learn how to work with the available terrain and get the right mix of skills on the battlefield.  Once you unlock more advanced weaponry then the real fun begins.
I honestly did not encounter any bugs.  There are a few things I might change to fix some immersion issues:
1. Let doctors heal themselves.
2. Make using a lantern or cannon expend a party members turn.
3. For the cannon, make it necessary for someone to be next to it.
Very minor things that at this point I don't really worry about.  An excellent game and if there is a sequel I will snatch it up immediately.

Expeditions: Conquistador is a hidden treasure of a game that rewards the stalwart explorer. It deftly combines role-playing, strategy and survival mechanics into a unique gameplay experience enriched and informed immensely by its rarely explored setting. Cast in the role of a Spanish Conquistador arriving in the New World you choose from a wide selection of personalities to form your expedition and set off into Mexico to find glory. The environment is harsh and survival is a concern but the moral choices you are presented with are the most troubling dilemmas. You have the freedom and burden of choice in whether to exploit the native civilizations or forge alliances, supress pagan culture or study it, seek riches or pursue nobler ideals.
Equal parts Fallout, X-Com and Oregon Trail, every strategy aspect interconnects seamlessly. The setting is fascinating, the characters and events memorable and the combat system robust. A solid twenty five plus hour experience that never stopped surprising and left me wanting MORE.

Expeditions: Conquistador is a tactical roleplaying game set in early fifteenth century Central America during the Spanish conquest of Mexico; this is such an interesting and alien feeling setting, that throughout I wondered why more games and movies did not take place during this unique time period. The game's historical fiction setting, morally ambigious choices, great artwork, and music make this an incredibly atmospheric game, even if the graphics can be very basic at times, and the initial learning curve a steep one.
There are three primary parts of this game: the first is exploration of the game's two overworlds, where you balance party management and discovery. The second is the well written and character-centric dialogue, where you are forced to navigate numerous choices that have a number of effects on the long and short term outcomes of your adventure, and generally nudge you towards being a brutal leader, which feels very appropriate for the time period (you can certainly take the morally high road, though you will usually be the poorer for it). The final, and most significant portion of the game is the turn based combat, where, due to story events, decisions you have made, and random encounters on the overworld, your party of up to six fights an equal or greater number of enemies on a hexagonal based battlefield. There is a suprising amount of depth to be found here, despite the seemingly limited class-specific and special abilities.
The most impressive thing about Conquistador is despite some clumsiness in execution, and a repetition that inevitable sets in, all the different parts come together very well, and after an initially brutal difficulty curve, makes for an all-round enjoyable and challenging experience. This entire game was essentially a one-man project, and deserves your support; the developer has created a great and unique game template here, and I would love to see another Expeditions game set in a different era with similar gameplay. Conquistador is hopefully a great first entry in a larger series of historical fiction RPGs, and this is a recommended title if any of those sound the least bit appealling to you.

One last thing to mention (again, for the Steamers): while I was browsing the forums for this game, I saw that the developers are very active; they engage in discussions, provide help and are awesome people.

In-depth analytical video on Hand of Fate: (written review below)
The
of Hand of Fate are undoubtedly stellar. The high quality ranges from great sketches for every card, to beautiful 3D graphics as soon as the brawling starts. Most notably here are the lighting and special effects that manage to bring the whole scenery to life. Especially the fight against the Queen of Dust did impress me with its flying sand everywhere. Hand of Fate makes it abundantly clear that the overall aesthetics are not meant to be overlooked and it succeeds in creating a very appealing style overall.
Almost the same could be said about the
of Hand of Fate. The dungeon master for example is exquisitely voice acted, the effects give precise feedback and underline every nook and cranny. Sadly, all of the event texts are not voice acted and have to be read, which is understandable in terms of budget for voice acting, however sad due to the competent voice actor already in the game. Since the music is mainly meant to create an atmospheric background noise instead of carrying emotion or story, it is competent in what it tries to achieve, however forgettable. All in all, the sound design of Hand of Fate is very good, could however be improved in terms of the quantity of voice acting.
Let’s delve into the rather
of Hand of Fate. For every story adventure you start, not taking the endless mode into account, you prepare two deck of cards. On the left hand side the equipment that can be found during your dungeon crawling. Which consists not only of stronger weapons, but also of armour, helmets, gloves, rings, artefacts and trinkets. Ideally you would want to include cards specifically against a certain type of enemy that you suspect to encounter, however I mostly threw in new cards that I had not used before to keep the game experience fresh. On the right hand side of the decks, you can select the encounters that you want to possibly face during your adventure. Hereby it is important that some encounters cannot be removed until you fulfil certain conditions. The same procedures holds true as previously: I mainly selected encounters that I did either not face before to keep experiencing new content or that I did not manage to complete previously. As soon as you are satisfied with your decks, you start the story. Depending on the boss you plan to encounter at the end of the adventure, the card dealer adds some fixed cards into the mix, indicated by their purple tint and as soon as all decks are shuffled the game begins.
The dungeon master begins by laying down the encounters face down in a randomly selected pattern. Now you strife to reveal the final boss and defeat said enemy to claim victory of this part of the story. Your character is indicated as golden statue and you always move by one card either horizontally or vertically hereby consuming one food, healing a bit and revealing the encounter you step on. One possible card is the choose-your-own-adventure style encounters, whereby you select an option and more often than not the final result is determined by your selection of one of four cards, ranging from huge success to huge failure and thus affecting the outcome rather randomly. While the encounters themselves are fun at their core, I do see a problem in the random nature of selection as there is no skill or learning involved from the player’s side and thus it fails to feel rewarding when selecting success and at the same time also unreasonably punishing when you hit that huge failure card, especially when this ends up costing you your weapon just before facing the final boss. I would have preferred a system similar to how FTL manages random encounters by which certain abilities or other pre-collected items can affect the outcome positively.
Another possible encounter is one of the multiple combat scenarios. This is where the third person brawling comes into play and the graphical fidelity turns up several notches. Depending on the encounter or just by random selection you will be spawned into one of several arenas together with a bunch of enemies and possibly even traps. These short brawling segments are highly reminiscent of the Batman Arkham series without being as fluent and as responsive. Make no mistake, the brawling in itself is good, however the animations are not quite as top notch as the basically perfect ones of the Arkham games. Also, at least in the first three hours, the combat is not as strategic and as deep as the inspiration. Hand of Fate mainly relies on counter-attacking on green indicators and dodging on red indicators, while there are only very few special moves or strategic approaches to the combat in itself. This problem obviously arises as the game relies on random generation and thus you are always dependent to create enemies that could be faced with the basic equipment, while other story-driven games can later on throw enemies into your way that require you to use the latest acquired item or special move and the like. To summarise, the brawling is competent and refreshing, however does feel repetitive after a while. A perfect example for this is the spawning animation. While it is highly enjoyable the first few times your character spawns and gets all his equipment step by step and lastly your huge hammer falls from the sky just before you charge the flabbergasted and underpowered bandits, after a couple of hours game time though, I wished this animation could be skipped or disabled entirely, as it eats up so much time, especially when going from combat to combat encounter and thus this delay turns to be obnoxious rather quickly. Oh, and speaking of annoying, the camera cannot be rotated while in the combat arena, which can lead to some weird angles and fighting directions. Hopefully that will be fixed in the future.
After defeating the final boss at the end of the adventure or by dying in between due to combat or starvation, the tokens you collected along the way are opened and thus new cards are unlocked, keeping the encounters fresh and empowering your equipment for future approaches. With these new cards you start the cycle over again, selecting a new boss, adapting your decks and facing the latest random encounters you selected beforehand.
As I now played a little more and stand before the Queen of Skulls, I must say that the further the game progresses, the more infuriating the random nature becomes. There are several encounters with three failure cards resulting in severe penalties like losing 50 health and 30 permanent health, basically rendering the whole remaining adventure impossible. Also, due to the entirely random nature of encounters, it happened multiple times that I died on the first floor. Regardless of the incidents manage your health, your gear, and your food well and you may stay alive long enough to defeat the boss at the end of each dungeon and earn some excellent rewards for your next trip through.

Hand of Fate is a strange combination of genres - collectible card game meets 3rd person action. The premise is rather vague at present, but it boils down to you gambling for your life in a complex card game. You have an Encounter and Equipment deck, which you can edit as you see fit, and the cards are dealt into game boards of varying shape. You move around the board, revealing challenges and encounters, which you must then complete to move on. Some of them are choise or chance based, others are pure combat encounters, some are a mix of the two.
Completing encounters sometimes earns you more cards, which you can add to the deck for future games, and undesireable encounters can be removed, allowing an interesting sort of customization. Which encounters you see in a given game is still random, but you can influence the pool of encounters that's available.
The game features 12 bosses, each of which has some unique encounters, rules or effects to contend with, and after each 3 bosses, the old enemies get stronger, new encounters are introduced, and the player's starting equipment improves, creating a very well-designed progressive difficulty curve, where the same encounter card will increase in difficulty as the pool of enemies and detrimental effects grows.
Combat is simple but very fluid and works very well for the game. Your equipment has a great impact on how combat flows, and with a few exceptions, the controls are very tight.
Movement is a little clunky feeling - turning 180 degrees causes you to move to one side slightly (picture a very tight turn on a bicycle - you're can't turn in place), which doesn't usually cause problems, but some encounters involve negotiating complex series of traps, and imprecise movement can easily result in taking otherwise avoidable damage from these. Overall, this is a fairly minor inconvenience, though, and certainly isn't a major detriment to the enjoyment of the game.
Some attacks in combat 'track' targets, which is good, but they do it from a very long distance (often resulting in the character lunging around the battlefield from target to target). This works, but it looks a little silly, and it can be both beneficial and detrimental - it makes it easy to hit targets that're a good distance apart, but at the same time, it feels a little unpredictable, and will sometimes cause the player to lunge into an attack that they were well out of range of otherwise.
Some of the encounters feel a little unfair - for example, there's a (very) late-game encounter that gives you a 50% chance of failure - and failure means instant death. Once you've unlocked it, you can't remove it from the deck until you've 'succeeded' at the encounter, and I died to it 7 times before finally making that 50% die roll. Since there's very few ways to see that the encounter is coming up before you step on it, this feels a little cheap, and I could have done with less of this, but the flavor of the encounter was at least appropriate, and a single 'game' only takes 15-20 minutes in most cases, so dying to this card at least wasn't as frustrating as it could have been.
Overall, the game is extremely fun. It starts off slow and ramps up quickly with a very reasonable feeling difficulty curve, and the recent addition of an 'Endless' mode adds a ton of replayability even after defeating the 12 bosses. The 'ending' is not yet in the game (early access), but even considering only the content currently available (which is very substantial), this game is absolutely worth the money - even at 'full price', which is not something I will often say - if you enjoy the genres it's combining.

I think this game is really fun.  I am a sucker for games with random events and permadeath mechanics.  This game plays out as an adventure told by cards.  The player chooses which card to travel next until they reach the stairs to the next level or the boss at the end.  A card may have different effects during each game.  Example: One card has a goblin who helps you out in a bar.  Sometimes he gives you a shield and other times he may teleport you to a different card or floor.
When you encounter monster/creature cards, the game changes to a small enclosed area depending on the event.  The combat plays out, like the Batman Arkham games or Shadows of Mordor, into a multidirection freestyle fight with a simple attack, stun attack, counter with overhead popups, finishers for downed enemies, and different weapon abilities.
After the first three bosses in story mode the Endless mode is unlocked.  In Endless mode the player sees how far they can get, with each new floor adding a curse to make it harder as the game progresses.
Each move costs 1 food.  After your food runs out, the player loses 10 health per move.  You are able to purchase food at various shops and traveling vendors, however food is expensive making it a precious commodity.
Some things I would like the developmental team to add to the game:
* Add a back button when you go into Story mode so you are able to go back to Endless Mode
* Add more player models in case you get tired of the default character
* Add a way for players to see previous Endless Mode scores
* Add a multiplayer setup so players may travel an adventure together, with each player alternating who chooses the actions during the next event.  (I don't really know how this would be implemented, but the idea just kind of comes from playing Divinity)
I can't think of anything else that comes to mind.  Things I really like about the game:
* The card master guy is very well voiced
* The changing backgrounds make for nice scenery
* The many event cards add for replayability
* Trying to get the best results/success from an event to unlock new cards adds a challenge that doesn't entirely revolve around the combat system.
* Different results from the same card adds to the replayability
* Endless mode is a good alternative if you do not want to continue fighting bosses in Story mode
I would highly recommend this game.  However, the early access price ($24.99USD) is kind of high especially if you are unsure whether you really want to try it out.  I would suggest watching some gameplay videos on youtube first or add this to your wishlist so you can be notified when it goes on sale.

I didn't really like this game in Early Access, but it looks like the balance issues have been addressed for the release. As such I've updated my review for the game.
The tags on this game say "card game", but it's really just a roguelike, one extremely similar to FTL where you go through a chain of events with the occasional combat interspersed (hack and slash in this case). It's got a pretty good presentation and is very controller friendly. The combat is basically cloned from the Arkham series, complete with counters, guard breaks and combos. This game actually has challenge to it though. As shown with FTL its concept is very solid and fun even if you don't win a whole lot.
Luck is obviously a factor in a game with cards. Hand of Fate has some really, really unforgiving draws, curses and failure rolls that result in nearly game ending situations: halving your health permanently, blocking your healing, making basic combat moves cost resources... In early access you were also given next to no gold or food to manage around them. However that's no longer the case. The game feels more in line with the "roguelike" genre now, albeit with more severe shocks and less dwindling resources.
One of the coolest things about the game is the dealer and the way you play on the table with the cards all laid out. It's clear the developers put a lot of time and effort into creating the dealer and giving him charisma. Playing through the earlier part of story mode he's really neat and makes the game atmospheric. Once you get to the end though and finish most of the card storylines his lines narrow he can get a bit annoying taunting you/ parroting the same words over and over. There's a voice slider though so no biggie.
Overall this is probably the only game to actually do Early Access right that I've played. Balance wise the game was a mess but otherwise done save for polish when it hit. And in its Early Access period it improved enough for me to change my opinion on it! It was all luck I got it too. Humble Bundle's own payment method didn't have a confirmation and I didn't mean to spend $25 on that bundle...
