Published by: Rising Star Games
Developed by: Speelbaars
Genre: Indie, Adventure, Relaxing
Release Date: 3 September, 2015
Time to complete: 2+ hours
Play as a bright, flying, fish-like species called Lumini, as you make your way through a beautiful colourful world, fending off evil creatures wanting to hurt you and escaping the dangers of a hostile planet.
Rather than controlling just a single creature, you play as an entire swarm of Lumini (unless of course you manage to kill them all!). As you progress, you reach large cube crystal-like checkpoints that emit an energy, allowing your force of Lumini to grow. The more little blue flowers you collect along the way, the more your swarm will grow. There are different types of Lumini with different abilities (for example a speed boost, or a bomb-like move which removes damaging objects in your path), and you can change which variety leads the swarm. Though the game mostly involves simply exploring the soothing atmosphere, there are a few puzzles to complete and bad guys to fight off. Some of the puzzles require your swarm of Lumini to separate into 2 groups, both of which you can control at the same time.
Honestly, 95% of the reason I play this game is because it is just so beautiful. There are crystals scattered around the Lumini’s path which light up as you pass them, different areas of the map that present a different theme, and bright, contrasting colours (for example the bright colours the crystals emit inside tunnels) throughout the game.
I also thoroughly enjoyed going through the concept art (can be found under ‘extras’), which displays a huge amount of artistic talent.
One play through of Lumini on the easiest setting takes roughly 2 hours. After completing the playthrough on ‘normal’, a harder difficulty will unlock. The replay value is highly dependant on whether you get bored of games easily, as it is fairly repetitive and linear. For me, the artwork is definitely reason enough to play it through numerous times.
There are enough achievements to give you a few playthroughs before you complete the game.
The soundtrack, much like the rest of the game, is incredibly calming. It’s enthralling, blissful and flows beautifully with the gameplay.
The first playthrough of Lumini is on the easiest setting, ‘normal’. It’s honestly very easy, and would be a good difficulty level for someone who is more interested in taking in the art of the game (rather than in engaging in more difficult combat), or even children. Because you have a whole swarm of Lumini, it’s hard to fail; you’re likely not going to lose every single one before the game ends, at least not on normal. After you’ve completed the game on this setting, a harder setting will unlock.
The controls are very easy to use (it is also recommended to use a controller), and the gameplay is very simple with very few dangers along the way.
Lumini very quickly became one of my favourite games; I could probably play it over 100 times and it would still have the same serene effect. With the different difficulty levels, I really think Lumini has something to appeal to everyone. For me, it was definitely worth the price.

However, there’s still some developers out there that like to break away from the fire, and keep the gentle, innocent, and enchanting world of games alive.

You need to actually try Lumini first hand to really gage how immersed you can become in this pleasant game.
Your character, or rather, characters, are what look like little fireflies that fly amongst the world. They bare the illuminating similarities to fireflies, but are far more alien looking in terms of features. In fact, these creatures, the Lumini, actually used to once inhabit the planet you’re introduced too, but they vanished, and since then time has changed their homeland. They come back to find a series of harsh, new species now running the caves, the waters, and the air. It’s up to them to restore their homeland back to how it was.

From the first article I read about this game I was hooked. Investigating your own murder and other crime scenes as a ghost? Yes please! The idea seemed so original and any screen shots I had seen looked awesome.
So I get the game and the first half hour is awesome. You'll have fun getting used to the controls and your own abilities as a ghost, but it didn't take me long to lose interest in walking through walls and making printers/TV's malfunction because at the end of the day, you rarely stumble across anything interesting or you get little to no reaction from the living people in the area. I mean come on! if I'm a ghost I want to be able to scare the living. Not just distract them from guarding that door for 20 seconds.
So let's get down to the things that really got on my nerves.
(1) Gameplay - It gets repetitive. Honestly, you'll find yourself running across the city/buildings where  your obstacles will be either one of  two things.
- Oh there's a demon there? better sneak up on them and extract their soul.
Or
- Oh would you look at that, a fiery pit straight to hell is blocking my path. Luckily for me there's  this person here I can possess, who's sole propose seems to be walking down this hall for the rest of their lives.
Oh which leads me to another thing, if you give us the ability to read minds, actually have the characters think interesting stuff that's personal to them, instead of the same thing like, "Oh its cold outside" or "I hope they find that killer" Seriously, a little variety never killed anyone. (There's a pun in there somewhere.)
(2) Skills/abilities - You will pick up skills as the story progresses, skills like teleportation....eh and umm teleportation. So on top of being able to posses people,(and don't be fooled, the most exciting thing you might get them to do is move their hand from blocking that page you want to read.) reveal the events that lead up to peoples deaths and maybe another ability that I have forgotten about, that leaves you with about 5 (give or take) skills. Not much and nothing that's gonna make you sit up and go F*** Yeah!! with excitement, which is disappointing.
(3) NPC's - If we were back in the early 2000's I might forgive this but there is a serious lack of character models for the npc's (there's about four different character's for each sex, who will either have  one of three different voices, all of whom usually say the same dialogue.)
(4) Collectables - For example once you've collected the 15 or whatever amount of saws, a memory is unlocked. Now considering some of these can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to collect, you'd expect maybe a flash back to the event. You know a cutscene, an animation. No, what you get is one image that is some what relateable to the story, with a bunch of  text in front of it (and I mean a bunch) and possibly the most life draining narration I've ever had to injure.
(5) Game length - The game is short! I finished it in under 10 hours and this is coming from someone who went out of her way to find as many collectables and whatever other extras there was. (Near the end I gave up, not caring any more and just wanted to finish the game so I stopped putting in any effort.) So for someone who'd only be interested in the story you might be able to get this game finished in 6-7 hours.
(6) Connecting crime scene clues. - Honestly I don't know how to describe this. Once you collect all the clues you'll be brought to a window that asks you a question. You have to click on a clue (or three) that answers that question. Being the generation brought up on CSI you're more than likely going to put on your Horatioto glasses and think long and hard about the choices and outcomes. My advice don't. Pick the clue that when you read it you think "Nah, that's not even a clue. more like a statement/common sense." Watch a lets play of one of these, you'll see what I'm talking about.
(7) Deus Ex desktop screens - Awesome the first computer screen I saw it on but when every police officer in the station seems to be playing Deus Ex on their work computer no wonder you haven't found the killer.
Whoa, okay I've complained a lot about this game. I don't want to come off too hard on it. There are some pro's.

Villian - I never wanted to punch someone in the face more. Well done on making a completle d*** of a villian.

A great shooting gallery with good class differentiation and the fairest compromise of classic RPG sensibilibities and standard third person shooter mechanics in the series. At first I was put off by the reduction of what I saw as RPG elements from the first game but I'm glad I moved past that. What ME2 offers is possibly the best case of a developer maintaining the player's ability to characterize their avatar through both statistics and narrative while pushing for seamless integration of the aforementioned with a more natural, real-time combat system and game world to do so yet. The golden ring Bethesda has been chasing, Bioware grabbed and ran with here. You have less to micromanage concerning combat related stats, but narrative control is at a series high here. And the stats are still there to be managed to a degree anyway, spread out over armor, weapon, and power customization. It may not be as much as the first, but I say it's in where it counts.
Every level, from a minor conflict picked up by scanning, to the grand galaxy shaping sorties offered here have a marked shift in design priotity from the first game. No level in ME2 feels stamped or generic. You can't buggy around looking for copy/pasted bunkers on varying colored planets any longer but what is gained manages to be far greater. Beyond the mechanical facelift there's also far greater attention to detail in their building of these fantastic sci-fi locales. Visual cues ranging from Alien to Star Trek abound. It's fantastic.
The narrative is at its best in the series here. They manage a fine balance of player freedom and the interweaving of optional content with primary story. You can manage much of the progression in this game as you see fit, the picture of the story you get a direct result of your efforts. Since a vast majority of the missions carry some significance you are granted further interaction with your crew after each. That coupled with so many crew members worth talking to gives even more incentive to get out there and do as much galaxy saving as you can. This all manages to be where the "RPG" went and hid in this gane.
Music's a high point too.
Get this game if you haven't.

I've only completed the first part of the game and it took me about 22 hours to do so. At first, the pace was very slow as I had to learn the core mechanics of Expeditions: Conquistador. After almost ten hours, I could easily complete quests and win battles without heavy casualties while playing on hard difficulty. From this moment on, I really fell in love with every bit of what makes this a truly great game.
First of all, the game comes up with a deep and rich combat system which lets you experiment as many strategies as you want. You can flank your opponents, hit and run, trap them... The AI is not that smart during the first fifteen hours. But as soon as you are about to complete the first segment of the main story line, things are really getting started. The AI is much more agressive and for instance, tends to focus on either your doctors or the biggest threats. It is also able to flank you and to incapacitate your team members in order to quickly win the match.
Besides, I really enjoyed the story so far. As a planescape torment fan, I was surprised to go through so well written quests. Wether main or side quests, every piece of adventures I came across was fantastic. You'll spend most of your time reading long texts but they are so interesting and thrilling... What a divine pleasure nowadays!
Then, don't even try to succeed without being proficient at managing your party turns after turns. You may lose a battle but you'll surely have to face the consequences. Moreover, you are accountable for every choice you make and your followers will react accordingly to their beliefs and ethic. Thus, sometimes you will be offered the possibility to know more about them and their background.
Finally, if you can bear to spend the few hours required to dive in the core mechanics, you'll be rewarded with a wonderful and well written adventure as well as a very deep and complex battle system.

I didn't really like this game in Early Access, but it looks like the balance issues have been addressed for the release. As such I've updated my review for the game.
The tags on this game say "card game", but it's really just a roguelike, one extremely similar to FTL where you go through a chain of events with the occasional combat interspersed (hack and slash in this case). It's got a pretty good presentation and is very controller friendly. The combat is basically cloned from the Arkham series, complete with counters, guard breaks and combos. This game actually has challenge to it though. As shown with FTL its concept is very solid and fun even if you don't win a whole lot.
Luck is obviously a factor in a game with cards. Hand of Fate has some really, really unforgiving draws, curses and failure rolls that result in nearly game ending situations: halving your health permanently, blocking your healing, making basic combat moves cost resources... In early access you were also given next to no gold or food to manage around them. However that's no longer the case. The game feels more in line with the "roguelike" genre now, albeit with more severe shocks and less dwindling resources.
One of the coolest things about the game is the dealer and the way you play on the table with the cards all laid out. It's clear the developers put a lot of time and effort into creating the dealer and giving him charisma. Playing through the earlier part of story mode he's really neat and makes the game atmospheric. Once you get to the end though and finish most of the card storylines his lines narrow he can get a bit annoying taunting you/ parroting the same words over and over. There's a voice slider though so no biggie.
Overall this is probably the only game to actually do Early Access right that I've played. Balance wise the game was a mess but otherwise done save for polish when it hit. And in its Early Access period it improved enough for me to change my opinion on it! It was all luck I got it too. Humble Bundle's own payment method didn't have a confirmation and I didn't mean to spend $25 on that bundle...

Summary: ArcheAge takes a lot of the things that are wrong with MMORPGs and fixes them. It's a game that's well worth investing time and money into if you're willing to pay to be a patron. The new mechanics are fresh and effective, and the game as a whole is probably the best MMORPG I've ever played and I highly recommend it. I will probably end up with well over a thousand hours of play by the time I move on.
Graphics/Environment: The graphics are definitely modern. They could use a little optimization, but that may come as we approach launch. The game is GORGEOUS. Every hour or so I find myself stopping everything and taking a screenshot. The land is beautiful and varied, and in some places absolutely stunning. It just adds that much to the immersion of the game. It's not going to win any 'awards' for graphical quality like Crysis would, but it's good looking and the scenery is amazing.
User Interface: Pretty standard for the most part. It's functional. Some people have complained that they wish it was more customizable, but for me at least it's okay.
Game Content: I've created two toons so far (one in alpha and the other in beta), and they're on opposite continents and opposite factions. A lot of the early game content is the same across the board, which is understandable. The game does a good job of introducing the core mechanics to you. The tutorial could be a bit better, but if you've played MMOs before, you should be able to figure it out. The community does fill those holes...most o f the time.
This game has a significant focus on economy and trading. There is an extensive framework set up, and it's being carefully balanced by Trion (who is in charge of the western version of this game). Be advised that some of the functionality is locked out for free players. You can't own your own piece of land without being a patron. This may tick off some people, but you can still farm on public farms, and you can definitely still play the game and enjoy it without needing to have 'your' land. If you really want to own land and delve into this wonderful world, you can afford to pay monthly for the game.
The gear that everything turns on is 'labor'. If you are a free player, you get 5 per 5 minutes of actual play. If you're a patron, you get 20 per 5 while online and 5 per 5 while offline. During my time as a free player I found that I never quite had enough labor (if they doubled they would probably be okay), and as a patron I had too much. Some people are really miffed by the system, because a lot of functions need it. You want to open those coinpurses you just looted (because there are no actual 'drops' from mobs)? You have to spend a little labor. You want to make that armor or mine that iron? You need labor. To me this makes logical sense. It also prevents bots from screwing up the economic balance. Sure, you can stay afk all day to collect it...but at the end of the day, you really don't have a whole ton. You can't skew the prices of items by flooding the market with them. As long as they balance the trickle of labor, I'll be okay with it.
What you're really looking to get are 'gilda stars', which are the valuable currency you're trying to collect. Some daily quests will give them to you in small numbers, but the majority should come from trading with the other continents (where there are enemies). This is intended to create a risk/reward situation where you have to go further and take more risk to get more gilda stars from your goods. This currency is used for ships, houses, land, and vanity gear. This is really what the game turns on.
Thus far, I feel the mechanics have been well put together. You get a free mount early, and it levels up over time, giving it abilities to help you inside and outside combat. There are gliders that you can use to fly around with (well...glide down from heights). There are little surprises here and there that will keep you amused...
Music: The sountrack is excellent, albeit a little bit repetitive after a while. If you play hundreds of hours, you may find it wears you out a little.
PVP: I haven't really had much experience with this because I'm not at end game content yet.
Conclusion: I haven't really found the game all that grindy, and for me that's a big deal. I like the variety in the gameplay and I like the mechanics. This game is sure to give me hundreds and hundreds (maybe even thousands) of hours of entertainment.

This seems to be a combination of a hex map TBS, Oregon Trail, a game with text-based events that require some cultural understanding sort of like those in King of Dragon Pass, and an RPG where you can freely roam around a "world map" in a non-linear fashion. The TBS aspect comes in when you get into a fight and must fight a turn-based battle, somewhat XCOM stye, except it's on a hex map. Like Oregon Trail you have to worry a lot about hunting or trading for food and medicine, as well as processing herbs you find into medicine, preserving any meat you can't eat right away, crafting objects to use in battle (like barricades and traps), and researching "inventions" that do things like improve your movement rate. Unlike Oregon Trail though, nothing is linear and your followers (except for your slaves/servants) are not anonymous statistics; they speak up and interact with you as events occur and will urge you to do things or object to things based on their beliefs.
One good thing about the game is that you have the choice of whether you want to act like a racist conquer, non-racist diplomat, or some combination of both, but regardless of what you pick the game won't go easy on you. If your party is full of aggressive rascists they'll be forced to work with the natives at times and forced to negotiate their way out of stuff, non-rascists will still be forced to deal with the rascist attitudes of others in society, and the peaceful will still be forced to fight. So whether you want to subjegate the heathen savages for the glory of the Spanish crown or promote their acceptance among the Spanish settlers, you won't be able to get by acting only according to one attitude or the other.
The mechanics of the game seem pretty well balanced, and they're rather unforgiving when it comes to things like running out of food or being unable to treat your wounded whether due to lack of medicine or doctors. The game is not quite as unforgiving as XCOM when it comes to death; if someone's "hit points" (endurance) reaches 0 in battle then they aren't automaically dead, but they have a good chance of being anywhere from lightly to severely wounded after the battle. This is a major problem because wounded people require a dedicated doctor and usually something like 5-8 medicine per day to treat, with one day of treatment needed per severity level of the wound. To make things worse, they can't hunt, guard, patrol, or do anything else useful until healed. On the other hand, the reason you get such an opportunity to save your casualties is that you can't just hire new people like you can in XCOM. While you can sometimes get a new fighter, hunter, doctor, or scholar, you have to *find* them and sometimes convince them to join because they're all essentially one-off special characters, not faceless minions.
Overall the game is a well made combination of several different types of game mechanic that I haven't seen all in the same game before this. When I was in high school all the kids used to play Oregon Trail and start out with 10,000 ammunition and no food or medicine because they just wanted to play the deer hunting minigame the whole time. I'm betting the same kids playing "Expeditions: Conquistador" would have their bloodlust satisfied by the TBS battles and they wouldn't have to pursue a really silly game strategy just to get in enough fighting. Because of that they might actually learn something while playing.

Having first learned of this game through YouTube, I decided to pick it up for myself and see what all the fuss is about.
It's difficult to put this into one category of games. It's essentially a roguelike adventure game, which uses cards to determine your journey and has a bit of combat that's somewhat similar to the Batman games.
The cards you draw affect various things, from your equipment, to your resources, to what enemies you face. Some cards are mini-quests which have different outcomes depending on your choices. I came across a card called "Devil's Choice", where I was given the choice to fight one of three cards: 2 of Dust, 2 of Dust and 3 of Dust. When I chose 3 of Dust, the Devil basically removed that card and made me fight the other two combined, "just for laughs".
You won't have many cards at first, but as you complete dungeons, defeat bosses and complete quest cards, you will receive tokens that unlock new cards. You can then choose which cards to use in your deck. This offers a good amount of player freedom in how you want to shape your experience for each run. For example, if you wish an added challenge, you can choose to play a deck that contains no armour or shield cards.
The game starts of easy enough, but after the 3 first "dungeons" it already gets exponentially more difficult, mainly because of what I like to call Roguelike Syndrome; basically, no matter how well you do, the game can mess you up worse than any one enemy can. My first attempt at the Jack of Plagues ended when I drew two consecutive Angry Mob challenges, and rolled the worst outcomes on both while I was already low on life and resources. While I'm perfectly alright with such events, do understand that if you're not used to Roguelike Syndrome, you will swear at this game for being unfair. A lot.
There are currently two game modes; story mode and endless mode. Story mode pits you against the dealer in a quest to defeat his lieutenants (who are based on the the regular deck of cards - 4 jacks, 4 queens and 4 kings, one of each for each suit) and ultimately, him. Endless mode simply allows you to play for as long as you can.
The few flaws I have found so far, I don't consider to be dealbreakers, and I believe these could be ironed out by the time this gets out of early access. The combat seems a little bit too easy. A "blind random" deckbuilding option would have been nice as well. And of course, more content is always nice.
Other than that, it looks pretty good, the voice acting of the dealer is pretty solid, and there's already a good amount of content to keep you busy. But DO play with a controller, it makes the game infinitely better to handle.
Highly recommended.

Lumini’s presentation is its trump card. It’s a game made in Unity so of course it’s beautiful, but it has a lot more to it than the typical “beautiful engine look” that can, and has, gotten tiresome as more Unity games have been released. You go to a lot of different environments in this game and it tends to be the reveal of each new area that has that emotional pull for me. They even ripped off Jurassic Park a little bit. The environments are extremely pretty, but on their own they wouldn’t be that impressive; it’s the timing. The music comes in at just the right moments, and the level design is timed with it so that when you pass certain triggers in the level the music does what it needs to. In other words the music is dynamic, and I have to say it’s maybe the best element of this game. But we’re not going to leave presentation without taking a look at another aspect of design that the developers seemed to neglect. Graphic design. All throughout the game whenever text appeared, or when I collected a purple gem, I have to be honest, I cringed. The font is not good, and the collectable overlay is straight out of Crash Bandicoot from 15 years ago. It might seem like a nitpick, but it really cheapened the whole experience and clashed with the otherwise beautiful game.
Unfortunately the weakest element of the game is the gameplay, which’ll be a dealbreaker for a lot of people and I don’t blame them for that. We’ll start with the negative and end on the positive. In this game you are controlling a school of flying.. fish dragonfly things called Lumini. Your health is represented by the number of them you have with you, and if you lose them all you go back to the previous checkpoint. The three colours each have unique abilities and you can switch between them; blue being speedy, red being aggressive, and yellow being… the gem collector. Yellow was really the third wheel throughout this game; it didn’t really have much of a place and I never used it. It does become slightly more useful towards the end when you are collecting gems from inside venus fly traps, and I think you could argue that getting lots of gems is important because that’s how you get more Lumini, but that idea is undermined by the fact the game is quite easy. There’s nothing wrong with that and there is a hard mode that you unlock after beating the game that I never tried, but honestly I think the biggest misstep with the difficulty is making it so that you have to beat the game to unlock hard mode. Assuming hard mode is hard, the difficulty wouldn’t have been an issue at all if I could have played it from the start. The game is already short, and it’s padded out with these unbelievably tedious and easy puzzles that just don’t belong in this game. They stagnate the pace and aren’t satisfying to complete; yet they come up again and again and they always have the same solutions. All that said, I actually did find it satisfying to switch between the red and blue schools of  Lumini to create a synergy and fight enemies in relatively tense action sequences. I felt powerful when I did it right, and it kept the battles fast paced and exciting.
The story is simple and things become clearer as you play. It’s not really a story that can be explained in words without using information from outside the game itself. The environment around you tells the story conceptually, with a few dramatic twists in tone throughout that keep it interesting. It has a satisfying but typical conclusion, and the world remains magical throughout the experience. There’s not much else to say about it, it’s really something you have to play and discover for yourself.
I think this game, that I completed in 90 minutes, is worth around 5-7 dollars. Right now, it’s priced at 13 dollars on Steam. I think Lumini is great if you want to scratch that goosebump itch, and if that’s you I’m talking about, my recommendation is putting it in your Steam wishlist and waiting for a sale when it gets closer to that 5-7 dollar mark.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is an excellent game. I don't usually write reviews, but I wanted to address the few issues that people do have with the game
The usual subject of criticism in Murdered: Soul Suspect is the combat system. The fact is, however,  that Murdered is not a combat-based game. If all you care about is fighting, this wasn't gonna be the game for you to begin with. The combat system isn't like most fighting games, but that's because it's not designed to be. Murdered isn't an action game - Murdered is about telling a story.
This brings up the other common complaint about Murdered: that the story is too short. Sure, you can beat the game in six hours, but, the fact is, you shouldn't. Murdered is also a game about exploration. As an example, each story mission gives evidence you'll need but also some you won't. This makes sense, as when you're looking around a crime scene, not everything you notice is going to be relevant. In the end, you have to choose what pieces of evidence are relevant to what you want to know. So sure, you could just find the necessary pieces of evidence and realize "Hey, I can solve this now." Alternatively, you could try to find all the evidence anyways. There are also hidden collectibles that explain some of the backstory but are not necessary to progress in the game. Side missions don't present the player with any rewards, but do provide short interactions with other ghosts (not to say that these side missions are perfect though). The atmosphere of the town of Salem is captivating and makes it fun to just walk around and explore. As a ghost, you can possess any human and read their thoughts. Granted, the thoughts of random civilians in the streets can get repetitive and reused, but in story missions these thoughts are more unique. So if you're the kind of person who likes to rush through the game, your experience will be short, but that's because it won't be the full experience. My personal playstyle was to seek out all the collectibles that I could (but not obsess over getting all of them), explore the town of Salem as well as the locations for the story missions (the police station and museum are particularly neat), read everyone's thoughts (at least in story missions), look for all the evidence I could find, and read anything I could find lying around. I'm not saying that everyone should play this way or that my way is the only way/correct way to play, but I do feel like gamers who like exploration will get much more out of this than players who don't due to the atmospheric nature of the game. In doing such, not only did it make it a more enjoyable experience for me, but it also lengthened the completion time a little bit
Anyways, pros/cons:
+ Graphics
+ Story/Atmosphere/Characters/Lore
+ Voice Acting
+ Unique ghost gameplay
- Side missions leave a little something to be desired
- Certain collectibles can only be collected during certain story missions, so if you miss them then they're gone
In short, Murdered: Soul Suspect is a great game, but make sure you know what to expect before getting it. Many of the bad reviews are from people who expected it to be an action game, when in truth it never presented itself as such. Murdered is more of a linear interactive movie. If you like story-driven games, this is the game for you, but if gameplay is all you care about then save your money.

Recettear is a game that should be fun. You run an item shop, you quest for new items, and sell those items to people. Along the way you make friends and a pile of money. Simple enough to grasp, or so I thought.
This game is so needlessly filled with dialog that it takes away from the fun. I'm all for a tutorial or a few helpful hints, but after 40 minutes of playing I hadn't even opened my shop for the first day yet. All I was doing was reading dialog AND not good dialog. It's not like there is a story line that will keep you on the edge of you seat. You are a young and very ditzy girl who is partnered up with a loanshark fairy. The fairy tells you everything you need to know to run a shop. She tells you, then you repeat it back to her and make a ditzy joke to go along with it, then she reiterates, and you make another ditzy joke. This goes on for far too long. The cyclical dialoge continues to ruin the game throughout.
EXAMPLE: Fairy: "To get out of item select, press the B button."  Girl: "But I don't have a B button. Does that mean I'll never get out of item select? tehehehehehehe."  Fairy: "No, you will be fine, just remember to get out of item select, press the B button."  Girl: "OKAY! But if I find a B button I think I wouldn't know what to do. tehehehehehe. But you're the boss I guess. tehehehehehehe."
Once you get through the 40 or 60 minutes of dialoge you get to actually play the game. This game is about questing for stuff. You play as another person, not the ditzy girl, and go to dungeons for loot. Then the girl you're playing takes all the stuff the other person you were playing worked so hard to get and puts it in her shop to sell for profit. Combat is a slight choir as you and monsters can move 360 degrees, but you can only attack in Up/Down/Left/Right direction. This means to attack something you have to line up to it, then move to attack, and then attack. It feels like it's been ripped straight off a Nintendo 64 title, and makes the combat more choir-ful than fun.
All that being said, if you skip every bit of dialoge, and don't mind old-school controls, there is a little bit of fun to be had here. However, I in good conscious can not recommend this game to any of my friends.

Started playing this game to see, if it would even be worth buying Destiny 2.
I got hooked way too fast, the movement and abilites feel really good. I played through about 7 planets so far and it's not getting boring in any way, because there is so much to do and it's up to you what you are doing.
Let it be a quest, farming materials, headhunting, searching for artifcats, grinding for specific loot or completing special events, that reward skins, materials or blueprints. I played about 50 hours and the game didn't even really begin for me, I am sure you can spend easily 1000+ hours in this game, just because of the fact, that the game becomes more and more rewarding.
Furthermore the developers really care for the game and update it regularly. The recent update added an open world to explore. You get to visit it after about 2 hours, if you like too. It has quests bound to it, that offer exclusive rewards upon completion. These quests scale from easy to very hard and become more rewarding.
There is much more to say, but you are better off just trying it out yourself, in the end it's free to play.
This may scare off some people, because f2p games are often bound to currency that can be bought ingame.
Yes, people who spend real money, are in a certain advantage.
Since the game mainly focuses on PvE, it's no 'real' advantage. You can unlock everything in the game, by playing enough. The only purchases, that can only be done with real money are certain skins, which were made by Steam users, that benefit their creator. But there are other skins to unlock without paying. And it should be said, that the real money currency, can be obtained by trading items with other players.
Games like PoE or this one live from ingame purchases and if I have spent a long time playing these games for free, I often purchase something equally worth a fully priced game, maybe more afterwards, since I spend way more time in games like these, than in AAA titles.
Although Warframe is a very good game, I bought Destiny 2 yesterday, I will try it out myself, but I can see me turning it down and returning to Warframe in a week or two. In the long run Warframe should provide much more content and is probably way more polished.

A fluid, unique, and entertaining adventure full of surprises.  A long-forgotten species, a hostile planet and a journey of discovery – welcome to the world of Lumini...
Having vanished without trace for thousands of years, an innocent race of creatures known as the Lumini have returned to their home world. Sadly, time has not been kind and the balance of the planet has shifted, turning the once gentle environment into a hostile landscape. Only the Lumini themselves can restore balance and help revive their long-dormant race, before adapting to preserve the future for generations to come.
Explore the Lumini home world in this relaxing flow-style adventure, overcoming obstacles and keeping your swarm safe while collecting the planet’s energy to bring back your fallen comrades. Split and reform your swarm, evolve and discover new abilities to bring the Lumini back to their former glory...  - Highly Recommended!

A fun little platformer, with a charming (and very scientifically inaccurate) story.
The key innovation is that the levels "wrap around" vertically, so falling off the bottom of the screen leads to you falling off the top, and jumping past the top makes you appear at the bottom, all momentum intact.  You can think of it as level-wide Portals connecting the top and bottom :)
As you progress in the story, a few more elements are introduced such as "bounce" blocks which pop as you hit them and bounce you away at high speeds, blocks which blink in and out, and "power-ups" which give you the ability to instantly arrest your vertical momentum. There are no enemies, and the only way to die are the ubiquitous spikes.
This game is quite short though, and if you're any good at platformers you'll likely get all the achievements by the time the last Trading Card drops.

Lets start with the leveling experience first off, its nothing new just think world of warcraft style macro based skill combat but with a much nicer skill stree system wich I will get into in a moment, the combat might be rather rotation based however, thanks to how the combo system works it actually ends up creating quiet a few different viable combos to pull of, if it be a CC focussed attack or something towards high single target damage, the game allows for you to mix it up quiet alot and still be effective towards whatever your target. Ready to accept my downvotes! (since it's a negative review! woo!~)
Archeage pulled me in by offering a seemingly variety in skills/builds and being able to combat other plays in a open world, rather than in battlegrounds.
Sadly, the game mechanics are very old school. There is no active dodging/blocking/kiting/aiming/cc breaks that many newer mmo's are starting to offer. Alas, I was still willing to give the game a chance!
For convenience sake, I will break my review up into categories.
Skills:
I was very much looking forward to making diverse builds with unique skill sets! Sadly I found myself being pigeon holded into using select skills that are typically the flavor. The biggest obstacle in the way of truly being diverse are the actions bars.
While there are many different spells and you can combine three skill trees together to make your hero feel diverse, you are not limited in how many skills you may put on your action bars, therefore you ultimately aren't choosing skills, only trees. Of course everybody eventually goes towards the same skillsets, or rather similar ones.
There is a combo system in play which does help making builds a little more diverse. It works like this: If you fear the target before using this spell you will do more damage.
Then pvp is very much who initiated and stunlocked who first (no diminishing returns!) There are a few spells that will cancel out certain cc's.
The biggest issue I have with the skills though would be the awful passives. A lot of the passives are activated by chance. Such as being hit by a critical attack will boost your own critical attack by #. This type of "random" mechanic is found very often on the passives. Then to top it off, using our example, if you proc the passive too often it will disable it for # seconds/minute. One passive that is randomly activated disables if you MOVE. Extremely poor passive design.
There are also a few (thankfully not a lot) of self using buffs that last ~a minute and have no cooldown. Why bother. Why not make this a passive. Just extremely annoying.
PVE:
The game does eventually open up a bit, but questing is really the only way to go. The quests are mostly very boring fetch quests (especially early on). Doing every quest I saw between 1 - 10 I killed less than 50 monsters. I understand that they want to introduce the game to you via quests, but it doesn’t take a genius to understand that you right click seeds in your inventory to plant them in a huge farm where tons of others are planting.
The loot is extremely lackluster. There a few typical set bonuses, etc. But I expect more from games now than just gaining a bit of stats from a set bonus. You also have to use labour points for everything, opening loot, opening gold, crafting, everything. From what I can tell, people who pay will gain an extreme deal more labour points.
Mounts are typical, except they can help you fight. I was never much of a pet guy, but I know a lot of people will enjoy this feature. Gliders can be really cool, especially in pvp. Boats have been done before in a mmo, but seem to have been put together a bit better in archeage.
Mobs and spells in general aren’t very exciting. You can’t actively block, dodge or even kite very well. Mob interaction is far and few.
Overall:
If all you want from a game is a very large, runescape esque, crafting mmo. This is for you, if you don’t mind grinding or paying for labour points.
If you want any kind of pve experience. Or are a seeker of unique treasure and lust after making a very individual and unique build, then no. This game is definitely not your cup of tea. Don’t bother buying into it.

By far, one of the best games I've played in my life
In Paradox's game progression this one is the first, and it occupies middle ages from 1066 to 1452 (or from 867 if you get the DLC for it). In game you basically have to choose dynasty and play till you die or till the game itself ends. And it's really ♥♥♥♥ing difficult. You might get kicked out of your throne and die poor with no heirs or you can survive and be emperor of whole Europe.
This game is great fun because:
1) It is really hardcore
2) The map is quite big, so variety of dynasties to play is really decent
3) Things go quite different every time you play, so it doesn't become repetitive
4) There are some quite competitive achievements in game, for example restoring Roman Empire or sample
5) It is quite historically interesting, you can watch how things changed around 1000 years ago
6) Nice graphically made landscape
7) It's not just about having wars. It's about being a ruler. You will have to do a lot of things there, from starting and ending wars to marrying your offsprings
Why this game isn't flawless:
1) Some really stupid and unrealistic things might happen. For example, Russian kingdom turning to catholic religion or black-skinned king of Britain (This is what I had only, most noticeable things)
2) There are really many DLCs and getting them can sometimes be worthy, the most significant ones are like 8$
3) Some DLCs are really stupid, for example the one with Aztec invasion. It's just plain idiotic.
4) This game might be sometimes TOO hardcore. You won't be able to play it normally before you complete tutorial, so bother yourself with that. And it's gonna take you a lot of time to start playing good. I actually started becoming good at this game after 100h only and still would sometimes get ♥♥♥♥ed.
Overall, this game is a great fun if you want some good time-spender, if you want some historical interesting events, if you're tired of real-time strategy games or if you just crave some difficult gameplay and not-so-stupid games. This is what you have to get then.
9.8/10, would play again and again

This is quite possibly the most addicting game that I've ever played. 438 hours poured in, and I still haven't ever finished a campaign to the end. How could I?! There are so many options and opportunities to play completely different games as completely different people. The learning curve is very high but the more you learn, the greater the scope of the game will appear to you. This may be the pinnacle of PC strategy gaming.

A brilliant game. Probably one of the best single-player games I've played to this day.
Everything listed below applies to both Last Light Redux as well as 2033 Redux. I highly recommend playing 2033 Redux first, as it gives a much better idea and understanding of the game world as well as storyline. Pick them in a bundle and enjoy a very good 20-30 hours long drive.
It has so many things done so amazingly that pretty much every player may like this game for at least something.
What are those things?
-Diversity. You can choose whatever playstyle you enjoy and go through the entire game with it. Sneaky or noisy, merciful or cruel, good or bad. Lots of weapons and upgrades as well difficulty options to choose from may create experience ranging from arcade Call Of Duty-like game to a patient and hardcore survival where every bullet counts.
-Setting. It's post-apocalyptic Moscow, where various underground structures are the only place where man can still survive. It has lots of various paranormal and mystical phenomenons, mutants, and, of course, the most dangerous enemy - humans. The universe is relatively unpopular and doesn't suffer from what plagues big universes, such as myriads of plot holes, gaps and inconsistencies.
-Storyline. Both games have an incredible almost forgotten feeling to them - a feeling of an adventure. You know, those times when you just rewind the entire game and recall what happened and how it all started. All those locations, experiences and different environments and how far they were from each other, it all gives a pleasant sensation of some kind of accomplishment.
-Atmosphere. Created by various instruments such as music, sounds, flashbacks and colour schemes it creates a very strong feeling of death, decay and survival.
-Philosophical undertone. A great showcase of how destructive the human nature is, as well as a marvelous reminder of how fragile and beautiful the world we live in is, and how improtant it is to preserve and appreciate it.
I highly suggest anyone playing this game. I know not everyone may fully appreciate it, but for those who will the game will become at least a very memorable piece.

-A Pretentious Roguelike That Likes to Think Itself A Much Higher Station than it actually Is-
I like roguelikes, hell, I love roguelikes. And the Pretense of thise game is pretty cool. Whereas most roguelikes have been a crutch for relatively rookie developers to lean on while they find their feet. This is no different for these guys, except that they managed to hire a voice actor to say things in their game so they've decided they're big time.
Although a lot of roguelikes are very similar this one is really quite similar to Faster Than Light. They both have the same format of traveling from point to point and facing random encounters. But when it comes to combat once opts for a top down RTS approach whereas Hand of Fate goes for an Arkham Series hand to hand combat schtick and I'll give it that, the combat is ok. It's smooth enough, there are some bugs which should have been priotities to fix even for an early access game (They're doing UI tweak patches now so they must feel they're near the end).

The main failure of this game is in between. The narrative of Faster Than Light is simple but direct. You come across a situation and you decide what to do. You weigh up odds, what your crew is like and  the outcomes to your decisions are rational. Stupid decisions get you killed. Whereas in Hand of Fate, everything is reduced to a game of 4 card trick to see if the outcome is good or bad. By the time you have enough information to weigh up the pros and cons of what you are doing, it is too late and you have to pick a card. Cards are deceptive and irrational. You will not be rewarded for being cautious or brave, you will either be lucky or unlucky and in Roguelikes I like to feel that my judgement and my skill as a player is one of the major factors in defining my progress.
If I wanted the experience that Hand of Fate provided I could just roll a D20 and punch myself in the nutsack every time I rolled a 5 or less then play 5 minutes of Arkham City every half hour.
Early access isn'r responsible for these problems. These are inherent failures in the decisions made by the game developers and their determination to drive home a pretentious card gimmick at the loss of things that actually make the game fun. Especially when a single run can take upwards of half an hour with a slow iteration time and poor communication.
There are plenty of Roguelikes out there that knock this game into a cocked had. If it's in a humble bundle or on sale for like $3 I guess you could buy it, but otherwise there are plenty of better games made by better developers who could use your money to make better games in the future.

It’s a bit or RPG Strategy mixed into a dungeon crawling type of story with some hack and slash combat. You interact with, use, or equip cards for the main aspects of the game, and gain more cards as time goes on (depending on your success/failure). If you don’t like a card, you can remove it from the deck and not play with it again later (as long as you have enough cards required for the play through). I will admit that it can become repetitive depending on how you arrange your deck, and the combat might turn into button spamming, but you don’t have to let it...you can play the game as you choose.
What is nice about this game is that you can either go “endless”, or use the “story mode” which gives you “break points” as you finish each piece once you beat the boss at the end of the dungeon. Like I said, it’s hard to explain...but you’re bound to like at least a couple aspects of this games layout. Lumini is a extremely relaxing experience that sees you controlling a flock of birds through beautiful scenery.
The difference with this game as oppose to others is that you control a whole flock of birds instead of just a single one. This I was expected would be difficult. But the developers have managed to nail the controls of movement perfectly. Monouvering the birds is simple and fluid and I never had a single problem. Each bird follows in a kind of trail.
The game uses a unique control method to make some puzzles. You are able to split your group into 2 different smaller groups. These are used to press buttons in different parts of the level. Some buttons have to be hold down both at the same time to open a door which is why 2 groups are needed. You can also control fans by spinning around them. Controlling the fans was sometimes a bit fiddly to do unfortunately. I really wish they had used this unique system to make some more intricate puzzles because the ones they used in lumini were extremely basic.
Lumini doesn't really have a goal as such. All you are really doing is exploring. The world that you are exploring is truly beautiful. The graphics style lumini uses isn't disimilar to the likes of trine 1 and 2. It's like a 3D environment but you only control in 2D. It's called 2.5D. The world is full of colour and depth. There is a lot of variety with environments such as caves, outdoors, trees and rain. This was such a pleasant experience just being able to explore the beautifully crafted world.
Interactivity with the environment is also something that the game uses a lot. When flying their are crystals in the background that light up, vegitation that sways, leaves that fall off the tree and loads more. It really does help to make the game actually seem real. There are always things happening in the background as well such as exploring animals or trees swaying.
Within your swarm you have 5 different types of birds. Each of them has a different ability. These include abilities like bomb, speed boost and electricity. Although in my playthrough I only used the speed boost and bomb ability to take out enemies. The others I felt were fairly useless. But this does create an element of strategy. You need to try can keep at least 1 of each of the types of birds alive within your swarm so you can use the abilities.
Throughout exploring you will find certain collectables and other pickups. The most important pickups would be energy and health. Energy is used to get more birds at each checkpoint. The more energy you have, the more birds you can get. The health just keeps your birds alive. Other collectables can also be found around the world. They don't actually seem to have a use though. The game doesn't explain what the other collectables are for so I have no idea. I found one that wasn't activtaed so I couldn't pick it up. But I had no idea how to activate it.
In the basis of the game there is prety much no challenge. You may loose some of your birds, but it is nearly impossible to loose all of them to a point of dieing out. I have no idea what happens in this situation becaue I didn't manage to loose them all. But if you do want a challenge there are some very difficult achievements. These include things like keeping all of the birds alive, not killing any enemy and getting all energy. You also unlock a hard mode after your first playthrough. They will add a tonne of time to the playthrough if you tried to get them all.
Overall the experience was extremly enjoyable and relaxing. It was a welcome break from some other hardcore games. Although if you are a strictly hardcore gamer this game is definitely not for you. The game unfortunately did only take me 1.5 hours to complete though. It isn't a very long length. So some people may consider £7.99 to be a slightly steep price for the amount of content. But I would personally recommend it at that price due to the perfect world you will get to explore. You really won't find the same experience anywhere else.
Disclaimer: I was provided a free review key by the developer to make this review.

6180 the moon, for as terrible a title that may be, plays a little like a platformer wrapped up in a children's book. The sun has gone missing, and with the people of Earth becoming distressed as the light disappears, you the moon have taken it upon yourself to heed their plight and discover where the sun has gone off to.
The writing, shockingly, actually wound up being my biggest issue with the game. Not so much because the narrative is flimsy and only the last handful of lines actually matter, but because it continually tries to fit in a rather odd, ambiguous meaning to the experience that never surfaces, and instead just floats around in the spectrum of weird space occupied by discarded poems and first drafts of better works.
If you disregard the story entirely though, 6180 is a rather delicious little platformer with an interesting (if basic and one note) mechanic of continual motion through the top and bottom of the screen. Falling through the ground pops you back out the top, and its with this in mind that platforms and obstacles are setup to require you to manipulate gravity and momentum to get past. The level designs are fairly simple and the difficulty consistently low (save a few frustrating spikes, pun not intended), but it's engaging and relaxing in a way that kept me interested in playing at least for the 40 or so minutes it took to complete the game.
Similarly, the modest but pleasant aesthetics and sleepy soundtrack fit in right along with an experience that seems designed to be played on a raining afternoon, sipping a cup of tea or cocoa without requiring you to process much more than a single button and the position of a few odd platformers. It's not deep, it's not innovative, and I likely won't remember it for very long, but I don't at all regret the time I spent with the moon and find it easy to recommend as a small snack of a game.

Fun little game!

This is a pretty nice and small platformer with a simple main mechanic: The screen wrap the top and bottom. Jump through the top, appear in bottom, and vice versa.
With this simple mechanic they challenge you in doing different jumps with timings and angles, introducing new elements and features slowly. They never felt unfair and I finished the game with a glass of whiskey being sipped on at the same time.
I played with a 360 controller, no setup required, didn't try keyboard.
The graphics are just as you can see on the store page, I personally like the simple glowy style and it fits with the gameplay and music.
The music is nice in an ambient kind of way and reminds me of Thomas Was Alone and to some degree Knytt Stories (check em out, also good games). But dont expect any rough tunes or hard beats. Very mellow.
Technical stuff: No Vsync, resulting in ugly tearing on the screen. No crashes. The only thing I can comment on is that the text in the cutscenes jumped up half a row all the time for no reason and that the particles could use some smoother spawning. Nothing major, just a dent in the packaging.
All in all, I liked this game, short but nice for a chill evening with a bit of whiskey in hand and a friend on skype/TS/Mumble. :)
Oh, and remember to select continue game after you reach the sun the first time, youre only halfway! :)

Another puzzle (though very low on the puzzle content, it's mostly just avoiding spikes...) platformer by the people who made Sugar Cube: Bittersweet Factory, this one about the everyday story of some celestial bodies instead of a sugar cube.
It's ... pretty much less good than Sugar Cube in every way - less amusing story, more minimalist graphics, terrible controls - and the puzzles mostly come down to figuring out how to best get the moon's frustratingly terrible jump mechanic (namely, it only has one jump speed/power, and it's very fast and very high, so the only time you can really make safe horizontal progress is when you're on the ground or at/near the very apex of your jump) to not destroy it against some spikes, which is why I'm going to have to give this game a thumbs down.
It's also really low on content, as I was able to get a 100% clear with all achievements in 71 minutes. That said, it's $4, so that might not be that bad - Sugar Cube was barely longer and cost nearly twice as much. Amusingly, though, the time I spent clearing absolutely everything wasn't even long enough to get all the Steam Trading Cards!

The sound design is amazing and fits perfectly for the game, anything else would just make it frustrating. The game is fairly short, i've only played about 1 hour of it and i'm almost to the sun stages (that's what I assume, might be wrong), but you can spend a lot of time replaying levels because there are a few ways of doing a certain run differently. It's definitely worth the $3.99. Buy it for yourself, your parents, your friends,  hell even gift it to your goldfish, it's that much fun.

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is a fun game where you take control of Recette as she attempts to start an Item Shop to pay back her runaway father's massive debt. I've only played through the storyline once, but it took me approximately 13 hours to beat.
There are multiple activities you can take part in within the game during the day. And each day is split up into 4 parts. Certain businesses are only open during certain times of day, or on certain days.
-    The activity the player will likely spend the most time doing is running the shop - which includes stocking your shop, tending to customers, haggling, ticking off scam artists, and making a profit.
-   The player can go to the town and buy supplies from the Market or the Merchant's Guild.
-   The player can interact with various characters during random events, which will generally increase their liking of you and may earn you a new customer or adventurer.
-   You can hire an adventurer from the Adventurer's Guild to go into a dungeon and gather loot for you. During this time, you control the adventurer and must fight enemies, avoid traps, and find lots of treasure (or be incapacitated trying).
There's more to the game then just these previous activities, but that's for you to find out for your own. When/If you beat the game, you unlock a few new game modes, such as
-   Endless, where you can continue to play your game endlessly without worrying about payments
-   New Game+ where you start over with your current items and Merchant Level
-   Survival Mode where you start over and your debt never ends, but constantly increases and you have to play until the debt overwhelms you and you lose your home!
Err... Aaaanyway, I recommend this game. It's fun... also...Capitalism, Ho!

It's Rune Factory for people that don't normally like Rune Factory or even know what Rune Factory is. If you play only one game about an adorable little girl running an item shop to pay down her negligent father's adventuring debts, you probably don't play many games from Japan.
Recettear is a cutesy, lighthearted RPG with tongue-in-cheek dialogue and a well polished shop management hook. None of the gameplay should give anyone trouble, with optional tutorials explaining the mechanics top to bottom: you stock your store, buy low, sell high, haggle with people, make your loan payments, and make friends with progressively weirder adventurers to comb dungeons for free items.
The genius is how it comes together. Before long you're tailoring your shop to draw specific clients, figuring out what each person is willing to spend, anticipating price spikes/drops, and preparing for the stampede of little girls who just have to have the latest Booze of the World. The fairly simple dungeon crawling probably wouldn't stand on its own, yet surprisingly weighty combat and your colorful roster of friends make it a net positive for the overall package.
And it's just so charming. It never commits to a full parody of RPG cliches - a playful ribbing at most - but neither does it get within shouting distance of serious business. It's just a cute little girl trying to convince someone the apple they found in their attic is only worth 70% of its current market value, armed only with a fairy accountant and her own made-up vocabulary.
It's fun. Remember fun? You'll have it when playing this, guaranteed or your money back*.

is a story-driven adventure game with a strong focus on collectibles and “detective” work, and very little action/combat.

You play in 3rd-person adventure style, progressing the story and moving throughout the game world from one spot to the next.  You collect clues and make deductions in the case you are working on in the primary story arc.  The game is pretty linear, which is to be expected for something so focused on story telling; but there is some freedom of exploration.  Much of the backstory and lore can be learned about through the extensive amount of collectibles scattered throughout the levels.
The graphics are pretty nice at max settings and the atmosphere of the game is fitting and done well.  The voice acting is among the best you will find in the realm of video games, which is important since the whole appeal of the game is the story.  It’s a pretty short game, perhaps medium-sized if you decide to get all the collectibles— but it is paced very well, and wraps up right around the time it starts to get stale.
There is really only one mechanic to the game, which is to move around and pick up clues or artifacts... and maybe use a few bland abilities here and there.  The combat is rare and one-dimensional and never evolves into anything more.  So it feels a lot like a show/movie where you control the main character.  To keep you busy, you can explore the levels to search for collectibles as you play through the campaign.
So in conclusion I would posit that I enjoyed my playthrough of this game.  It is pretty minimal in terms of gameplay mechanics; but if you are one who enjoys good story-driven games with atmosphere, and who enjoys collectibles in a 3rd-person adventure setting: then you will probably enjoy
.

Side quests are often dull & unspired. The NPCs you can mind-read only have 2 bits of dialogue,and some even have the same speech within metres of each other. Compare to Dishonored and Bioshock,where the lore was positively overflowing with extra tidbits and engaging backstories.
The checkpoint save system is disappointing in that if you complete the game with quests unfinished, you cannot go into the relevent chapter and re-do the missing quest. It would have nice to revisit these quests without having to start the game over.
Voice acting of the leads is excellent,but the NPCs are phoning it in. By the end,unless I thought the person I passed was integral to the story,I skipped passed them entirely.
Ending is a double-edged sword. A genuinely surprising ending, but the final challenge,where you have to do a quicktime event to a timer is unpleasant and confusing. Why does the key combo for the SAME act change from D + LB to S or A+ LB from one save to the next? It makes no sense! You will likely fail this at least more than once & the loooooong unskippable cut scene before the final denouement only serves to make a hard task even more irritating & stressful. Just let me press 'esc' to get to the challenge,dammit.
The game crashed  or froze repeatedly during play and every 90 minutes or so I would have to use Task Manager to close the game & re-load. I had it on the lowest graphical settings,but still these things persisted. Items that were supposed to be highlighted by the 'e' key often refused to do so.
Not a terrible game at all. But the technical bugs and somewhat half-hearted aspects of the gameplay and lore made this a less than optimal experience. Nice little  thriller that is best enjoyed if bought on sale,and you are pre-warned about the technical glitches. A shame as it had a lot of elements that I liked that could have made it outstanding. 7/10 when the bugs behave. 5 when they don't.

This isn't a game. It's more like a barely interactive movie. The gameplay is nearly non-existent, besides the 3000 quicktime and other single-button-press events. You get cool powers like "Reveal" and "Remove" but are never given the opportunity to use them for anything other than the aforementioned single press events. I was waiting for the puzzle where you have to combine your powers in some clever way. But unfortunately, that never happens. There is not a single puzzle in the entire game where you actually have to use your brain.
The only positive is that the story is actually pretty good. I was engaged enough that I really did want to find out who the killer was. And the history parts of it were pretty entertaining yet educational.
It's unfortunate that the rest of the "game" is so poor and lacking any sort of polish whatsoever. For example, when you walk near an NPC, they have one voice. Then you possess them and read their mind, they have a totally different voice. Very jarring. Not to mention the incredible amount of voiceover repetition amongst all NPCs. Another issue is trying to target objects and enemies is often a frustrating mess. Walking up to an enemy, seeing the prompt to "attack", and then having it suddenly disappear causing you to die is maddening beyond belief. It's made worse only by the fact that it happens so often. The targetting is really, really off in this game. These are small issues, but I bring them up as 100% undeniable proof the game is filled with small details like this that really show a lack of polish, and probably indicate the greater motivation (or lack thereof) to make this game truly shine. As with many things, the devil is in in the details, pun intended.
Do yourself a favor and watch a YouTube video of this game being played in action so you see how the gameplay really is. And for Pete's sake, absolutely do not buy this at full price. Wait for a Steam Sale. I got it for $5.50 via GMG coupon, so the disappointment isn't too harsh for the price I paid. It's unfortunate because the story was actually enjoyable. The story deserves to be told by a greater game.
You want a much better mystery game? Try The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. The UI, voice acting, ambience, and even graphics, are light years ahead of this game. Buy it on sale too though, since that one is very short.

It’s a bit or RPG Strategy mixed into a dungeon crawling type of story with some hack and slash combat. You interact with, use, or equip cards for the main aspects of the game, and gain more cards as time goes on (depending on your success/failure). If you don’t like a card, you can remove it from the deck and not play with it again later (as long as you have enough cards required for the play through).  This deck building aspect allows you to choose what possible events you encounter in your adventure.
I will admit that it can become repetitive depending on how you arrange your deck, and the combat might turn into button spamming, but you don’t have to let it...you can play the game as you choose.
What is nice about this game is that you can either go “endless”, or use the “story mode” which gives you “break points” as you finish each piece once you beat the boss at the end of the dungeon. Like I said, it’s hard to explain...but you’re bound to like at least a couple aspects of this games layout. I enjoy the dialogue from the card master quite a bit and it really adds character to the game.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a game I hadn't heard anything good about. Even prior to release, all the buzz was fairly negative. I can sort of see why. Soul Suspect is a strange cousin to a few genres. Its engine feels like it should be third person action adventure, but there is little action. The action (when it occurs) relies on limited stealth and is a bit rubbish. It operates mostly like a point and click, but investigative sections are few and far between. The main crux of the game is the deductive reasoning which is frankly utter tripe.
Now none of this looks very good for Soul Suspect... You know what let's get this out of the way - the title is dreadful. Soul Suspect is a play on words that doesn't really make sense, except that you are a soul, having been murdered in the opening minutes of the game (spoiler!). But that's it. It would have been acceptable, but the "Murdered" title makes it unwieldy. Are we to expect a spate of games in the "Murdered" series? I would suggest "Murdered: Going Ghostal" about a murdered postman. I digress.
On the surface, Soul Suspect is very much on the ropes here, so let's take it back to the beginning, where the game actually makes a very good first impression. Essentially, you play a policeman who is killed by a serial killer while investigating said serial killer and has to solve his own murder before he can move on to heaven. A neat, fun premise that isn't too demanding and immediately has you suspending your disbelief. What I found exceptional was the telling of your character's history in a well done cutscene showing his tattoos and reasons for getting each one. It really adds some layers to your character and I have to say that I liked the guy. There, I said it. He isn't too much of a wisecracking smartarse, he isn't all whiny and angsty about dying, and his voice actor does a cracking job. Great. I'd go as far as to say that all the characters are well written. You eventually befriend a teenage girl and even SHE is well portrayed, with the right amount of attitude to stay interesting without getting annoying.
Now, sadly it starts to go downhill. Not quickly or dramatically, mind you - you just start to feel that many elements could have be far better implemented. The meat of the game is made up of investigating crime scenes, very similar to L.A. Noire, but without the depth. It can feel a little bit clumsy walking around the crime scene waiting for the "investigate" prompt to come up. It tells you how many clues you need to find, but finding some is needlessly difficult, requiring some odd maneuvering into the exact position. Using the clues themselves is even more frustrating.
An example from early in the game is when you have to investigate a young woman who tells you she was murdered by an old couple and needs to know where her body is so she can move on. After investigating the old couple's apartment, you are given the question "What happened to the young woman's body?" and you have 6 clues to work with. Intuitively, you might select the ones that give physical evidence or point to what happened to her body, but you'd be wrong. The clues you have to select are actually 1) the girl is dead; 2) this person murdered her; 3) yes, this person definitely murdered her. It doesn't make any sense, because the clues you have to use don't really point to the question asked. This is a recurring problem throughout the game, but swings wildly between obtuse clues and such stark simplicity that you are constantly thrown. For example, later you are asked "What made that cracking noise?", a rope, branch or something cracking into a tree. Here it seems like the answer with "crack" in it is too obvious, but that is the actual answer!
This all leads to a rather odd issue with the game in that there doesn't really seem to be a way to fail the investigations, you can just keep trying combinations of clues until you get it right. You get 3 shields next to a clue if you get it perfectly, dropping down to one as you fail. I don't really know how I feel about this. I like that it keeps the story moving, but it also makes the game feel trivial.
What can slow the pace of the game are the fairly boring stealth sections. There are two types - one where you simply have to distract a living person with a possessed electrical appliance in order to let your companion slip past (I never failed any of these sections), and the second is when demons decide to show up. These sections are incredible dull and annoying simultaneously. You need to either slip by the demons' very short, predictable patrol paths or get behind them and kill them with mercifully simple QTE. There is some nonsense about using ghost crows to distract them and hiding in ghost residues if they spot you, but it all seems hastily cobbled together.
When you're not taking part in the main parts of the game, you'll be collecting collectibles. Lots and lots of collectibles. There are journals, memories, ghost stories and ghost graffiti to collect and are also the subject of ambivalence. They are very easy to find which is sort of good as they add to the story, but are so easy to find that they seem a bit pointless. The only hard ones to find are the graffiti collectibles, but that's because they're invisible and there's the problem of you being in the right position to tell you that you can interact with them.
So all in all, boring, pointless and needlessly obtuse. What a terrible game! Well, no, actually. It all sort of comes together. It gels very well. It initially feels weird moving around the levels and into crime scenes because you might feel like you should be sneaking, but you are completely invisible, so you walk around completely unimpeded. You can walk through walls, possess people to see what they're thinking and (in a great highlight) even possess a cat and run around meowing. The execution of the game might be lacking, but the intention is so clear that I found myself forgiving it most of its flaws.
The story is a high point as well, I have to admit that it drew me in very and had me second guessing myself a few times. There are lots of clues around as to what is happening and if (like me) you pick up on them, you will find yourself slightly thrown as you try to piece it all together and re-evaluate your theories. I even found myself pleasantly surprised by the denouement - it wasn't overlong, over complex or a ridiculous boss fight. I was very impressed by the writing and performances in the game, they turned a mediocre game into a good one.
I did get the game very cheap, I have to say, so I don't know how forgiving I would have been at £39.99. I paid around £4.50 for it and feel that that is very cheap, but I would have been happy to pay up to £11.99 for it, and that is praise indeed!

Lumini is a beautiful, simple and relaxing game to play.
The creatures you play as are cute little creatures that light up the place as you traverse caves.
Your main goal in the game is to make it to the next checkpoint, collecting little orbs of light along the way. Once you reach the checkpoint, you add more Lumini to your pack. They will replace the ones lost due to enemies attacking you.
Different coloured Lumini have different abilities. Allowing you to play in a more offensive way, killing all enemies you see, or evading them with speed boosts.
There are quite a few hidden areas in the game, which gives you a purpose to explore the caves apart from just enjoying the beautiful scenery.
The music is quite beutiful, and helps immerse you in the world.
It's a great game overall, check it out!
