It´s a good game, not perfect, but it has the potential of being the best mmo of the year.. and maybe even beyond that.
But why?
First of all, the graphics are good. The used engine (Cryengine 3) does it´s job, and still has potential for the future to look even better. In addition it´s an engine suitable for mmo´s, i have jet to experience engine related problems in this game. After playing Aion for 5 Years thats something quite positive and important, as that can severely influence the pvp experience in a bad way, especialy for melee classes.
But lets talk a bit about the combat, it´s tab based, which in my opinion ist the best way for mmo´s, it´s well paced, and you can move during all of your skills, exept for the cast skills of cause. The need to stand still on a spot, even when using instant skills was always bothering me (although thanks to the nuggy engine there was a way around that in Aion). That makes for a dynamic and movement based combat. But thats not all, spamming just some skills wont get you anywhere (at least it shouldn´t), but using the right combinations and synergies will bring out the full potential for your character. The combination system, which at first glance seems rather complicated can be learned by simplyplaying, because soon you´ll notice the *combo effect* written over the targets head als you´re accidently using a combo.
But lets talk a moment here about the classes. There are 10 Skill trees, and you can combine 3 of them into your own class, and put your skill point them accordingly to your playstyle. This means there will be so much diversity in PvP and PvE, as you can have your own unique playstyle. Wanna be a ranger play can unleash a roaring thunder? no problem.. a sneaky mage, attacking you out nowhere? You can do that, or just a simply cleric like character... there is a class combination for everyone here. Even if you have chosen a combination, that doesnt seem to work for you anymore? No Problem, you can rechoose your classes, without having to create an all new character.
Of cause not everything is perfect, for example the questing system is not really exiting, quests are rather repetetive and and the rewards pretty much always xp, cash and maybe some armor/weapons. It´s been done in a lot of mmo´s and this one is no different, BUT the questing areas are well highlighted on the map, and I have never had any trouble finishing a quest. But you´re not playing Archeage for the quests, those are just the means to lvl up, get some starter gear (which they do offer) and get to the end content smoothly, which again, works.
So graphics, combat and quest are fine, but what about the rather hyped crafting system? As I have not played this game too much, i can only say.. it works for me, I have done some gathering, crafted a few things, and the system works. The amazing part of the crafting in Archeage is actually not the way it works, but the sheer diversity of what you can actually craft. Ships, houses, armor, weapons, your own sheep farm, even castles, submarines and a frigging tractor that can honk can be crafted.
But no matter how amazing the things are, that can be created, if that materials needed for them are too easly obtained, or to hard, this crafting system can be the downfall of Archeage. You won´t be able to big scaled crafts on your own, as you´ll need a big guild to achieve your, and your mates goals because of the complexity of the system, which is good, as this will create the need to work together and keeps egoism down.. which for me means that the game will be a lot more enjoyable for the majority of the people
As I have not done PvP so far, only watched some videos of it, I can´t really judge it, but it seems good as far as I´m concerned.
In conclusion: in theory this is not just a great game, but THE next big potential MMO,  but it all depends on the publisher and
the community, as it´s a player based economy that´ll only work if the community gets it right. I sincerely hope that it will, because Archeage has so much potential.
If you´re looking for an MMO few retricions, and a lot of ways to play it in addition, and dont mind the need of having to purchase the patron status (you can buy it with in the ingame currency or rl money), it´s a must try.
For those, who always need a guiding hand, leading you through the entire game this might not be your choice of MMO, but with some friends who can lead you, it still might be quite the joyride. Since it´ll be free to play, anyone can test it, although again, without the patronage status your experience will be limited.

Floor 3, do I chose to run from the angry mob and chance keeping all my remaing food but risk losing it all and thus succum to the subseqent inevitable starvation? Do I risk searching the remaining cards on a floor in hope of finding better equipment but risk losing everything trying to cross a river, leaving myself bare of armour and weilding only a rusty axe when it comes to challenging the deck boss? These are just some of the many difficult decisions you will face in Hand of Fate. Gripping dialogue and voice acting straight from the off. (The voice actor of the dealer is superb). Immense replayability and customisation through the use of the randomising deck system. Challenging bosses, enemies, events and decision making. I have not seen a game that can blend card based gameplay, with RPG elements such as your equipment, curses and 'artefacts', and actual in game combat. (One criticsm would be the combat system is a bit, well lots of rolling around randomly dodging enemies whilst mashing the LMB...But theres potential for a more substantial combat system in the future, furthermore this is only a minute criticsm in my opinion and should not overshadow the vast quality and diversity this game offers). Icant wait to see what the developers include in later patches and updates, perhaps character facial customisation? Some sort of tech-tree or research tree to go alongside the RPG aspect of the game? Hope everyone, developers included if you are reading this, found this a useful and honest review. Definately recommend getting your hands on this game!

This is an absolutely mind benidng platformer with mixed elements that you have never seen before, all packed with a fairly good and quite calming soundtrack.
Walking into this game you must toss aside most of your traditional platforming wisdom. The game takes a completely new take on platforming mechanics and executes a great 2-3 hour experience with it. In this game, falling off to the bottom or jumping through the top (or in the later half of the game, the opposite!) will instead loop you around to the other side, as though your jump went across a cylinder. On top of that, you can't control how long your jump is, making for even more careful (not torturous) platforming. It's completely wild and in the same kind of way that portal does, it just absolutely bends your mind for nearly the entirety of the game.
The soundtrack of the game is zen-like in its nature and even if a level would otherwise be particularly hard and mildly rage inducing, I even found myself just saying "Damn." calmly after multiple failures at just the first part of one level. In fact, I have yet to be actually mad from this game just from it's soundtrack. Your experience may vary, but it is still a great feature.
The only unfortunate thing about this game is that its story is completely lost in translation. You can certainly understand what's being said if you mix and replace some words, but the story is extremely minimal and unless you are someone who plays games almost exclusively for a story then this shouldn't be an issue and may even further lighten the mood because of some silly translations.
Overall, I would recommend the game, espeically for its price point. It knows exactly what it's worth, so if you're interested, give it a whirl.

Metro: Last Light Redux is why I play video games, this game is fantastic and one of my all-time favourites. It runs great for me at 60 FPS, on a GTX 980, with Windows 10. However, the maximum Antialiasing setting appears to be broken. So, I play with everything maxed out except Antialiasing, which I leave at the default setting. It looks and sounds incredible, with clever gameplay elements, that help to make it one of the most immersive games I’ve ever played.
The game can be played with both a shooter or stealth play style, with different endings depending on decisions you make throughout. There are also hidden depths contained within the game world including a ‘moral system’. Which encourages the player, to take notice of the extensive attention to detail, contained in Last Light’s design. As a sequel to Metro: 2033 Redux, Last Light continues the entertaining and immersive story from that game. While adding more fun scenarios and well-designed chapters of its own.
This version of the game also includes all of the DLC content, which can be found in the ‘Chapters’ section of the main menu. The first time I played through the campaign, I didn’t know about the DLC, as it can be easily missed. When you go into the ‘Chapters’ menu, you can press ‘x’ (XBOX 360 controller), to switch between the campaign and DLC chapters. These DLC chapters are great, each one demonstrates different aspects, of ‘Last Light’s gameplay and design. My favourite of these chapters are Kshatriya and Khan, over all though this DLC content is probably the best that I’ve ever seen.
I highly recommend Metro Last Light as a fun and immersive video game, which stands as a shining example of great game design.

My 772 hrs of Steam game time only represents less than half of the time I've spent with this game. The total, as of writing is actually 15,542 - 647 days. I'm still nowhere near done exploring what this game has to offer.
There are three ways to play this game: on Steam, in an internet browser, and on mobile devices. Steam is the first and still the best way of playing but, for a long while, I was unable to do anything other than play on mobile. Handily, all three methods of play link up with each other, so you can progress nomatter what method you use.
I started playing around February of 2015 (after I 'won' AdVenture Capitalist) and the game is still in beta - it's had several major improvements in that time: Tired levels of difficulty, missions for crusaders that you're not using, a crafting system, changing the way 'Enchantment Points' are earned, and an established calendar of holiday events. The core mechanic is still the same though: earn gold by killing monsters while you play through a loose, tongue-in-cheek adventuring plot. Use the gold to level up and unlock more crusaders. Gold is earned by clicking or through the passive Damage Per Second of your crusaders. Crusaders interact with the other crusaders in different ways, creating a strategic element where you try to find the most efficient formations to provide the most click damage (which will not be the same for everybody before long), DPS and/or gold find bonuses. Reaching a pre-defined objective and 'resetting the world' (read: blowing the planet up and starting over) awards you the 'Idols' from the title, which give you a passive DPS & gold bonus regardless of your formation (and can be used to purchase other bonuses) as well as other rewards.
As I said, after a short while, nobody's formation strategy will be the same as differences in crusader equipment will change things.
The game is by no means pay-to-win. The exclusive stuff you can get by dropping real cash just adds a few extra animations and enhances item effects by 50%, which is really powerful in tier 1 but markedly less so by the time you've managed to get to tier 3.
New content is added at least twice a month, every month, sometimes as often as weekly, so there's always new things to do and new challenges to face. The developers are all friendly, hosting frequent Reddit AMAs and are incredibly approachable and helpful.
I'd also recommend Codename Entertainment's other Steam game: Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms - a licensed D&D game, similar but functionally different to CotLI.

Brilliant strategy game with a very steep but rewarding learning curve. A bit like the total war series, if you completely removed the realtime battles and focussed on designing the most in depth and rewardingly complex grand strategy element possible.
The emergent narratives that are created by the multitude of smaller systems and simulations working behind the scenes is what makes this one of my favourite games of all time. Be warned though, this is not for the faint hearted in terms of the ammount of time you need to put into the game to get the best out of it. If you love complex strategy games and if you have plenty of free time or are looking for a game to focus on for a few months or more then this could very well be the game for you.
My biggest criticism would be that although the DLC is for the most part very well crafted, it is in my opinion hugely overpriced. This is mostly forgivable however as you still get to see and get the benefits to the main game, for free, that all the DLC brings. You are just unable to play with the main new mechanics the DLC introduces without forking out as much as £10 or more for each peice of DLC.
Unlike a lot of major publishers, Paradox have been really good about patching and updating this continually for more than a year after it's release and are still making improvements and releasing new content as of the date of this review. All in all this is a worthwhile purchase if you are not afraid of having to try and play for a few hours before you have actually learned enough... to start playing. It's a tough nut to crack but a few hours of wrapping your head around this gem can lead to literally years of entertainment and replayability.

I really, really want to get into this game and enjoy it, but the learning curve is so huge it is virtually impossible for me. It is exactly the sort of game I want to play, but there is quite literally nothing to help players along the way.
The official tutorial included in the game is awful, either it has become broken as new patches have come out, or the content of the tutorials have just never worked - there is a point where you just can't move on with it as the button it references doesn't exist.
Overall I feel like I have dropped money on a game that I will never play again, I just can't get my head around anything in the game which is unfortunate honestly. So, if like me you are new to RTS-RPG games don't pick this up, it is not noob-friendly.
I would love it if someone could teach me how to play the game, see that would be awesome - but I know of no-one personally that would be willing to do that.
So yeah, not recommended for beginners, including myself.

After playing Expedition Conquistador for the last several hours I have been compelled to write a recommendation for this amazing indie game. This is an under-the-radar hidden gem that deserves a huge player base because it is simply that good,
As the name suggests you take charge of a group of Spanish Conquistators venturing to the New World. Are you there for fame, glory or riches? The choice is yours!
The game itself is an excellent mixture of RPG, map exploration, character/resource management and turn based combat. You can be diplomatic and seek alliances with natives to add local units to your group and peacefully aquire what you need ... or .... you can cut down the savage  and take what you want fom them without pity!
Its great that a game like this doesn't shy away from topics because of politically correct considerations and just lets you play however you want.; as a bloodthirsty conqueror, a peaceful diplomat or somewhere between those too extremes.
The battles are a lots of fun (and genuinely hard! even at normal difficullty) and take the form of  turn based and hex-centered combat. The games graphics aren't astounding like say, Skyrims are, but they are in my opinion definately above average for a game that focuses as much on the RPG side of things as the combat.
I took a chance on this game because it was on sale and because  I love the period in history its based on . However, if I could go back in time I would honestly have donated to the kickstarter campaign for this game and/or bought it at full price. It really is that good, and is probably one of only a handful of games I would ever say are worth their full price on Steam
This is a completely underrated gem that I would highly recommend to anyone and everyone, you could honestly pay full price for this game and not be disappointed. However if your still not convinced, add it to your wishlist and get this the moment its on sale.
So, what do you say ... are you man enough to seek your fortune across the seas in the New World? Are you a modern day Christopher Columbus or Hernán Cortés? Play Expeditions Conquistatdor and find out!

Expeditions: Conquistador is billed as XCOM set in an Age of Explorers historical fiction.  And as far as that goes, it is accurate.  Expeditions: Conquistador is in fact substantially more complex than XCOM, and also quite a bit more unforgiving.  The moment you leave the first island fort-town in Hispanola, you will end up fighting outnumbered, outgunned, and outclassed.  To wit, I have yet to win a non-tutorial fight.
Am I merely doing it wrong?  Have I utterly failed to do some basic this-or-that which would make the game play more smoothly?  Perhaps so.  I don't know what it would be off-hand.  To the extent that there is immersive schadenfreude in getting run off by spear-waving Caribbean natives, this game is effective.  But is it too much to ask for the newbie levels to be a little more forgiving?  It's one thing to sally forth into the jungle with your caravan laden with equipment and supplies only to return a couple weeks later starving, robbed, and bleeding; and quite another to have at least some success early on.
I suspect I'll give Expeditions: Conquistador another run in time.  But for now, I'll suck my thumb and play something that won't flay me for having the temerity to hit the New Game button.  Hello Kitty Island Adventure was certainly not on the island of Hispanola.

I will write a better review later on after playing some more of this, but since it is currently on sale, i wanted to write this for those interested but not 100% sure.
This game is a turn-based game in which you have limited amount of distances you can travel and thus you have to think like a strategist.  Planning your route and plan of attack, is vital.  Failure to do so, will result in either you losing because your soldier was a derp and ran out of energy to run to cover, or you simply losing comrades who will not be revived.   It is tricky, but there are many ways to skin a cat, and for this, there are many ways to win the battle.
There are various classes of soldiers to use in battle, each with their own strengths and personalized weaknesses.   There is ways to grind for exp and money, while it is never needed, it is good for things in general.
The Art style, is very unique looking and while it is not a 4k texture package with 60+fps and all of that modern stuff you hear, it is a nice change of pace and it honestly looks good, period.   The outer white line that borders the video, can be odd at first but it gives off the effect of you being in the story.
Speaking of story, there  is a nicely done story for this game which I am still learning about, but it sounds like one that has potential for a lot of good, and bad, things to happen.  Also, the game has a "episode" like feel to it.  What I mean is that to play the game, you go to this book and "Play" the episode.  Doing this will either cause a video to play and can be skipped, or you will see a fe wshort clips that ends in a fight.
overall, it's a great buy, the price is cheap, and the game is amazing.  Is it 10/10?  I don't know yet.  Maybe, maybe not, but for the current price, it IS worth it.

Edit: Having now finished the game with a couple of play-throughs, I have to admit to being somewhat let down by the finished product. I was eagerly looking forward to playing with some of the things I loved in the first, that were lacking in EA. I thought their omission was due to it still being in EA... alas it wasn't... So if you loved the crafting in the first, well, forget about it for DOS2, it basically dosen't exist.
CRAFTING: Forget about it, it doesn't really exist and what there is, is almost negligible in it's use unless you are playing hardcore- and very few gamers do. You can make a few potions, but why bother when there is no need and what you might potion up is better dealt with by a cast spell.
ARMOUR: Like crafting, they have taken one of the pleasures of the first and ruined it to such an extent, that what little crafting ability they allow you to play with, is almost totally useless, and a complete and utter waste of time. In the first, you could get a semi decent piece of armour, and mod it to your characters ability and it would be with that character for a large chunk of the game. Now, it's with your character for one character level - two if you bother to mod it - and then it's useless and sold. Larian have managed - very successfully -  to make Legendary and Epic armour anything but. And that is no mean feat. Seriously, you won't keep Epic/Legendary/Supermarket-own-brand armour much more than two of the characters levels, as by that point it's quite simply, crap and very un-Epic in stats.
And that leads to the next bug-bear. Because of the rubbishness of armour, you spend less time exploring the wild as an adventurer of (dubious) repute and more time as a shopper of armour, sick in the knowledge that in 2 levels time, you are going to have to repeat the whole tedious process all over again...
WEAPONS: Pretty much the same as ARMOUR; Buy some glitzy cutlery, level up twice, sell old cutlery, buy some new, rinse repeat. It gets tedious quick. Real quick.
GRAPHICS: It looks nice, yes, I will give it that.
ENVIROMENTAL EFFECTS: Yes, wonderful, have a pat on the back, but after a few hours playing, you tend to ignore most of it except for Boss fights. (That was on normal difficulty-it becomes more of a requirement for the harder play throughs, but again, that's only going to be an issue for a (very) small number of players.)
STORYLINE: It was alright, nothing to write home about and pretty much standard fare for this genre of game. Larian have tried to throw in some curve balls to increase the re-playability of the game, which was nice, but looking at Steam Achievements for the game, a quarter of players haven't even made it past the first chapter yet, and to be honest, I don't see that score getting much better in the future. So all that effort to make the game replayable when finished, could have been spent better elsewhere... Like on bug testing for a start. Gosh, there was an astounding amount of bugs, many of them game/quest breaking.
OVERALL: The game was alright, but the problems with the lifespan of armour and weapons quickly meant the game became less DOS2 and more Divinity-mad-dash-around-map-for-shopkeepers-to-up-grade-rubbish-equipment, or" Divinity Original Shopping Trip 2" for short. Yes graphics are good, environmental effects have been made more effective, if you can be bothered to use them and a lot of effort has been spent on the ending scenes for the 48 people that will finish the game.
Not played a DOS game and thinking of grabbing a spell book and jumping in? Then buy DOS1 instead. It's more rewarding, most of the bugs have been squashed, it's cheaper and hasn't been dumbed down for console players like this one has. I had high hopes for this game, enough to buy it months before release, but would I do so for DOS3? No. Not if this is the direction Larian are going in.

Highly overlooked gem.  Just finished playing this and I thoroughly enjoyed it from beginning to end.  I do not understand why this game received such negative reviews. The story is entertaining and you're kept guessing until the end (although I had my suspicions - which turned out to be incorrect). The graphics are quite beautiful overall - the animations are very good.  The voice over work is very good - I really liked the main character. The gameplay on a computer keyboard is a tad clunky but I got used to it very quickly.  There is nothing that deterred me from being truly engaged in the story of Ronan, the main character - a detective who is murdered while trying to track a serial killer.
NOTE: this is an adventure game.  In fact, I'd argue that it's almost an old-school adventure game wrapped up in a shiny, modern day package.  The goal of the game is to gather clues and solve puzzles.  There are a few moments that require stealth: when demons roam the area your character is traversing.  The demons look for ghosts and eat their essence (including Ronan's). But this is not an action game in any way - in fact, you can probably get through the whole game without ever having to fight one of the demons - simply run and hide from them (ok, not always so simply).
Even searching for the hidden side quests is entertaining (something I still haven't finished - I'm about 83% of the way there as of my writing this). Scattered throughout the locations are hidden objects that need to be revealed and collected.  Once collecting all of them, you are treated to a ghost story - the history of that particular haunted object.  The ghost stories are well written and well voiced - I would have liked there to be some video or a slide show to go along with them instead of only audio, but I enjoyed them nonetheless.
The game is quite inexpensive during Steam's seasonal sales and I highly recommend picking up a copy if you like a good detective story with some simple, but clever puzzle solving.  The game is engaging, the story is well-written, the characters beautifully rendered with excellent acting, and the sets are detailed and moody - perfect for a ghost story. I cannot say enough good things about this wonderful game.

Surprisingly enjoyable. A not so long adventure game with an original idea but plagued by an average execution.
Murdered takes the interesting concept of playing a dead man stuck between two worlds and having to solve his murder to be able to get to heaven. I really love this idea, you're investigating in two embedded worlds : the living and the dead. You can clip through most environment from the world of the living but get stuck against the environment of the dead. The setting is very well made with ghosts appearing and disappearing as well as people in an alike situation as yours : unable to let go and go to heaven. There are 4 side quests where you're helping someone to understand his/her death.
I personally loved the aesthetic of the game, a mix of color and black and white. The game also is very well optimised and runs flawlessly on my laptop (i7 4500U, Nvidia GT750m) @ 900p/1080p. The story is enjoyable for the most part and the collaboration and interactions between Joy and Ronan are well-executed. Finally, the game has a lot of collectibles (242 to be precise), this can be either a positive or a negative point depending on the player.
The gameplay is below average even for an adventure game. Every step of the story involves you looking for clues in a small area, when you have enough clues you are able to link a few of them to each other to solve one question.... and that's it, for the whole game. The clues are either stupidly obvious or stupidly useless and the solving questions are terrible. The combat system sucks terribly too, it's simply about sneaking behind enemies and doing a simple QTE. Murdered won't be remembered for its gameplay.
The story is very unbalanced. The first hour is basically setting the story and characters, the pace is slow and isn't very compelling. When you start seeing a bit through how the investigation is going to take place, it becomes enjoyable and that until the end of the game where you are faced to a completely stupid and abrupt ending. The ending feels rushed and I hated it because of this, the last chapter is like 5 minutes long... The rest of the game isn't very long either, count between 6 to 8 hours depending on whether you want to find all the collectibles or not.
It might seem that the game is terrible but I personally enjoyed it anyway despite all of its flaws. The aesthetic and most of the story felt original. Many good ideas, poor execution but still worth it in my opinion. I wouldn't recommend it at full price though, buy it on sale.

Very fun RPG where you take the roll of an item shop keeper.  While sitting around hawking broadswords all day may not sound very fun, the shopkeeping element is oddly engauging and surprisingly deep - with different customers having behavior quirks and fluctuating budgets, mechanics that reward a concientious approach to pricing (the most someone will pay for an item is not always the best price to sell it for), and different ways to sell items including advance orders and vending machines.  If you ever get bored of the daily work grind, however, you can always hire an adventurer and spend the day exploring a dungeon for exp and loot (which you can, of course, sell in your store for 100% profit)
Lots of postgame content (there will be entire dungeons and playable adventurers you wont even see on your frist playthrough). Worth $20, but a definate pickup on its frequent 50% off sales.  Play the demo.  9/10

Expeditions: Conquistador is the best RPG I've played in a long while, because it's roleplaying in its purest essence that goes beyond the usual combat statistics and dice rolls. Set in an unique historical time period (the Spanish conquest of Middle America), you can pick your party members at the start of the game, each with his/her own background stories and character traits. Your party members will talk to you and react to your actions, and their stories and opinions really matter. You might want to leave passive characters behind if you're about to behave aggressively. And don't be surprised if discriminating characters react negative when you act friendly to the native Americans. Add a HoMM-ish overworld that can be very hostile (especially at the start), some very unique gameplay mechanics and enjoyable turn-based combat, and this game is pure awesomeness. Highly recommended!

This is something truly cool and unusual. A very unique mix of tarot, roguelike, flowing combat, turn based adventure.
It's not often I gush about the very concept of a game, but this is such a fantastically new thing that I can't help it! The Dealer lays down cards which represent one leg of your journey, somewhere in the cards is a "Stairs" card which leads you to the next step of the journey. In between are combat encounters, small challenges to defeat, overcome, or just survive, with a cool "keep your eye on the card" shuffling minigame that, if you're good at that sort of thing, works quite well as a personal challenge to the player's skills. There's also shops to buy and sell equipment (also portrayed by cards, such as Axe, Sword, or blessed or cursed weapons with various extra abilities) and food, which is used with every card you encounter, or sometines specifically in certain encounters (Goblins steal your food, attack them to get it back. An angry mob from a starving village approaches you, will you give them half your food? - if it's not enough, they just might attack you!). Your rewards are gold, new equipment, new blessings or curses.
And, every time you complete a certain challenge, conquering it fully, you are given a token which unlocks new cards to be shuffled into the deck for your next game. More weapons, equipment, curses, encounters, enemies unlock as you progress.
Seriously, this is just a MASTERFUL concept that feels so right. The only real weak point so far is the combat, which isn't bad, but it feels a bit unpolished and simple. That said, the most recent patch included some serious improvements in even this area, following player feedback.
It is abundantly clear that Defiant Development are set on making something that is truly unique, clever, fun, and above all, excellent. They are absolutely on the right track. I would love to see more fantastically new ideas like this in gaming, and as it stands, they deserve their hard-fought success in this beautifully designed piece of unusual game-design brilliance.

Expeditions: Conquistador is a tactical RPG, set, as implied by the name, during the historical Spanish invasion of parts of the American continent. You play a Spanish nobleman, in command of your military unit, set on a ship from Spain to America.
Your first duty is to choose the members of your unit. I really like the idea that you don't only have to consider their tactical roles (Soldier / Scout / Hunter / Doctor / Scholar) and how many of which class you're going to need, but also their personal views and agendas. Some of those people are either racists or extremely religious, while others are more tolerant and open-minded. Some are adventurous and like taking risks, while others are more cautious and calculated. As squad-leader, you must consider how well those people are going to be able to interact and get along with each other, and how easy it is going it be for them to accept your leadership, considering the differences between them. Having half your squad be adventurous risk-takers and the other half very cautious, for example, is probably not a very good idea, as any decision you make during the game which will have anything to do with taking risks, would end up making half your squad lose morale.
Next up, as soon as you set foot on "The New World", you're challenged with tough decisions to make, one after the other. Some issues can be solved either peacefully or by force, while others will require unavoidable violence to deal with. One of the things I really like about the game, is that it lets you face some of the obvious moral dillemas of the period and the context from a refreshing and flexible perspective. You can be the barbaric warlord who uses violence to solve every problem, you can be something more alike an enlightened diplomat, or anything in between, according to the options the game presents to you. While you're obviously led by the general way history was set in reality and are expected to bring money and treasures back to the King of Spain, the game gives you quite a variety of ways to do that. Some of those ways are filled with violence and bloodshed, and others are much less so, although fighting is an integral part of the game, whatever path you end up choosing.
The battle system is complex and interesting, yet not too difficult to learn. The ingame tutorial is effective, short and to the point, so I won't get into it in too much detail. The main principle is choosing which members of the squad to send on each battle, based on their skills, experience and character. Also, some of your people will trigger all sorts of plot events during the game, which gives the game a higher replayability value. I've found it interesting to start another playthrough, this time with different people, just out of curiosity regarding their personal plot events.
As the game is very story-driven and there's (almost) no voice acting, there's a lot of reading to do, which you shouldn't skip if you want to stay in the game. Your choices and decisions have a significant effect on the plot, and in order to make an informed decision, you should know what's going on. Skipping text will only put you in a position of having to choose an arbitrary action, which in my humble opinion, takes most of the fun out of the game. If you generally don't have what it takes to be patient and take the time to read, maybe this is not the type of game for you.
The graphics are not bad at all, and the soundtrack is one of the best I've heard (composed by Leonardo Badinella, a musician from Chilli), which really helps keeping the game alive, even along the slower parts.
All in all, this is one of the best games I've encountered during the last few years, and I recommend it to anyone who likes Tactical RPGs.

If you land on combat it can cost you food and if you land on a shop you can spend your money.
The main reason for not recommending the game is the combat. Although it's definetly not the worst implementation of a fighting system in a game, it doesnt feel fluent enough to feel good. This is a game near and dear to me.
First off, the aesthetic. Oh my God, the vehicles and the weapons and the costumes are so gorgeous in this game. From the saddle bags on the tanks to the little map pinned to Welkin's shirt. Its incredible. The setting is fantastic as well. I love worlds created out of 1930s-1940s technology. There's not many of them compared to the ocean of fantasy and steampunk worlds, but this is one of the best the genre has to offer. The gameplay is a lot of fun. Due to a bug, the damage inflicted on my units was far higher than usual. It had something to do with the framerate and the game registering several consecutive hits at once. It wasn't a problem though. I actually preferred how difficult it made the game. There's a forgiving permadeath system. Units can die but it takes a lot of negligence to let that happen before the difficulty ramps up in the second half of the game. Leveling up classes instead of the units themselves is ingenius and perfect for this sort of game.
The story, and on this I'm going to differ in opinion from a lot of my collegues, is nothing special. Its totally workman, there's nothing especially good or bad about it. It can get a little "anime-y". And don't get me wrong, I love anime, but it can get a little more K-On than Venus Wars, if you know what I mean.
The game is not perfect. The Engineer class is severly underpowered, and there are certain tactics that can be exploited to make the entire game a complete joke. I reccomend not spoiling it for yourself and just playing the way you like. And not to beat yourself up over losing or letting people die. Just have fun.
There are sequels to this game. They are PSP exclusives ( :^( ). I've played a lot of V2, its fun, but it doesn't hold a candle to this one. I really hope Sega wakes up and realizes this series deserves another proper fully fledged entry, not a portable grind fest.

Many developers set out with clever genre-crossover ideas, and this may not be the cleverest but it is by far the best executed. The card system doesnt feel like its forced onto the arena-fighting element, nor do the rogue-like elements are not ever compromised for the sake of story or the card mechanic. The game has the same replayability of games like Binding of Isaac or Rogue Legacy. Even simple things like "draw 2 gain cards" (each of which is slightly different) instead of just "gain 10 gold" make you glad nobody else thought to make this game first. And if they did and I just don't know about them, they probably didnt make as smooth (or graphically impressive) a game as this.
As for the mob-fighting type of combat that people keep comparing to the Batman: Arkham series, dont let that scare you off. Its not the 'repeatedly tap x' kind of fighting, but a type of combat were you still have the cool animations of batman, but you actually need to control your character's direction and time your attacks and counters.
This game would still be the best digital-card-game/rpg/rogue-like/text-adventure/arena-fighter even there were two of them.

Shaping up to be an amazing game.
A brilliant mix of deckbuilding and table top adventuring with 3rd person combat akin to Batman (Arkham series).
- Combat feels meaty and relatively smooth. Sliding across the room to slam an axe into a bandit's face hardly ever gets old, countering is satisfying and taking on a group of tough enemies and coming out on top feels awesome.
-The game is hard (maybe not dark souls hard but you'll definitely be rolling and parrying a lot) and as with any chance based games you're gonna get screwed over every now and then.
- AND yet with some strategy and skill you can overcome some of the bad luck thrown at you.
- Even if you do lose you rarely leave a playthrough completely empty handed. i.e. you'll find new cards that you can add to your deck that bring more useful weapons and items into the mix as well as new events/scenarios.
- No two games will be the exact same, you will feel like coming back for more.
- Play sessions tend to be short and sweet, (anywhere between 15 - 30mins) great for gamers who don't have the time to sit down and play long haul RPGs.
-I'm 8hrs in and I've still got plenty more to do. At the very least another 5-8 more hours of gameplay.
Cons
-Still a little buggy and in need of some fine tuning but overall definitely worth your money.
Definitely worth getting if you're looking for something a little different.

This remake and extension is second to none.  The graphics for a game from (technically) 2004 are extremely good and fit the entire aura the game tries to create.
If you're not familiar with the Fable franchise, you essentially experience the life of a hero but also mould and shape his reputation and stature within the town. You are faced with many problems that need solving either through being 'good' or 'bad'. These decisions affect the story-line, those around you and even the town itself. The Lost Chapters offers new content as the story continues from where the game ended in the original version, giving you hours of fun.
Not only is the playability of this game exceptional, it also has a great feel to it and feels natural when in combat etc. This makes combat fun and not tiresome despite some repetitve enemies and repetitive movements. The AI in combat are actually pretty smart which adds to the fun, they can dodge, block and counter, often making it difficult to hurt them... not too challenging, but challenging enough for a fun battle with every encounter.
The length of the game is not bad at all, it should take you around 10-11 hours to complete the game with minimal exploring... whilst this is significantly shorter than the following titles, this captivating story is definitely worth at least a run through. It's the sort of game you want to play again and again, doing things differently each time and seeing how that affects your hero and also those around you. I'm currently on my fourth time round this game (just on this platform) and not bored even in the slightest. In regards to the other Fable titles, I'd say they're all equally awesome and enthralling. If I had to pick an absolute favourite it would have to be Fable 2. Yet, this game is almost up there and transitions you well throughout each game if you follow the titles from the start up, seeing the development of this game is very rewarding. Yes, people who spend real money, are in a certain advantage.

The only purchases, that can only be done with real money are certain skins, which were made by Steam users, that benefit their creator. But there are other skins to unlock without paying. And it should be said, that the real money currency, can be obtained by trading items with other players.
Games like PoE or this one live from ingame purchases and if I have spent a long time playing these games for free, I often purchase something equally worth a fully priced game, maybe more afterwards, since I spend way more time in games like these, than in AAA titles.
Although Warframe is a very good game, I bought Destiny 2 yesterday, I will try it out myself, but I can see me turning it down and returning to Warframe in a week or two. In the long run Warframe should provide much more content and is probably way more polished.

Wow.
It's hard to overstate how much I enjoyed this game. It is masterful on every level - story, writing, scope, decision making, combat, environmental design, artwork, lighting effects, cinematography, musical score, sound design, and virtually any other area I can think of. It is, without exaggeration, that good.
(mini spoiler) And the last mission - any team member you have come to know in the game can die a very permanent death based on your decisions, giving the finale a weight and consequence rarely experienced in video games. (end mini spoiler)
What is perhaps most staggering is that even after a 50-hour playthrough (DLC included), you can be sure that you have seen far less than even half of the possibilities that the game has to offer. The original game isn't nearly as perfect, but still worth a run-through for the storyline and decisions that will carry over into the sequel.
No, the game is not without faults. For one thing, it's overly easy and overly simplified compared to the original.
It doesn't have the same level of cinematic polish that we've come to expect from AAA titles in 2013 and beyond.
It gets excessively talkative and stale in certain areas.
Much like the previous game, the romance subplots are stupid. If you want your Commander Shepard to get some quick and casual sex, it's not gonna happen. It's deep love or nothing. And that deep love comes out of nowhere, since your intimate conversations with any given love interest are extremely limited.
But by far the worst of Mass Effect 2's problems is the very time-consuming process of grinding for resources, which isn't any fun at all. There are nearly endless amounts of resources available, but the game doesn't tell you how many you need. While there are ship upgrades available later in the game to make these processes quicker, the game doesn't tell you about them, and so you may waste much time in the first half grinding before acquiring them. My advice: grind at a minimum until you get the upgrades, and then only focus on "rich" planets, since there are more than enough to get you through.
(Issues)
I want to mention a few minor issues that you might run into. I frequently clipped through objects and got stuck, forcing a reload, and there are a few missions tied to DLC that resulted in game-breaking crashes. The latter problem was easily rectified by creating a shortcut to the .exe and putting -nomoviestartup in the parameters. One last very strange glitch resulted in my player character stretching her arms out to the sides, unable to shoot or interact anymore, solved only by reloading an earlier save and trying different dialogue choices before the bug. With a game this big, my recommendation is to keep numerous save files and save often.
Overall, Mass Effect 2 is definitely one of my favorite games of 2010, matched only by Red Dead Redemption. In my book, that's saying a lot.

Looking at the amount of hours (plus several hundred more), you can tell that I clearly love this game. I would not invest so much of my time into a game I did not enjoy. There are so many characters, classes, skills, dungeons, and more to discover! By the time I have finished playing every single character, class, and gotten to the maximum level, I would no longer be a teenager.
In a more serious note, there are obviously flaws to this game. All games do really. As for this, the main issue people have with this game is the balance between classes. It is understandable. I get it. Many classes are more overpowered than others. Just look at the recent renewals there have been lately. Old classes that were rarely seen before the renewal have been making a comeback because of their new skills, textures, stats, combos, etc.. However, the renewals are pretty cheap. Many of the renewed classes have skills that are constantly spammed. I would also like to include the recent balance patch made in KR. There has been A LOT of talk about it. It is one of the most impactful balance patches I believe.... Many of the overpowered characters are getting nerfed. That is interesting. It'll wreak havoc when the patch comes to NA in several months. PVP will be more balanced I hope.
Yes, the current balances are quite an issue in PVP, but there is so much more to the game than that. Events, Henir, Secret Dungeons, Field, Raid Bosses.... There is so much more to do. Whether a player is stronger than another does not apply to those. You can still have fun. You can have fun exploring skills and combos and getting to know each individual class. You can have fun meeting the community (outside the salty Arena ofc) and make friends and join guilds.
There is also the arguable fact about the phrase "Pay to win." Now, I do admit, I have spent A LOT in this game. That is only because I see myself playing this a lot, so I invest money into it. I do not pay to win. I more pay to make the experience of playing the game more enjoyable. Yeah, a skill B-Slot takes a big role in playing the game, but I feel like it could also be taken as a challenge. Not investing any money into a game is quite a challenge. I would admire anyone who could truly know the game without having to pay once. Luckily, Elsword has something called a board where you can not only sell craftable items and consumables, but you can sell items that come from the Item Mall where you could only use real money. On the board, people could use ED to buy those items, free of any real life charge. Yeah, it takes long to farm for that ED, but if you invest enough time into the game, it should not be a big deal.

Archeage is a very interesting, visually pleasing and in-depth game.
The game allows players to create a lifestyle in which they construct their own house and farm their own produce. While doing so, players can also follow a line of work which could vary from carpentry, cooking, alchemy and plenty more.
Players can also become a Jury to help decide what happens to players who commit illegal activities such as murder, stealing and various other activities. This gives players the ability to decide as a team of 5 how long the criminal's sentence should be depending on his actions; each player gives a decision and an overall sentence time is confirmed - this is only if the player is found to be guilty.
The class and skill system is quite in-depth with a over 100 possible classes. When first creating your character, you choose between 6 main skillsets; Battlerage (Warrior Melee), Sorcery (Spellcasting Ranged), Archery (Hunter Ranged), Vitalism (Healer Range), Occultism (Necromancer Range), Shadowplay (Assassin Melee). Once you hit level 10, you can then select your final third skill to finalize your class; each class has a specific name, for example Archery/Shadowplay/Auramancy is known as 'Primeval'. You can choose another skillset whenever you want however you will be penalised by being reduced back to level 10 in that skillset. Similarly, you can respec each skillset by paying a currency fee allowing you to re-choose what abilities you would like from that particular skillset. This allows players to change their abilities to suit the situation.
Instances are enjoyable with various mechanics being responsible for how you progress towards the end of the instance. The first instance is an underground mine whereby a bridge collapses forcing the players into a small area to fight a pack of weak enemies. It is then the player's job to flood the hole to bring the player back up to the bridge and continue. Next, the player must use explosives, found in an area only accessible by killing the first boss, to blow up a part of the wall allowing passage to the next area of the instance. These little features add to the experience making it more than just a mob-clearing exercise.
The quest line has a lot to offer with a main questline, which sadly dissapeared at around level 28-30, and various side quests, all of which offer rewards such as gear, currency or potions. One issue with the quests is that a large proportion of them consist of "Kill X/X (Enter mob name here)" which can become extremely tiresome and dull very quickly, unless you enjoy killing the same enemy over and over again. Let's not forget that you can overachieve certain quests in order to yield larger experience rewards, and for some this means killing even more enemies than is required.
I can honestly say that I thoroughly enjoyed Archeage and I look forward to participating in more Beta events and will certainly be playing the game once fully released.
As usual, this is my own opinion of the game and is not to be used solely to determine whether or not it is a game for you; please read other people's reviews for a wider understanding and varying opinion.

Elsword is a fun game in general with surprisingly a lot of content.
The side-scrolling style of gameplay makes the game unique from most other MMORPG's and is simple to navigate through. The game can be played either on the keyboard or on a gamepad; picking either one is based on preference. The story is quite interesting but if players are not interested, they can skip through the story if they want.
Elsword has a variety of characters and class progressions so players can make themselves different from one another. As well as Skill Progressions, which make players even more unique. Leveling up your character is easy in the beginning and getting to your first class makes a small giddy feeling in some people. Leveling up becomes harder as you progress through the game and so do the monsters.
The PvE aspect is quite interesting. The player can either find themselves playing in a Dungeon or in the Fields. Both have monsters and bosses. The level designs are very creative and shows that a lot of effort was put into making them. My favorite dungeon so far takes place in the town Lanox, "Ash Covered Village". Toward the last part of the dungeon, your party are left on a giant rail cart and the cart speeds down into the mines of the village which is in the background. Visually it is my favorite dungeon. The Fields are a good place to grind up on quests and leveling up your character.
The item-revamp from earlier seasons made the Equipment system simpler. No longer were characters forced to find specific pieces of gear for a specific character-class. It became much much simpler. Organizing is easy and there is a "Organize" button if players don't feel like organizing themselves. Just don't spam the button.
Crafting is also a necessity in the this game. Players can craft weapon, equipment, potions, etc. Players can also enhance their items through the Blacksmith which enhances your stats. Or players can give their gear some valueble elemental attributes which varies depending on individual playstyles. Players learn as they play through the game learning these aspects becomes a must.
If players want to give their character some flash, they can spend real money in the Item shop. There are a large variety of goods in the shop. You can spend money to buy a pet, buy accessories, buy more inventory space, skill notes, customization options, the costume sets or the Ice burners that carry mysterious and rare goodies. However, in my personal opinion Ice Burners are not entirely safe to spend on for the goods that are found are ULTRA RARE statistically.
Occassional events in the game are fun. They liven up the game somewhat and allow the player to gain some special items as well. And cool new stuff gets announced in the Item Mall. Best be on the look out!
The most important aspect of the game would be the community. In Elsword, I found myself participating in almost every way I could in order to find and interact with other people. In one mode in particular known as Sparring mode, I found many different people speaking in these premade sparring rooms. Conversations are fun and are a joy to have. Guilds also offer many opportunities to speak with others and as a little bonus, that guild gives you buffs to help you through the dungeons. There are a lot of people in Elsword so players will be able to meet someone they can talk with. While there are some folks on Elsword that may be antogonistic, the majority of the people online are open-minded and refrain from being negative. Besides MMORPG's are best played with friends.
Overall, like I said, Elsword is a fun game. It's constantly getting more and more content and has a very nice community.

I played through Assassin's Creed (AC): Liberation. I just wanted to share a couple dot points.
+ I liked the story. It was interesting trying to understand the different personalities. Likewise, I liked the connection to the broader AC story of Templars vs. Assassins. And for the characters, I really liked Aveline and Gerald. A nice blend of contrasting personalities mixed with a hint of love, creating an interesting dynamic.
+ I loved the landscape of New Orleans. There were many contrasting suburbs within the city with their own personalities, for example, the dock being full of fishers, contrast to the mansion side of the city with everyone dressing in luxury outfits.
+ Music fit the environment and atmosphere of the game.
+ Weapon variety is nice. I did not have the DLC, but there were a few choices. Likewise, I loved the Whip and Blowpipe as side-weapons.
+ Technically, I did not experience a crash as other people experienced. I play on a i5-6600k with a GTX 1070.
- Despite interesting, the story was short and it was a mess on trying to understand the situation in New Orleans.
- Side content was purely filler. I did not touch much of the collectible quests.
- Movement, as usual in the series, was very clunky, such as the random jumps off buildings when climbing.
- Framerate issues. I experienced frame rate drops, particularly when sychronising on the towers.
I believe Liberation is average. I liked the story and the interesting twists in it. But, it is short and therefore rushed. More broadly, I didn't overly enjoy the game, it felt like a chore, so this review is more of a ''thumbs in the middle'' review. To note, I didn't buy the DLC and I did maybe 10% of the side-quests, so I mainly played just the story. I recommend buying this on sale.

Ok, so I stand by the plusses of my previous review, and am redacting the negatives. This game is fantastic. It presents a rogue-like style of dungeon delving with an entirely new and unique setting, story, and progression. The combat is smooth with each weapon style feeling unique enough, and the special abilities of the better ones creating a more exciting combat flow. Also, they added a slew of game modes that modify the experience through giving bonuses and negatives that change combat, as well as what tools you have available to you.
If you haven't picked this game up yet, and you love new gameplay experiences, I say you have done yourself a disservice. This game is fantstic!
*DISCLAIMER* This review is for Early Access.
To start, I have had very mixed experiences with early access games. Some have been so incomplete or fractured experiences that I hardly feel they constitute "games" when I play them, and others are a good view at what the game holds as a promise.
Hand of Fate is SOLIDLY in the latter category.
I purchased this game through the Humble Bundle - Extra Credits bundle (which is a fantastic combo). As a result, not only is my faith in Extra Credits validated once again, but I have been able to play an extremely unique game that holds a LOT of promise for its future. Combining deck building, Arkham Asylum style combat, text adventure games of chance, and a new approach to story telling, this game is truly a one of a kind experience.
You find yourself in front of a kind of fortune teller who shuffles up a deck of cards in front of you, inviting you on a journey. You are represented by a game piece, and the level is laid out in a series of face down cards. as you move your token, the cards are revealed. Each card can present you with a combat scenario, an event that forces you to choose, or a merchant (at least as far as I have adventured). Through your successes and failures you accrue new weapons, armor, and skills (which you can equip to make yourself more capable in combat), gold, food (which you comsume each time your move, healing yourself, or taking damage if you run out), and tokens (which at the end of each boss fight will reveal new cards which you can shuffle into the deck for the next level).
So far, although this game is incomplete, it is a fantastic new game and it deserves your money.
The rough edges:
The combat suffers from a low frame rate (at least this has been an issue for me), is not unplayable as a result.
The "tutorial" level was a steep learning curve for me, due mostly to the somewhat sluggish combat and somewhat randomness of gear that you gain (which is part of the fun, but if you get a rough starting run fo cards it can be hard to come back from).

I'm going to begin by voicing my displeasure at the fact that steam has only a two means of reviewing a game. The bright blue thumbs up or red thumbs down is the first thing people see and it is criminal that I'm forced to open my opinion with either a blatant recommendation or condemnation, as it is often never that simple. Murdered: Soul Suspect is one of those games that I feel very ambivalent towards. It gets a thumbs down though for reasons I'll gladly expound upon here but I'll start by saying that If you do want to buy this game, go ahead, but do it at a discount as there isn't enough of it to warrant its full price by a long shot.
Murdered: Soul Suspect is a supernatural intrigue game where you play as Ronan O'Connor, gangland warrior turned detective and wandering samurai warrior, who is tracking a mysterious serial killer. Ronan is about apprehend the killer in the opening cutscene when the killer decides he's had enough of the law and reenacts the opening scene from Watchmen all over Ronan's face before shooting him seven times in the chest. So Ronan is dead, but you knew that already. Ronan now has to endeavor to do in one night what the entire police force couldn't do in years worth of time and solve the case of the Bell Killer. M:SS reminds me of two very specific games I actually liked, the first of which is Alan Wake. Like Alan Wake, this game is about supernatural dealings with a distinctly traditional American feel. Also like AW, the rules for the supernatural stuff in this game are very well defined.
The supernatural lore being dealt with this time is ghosts, exploring all the traditional facets of what you might think ghosts are like, but before you go hog wild there is an exception to each of your abilities. You can pass through walls but not consecrated or ethereal walls, which mark the level boundaries. You can jumble electronics, but not to any meaningful degree. You can possess people but not control their actions. You can teleport, but not over demon holes so you still have to circumvent those on foot. Also like in Alan Wake, there isn't a whole lot to do in between plot points except hunt for collectibles. This leads me into the real issue I had with this game: its design.
Murdered: Soul Suspect is a game of extra steps. I kept a running list of things the game took more than one step to complete without needing to: Often the game will end a cutscene just to have you press the interact button to continue the same cutscene. When questioning a suspect, you have to press a button for each option you want to explore but the interrogation doesn't end until all options are explored, so it might as well be one long cutscene. You can read the minds of people you possess but each person has exactly two things to say and you have to press the button twice to hear both things when they could just say them both at once. When piecing together the clues of an investigation, if you pick a wrong option you get booted from the screen, having to reenter the screen to continue. When grabbing collectibles, you have to reveal the object first before picking it up. The collectibles are half hidden but the game tells you where they are so there's no need for hiding them. Speaking of collectibles, there are a plethora of them, all of which have very little to no bearing on the actual game. Each area has a unique object that, once all are gathered, will unlock  a spooky campfire story unrelated to what you are doing. There are a series of over arching collectibles including diary pages from Ronan's dead wife (really the only means of character development), handy info blurbs copy-pasted from the Salem tourism comity website, and newspaper clippings reminding you how creepy and invincible the serial killer is.
While Alan Wake also felt the need to boldly announce the appearance of an enemy so that there is no way for you to be caught off guard, at least it had engaging combat. Every once in a while the game breaks up the monotony by presenting you with enemies to sneak up behind and quick-time-event to death. Once or twice a level, there will be demons that half-heatedly wander around in an enclosed area. You have to hide in the hiding spot and wait for the monster to turn around so you can slowly walk up behind it and kill it. This ends up being tedious and non-threatening, unit you mess up. If you manage to not properly dispatch your spectral foe, the backlash is absurd. Demons will kill you within a 3-5 second window unless you can scurry back to a hiding spot. However, once detected, the demons can see you in hiding spots; forcing you to shift between them as fast and erratically as possible until they give up. This turns what little combat there is into a game of Red Light, Green Light. These sections make no sense to the lore of the game either as there is no reason given as to why Ronan seems to be the only ghost that can dispatch the demons. No introduction is given to the power nor is it explained that Ronan is the only one capable of it, leading me to wonder why the other ghosts all flee in terror when the demons show up.
The second game I'm reminded of is L.A. Noire, because the investigation sections are reminiscent of the ones in that game. You have to walk around the crime scene and collect the clues, using them to piece together the motive of the criminal. There are six to fourteen clues per scene but only three of them at most are ever necessary to continue. It's no secret that detective work is not as flashy or intriguing as it is portrayed in popular culture, but no where is this more obvious than video games. L.A. Noire had a good mix of action and detective work, due (I think) to it's structure. All the clues were relevant because solving the case was the goal of the mission and everything unfolded naturally. Murdered, by contrast, has you investigating glaringly obvious crime scenes which, more often than not, inform you of something you already knew. For example, one crime scene later on in the game has you investigating a room full of people the Bell Killer murdered all at once. At the point of investigation, however, you have already been made aware of what the killer did afterword, so the reason for killing the room full of people is obvious. Then, once you investigate the room, Ronan stands there and tells the the reason the killer did it, even though you already knew. Really the investigating is just being a master of the obvious. It's also impossible to fail to find all of the clues, because the game tells you how many are present in the scene.
Murdered, like many games these days, would have probably made a better book or movie. The game play really just consists of different kinds of walking around and looking at things. Despite being a game made by an established developer and publisher, this is something any indie dev could have made, if not made look quite as good. In the end, games are meant to be interactive; that is what the medium excels at. Yet more and more it seems like games are being made with interactivity at the bottom of their priority list. Once during the middle of a cutscene I caught my self replying to text messages. It was then I realized how bored I was with the game; how absolutely unengaged I felt. The story was really not all that bad but being set in Salem, you can bet with reliability that it will have to do with what Salem is famous for. I would rather them have just made a movie out of it and cut out the game play entirely. At least then it would have taken me only 120 minutes to get through.

First of all, this game has a Metascore of 59/100 and I can kind of understand why. This is not about the story or the characters, but mainly because of the gameplay.
minor spoilers (not really spoilers, but just in case, you know). Marked them.
The story is simply ah-ma-zing. In my opinion, it’s a great murder mystery in which you have to solve your own death (and prevent others from dying too). The whole ghost-idea is greatly elaborated in the story and makes the whole thing quite original: you’re not the usual cop who has to solve the usual murder mystery. The game has some great (and by that I mean unexpected and mind-blowing) plot twists. And, honestly, I didn’t expect the actual murderer to be the murderer, if you know what I mean.
I LOVE how the characters’ stories become clear throughout the game. Most of the characters’ stories are quite vague when you start the game, but as you progress and collect artifacts, you learn more about each one of them. It made me want to keep playing, not only to know who my killer was, but also to know more about other people’s lives and deaths (and Ronan’s tattoos, for example). The side quests are nice additions to the story; they aren’t very long, but quite interesting, too. The main characters aren't really stereotypes, in my opinion. For example,
(not really sure if spoiler, but marked just in case). It makes the game much more interesting than your usual detective story. The side characters, on the other hand, are much more flat and typical.
Not great. Even boring, after a while. You walk around in Salem, investigate surroundings to find clues, possess people (and cats!), hide from and defeat demons, poltergeist stuff, and, well, that’s about it. It’s the same thing over and over again, for the maximum of 15 hours of gameplay the game has to offer (one playthrough). No real puzzles, just looking around and finding things. No real action, I believe there’s a maximum of 20 demons to defeat throughout the game. The combat is boring: you have to sneak up to them and kill them with nothing but your bare hands. You have no defense apart from some hiding spots. The demons are in my opinion unnecessary and only a burden to the game. The game’s pretty linear, too. You have no choice but to follow the storyline. Between cutscenes, you can walk around freely in Salem and the areas you’ve already visited throughout the story.
Also, it’s obvious this is a game made for consoles, not for pc. I mean, “Press START”? You’re joking, right? You’re unable to change the controls, so if you’re playing with an AZERTY-keyboard, you’ll have to change the language settings of your pc. I really recommend playing this with a controller, if you have one: it suits the overall gameplay much better.

This review is also somewhat relevant to the other Metro titles Redux & non-Redux. When I first launched a Metro title is was Metro 2033 original and I was immediately immersed into a post-apocalyptic world with mutants, communists and "♥♥♥♥♥es" as bourbon so eloquently put.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is some of the most realistic combat I've seen (on higher difficulties) and it handles like a dream, its nice to finally be brought back to a game where taking cover is important. 10/10
Audio:
The audio in this game is outstanding, with 7.1 surround sound you can be listing to people in the background, hear a fire crackling, maybe someone coughing. Its a immersive experience, however I always turn the music down so I can get the most immersion as possible. (Am I using that word too much "immersion"? Well I cant lie this game is a masterpiece) 9/10
Graphics:
The graphics are incredible! Some of the best graphics I have ever seen. The shadows blend with object incredibly well and the texturing on 4k resolution doesn't look stretched. The developers really took allot of time to assure each and every object blended in well with the gloomy underground atmosphere. 10/10
Storyline:
Most games that are 10+ hour's generally start to feel dragged out and just repetitive, however metro has you immersed for each and every second. The characters are loveable, relatable and the story has no boring downtime. 9/10
HYPE!:
Plain and simple, If I ever need to be hyped up I just listen to Colonel Millers speech at the end of Last Light and it brings tear to my eyes. (not rating this but just saying damn dude)
Things I didn't enjoy:
Children voice acting sounds like pandaren children. (WoW players remember "I'm growing a beard" * shivers *). Sometimes the dialog seems to not fit the circumstances (more so in metro 2033).
Recommend?:
I would highly recommend this game and go as far as to say this is my favorite game of all time. 9.5/10!

Conan Exiles is very much like Ark Survival Evolved and it shares some of the flaws, adds some of its own, but does a few things a lot better.
The good things:
1. There's a much more coherent world here, Ark is all over the place, no idea what it's trying to be or what it's trying to do. Conan Exiles has focus, feels like it knows what it wants to be.
2. The art style and character design is a class above what Ark has going on.
3. I get the sense from what the game is about that it should develop better than Ark has done. Ark's development has been fun to follow, but it has largely consisted of adding more dinosaurs and little consideration for balance or technical issues. I expect that Conan Exiles is going to see more technical updates (And boy does it need them).
4. The buildings look good. Didn't get far with that side of it, but it looks much more promising than Ark and again it's helped a lot by a coherent style. Having human workers sounds much better than tamed dinosaurs, I mean in theory tamed dinosaurs sounds like the best thing ever, but when all most of them end up doing is standing around honking and pooping they lose their shine a bit.
The bad things:
1. Combat is really poor. Ark got around this by making the combat kind of asymmetrical, you're a man poking a dinosaur with a spear, or a dinosaur chomping somebody, or most often in the late game you're shooting things. This meant you kind of didn't notice that hand to hand combat sucked. Conan Exiles is a game that needs good hand to hand combat, it's fricking CONAN, but the combat here is weak. Ranged combat not great either, but in a Conan game you've got to have good melee or why are you even a Conan game.
2. The game has inherited Ark's horrible crafting system. You level up, you pick recipes to learn, you level up some more and so on. It's a bad system that wastes the players time. It's a worry that the developers would look at Ark and say, "Hey guys, I think we want that crafting system."
The future could be bright for this game but it is vital that the developers focus on fundamental improvements over content additions. My main worry is that the areas that need to be improved most urgently, the combat system and the crafting system, seem like the hardest things to fix.

This is probably the grindiest game I've ever played. It's not a bad game at all, but it has a few hours of fun gameplay spread out over 25 hours repeating the same missions over and over. There's no real reason to explore systems, especially if you don't need a technology upgrade. A little blip of story in random systems or random FTL-style encounter would make it more compelling to explore.
The devs in the forums confirm that the best way to play is to put all of your points into one type of weapon. If you don't, you'll have to grind 2-3x as much to viably use multiple types of weapons. Despite all the fancy looking weapons, attachments, and mounting points in this game, you'll probably end up with a ship loaded with all of one type of weapon. You'll also quickly learn to never die so much that you run out of rez, or you'll have to grind away at a mining station for a while just to have enough money to start playing the game again.
If I played again, I would play without bounty hunters. It looks like they a balancing mechanism, because the only thing they do is provide a constant drain on your resources. The diminishing returns of their arena-style missions weren't very worthwhile.
It does look very good, especially when battles involve different kinds of ships, weapons, and drones flying about. The movement and turning speed plays a major role in the game, so I did like how I feels like naval warfare. Throughout the 25 hours there were fun bits unlocking new ships and figuring out what works well too, but once I figured it out it was back to the grind. It's a decent game to play while watching TV or listening to some podcasts, but it wouldn't hold my interest alone.

The potential was there but the ball was dropped.
You’re Aveline, an Assassin in Louisiana that… kinda does stuff. She has one contact to the Assassin order and just does what she wants and thinks right. The story starts off from finding disappearing men to murdering all the local templar leaders. The story has substance and Aveline is WAY more interesting of character than Conor. However, the story just jumps around a lot and seems completely incomplete. For example, there is a point in the game where you find your mother and instead of having a discussion about what’s going on and what happened, they say two sentences and she teleports to a different location with another mission. There are gaps like this EVERYWHERE in the damn plot and it’s very hard to get invested in the plot as it suddenly stops or changes courses every other mission.

It’s AC. Sneaky stabbing, long range stealth kills, and a whole bunch of extra crap you never use. The sneaking is there and you can stab people but there rarely are missions where you actually need to sneak through a fortress or some guarded area and kill a person. Most of the missions have you tail someone or kill a small group of people in the area. It’s diverse but boring mostly. You also have a mechanic where you can change your outfit and blend into different occasions. This would be cool but there were 1-2 missions where this thought even came up in my mind because most missions have the outfit preset. The hub worlds are pretty big and there are like 3 of them which is awesome but they have nothing interesting to see or explore inside of them so what was the point?
Overall, the gameplay just felt like it was lacking. The pieces were there but they needed more substance in order to be fun
Running in the open world looks fine but zooming into models for cutscenes or animations is really bad (along with this voice acting. WTF). Runs at 60 but dips in the bayou though.

The pieces were there with character, plot, and actions. However, they needed to be developed into something good and with substance instead of this half baked mess.

Having played online with friends, and alone, this game is great!
