Introduction
Having played most of the AC games until this one I wasn't having great expectations. AC3 was ok, but seemed a bit lacklustered because of uneven gameplay and uninteresting main character. I took a break from the serie after playing the downright bad dlc Tyranni of King Washington which didn't even work properly and crashed at a very specific point.
Assassin's Creed Liberation is more of a stand alone extension of AC3 , as it use the same game engine. It was originally designed for the Vita but upgraded for the PC in this "HD version"
Gameplay.
I felt the parkour part was actually a bit smoother than AC3, however the improvements were slights, and occasionally Aveline would still involuntary jump on a wall  or fall on her face, and the jumping in trees while also improved did give me headaches on occasions.
when it comes to fighting the game is ok, but as usual the assassin is overpowered and you rarely if ever feel threatened by the guards you meet. You can counter most of the moves the make , on top of that use of guns and smokebombs will make you virtually unbeatable when outnumbered. This is a recurring problem in AC games and the only thing done to balance it is the ridiculous 100 % synchronization system that requires you to perform the mission in a very specific ways to get a perfect score. This is annoying as the game feel too easy because of the fighting but extremely frustrating when you don't get the 100% synchronization as you feel the job is half-done.
Personally I would rather have the game throwing a bit more difficult missions with more dangerous guards and less (or any for this matter) demanding synchronization demands. This is also something that has plagued the AC games for a long time.
New game-play technics like disguises are a welcome new addition in the game, Aveline can disguise herself as Assassin, slave or lady , each one of the disguises have their pluss and minus and some are required for specified missions. Unfortunately the disguise part feel underused in the game which is a shame because I quite liked it.
Story
I quite liked the story in Liberation , set in Louisiana New Orlean in the 18 century , young Aveline , an half african , half french young lady must navigate the traps and machinations of the templars and assassins while assessing her rolle as a person of high  society where slavery is part of everyday life.
To make things more complicated , the game is set from a somehow "templar" perspective but a mysterious entity informs you of deleted scenes in the game in small but smart sections of the game. It's a bit convulated but it beats the rather dull and overbearing Desmond parts of AC3.
The main plot unfortunately feel underdeveloped and hasted ,  we also never really get to know the characters as the game feel too short fort that, which is a shame given that the setting is colorful and interesting . I honestly feel like Liberation given a bit more care and ressources from the devloppers could have been a great Assassin game in itself rather than a "shortish" expansion to AC3.
Conclusion
All in all I enjoyed the game despite the frustrations I got from some of the mechanics ,lke  the 100% synchronizations tasks, and was left wanting for more when it ended. This game isn't great and is rather short, but it still holds its own, thanks to interesting characters and beautiful settings.
Despite the obvious flaws I still recommend this game , especially if you're a Assassin Creed fan.

Had a blast on EA, impatiently awaiting download of full game. If you love RPG's you will love this. Miles better than the first- and that was pretty good as well. More choices, more decisions, and if you don't like someone, you can always eat them. Eat them! Mmmm brains...
Edit: Having now finished the game with a couple of play-throughs, I have to admit to being somewhat let down by the finished product. I was eagerly looking forward to playing with some of the things I loved in the first, that were lacking in EA. I thought their omission was due to it still being in EA... alas it wasn't... So if you loved the crafting in the first, well, forget about it for DOS2, it basically dosen't exist.
CRAFTING: Forget about it, it doesn't really exist and what there is, is almost negligible in it's use unless you are playing hardcore- and very few gamers do. You can make a few potions, but why bother when there is no need and what you might potion up is better dealt with by a cast spell.
ARMOUR: Like crafting, they have taken one of the pleasures of the first and ruined it to such an extent, that what little crafting ability they allow you to play with, is almost totally useless, and a complete and utter waste of time. In the first, you could get a semi decent piece of armour, and mod it to your characters ability and it would be with that character for a large chunk of the game. Now, it's with your character for one character level - two if you bother to mod it - and then it's useless and sold. Larian have managed - very successfully -  to make Legendary and Epic armour anything but. And that is no mean feat. Seriously, you won't keep Epic/Legendary/Supermarket-own-brand armour much more than two of the characters levels, as by that point it's quite simply, crap and very un-Epic in stats.
And that leads to the next bug-bear. Because of the rubbishness of armour, you spend less time exploring the wild as an adventurer of (dubious) repute and more time as a shopper of armour, sick in the knowledge that in 2 levels time, you are going to have to repeat the whole tedious process all over again...
WEAPONS: Pretty much the same as ARMOUR; Buy some glitzy cutlery, level up twice, sell old cutlery, buy some new, rinse repeat. It gets tedious quick. Real quick.
GRAPHICS: It looks nice, yes, I will give it that.
ENVIROMENTAL EFFECTS: Yes, wonderful, have a pat on the back, but after a few hours playing, you tend to ignore most of it except for Boss fights. (That was on normal difficulty-it becomes more of a requirement for the harder play throughs, but again, that's only going to be an issue for a (very) small number of players.)
STORYLINE: It was alright, nothing to write home about and pretty much standard fare for this genre of game. Larian have tried to throw in some curve balls to increase the re-playability of the game, which was nice, but looking at Steam Achievements for the game, a quarter of players haven't even made it past the first chapter yet, and to be honest, I don't see that score getting much better in the future. So all that effort to make the game replayable when finished, could have been spent better elsewhere... Like on bug testing for a start. Gosh, there was an astounding amount of bugs, many of them game/quest breaking.
OVERALL: The game was alright, but the problems with the lifespan of armour and weapons quickly meant the game became less DOS2 and more Divinity-mad-dash-around-map-for-shopkeepers-to-up-grade-rubbish-equipment, or" Divinity Original Shopping Trip 2" for short. Yes graphics are good, environmental effects have been made more effective, if you can be bothered to use them and a lot of effort has been spent on the ending scenes for the 48 people that will finish the game.
Not played a DOS game and thinking of grabbing a spell book and jumping in? Then buy DOS1 instead. It's more rewarding, most of the bugs have been squashed, it's cheaper and hasn't been dumbed down for console players like this one has. I had high hopes for this game, enough to buy it months before release, but would I do so for DOS3? No. Not if this is the direction Larian are going in.

I’m not sure where to begin with this so I’ll just jump right into it. I could go on and on about the Countless class combinations, or the sheer insane amount of things you can branch off into to spend your time doing, but it’s been said so many times ill just keep this to a personal experience point of view. I just started playing this game on this last Beta, so take that knowledge ahead of time.
I went into this game with really high expectations, I won’t sugar coat it, everything that I read about it and everything I saw about it made me want to play it from the start. I am up to level 25 at the moment and have 48 hours logged into the game, I’m the kind of player who explorers every area and talks to every NPC before moving on, and at that point you should be able to tell if you’re going to want to invest time into a game or not. Without a doubt I am 100% sure I will be playing this game again and CANNOT wait till launch. Even though I’m still in the “Classic MMO Phase” (Get a quest, do it, move to the next area) the entire game play is just amazing. The game itself is beautiful. Attack, casting, moving animations are always fluid. Footsteps and other audio blend amazing well. One of my favorite parts of the game was climbing to the top of a hill and looking into the ocean, seeing every wave for miles, seeing islands in the distance, and seeing player operated ships sailing where they wish. Another thing that I thought was a nice touch is the entire way that you control your mounts, you raise them from little ones to a full grown mount, and you can name your mount, and equip armor to them so they can take more damage without getting knocked out. (Wait what? What do you mean get knocked out?) Yes your mount can be knocked out and you’ll have to heal them to ride them again. (That sounds dumb why would you do that?) The way that they do it is much more realistic then other MMO’s and I personally enjoy it, when you dismount if you don’t dismiss your mount they will follow you around while you fight or whatever you do. Now this is good and bad, it’s bad because they can draw agro and pull mobs if you’re not careful, but it’s also good because all you have to do to get on your mount again is press one button, without having to summon them again. Mounts also level with you as you use them allowing the use of better armor, better stats, and more skills. While they won’t fight with you the skills they offer are very helpful while traversing the game, everything from a movement speed up, to a charge that lets break through enemies in your way. Speaking of which I should mention, there IS player to player unit collision which I, again personally, like.
TL: DR?
>Beautiful graphics, amazing amount of possibilities, amazing character customizations
I would 10/10 recommend my friends and others to play this game.

Hand of Fate is a great example of an Early Access game worth the asking price despite being unfinished. Even if the developers cut and run at this stage I wouldn't regret my purchase.
The game is an Action RPG Roguelite, which, like games in this broad genre such as FTL and Binding of Isaac, will serve you with a random selection of items to face an escalating challenge. The chief innovation of the way Hand of Fate plays out is that the pool of encounters and items in every "dungeon" is defined by a deck of cards, a few of which are semi-random, some of which are defined by the boss you've picked to face (which are offered in a linear sequence), and most of which are picked from the decks you build of encounter and item cards. It plays out better than it sounds. The game plays out iteratively; you'll build a deck, choosing mostly encounters you haven't beaten before, and the best items you have access to, choose a boss (probably the highest level boss you haven't yet beaten) and play through the "dungeon", which is a grid of encounter cards played face-down. Whether you get to the boss and defeat it, or die trying, you'll probably have succeeded against some encounters you haven't beaten before, thus unlocking new cards to put in your deck, so that the next time you're going to see new challenges and have a chance of getting new gear.
This amounts to an excellent way to manage the randomness of roguelite games, as you can generally remove encounters or items you're bored of and tailor your experience, ensuring you always feel like the next dungeon will have something you're eager to see in it.
The combat recalls both Dark Souls and the Batman games, though... not as good. There's a good array of cooldown abilities and interesting magical items, only half of which I've yet unlocked. Some tweaking needs to be done to the counter/block/combo systems, as currently it feels horribly difficult to counter as you're almost always locked into another action for too long to exploit the counter/deflect windows, but hopefully this will be reviewed and show that the game was just a few timing-windows shy of having a genuinely great and enjoyable combat system. Currently there's no difficulty options, and combat - and indeed the whole game - is punishingly difficult. If you don't like games that kill you, lots and lots, you won't like this. Because it kills you. Lots.
The graphics are genuinely beautiful; with the exception of faces, this feels like a AAA quality game in terms of polish most of the time. In some respects more care has been taken with graphical polish than most AAAs manage, with some very unusual touches in areas which you could expect to be neglected. The animation of the cards is noticably beautiful. It seems weird to so strongly compliment the way imaginary pieces of cardboard are animated, but the way each card's physical location is actually accurately simulated adds a strangely immersive charm to the game-table aspect of the game. To explain, there's a kind of Three Card Monty minigame (except it's... four... four card monty...) which determines your success or failure in many encounters, and it's possible to track where the cards are moving a lot of the time... with great care and difficulty, rather than the final positions simply being randomised with a virtual shuffle.
The atmosphere of the game benefits from the oppressive difficulty being complemented by the doomsaying narration of the game-master, who takes delight in your misfortune and is angered by your success or luck, giving the game a very characteristic feel. You really feel like the odds are against you, which gives an almost Dark Souls-ish sense of accomplishment when you finally manage to prevail. If anything offsets this difficulty, it's that you're constantly unlocking new cards, so that even though, by the sixth level, if you're anything like me, you'll be dying over and over, you get a sense of *some* progress, even if you didn't make it to the boss level.
Overall, I'm surprised how well this game is shaping up and have no trouble recommending it to anyone who likes challenging action RPGs and roguelites.

‘I Know a Tale’ has nice sceneries, great hidden object scenes, and charmingly amateurish cut-scenes—but even they cannot hide how tedious it can get towards the end with the endless backtracking.
Despite its 2015 release, I Know a Tale mostly looks and acts like a hidden object game from around 2010: pretty, but low-resolution 4:3 format graphics, plain hidden object scenes, no map feature… and it is one of those HOGs that tries to include live actor footage to spice up the story.
Well, these live segments are… charmingly amateurish, both in terms of acting and the English dub. The same goes for the plot itself: it starts out as an interesting heist/kidnapping story, but eventually regresses to the standard “stop nameless evil entity from being evil” formula.
The hidden object scenes are probably the best part in the game; rarely can we see so nicely balanced object placements and density. In exchange, the classic item-using adventure game parts can be annoyingly fidgety, because there are too many items and places to use them at. With no map and a half-broken hint button, it is easy to get lost, especially in the later segments.

Platforming games are perhaps the most common genre out there, even before the rise of Steam and being able to grab a bunch of them for less than twenty bucks on a sale. But they’re also perhaps the hardest to do well. There’s really no getting around making the gameplay of one good, and failing to do that is practically a kiss of death. While Splasher doesn’t reinvent the wheel, it does provide a very enjoyable experience.
The story takes place in a massive paint factory, Inkorp, whose owner has suddenly revealed himself as a mad scientist, kidnapping workers and experimenting on them, as well as using an army of killer robots to do the task. You know, as you do. As the only unique-looking worker in the bunch you have to put a stop to that using a gun that can fire water, and later on a few different kinds of paint. Red lets you walk up walls and on the ceiling, while yellow bounces you around.
Your water gun is used to flip switches and defeat enemies, although aside from some moments where you’re locked in combat is a bit of an afterthought, thanks to some liberal auto-aim on the game’s part. That isn’t to say enemies aren’t dangerous though, as even the ones not trying to kill you directly can still cause your death by washing away the paint you’re using to get around. Thus far they’re placed fairly, to make the levels harder but still doable.
In each level of the game you’ll find seven workers in peril that you can rescue that spell out Splash! Six are strewn about the level behind some tough jumps or puzzle rooms, and the final one is at the end, locked in a cage you’ll need to have enough energy from the stage to unlock. You get that by destroying enemies and washing off special glowing patches of paint.
This set-up reminded me a lot of Donkey Kong, particularly the newer games by Retro, as well as the newer Rayman titles. The latter thought turned out to be quite appropriate, as three of the game’s staff are Romaine Claude, Richard Vatinel and Aymeric Schwartz, the level designer, art director, and composer for Origins respectively. I can safely say all their talent is not wasted on the game.
Each level I’ve played - about six of the twenty-two the game seems to have - has been well-crafted, and built around speed. Apparently Splashy was made through a collaboration with speedrunners, and I can see why. If everything lined up perfectly, you’d be able to get through levels quite fast.
The levels themselves are also a treat to look at as well as play. Factory levels in games tend to be really dingy, dark places, but owing to it manufacturing paint the one in Splasher is very colorful and almost feels alive. Water spouts up from pipes to propel you upward, turrets paint the walls and ceiling automatically - even things that kill you are very comfortable. You die in one hit, but so far I haven’t felt any real frustration. The music is also very nice, being jazzy and upbeat.
About the only knock I can think of to the game is that it’s one of those games that takes it for granted you’re playing with a controller. All the prompts are for one, and you can’t change keyboard controls, which are WADS for movement and IJKL for shooting water and paint. Obviously not everyone plays games like this on a keyboard and that’s fine, but it is something to be aware of. I’d say it’s perfectly playable on keyboard, though, aside from jumping over saws while wall-running, which I found a bit awkward.
Another thing that might be a flaw is that advancing through levels is gated off by you rescuing the workers in levels, so it’s not entirely an optional goal. So far it’s not too strict, but if you’d just prefer to blaze through levels it could be a flaw. Some of them did take me a few tries to rescue.
Overall, if you’re looking for a well-done, if not exactly an innovative platformer, or a new game to speedrun, I think Splasher would do nicely despite these minor flaws.

Long story short: This is a really good game that everybody should try at least once. Welcome to the ultimate feudal simulator.
While in many grand strategy games you control a country, raise troops and build an empire through conquest, Crusader Kings II brings on a more complex and interesting experience of country management where you will not actually control a country as a whole, but just a male or a female ruler who will have a limited authority upon the land he or she has through his/her nobility titles.
These titles vary from being a count (a minor ruler who usually has one or two provinces) to being an emperor (who can even control kings), but each of them has it's advantages and challenges. Although there are other titles (such as Emir for moslems or Jarl for norse pagans), most of them follow the classic feudal system of Baron/Bishop/Mayor<Count<Duke<King<Emperor. There are many ways to get new titles, but the most common ones are through conquest and through inheritance.
Laws can be changed in your domain, but your vassals have to approve them, so try to keep them happy. There're also inheritance laws, that include the way the titles will be given or if a woman can hold them or not.
Speaking about women, marriage plays a pretty important role, being the key to your blood line's survival. Following traditional feudal diplomacy, many alliances and agreements can be reached by marrying another character.
Wars, crusades, rebellions and infight are not as important as in other games such as Europa Universalis IV, but every ruler will eventually have to live by the sword. Since you don't have an army of your own, you will have to ask your vassals for their leavies, that will remain loyal to you for as long as you don't overuse them. In this game, you cannot declare a war without a casus belli, so you may need to fabricate one. Crusades and Jihads are called by the Pope / Caliph, and you can choose to join them or not.

I think I can pretty definitively say at this point that this is one of my favorite platformers of all time, and I've only really scratched the surface of it.
To start off: This game is very, VERY meticulously designed for speedrunning. The game's controls and level design are fluid and fast. Levels are designed in a way that rewards quick movement; lots of cycle-based stuff that you can make and just looks awesome when you do, but only if you're fast enough. Pretty dang tight platinum medal times to beat in single-level time-attack. Built-in full game speedruns for three different categories. An integrated split system that lets you easily track just how far ahead or behind you are of your best runs. The only things really missing are time attack ghosts and a quick restart (the latter of which is intended to be added soon and feels very sorely needed). As well there are a small number of short unskippable cutscenes but those are pretty minor.
The game is pretty dang great to play casually, too; a smooth progression of gameplay mechanics and difficulty across 22 levels, with the first few levels getting you used to the basic mechanics, then giving you the stick ink and bounce ink at about a quarter and 2/3rds of the way into the game. The levels tend to be focused on one core mechanic but still incorporate some of the other mechanics to keep levels diverse and interesting. And the last level ties everything together and adds a simple boss fight to boot. There's 7 splashers to rescue in each level, the last of which requiring you to collect 700 yellow ink, which tends to require nearly every speck of the level to be scoured, but never feels too hard to get (I never actually had to replay a level to get the 700 ink myself).
Visually the game is also pretty gorgeous, a nice cartoony style with lots of vibrant colors. The level design itself is fairly blocky but it works well with how movement in the game works. And the control scheme makes quite a bit of sense (if you use controller, at least; I found it near unplayable on keyboard and I wouldn't recommend it regardless given how important aiming with the D-pad is). The soundtrack I'm pretty indifferent on, it's solid enough & doesn't annoy me, and it fits the mood of the game well enough. The plot's very simple and conveyed entirely without dialogue but it's basically an excuse plot to get the whole thing rolling and I'm totally fine with that.
You can definitely tell this game was made by a designer for the Rayman Origins/Legends games, up to using both those games as level titles (alongside quite a number of pop culture references). The atmosphere is pretty similar (though not as wacky), the level design is absolutely up to par with the Rayman games (heck, might even be better), it's just a great experience all around. The kind of game I am very seriously considering getting into speedrunning the full game for (though I haven't gotten there yet; soon, though, once I at least gold medal all the levels in time attack).
It's got minimal frustrations, clever and varied level design, a great length to not feel too short but keep the whole game plenty replayable, a lot of obvious fine-tuning to make it as player friendly as possible while still providing a decent challenge... absolutely worth checking out for any fans of 2D platformers.

I urge everyone who purchases this game to not throw in the towel after a mere couple of gaming hours. With over 11,000 buttons to click, terms to remember and legalities to learn, it is definitely more complex than your average hack-and-slash, but an extremely rewarding experience when you stick with it.
I would most likely compare this game to chess, especially its tutorial. When my grandfather taught me chess, he showed me all the cute little figurines, showed which way they could move and kept winning for seven years, until I finally mastered the game enough to beat him.
This is exactly how I feel like with CKII. I played through the tutorial, read several different guides and have an extremely helpful friend with over a 1000 hours of this game under his belt - and I still very vaguely grasp what I'm doing. My daughter is the wife of the Kaiser - good stuff - but is it - but who should I kill... That's what a fraction of a second of the game feels like.
All of this is emphasized by the fact that you literally don't know what you are supposed to do  - you choose it, there are no built-in goals.
In conclusion, this game has an extensive learning curve. It takes time to master, but is very rewarding once you do.

This is a game that has the potential to be a great little minigolf game, but isn't quite there yet.  The main issue is that the dividing line between success and disaster is too fine.  When the only way to complete a hole is to hit
one spot, with no margin for error, the frustration level piles up quickly.  You're not alone here, Blacklight - Vertiginous Golf has essentially the same problem.  Having a rotten angle or needing to just putt out to safety is enough of a penalty; having to replay a stroke until gotten
right sucks the fun factor way down.
It's a principle of golf course design -- and the same applies to minigolf -- that if the route to the hole is high-risk, there should be a bail out option for players who aren't at that level yet.  I certainly wouldn't play a regular golf course where every tee shot required a 300 yard carry over water with no other way to the hole.
A little on-course direction would be a good idea -- it doesn't need to be precise, but when you're on a timer and don't know which way the hole is, that doesn't help the frustration level either.
That said, it is a very good game.  The graphics are excellent (if a little eye-twisting on Candy Land), the mechanics are straightforward, the play is smooth, and the music is not only appropriate, it's even kind of charming.
Overall,
.  If the vast gulf between risk and reward narrows, I would even change that to Highly Recommended... but not yet.

DOS II is a herald to old rpgs from the 80s-90s.  RPG’s like Fallout, Wasteland, Baldur’s Gate.  All of them rewarded you with exploration, dialogue, minute journal-keeping and little to no quest markers.  You relied on your wits alone to get you through the game.  Choices mattered in those games.  If you ♥♥♥♥ed up a quest, the game would make damn well sure you knew it – and felt it.  Unlike most modern RPGs, Divinity is open-ended and not just with classes.  You want to be a magic-wielding rogue?  Go for it.  Pure rogue that steals and kills everything that isn’t nailed down or moves?  Go for it.  The choice is yours!  Be whatever mixture of class/skills that you want.  What this game is is a love letter to rpgs of the past and it has little to no hand-holding.
Pros:
+ graphically one of the most beautiful CRPGS I've played.  Varied enviroments, painstaking details, vivid colors.
+ Written dialogue is very well done - characters have stories they're willing to tell
+ the story is intense; it leaves your morals confused and often conflicting
+ Incredible customization for characters.  Skills, weapons, attributes.  This really is a game that harks back to working your character out
+ Challenging.  This isn’t your momma’s half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥RPG.  This game WILL kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you don’t play your cards right
+ The world is massive and rewards players for exploring and roaming
+ Multiple solutions to quests.  There isn’t one way to do everything.  Find one solution you like?  Quest on!  Find another way that suits your fancy better?  Game on.
+ Graphically very pleasing to look at!
+ Music is what you’d expect from a fantasy game and it’s pleasing to chill out and relax to
+ Party members are interesting and have their own backstories/quests
+ Multiplayer/Co-op!
+ Option for fast travel when you discover waypoints
+ VO's are nice but I've played the game for so long without them that I find the experience more enjoyable with it off completely
+ loot in certain vendors has changed or does change so there's always plenty of variety
+ crafting is so optional that you almost don't really have to bother with it unless you want to
+ The Gamemaster mode is probably the best thing since tabletop simulator
+ The freedom to do what you want in-game
+ Loot once you hit just before leaving Fort Joy and after is beyond plentiful
+ Variety of characters, both recruitable and NPCs alike are astounding; everyone has a story worth listening to
Cons:
- Gold can be hard to come by.  Or... you know, cheat
- A lack of direction can often be confusing; especially for gamers just getting into the game/series
+/- Multiple quest solutions can be missed or completely over-looked.  Although exploration/deep digging can help you find them
Final verdict: 9/10: would play love letter RPG again.  And again… and again.

Sure, the game starts off as your typical Japanese cutesy thing. But soon enough, you realise things.

Adventurers will be your tools. Cavediving may seem like an extra, but it's the only way of finding some of the most profitable treasures. You don't wanna buy from a wholesale seller or such - after all, that means less profit. You'll give them some equipment, maybe some food, and then hope they come back alive.
Perhaps they will. After all, you play them. But if they die, you can only take a few things with you back up. Maybe you'll sell something to them, later, when they come browsing. At just under 150% of it's base price.
Underneath that cute exterior is a game about making money.

I wish there was a "meh" button on Steam. This is definitely not a bad game, but not a great one either.  Let me break it down:
+ The story, when it picks up towards the end, becomes quite interesting, especially considering this is originally just a Vita game.
+ The design of New Orleans is quite good; it really feels like a town that is slowly becoming a proper city.
+ The voice acting itself is quite acceptable, again considering this is just a Vita game.
+ The trade system is a nice touch, and an intuitive way of earning money. It's perfectly integrated into the gameplay and the story.
+ The facial expressions are impressive, a thousand times better than Andromeda.
+ The animations are nice, especially the combat ones.
+ / - The new weapon, whip, is very lackluster. It's not especially useful and I've almost never used it.
+ / - I get that the Lady persona can't be seen sprinting through the streets like a common slave, but playing as the Lady gets boring really quick as it takes too much time to arrive anywhere. However, I can't really put this into the negatives as it makes sense.
+ / - There is no need to play as the Assassin persona, as its advantages are not really necessary. As long as you are careful and have not-too-bad reflexes, you can solely play with the Slave persona. It earns notoriety much slower and does not have the "at least one level of notoriety all the time" problem.
- The story takes way too long to get exciting. The first half of the game (story-wise) is literally sleep-inducing. You vaguely get the impression that there are some slaves missing, and that's all. It doesn't go further than that until you get to the last few sequences.
- Although the voice-acting is good enough, the ambient sounds are terrible. Terrible as in they don't exist. You wander through New Orleans, a big town, and the ambient sounds are pathetic. It feels as if you are walking down a back alley whereas there are actually more than 50 NPCs on that street. It makes the urban environment feel dead. The same can be said for Bayou. There should have been non-stop bird and insect noises all around, but it's quite silent (for a bayou, I mean).
- The collectibles don't earn you anything meaningful. They are all (almost purely) cosmetic. The armors and weapons you normally unlock in other AC games change the gameplay considerably with their bonuses; there is no such thing here.
- The reward system is broken. I unlocked a ton of achievements but got no Upoints in return.
All in all, I still recommend this game as I had quite fun while playing it. Just keep in mind that this is a Vita game and don't expect too much.

But the way you can command troops and do combat in two different stages with an overview and Third person shooter make the combat attractive.

Note: I played this for months before it was released on steam.  I reached level cap, build my ship, farmed Hasla, etc... So ignore my 0.0 hrs logged on steam for this game. They were late to the party on getting it on steam.
Very innovative, but Dev's and the parent dev company are compeltely lost on what the community actually wants.
At its core, this MMO is BETTER than any other MMO.  It offers more in it's general idea.  The aspect of building your own ship from scratch, sailing the open seas, diving for treasure, exploring shipwrecks, and killing sea monsters... These things are groundbreaking to the MMO genre.
It has a very decent questing system that doesn't feel too grindy.  The class systems are very well done, and they avoid falling into the cookie-cutter rut of class building that 99% other MMO's fall into.  You really can play your way, choose your own skills, and build the class you want, as long as you play smart about it.
It does lack in some skill trees though.  I wish there were summoner type classes, as well as psionic/telekinetic types that never get any love.
Items are unrestricted, you can use anything.  You're given great freedom over how you want to play and theorycraft your character. This is another aspect where AA beats other MMO's.
The game looks great, and plays great. It's easy to get around, explore, do quests, form parties, etc.
Where the game fails is at its developement team.  They aren't doing a good job of protecting the game against botters or hackers.  They DO NOT listen to the community at all, no matter how they might try and comfort their fans on the forums.. It's often "We'll say we'll fix it, but we will show we don't give a !@#$."
A MAJOR problem with the game, that caused me to quit playing after reaching 50 is that there is not NEARLY enough housing space available.  And you need a house to craft properly, and you need to craft properly to build the ships you want, and weapons you want.  You can try to otherwise, but it will take you 10 times longer than everyone else. You will fall behind the curve, and get smashed in PVP encounters.
The crafting of end-game items requires so many materials, it becomes a grindfest.  To the devs i say this: THIS ISN'T FUN!
All in all, you have a game that looks good, plays good, sounds good, and has a ton of content and options.. It's technically better than every other MMO out there.  But the way it's crafting and housing system has been designed is poorly balanced and is killing off numbers of players for the game.  And its supported by 2 dev teams (Trion and then AA's parent Korean Dev team) that can't make ends meet in providing support and care for their game.
I can recommend playing through to level cap, but don't get any big ideas of crafting a Black Pearl pirate ship, or building a big house for yourself - Those are unrealistic ideas in this game.  Which is a shame because they are the funnest aspects.
ArcheAge really should have taken a page out of Ultima Online, and really given more freedom to players on where to build houses and made land more available.
What a giant let down... This game was supposed to revolutionize MMO's. and it could have.  But the dev's ruined that opportunity.  This could have been a WoW killer if they would have done it right.

UPDATE:  This review was written right before the game launched. That was before it mysteriously got removed from the Steam store. I no longer reccomend this game. I feel that it is fine if you don't fall into the RNG box trap. But, if you are a player who likes things fast, easily accessible, and/or like to collect in-game items, this is not the game for you. I played this game longer than the hours shown on here. I played it for about 6 months straight after launch. The continuous issues with communication between Trion, XLGames, and the community, made this game unplayable for me. I know there are those who will still enjoy it, and I'm happy for you. I wanted it to be more than it ended up being. Good luck to those still playing. <3
Pros:
- It allows you to customize your gameplay by giving you the freedom to mix three classes of your choice.  This means that if you wanted to, you could be an Archer/Mage/Rogue or a Warrior/Monk/Necro.  There are combinations that make the most sense and probably have the most synergy indicated by flame icons when you go to choose your second and third "skillset" (class).  But, it does not prevent you from making up your own combinations.
- Character customization in this game is pretty fleshed out.  There are many options for hair/makeup/skin, etc.  And it allows you to go even further and apply scars that you can move to new locations on the face, alter the size, and even change the angle.  Some of the options look silly, and it's easy to make a "derpface" character if that's what you're into.  And, if you're one of those players who doesn't like spending hours customizing a character, there are many premade options available to choose from.
- The combo system is interesting.  While watching players fight mobs, it's obvious who has paid attention to the skill info and who hasn't.  The combo system is incredibly rewarding if used correctly.  The amount of damage you do becomes less about having the "strongest" skill and more about reading through all of the skills and finding a combination that has synergy.
- You get a mount before you hit level 10.  It will be in your quest log before you even notice.  While the game will be f2p, and many "fancy" mounts will cost you a pretty penny, they do supply decent mounts for the 100% f2p playerbase.  This mount also has set skills that you unlock as your pet levels up.  And, you can gain armor for your pet through quests.  So, again, the game doesn't force you to spend money to be able to move throughout the game.
There are more pros to the game, but I suggest for anyone who is weary after reading the cons to just wait until open beta and find them out for yourself.
Cons:
- You don't start off with many skills.  Unlike many other MMOrpgs, you do not recieve a skillpoint with every level achieved.  And, you don't start off with the 2 extra skillsets, those are unlocked at level 5 and level 10, respectively.  Some players feel limited by this setup.  This especially becomes an issue when you mix the limited skillpoints in with the level-gated and point-in-class-gated system (the passives for the skillsets are locked until you spend a certain amount of points in that particular skillset).  So, when a player wants to save those precious skill points for the level 20+ skills, they are severely limited in their number of skills available to them.  It becomes a choice, and I would reccomend just purchasing the skills that you really want, but still getting enough in the beginning that you are having fun.  Afterall, that is what playing the game is all about.
- There is an issue with some quests where the arrow at your feet, pointing you in the direction of your quest, takes you to a location and nothing is there.  Why is that?  Because your quest objective is either above or below you.  Usually, this issue only occus when it is below you.  While you will eventually find where you need to go, and faction or general chat can be helpful, it can become frustrating and in some ways takes away from the immersion of the game.  You end up no longer pretending you are a member of a criminal society and just focusing on "UGH WHERE THE HECK IS THIS NPC" /rage.  It isn't a huge issue and it is in no way occurring frequently, but I figured it was worth mentioning.  And, this game isn't even in open beta yet so issues like this may be fixed.
Now in order to do some of these cons justice, I need to make them Pro/Con, bare with me.
Pros/Cons:
- There is a resource called "labor" in this game.  You gain it over time, but those without Patron status gain it at a much slower rate.  I feel like this resource is a good idea within the game and it gives a truly rewarding boost to those actively supporting the game developers.  But, it can become an issue in the early stages of the game.  New players want to explore these new horizons.  You can create trade routes, become a farmer, sail the seas, craft like a boss, or build a house and maintain your land.  All of this takes labor and in some cases the amount is rather substantial.  On the forums I saw someone mention that it may be a good idea to eliminate the labor costs from the beginning quests that are simply showing players what the game has to offer.  I agree with this sentiment and I think it would make "labor" more of a Pro than a Con.  I also think that if the developers let players fully experience the boundless opportunites of the game, they may be more likely to purchase Patron status in the future.
- If you don't tag a mob first, you won't get XP or any loot from it unless you were in a raid or party with the person(s) who tagged it before you.  This is a Pro/Con because it depends on how you like your MMOs.  Obviously, some quests will become infuriating if someone decides to sit there and troll a boss spawn, but, so far in my experience, people accept a party invite.  Do not expect the stranger sitting at the corpse's feet to initiate contact.  You have to be willing to set up the party if you don't want the guy to tag it before you and if you don't want to be one of those players who runs in right before it spawns and steals all the progress from the player who has been waiting there for a long time.  It encourages group play, which I think is necessary in some ways.  I feel like it is a nice kick in the pants for the outcast players to try to find a guild or a group of friendly players, which will ultimately enhance their entire gaming experience (this is coming from a singleplayer4life "outcast", I'm one of you).  It really isn't the worst thing in the world, but it will turn away some players.
- Freemium is always one of those iffy business models that I generally try to avoid.  At this point, I don't see anything truly gamebreaking from playing it without putting money into it.  However, sometimes these games can take a turn for the worst and suddenly quests are for sale (I'm looking at you LOTRO).  Or, they may stop putting real content (armor, weapon, and glider skins) into the questlines of the future and instead place them all in the marketplace (I'm looking at you Guild Wars 2).  It's too early to tell what direction this game will take, but it's definitely full of interesting content and it's complex enough (tons of tradeskills, skill combinations, mechanics, travel options, etc) to entertain a f2p player.
Final notes:  Not sure about it?  Don't pay for the packs that give you super duper special shiny early access.  It's a lot of fun, but if you don't have the money right now, or should be putting that most recent paycheck into the bank, just wait.  If you wait until open beta/launch you have spent $0.  Then, if you fall in love with it "LIEKOMG", then you can consider putting in the big bucks to attain Patron status.  Hopefully that helped.  Happy gaming. <3

This is my first JRPG in Steam and I'm very pleased in my purchase of this game. I highly recommend this for JRPG gamers and for RPG gamers that wants to add an anime feel on their RPG experience. The story is immersing and the characters have certain interactions with the main character that makes you feel more "into the game".
The only thing that I don't like with some of the JRPG games are the "true endings" route wherein if you make a false move, even for just one decision, you'll never be able to get a good ending. This made me become reliant on walkthroughs for the game since I always want to finish RPGs without walkthroughs in my first run. But since the story is so epic, I wanted to have the true ending in first run.
That is the only CON that I can think of. The graphics are great and very anime styled. The characters profiles and stories are in-depth. The game mechanics are unique and very interactive since it has this combo feature. Overall, this is a good buy in the Steam store (you can always wait for a sale and its even better...  I bought it at a sale price plus all DLCs and I don't regret doing that) for the JRPG fans and RPG fans that want to try a new twist to their games.

This game is pleasantly surprising. You are not trying to build an RPG character who can survive hordes of enemies. You are trying to arrange fate to favor one warrior's quest... and since the damage carries from one encounter to the next, you really feel every outcome and blow.
And you can decide you don't like a specific encounter. Effing goblins took my good sword! Although, I did beat some food out of them when I was out. But there's often trade-offs.
It's a rogue-like where I feel like I have a chance. When I fail, I can usually point to a choice I'd rather I'd made differently... or five or ten blows in combat I wish I'd dodged. It doesn't feel like solitaire, where you can't win a lot of hands. I mean, it is a solitaire, and I do lose a LOT. But even if I just manage to unlock a few more cards, I've gotten some new twists to explore. And it is exploration... you don't get to know what a card does until it's been in play.
[Post-EA followup]
Finally managed to beat the end boss! :D There's a big difficulty spike in the last 4 levels, and the end boss includes a full boss rush. It took a few tries to get the deck adjusted for a decent shot at victory. A lot of late-game cards will take a few attempts to unlock and may ruin your chances at the current run. Not sure that's such a bad thing. It's a matter of priority... and luck.
Still have a couple cards to unlock. It's like being at the end of a nice RPG but there's a sidequest or two remaining.

The store page reads.
"Besiege castles and raid villages in Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a first-person slasher with a focus on multi-player. Featuring competitive online combat that seeks to capture the experience of truly being on a medieval battlefield. Inspired from the intensity and epicness of swordfighting movies such as 300, Gladiator and Braveheart, Chivalry: Medieval Warfare aims to bring that experience to the hands of a gamer."
Which is the perfect example of a game sounding better in theory than it delivers in practice. The graphics are fine, but when it comes down to the laughably bad animation system  (The kind of laugh you deliver before shutting down the game) it really doesn't matter how high of a resolution your textures are. The combat is mediocre, helped some by the sound design which they surprisingly didn't screw up. The only good thing to say about this game is that there aren't many out there like it, so while the medieval time period has been played out in both history and television, it still has some legs to stand on when it comes to gaming. It's almost too bad since after playing this game you know it couldn't get much worse, while still hoping someone else can do it better in the future.
This game was a fun mod back in the day, and today the only thing keeping it somewhat relevant and not so offensive to your eyes (Besides the crud animation system) is Unreal Engine 3. My closing comments are that patches and substantial updates to the game are few and far between, if non-existent when it comes to the latter part. If you see this game on sale make sure you don't want any one of the 6000+ games in the Steam Store before you buy this one, you'll thank me later.

If you like card RP games, then this shoud suit you.
I've never been a massive card game fan, choosing your card, rolling the dice. Didn't quite take me.
HOWEVER.. I started playing this game, and I am really enjoying it!!
The best way I can describe it, is that you choose cards to play within a deck that is dealt by the dealer, and your 'card warrior' acts that scenario out.
Your cards contain weapons, armour, mystical items and the such, which you can choose to have before traversing the card path that is laid by the dealer. Some 'area' cards that you choose, prior to play, are locked, and you have no choice in the matter, whether that be being attacked or trading.
Trading is the usual buy, sell kind of thing, but you also have the option to buy food.
The battles are fairly straight forward, attack, block, dodge. If you have equipped your card warrior with certain items, you can play these during your battles, so you can gain more coin etc. The biggest issues I have with the battles is the slow mo finishing mini cinematic. I see enough of this playing Batman, but I'm being overly picky there, and the camera angle. A nasty can be out of sight, but still shoot you.
In general though, the animation is good, voice acting is good, the fighting mechanism is good,  the concept (for me at least) is brilliant.
Apart from the slow motion part, and camera angles, there's nothing I've happened across to cause major distress. I've played games that have had general release and are proper pigs ears. For an early release game, this is pretty cool.
If you like a traditional type game, but without all the faffing about with cards and dice, then this is a good purchase.

I'll try to keep this short and somewhat readable :
If you were an Euro Truck Simulator 2 fan and are intimidated by the seemingly small size of the current content - don't be.
SCS has shown more than high aptitude to deliver high quality content with time. It may be less content than you are used to, but it's fresh, and my god is it polished.
It's beautiful, the controls are tight and intuitive, as well as incredibly configurable - and it seemingly runs smoother the prettier it looks - don't know what kind of nail polish SCS works with, but it works perfectly on my 2012 war victim.
As a final note : remember the devs took several steps to have the world size of Euro Truck Simulator 2 as it is. There was its prequel, and the prequel to that (Scania Truck Simulator). And on top of that, the game got massive expansions, and multiple patches that added cities in Italy, Austria and Hungary.
You honestly think SCS didn't or won't deliver? Well if you do, I can't do much to convince you otherwise. But they can. For 20 (local currency) it's worth it.
tl;dr : BELIEVE in the developer. Particularly this one.

After playing (and getting hooked on) a number of clicker/idle games, I've got to say: this is the best one.
Rather than just going on forever or repeating the same thing endlessly, CotLI introduces variety at every stage of the game. Keep up your long-term strategy while managing the intricacies of the various challeneges and organize your varied team of Crusaders to get the most beneft for each run.
There are some purchasable options that may help speed you up (especially as a new player), but if you are 100% F2P, you're still going to be good to go.
The game has in-game chat that is full of silly banter, but also helpul players who will actually offer advice and answer questions for those in need. The in game community (which generally doesn't exist in this genre) is excellent.
Frequent events keep up the variety while offering a plethora of attainable bonuses that add on to the original experience. Everything's always changing.
This is a great take on a clicker/idle game and really recommend it to anyone who enjoys them.

I really wanted to love this game. Unfortunately, I can't.
Pros:
- Very detailed, focuses on a lot of features in the medieval world.
- Interesting take on things: you don't control a country, but a nobleman, forging his dynasty through the middle ages.
- Great theme.
Cons:
- Steep learning curve. I've probably spent time equal to the gameplay watching walkthroughs and tutorials
- Feels grindy. Instead of building, researching, exploring or fighting, you wait a lot in this game. A lot.
- Once you find a method to win more territories ( press claims, alliance through marriage, hire mercenaries, fight ), it's pretty much the same.
- Battles are boring. And I'm not usually the warmonger type of player, but it'd be nice to have a way to actually control the battles ( or to turn the tides in your favor when outnumbered ), instead of just watching stats and percentages.
- Improving your cities is rather pointless. First, because you'll improve only the cities that belong to your own dynasty, not the whole empire. Second, because the benefits of improving your cities are barely there.
- Researching is, also, pointless. In a game, my dynasty got from a lowly count on the outskirts of the empire to the Basileus of the Byzantine Empire and I didn't even open the research tree once.
- Its goals are uni-directional: acquiring more territory.
- THE MOST IMPORTANT ONE: you get no satisfaction when winning something. There's no pleasure involved in it.
So my suggestion: if you want fun, stick to Civ V, Knights of Honor ( another Paradox title that's unfairly overlooked ) or Total War.

One of the first things to note about ME2 is that, especially with relation to the PC version, this game was originally intended for controller use.  This is primarily because there is a one-button-do-all feature that, while the mouse may provide more accuracy for hacking and small tasks (aim assist in console versions making up for accuracy loss), shows us that this game is intended for primarily "A" button usage.  The PC versions DO NOT feature any controller support, and the 'mods' that are out there do not let you properly use your weapon/power selection radial, making them completely pointless (in my opinion, maybe if you memorize it it'll work, but the stick is still inverted-upsidedown on the menus).
To get deeper into the controls, there are a number of people who like to jump on those who indicate that the controls are clunky, compared to other TPS games.  First and foremost, I would address that Shepard can apparently only sprint for about 4-5 seconds.  Now I get that he is in a space suit, but that armor is pretty thin given his actual size and is likely light-weight so that should not be slowing him down, and if he is a military trained individual we should all hope that sprinting would in actuality be near-infinite since his normal movement is a light jog at best (thinking in comparison to Gears of War or Army of Two).  Now to get to the cover combat; yes it's nice that he sticks his head around the corner like it's realistic, but there are many places where for some reason you cannot aim around corners for no reason, unless you are perfectly locked into the flush-opening position.
To wrack on the controls a little bit more (which aren't bad to get used to, but lets face it Resident Evil 4 had better mobility at higher skill training), there is no intentional crouch and zero jumping, and very few places where you can actively leap over cover despite a very slight slide into some cover spots.  The lack of jumping has created a number of instances where, for example, the character gets stuck on top of a medical bed with the only fix being to reload your game (hope you used your quicksave) due to the lack of full world programming.  Not being able to crouch greatly reduces the ability to move throughout the battlefields as well, and makes you feel like a derp sandwich running around with your head up between cover spots.  So for all of you who have said the controls are not clunky or are looking for a smooth combat experience, you now have a nice detailed explaination of what to expect and why, compared to other games, ME2 is still lacking.
However, the game is not 100% a combat game, probably not even 50% to be honest, so this really creates less problems for game enjoyment than I make it out to be.  The dialogue is really fantastic, especially in that when you choose a dialogue option it is what your character is thinking, not your exact words.  You can effectively play the game from a Cpt. Picard standpoint, making just about the right decision and resolving issues in an acceptable manner.  However, city affect (yes I mean 'affect', not 'effect') and conversations really do feel like KotOR, almost like it's just a reskinned version of the game with surprisingly more realistic characters.  The paragon/renegade options do work nicely in the dialogue, which is enjoyable to watch in and of itself and good that it is since it makes up a large portion of the game.  Unfortunately, there is no chance to fail in dialogue options, most likely to ensure that all dialogue is spoken and not simply text-based.  A trade-off most gamers can live with for the experience, but limits replay value to an extent.  I mean lets face it, many gamers would be quicksaving before every room and reloading if they didn't get their dialogue to go the way they wanted if there was a chance to fail.
Overall the game is very fun, and I do recommend at least experiencing Mass Effect for the visuals and cinematic feel to the game, though the lore seems a little cheesy at times with how it is presented (though that could just be satire).  Also it's very odd to deal with well-known actors voices; I spotted Seth Green's voice immediately but had to look up when I heard Martin Sheen's; I knew I knew that voice!  It's a nice touch in the end however.
Final rating; 81% approval; lots of things could have been better, yet it's good for a playthrough or two, but I would not pay top dollar; wait until it's $5-10 to pick it up.

UPDATE: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME, at least its Mac version, for there is something that prevents you from using any DLC or mod you get. I repeat, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME unless you want to have non-DLC-non-mod vanilla version.
Long story short: This is a really good game that everybody should try at least once. Welcome to the ultimate feudal simulator.
While in many grand strategy games you control a country, raise troops and build an empire through conquest, Crusader Kings II brings on a more complex and interesting experience of country management where you will not actually control a country as a whole, but just a male or a female ruler who will have a limited authority upon the land he or she has through his/her nobility titles.
These titles vary from being a count (a minor ruler who usually has one or two provinces) to being an emperor (who can even control kings), but each of them has it's advantages and challenges. Although there are other titles (such as Emir for moslems or Jarl for norse pagans), most of them follow the classic feudal system of Baron/Bishop/Mayor<Count<Duke<King<Emperor. There are many ways to get new titles, but the most common ones are through conquest and through inheritance.
Laws can be changed in your domain, but your vassals have to approve them, so try to keep them happy. There're also inheritance laws, that include the way the titles will be given or if a woman can hold them or not.
Speaking about women, marriage plays a pretty important role, being the key to your blood line's survival. Following traditional feudal diplomacy, many alliances and agreements can be reached by marrying another character.
Wars, crusades, rebellions and infight are not as important as in other games such as Europa Universalis IV, but every ruler will eventually have to live by the sword. Since you don't have an army of your own, you will have to ask your vassals for their leavies, that will remain loyal to you for as long as you don't overuse them. In this game, you cannot declare a war without a casus belli, so you may need to fabricate one. Crusades and Jihads are called by the Pope / Caliph, and you can choose to join them or not.
Of course, religion has an important role in this game, so there are many religious options you can follow in order to make your religion stronger. Christians, moslems, norse, jews, suomi, zoroastrians, buddhists and many others have different religious options you can use in your benefit.
As a whole, this game is really fun to play, and you can play it just for doing stupid things with your realm or try to go on and build a new empire. There are many choices, and there's always a new surprise waiting for you.
The only flaw this game has, and it's a big one indeed, is that you cannot do many things (like playing moslem or pagan countries) if you don't buy the DLCs. So get your wallet ready to spend a lot of money here.

So far I like it.  It's still early hours yet, but I've run into no major difficulties and have had fun kicking the tires and learning the mechanics.  Some major points:
Singleplayer - It has this.  This is major for me, because I game to relax, I don't game to deal with other people.  Day one it has more difficulty sliders than I will ever use or need, which is awesome as it lets you tailor the game to your playstyle.  So far the only thing I've changed is upping the respawn rate a tad because I hate looking at a barren landscape after I've gone and destroyed everything, and was glad to see that the respawn radius is pretty close to where I was building.  My hidesously uncreative box base has pretty trees to look at again!
Bugs - I actually haven't come across a single one.  I realize I may be an outlier here, and also I'm playing singleplayer and most people seem to be complaining about server lag, but still.  It's been a pretty smooth run in the time I've played.
Price - Am I the only one pleasantly surprised by it?  I've seen worse and have paid more.  This is about what I spent on Ark and Planet Explorers, off the top of my head, and if I get half the playtime out of this as I have from either, it'll be more than worth it.  Plus, I am totally down with supporting devs when they've got a worthwhile product to offer.
Early Access - Just like half of my hours played are in sandbox games, half of them are in Early Access games as well.  I know exactly what I am getting into with an EA game, which tends to make me more patient with them.  That said, there seems to be a good game here, to the point where I'm more excited than impatient for future updates, in that I currently have plenty to do.
Difficulty - Still learning the ropes, obviously, but it's neither hand-holdy nor overly punishing.  Died like six times in the first hour and nearly ran out of water once from sheer inattention.  A lot of the mechanics are similar to other games, but I actually find that to be a good thing--as I'm running around fresh off the cross, I start spamming the "E" key for rocks and things and yep, it works.  Which is awesome, because I am naked and unarmed and there's no pause button; I don't want to have to stop and research basic survival mechanics if I can just run with what I already know!  Research can wait until I've got food, water, and somewhere relatively safe to put my back against, thanks.
Graphics - I have kind of a beefy computer, but I literally forgot to even check what settings I'm playing at with this game; it looked great out of the box and ran without stutter, so I honestly don't even care.  Whatever it is, it's working.
Overall - There are some very minor quirks I would hope to see changed--more directional sound from enemies, for instance, as even with headphones I have no idea which direction danger is coming from without spinning around looking everywhere--but my few complaints are just that--few, and minor.  Can't wait to see where this game goes, and quite enjoying it so far!

I'm not sure what to make of this game, but it's undoubtedly got some weird stuff going on with the achievements. Ignoring that, I have a few things to say about the actual game, and I'll try to keep it simple.
Gore - The gore is absolutely glorious. It's nothing state of the art or high-tech, but man is it great. Enemies literally explode into a shower of gibs when killed and it's truly a sight to behold
Weapon feel -
of the weapons feel pretty satisfying to use, especially the shotguns and the minigun
Performance - the game runs well over 60 (most of the time even over 100) at all times with everything set to highest, although your results may vary
The price is right - 99 cents for a game is not a big ask, let alone the 50 cents it's going for on sale right now. I've spent a hell of a lot more on worse games.
Audio - A lot of sound effects are either over or under volume. Explosions play loud enough to distort the audio and the footsteps of enemy dinosaurs are too quiet and too similar to your own.
Story - The storybook style narration segments seem to have little or nothing to do with the gameplay segments. For example, the narrator will talk about being in a jungle, but neither the level prior to or after the cutscene are set in a jungle
Movement - Your player character moves
If you see a boss coming and it's already kind of close to you, you'd better kill it pretty damn fast. Backing up normally isn't getting you anywhere and turning to sprint will only match their speed, making escape futile.
I want to end by making it abundantly clear that I have recieved no compensation for this review. I paid for the game myself (all 50c of it) and these thoughts are my own. The developer asked for my feedback, but that is the only interaction I have had with them.
So, what to make of this game then? Well, it's not for everyone. If you like easy achievements, then I would definitely recommend the game to you, but if you don't, then it might be a tougher sell. With that said, for such a low price you're not exactly losing much if don't enjoy it, and it can still be a bit of fun if you've got time to kill

While the core gameplay loop - the fluid movement mechanics and satisfying gunplay - is fun, I can't recommend Warframe because of its business model.
The running and gunning is unfortunately just a shiny veneer on an otherwise unpleasant and grindy gameplay experience. The missions themselves aren't particularly rewarding and it becomes clear that the real meat of the game is in gathering resources for equipment - a long, drawn out process that usually requires farming the same missions over and over... unless of course you pay them and bypass all that tedious grind.
Devaluing the gameplay like that is sad enough, but what really came to bother me was the suspicious random log-in reward. When you log in, the first thing you're greeted with is a scrolling loot-crate-style reward system that usually gives you a handful of crafting resources... unless you haven't played for a few days, in which case it gives you 20% off the premium currency 100% of the time. I'm not the only one to have noticed this.
There's two things wrong with this (if confirmed):
1) It's deceptive. They know what they're doing when they show you scrolling loot crates. They're implying the reward is random when it isn't. Right off the bat Digital Extremes appears to be using your data to manipluate you into spending money. They are already setting themselves up as untrustworthy the second you log in.
2) If they're using data about you (your last log-in time) to manipulate the pricing of platinum, how can we trust them to not use other data. There might be better examples, but off the top of my head what's to stop them from watching when you queue some research in the Dojo and then just subtly decreasing the droprate of the resources you need, nudging you towards giving up and paying the platinum price.
With the recent revelations about Activision's microtransaction-based matchmaking patent and plugins like Scientific Revenue, I can't trust any company that even appears to be using similar deceptive tactics.
It's a shame really. If this game was available for a straight-up £40 and no microtransactions, I would've bought it. And I would be willing to bet it wouldn't be quite so grindy, and the loot system much more rewarding. I guess we'll never know... Although you never know, Warframe *is* still in beta (WHY!?) so maybe they'll get rid of the microtransactions, revamp the loot system and charge an honest, upfront price for the game before release... sigh.

I'd been itching to find another good strategy game and this little number I found sitting in the "well-user rated" page of the strategy games caught me by surprise. When it said soemthing along the lines of turn-based strategy which is evidently similar to XCOM despite never playing the series, I was unsure of what to think, since most strategy I stuck to was RTS like C&C or Starcraft. Plus, I am an avid story-interest guy when it comes to anything, and the allure of a (supposedly) riveting story coupled with strategy seemed like it was worth the 20 dollar leap. And it was oh so worth it.
I didn't expect to get this absorbed into a strategy game with a huge slew of characters with whom I thoroughly enjoyed, both main and side characters. The story itself is quite magnificent seeing as how its essentially a re-envisioning of the real-life WWI/WW2 with some, extra, mystifying elements added into the mix, which didn't seem to detract at all from the story, in fact it made it even more unique and interesting. The world of the game is intriguing and the gameplay itself was fresh and magnificent for me since I've never played anything of the sort, although I did have some qualms with playing this game at the start and as it went along.
Most apparent of issues from the beginning, although it quickly became less of a nuisance, was the menu; no mouse needed anywhere and was heavily reliant on the keyboard if not only keyboard-reliant. I had initially found keyboard operation in battles choppy and not very accurate until I found the right keys for them so that removes that issue. Probably the most struggling of features in this game is just the pure chance of things. Even though battles are fought through the player's actions and actual real-time decisions in aiming and movement, I found it incredibly frustrating seeing how bad chance could play out at times where bullets at point blank range would miss and cost my team valuable CP ("command points" which are the lifeblood of every match) and even their lives. On another less-immersing and troubling note was that to obtain high ranks, battles had to be won with lightning speed and blitzkrieg tactics mainly involving the scout class alone, meaning slow, methodical pushes with all your forces were usually not advised for high-scoring missions, which made it feel less like a full-scale battle, but those are hardly bad points.
Aside from those only sour points I had with the game, everything good with the game easily made up for its annoyances. The amount of strategy and decision one can put into the team BEFORE the battles even start is astounding and almost felt overwhelming. You had to handpick each of your squadmembers from the command roster and each person had their own strengths and weaknesses, and each of those strengths and weaknesses would pertain to their fellow teammates, the battlefields they would tread upon, and so many more criteria that made soldier selection so very diverse for every situation you will be faced with. Even better, the very gear and equipment you would bring into battle had many branching upgrade and choice options making the depth of pre-battle planning so incredibly diverse and immersive. Nearly a third of the time logged into this game has admittably been me listening in on mission briefings, choosing the most acceptable soldiers, gearing each one for their roles, and inspecting the other various side elements outside of battle like the extremely vast amount of backstories, world mythos, and "reports" or side missions per-say, that kept me at this game for nearly 40+ hours, with free DLC to boot with the 20 dollar tag.
I don't know what else to point out at this point, this game just has some much fun to it despite some of its slight shortcomings. I even hear they have VC2 and VC3 available on the PSP, so here's hoping they port some of those to other consoles someday because I want more of this stuff. Gripping story, gripping gameplay, this thing will have you glued for hours to come. Definitely worth the buy for only 20 bucks. 9.5/10 for reals.

Closed Beta 2 Review:
Ok this game is called Archeage.
I got interested in this game about 1 year ago.
Thought it looked like a promising MMO.
The graphics look similar to a Dynasty Warriors Game.
(I do enjoy the dynasty warriors franchise)
Ok back to the topic at hand.
I have only leveled to 17 in this game at the moment. During the Closed Beta 2.
To a person who has played MMOs this game can get kind of confusing at a first glance.
COMBAT:
The combat is generic to most mmos having to press the number keys to activate certain abilities.
You can combine 3 main skill lines together for example  as Sorcery, Occulism and Auramancy.
Each combination has it's own class name like this one is the revenant skill line.
Each skill tree gives you the ability to combine these skills in tandem to create formidible combinations that can make you undefeatable or practically immune from attacks.
PVP:
I haven't got involved with this part so i can't really say anything.
Crafting:
I have started the crafting system. I started to try it. It feels kind of complicated making you have to learn each individual skill from purchasing it from NPCs (at low levels this would be best to be avoided) I believe this should only be encountered either end-game or if you want to create yourself a goal in future. This also requires Labour points to even get involved. The game limits you on what you can do.
Patrons get more LP (Subscription) and Non-Patrons less LP. (It's a good system to get people to keep the servers up)
Housing:
- Not really got into it.
Farming:
- Similar to farmville requiring LP though.
Mounts & Pets:
Mounts & Pets gain exp from the monsters you kill this eventually unlocks more skills for them.
If a Mount dies in battle they will die and get a -30% speed debuff making it risk and reward.
You will then need to heal them at a Stablehand to remove this debuff.
Gliders:
Fly from the highest cliff and glide down to enjoy the sights.
At this moment in time i would recommend this game as it has potential...
Only time will tell.

I will be updating this review as I play more and more, I read some reviews about this game and looked up some info on the site. Bought the lowest package to get in the beta and see how things are.
My MMO history: Ultima Online (favorite MMO), WOW started at beta and stopped when wrath came out, Age Of Conan :(, Darkfall Online (second favorite, played on EU servers with the goons and on US servers), Guildwars 1 and 2, then a mix of some that don't matter.
Started this one up last night, the story for my race is pretty neat. Sounds like they have taken a beating over the years. There are 4 races, two are buddy buddy and the other two are close. So you can understand your own race talk and the friend race but not the other two. I guess you can learn the other languages and I like that aspect of it.
I believe I am level 8 now and around level 5 you get a pet/mount, you have to kinda care for them for a bit as a quest then they grow up and you give them a ton of hugzzzz :P. Not really, but you do bond with it a bit first. You can ride the mount or jump off and have it follow you, I think as you travel and I know as you fight with them by your side they gain xp. They will gain levels like you. They get new skills and you can gear them up. Far better than the old school WOW mounts.
I have gathered some resources so far, I have not done anything with those yet. Also as you play you gain these points (labor points) but you gain so many over time while you play and when you're offline if you paid for the game. These points so far have been used for items in my pack. Quests or drops will be closed up or unidentified and you use 1 or 5 of these points to see what the item is. I was worried about this at first but i have not dropped too low on points to be able to open up some of the loot that comes packaged up.
While riding around on my mount I have found people flying/gliding over me which is pretty cool. The villages I have passed through seem very alive with NPC's and players, everybody is up to something.
Fighting system: This seems very similar to Guildwars 2. There are combos where if somebody is stunned or poisoned or something then you do this other ability it will proc or something. I could put 20 stacks of debuffs on a mob then hit them with one move that would stun them if there was 20 stacks. Most of the abilities I have seen do something like this.
Skill points: After leveling up you get skill points to assign out. You first start with 1 set of abilities, then once you hit level 5 you can add another whole set of skills to pick from. I had 3 choices to use, and it actually looks like you can reset these decisions at any time. Which i might do just because gear now is not as important since i just started. Just to see how i can play this character in different ways.
One thing that bugs me about this game right now.. every time i load up the game my character loads only the hair. So the character model is just a wig basically and it takes a while to load. Then in game it will do the same thing if i have never been to the area. My computer is not great but still seems like an odd problem. Other issues similar will happen like the whole left face of a mountain will be missing and take a while to load.
Ok thats it for now, I should be playing more over the weekend if i have time. I will update this review again. Right now its a YES for this game and I'd give it a 7.8/10.

An old-style (ie, 2009-ish) game featuring some Mystery Case Files type gameplay, including middling live-action clips combined with finding needful things via both hidden object scenes and zooming in to parts of the larger scene.
