There are a few negatives, mainly the fact that the dubbing into English is terrible in parts, with a lack of certain grammatical elements that can be jarring at times. Also, as with all games like this, some scenes defy logic (such as why can't somebody with long arms just reach under a bed to retrieve an object, instead of having to find something else beforehand).
Otherwise, it's a relatively-short, but satisfying puzzler.
Edited after three hour playthrough: My previous comments stand, but with a couple caveats.
I realize the creators of the game are not native English speakers, but a proofreader with better English language skills would have been helpful. It wasn't a game-killer, but I did cringe a few times at some of the grammar. It was pretty bad in spots.
The other additional caveat is that the game is VERY short, even playing on expert. I would have taken less time than listed, but sometimes my brain doesn't work at two in the morning.
Oh, and kudos for using live actors in the cut-scenes. The little girl was properly scary, although one character reminded me of somebody who would have been right at home in Dukes of Hazzard.
Enjoy!

This game is a very pleasent suprise. It's randomly generated dungeon board game. It's also a solid roguelike action rpg. Lastly it's a strategic card game. You unlock cards to build a deck that that you randomly draw from during each game. Unlocking cards feels reawrding since you get to 'load your deck' with them later.
If you get bored with table top games, or hate having to start your character over, then this game isn't for you. If you dislike the combat in the Batman Arkham games then you should stear clear. The combat has some actual depth with a dodge/counter/block system. It's pretty easy to view the combat as a button smashing action rpg, but you'll get your butt kicked pretty fast if you do that. It's not my favorite part, but taking time, planning out the order of your attacks, and being ready to counter is key to victory.
I give this game 8/10

-Lacks a story
Play if you like:
Munchkins (tabletop), Dominion (tabletop), Magic the Gathering (tabletop), FTL, Fable, or Dark Souls.

Greetings ! Fable : The Lost Chapters is a game I have been playing on Xbox 360 for little less than 10 years now, before which I played the original Fable.
It definitely is one of my favorite video games across the many many years of video games experience that I have gathered under my belt. With more than a thousand hours of gameplay in total (if we sum up both the time I spent on the original Fable and on TLC) — and I plan to keep on playing — I thought it would be nice to put the experience to good use and share my impressions on the differences in gameplay between Fable : The Lost Chapters on Xbox360 and on PC.
First of all, even though it is not gameplay related, the quality of graphics is atonishy on computer compared to its console counterpart; it might seem obvious said like this, but for those who didn't get to play on Xbox, now you know.
Then, the fact that xbox controler is not enable by default is quite sad, even fustrating for some from what I read on the conversation topics. Surely there are many altenative to fix that problem, but it remains a nuisance.
Now, for the actual criticism; the lock-on target engine works very badly on computer compared to how it did on xbox. With the controler, all you had to do was press the L trigger to activate the targetting system and the switch between targets with the C-stick (or right joystick). These mechanics were usefull for they were not compromising your combat at all, compared to the hold-and-release-to-target mechanic of the keyboard. Personnaly, I came to a point were I no longer use the targeting system anymore, and I would say the game is still fully playable without it.
That being said, I would also like to point out the fact that the spell mode (when holding a specific key to access your spell with the right and left mouse buttons) is more limited on computer since you only have access to 2 spells at a time and have to use the mouse wheel to circle between your spells sets when, with the controler, you simply had to hold the R trigger to switch into spell mode and you had access to 3 spells (on X, A and B) and used Y to circle between you spells sets. It is not that much of an hindrance but still a limit that cannot be left unnoticed if you heavily rely on spells.
As for the good point, I believe the menu is easier to use, and the shortcut bar at the bottom of the screen for rapid access to your favorite expressions or items is very useful (you have 9 slots plus 3 contextual slots on computer while you only have 3 slots and 3 contextual slots on Xbox; a very praised amelioration by those who like to express themselves within the world of Fable).
And finally, the use of a mouse permits a lot of new camera angles that couldn't be achieved on Xbox. So far I like it.  It's still early hours yet, but I've run into no major difficulties and have had fun kicking the tires and learning the mechanics.  Some major points:
Singleplayer - It has this.  This is major for me, because I game to relax, I don't game to deal with other people.  Day one it has more difficulty sliders than I will ever use or need, which is awesome as it lets you tailor the game to your playstyle.  So far the only thing I've changed is upping the respawn rate a tad because I hate looking at a barren landscape after I've gone and destroyed everything, and was glad to see that the respawn radius is pretty close to where I was building.  My hidesously uncreative box base has pretty trees to look at again!
Bugs - I actually haven't come across a single one.  I realize I may be an outlier here, and also I'm playing singleplayer and most people seem to be complaining about server lag, but still.  It's been a pretty smooth run in the time I've played.
Price - Am I the only one pleasantly surprised by it?  I've seen worse and have paid more.  This is about what I spent on Ark and Planet Explorers, off the top of my head, and if I get half the playtime out of this as I have from either, it'll be more than worth it.  Plus, I am totally down with supporting devs when they've got a worthwhile product to offer.
Early Access - Just like half of my hours played are in sandbox games, half of them are in Early Access games as well.  I know exactly what I am getting into with an EA game, which tends to make me more patient with them.  That said, there seems to be a good game here, to the point where I'm more excited than impatient for future updates, in that I currently have plenty to do.
Difficulty - Still learning the ropes, obviously, but it's neither hand-holdy nor overly punishing.  Died like six times in the first hour and nearly ran out of water once from sheer inattention.  A lot of the mechanics are similar to other games, but I actually find that to be a good thing--as I'm running around fresh off the cross, I start spamming the "E" key for rocks and things and yep, it works.  Which is awesome, because I am naked and unarmed and there's no pause button; I don't want to have to stop and research basic survival mechanics if I can just run with what I already know!  Research can wait until I've got food, water, and somewhere relatively safe to put my back against, thanks.
Graphics - I have kind of a beefy computer, but I literally forgot to even check what settings I'm playing at with this game; it looked great out of the box and ran without stutter, so I honestly don't even care.  Whatever it is, it's working.
Overall - There are some very minor quirks I would hope to see changed--more directional sound from enemies, for instance, as even with headphones I have no idea which direction danger is coming from without spinning around looking everywhere--but my few complaints are just that--few, and minor.  Can't wait to see where this game goes, and quite enjoying it so far!

American Truck Simulator is basically Euro Truck Simulator 2, set in the West coast of the USA. So if you didn't like Euro Truck Simulator 2, you're probably not going to enjoy this Sim.
So just like ETS2, you start off by creating your new, exciting delivery company and character. You then take on a few quick delivery jobs around California and Nevada (More states coming soon). Eventually, you can get loans which then allow you to purchase your own truck so you can do freight jobs where you use your own equipment. (You get more money for this)
You can then upgrade your garage to allow more spaces for employees, buy more trucks and hire employees to make more money. There is a skill tree and as you level and progress through the game, you can unlock delivery jobs such as hauling Dynamite, gassess and whatnot.
The game is highly addictive if you're the type of person that gets satisfaction from a mundane task; it's the thought of developing your own company and working really hard to get by which is really fun. After quite a few hours on this game already, I can tell I'm quite hooked and I find that driving around isn't as boring as it looks.
The driving is just as good as ETS2, the physics are really decent and it's pretty damn realistic. But then again, I'm not a truck driver, so how would I know?
More content coming soon! This game only has 2 states so far and only two truck brands, but more is on the way, such as the Arizona state and a few more truck brands.
This game like every other Simulator, is a massive grind and I can see myself eventually getting bored or tired of repeating myself. But you've got to remember, it is a Simulator and you're supposed to work hard for little reward.
The lack of states in this game is slightly dissapointing as you feel like there should be more places to go, however I found that after my current play time, I have seen a lot and there's still a lot to see. There are also only two car brands which is a shame as there's not much choice in what truck to buy at the start. It's 50/50 chance you'll get the same truck as me.
Speed Limits! Every country has them, but God damn! I want to scream when I'm in a 55 Mph zone when you could clearly do 70! And don't get me started on the 30 Mph limit, it's so painful!

I urge everyone who purchases this game to not throw in the towel after a mere couple of gaming hours. With over 11,000 buttons to click, terms to remember and legalities to learn, it is definitely more complex than your average hack-and-slash, but an extremely rewarding experience when you stick with it.
I would most likely compare this game to chess, especially its tutorial. When my grandfather taught me chess, he showed me all the cute little figurines, showed which way they could move and kept winning for seven years, until I finally mastered the game enough to beat him.
This is exactly how I feel like with CKII. I played through the tutorial, read several different guides and have an extremely helpful friend with over a 1000 hours of this game under his belt - and I still very vaguely grasp what I'm doing. My daughter is the wife of the Kaiser - good stuff - but is it - but who should I kill... That's what a fraction of a second of the game feels like.
All of this is emphasized by the fact that you literally don't know what you are supposed to do  - you choose it, there are no built-in goals.
In conclusion, this game has an extensive learning curve. It takes time to master, but is very rewarding once you do.

The first clicker game to actually keep my interest, and even got me playing other clicker games in an admittedly unhealthy fashion.  Remember to go outside folks!
From what I’ve seen of other clicker games, Crusaders has done quiet a bit to keep you interested in whats happening for a lot more of the game’s progression than just buying upgrades.  RPG style formation abilities add a large amount of thought to this, aside from it being “keep grinding till I can get the next upgrade”.  The goals given during different missions also give a more significant impact to when you reset, making it more satisfying when you do reset, and more motivational to reach those individual goals.
I will say that the assets look fairly silly, and that the sound design in my honest opinion is unbearable.  I muted the game 5 minutes in, haven’t had any issues with visual/audio appeal since.  I imagine a lot of clicker games are unplayable for long periods of time if you keep the sound on.  This game also has typical clicker game humor, to which I have mixed feelings on.  Sometimes I have a few snickers, other times I cringe so hard it hurts my stomach.
You can’t play offline, and I have had a fair bit of connection issues.  I usually don’t mention stuff like this because my home internet provider is awful and does this normally, but there are other users who have reported issues on the Steam discussions, so might want to look into that before installing.  The constant events are nice though; always something nice to look out for while playing, but won’t force you to play cause you are too scared to miss out(they last over a week anyway so..?).
The characters have… character to them :s I mean, they aren’t just upgrades that you forget about a few minutes later.  Their designs are a lot more memorable, even if they can be a bit basic at times.  Majority of the Event Crusaders are parodies too; I actually appreciate a lot of the Crusaders you get over time.  Lots of different fandoms, cultures and genres of characters have been covered.
The DLC seems over priced, but I can safety say you can enjoy progression while being F2P the entire time.  I consider it over priced because it doesn’t seem like much for what you are getting.
All things being said, I do recommend this game.  Its a very nice time waster that has enough depth to have you thinking about what you are doing, but can also be played without focus and still be relaxing.  I would personally recommend this to those who want a nice casual game that can be more than just a mindless distraction.  Fair warning, as someone who had never played clicker games until Crusaders; they are addicting and can form serious depression issues.  They are great for filling in the
in your life; do not
for them.  I have sank time into games before, but addictions to clickers can leave you even more empty over time..

This is not to say that AC Liberation is entirely devoided of fun factor - it isn't and I'd rather played it through then not. But such a mess is just unacceptable. To sum it up:
Pros:
- Good story line
- Nice looking locations, like swamps and Chichen Itza
- Canoe
- Chain kill option
- Variety of weapons and outfits
- New "personas system" which allows Evaline to switch between assassin, slave and lady.
- Some very nicely developed characters (like Dominiquez) !
Cons:
- Game is poorly optimised. I know it's a port but it could at least be as good as AC III, no?
- Evaline is on speed. Literally - she moves fast, which may be kind of nice when you get used to it, but when action begins (and bloody sync requirements), you just stop appreciating it, since operating Evaline becomes a hassle.
- Movement: Evaline will often get stuck in canoe when you want to get out of it, will jump when you don't want her to (in slave persona it will often have unpleasant effect of rising notoriety), during mission in cave in canoe you'd swim too fast for mouse to rotate camera (and you cannot adjust mouse sensitivity), etc, etc.

I'd been itching to find another good strategy game and this little number I found sitting in the "well-user rated" page of the strategy games caught me by surprise. When it said soemthing along the lines of turn-based strategy which is evidently similar to XCOM despite never playing the series, I was unsure of what to think, since most strategy I stuck to was RTS like C&C or Starcraft. Plus, I am an avid story-interest guy when it comes to anything, and the allure of a (supposedly) riveting story coupled with strategy seemed like it was worth the 20 dollar leap. And it was oh so worth it.
I didn't expect to get this absorbed into a strategy game with a huge slew of characters with whom I thoroughly enjoyed, both main and side characters. The story itself is quite magnificent seeing as how its essentially a re-envisioning of the real-life WWI/WW2 with some, extra, mystifying elements added into the mix, which didn't seem to detract at all from the story, in fact it made it even more unique and interesting. The world of the game is intriguing and the gameplay itself was fresh and magnificent for me since I've never played anything of the sort, although I did have some qualms with playing this game at the start and as it went along.
Most apparent of issues from the beginning, although it quickly became less of a nuisance, was the menu; no mouse needed anywhere and was heavily reliant on the keyboard if not only keyboard-reliant. I had initially found keyboard operation in battles choppy and not very accurate until I found the right keys for them so that removes that issue. Probably the most struggling of features in this game is just the pure chance of things. Even though battles are fought through the player's actions and actual real-time decisions in aiming and movement, I found it incredibly frustrating seeing how bad chance could play out at times where bullets at point blank range would miss and cost my team valuable CP ("command points" which are the lifeblood of every match) and even their lives. On another less-immersing and troubling note was that to obtain high ranks, battles had to be won with lightning speed and blitzkrieg tactics mainly involving the scout class alone, meaning slow, methodical pushes with all your forces were usually not advised for high-scoring missions, which made it feel less like a full-scale battle, but those are hardly bad points.
Aside from those only sour points I had with the game, everything good with the game easily made up for its annoyances. The amount of strategy and decision one can put into the team BEFORE the battles even start is astounding and almost felt overwhelming. You had to handpick each of your squadmembers from the command roster and each person had their own strengths and weaknesses, and each of those strengths and weaknesses would pertain to their fellow teammates, the battlefields they would tread upon, and so many more criteria that made soldier selection so very diverse for every situation you will be faced with. Even better, the very gear and equipment you would bring into battle had many branching upgrade and choice options making the depth of pre-battle planning so incredibly diverse and immersive. Nearly a third of the time logged into this game has admittably been me listening in on mission briefings, choosing the most acceptable soldiers, gearing each one for their roles, and inspecting the other various side elements outside of battle like the extremely vast amount of backstories, world mythos, and "reports" or side missions per-say, that kept me at this game for nearly 40+ hours, with free DLC to boot with the 20 dollar tag.
I don't know what else to point out at this point, this game just has some much fun to it despite some of its slight shortcomings. I even hear they have VC2 and VC3 available on the PSP, so here's hoping they port some of those to other consoles someday because I want more of this stuff. Gripping story, gripping gameplay, this thing will have you glued for hours to come. Definitely worth the buy for only 20 bucks. 9.5/10 for reals.

I'm playing the series in order of release date, so this is the newest game I've played, and I've played the previous six games (plus The Tyranny of King Washington).
Of those, unfortunately I think Assassin's Creed Liberation is one of the weaker entries-Bloodlines is the only other one I might put at the bottom so far. Even still, I mostly had a lot of fun with it.
There are really two problem areas here-the story needs some work. I like the basics, but it's clunky in places compared to the other entries in the series, and leaves some things (some relationships in particular) unexplored that seem like they should be. The storytelling in the previous games feels much stronger.
My other complaint is that it feels like it needs months if not a year of polish. I didn't run into anything game breaking, and the rapid release schedule has left many of the games with some unpolished elements, but things feel worse here than in 'III'. Mostly it just feels like they needed more time to run through the game and make sure everything executed properly-you've got some fights and various elements of animation that (sometimes) just don't look half as cool as they should...it's difficult to describe, and not game breaking, but it just clearly needed more time.
Really both elements I have issue with come down to that-it needed more time for polish, in storytelling and other elements.
Obviously that's the fault of the publisher, not the people who worked on it, and again, I never ran into anything gamebreaking.
I'm a bit disappointed that the first outing for a female assassin, and (as usual) quite an interesting character, couldn't have been a bit better executed. I wouldn't start here if you're new to the series, but if you love it like I do, I think you'll get enjoyment out of it too.
I suppose it's worth noting that the areas in the game feel smaller than in pervious entries-I'd imagine that's because of it's origins on Vita. Vita may not have the CPU or GPU power to pull off areas as large as in the previous games, or it may be entirely down to the smaller storage size of cartriges. Regardless I really don't mind. There's still variety, still quite a few interesting locations, and I don't see it as a big deal one way or the other...in fact I don't want Ubisoft to feel restricted in telling stories set in smaller towns or the like.

I first played this game on a PS3 I borrowed from a friend few years back. I didn't finish it and always regretted it. So when it came out on the PC - Yeah, I'm buying it.
It's a solid port. I've had not technical issues with it.
Biggest problem I have with the game is:
The clunky book/chapters out-of-combat interface remained unchanged. I didn't like it in the original game, and was disappointed to see it persist in the PC version.
Smaller issues that may stem from me being me, rather than the game being flawed:
Skirmish battles could have had been updated to feature some randomness in opponent behavior or placement. They tend to get boring immediately after the first time you play through them.
A faster way to get back into the game after failing a mission would've been good. I currently can't motivate myself to pick the game back up because the idea of failing and needing to repeat the mission(cut-scenes and all) mentally tires me.
And that's the basic way the game progresses after a point. You start a new mission with little to no idea what's going to happen or what you're facing. You fail, naturally. You load the save. Try again with the update to your strategy. And repeat the process until you beat the mission.
I'm just saying, the restarting process could've been faster.
That said.
The game is pretty cool. Turn-based squad battles that are affected by various quirks your soldiers have.
Speaking of soldiers, you don't get as attached to them as you could, if they were given a more robust progression system or more dialog lines, but you do tend to stick with a few favorites that seem to cooperate well.
The story is anime-ish. Take that as good or bad depending on your own opinion on anime/manga. With characters being pretty one-dimensional. But it does serve as a good motivator to keep pushing forward and seeing how it develops.
I do recommend this game for people that fit one or both of the following:
Like turn-based games.
Like anime/manga.

TL;DR - Watered down version of AC3 gameplay with a very shallow story which makes no sense.
The game tries to introduce a NEW exciting system of gameplay by breaking down the assassin persona from AC3 into three different personas: assassin, slave and upper class lady. Each persona should possess unique abilities, advantages and disadvantages, which makes one or the other better suited for certain missions, in theory. As cool as it sounds it just creates more problems in practice. The game basically punishes you for playing as an assassin (which IMHO can do any mission with ease) by adjusting your notoriety bar from basically anonymous to maximum notoriety. The whole notoriety system is a clusterf*ck. Enemies will only see you when you're basically in front of their nose but will also immediately forget about you when they turn around or you take a turn. Redefines the whole concept of "stealthy gameplay" by making you hide behind a f*cking lamp post in order to be invisible. The other two personas have mainly reduced abilities with a lower notoriety penalty.
Other than that, it features familiar aspects of AC games like a big weapon and equipment repertoire, a trading system to gain ridiculous amounts of money, pointless sidequests to unlock that one SPECIAL HAT or other wardrobe pieces, collecting neverending amounts of pages (WHICH ARE STATIONARY HERE, THANK GOD) and other useless trinkets which should expand on the actual story missions. The latter make up the story as much as a few bread crumbs make up an entire loaf of bread. You are left with countless open questions which are just ignored as the game restarts and you are allowed to freely go and collect those 3 crocodile eggs you skipped because what else is there to do.
This game comes with its own set of glitches and bugs, yay! You will see things like citizens floating off into air, gravestones and other random objects floating above ground, entire houses leaving gaping bottomless holes in the environment and of course endless exiting and restarting to get to get unstuck from somewhere because just F U.

Most unexpected fun you can ever have out of a shop-sim. Recettear is about management, of both time and resources, and it's good at that. It also has an overview-grid action RPG-mechanic that isn't as interesting and at times gets pretty tedious, but it's still head and shoulders above average.
The real draw here is the store. Not only is the shopkeeping gameplay plenty addictive for its beautiful aesthetics and atmosphere, but it's also very understanding about difficulty. Every time you happen to fail your quest to save your store from bankruptcy, you get to keep your experience points from the previous go and the next attempt will be a whole lot easier afterwards. You simply cannot fail if you just keep failing long enough, so experts will complete the game in one go, while beginners will slowly learn by getting stronger from failure. A very balanced system for all kinds.
Plenty of replayability if you know what's good for you. Capitalism, ho!

Ok so this is a weird one.
The game has a fun combat system that can take a little time to get your head around. The flashy attacks, and fluid sprite animations are a joy on the eyes. Despite the fact some attacks can take a silly amount of time to complete, you may just end up never skipping them because they are so over the top, they're fantastic. Japanese anime like attacks at their finest.
However everything else is just... meh. The characters are typical japanese anime tropes for the most part. There isn't anything wrong with this if they are done well, but I thought that only a few of them were entertaining to watch. The writing isn't too bad though and the japanese voice acting is above average. There is no english dub for the voices so if you don't care for reading subtitles this might irk you.
The story is also sort of nonsensical. Nobody ever questions some of the stuff going on. For example you proceed through generations of characters where the child of the previous protaginist will continue on 18 or 20 years in the future (I think its around that long...). So some characters pass away yet another character who should be dead somehow manages to stay alive and, no one seems to bat an eyelid about it, despite him being human. The reason why is given later but you'll have probably worked it out yourself way before this happens. And generally the plot towards the end gets so little explanation that the objective for their quest begins to become questionable. I won't spoil anything but I've read better stories out of a childrens book.
Also
Seriously there are minigames where you have to massage your female companions in order to improve affection, their stats, or technique points. And if you are going for a paticular ending this may be seen as mandatory, unless you want to spend hours grinding. The fanservice was toned down in this version though as it seems to be censored during some scenes and images/dialogue was removed or altered.
And you will grind in this game. Not for levels however, more for the comissions and materials to make better weapons. If you do purchase the game I'll give you a hint and say that the strength of your equipment if far more important than your levels, especially when you start reinforcing them.
So despite the fact I've put around 143 hours into the game I can't recommend it. I like it despite the negativity you might be seeing from this review but honestly you could put those hours into a game that is far better than just anm average game. Proceed with caution if you do decide to play it, and
for your own sake! Go for the true ending path (Might need a guide for this one.) The normal ending is a punch to the stomach after the time you put into it. Hope this review was helpful!

Super addictive, extremely fast-paced, challenging but learnable... I really don't know much of what's wrong with this game, besides some bearable (and fix-able) Early Access probs.
The matchmaking can be a bit doo-hicky somtimes. I was in the entry league still, and two of the other guys were entry and suddenly we get matched with an expert, so pretty much that match we were doomed to lose points. But hey, it's not really a huge problem, just occasionally annoying
The character select menu is odd, in the fact that you don't "select" a character, you mouse over one. If you are playing with a controller, and you hover over your character, then bump the mouse, if the mouse moved over a character, you're suddenly selecting that one. And sometimes then the match starts before you can correct it. But again, it's not a huge thing, just 1 out of thirty matches you're not the right character. It's certainly bearable
And finally, there are just gameplay bugs. Like, one out of every, maybe, 60 matches, the camera will bug out for everyone and go searching around the map, and everyone dies and someone randomly wins.
Every once in awhile an item will not activate, and sometimes it WILL activate, but won't work in some way or another
Now, on to the pros:
It's very, very fast paced. If you play too long you might even get a tiny bit shaky. BUT, it's not SO fast you can't keep up. You'll still be able to play with even the smallest amount of practice. And once you get into the swing of things, and get your grooves, you'll start to feel like you're flying
I kind of touched on this already, but I'll say it again. It's not hard to pick up, not hard to learn, and not hard with a bit of practice. I picked this game up and within twenty minutes I was doing pretty well, an hour later I was beating a good number of matches, four hours later I was doing just as well if not better than my competition, and now, ten hours in, I feel like a Speedrunning-god somtimes. And I'm only in the beginning league, which is the second tier.
The items are well balanced.
Missile: Sometimes devastating if it works, but it can be hard to work. But, not impossible
Boxes: Good to just add some more bits to the map, and if placed/dropped in just the right moment, can mean a win
Hook: Possibly the most devastating of the items, you hook on to the person nearest-in front of you. You pull forward,
and send them backwards. But, again, it's not OP. You CAN dodge it by sliding if you see it coming fast enough,
and it can hit walls and stop
Bomb: This one's hard to use, but in the right moment, can mean a win. You drop a bomb, and when you press the
button again, explode it. Sometimes you miss, and it does nothing, sometimes you hit, but it's only a temporary
setback for them. But other times, it lags them behind just enough for you to sprint forward and win
Drill: This one doesn't seem to be very common. But oh, is it nice. I think this one IS a little more OP, but it's not
perfect. Basically you start rushing forward a bit faster, and you're completely invincible. But then again, it only
lasts for a few seconds
Shockwaves: This basically sends out a circular wave out from you. It destroys any boxes in the immediate area, and
pushes enemies back a bit. Usually doesn't do too much, but if you and your enemy are swinging up
high, it can give them just enough of a push to fall, and possibly to their death
The Game "flows". Every action leads to the next, and you'll be swinging, then grappling on to someone to jump then quickly swing and jump again, to then boost to get a win. It's amazing how much you feel like you're flying sometimes.
The Characters are nice. I know this may be a bit weird, but seriously, thought and care went into those models, and it shows. They each move in almost unique ways, and they all look amazing doing it. Whenever Gil the Shark Man jumps, he dives back down. A few of the characters slide on their backs, some of the others their stomachs. One guy, "The Falcon", is a big chicken that flaps his little chicken arms when he jumps. It's just so fun to watch and control the characters.
So yeah, I think that's about it. I bought this game yesterday, and I already have ten hours. It's so, so good. I highly suggest. 9/10, just because of Early Access probs. But really, a tiny bit of polish and this game is perfect.

My exposure to the Agarest series has been quite long. In fact from the very first Generations of War, up until ZERO and now this. This installment was supposed to be the defining chapter for the series and to me, it fell quite short in very many ways. For every positive outlined below, there will almost certainly be an overbearing glaring negative.
To begin with the new animated character portraits during spoken dialogue mark a fascinating turn for the series going forward. This simple addition to the
provides some flair to the tedium of still having to read through text "visual-novel" style. Did I mention that despite the voice acting present, all voices are in the native Japanese? While not inherently bad as the voice actors are competent, expect a lengthy script with PLENTY of reading. As for the environments, well there's some variety and even change when it comes to battle transitions. Sadly there's still no environmental interaction to be had within battles
revolves around traversing a world map, transitioning to a battle screen, then taking part in grid-based turn-based combat featuring members of your party. In a marked departure from the earlier games, you don't position all your characters on the grid with a Move phase then Attack phase. Instead you can now determine formations prior to fights, obtain stat bonuses per formation then switch leaders around to change the formations (hence bonus) mid-fight. Since there is no separate move phase you get into formation and then press one of 4 Face buttons onscreen to perform attack types such as Launch and Stun etc. Since this system has become combo based in order to maintain high damage strings it's become a case of button-mashing with minimal strategy involved. And since the battles are RANDOM in nature......... Now, levelling up. This title has THREE separate level up variants consisting of "Technical Points" (for moves), "Party Points" (ability points shared out within the party) and "Control Points" (enabling you to SET moves in your character's repertoire including combinations). As you can imagine, juggling all these is complicated and tedious at best.
The
...... is quite atrocious really. On top of the usual kill the demon and marry one heroine per generation (max out at 3), motives for doing what is needed are pretty much non-existent. Add to this the lack of any sort of intrigue (the light political intrigue of the earlier Agarest wasn't bad) and you end up with an unnecessarily lengthy tale whose characters fit set cliched molds.... At least the music especially in special boss dungeons is great. Don't let me even get started on how long it will take before you start fighting the heavy hitters with their loads of three-tier experience points.
So, should you buy this game? Proceed with caution if you must, but if you are prepared for a LARGE chunk of your time being eaten up by a mediocre tale, then be my guest. Get it on a sale. A significant sale..... Ahhh yes. There's plenty of DLC offering weaponry, add-on dungeons, smithing loot and experience points for the spikes in difficulty. Which brings me to another demerit. Every single piece of DLC for this game is just pricey... Why would I have to PAY for stuff that should be ingame and unlocked especially if you meet special battle conditions/story conditions?
You've been warned.

So far, a really great Beta. Certainly one of the better Early Access titles that I've played in terms of content and completed gameplay.
In the game, you play as a pawn in a dealer's game. You have a choice to move between cards and randomly attack enemies, complete tasks (the success of which depends on your draw), visit shops, and gain equipment. The gameplay is less card game (which I think people might surmise from the title) and more of a 3rd person action game with "Chance" components.
The graphics are well-suited to the game and have good art direction. The voice-overs (when present) are good and add to the atmosphere.
The only (exceptionally mild) complaint I have is that the controls seem somewhat "floaty" at times. More along the lines of "Fable" or "Kingdoms of Amalur". It tends to snap to enemies in a slow way, and as such combat seems as though it's in slow-motion. This is a matter of personal preference and really doesn't detract from an otherwise wonderful game.
As a recommendation to the developers, it would be nice also to hit enemies on the ground. In my playtime it didn't appear this was possible, which seems off given that enemies spend a lot of time knocked down. I don't know if this is meant to keep fights more balanced, but it's a mechanic that I think would help speed up combat without lowering health or boosting character stats.
Great game, and I'm glad to see it's shaping up so nicely!

The controversy with EA and Mass Effect 3 being an Origin exclusive when that program was getting considerable bad press for spyware and peeking into people's computers remains a bitter memory for me. It went from my #1 wishlist item to becoming the first and most trying test of my resolve to never buy anything from EA again. I still have never played Mass Effect 3 because of it, and might not ever because of other issues that that game had. Though... not having played that allowed me to be insulated from ME3's ending, which♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥a huge number of fans of this series off enough that it led to Bioware redoing the ending (a bit).
What does all this have to do with my opinion on ME2 do you ask? Well, it's important because it points out that I ended the series with ME2, and therefore cannot make a review of this game in context as the middle part of a trilogy, but just as the second chapter to a story that I may never finish. So how is it? Well, "#1 wishlist item" might have tipped you off to this: it is one of the best games I have ever played. Which is why that ME3 stuff bit as hard as it did for me.
It is true that this game is considerably different from ME1 in its gameplay, and some don't like the loss of some "traditional" RPG elements that resulted from that. But it wasn't a real problem for me because it also got rid of much of what was wrong with ME1 and replaced it with a more solid game attached to the quality storytelling that the first game had. If there's anything bad i'd have to say about the gameplay, it's this: it plays much more like a shooter than an RPG in combat (which can be exhausting for a game this long), and whoever thought that planet scanning stuff would be fun needs to have their head examined. Preferrably with a sledgehammer. Oh and a note about how Paragon and Renegade are lame and limiting on your ability to roleplay stuff (kinda did in the first game too, but not as much).
But that's it. The gameplay is solid, reasonably difficult at times, and, if you imported your save from ME1 (which you did because continuation of your specific storyline is a major selling point of this series), it makes for a great storytelling experience. This game is a smaller, more personal, story than ME1, which leads to considerable investment into the characters in your party. It's a mix of excellent characters, with a few notable standouts that probably are obvious due to their huge fanbases.
And the answer to the question that just popped in your head is no. I never romanced Tali despite her being one of my favorite characters. I never played a male Shepard beyond the intro level of ME1. Come to think of it, I never romanced my favorite character (Garrus) either.
And it is this focus on characters that makes the final mission of this game all the more affecting. At least the first time you play it and/or if you don't just grab a guide. Seriously, for your first go at the final mission, or really this whole game in general, don't read a guide. It will ruin it for you. And if you play it without knowing what's coming like I did, then you are likely in for one of the darkest and tragic final missions of any game out there when those party members you have spent dozens of hours getting to know and like start dying like flies. It makes the term "suicide mission" much more impactful if you go in with nine party members and walk away with only two and feeling lucky for that.
And that's all i'll say about the gameplay. I think this is a great game, and even my sour feelings about ME3's various controversies did not dampen that opinion. Still, I would only play this if you went through ME1 first, because importing saves is cool. Whether or not you want to continue beyond this into ME3 depends on how high your tolerance for EA's BS is. Mine, sadly, is nonexistent.
Have fun. :)

After having lost a few weeks of sleep to Agarest: Zero, I was eagerly awaiting Agarest 2. Infact when I saw it release at about 4am on steam finally, I could not have clicked the "Buy" button any harder. And for sure a lot has changed in the third game. Now that I found time to actively play through it thoroughly, figured a review wouldn't hurt.
Overall, it's very fun. There are many, mostly positive changes to the series compared to the previous game, Agarest Zero.
Story:
If you're able to immerse into a game's plot or story, you'll enjoy Agarest 2 or any Agarest game. But whether you're a returning fan or new to the series, be warned that Agarest 2's story is far darker, cuder, and more of a "grim reality" compared to previous games. However, just like in-game, there's always light in the dark. You'll end up appreciating the happy moments all the more. Just don't go into it expecting child-friendly content. Just like in a good anime, there will be swearing, inneundos, and action a-plenty. Not for the easily-offended or too-uptight.
(Personally, I loved Gen2. The character developement and characters overall were by far my favorite by the end.)
Combat & In-game features:
As opposed to previous entries where you would move your party around a board, then initiate attacks in turn order, Agarest 2 tried, and very well succeeds in changing the combat pace of the Agarest series. You no longer move around a board, rather you sit on "your side" and launchs attacks at enemies, which can move you out of formation or into enemy territory. And rather than picking a bunch of commands, you now input the attacks as they happen. While it will seem basic at first, eventually with practice you'll be chaining many different combo and group attacks in one long chain (and as a bonus, the bigger you combo chain, the more damage per-hit you deal for that chain).
A few things were blundered with though. Firstly, navigation and finding events or even the main quest can be extremely irritating. You have no markers on the minimap, no arrow, no way to re-read the last event to see where you're meant to go, so if you stop playing the game for awhile and can't remember or did not write it down, you may spend a lot of time searching for it. And in the same suit, the game will often unlock 'optional' event fights or mini-bosses you can find around the maps when you complete Commissions, but it tends to be cryptic in that fact. I was nearly done with Gen1 before I even realized some of these events were actually spawning event-monsters.
Balance:
I remember one fight in Agarest Zero's 2nd Gen, that I shamefully admit was a brick wall, I could not beat it until I caved in and purchased the best weapon DLC pack they had. However, I've yet to encounter such a "great wall of china" difficulty spike in Agarest 2 (I tribute this partially to the new combat system, when learned it can be heavily abused in your favor).
The temptation of DLC will always exist, and there are times when it does seem like it'd be a good idea to spend $5~$10 on a pack, purely for the sake of breezing through. I haven't needed to do so, but if you really like the game and are having trouble or don't want to spend a fair amount of time farming/upgrading, pick up any of the packs when they go on sale, even just 1 can make all the difference. But unlike previous games, some insanely powerful gear can be obtained early on with some time investment. But whichever is your personal preference, either route is enjoyable.
Customizing & Chars:
As usual in an Agarest game, there's a healthy and entertaining cast of chars you'll have throughout the game. And while they all come leaned towards one playstyle or another, the amount of customizing in terms of skills and stats you can do with them is rather interesting. Which is nice considering Agarest: Zero was rather restrictive in that sense.
(I do miss the dynamic changing outfits based on their affections from Zero though).
Overall it's a great addition to the series, as well as a good game for anyone new to the series, great game series overall, you'll spend a good amount of enjoyable time in any Agarest game really. But I will re-iterate that of the series, 2 is the darker of the games (not a bad thing, if you're more of a fan of the more serious stories. If you're more into light-hearted, I recommend Agarest Zero as your starting point)

First concern people have with a game in Alpha is: "Is it playable or am I buying a broken mess?" Hand of Fate is absolutely in working condition. You may encounter a bug here or there, but I just beat the alpha version of the game yesterday - or at least all 12 current encounters.
So what kind of game is it? It's a mixture of board game that you can customize + real time action brawler (like the arkham series) wrapped in a rogue-like shell. It's fun to engage on a strategic level when dealing with card choices and then on a visceral level when fighting monsters, you're learning two different aspects as you go. Also, if you enjoy punishing games like Demon's/Dark Souls then this game would be something to think about.
Devs are also active in the forums and are releasing updates so not only do you get a game to play, you also get a game that the devs care about making better.
All in all, highly recommended.

What does it feel like to be staring down at your own dead body, lying helplessly in the street? To see police agents discussing what might have happened to you, without being able to tell them? The first thing you might notice is that being a ghost actually renders you painfully limited in your ability to interact with the world. Thankfully, there are advantages as well. And, as you will soon discover - what you can't do, someone else might be willing to do for you.
I imagine some people are holding off on buying this game due to the moderate-to-bad reviews it has received. I'd like to argue differently. It is by no means perfect - I ran into a few bugs and the game even crashed on me in the final chapter. I was also not happy about not being able to change the key bindings. But the story and its two main characters made it easy to overlook these issues. A unique idea for a video game - not perfectly executed, but more than well enough to warrant a playthrough.

I've played this game twice in the past couple weeks, so I'd say a game that has stuck with me like that already deserves a thumbs up. But lets look into why...
First up you're going to get around 8 hours in a single playthrough, although you can take that up to 16 since you will want to at least play it twice for all the endings and decisions, and on top of that you may want to do more playthroughs for ranger hardcore and the spartan and survival modes. If that's not enough there are additional missions that are great for practice, or giving context to parts of the story that were not so well flushed out.
You could probably get just about 30 hours out of this game before exhausting it all.
Story, it's easy enough to follow although you will want to play 2033 first in order to understand who specific characters are as a lot of returning characters play major parts in the story, best do your homework on that.
There is a lot of tension in the story, very likeable characters that face a lot of ugly situations in a world without mercy.
Environment is outstanding, intense levels of detail are poured into this game indoors and outdoors, home stations look like people live there, it is easy to get sucked into this world as the voice actors, animations, models, facial animation and lighting do wonders to getting you immersed.
the game has multiple ways to be played, a lot of areas can be completed without firing a shot, taking a life or disturbing the enemies entirely. Passive runs are not possible however as some areas will demand you defend yourself in some capacity, although this typically only applies to mutants for most situations, although the story will force blood to be spilt.
There is a moral system, technically, and it is not fun. If you plan to get the best ending then you need to get nearly every moral point, and these points are distributed without making sense, explain to me how you are a better person for finding a old ammo stache, or looting the corpse of a long dead stalker? Keep a guide with you at all times if that's the run you're going for, although don't bother on the first playthrough.
TL:DR - A great game with a lot of replay value that is only held back by a poorly executed and explained moral system which locks away the cannon ending to the game.

Had a blast on EA, impatiently awaiting download of full game. If you love RPG's you will love this. Miles better than the first- and that was pretty good as well. More choices, more decisions, and if you don't like someone, you can always eat them. Eat them! Mmmm brains...
Edit: Having now finished the game with a couple of play-throughs, I have to admit to being somewhat let down by the finished product. I was eagerly looking forward to playing with some of the things I loved in the first, that were lacking in EA. I thought their omission was due to it still being in EA... alas it wasn't... So if you loved the crafting in the first, well, forget about it for DOS2, it basically dosen't exist.
CRAFTING: Forget about it, it doesn't really exist and what there is, is almost negligible in it's use unless you are playing hardcore- and very few gamers do. You can make a few potions, but why bother when there is no need and what you might potion up is better dealt with by a cast spell.
ARMOUR: Like crafting, they have taken one of the pleasures of the first and ruined it to such an extent, that what little crafting ability they allow you to play with, is almost totally useless, and a complete and utter waste of time. In the first, you could get a semi decent piece of armour, and mod it to your characters ability and it would be with that character for a large chunk of the game. Now, it's with your character for one character level - two if you bother to mod it - and then it's useless and sold. Larian have managed - very successfully -  to make Legendary and Epic armour anything but. And that is no mean feat. Seriously, you won't keep Epic/Legendary/Supermarket-own-brand armour much more than two of the characters levels, as by that point it's quite simply, crap and very un-Epic in stats.
And that leads to the next bug-bear. Because of the rubbishness of armour, you spend less time exploring the wild as an adventurer of (dubious) repute and more time as a shopper of armour, sick in the knowledge that in 2 levels time, you are going to have to repeat the whole tedious process all over again...
WEAPONS: Pretty much the same as ARMOUR; Buy some glitzy cutlery, level up twice, sell old cutlery, buy some new, rinse repeat. It gets tedious quick. Real quick.
GRAPHICS: It looks nice, yes, I will give it that.
ENVIROMENTAL EFFECTS: Yes, wonderful, have a pat on the back, but after a few hours playing, you tend to ignore most of it except for Boss fights. (That was on normal difficulty-it becomes more of a requirement for the harder play throughs, but again, that's only going to be an issue for a (very) small number of players.)
STORYLINE: It was alright, nothing to write home about and pretty much standard fare for this genre of game. Larian have tried to throw in some curve balls to increase the re-playability of the game, which was nice, but looking at Steam Achievements for the game, a quarter of players haven't even made it past the first chapter yet, and to be honest, I don't see that score getting much better in the future. So all that effort to make the game replayable when finished, could have been spent better elsewhere... Like on bug testing for a start. Gosh, there was an astounding amount of bugs, many of them game/quest breaking.
OVERALL: The game was alright, but the problems with the lifespan of armour and weapons quickly meant the game became less DOS2 and more Divinity-mad-dash-around-map-for-shopkeepers-to-up-grade-rubbish-equipment, or" Divinity Original Shopping Trip 2" for short. Yes graphics are good, environmental effects have been made more effective, if you can be bothered to use them and a lot of effort has been spent on the ending scenes for the 48 people that will finish the game.
Not played a DOS game and thinking of grabbing a spell book and jumping in? Then buy DOS1 instead. It's more rewarding, most of the bugs have been squashed, it's cheaper and hasn't been dumbed down for console players like this one has. I had high hopes for this game, enough to buy it months before release, but would I do so for DOS3? No. Not if this is the direction Larian are going in.

First off, this might sound a bit biased. That's because it absolutely is.
I grew up playing this game on my old Xbox. My mom would tell me "[redacted], you can play this game, but only if you're a good guy". I would run around, only killing evil things, eventually becoming a shining beacon of happiness and hope throughout Albion.
Then I turned 10. Things got a bit crazy. May or may not have "accidently" slaughtered a couple villages and grew a set of horns.
Anyway.
That was in the past.
I hadn't played this game in at least 7 years (which is crazy to think about) and for some reason, never checked on Steam for it. When I saw it at the Summer Sale, I froze. Oh my god. It's my game.
I picked it up without thinking about it, and am 100% happy with my decision.
The game is great. The voice acting is horrible. The faces and lip movements are really bad. The Guildmaster is annoying as hell. But the game is a rare gem from the past that I don't think anyone should miss playing.
This is the Lost Chapters. It adds much, much more to the base game. It no longer ends when you beat the main villain the first time. Instead, you find yourself with another HALF A GAME to go. More weapons, more enemies, more armor, more quests, and more fun.
It also runs really, really well on my laptop. I still haven't felt it get hot, even after a 5-hour gaming session. Camera is a bit wonky, and I had to rebind a few keys (who would want to block with the middle mouse?). Once I got used to it, I've done very well with it.
One thing I love about this game, is that it can give you a sense of being overpowered, but only if you play it well. If you mess up, you can easily be overwhelmed by enemies and lose half your health. Play it right, and the only damage you'll take is from a few stray crossbow bolts.
If you like rpg games, this game is one of the best out there, even today. I highly, highly, highly recommend getting it and trying it out. After you endure the first hour or so of not-so-great "gameplay", you'll come to love this game as much as I do.
Well, not as much.
Not nearly.

Roughly 5-6 hours in and I'm having fun exploring, dying to wild beasts and struggling against savage african tribesmen. Haven't experienced any technical issues yet and loading screens are quite fast (most settings on ultra with a decent PC).
That said, there's not super much content currently in the game. Just looking at the amount of craftable stuff the list isn't super long, and environment interaction seems a bit limited (ie. not enough unique stuff like loot chests, unique loot, caves, bosses etc). But this is to expected since it was just released into Early Access.
The biggest problem right now is to fix animations and make combat enjoyable. There's also apparently some rubberbanding going on for players who play on large servers with high population.
All in all this game has great potential and I do recommend it for anyone who enjoys the world of Robert E Howard and has read the books like I have. The music is pretty good too! A big plus to them reusing some assets from Age of Conan as that game had a lot of good stuff.
Just don't expect a full fledged game for obvious reasons. But if you don't experience any technical issues like me, you should easily get at least a dozen hours of fun before the content starts to run out.
Let's hope Funcom patches often and adds more content for our enjoyment!

This is a short AC game (For me, it took about 18 hours). That said, what it does is done well.
It is much more stealth focused than the other AC games and has less attention towards combat. This is largely done through the persona system, essentially three identities to build and reduce notoriety on. While recruitment of assassins is done away with, I personally didn't notice the absence of it. The engine feels like that of AC:3, allowing for climbing of trees and less micromanagement. However, on PC it runs much better. Honestly, I feel like this is the kind of game that the creators of AC:3 wanted to make, but failed to produce. The fast travel is limited, with single-destination portals at the edges of the map, to the three locations in the game: the bayou, New Orleans, and Chichen Itza. As always, there are collectibles and side-quests, although the side-quests are slightly lacking. There is little coverage of the "present-day" story.
The narrative was well done. There's a good connection between the mechanics and the story. AC:Liberation goes over topics like racism and slavery, and the roles of women in the 18th century, but not overtly. None of the characters feel like charicatures or two-dimensional. It's a decent introduction to the AC genre, but I'd definitely reccommend AC:2 or AC:4 over this for that purpose.

There are a lot of things I like about this AC. For one, the protagonist, who actually realizes that running around in a white hood isn't very subtle for an assassin. I think the persona mechanic (basically disguises) was a really intriguing idea, but its actual implementation falls flat. Certain personas are a requirement rather than a choice for each mission. I thought it would have been great if you could play through the entire game with any one of them.
Sadly, the characters, story, and setting are all held back by the game's (former) mobile limitations. There is practically nothing to be done outside the story except for finding collectibles. While there are a handful of side quests, none of them contain cutscenes or even voice acting. A typical story mission takes probably less than 10 minutes to complete and they are often very linear. I also noted that it's practically impossible to die in this game, it's simply too easy. There's even a feature that lets you automatically kill multiple enemies just by pausing the game for a moment.
I would have loved this game if it had been made with actual gaming consoles in mind but sadly it remains a half-baked mobile spinoff.

This is a difficult game to write about.  What it does, it does very well for the most part.  It's just that "what it does" may not appeal to a broad audience.  This Agarest game has the sort of epic, sweeping plot we expect from JRPGs, complete with deicide, ancient mysteries, untapped powers, and (of course) amnesia.  The amnesia on the part of the rather unlikable protagonist makes it easy for a player to jump in even if they have not played Agarest 1 or Zero.  The characters are much more central to the movement of the game than the epic plot tropes are.  There are many characters, each with distinct, well-written and fleshed-out personalities and motives.  Each has a role to play and the player has some minor control over the direction that role takes.
So what is the actual gameplay like?  There are two basic types of gameplay in Agarest 2: tactical battle and visual novel.  The visual novel portions, though very well-written, are long and unavoidable.  The choices you make in these sections affect the love characters feel for the protagonist- because like any good visual novel, these sections ultimately amount to a dating sim, in this case spanning three generations of characters.  The tactical battles are curious.  If you are expecting something in the vein of Final Fantasy Tactics look elsewhere.  The grids on which the battles take place determine the viability of your various combos and is not a field you can manually move around.  What's more, the combos in question are executed arcade style- I found myself mashing buttons maniacally to maximize damage.
If these types of battles don't appeal to you, be wary.  Agarest is a grind, a very serious grind.   The vast majority of game time is spent fighting battles again and again and again.  I find them to be pretty fun battles, but after a while I find myself throwing on Netflix while I absently mash through battles to fulfill my goals.  The battles become more fun once you unlock all the various character customization options, but just getting there takes a good five hours of grinding.
Which brings me to the last point I want to be sure to mention.  I found the text-based in-menu tutorials on how to use the various systems so confusing that I actually understood less after reading them.  I learned how the systems worked through trial and error.  I'm not sure how much of this is due to obtuse writing and how much is due to ADD.  The menu pages are ornately decorated to the point of gaudy opulence.  These decorations add nothing to the information and for me, someone who struggles with ADD, I found them incredibly disruptive.  I know others out there have the same struggle, so prepare yourself if you do.  For those who don't struggle in this manner, enjoy the gorgeous menus.
6.5/10 Recommended to fans of visual novels and folks who play JRPGs for the plot and don't mind a good long grind.

People may call this game "Pay to Win", and I tell you now. It. Is. Not.
Nothing in this game says that you *have* to buy things. And even then, you don't win if you buy stuff, you just get some more skills, which can be done via quests, quick ways to get Job Change, which is more worth it than you think, more items, EXP boosts, and a couple other things. It doesn't make you win. It just makes the game *slightly* easier.
Now, I say this game is great, if they polish out a few things, this game could easily be the best game i've played. Please, don't knock this game by reviews of people saying "Pay to win", cause it's a lie.

First concern people have with a game in Alpha is: "Is it playable or am I buying a broken mess?" Hand of Fate is absolutely in working condition. You may encounter a bug here or there, but I just beat the alpha version of the game yesterday - or at least all 12 current encounters.
So what kind of game is it? It's a mixture of board game that you can customize + real time action brawler (like the arkham series) wrapped in a rogue-like shell. It's fun to engage on a strategic level when dealing with card choices and then on a visceral level when fighting monsters, you're learning two different aspects as you go. Also, if you enjoy punishing games like Demon's/Dark Souls then this game would be something to think about.
Devs are also active in the forums and are releasing updates so not only do you get a game to play, you also get a game that the devs care about making better.
All in all, highly recommended.

Agarest 2 is the third installement of the agarest series and for me, it was the first agarest I had played.
The game could be best described as visual novel with strong and stratetic gameplay elements. It should be noted that you can easily sink a lot of time into this game, once you understood the gameplay machanics. If you are searching for some quick fun and a easy-to-understand-gameplay, you may be better off with another game.
Story: 6.5
Characters: 5.0
Gameplay: 9.0
Sound/Voices: 6.0
Story
To keep it short: There is probalbly not much in here, you haven´t seen somewhere else allready. The story is nice but ovarall pretty predictable. You have to become a vessel for a new god while fighting of demons. These two things are what keeps the story going. To be absolutly honest, I found myself skipping through the story in the later parts. It just didn´t catch me. Regardless, I can see that the developers really tried and at time I liked what they presented. So I give a 6.5 for the story.
Characters
Maybe I will receive alot of hate for saying this, but the characters where the main point which almost made me drop this game. Firstly I want to make a general statement in terms to character presentation. I found it really hard to take any of them serious. Why? Because of the *breast bouncing* thing.
Conversations with the heroins normally go as follows:
"We have a very serious discussion about the future of this world" *breast bouncing*
"Your deeds where a terrible mistake" *breast bouncing*
"You have to make up for your errors" *breast bouncing*
"..." *breast bouncing*
While I do like breasts, this was totally ridiculous. I was irritated by it the whole time and can only assume the developers did this to make the heroins appear more attraktiv. Which in my oppinion absolutely failed.
As this section is allready pretty big, I will keep things a little bit shorter as I originally had planed. There where a few characters I liked but the main problem is that there where to many that ranged from "I don´t care about you" to "Please shut up...seriously just shut up". The Fiona-girl got especially on my nerves and the third generation MC made me start the whole game all over again to get a second-generation MC I could use further in battles, as I my first thought after a battle with the third gen MC was...ugh nope...
Some people mentioned that they didn´t like the sec gen MC. In my opinion he was the most human of the three MCs and the one I liked the most too. To keep things fair I also have to say that I really liked the more mature Fiona of the third gen. Nonetheless, I can only give a 5.0 for the characters in this game.
Gameplay
This is where the game really shines. I have to admit, it almost took me 20 hours of gameplay-time to understand the battle and character system. The tutorial really doesn´t help much and I really had to google many things. If you are into these kind of complex things (as I am), you are rewarded with some of the best combat and character system I have seen in a long time. The system is complex without giving the impression of anything in it to be unnecessary. You have to micro-manage many things to build a powerfull party. I really liked that. I give a 9.0 for the system while reducing a point for the fact that you have to google even the tiniest bit of information. That includes the lack of quest markers and others things that would really had made your life so much easier.
Sound/Voices
The soundtrack of agarest 2 is decent. There are some tracks, especially the battlethemes, that are really nice. The voicecast is done nicely too, but then again I have to admit that I had to turn it of because some characters drove my blood pressure into higher grounds (Oh just shut up Fiona!! I don´t care if you got a level up). I give this section a 6.0 while reducing a point for the need to turn the voices of.
Conclusion
Agarest 2 is a nice game in which you really can sink your time into. Sadly the Story and Characters aren´t as strong as the gameplay. I would still recomend this game as something you can enjoy while ignoring the story, as it offers lots of challenging fights with the possibility to customise your character alot.
If you are looking for something that has a strong story and good characters try "G-senjou no Maou" (Yeah, it has sex in it, but as I said, I like breasts).
If you are looking for something that is easy to get into, try Final Fantasy 14: A Realm Reborn.

If you try to avoid damage, cover, take advantage of all your soldiers, ambush the enemy or anything of the sorts you'll be rewarded less xp. That's it.
Eventually I suppose you'll be forced to balance this frantic speed run with minimal survivability, but nevertheless it is a game about warfare and strategy that plays like kindergarten simulator.

I'm checking "no" because this game MUST NOT BE PURCHASED AT FULL PRICE. wait for a discount like i did, because this game is just a glitch fest.
now, let's go over the positive things that this game has:
+great atmosphere, great story and good graphics
+fight scenes are both awesom and tedious (more on that later)
+the linearity isn't an issue, it's a game based on a book about a post apocalyptic future, so the lack of exploring is excusable
+even though it lacks a save feature and relies on checkpoints, those are plenty, hard to miss (the icon pops up in the botton left corner, a place where you are constantly looking because it also features your "visibility gem" and the minutes of air you have left with a gas mask) and the levels aren't that long either.
+the double endings are quite nice
unfortunately, it has a couple major problems, one of which is, sadly, game breking.
-sometimes, for no good reason, the enemy will see you because he will shine his flashlight THROUGH a wall, or he will just hear a comrade getting killed with a silent weapon even if you tryed the level 4 times before and all of those times nobody noticed that.
-Hit detection is totally ♥♥♥♥ed up, you can aim at someone's torso, shoot an arrow or a throwing knife at him and it will go through him, MISS HIM and alert everyone of your presence. and, no, i didn't miss anyone when this happened. one time this happened to the last enemy in a room so i didn't have to restart the checkpoint, after he went down i saw the throwing knife stuck in the wall where the enemy torso should have been, so it genuinely passed through him.
-and the game breaking glitch is....in the last level. you have to fight some dudes and if you die, it's all fine. the problem comes when a tank arrives, if you die at ANY POINT AFTER THE TANK APPEARS your game will crash without warning upon clicking "load last checpoints", so basically you have to do an entire level of precise shooting where sometimes the hits don't register WITHOUT DYING
so, yeah. don't get this game at full price, i got both 2033 redux and last light redux for 7 euros in a boundle and, barring the last level, it was a fun, albeit frustrating, experience.

Conan Exiles
First off; this game came out on the 30'th of January - just over a week ago. It's gotten plenty of negatives reviews even though it's in EA and has literally only been out for just over a week.
That said...
In my experience this game has been great so far. There is some truth to a lot of the negative reviews when it comes to lag. New servers don't seem to lag at all - for me at least. However, when it gets closer to 30+ people and people building structures and leaving it seems to clutter up and start to get a bit jumpy. I haven't experienced such ridiculous lag that it's unplayable as most of these negatives reviews seem to say. I'm running the game on an i7 4790k / 970 / 16GB ram and I've had barely any issues apart from slight rubberbanding at high populations.
1) So far I've experienced a great community (I play on RP/PVP servers) - There's a selection to the type of community you want to play with which is very unique and a welcome addition to the server selection menu.
2) Similar to Ark, the crafting system is intuitive and if playing on slower settings you'll find yourself immersed for long gaming sessions. It is immersive enough to generally always be doing something such as collecting ores, leather, or even chopping up human corpses for rituals to whatever Gods you serve.
3) The leveling system is in combination with the crafting system, which makes it give you the urgency to want to and have to level before being able to unlock more effective equipment. Even at this stage of EA there's quite a lot to do - even if it feels a bit grindy at times, you always feel like you're making progress towards something.
4) The environment... Sandstorms are quite awesome to experience. Footprints in the sand, and ruins of a past civilization are all a sight. I quickly became immersed in the environment after finding journals that give some light to the story, caves filled with exiles and random small bonfires with NPCs.
EDIT: 5) Thralls. Thralls are a great addition to this game. You can bash an NPC over the head with a Truncheon, knocking them out, and drag them back to the wheel of pain to break their spirits having them join your cause. You can outfit your base with Thrall archers to defend it while you're offline. Have Dancers, Fighters, Blacksmiths, Carpenters, Armorsmiths - which all benefit you in different ways. I look forward to this feature becoming more refined.
6) Building. The building is pretty great. I've seen some amazing structures and the amount you can do with the more simpler buildings, like Sandstone which happens to also be quite easy to make, are quite awesome. Building around hills/mountains using stairs. Player buildings quickly become something that seems visually possible and immersive - apart from the occassional completely ridiculous building.
Ultimately, the game has a lot to do. If you're willing to take the game for what it is - an EA title in a vast wasteland - you'll probably enjoy it a lot more than a lot of the negative reviewers. If you want to enjoy the game but can't stand the lag enjoy SINGLE PLAYER with your selection of preferred MODS. At least until the memory problem with the online gets fixed and makes it more playable for the people experienced rubberbanding issues.

I love the game.  I recommend it, with some caveats and observations:
1. This is essentially a reskinned Euro Truck Simulator 2 in terms of gameplay.  There are some tweaks minor new additions (most notably, the optional trailer parking 'minigame'), but if you don't like playing ETS2, you're probably not going to like playing ATS.
2. The current sandbox area of ATS is small, relative to ETS2.  To my mind, this is not unreasonable, because A) ETS2 had a great deal of its content offered well after its release, and there's every indication that this will be the case for ATS; and B) ...
3. While primarily a reskin of ETS2, ATS's assets are extremely detailed and do a wonderful job of distinguishing ATS from ETS2.  The setting has a definite American feel, and the surroundings do a much better job of feeling like a lived in world.
If you like ETS2, this is a no-brainer.  If you haven't played ETS2, I'd recommend watching some YouTube gameplay examples before buying.  If you're scratching your head after watching, trying to figure out what could possibly be enjoyable about hauling cargo in a truck, this may not be the game for you.

NOTE: expect the usual AC-Ubisoft BS, if you can't handle that, DO NOT SPEND YOUR MONEY ON THIS GAME
Game Mechanics:
It's an Assassin's Creed game, it's got every game mechanics you've gotten used to in the previous ones. It does add a little variety by allowing you to switch between 3 different personas (with no real use except for persona-specific missions and collectibles), each with a slightly tweaked playstyle. On top of that it adds the exotic, game-breaking sport of land swimming; the comic relief of twitchy corpse physics; the inscrutable delights of broken cinematics; disappearing character models; the rushing sensation fo falling through the world; inescapable canoes; the return of jerky and wonky tree-based freerunning; and instant-death, nearly-impossible to predict alligator attacks in the water.
Plot:
The plot is pretty decent, mostly because I tend to forget what the hell is actually going on after doing all the available side stuff (which for some reason doesn't always register for your achievements by the way). There's a half-decent twist at the end, so long as you don't read the massive spoiler you get by reading the redacted Database entries after doing some Citizen E-missions (seriously, didn't ANYONE catch that during development?).
Presentation:
I've fallen through the world only once, but regularly found myself climbing vertically up 45 degree angle slopes; seen people move in an escalator-like trajectory through thin air; witnessed rats scurry off several meters above the water as if they had mini-jetpacks; had to restart the game a couple of times because my character decided it was still swimming, even though I'd left the water for 30 seconds; so yeah, it's usual Assassin's Creed Ubisoft ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Disregarding that most of the alternate outfits are just recolours, though the unlockable Assassin costume is pretty cool (but completely wrecks any and all cut-scenes in which you wear it).
Completion:
The completion is pretty alright for this game, just collect the McGuffins (mushrooms, coins, brooches, voodoo dolls and more!) and follow the set guidelines for full synch. Then if you're lucky maybe the game won't bug out (like it did for me when clearing out the enemy camps in the bayou) or fail to register the missions you've done (like my Free Slaves and Ship Crew ones).
