If somebody asked me to describe Murdered: Soul Suspect in one word, I would say: Unfinished.
It's evident from the start that this game was rushed out the door too early in order to meet a deadline. Many things that you'd expect from a modern, full-priced AAA game are not present here. I knew something was up even before I jumped into the actual game. The menu was just a static image. There were no flashy effects when you highlighted any of the options. No bells and whistles whatsoever. Of course, none of that is actually necessary, but it is odd to see a big-budget game cut corners like that.
Unfortunately, this was just the tip of the iceberg.
After the game's opening cutscene, you're immediately tasked with investigating a crime scene. Games like Ace Attorney and L.A. Noire have already demonstrated excellent examples of how to simulate actual detective work, so it's pretty baffling to me that Murdered: Soul Suspect would take the most basic, and un-intuitive route possible.
You point. You click. You win.
There's almost zero deductive reasoning involved in investigating these crime scenes. Gathering evidence presents no challenge, since the "clues" are ridiculously easy to spot in the environment. It's depressing that the biggest problem I ran into when solving the mystery behind these crime scenes was my tendency to overthink them. Turns out, the most obvious solution is ALWAYS the right one. Once you figure that out, the rest of the game is a cakewalk.
So what else is there? Well, your ghostly character can possess people. This is a great idea on paper, but your enthusiasm will quickly wane once you realize that you can't actually control your posessee's. However, you can read their minds. Better than nothing, I suppose, but you'll be in for a rude awakening once you find that NPCs in the town only have a handful of phrases to recite, none of which are actually relevant to the investigation at hand. What could've been an excellent and inventive way to acquire information about the details of your case is squandered by the complete ineptitude of the developers.
Soul Suspect isn't entirely without merit though. The story held my attention for the duration of the game, and even though the characters are archetypes that we've already seen before from the detective/mystery genre, it still managed to be a moderately intriguing tale. The pay-off is also decent, with a twist ending that even M. Night Shyamalan would be proud of.
What saddens me the most is that Murdered: Soul Suspect is a very solid idea, and it could've easily been a great game with a little more TLC. It's painful to see a game with this much wasted potential. I liked the ideas here, but the execution left a lot to be desired. I'd love to see a sequel to this game where these ideas are more expanded upon, but as it stands, Murdered: Soul Suspect is half-baked, and it shows.

Welcome to Assassin's Creed: Liberation, where the Templars have become a mere afterthought to the much more looming threat: game controls. The developers clearly wanted to break the mold of tight, fluid game controls and go in the polar opposite direction with design. Every spare moment between cut scenes and dialog is dedicated to combating Aveline's sense of direction and agility. Want to chase someone on the ground? Good luck not jumping into a tree 90 degrees from the angle you're trying to run. Want to race someone across the rooftops? "Are you sure you didn't want to fall into a crowd of guards on the ground while making a simple, obvious, short-distance leap?" asks the game, then takes its own advice with your character. And hey, that combat system, right? Most people would think improving the notoriously quirky combat system is the right direction for development, but Ubisoft is obviously thinking on a whole different level and decided to go meta, making the battle actually take place in the real world, against your game pad.
The story is probably the most confusing and pointless in the Assassin's Creed universe, and that's saying something. There are several head-scratching moments where it appears the story editors either forgot a whole scene or accidentally cut the wrong segment. There are side missions missing dialog to make any sort of sense of them, and cut scenes irrelevant to the missions. Meanwhile, overlaid on all of this is the baffling notoriety system that doesn't follow a reasonable logic (accidentally climb on a box while running through the streets in the slave persona, suddenly wanted posters are plastered on all buildings across the Caribbean). The notoriety doesn't mesh with the fact that a well-known noble woman is hiding her activities from her father, a well-known business man, or from the rest of the city for that matter.
All that being said, Aveline is a nice addition to the Assassin's Creed character lineup, even though no one else in the game, aside from a cameo from another important character, is interesting and all the rest border on annoying and/or excruciating (Gerald would have been vastly improved if his entire dialog was just removed from the game). She is the only compelling reason to play all the way through this otherwise frustrating, confusing, thin game.

This is one of the greatest games I have ever played. It is my go-to game when I seem to get bored with all other games. With that said.. the game is not perfect, and it has several flaws in it. I'll go through my honest thoughts starting with the few down sides and then list all the plus sides to the game.
Cons:
-Lore is lacking / incomplete. (there isn't a lot of story involved yet, and thats a bad thing imo. however this is something that the developers are working on. i'll go into more details in the pros section but basically this con is not going to remain as such forever)
-Heavy grinding (this is both a con and a pro, and really is more to personal taste. some people don't like a lot of grinding in a game while others do... i do find it annoying if the grind goes on too long but thats unavoidable in some games..)
-The cash shop (i'm putting this as a con but not for the reasons people think. its a con because of how money shops are generally viewed.. a lot of people see an ingame shop that sells things for real money and instantly think "pay-to-win" and it gives the whole game a bad reputation. NOTE: this game is NOT pay-to-win.. everything ingame can be obtained without spending any money.. the currency you buy with cash is tradeable and you can trade with other players for said currency.. and said currency is really only needed for cosmetic effects or more slots to store items.. nothing that breaks the game. everything else on the cash shop is if you are being lazy and want to cut down on the grind, which given that this game is all about grind you basically pay to cut down on half the gameplay.. but its not all bad, as the developers need to be supported some how.)
**again: this is not pay-to-win**
-some things may not be fully explained to new players (honestly, im not 100% sure on how bad it is anymore as the new player experiance has improved a lot since i started years ago.. but i have seen new people ask some regular questions so i thought i'd make this a note. but, like with the lore, this is something the devs are working on and shouldn't be a problem forever.. and really, the need to ask questions does make you talk to people, so i guess its not all bad)
-many missions are almost dead (the missions are spread across the solar system on many nodes for each planet. while this is a nice idea, the planets are seperated by levels of enemies and the lower leveled nodes are often empty as veterans usually never need to return to those nodes. this often makes it harder to get groups to run with. however this does have some good sides, as it allows you to take your time and learn what you are doing.. and there is also a recruiting chat and public relay nodes that you can ask for a group to help run missions so there are ways to cope with this down side)
Pros
-Heavy Grind (Again, this is a con and a pro, depending on personal taste. the grind gives you something to do, a reason to return playing. the game isn't about an end goal but rather the trip taken, so to speak. it this regard, its like diablo or path of the exile in that there really is no "end" mission.. you play simply to play.)
-Easy to learn, hard to master (the gameplay is easy enough for any new person to learn to play.. but there are moves that are hard and take real effort and skill to master if you choose to do so. at its base form, its a third person over the shoulder shooter with sword fighting. add parkour, sword combos, mixing damage types for maximum damage, and your character's powers and you have a unique mix of gameplay thats all its own)
-access to all "classes" on one character (you don't have to log out of a character and log into a new one to get a new "class" to play. your one character has access to all warframes, the "classes", and can switch between them before each mission. all that is required is you to actually collect/build the warframe itself and have a slot to store it in, and there is no limit to how many slots you can obtain.
-Large variaty of "classes" to choose from (beefy tank? check. expert healer? check. elemental casters? check. archer? gunslinger? swordsman? stealth? check, check, check, and check... dragon? monkey king? musician? fairy? someone who control a different plain of existance? yep, all there... and thats just the start of the roster of over 30 frames... with new frames in the work as we speak)
-weapons, weapons and more weapons (assault rifles, shotguns, beam weapons, snipe rifles, blasters, bows, pistols, crossbows, ninjastars, nunchuks, sai, swords, polearms, daggers, gunblades, glaives, claws, whips, tonfa, granade launchers..... the list goes on and on... almost any weapon you could think of with more on the way.)
-Mission variaty (theres all sorts of missions, most are on dynamic maps.. each time you load into a node the layout is different. missions vary from sabatage, slay all enemies, capture a target, sneak into computer vaults to steal data, fly through space to capture a ship, and so on. their most recent update has even added a map that has 9 square km of free roam that lets you do bounties, fish, mine, and explore at your leasure.)
free to play (everything listed and more is all free to play.. like i listed above with the cash shop, everything can be gotten without spending real money, all it really takes is time and patiance.. )

In CK2 you control a county/duchy/kingdom, assign your own council, propose marriages for your courtiers, develop your regions, ally or go to war with your neighbours, venture on crusades/jiihads, buy mercenary armies... and this is just the normal part of the game.
But CK2 is not just your regular strategy game. In this game, it's all about your dinasty! You marry per convenience in order to form better alliances, you plot against vassals that have claims on your lands... sometimes even against your own family, you murder your wife and children if the heir is not your own blood, you assassinate opponents or friends as needed, fabricate claims on lands, instigate other kingdom's vassals to rebel against their lieges, execute, free or ransom prisoners, get maimed on battles and become a useless peon, die of syphilis or other nasty diseases, get assassinated by your own brother/uncle/mother in a plot conjured by your own spymaster, allies will turn their back on you and join your rivals when you most needed them, you will rise slowly and steadily and then lose everything because you were either too greedy or just because you died naturally without being able to set the right strategy to give continuity to your dinasty, popes will excommungate you or give you gold for your contribution against infidels... and countless of other situations that make this game pretty unique.
If you want something different and special, this is the game for you!

I was largely dismissive of Warframe for years because I did not trust any free to play game to be anything more than just a manipulative microtransaction platform moreso than a game. Heroes Tactics is another mobile port to PC game. The game revolves battling on a hex-tile grid similar to Heroes of Might and Magic 2. All the creatures that you use basically follow the same rules as in HOMM 2, with the ability to defend and wait. The objective is to try to form a team of 5 characters to beat the same loop over and over again. The only difference is that the subsequent loop is just of a harder difficulty with the opponent having immensely more stat points than the previous loop.
Gameplay-wise, you control up to 5 character summons on a hex grid. You can choose to attack, defend or wait. If you upgrade your hero, they will have special attacks that naturally come to them on specific turns. E.g. Turn 1, 4, 7. The main gist of the game is to just stat/level up and you will beat the level. While the skins on each hero are different, each hero's skills have to be unlocked by a major grindfest. This is the main part of the game, doing a grind feasta. In order to unlock them, you have to grind/raid certain locations for items to equip to your hero to improve their stats. Once you unlock all 6 of them, you can promote your hero to the next level and improve its combat rating. The rating levels follow the green, blue, purple system and come with stars to highlight which ones are stronger in stats. To upgrade your skills, you need to have skill points and gold. The higher your skill level, the more damage/heal/defence it does.
Conclusion, skip this Pay To Win Game. You can try old games like Heroes of Might and Magic 2 that will give you deeper and more diversified content, rather than an infinite loop of increasing difficulty.
Note: Developer is Lilithgames, an Android app maker from Shanghai, China. It's basically partnered with Ubisoft, the owner of the HOMM series. Lilithgame's CEO is Wang Xinwen.
1. Simple to play
Click and go. Not very in depth but easy for anyone using a mobile.
1. Pay To Win
Another P2W game. They use Crystals as the in-game cash currency. It's around 100 USD for 8000+8000 = 16,000 Crystals.
2. Energy/Stamina System
Sigh. Facebook and Zynga truly created a horrible mess of timed energy/stamina genre.
3. Timed Skill Point System
If you want to upgrade your heroes, you have to wait for skill points to be allocated to you by a timed system or buy crystals with real cash and convert them.
4. Grindfest
To progress in the game, you have to unlock
5. VIP Levels
In order to get rewards, Heroes Tactics sets up VIP tiers that gives you more rewards if you spend cash to purchase in-game rewards. This is part of the P2W system.
6. Repetitive Gameplay
You go from one map to another doing the same thing over and over again. The only difference is that the subsequent loop is of higher difficulty with the enemy having significantly more stats.
1. Hex Grid
It makes straight line movement extremely awkward and it's mostly used for large maps. In this case, it's too small to be used.

Crusaders of the Lost Idols is as if someone decided to clone the venerable Clicker Heroes game, but then added much new stuff and improved it along the way.
CotLI contains a strong echo of Clicker Heroes as its base:
-- A boatload of heroes to recruit and purchase each reset/prestige round.
-- First hero is granted to you, and represents your clicking power.  All others provide DPS at increasing rates.
-- Leveling said heroes unlocks permanent buffs to them and the party, as well as abilities to trigger to get past a difficult level.
-- One of the hero abilities is what resets the game for prestige.
-- The prestige items (here, the Idols of the title) are earned based on total party levels.
-- Prestige items grant bonuses and can be spent on additional permanent buffs.
But then it adds
The first thing you notice different from Clicker Heroes is
!  Some of the hero buffs are based on where they are in the formation.  Some heroes may gain strength from those around them, while others prefer to be lone wolves.  Others may support the heroes near them through protection or healing.
Note that for a hero to be effective for anything, whether fighting or abilities or even counting toward Idol earnings, they MUST be in the formation.
Every few hours (offline, too!) spent in formation earns a hero an experience point that adds a whole hundred percent of base DPS to them.  This is useful once you've maxxed out your formation and are trying to pass a difficult area or reach the high-level objectives.
The other thing you notice is
!
You know how Clicker Heroes' gameplay consists of fighting ten monsters a level for four levels, then defeat the boss within 30 seconds or so, then repeat ad infinitum?  In that game, you cycle through a bunch of areas and monsters, and the bosses are swapped out for holiday events, but that's about it.
With Crusaders of the Lost Idols, each level is characterized as a quest, with every fifth level being the boss level.  Each five-level chunk is forms something of a quest story arc.  Quest objectives include "kill X monsters," "kill monsters until you gather X items," "kill monsters until single quest item drops," and "defeat the boss."  You're still killing monsters, but there's now more variety, and the numbers vary instead of being the exact. same. number. each time.
This variety continues when you reset for prestige.  After the initial round, each time 'round, you can choose an objective.  They're all built around hitting some level milestone, but the more advanced ones also add wrinkles such as something taking up one or more of the formation slots and/or otherwise affecting play.
Also, if you prestige during certain events, you can choose to jump into a campaign designed around that event.  Some event objectives will allow you to earn a new hero, but most event heroes are slotted into a seat on the "bench," and can be swapped in or out with the default hero on that seat.  In other words, you will usually NOT earn a more powerful hero than the topmost guy you can unlock upon first firing up the game.
This game also has
!
Every boss can drop a chest.  Each chest contains three cards.  Cards represent a haul of gold, a buff that can be triggered at any time (as opposed to the hero-based abilities that can only be triggered if said hero is in formation AND you have purchased that ability), or equipment.
You can also purchase a pack of jeweled chests directly with real cash money, or with the rubies that is the premium currency, which is also earnable through other means.  Chests purchased this way give you FIVE cards and a chance for better loot.
Each hero has three equipment slots, which is another way to grant buffs.  There is no way to mix-and-match equipment; each hero gets his or her own specific equipment.
Equipment comes in Common to Legendary flavors.  Common, Uncommon, and Rare equipment all drops from normal chests.  Epic loot drops in the jeweled chests, except for whatever rare epic equipment they offer in the sales events, and those can only drop if you pay real money.
Equipment can also be crafted, with materials gathered in missions.  You are granted the recipes for the first three levels of equipment, but the recipes for the other two must be earned in missions, and are random drops.  Legendary equipment MUST be crafted.
When you draw duplicate or lesser equipment, you can disenchant the item and reclaim a portion of the materials that would have been used in its recipe.
As mentioned, CotLI also has
that you can do after your first reset.  These come in two styles.
One is very simple and always earns rubies so you can occasionally buy a jeweled chest with five cards.  These objectives are to do some easy game stuff:  Use a hero's ability a few times, use a buff, level a hero up a few levels, or click a few hundred times.
The other version has you send heroes out to retrieve stuff.  Every hero has a few tags (gender, tank, support, magical, human/animal, if earned in event, and others) based on what they are.  Some tags can only come from heroes earned in events.
The more such tags you can tick off on a particular mission, the more likely it will be successful.  Some missions also might require heroes have a good piece or equipment to be more successful, and some are flagged as dangerous enough to possibly injure a hero and take them temporarily out of commission.
Rewards are decently proportionate to difficulty and time needed for each mission.  You can earn anything from more rubies to gold to crafting materials (including the only way to get the ones needed for Epic or Legendary equipment), recipies for Epic and Legendary loot, and even heroes from past events.
One of the most useful items you can get only from these missions are Enchantment Points.  EPs are BIG (25% of base per EP) DPS boosts specific to the hero that earns them, and they last through resets.  The only way you'll pass the higher levels is with mucho Enchantment Points and Idols.
Two benefits to earning Event Heroes is one, using them is the only way to satisfy some tags needed for the better missions, and two, the EP count for a hero is all those that he or she has earned, plus a third of those of the other heroes in the same seat.  Thus, "benchwarmer" heroes that you pass over on your way back up to full strength in the main game are still useful in the side quests.
The game's been around long enough that they've begun repeating holiday events, with additional content for the second year, making another chance to earn their heroes.
The ONE thing that Clicker Heroes has on Crusaders of the Lost Idols is the ability to auto-pass a level once the objectives were finished.  That is, here, you must click past every single level, meaning you need to babysit the game to pass many levels in a session.  On the other hand, the level you stay on simply repeats (including boss levels), so you keep gathering gold regardless.  You just cannot advance automatically.
Oh, and the flavor text is amusing, more lighthearted than Clicker Heroes, with several sly references.  Many of the event heroes are obvious parodies.
I'm only a few weeks, and so far, Crusaders of the Lost Idols feels pretty fair for a freemium clicker game of the wash-rinse-repeat style.  I lasted a couple years with various iterations of the relatively boring Clicker Heroes, so let's see how long I last with the Crusaders.  ;-)

In short, this game is good and much different to FlatOut 2, with some quirks and annoying issues that were ironed out in the sequel (and shouldn't have been ironed out, some will say).
A bit of a disclaimer: I was introduced through the FlatOut series with FlatOut 2, which I very much adored, but I never played the first one. So naturally, I was curious about it (I apologize in advance for the numerous comparisons in this review).
Let's get the technical stuff over with. It's an older game, and while not as visually polished as the follow-up title, I actually preferred the gritty, stripped down graphics and overall art-style. It just seems to fit the game better. The sound design is also great, again, I can't help but feel it's just a nudge better than FO2. The soundtrack is, for me at least, a let-down, sadly. I imagine they couldn't really get any big names due to budget constraints and such, but dear Jeebus are some of these songs awful (the fact that one song loops per race is also kind of annoying). I know bands my friends play in that would do a better job as a FlatOut soundtrack. Since Steam has a Music option, I just loaded up the FlatOut 2 soundtrack and off we go (it fits surprisingly well).
The gameplay, then! Well, it's a lot more challenging IMO than FO2, for a number of reasons. The tracks, especially some of the later ones, are a lot more bendy and relentless. I'm curious as to why there were no winter tracks in FO2, those are present here and they're fun and refreshing. Then, there are the environments and the various crap found in them. While in the second game, it sometimes feels like the objects you're hitting are made of cardboard, here, some objects will really knock your soul (or at least your driver) out the windshield. Also, the cars feel more fragile and more... hefty, for lack of a better term. In essence, this means you have to be a much, MUCH more cautious racer than in the next installment. The reset button is also not as (overly) powerful. Nitro is gained by destroying things and the environment and ONLY by doing that, and it becomes a rare commodity. The cars feel great, though and as with the sequel, there are a number of different types of cars you can choose from, though I can't help but notice there is a little less variety in the way they actually handle.
This game is also noticeably shorter than FO2, with 36 races total and 12 bonus events. The races are split up into Bronze, Silver and Gold classes, and the cars get better once you move up the ranks. One cool feature is that the bonus events are always available and they are noticeably more challenging than FO2's stunts; the derbies in particular are really, really hard, I'd even go so far as to say I question whether or not they're really fun anymore. These would be greatly improved upon in FO2. All in all, there's still enough to satisfy a good racing/smashing itch.
So what's wrong with this game? To be honest, aside from the questionable soundtrack (thing of personal preference of course) its relatively short length (still decent), there is one thing I wasn't terribly a fan of. The damage mechanics, mostly the blast-outs seem wildly inconsistent to the point where it becomes frustrating and annoying. Now, to be fair, I've never raced in a proper race myself. I'm pretty sure smashing head-on into a tree without a seatbelt will send you flying through a windshield at 80+km/h. But hitting a wooden barn door at 25km/h? Slowly (30-40km/h) drifting into a fence? Hitting a haystack? I dare say you'd probably get beat up, sure, I've been in a car accident and it ain't pretty, but you wouldn't spectacularly fly out the front of your ride. These moments aren't very common, but when they happen, out-of-the-blue, especially if they happen in the last quarter of a 5 lap race, you tend to want to break your controller in half, which is never a good thing.
Overall, this game is a solid first entry, and while there are some minor annoyances (that were more or less ironed out in the sequel), this is a very enjoyable and unique racing game that any racing fan should definitely play at least once.

Murdered: Soul Suspect is a console port detective game with a horror
atmosphere that plays more like an interactive movie than a game.  Right off
the bat, I was unimpressed by the whopping 30 frames per second that this
game runs at, followed shortly by the delayed lineup of subtitles to speech.
The story was cheesy and doesn't fit with the objective of the game;
starting out by stating that your ultimate goal is to reunite with a lost love,
but then not mentioning that relationship for the bulk of the game.  As for the game
being a detective game, I would disagree with that and state that it is more
like a hidden object game that requires you search out 'clues' in a predetermined
location.  There is no deduction needed; all the clues are in one place, and
the game holds your hand by leading you to the next clue and asking
rediculously obvious questions.
The ghosts, while contributing to the atmosphere, did absolutely nothing
to add to the game.  For the most part, they were all from the same time period,
and were supposed to add a spooky element, but as you are also playing as a
ghost, and they disappear when you get close, they were more of a waste of time
than anything else.
I enjoy watching movies, but I buy games in order to, oh I don't know,
play a game!  This game played like a cinematic movie, with about 20-25%
of the game actual gameplay, and the rest being cinematic movies or dialogue.
Being made to move all across the mapp to get to the next action point does not
count as gameplay;  it is wasting time.
If you are interested in the story of this game, I would recommend going
to YouTube and watching the cinematics strung together rather than buy this game.
It treats you, the player, as if you are an idiot that can't figure out anything
for yourself.  Graphically the game gets by, as well as the level design.  The
story is acceptable, but what little gameplay there is designed for those
that can't deduce anything for themselves.  As a game, I cannot recommend this,
if it can even be called a game.
For more details, see the linked video review, as this is a basic summary of
what I cover in my video.

The greatest injustice that can be inflicted upon “Kotonoha no Niwa” is to falsely and narrowly label this 46-minute film a simple story of love. Too often do you see people claim that this movie is one about a "forbidden love" created by an age difference and it is through these lens that unwarranted and confused criticisms of the show sometimes emerge. The Garden of Words has a level of nuanced complexity that is concealed for the presumptuous as it requires you to think and pay attention to its use of visuals as well as its dialogue to realise this. Indeed, Makoto Shinkai himself stated that he wanted to write a tale of “lonely sadness” and whilst romance is definitely a prevalent theme, it is not portrayed nor explored in a traditional fashion.
The entire plot centralises around the interactions between our two main characters: a young student and a mysterious grown-up woman. Be that as it may, the dialogue is very minimal but simultaneously so potent for a vast majority of the development that occurs and the insights we gain into our protagonists hinges upon brief and restrained conversations. It is the absence of dialogue in many cases that convey human emotions more eminently and passionately than when spoken and the visuals play an incredible role to enhance this. Given the film’s brevity, it requires every element to contribute to the plot and no element exists without a reason – be it simple movements, scenery, music or dialogue. It is truly impressive to see how effectively and concisely deep emotions and their underlying intentions are conveyed. The story is told elegantly for nothing is wasted.
Rain is a fundamental aspect that initially represents the condition necessary for our protagonists to meet. I think with regards to the symbolism that Shinkai has employed to explore key themes, it is better if you watch and contemplate yourself on them as this is where the majority of the satisfaction lies in this movie. The most impressive aspect of the Shinkai's film was how effectively extended metaphors such as the rain were used consistently and in an enlightening fashion which keeps the film short yet brimming with sentiment. These themes coalesce with our characters and their self-discoveries to tell a larger story at hand in a modern social context exploring the Japanese traditional notion of love. Takao’s burning desire to transcend into adulthood and realise his dreams is beautifully embodied by the older and seemingly sophisticated woman but even during the film’s brief journey, Takao’s preconceptions are deconstructed and despite their differences, they come to realise their similarities through their interactions under the rain which are painfully human. Perhaps my only significant issue I found was the lack of emotional intensity or potency that led our female main character to the position and predicament she was in. By no means was it weak but it seemed lacking compared to how brilliantly Takao was characterised and this slight imbalance for me, hampered the final climax to a certain degree.
For a film whose strengths lies in its representation through resigned soliloquies, much of the portrayal lies in the hands of the artwork and animation which are nothing short of a masterpiece. This is the most visually impressive work I have ever seen in the entirety of the anime medium. The animation is flawless with excellent cinematography such as clever use of deep focus in more intimate scenes that successfully emphasise key metaphors employed and well angled panoramas boasting the vast and gorgeous landscapes that are a sight for sore eyes. The sceneries and landscapes are meticulously drawn with details that are exceptionally similar to real life further enhancing the immersion of the experience. The musical score has a larger focus on softer pieces that almost act as an addition to natural sounds of rain and nature or the cacophony of city-life. The soundtrack is entirely piano-based and range from subtler pieces that capture the ambience of the moment to more prominent pieces such as “Greenery Rain” (one of my favourite anime OSTs) which accompany many of the visual experiences.
“Kotonoha no Niwa” is a magnificent movie that adopts a more nuanced and authentic approach in exploring human relationships. As stated initially, this is not simply a bittersweet romance that many condemn it to be but a subtle journey into the solitude and desires humans hold, within a prominent and relevant modern day social context. All of this is delivered to viewers in a film that entirely takes advantage of the anime medium, showing just how much artistry and cinematic storytelling that resonates within you (as most Shinkai films do) can be achieved in a what is fundamentally 46 minutes of animated images.

TL;DR Great game but unfinished, no support, and P2W.
This game is well designed and very fun. It's extremely dirivitive of Heroes of Might and Magic III (right down to the loading screen being an angel bearing a firey sword down onto a demon), but the thematic elements and game play are both super solid and, for some, will feel freshly nastalgic. Character progression is steady and I didn't feel it was very "grindy" until late game (200 hours+).
Unfortunately there are major things left unfinished in the game. There are heroes that there is no way to attain, and game modes that there is no way to access. The last comment I saw from a developer was in August, saying that they are 'working hard on new content', but I'm not sure what that means since there are no updates and no communication with players. Today, you can't even log in and we have no way of knowing if it's because they are updating, or the game is gone forever.
The second downside is that paying real currency directly affects your power level in the game. In most games now, you can pay for convenience or cosmetics. But in Hero Tactics you can get overpowered heroes that are not available otherwise. I wounldn't say this is a deal breaker, because you can still get towards the top of the rankings without these, and still beat the PVE sections - but of course it is annoying anytime the P2W concept is introduced - even moderately.
You can tell from my logged hours that I still had a lot of fun with the game. I think I spent $3.99 on crystals or something, and I'd say I got my money's worth overall from the fun I got out of this game. But I definately wouldn't recommend spending money on it since it could feasibly go down at any moment... and never come back.
*Edit* Servers are back up - they combined all into one giant US server. They also say that a large update is coming, so it could be that the game is not abandoned after all. :D

Basically, it is 90% the same as ETS 2, so if you're umming and ahhing over this game, you should get ETS 2 and if you like that, then get this. If not, on Steam, Refund is always an option.
I'll base this review on the negatives, because frankly, there is little more that you can say about this game that you can't about ETS 2, which is a bit of a negative, but I give it a fairly stable 7/10.
Cons:
- Steering at times can be rather dodgy. There have been times where I have literally had to reverse in the road just to make it around the corner and avoid oncoming traffic.
- Many of the locations are simply too small for the type and size of trailers that are available. Fuel stations and even some junctions are WAAAAAY too tight do drive through.
- Although it has been slightly improved from ETS 2, it still takes a while to set off from stationary and after about 30MPH, forget getting up to speed which on a slip road where every car stops, joining can be a b**ch.
- Graphics are quite dated and aren't really up to par with a game for 2016 - maybe for 2011/12. Though, detail on the trucks aren't too bad.
- AI can be pretty dumb at times. I'm not sure if it is an American thing, but right of way doesn't seem to mean the same thing - they just stop at the end of slip roads or just pull up on the carriage way to let someone through when they should slow down to let them pass or change lane. Also, a problem carried over from ETS 2, no one seems to understand the meaning of reverse lights and the size of my vehicle when I have to reverse to get out of a tough spot. First time reviewing a game, but felt I should on this one. I never did play the first game though heard good things about it, so figured give the second a run. So far...even in early access I can't say I was disappointed. The game it's self reminds me of classic computer RPGs and pen 'n paper RPGs I played when I was much younger just a bit more fair and easier to understand yet still maintaining a lot of what made them challenging. Character customization starts a bit limited but as you get higher in levels its more about what you want to play and what your party members be. You are not locked into your starting class at all and I love that, hoping they have a lot more choices in the full release.
Gameplay wise is point and click, though I found there is a lot to interact with in the world in different ways, one of the more different ways I found was that playing an Elf or having an Elf in your group, the elf can eat a corpse and gain the memories of that person, and it actually does play a part in the game. Combat is much of the same, point and click with a lot of tactical choices to make, the enemy AI is well refined and act in actually very smart ways even on the easier difficulties. I also found it pretty neat how your spells, items and attacks can change the battle ground and make hazards for yourself and your enemies, with the enemies able to do the same. Such as freezing a wet spot on the ground to give a chance of someone slipping on the spot or shocking the water with lighting to stun everyone standing in the wet spot. Though at times at least for me I found it hard to move to avoide these hazards at times like the area they were affecting were slightly larger than they really were.
I even tried a bit of co-op with friends and a bit hidden in a sense once we figured it out, connecting with one another was clean and easy to do.
Storywise I found interesting enough, a dark world with many dark themes with demons, torture and corruption. The premade characters have backgrounds and behave well according to their backgrounds. Another different system in this game is the tag system. Basicly pick tags for your character and you will have in game choices that you can make based just on those tags you pick. The pre mades having different choices as well they can make based on their stand alone backgrounds. Though it does feel you can get same results no matter your background still, it does help with immersion and at in making your created character feel seprate from the rest.
Graphics, are not that important to me, but they are decent enough in this game. Though playing completely zoomed out (pretty much the only way to play an RPG like this) I found it a bit difficult to notice things I could pick up or interact with since they are so small. A few rare times I misclicked on something because of how small it is. I have an older system, so I wasn't able to play on the highest settings, I was able to however able to play on high even though the game suggested I play on low. So I can see pretty much everyone able to play this game with no issues. Even when I tried the highest settings I just had a slight drop in Frame rate.
Overall Divinity 2 I recommend highly, especially if you are a fan of old school RPGs and Pen 'n Paper RPGs, you will feel right at home playing this with a high level of immersion and ability to costumize your character however you desire. Story had been done before but it's presented well in the world, and should be interesting enough to keep you playing. Combat is deep, and will challenge the thinking sides of your brain to approach each encounter in most effective way possible, plus have you thinking best way to build your characters to deal with threats in your prefered way. You might find a little frustration in interacting with the world due to how small things are and will even miss a few things if you aren't careful, but it shouldn't be a big enough issue to remove any enjoyment in the game.
Hope you found this helpful if you took the time to read it.

Original Sin 1 was probably one of the best CRPGs I had ever played to that date, and I could find little to no flaws with it, many of which were improved upon in the Enhanced Edition of the game.
Original Sin 2 somehow manages to take that mastercraft and make it even better, the new systems and mechanics implemented in such a way that I find it almost hard to return to the original. I have spent an absurd amount of time on the Early Access alone, and cannot believe the amount of variety and feasability to the different ways to approach each situation.
I was a bit taken back by the new changes to the armor system -- having physical and/or magical armor protects you (and your enemies) from those CC abilities, which made the first game a bit of a race to CC the enemies before they could do it to you. Original Sin 2 found a interesting way to handle that, and building your team and skillset to tackle this new problem has made the combat far more interesting and more satisfying, while not over complicating things. Instead of a party make-up being almost required, you're now a bit more free to experiment with your set up, and the changes to the skill system allows you to experiment more with being a hybrid build, instead of having to take a strict path in order to maximize gains.
This game seems far more friendly to newer players, while still keeping much of the spice and charm that I've come to expect and love from Larian, and this newest entry has done nothing but please and delight me.

A true masterpiece of a game. The fantastic metal soundtrack to rival even Doom and gunplay better than anything I've ever played mix to create this game. No, experience. It has a LOT of achievements that only the most professional players such as myself could achieve. Let's talk about some features.
Weapons: There are a variety of weapons, ranging from RPG that hits sometimes to a katana to a minigun. We in the pro Dinosaur Hunt community like to use the minigun because of its power to kill anything in one clip at most. It's a very strong choice and I personally believe it's the best weapon in the game.
Voice acting: Pristine and beautiful voice acting made by angels. The voices are so badass and so dreamy it makes me rethink my sexuality.
Levels/Graphics: The level design is flawless. You hunt dinosaurs basically everywhere. I'm baffled by the creativity. You have the icy tundras where you're fighting off hypothermia as well as bloodthirsty reptiles. There are the deserts so real that you'll start sweating at your computer. You have forests so pretty you want to just walk around in nature for a while. I've often found myself distracted with the sheer beauty that I died a few times. These graphics are revolutionary.
Plot: The plot in this game is perfect. You follow Hunter Guy on his quest to eradicate the planet of dinosaurs. They come after you in 2 waves. One of regular dinos, and one boss. His edgy murderous intent keeps you coming back for more every time. It's a plot worthy not of people, but of gods and goddesses. Truly amazing how far we've come with storytelling in gaming.
Overall: I give this amazing game a 10/10 and I believe everyone should. If you haven't played it yet, please do. The character development and gameplay both intertwine so well that I can't help but give it this high of a score. Dinosaur Hunt is the greatest game I have ever played and everyone needs to experience it.

Here we go... Finally I am reviewing a grand strategy game. First off, I just want to say that this game is definitely NOT for everyone. Due to the learning curve of the genre (more on that later), this game will inevitably have haters, but this is okay. Personally, I absolutely LOVE this game. Everything about it is just simply amazing. In this review, I will talk about pretty much everything that is important about the game.
First off, let's talk about the least impressive part of Crusader Kings II: the graphics. They are decent, and do the job. The map is more detailed than in any Paradox game before this (excluding Sengoku), and is actually pleasing to look at. The models of soldiers and your council members on the map aren't too great either, but once again they get the job done. There are map modes which essentially display information to the player through colors/words on the map, and these are incredibly useful. It should also be mentioned that the interface displays a lot of information, and can be a bit overwhelming for the player.
Now, on to the good stuff. The music is simply incredible. I love video game music, and honestly I have never heard a soundtrack like this one before. If I made a person who wasn't a gamer listen to this music, they would never guess it was from a video game. It is hard reviewing music, so just Google the soundtrack. Paradox was awesome enough to upload the whole soundtrack to YouTube for your listening pleasure, so what are you waiting for? Also, Paradox included the soundtrack in the game's Steam directory, which was incredibly kind for them to do. Before moving on to the next topic, I should also mention that the main theme is simply incredible. It plays when the game loads and on the main menu. The first time you hear it, you will inevitably get goose bumps.
While the previous things add up to an amazing experience, the most important part of any game is its gameplay. Explaining the gameplay would literally take me all day, so I will sum it up in a few sentences. Essentially, you play as a feudal lord (either a count, duke, king or emperor) in the timeline of 1066-1453 (the starting date is pushed back to 867 if you have The Old Gods expansion). Yes, the game is long, and can last for over 30 hours easily, and with all of the DLC there are over 1000 different characters on the map of Europe and a bit of Africa and Asia you can play as, all with different dynasties and play completely differently. Also keep in mind that the game has completely random events, which means that every play through is different and unique in its own way. Also, this game is a sandbox: you make your own goals. You win by essentially getting to the end date, which is  rather easy to do, so you can almost do ANYTHING. One day your wife can become pregnant randomly. If you already have a son, you might want to plot to kill your wife so that the child isn't born, and therefore cannot become jealous and kill your heir to the throne. This is just one example out of many thing that will happen to you in Crusader Kings II. Honestly, CKII is the void of ethics in almost every single way. You can either be the nicest guy possible, or can be the cruelest ruler anyone has ever seen. The possibilities are nearly endless, and you can spend hundreds upon thousands of hours in the game. At the time of this review, I only have about 30 hours in the game, but I can definitely see myself playing hundreds of hours because I feel I have barely touched the surface of this game. While all seems good so far, the game has one major flaw: the difficulty curve. I came from Europa Universalis IV (another fantastic Paradox game), which has a much easier learning curve because the tutorial is amazing, so I was able to adapt in about 5 hours. For someone that has never played a grand strategy before, learning this game will take a lot of effort and time. The in game tutorial is terrible, and the player will have to read forums and watch videos on how to play. If you want my advice, the Crusader Kings subreddit (r/crusaderkings) has a great tutorial on it, and it is the shortest one, too. If you have a friend that knows how to play the game, I am sure they would be happy to teach you how to play. One more thing I should talk about is the DLC. There is a lot of DLC for the game, and if you can I recommend buying the Crusader Kings II Collection. It doesn't actually come with all the DLC, so the important ones that you will also have to buy are The Old Gods (pushes the starting date back and allows you to play as the Pagans), Rajas of India (adds Indian nations) and Sons of Abraham (adds Jewish nations). If you have Europa Universalis IV, you should also get the save converter which allows you to easily export your game to EU4, allowing for even MORE gameplay!
tl;dr - Crusader Kings II is an amazing strategy game that is will keep you hooked for hours at a time. I'd highly recommend it.

This is a pretty good game. If you think about whats in it and the scale of it, you'll be able to see this is definately a complete game, however, that doesn't mean that there aren't things people (Myself included) wanted more of.
If you look at all these reviews you'll more than likely see a bunch of people saying that the game isn't a full game, but it is, I could understand how it might not feel like one to others, but again, that doesn't change that it is. The developers decided to phase out a few ideas (Some channels they were considering or planning before), because with the way the game was modeled, the gameplay wasn't that different and the mass of users ended up only playing one channel type, but even when presented with that, people are still upset for some reason about the lack of channels. Anyways, that's just my personal view on the people that negatively reviewed this just for the sole reason of me being personally annoyed. (I ran into a person on the forums that was whining about being "entitled" to a refund, and he was quite literally slandering the developers and trying to urge others into false reporting the game so he could get one for himself; disliking the game is one thing, but you shouldn't attack people or their product to that severity just because you dislike what you invested in.)
Anyways, onto the game itself and not the development stand-point
If you like this genre, you will like this game. When you start and get into it, I believe you'll most likely enjoy it. However, there are people out there that say they like this genre but only like instant results, so this isn't really targeted at them. This game will be easy, and it might feel repetitive from time to time, but there will be twists and turns for quite a bit that make it more interesting. Now, there could be more to it, as there could to all games, but the amount of content in it should keep you playing for a few hours if you're an actual fan of games in these genres. There are three channels currently, potentially more in the future, but while the channels have new objects, a few new mechanics and other things, the gameplay itself is the same. After all, this is a game where you take up the role of a youtuber and aim for the top; the channels are more or less just different paths you can take.
The development itself has come to a standstill unfortunately, however, before this, a few updates came out along with a roadmap. I'm choosing to trust the roadmap, just because it tackles a lot of the issues I've seen some people upset about. They clearly state that they plan to continue working on the game, and to add more things; however, long term, not short-term. However, at the time of writing this, it's possible that the development will start up again sooner or later, as one of the staff members that work with the developers (I don't mean someone chosen as a forum moderator, I mean an actual paid employee that shows up to their offices.) has started becoming active. It seems like they took a break, which, was well deserved considering the game they released.
Tl;dr
If you like games in this genre, buy it. If you aren't satisfied with the amount of content, even though theres enough for it to be considered a full game, then don't. However, if you do buy it and play over the two hours, don't feel like you're somehow entitled to slander the developers and demand an unjust refund.

As an economist and nerd, I knew I was going to pick up this game eventually.  Not many people consider what goes on in the lives of RPG store-owners, and this game attempts to address that.  The story is entertaining enough, and for those who don't like business management as much as I, adventurers can be hired to go on dungeon crawls.
The game has a few flaws, though.  First, the loan payments go from challenging to excessive too fast, and then stop way too early.  After that, the entire reason to earn money goes out the window (aside from some optional modes).  Second, while the dungeon crawls are fun, and can be rewarding, they take so much in-game time that you're almost always better off just running your store, and going to the guild or market when your stock is low.
Still, you'll likely enjoy the game if you have even a bit of interest in business, so it's worth purchasing during a sale.

This game is what I would call an action-adventure with simple puzzle elements. The gameplay itself is not very original and repetitive, but the game stands out due to the excellent presentation and good storytelling.
In "Murdered: Soul Suspect" the player steps into the role of Ronan O'Connor, a police detective who gets killed right during the intro. In this first cutscene, Ronan sees his dead body and realizes that he has become some kind of spirit (which reminded me of the similar scene in the 1990 movie "Ghost", starring Patrick Swayze). As a new inhabitant of the spirit world he sets out to find his murderer, seemingly some kind of serial killer on the loose targeting women who at first don't seem to have anything in common. Ronan saves Joy, a young medium, from the killers grasp. She is in search for her (also medially gifted) mother. The two start to work together to unravel the mysteries behind the killings.
The game is set in the small town of Salem, USA. The entire story occurs during one (very long) night. The streets of salem provide the starting point and are also the main "level hub" during the game gaining access to different locations which are unlocked by advancing in the main story line. Allthough story and level design are quite linear, this allows the players to travel back to previous visited places to look for clues or collectables they may have overlooked, giving the game a small whiff of "open world".
While following the main storyline, the player is free to pursue side quest for other ghosts, in other words doing detective work on their "cases" to help them find peace and thus the way into the afterlife.
Most of the time you search for different clues, either physical or mental - Since you are able to slip into the bodies of every human NPC you encounter, you can read their minds to find valuable clues or just spy on their thoughts, which is quite fun most of the time and adds to the atmosphere. When you have enough clues, you can "solve" a crime scene by combining the clues that matter, which I found sometimes confusing and not very logical. Since you can try the combination out as often as you want, try-and-error is always the way to go, making these puzzles somewhat obsolete.
One of the most fun elements in the game are the few cats throughout, you can possess their bodies to jump and climb into otherwise unreachable areas to open passages or unlock secrets. A feature I could definitely have had more of.
Scattered during the different levels are several sets of collectables which, upon completion, each unlock a small, fully voice-narrated ghostly short story.
There are no time-limited missions, which I found very comforting.
(Unfortunately, the developers decided to change this in the final battle, see below). The player is always allowed to take hers/his time to inspect the surroundings (with the exception of the recurring hide-and-seek from the demons), giving the opportunity to enjoy the remarkable atmosphere the developers created here.
The only physical confrontations in the game happen in some scattered events where "demons" show up. These entities are described as former ghosts of humans that were unable to solve their "soul quests", and as a result descended into madness and turned into vile creatures, preying on other spirits. If they spot the player, they rush towards him and attack, resulting in a game over after a few hits. The only way to defeat them is to perform a sneak-attack. To avoid being seen, the player can use one of the variuos "ectoplasmic residues" (some astral, human-shaped clouds that are found all over the game world) to hide inside.
These sequences work like a stealth game where you approach your enemies from behind and finish them of by a quick keypad-key & mousekey combination that is displayed. I despise quicktime events in general (in my opinion they are the distinctive mark of the lazy game designer), and I found these short "battles" against the demons just annoying. If you hit the wrong button, the attack fails and you have to flee and hide again, while the monster search the hiding spots. Most of the time you hop from one hideout to another, till the demons stop looking for you. This can be quite frustrating if you are in a limited space (like the asylum) and three demons are hunting you simultanously. These sequences often feel random and half-baked, resulting in hectic hopping-around until the enemies let go. In some levels there are spectres of crows placed in certain spots which the player can activate to distract the demons. These are quite helpful, but there are few of them and they are seldomly encountered inside buildings.
When I started playing, I was drawn into the eerie atmosphere and loved it. Unfortunately, the feeling vanished the more I approached towards the "final battle" sequence. Without spoiling the story, it is basicly just a longer quicktime event. You have x seconds to find out that you have to push key y, then you have x seconds to do z. Otherwise you lost. I tried to beat the sequence about four times, then I uninstalled the game (yes, I am a wimp!).
The strength of "Murdered" lies in its strong storytelling and stunning depiction of the spirit world, and if it were not for the uninspired gameplay mechanics, it could be one of my all time favourites. Since steam does'nt have a "thumbs sideways" button, I give it a thumbs down, although it would deserve better.
I recommend it for people who are into "haunted house" stories (It reminded me of movies like "Ghost", Peter Jackson's "The Frighteners" with a pinch of "Se7en" in the mix.), and who are not easily frustrated by quicktime events like me.

I finally finished this game today and I'm finding it incredibly difficult to decide how to score/review it, since my thoughts about it are so mixed. I chose to give it a positive overall score because I don't feel it's a *bad* game per se, and it certainly does have an audience. I did enjoy the game, even while at the same time I had so many issues with it.
Since I first heard about this game, I couldn't wait for it to come out. The premise sounded fantastic. Salem is very close to my heart IRL, and I'm inclined to adore any game that explores occult/supernatural themes in a unique way. And this game certainly did that. However, it just doesn't have the polish that it deserved, and I feel as though it doesn't give itself license to be what it is. In stark contrast to this is another game that came out this year with very similar themes and gameplay, which I found to be executed far more effectively. That game is the Vanishing of Ethan Carter, and it was made by a much smaller studio no less! Of course, these games did not invent detective games, however they explore mechanics that I haven't seen much of before. While I won't spend this whole review comparing the two games, I will say this: if you enjoyed the detective mechanic and occult themes here, do yourself a favor and look up the Vanishing of Ethan Carter as well.
With that said, I did enjoy Murdered: Soul Suspect. Wandering around the streets of Salem as a ghost, deciphering clues and uncovering hidden remnants of the past is a fun and unique experience. The game looks great and plays smoothly, and the difficulty level is appropriate for the casual player, nothing quite too challenging. I also enjoyed the story, which wove together some pieces of Salem's darker past with modern times, as well as stories from in between. Exploring a Salem full of ghostly objects and remnants was an interesting idea, even if many of those objects were clearly just placed at random to place limits on the world. I didn't really feel like this is what an "in-between death realm" would look like - random boats and carts all over the place, the occasional demon grabbing for you and other dead people standing around that disappear when you get close. These effects start to feel more like decoration than a living world, which is a shame. This is Salem after all, there was such potential here. Some of the locations outside of the town proper were much more interesting, such as the cemetery. While you can roam around Salem (mostly) freely, at the end of the day, it's a very small place with a finite number of activities. And while walking through walls and objects never gets old, using your other ghostly abilities such as "possessing" living people does. 90% of the time, all you can do is read their thoughts, and most people have only 1 or 2 thoughts, neither of them interesting. After doing this a few times with different people, you'll hear the same thoughts over and over, and this feature will lose all of its appeal. Only very rarely do people's thoughts contribute to gameplay or add any interest to the story, mostly it's just a bore. A few times, the possession mechanic was used to inhabit and move through other characters, including a cat, which was very interesting. I would have loved more of this, it would have provided a bit more variety in gameplay and made the ability feel a bit more tangible. I'm also left wondering why the devs developed the ability to inhabit and move through a secondary character, but this was only used for a combined total of 30 seconds throughout the game. Much more potential for stealth here. Instead, all we can do is "poltergeist" objects like fax and soda machines while the other character runs around, and it's almost impossible to mess up.
Which brings me to the other stealth mechanic, the demons. I did not like the demons at all. Very tedious and unnecessary piece of gameplay. This is what I meant when I said the game should embrace what it is, a detective game. Instead, it tried to add some action into the mix, with a half-hearted attempt at stealth mechanics. I love a good stealth game, in fact it's one of my favorite genres, but this was painful. The demons just wander around set courses, and you have to either slip by them or attack them with what is essentially a quick-time event. The only thing that makes this remotely challenging is that you have to press (if playing with keyboard and mouse) a random WASD key and either left or right mouse button at the same time. It just ends up feeling like a cheap attempt at adding challenge to a very boring mechanic. Essentially, the only weapon you have in this game is how fast you can press those keys. The demons don't change throughout the course of the game, and you don't develop any new abilities for dealing with them. They merely serve as padding to prevent you from getting from one area to the next too quickly. The "action" culminates in a very disappointing "boss battle" which strangely attempted to weaponize the game's detective mechanics. It all just felt very strange and unnecessary. Again, in contrast, VEC allowed itself to be a detective/exploration game without injecting unnecessary action, and as a result achieved a much more cohesive experience overall. Perhaps if M:SS had developed the stealth/action parts a bit more, it could have integrated that gameplay more effectively. But as it is, I felt the game would have been better off without it.
M:SS does have a few other redemptive qualities that I want to mention. There are stories in the game that you uncover by finding objects and letters, and these, along with the main storyline, are what kept me playing. It is definitely fun, at least for me, to explore the various scenes and settings in the game and uncover the secrets of what happened here. Perhaps that is what this game does best - it allows you to unravel the story through experience rather than just telling you what happened. Many of the locations are great and kept me wanting to explore every last nook and cranny to make sure I didn't miss anything. Not all of the stories are interesting though. Most of the notes you'll find are sad journal entries written by the main character's wife. Both her and the main character himself are beyond boring and cliché. All of her journal entries are about how Ronan is such a bad boy, but she's irresistibly drawn to him nonetheless. She's afraid of him, but she loves him. If you've read one, you've read them all. It became disappointing to pick up a note and see her sad face on it. Ronan, however, is even worse. I just found him incredibly uninteresting and unlikeable. Keep on ghost-chain-smoking your ghost-cigarettes, Ronan. Most of the other characters and stories in the game were much more interesting, so at least there's that.
Another gripe - where are all the witches? We're in Salem, and there are basically zero witches. Huge missed opportunity there. To this day, Salem has a thriving Witchcraft community, and it's an essential thread in the tapestry of the town for obvious reasons. While the story references the witches of old, I was left wanting more than that from this part of Salem. And further, for a ghost story full of demons set in a town famed for Witchcraft, there is no horror to this game at all. The only thing scary in this game is whether you'll continue to fail at QTEs and have to do them over and over again.
Alright, I feel this review is just devolving into me listing off complaints about what I wanted this game to be, which isn't quite fair. There is much more I could say about why this is overall a decent game, but I would say that if this game piques your interest, if you want to try something different and aren't scared off by the mixed scores, then I'd say go for it. Get it when it's on sale and go in with low expectations, and you'll probably enjoy it. 6/10

Before I begin, I want everyone to know that I've been waiting on this game for years now. Ever since we were told they began development. I knew exactly what I was going to get, so I'm basing my review on that.
____
When you first see the game, it looks exactly like Euro Truck Simulator 2. The only differences include it being in the United States, having vehicles driven in the United States, trailers that are used in the United States, and a couple states in the United States.
After you get past the $20 price tag and actually get in the game, it's exactly as it seems. Just a reskin of ETS2. But what was to be expected? It's the same engine used to rebuild ETS2 for a different region. That's what we were told we were going to receive and that's what we got. I am not at all upset that we only get 2 states at release with Arizona coming a little later for free and 2 trucks. I knew I was getting that and I paid the price for that.
The developers wanted to go the correct route with the game and get licensing for the vehicles used so the lack of vehicles is okay. As time goes on, we'll get loads more. As far as states go, 3 might not seem like much. With the scale, it definitely seems lacking in content. But you have to remember. If they went to a more in-depth scale and added more content, then it'd take years for a single state to come out. I don't know about you, but I'd like to have 48 states before I turn 70 years old. :P
And the game is called American Truck Simulator. American. The United States is only one of dozens upon dozens of countries in America. Canada and Mexico are 2 more countries in NORTH America. Meanwhile, there's still South America that has to be scaled in. By the time we get all of that(if we ever do, the plans could change), we'd have so much map, we wouldn't be able to explore it all in a reasonable amount of time. Sure, California and Nevada might not seem like much, but they are comparable to Great Britain and France in ETS2 when you talk about size. Now add the equivelent amount of states as there are countries in ETS2 and you have the United States completed. UK and France might not seem like much on ETS2, but when you travel from one to the other, and then all the way to Poland and then up to Sweden, you start to realize that even though the map is small now, it will be much bigger later on when we have more content to play.
Not much of a regular review that you'd see on Steam, but these are my opinions on the game so far. It's a reskin of ETS2 and that's what we were told and what we paid for. No complaints here. Still a billion times better than most simulators out there.

An amazing game if you know what your paying for..
It's not a 3rd person adventure game like Assassin's Creed or Sleeping Dogs
If you go into the game realizing that it's a new take on the old point and click adventure games where you solve puzzles and experience a narrative, then your much more likely to enjoy yourself.
That being said, Murdered: Soul Suspect, does a few things really well.
- Great Characters, they're very well done and you'll find yourself really caring about what happens to them.
- Voice work is top notch
- Extra items / Side Cases come with their own ghost stories that will have you scouring the area to make sure you collect all of them.
- Setting is dark and creepy yet it feels alive thanks to all the townspeople spread throughout salem
As with any game though there are negatives of course
- The demonic / exorcism dynamic of combat feels more like an afterthought meant to draw in more gamers than a mechanic that was developed to really add depth to the gameplay.
- While the voicework itself is excellent.. the characters lip syncing is not as great.  Not terrible, but it's something you'll definitely pick up on from time to time.
- Even though there are plenty of citizens walking about and interacting with the enviroment; there is a lot of dialogue that's used on multiple people.  Also once you decide to read their thoughts and the voiceover starts; you have to wait for it to finish before  you can listen to the next or disposses them.
If you see it on sale definitely pick it up.  I managed to find this on Gamer's Gate for 13.99

Okay, it has a lot of the elements that make AC a lot of fun.  But they skimped on the story, so that leaves gameplay as the sole draw.  AND IT DOESN'T FEEL LIKE THEY FINISHED IT.  I just spent 5 minutes trying to QT kill an alligator, which needed 5 correct button presses.  After the first 2, some were insta-fails no matter how quick I pressed.  Obviously the keyboard-mouse doesn't get the same love in a console port.  Also, despite far exceeding every requirement, anti-aliasing comletely crashes my framerate.  There is so much good about this game, but QA wasn't the top priority. One of your "personas" cannot parkour, yet she is capable of falling into the water but not able to climb out---must be lead weights in her dress.  At one point I was mugged while dressed as the "Lady," and as I was blocking the town guard comes running up and starts bayonneting ME, leading to an enormous WTF moment.  And finally, in a game that really revolves finding all the little guffins and bawbles, there is no Quick Travel within the maps.  Add in that each of the 3 personas highlight a different set of doodads, and it means you will be running.  A lot.  I officially give up on 100% synch.  I will finish the game, but they could have had a home run here instead of a limp first base hit.
Though there are glitches (like the original game), I still enjoy and love it! <3

I've played all 3 Escape Velocity games, if that is what these guys were trying to emulate they failed.
This game is overly complicated from the beginning, it has a difficulty curve like a mountain and has combat that simply doesn't have a good feel to it, which is important as there isn't much more to this game.  There is a plot, some narration, but honestly the level of the dialouge and the amateur art designs for the charcacters caused me to ignore it after about 10 minutes.
This is Diablo in space, you manuever around, try to damage opponents and mostly are just trying to click at the right times to line up shots against VERY agile opponents.   You also constantly have to keep track of how allies are doing, your ship is usually worse then your competitions and there are more of them then there are of your fleet (as opposed to most ARPGs where you have an advantage but you are facing a horde).
It is very easy to die but that's ok, because using your mined resources you can then use them to respawn yourself and your fleet.  But you can and will run out of resources, therefore making you not be able to respawn, at which point the game tells you to go get in a very very very crappy ship and start mining, but anyone with common sense will tell you to reload your save instead to save you the mindless grinding that would entail.
This is grossly dissapointing because I feel there is a lot to this game, it generates a new galaxy for every game which would seem to have a huge amount of content but I couldn't get past the second star system and had great difficulty getting past the first (which was the tutorial).  Maybe this game was made for the nintendo hard crowd, or maybe I just suck, but I just don't have the time or patience anymore to deal with that.  Although after looking at the universal badge progress on this game, I can tell I'm not alone.
Don't trust the metacritic score, although I will say there is something here but you have to be pretty dedicated/skilled to find it.
